​Did you know that the grand autumn festival of Durga Puja has its roots deeply connected to the Ramayana? Why is Goddess Durga awakened specifically on Maha Shashthi? Let’s dive deep into this sacred epic of devotion and triumph!

📜 What is 'Akal Bodhon'? (The Untimely Invocation)

According to Hindu scriptures and the Krittivasi Ramayana, the autumn season (Ashvin month) falls during the period when deities are resting or in a state of celestial slumber (Devshayani).
Invoking the Divine Mother during this off-season period is known as 'Akal Bodhon' (an untimely awakening). When Lord Rama needed supreme cosmic energy to defeat the demon king Ravana, He chose to awaken Maa Durga out of season, defying conventional cosmic timelines through His absolute devotion. 🙏✨

🔱 Why Shukla Paksha Maha Shashthi?
​The sacred rituals officially began on the Shashthi Tithi of Shukla Paksha in the Ashvin month. Under the guidance of sages, Lord Rama performed the Bilva Nimantran (invoking the Goddess beneath a sacred Bel/Bilva tree) on this very day.
By offering prayers and awakening Her from Her divine sleep, Lord Rama established the spiritual foundation for the final battle, seeking the grace of Shakti to restore Dharma on Earth. 🚩🌿

🌸 The Ultimate Test of Devotion: The Offering of the Eye

A fascinating climax of this worship occurred when Lord Rama needed 108 blue lotuses (Neelkamal) for the Chandi Yajna. Just as He was about to complete the ritual, one lotus mysteriously went missing.
Known as Kamal-Nayan (one whose eyes resemble lotuses), Lord Rama immediately prepared to pierce His own eye and offer it to the Goddess to fulfill the count of 108. Deeply moved by this supreme sacrifice and unshakeable faith, Maa Durga physically manifested before Him, stopped His hand, and granted Him the ultimate boon of victory over Ravana! 🏹✨

🚩 An Enduring Legacy of Triumph Over Evil

Ever since that historic moment, the grand celebration of Durga Puja officially commences globally on Shukla Paksha Maha Shashthi with the traditional 'Bodhon' ceremony (opening the eyes of the deity).
This timeless narrative serves as an eternal reminder that no obstacle is insurmountable when one walks the path of righteousness, truth, and unwavering devotion to the Divine! 🌺🙏

text:
Your reply anachronistically  blames Rome and simplifies the complex historical events that actually occurred.

The Fourth Crusade’s leaders had contracted with Venice in 1201 for a large fleet based on an expected army of roughly 33,500 men. Far fewer actually arrived (around 12,000), leaving them deeply in debt (about 34,000 silver marks still owed after partial payment). Venice had suspended normal trade and spent heavily building the ships, so Doge Enrico Dandolo would not simply write it off. 

Dandolo proposed that the crusaders help Venice recapture Zara (Zadar), a Christian city under Hungarian control, as a way to defer or offset the debt. Many crusaders objected; some left the expedition. Pope Innocent III forbade the attack and later excommunicated participants. The leadership largely suppressed his letters and proceeded. 

While wintering at Zara, the exiled Byzantine prince Alexios Angelos (son of the deposed Isaac II) offered 200,000 silver marks, troops, and submission of the Greek Church to Rome if the crusaders restored him and his father. The leaders accepted this as the practical way to clear the Venetian debt and continue toward Egypt/the Holy Land. Rank-and-file opinion was divided; some sailed on separately

Alexios IV was restored in 1203 but could only partially pay. Growing hostility in Constantinople led to his overthrow and death in early 1204. The new regime refused the promised sums. At that point the crusade leaders and Venetians agreed (March Pact of 1204) to take the city themselves, citing the unpaid debts, the need for funds and provisions, and the opportunity to secure control. Venetian ambitions, trade dominance in the East, recovery of Zara, and long-standing rivalry with Byzantium, were central throughout, with Dandolo a key driver. The common soldiers did not simply mutiny over unpaid wages against their own commanders; the leadership was deeply implicated in the debt-driven diversions.

Innocent III repeatedly prohibited attacks on Christians and condemned the sack’s atrocities once reports arrived, distinguishing the unauthorized actions of the army and Venetians from papal intent.  The diversion unfolded through a clear sequence of debt leverage leading first to the attack on Zara, then to Alexios’s unpaid promises, and finally to the conquest of Constantinople, with Venetian commercial and strategic interests accelerating every stage.

Pope Innocent III explicitly forbade and condemned the attack on fellow Christians. He called the Fourth Crusade to recover the Holy Land (via Egypt). He ordered the army not to attack Christians and excommunicated participants after the sack of Zara Upon learning of the Constantinople sack and its atrocities (looting of churches, violence against civilians and clergy), he rebuked the leaders and his legate in strong terms, writing that the Greeks now “rightly detest the Latins more than dogs” because of the crimes, that the crusaders had turned swords meant for pagans against Christians, and that they had preferred earthly spoils to the Holy Land. He did not order or authorize the sack; the diversion stemmed from Venetian debts previously explained, the deal with the Byzantine claimant Alexios IV, and decisions by the crusade leaders

 Later, Popes repeatedly sought church union partly to enable coordinated defense (notably the Council of Florence, 1438–39, which produced the decree Laetentur Caeli). Byzantine Emperor John VIII sought Western military aid precisely against the Ottoman threat; the union was accepted under that pressure but rejected by much of the Orthodox clergy and populace. Separate crusading campaigns against the Ottomans (Nicopolis 1396, Varna 1444) were organized with papal support and failed due to military outcomes and incomplete European commitment, not papal indifference. John Paul II later expressed sorrow and regret for the 1204 events on behalf of the Catholic Church.

text:
Astronomer J. Allen Hynek created the original Close Encounters scale (First to Third Kind) in 1972 to classify UFO (Unidentified Flying Object) reports based on increasing proximity and interaction. Later Unofficial  Additions came into play (Fourth and Beyond). 
WHO has experienced a close encounter of any kind in their lifetime? 
Here's my story -

Close Encounters (of my own kind)

It was early January and cold. I was southbound on U.S. Highway 101 and driving in Washington State on my way to Alameda, California. I was on active duty in the United States Navy and a crew member assigned to the USS Enterprise CVN-65. We had recently completed the Extended Selected Restricted Availability (ESRA) at the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard in Bremerton, Washington, where the Enterprise was altered and refitted to support the Navy's newest fighter aircraft, the F-14 Tomcat. Crew members who owned personal vehicles were offered the option of driving to NAS Alameda, California (where the carrier was home-ported) or arranging to have a shipyard crane lift their vehicles onto the flight deck of the carrier for transport back to our homeport. I elected to drive solo, believing it would be a pleasant break from duty aboard ship. My trip also included a stop and short stay to visit a friend who resided in southern Oregon. Nevertheless, as events unfolded,that visit would never materialize. 
I began the drive approximately 9 pm on the day I departed. Drive time to arrive in southern Oregon would be approximately seven hours. I decided to make the drive at night to minimize traffic, and to time my arrival to occur early to mid-morning of the following day. I factored in several short stops for fuel, a bite to eat, and bathroom breaks as needed. I remember the sky as cloud free, moonless, with unusually cold temperatures. I adjusted the car's heater to its highest setting as it was only barely keeping me comfortable, even with the heavy Navy 'foul weather' jacket I was wearing. With no moon as a beacon, it was (as they say) dark as ten feet down. I had to be particularly vigilant as I 'wound' my way down the Washington and Oregon Coastal Highway. I was trying very hard to avoid small animals that occasionally darted out on the road, and especially deer, losing count before the clock even struck midnight. It was around 3 am when it happened.
"What the hell?" I yelled out loud. I was in northern Oregon and had slowed to navigate a sharp, round curve in the highway. A soft blue pulsating light about two miles ahead and on the other side of a hill seemed to appear out of nowhere. I was a little 'zoned out' to begin with, considering my time behind the wheel and the miles I had driven. 
As I slowly completed the curve in the road and straightened my car, the soft blue pulsating light I previously noticed was now an intense, pulsating blue/white light, round to oval in shape with a distinctive humming sound. It was hovering approximately fifty feet off the ground over a space devoid of any trees, brush or other vegetation. The craft appeared to be rotating in a clockwise direction, or giving the illusion it was rotating. My best description was that it looked almost identical in appearance and size to the interplanetary vessel from the movie, "The Day the Earth Stood Still," except it was silvery in appearance, like stainless steel.
Then it happened. The hovering saucer moved in an instant over the road and directly in front of my car. The craft then advanced slowly toward me, and to avoid contact I turned and drove to my right off the road and onto the spot the UFO had previously occupied. I turned my car around to face the highway and the unidentified object. I was attempting to position myself so I could put the 'pedal to the metal' at my first opportunity, but the UFO moved again in my direction, blocking any chance to escape. It then slowly descended, coming to rest on the ground less than one hundred meters in front of my mustang. 
Over the next several minutes, the pulsating lights dimmed, the humming sound slowly faded. Finally, the rotation stopped and an opening became visible. The UFO appeared to split in a straight line all the way from its apex to its bottom ridge, a ramp now extending, only smaller and steeper than in the movie I previously mentioned. 
The cold was no longer an issue. The combination of adrenaline and fear soon had me perspiring, beads of sweat forming on my forehead. I remember turning off the car's heater. It was difficult to think clearly or logically. 
I reached down under the right front seat of my mustang. I grabbed my colt python .357 magnum I carried whenever I was in unfamiliar territory, except this time I was scared out of my wits, and definitely not ready to be a captive ... or worse, their guinea pig -- not even their well treated 'guest'. Yes, I had read and heard about alien 'abductions' and the stories about what they do to their captive humans. I had absolutely no desire to be their next 'victim.' I wasn't going anywhere without a fight. 
I sat there, my heart pounding, waiting for one or a group of extraterrestrials to walk down that ramp. I was going to blow its (or their) head(s) clean off at even the slightest hint of hostility or foul play. What else could I do? I was trapped. Personal cell phones were not available to the public at that time. I couldn't call anyone for help. I waited for what felt like an eternity for someone -- some being or some life form to exit that ship, but nothing happened. When I couldn't stand it any longer, I opened the car door and stepped out. It was time ... one way or the other to end this.
With my gun in hand, I moved cautiously in the direction of the alien spaceship (or whatever it was). And then something totally unexpected happened. The ramp began to retract, followed by the opening in the ship closing as seamlessly as it had opened. Simultaneously, the pulsating lights began to flash brighter, the humming sound rising as if the UFO was powering up its propulsion system. I began to slowly step back, past my vehicle and well away from the energized vessel. 
The saucer rose steadily until it was above the surrounding trees, then accelerated at an angle of approximately sixty degrees at an astonishing rate of speed. In the blink of an eye it was out of sight, and I just stood there, now in the dark and totally bewildered. 
I finally walked back to my car, placed the gun back under the seat and left. I never stopped in southern Oregon. I was in no frame of mind at that time to enjoy a visit with anyone, not even a good friend. I continued on to Eureka in Northern California before checking into a hotel and sleeping the remainder of the day. I wouldn't have slept a wink had I not been so mentally and physically exhausted. When I finally reported back aboard the Enterprise, I just kept my mouth shut. No one would have believed me anyway.
Over the years I've revealed this story to only a few people -- up until now, that is. The primary question asked is: "Why do you think they left without making contact?" 
"One of two reasons," I always answer. "They (whoever THEY are) were wary about the weapon I was carrying, as they certainly must have noticed, or simply changed their minds in spite of it." Having said that, however, I firmly believe had the occupants wanted to take me, they probably could have. If they're technologically advanced enough to get here (wherever they're from) and back -- well, what do YOU think ? 

P.S. I have attached a re-enactment of the 'alleged' examination of Travis Walton from the movie "Fire in the Sky" about a lumberjack abducted by aliens and subjected to a brutal physical examination during a day of tree cutting in the Arizona Forest in 1975.

text:
Its the Savior.  You have to read it with context from verse 24 where "one" has a footnote reference to Jesus Christ...

The verse has the "one" speaking in the first person to verse 27 where "The Lord" has a footnote to God the Father...

The "send" has a footnote to Moses 7:39 where it declares the "Chosen" which footnotes back to Abraham 3:27 but also Moses 4:2

The second "send" in Abraham 3:27 has a footnote to Jesus Christ.

---- Now on to Apostolic Commentary:
axwell gave some of the clearest apostolic commentary on the verse:
•  “Never has anyone offered so much to so many in so few words as when Jesus said, ‘Here am I, send me.’” (April 1976 General Conference, “Jesus of Nazareth, Savior and King”; also in Plain and Precious Things, 1983, p. 53).
•  “It’s extremely important to get straight what happened in that premortal council. It was not an unstructured meeting, nor was it a discussion between plans, nor an idea-producing session, as to how to formulate the plan for salvation and carry it out. Our Father’s plan was known, and the actual question put was whom the Father should send to carry out the plan” (Deposition of a Disciple, 1976, p. 11).
•  He emphasized that the Father already knew whom He would send (“My Beloved Son… was my Beloved and Chosen from the beginning,” Moses 4:2). Asking “Whom shall I send?” allowed Christ to offer Himself “of his own voluntary will,” establishing a pattern of willing, non-grudging sacrifice.
•  Maxwell repeatedly described Jesus as the “prepared but meek Volunteer” who stepped forward humbly and courageously.
Bruce R. McConkie
McConkie expanded on the scene in several settings, including the BYU address “Who Shall Declare His Generation?”:
•  He paraphrased the Father’s call as: “Whom shall I send to be my Son, to work out the infinite and eternal atoning sacrifice? Whom shall I send to be born into mortality…? Whom shall I send to lay down his life for the sins of men…?”
•  He identified the first volunteer as the firstborn of the Father (Jesus), who said in effect, “Here am I. Send me. I will be thy son. I will do thy will.”
•  He identified the second as Lucifer, who proposed an alternative that would take away agency and sought the Father’s honor (drawing on Moses 4:1).
•  The decree was “I will send the first” (Abraham 3:27), after which the war in heaven followed.
•  McConkie consistently treated this as the moment Christ became “the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.”
Other apostolic references
•  Dallin H. Oaks has discussed the scene in the context of agency. He notes that Satan’s proposal (Moses 4:1) would have destroyed agency, while Christ responded “Here am I, send me” (Abraham 3:27) and “Father, thy will be done, and the glory be thine forever” (Moses 4:2). Oaks stresses that the war in heaven was over agency and that a third part of the hosts of heaven chose to follow Lucifer.
•  Marion G. Romney described the plan as having been presented to and approved by the hosts of heaven, with free agency as a foundational principle that Lucifer opposed.
•  Henry D. Taylor (then of the First Council of the Seventy) contrasted the two proposals: one preserving agency and giving glory to the Father, the other seeking to force salvation and take honor for himself.
•  James E. Talmage (earlier) identified both Christ and Satan as among the “exalted intelligences” of Abraham 3:22.
Common themes across apostolic commentary
•  The first who answered “like unto the Son of Man” is Jesus Christ; the second is Lucifer.
•  The Father’s plan was already known; the question was who would carry it out.
•  Christ’s response was voluntary, meek, and glory-giving; Lucifer’s was self-exalting and agency-destroying.
•  The rejection of the second volunteer led to the rebellion described in Abraham 3:28 and Moses 4.

Traders analyze charts, choose their leverage, and wait for the market to move. But behind every trading interface is a bigger question: how does the protocol actually execute those trades and source the liquidity to support them?

Which is where 𝐇𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐳𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐰 brings in a difference.

Built on BNB Chain, @Hertzflow_xyz uses a request-for-quote (RFQ) execution model rather than relying on a traditional order book. Trades are executed against liquidity pools, with prices validated through multiple oracles.

text:
⚽ Sjoe! Correlation’s Shadow: The Match Between Claims and Evidence🖥️🔦 The servers fell. Who awarded the political goal? ~ 🧾🏆 No trophy for a theory without receipts.
When the servers fell in Russia, the stories rose in South Africa. The question is whether the two events were ever the same event at all.

In the second week of October 2026, Ukrainian drones struck three data centres belonging to the Russian technology company Yandex. Network monitors recorded a sharp, stepped collapse in automated traffic leaving those facilities. 

Within hours the collapse was being read, on platforms and in commentary, as the silencing of Russian influence operations. 

Some of that commentary reached South Africa and attached itself to an older claim: that the same infrastructure, or something very like it, had been used against the Democratic Alliance. 

The attachment was swift. The proof was slower. 

In the space between the measurable drop and the political meaning assigned to it, a shadow formed. This article examines that shadow.

1. The Servers That Fell

Between 8 and 11 October 2026, Ukrainian forces struck Yandex facilities in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir. Public traffic data showed automated requests from Yandex networks falling in clear steps that matched the strikes (Cloudflare Radar, 2026). 

Independent technical assessments of the same data characterised the bulk of the lost traffic as the company’s own search crawlers and internal service bots rather than accounts engaged in social-media posting. 

The political inference drawn from the drop—that Russian social-media influence networks had been taken offline—rested on a category error. A real kinetic and network event was treated as proof of a different kind of event.

Researchers monitoring known influence clusters in the same period reported continuity rather than collapse. The distinction between what the monitors could see and what the narrative claimed became the first hard edge of the story. 

In information environments already saturated with competing claims of foreign interference, the temptation to treat any dramatic technical failure as confirmation of prior suspicions is strong. The temptation is also costly. 

Once a measurable event is allowed to stand in for an unmeasured political effect, subsequent analysis begins from a distorted premise.

The South African reception of the outage illustrated the pattern with particular clarity. Commentary quickly linked the Russian infrastructure failure to domestic political pressure on the main opposition. 

The link was offered as self-evident. The technical record did not support the leap. What the monitors recorded was the interruption of automated crawlers. 

What the narrative required was the interruption of coordinated social-media activity directed at South African political actors. 

Those are not the same phenomenon.

Sjoe!
A server farm goes dark in Russia and, somewhere between Kaluga and Cape Town, the darkness is already being asked to explain a local election. 

The shadow arrives before the light has even finished leaving!

Stirring Questions:
If a measurable technical failure is immediately read as political victory, what standard of evidence is being applied?
When does the speed of interpretation become a liability rather than an asset?
Why does the absence of corresponding social-media disruption receive less attention than the presence of the infrastructure failure?

What these questions together reveal:
Taken together, they expose the precise moment at which observation ends and narrative begins. They matter because democratic accountability depends on keeping those two moments distinct. 

When the distinction collapses, every convenient technical event becomes available for political use, and the cost of verification is quietly transferred to the public.

2. The Documents That Named a Target

In early 2026, investigative reporting based on leaked internal material described a Russian-linked influence network that, in 2024, produced racialised content targeting the Democratic Alliance (Forbidden Stories & The Continent, 2026). The stated operational goal was to keep the party away from Foreign Affairs and Justice portfolios in order to protect Russia’s political and defence relationship with South Africa. 

The documents were specific about intent. They were silent about the precise technical infrastructure used to deliver the material.

Nothing in the primary record placed those 2024 operations on the Yandex facilities struck two years later. Shared strategic interest and chronological proximity were offered as bridges. Neither constitutes hosting attribution. 

Influence networks are routinely designed for geographic and technical resilience precisely so that the loss of any single domestic facility does not end the activity. The claim that the October strikes had interrupted the earlier anti-DA operations therefore required an evidentiary step that has not been supplied.

The historical context sharpens the difficulty. South Africa’s bilateral relationship with Russia rests on long-standing networks that predate the democratic transition. Those networks have always mixed genuine solidarity with practical utility. 

When a foreign influence document records an interest in keeping the main opposition away from sensitive portfolios, the interest is intelligible within that longer pattern. 

Intelligibility is not the same as proof that a later technical event interrupted the execution of that interest. The two claims must be kept separate if the analysis is to remain honest.

Sjoe!
A foreign network writes down its preference for a weaker opposition. Two years later a different set of buildings loses power. The preference is real. The power loss is real. The assumption that one caused a pause in the other is the part that still needs to walk across the room on its own legs.

Stirring Questions:
How much weight should strategic alignment carry when technical continuity is absent?
What would actual infrastructure attribution look like, and who is in a position to produce it?
If a foreign network records an interest in weakening an opposition party, does that interest automatically explain every subsequent instance of domestic criticism directed at the same party?

What these questions together reveal:
They force a separation between documented foreign preference and unproven technical continuity. They matter because without that separation, every domestic political contest that disadvantages the opposition becomes available for reinterpretation as the residual effect of an earlier foreign operation. 

The reinterpretation may be politically useful. It is not yet evidence.

3. The Signal That Did Not Appear

Attempts to measure anti-DA volume on X around the strike window—using markers associated with the 2024 material and common oppositional hashtags—returned sparse, low-engagement posts. No continuous public time-series of keyword volume, unique accounts or amplification showed a clear collapse timed to the outages. 

Ordinary domestic political traffic, including court proceedings and campaign activity, continued through the same period. Full historical data capable of resolving the question sits behind commercial access regimes (X Developer Platform, 2023–2026).

The absence of a detectable signal in the available samples is itself a finding. 

The narrative of a quietened anti-DA campaign lacked the quantitative foundation required to move from hypothesis to demonstration. This is not a claim that no activity occurred. It is a claim that the activity, if it existed at the scale suggested by the stronger narratives, left no clear trace in the publicly accessible record during the relevant window. 

In research design terms, the expected effect failed to appear in the only dataset currently available without substantial payment.

The commercial character of platform data introduces a structural asymmetry. Those who wish to assert a causal link between a foreign infrastructure failure and a domestic political quietening can do so at low cost. 

Those who wish to test the assertion must either accept limited public samples or purchase enterprise-level access. The asymmetry favours narrative speed over verification depth. 

It is not unique to South Africa, but it has particular consequences in a political system already contending with contested claims of foreign interference.

Sjoe!
The expected quietening was announced with confidence. The data that would have confirmed it remained behind a paywall. In the interval, the announcement continued to circulate as if the invoice had already been paid.

Stirring Questions:
What volume of data would be required to confirm or refute a strike-timed drop with reasonable confidence?
Why does the commercial character of platform data make verification of influence claims systematically expensive?
If the expected quietening cannot be shown, what remains of the causal story that depended on it?

What these questions together reveal:
They convert an expected political effect into an empirical test that the currently accessible evidence fails. They matter because the failure of the test does not prove the absence of all activity; it does prove that the stronger public claims have outrun the available measurements. 

In a democracy, that gap is not a minor technical detail. It is the difference between allegation and demonstration.

4. The Doors That Stay Closed

Historical volume data from major platforms is sold, not given. Standard access is limited and metered; full-archive capability is priced for enterprise clients. Political parties and civil organisations have no automatic right to compel bulk release. 

Inside South Africa the Independent Electoral Commission, as a Chapter 9 institution, holds the clearest statutory mandate for examining foreign interference that touches electoral integrity (Electoral Act; Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996). 

Specialised police structures remain inside the executive hierarchy and are subject to ministerial direction.

Formal requests for the data required to test the stronger claims therefore confront both commercial barriers and institutional proximity. Verification is not merely difficult; it is architecturally constrained. 

The constraint is not the product of any single decision. It is the cumulative result of platform monetisation strategies, the design of Chapter 9 independence, and the placement of investigative capacity within the executive. 

Each element is defensible on its own terms. Together they produce a situation in which the most serious claims of foreign electoral interference are the hardest to test with independent data.

Comparative experience is instructive. Jurisdictions that have created clearer statutory pathways for researcher or electoral-body access to platform data have not eliminated influence activity. 

They have, however, reduced the asymmetry between those who assert and those who must verify. South Africa has not yet closed that gap. 

The result is a recurring pattern: claims travel quickly; the evidence required to settle them travels slowly or not at all.

Sjoe!
The institution with the cleanest mandate looks at the door. The data sit on the other side, priced for clients who already know what they want to find. The public is invited to trust the process while the process waits for a budget it does not control.

Stirring Questions:
Which institutions possess both the legal mandate and the practical independence to compel or purchase the necessary data?
What happens to democratic accountability when the evidence required to test influence claims is locked behind paywalls or executive discretion?
If the most independent available body is asked to investigate and the data remain commercially gated, where does the inquiry go next?

What these questions together reveal:
They move the problem from the realm of narrative into the realm of institutional design. They matter because a democracy that cannot test its most serious claims of external interference is forced to choose between credulity and paralysis. 

Neither choice is healthy.

4. The Resemblance That Is Not Proof

Julius Malema’s period as ANC Youth League president (2008–2012) coincided with a temporary elevation of South Africa’s ranking on one international risk scale, explicitly linked by that organisation to his rhetoric (Genocide Watch, 2011–2012; Africa Check, 2016). 

After his expulsion the ranking was lowered. In 2026, Youth League and party structures directed strong criticism at the Democratic Alliance during a Constitutional Court dispute over candidate lists (Constitutional Court of South Africa, 15 October 2026). 

The 2024 documents had recorded a foreign strategic interest in precisely such weakening of the opposition.

The stylistic similarity is real. Similarity of effect, electoral timing and historical networks do not, by themselves, demonstrate ongoing foreign direction. Domestic political competition generates polarising language without external instruction. 

Only primary evidence of coordination, funding or shared infrastructure can convert resemblance into direction. The insistence on that threshold is not a refusal to take foreign influence seriously. 

It is the condition for taking it seriously without dissolving every domestic contest into an extension of an external plot.

Political science has long recognised the risk of over-attribution. When an external actor records a preference for a particular domestic outcome, later occurrences of that outcome become available for reinterpretation as success. 

The reinterpretation is tempting precisely because it is difficult to falsify without access to private communications or financial trails. The difficulty does not make the reinterpretation true. It makes the demand for higher-quality evidence more, not less, necessary.

Sjoe!
Two periods of confrontational youth-wing rhetoric, separated by fourteen years and a change of organisational address, are invited to share a single foreign parent. The family resemblance is noted. The birth certificates remain outstanding.

Stirring Questions:
How should a democracy weigh functional similarity against the absence of direct evidence?
What threshold of proof should be required before domestic rhetoric is treated as the execution of a foreign operational plan?
If the same strategic interest can be served by both coordinated external activity and ordinary internal competition, how is the difference to be established?

What these questions together reveal:
They protect the distinction between what looks connected and what can be shown to be connected. They matter because the collapse of that distinction would hand every domestic political actor a permanent excuse and every foreign actor a permanent alibi. 

Neither result strengthens the constitutional order.

5. The Shadow That Remains

Across the sequence the same pattern recurs. A measurable event occurs. A political narrative attaches itself with speed. The data required to test the narrative prove either absent, commercially locked, or institutionally difficult to reach. 

Functional similarities appear and invite causal stories that remain, under scrutiny, unproven.

The core difficulty is not the existence of foreign interest in South African politics. The difficulty is the distance between observation and demonstration. Correlation is cheap and rapid. Causation is expensive and slow. 

The institutions and data regimes that would shorten the distance are themselves constrained. 

Accountability begins when the shadow is recognised as shadow rather than mistaken for the object that casts it. The alternative is a politics in which every convenient alignment is treated as proof and every missing dataset is treated as confirmation. 

South Africa’s democratic health depends on refusing that bargain.

The cumulative evidence does not prove that foreign influence is absent. It proves that the gap between measurable events and the political narratives constructed around them remains the decisive terrain of accountability.

Closing the gap will require better data access, clearer institutional pathways, and a public culture that values demonstration over narrative speed. 

Until those conditions improve, the shadow will continue to lengthen each time a server falls and a story rises to meet it.

text:
The Third Who Walks Beside You

At the edge of death and in deep grief, people report an unseen companion who stays close, steadies them and sometimes seems to know the way. Many never tell anyone.

The Stairwell

On the morning of September 11, 2001, Ron DiFrancesco was in a stairwell of the World Trade Center's South Tower, above where the plane had struck. The smoke was thick. He lay down on a landing. Years later he told the writer John Geiger what came next; Geiger opens his 2009 book The Third Man Factor with it.

DiFrancesco had the sensation that "somebody lifted me up." In a CNN report on the book in 2009, he says it told him to get up. "I was led to the stairs," he told Geiger. "I don't think something grabbed my hand, but I was definitely led." The presence, he said, took him toward the fire rather than away from it. "That's not where you go, you don't go toward the fire." He ran through it. Geiger writes that the helper stayed with him for about five minutes, and DiFrancesco says, "I think at that point it let me go." To CNN he put it plainly: "It was a higher being rather than an internal being. Maybe it was an angel. I didn't see the face of God, but I know somebody came and helped me." CNN reported that Geiger calls him the last person out of the South Tower before it fell.

Why a helper no one could see would send him toward the fire, and why he came out alive, is a question the record has never answered.

That is the shape of the experience this essay follows: a person at the limit, a helper no one else can see, and a way out the person would not have chosen alone. Researchers call it a "sensed presence," meaning the strong feeling that another person is near when no one visible is there. Geiger called it the Third Man Factor. The record runs from Antarctica to Everest to the homes of the widowed. Three features recur. The companion comes when a person is at the end of their strength. It often helps. And many of the people it helps keep quiet about it. No one has explained where it comes from.

Four, Not Three

On May 19, 1916, Ernest Shackleton, the ship's captain Frank Worsley and the seaman Tom Crean set out to cross the unmapped mountains of South Georgia, an island in the far South Atlantic, toward the whaling station at Stromness. Their ship, the Endurance, had been crushed by ice the year before, and the rest of the crew was waiting on Elephant Island. If the three men failed, no one was coming for the others.

In South, published in 1919, Shackleton wrote that during "that long and racking march of thirty-six hours over the unnamed mountains and glaciers of South Georgia it seemed to me often that we were four, not three. I said nothing to my companions on the point, but afterwards Worsley said to me, 'Boss, I had a curious feeling on the march that there was another person with us.' Crean confessed to the same idea."

Worsley left his own account, quoted in a 2018 article in the medical humanities journal Hektoen International: "even now I again find myself counting our party – Shackleton, Crean and I and – who was the other? Of course, there were only three, but it is strange that in mentally reviewing the crossing we should always think of a fourth, and then correct ourselves." The two men first compared notes, he wrote, "three or four weeks after" reaching Stromness. Each of the three exhausted men felt a fourth, and each, by these accounts, kept it to himself for weeks.

T. S. Eliot read the story and put it into The Waste Land in 1922: "Who is the third who walks always beside you? / When I count, there are only you and I together." His note says it was "stimulated by the account of one of the Antarctic expeditions (I forget which, but I think one of Shackleton's)."

The Pilot of the Pinta

In 1895 Joshua Slocum was sailing alone around the world in the Spray, a rebuilt oyster sloop, a small sailing boat with one mast. Off the Azores, sick from plums and white cheese and with a gale building, he collapsed in the cabin. In Sailing Alone Around the World (1900) he wrote: "looking out of the companionway, to my amazement I saw a tall man at the helm." (The companionway is the ladder from the deck down into the cabin.) "His rigid hand, grasping the spokes of the wheel, held them as in a vise." The man said, "Senor, I have come to do you no harm," named himself the pilot of Columbus's ship the Pinta, and scolded him about the cheese. In the morning the Spray was still on her course.

Slocum knew his boat. He wrote that she could hold a course for long stretches with the wheel tied in place. He still raised a toast "to the health of my invisible helmsman--the pilot of the Pinta." The man who understood the boat best was the one who thanked the helmsman.

Voices Over the Atlantic

In May 1927 Charles Lindbergh flew alone from New York to Paris in about thirty-three and a half hours without sleep. In The Spirit of St. Louis, published in 1953, he described what came into the plane in the worst hours: "These phantoms speak with human voices – friendly, vapor-like shapes, without substance, able to vanish or appear at will, to pass in and out through the walls of the fuselage as though no walls were there." The voices, he wrote, were "familiar voices, conversing and advising on my flight, discussing problems of my navigation, reassuring me, giving me messages of importance unattainable in ordinary life."

When he reached Ireland he was, by his own account, within about three miles of his planned route, after a night over open ocean with no radio. But when he tried to recall the messages, he could not: "I can't remember a single word they said."

According to the historian Chris Gehrz, writing in 2017, none of this appeared in his first book, We, written within weeks of landing in 1927. The phantoms reached print twenty-six years after the flight.

Mint Cake on Everest

In 1933 the climber Frank Smythe pushed on alone high on Everest after his partner Eric Shipton turned back. In Camp Six (1937) he wrote: "After leaving Eric a strange feeling possessed me that I was accompanied by another." The presence "was strong and friendly. In its company I could not feel lonely, neither could I come to any harm. It was always there to sustain me on my solitary climb up the snow-covered slabs." When he stopped to eat a slab of Kendal mint cake, a sugar bar climbers carried, the companion felt "so near and so strong that instinctively I divided the mint into two halves and turned round with one half in my hand to offer it to my 'companion.'"

Smythe guessed at a cause, lack of oxygen and the strain of climbing alone, then declined to rest on it: "I do not offer this as an explanation, but merely as a suggestion."

The Widowed of Mid-Wales

The most careful count of the experience was made not on a mountain but in ordinary homes.

In 1971 the Welsh doctor W. Dewi Rees published "The Hallucinations of Widowhood" in the British Medical Journal. In medicine, a "hallucination" means perceiving something that others present do not perceive; the word describes the experience and does not settle what causes it. Rees interviewed 227 widows and 66 widowers, 293 people in all. Of them, 137, or 46.7 percent, reported experiences of their dead husband or wife. The most common was not a vision or a voice. It was, in Rees's words, "the illusion of feeling the presence of the dead spouse." At the time of the interview, 106 people were still having these experiences, some many years after the death. Rees found they were not tied to social isolation or to known depressive illness, and they were more common among people whose marriages had been long and happy. He described them as "normal and helpful."

"Most percipients" (the people who had the experiences) "were helped by their hallucinations," Rees wrote. Of the 137, 94 (68.6 percent) found them helpful and 8 (5.9 percent) found them unpleasant. Of the 115 who felt the dead spouse's presence, 84 (73.0 percent) called it helpful.

Then Rees asked who they had told. Only 38 of the 137, 27.7 percent, had told anyone. "No doctor had been informed and only one person had confided in a clergyman."

Outside grief, the feeling is less common but not rare. In a 2024 survey of 10,447 Dutch people aged 14 and over, published in the British Journal of Psychiatry, Brederoo and colleagues found that 165 people, 1.6 percent, had felt a presence in the past month. That is about one person in sixty, every month. The researchers linked it to loneliness, poor sleep and hard life events.

The Silence

A thread runs through many of these cases. Shackleton "said nothing to my companions on the point" until Worsley spoke first. Crean left no account of his own; his experience exists only as the other two reported it. Lindbergh waited twenty-six years. Most of Rees's widowed told no one, and none told a doctor.

The silence matters because it shapes the record. The accounts that exist come from people who lived and who found someone willing to listen. What came to the people who did not survive the mountain, the sea or the stairwell is not written down anywhere. The record is a set of private experiences, carried by explorers, a pilot and widowed villagers alike, that mostly stayed private.

Protector and Watcher

Not every presence is kind. In three surveys published in Psychological Medicine in 2023, Alderson-Day and colleagues coded descriptions of felt presences. Psychosis is a condition in which a person loses touch with shared reality. Presences described as "scary, frightening" made up 25.4 percent in a sample that included people with psychosis, 9.3 percent in a spiritual sample and 19.1 percent among endurance and solo athletes. In that athletic group, the people closest to Smythe and Lindbergh, the experiences "were most likely to feature a feeling of being watched."

The same athletes reported both faces. In that group, 27.7 percent described the presence as a comfort, 19.1 percent felt fear and 19.1 percent felt watched. One population, in the same kinds of settings, meets both a protector and a watcher.

The names witnesses give it run the same range. DiFrancesco said, "Maybe it was an angel." Rees's widowed felt a husband or wife who had died. Smythe called it his "companion."

The folklorist David Hufford, in The Terror That Comes in the Night (1982), documented the "Old Hag" of Newfoundland: waking unable to move, with a presence in the room and a weight on the chest. Hufford reported the same experience in cultures with no contact with each other, explained differently in each. His conclusion was that the experience came first and the explanations came after. The companion that walks beside and the presence that presses down are reported with the same core feature: someone is there.

What the Lab Can Switch On

Why a feeling the brain can produce on command should so often arrive at the moment of need, and so often as a helper, is not answered in the lab. What the lab has done is find one place where the feeling can be switched on.

In 2006 Shahar Arzy, Olaf Blanke and colleagues reported in Nature on a 22-year-old woman being evaluated for epilepsy surgery. When doctors stimulated her left temporoparietal junction, an area above and behind the ear where the brain combines touch, balance and body position into a sense of where the self is, she felt a person behind her who copied her posture. Given a card to read during stimulation, she said, "He wants to take the card," and "He doesn't want me to read."

In 2014, in Current Biology, Blanke's group used a robot to touch blindfolded healthy volunteers on the back slightly out of time with their own hand movements. Many reported an invisible person standing behind them, and some counted more than one. According to the researchers' announcement, the feeling was so disturbing for two of the volunteers that they wanted to stop.

The lab shows that the brain has a door for this feeling, and that the door can be opened with an electrode or a robot. It does not show what comes through it on a mountain or in a burning tower. The presence in the lab did not help anyone. No one in the lab was in danger, so there was nothing for it to help with. The companion in the field stays and steadies. The presence in the lab reached for the patient's card. The one in the field pointed the way: toward the fire, along the route.

Older Names

Older traditions have names for a companion on the road. In Greek religion Hermes guarded roads and travelers and guided souls of the dead. In the Book of Tobit the angel Raphael walks beside young Tobias disguised as a kinsman and reveals himself only at the end. In Luke's Gospel two disciples on the road to Emmaus walk with a stranger, "But their eyes were holden that they should not know him."

The researcher Jacques Vallée, a computer scientist who studied UFO reports for decades, proposed a reason the costume changes. In Dimensions he wrote, "I propose that there is a spiritual control system for human consciousness, and that paranormal phenomena like UFOs are one of its manifestations." "Paranormal" here means events that fall outside what science currently explains. Read this way, a control system works something like a thermostat: a process that nudges human belief over time and adjusts its form to the culture it meets. In Messengers of Deception he called it "a control system which acts on humans and uses humans." Much of what Vallée described, as that title suggests, has a cold side. The companion would be the warm side of the same system, if it belongs to one: it appears at the moment of greatest need, in a form the person can accept, and, in the explorers' accounts, leaves when the crisis is over. That is an interpretation, not a finding.

A Working Frame

One frame, offered as a frame and not a fact, reads the record differently. Suppose the world is a built environment, a simulation, meaning a reality running on rules its inhabitants did not write. The Book of Enoch describes Watchers, beings set over humanity who came down among people. Under this frame, could those texts be early notes on how the builders reach the people inside? A companion that appears at the limit, helps quietly and leaves no trace would fit that description. Nothing in the record proves or disproves it.

One comparison fits the frame. Investigators working under AAWSAP, the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program, a Defense Intelligence Agency contract awarded in September 2008 to the company Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies and run to about 2010, described what they called a "Hitchhiker Effect": anomalous events, sometimes shadowy figures, that followed people home after they went looking for the phenomenon. The claim comes from Skinwalkers at the Pentagon (2021), written by the program's originator James Lacatski with Colm Kelleher and the reporter George Knapp. The Pentagon's 2024 historical review of the subject did not support the Utah claims. The Third Man arrives to help someone stranded. The Hitchhiker arrives to watch someone investigating. Are they the same thing, seen from two sides?

The Question Eliot Asked

The record leaves its questions open. Why did a voice in a smoke-filled stairwell send a man toward the fire, and why did he come out alive? What walked beside the people who did not come back? Why do so many keep it to themselves? Why does the same presence lift one person and press down on another?

Eliot's line has never been answered, only repeated. The record shows people who counted one more than were there and kept walking. It does not show who they were walking with.

@JacquesVallee @GeorgeKnapp @johngeiger

1 | Strong quarter led by strong demand for leading edge, and revenue was above the high end of management guide, expect similar for Q4.

Third quarter revenue increased 17.6% sequentially in TWD, supported by strong demand for our leading-edge process technologies. In U.S. dollar terms, revenue increased 16.2% sequentially to $46.7 billion, above the high end of our third quarter guidance.

Moving into fourth quarter 2026, we expect our business to be supported by continued strong demand for our leading-edge process technologies, including the steep ramp-up of our 2nm technology.

2 | Gross margin continued to face dilution due to 2nm ramp and dilutions from overseas fabs, closer to 2% for 2026, and widened to 3-4% in the next few years.

Gross margin decreased by 130bps QoQ to 66.4%, primarily due to margin dilution from 2-nanometer ramp….We have just guided our fourth quarter gross margin to decrease by 40bps to 66% at the midpoint, primarily due to the continued margin dilution from the steep ramp-up of our 2nm technology as well as dilution from overseas fabs. These impacts are expected to be partially offset by cost improvement efforts, including productivity gains and across node capacity optimization.

While the cost of overseas fabs remain higher, thanks to the company's overall larger scale and cost improvement efforts, we now expect the gross margin dilution from the ramp-up of our overseas fabs to be closer to 2% for the full year 2026. As we put more effort to support the strong structural demand from our customers, more fabs will be ramping up in the U.S. Thus, we expect the dilution from our overseas fabs to widen to 3% to 4% in the next few years.

3 | TSMC observed consumer- and price-sensitive end-market segments being challenged due to the impact of rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainties.

Looking ahead, we continue to observe consumer and price-sensitive end market segment are being challenged due to the impact of rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainties. As such, we are being prudent in our business planning going into 2027, while focusing on the fundamentals of our business to further strengthen our competitive position. Having said that, demand for our leading-edge technologies continue to be extremely robust, supported by our strong technology differentiation and broad customer base.

4 | TSMC remains confident that they can be the most cost-efficient semiconductor manufacturer in every region they operate in, i.e. in Taiwan and the US.

We will leverage our increasing size in Arizona and work on our operations to improve the cost structure. We will also continue to work closely with our customers and suppliers to manage the impact. Overall, with our fundamental competitive advantages of manufacturing technology leadership and large-scale production base, we are confident that TSMC continues to be the most cost-efficient manufacturer in every region that we operate.

5 | HPC was the largest growth driver, grew 22% QoQ, 80% YoY

HPC increased 22% QoQ to account for 68% of our third quarter revenue. Smartphone increased 10% to account for 21%. IoT increased 5% to account for 4%. Automotive increased 23% to account for 4%, while DCE declined 12% to account for 1%.

6|  AI market continues to be very strong, fueled by rising adoption of agentic AI as the market transitions from chatbots to AI assistants.

Next, let me talk about the AI-related demand outlook. The AI market continues to be very strong. Recent developments are very positive to AI's long-term demand outlook. We observe increasing AI demand fueled by the rising adoption of Agentic AI as we transition from chatbot to AI assistants. In addition, we are observing great adoption of open source AI models. This will drive greater efficiency and help lower the barrier to future AI usage and result in more and more demand for leading-edge silicon.

7 | TSMC still sees demand as being higher than supply, and they are narrowing the gap. Don't see any sign of slowdown. Expecting AI accelerator CAGR to be higher than 50%.

And then based on our assessment of the demand, we still think the demand is higher than the supply, and we are working very hard to narrow the gap….all I can say right now is the demand is very extremely robust, okay? And we did not see any sign of slowdown. Whether it's a high 50 CAGR, it doesn't matter. It probably will be higher.

8 | AI demand is supported by strong underlying demand for AI accelerators, agentic AI, CPUs, and networking chips.

AI-related demand is being supported by strong underlying demand for AI accelerators. In addition, the emergence of Agentic AI, CPUs and the continued demand for networking chips are driving further silicon demand. Therefore, semiconductor will remain essential in the AI megatrend. The value of semiconductors in the global supply chain is set to continue to increase in our view. This will create more value opportunities for our customers to capture and more value opportunities for TSMC as well.

9 | CPUs are not included in TSMC’s AI demand calculations.

It's not included in our AI demand calculation. The reason is very simple because we cannot identify which CPU user in the conventional server CPU or AI server CPU. And also that it depends on our customers' application and their own allocation also. So no. So far today, we stick to our initial very narrow definition on the AI demand.

10 | With TSMC's technology leadership, manufacturing excellence, global capacity expansion, and customer trust, they are well positioned to capture the full multi-year structural AI-related demand. All AI players are working at TSMC.

No matter which approach is taken, it will require use of the most advanced semiconductor process technology. With our technology leadership, manufacturing excellence, global capacity expansion and customer trust, we are well positioned to capture the full multiyear structural AIrelated demand. Therefore, all the AI players are working with TSMC.

11 | Higher capex is always positively correlated with higher growth opportunities. Reiterated 2026 capex and expect capex to be significantly higher in the next few years.

At TSMC, a higher level of capital expenditures is always correlated with higher growth opportunities in the following years. Given the continued robust multiyear demand from our customers, including the emerging Agentic AI market, we reiterate our full year 2026 capital budget to be between USD 60 billion and USD 64 billion. We continue to expect our CapEx dollars investment from 2026 to 2028 to be even more significantly higher than the past 3 years as we continue to invest heavily to support our customers' growth.

12 | TSMC is checking not just with their own customers but with their customers' customers. Going one step further to send their own teams of people to check on the data center build progress and power supply situation in the U.S. on a continuous basis to assess the market demand from its top-down and bottom-up approach.

To address the structural increase in the long-term semiconductor market demand profile, TSMC collaborated closely with our customers and our customers' customers to plan for our capacity. In addition, we are now going one step further and sending our own teams of people to check on the data center build-out progress and power supply situation in the U.S.

The feedback is so far so good, and the CSPs has been well prepared. Internally, TSMC employed a disciplined capacity planning system to assess the market demand from both a topdown and bottom-up approach. This is a continuous and ongoing process. Given the fundamental complexity of leading-edge technologies and the design-in and lead time involved, we already have a very good idea of customers' multiyear product road map and production plans.

13 | TSMC continues to hold strong conversion in the AI megatrend. Confident in expanding capacity to fill the large demand-supply gap, moving at full speed to step up capex and increase capacity.

All the results we put into our judgment and our assessment, the result is the demand is very, very high. And so the gap between demand and supply are still quite big, and that's why we put all our strengths to increase the capacity, as I just mentioned.
Thus, we continue to hold strong conviction in the AI megatrend. We are moving full speed ahead to increase our capacity to meet our excess demand and stepping up our CapEx investment to support our customers' future growth. TSMC is expanding at an unprecedented pace with a near 20 fabs worldwide in progress. We are building 13 leading edge and advanced packaging fab in Taiwan over the next several years and another 5 to 6 fabs overseas.

14 | TSMC has very strong conviction in the AI mega trend and expects capex from 2026 to 2028 to be significantly higher than the past three years. They have no intention to leave any food on the table for competitors to take.

we have very strong conviction in the AI megatrend. Therefore, our CapEx from 2026 to 2028 is expected to be significantly higher than the past 3 years. And this is a step-up of our investment to support the customers' growth. We have no intention to leave any food on the table for others.

15 | Tool price inflation from ASML is real. But TSMC expects the revenue growth to outpace capex growth.

The tool price inflation is real. The tool price, material, labor costs, et cetera. However, the majority of the CapEx is always related to the long-term demand. So that will be the composition going forward. And capital intensity-wise, as we always said, if we do our job right, the increase in revenue will outpace the increase in CapEx, and that is still the case from what we are looking at.

16 | TSMC continues to work very hard to expand their capacity in the US because that is what their customers are demanding, and with strong support from the U.S. government.

we work very hard to expand our capacity in U.S. This is necessary because of all our customers, most of our large customer in U.S. and they requested TSMC to increase the capacity. And also U.S. government are very helpful. So that's a place we want to expand. So recently, we did expand our capacity consideration to see outside Arizona, whether we can get another chance to expand our capacity. And Texas is one. So we send the teams to Texas to do all the evaluation.

17 | Nothing with Tesla, SpaceX on Terafab joint discussions as of now. The fab has got to be run by TSMC, not them.

And we also talked to one of our customers who try to build a fab, Terafab, let me be more specific. And we discuss with them to see whether that we can be utilizing that actual capacity also. So we joint discussion, if we have any solid conclusion, we'll share with you. But today, and that's it, yes, from Arizona to Texas, yes. We are still in discussion. Let me say that. It's not either way, it will be possible, but the fab got to be run by TSMC.

18 | TSMC does not allow their customers to sublet or auction the capacity that they have with them. While customers can collaborate through a mask licensing agreement, it is small.

To say whether this is a new strategy, new methodology, the answer is no. The principle of TSMC is we do not allow our customer to sublet or auction of the capacity. But in certain cases, customers can collaborate through a mask licensing agreement, but this is not our common practice. And the amount is very, very small.

19 | Adding more new fabs and converting to support N3 capacity expansion

Now let me talk about TSMC's global N3 capacity expansion update. As we said before, historically, we do not add additional capacity to a node once it reaches its targeted capacity. However, based on our assessment, we are executing well on our global capacity plan to add 3 new fabs to support a robust multiyear pipeline of demand for 3nm technologies. In Taiwan, volume production for our new 3nm fab in Tainan Science Park is well on track to begin the first half of 2027.

In addition, driven by the strong demand from our customer, we have decided to add one additional 3nm fab in Tainan. Volume production is scheduled for 1H28. In Arizona, we have completed the construction of our second fab and are in the process of tool moving and installation. Volume production will begin in 3Q27, slightly ahead of our previous schedule. In Japan, we are progressing well to our plan to utilize 3nm in our second fab and volume production is scheduled in 2028. In addition to all the new fabs, we continue to convert 5-nanometer tool to support 3-nanometer capacity in Taiwan.

20 | N2 has entered high-volume production manufacturing in 4Q25 and is ramping well. Expect N2 capacity to 2x in 2027

Our new node, N2 has already entered high-volume manufacturing in the fourth quarter of 2025 with good yield. N2 is ramping successfully in multiple phases at both Hsinchu and Kaohsiung site. We expect our N2 family technologies annual capacity to more than double in 2027, supported by strong demand from both smartphone and HPC AI applications. We are also leveraging our manufacturing excellence to generate more N2 wafer output, further increasing our capacity support to customers.

21 | Preparing capacity for A14 on track for 2027 and volume production in 2028. Expect A14 to be an even bigger node than N2.

In addition, we have already begun preparing the capacity for our A14 technology. Risk production is well on track for 2027 and volume production will start in 2028. Thus, TSMC's semiconductor technologies and manufacturing will continue to play a pivotal role in supporting the global semiconductor industry while unleashing our customers' innovation. Now let me talk about TSMC's global N3 capacity expansion update…And we expect that the A14 will be a bigger node than our current N2 technologies.

22 | TSMC's advanced packaging remains very competitive. Their CoWoS is still the number one choice for customers. And they are in real-world production of 5x radical size.

Actually, I still think that TSMC's advanced assembly or they say, packaging technology are very, very competitive. But the most important thing is that we're using that one to help us help our customers product can be introduced in the market smoothly. That's our #1 priority. And so we have to offer them the best technology with enough capacity. 

So far, let me share with you today's situation. We are in the real-world production of 5x reticle size. I don't believe that anybody can do that today, except at TSMC. And the yield is excellent. So our customers are very satisfied with the result. And then we are working on the 9x reticle size and moving into the 14x reticle size. Of course, we are also working on the CoWoS and to make sure that in the future, we can offer a reasonable cost reduction. But so far, the CoWoS is still the #1 choice for our customer. As time goes by, yes, our competitors offer a very competitive solution. Still, I want to say that today's situation, we are the only one that make sure that the advanced packaging is a 5x reticle size and still, we are very competitive. I want to emphasize that.

23 | See High NA as a very good tool and plan to use it in 2030, expecting higher capex. But not using High NA now because it is too expensive and not at the best maturity. With the 12-inch photo mask by 2031, the cost of High NA should be more reasonable.

Yes, for the long-term productivity, we continue to improve it and High NA definitely is a very good tool. And so far, I think our plan is to use it in 2030. Again, our CapEx will be much higher than today.

We always evaluate a new tool. And if we want to put into the mass production, it got to be the best technology with a very reasonable cost and most important is the best maturity, okay? So we say in 2030, we'll start to use it because we also think at that time, High-NA will be mature.
And we're also working very closely with ASML to establish a 12-inch photomask by 2031. And at that time, we think that the high cost will be reasonable and for TSMC to make it into the mass production.

24 | There is no ceiling for TSMC's profitability, but they are not profit-maxing and always seek to earn their higher profitability by providing growing value to customers

And so you're talking about whether the gross margin or the profitability can be increased or not. Let me say that. There's no ceiling for TSMC's profitability, but a dramatic increase will not happen overnight either. So our philosophy or our strategy always works with our customer, and we want to make them be successful and then we can get our value.

➡️ Key takeaways from TSMC:

Expect TSMC to continue its outperformance against the foundry industry, supported by long-term structural real demand from AI accelerators be it GPUs, custom ASICs, and CPUs. All roads in AI ultimately lead back to TSMC. Raised CAPEX guide reflects the even faster growing opportunities. Advanced packaging supply capacity remains tight. Expecting 2nm and overseas fabs to weigh on GPMs, offset by efficiency and gradual higher pricing. TSMC continues to be the dominant foundry for advanced semiconductor manufacturing with its scale, efficiency, and technological expertise. Appreciate its philosophy to not “profit-maxx” from its customers.

text:
“God cannot be bribed, His power cannot be auctioned, and His sovereignty cannot be challenged with UGX 200 million.”

Yet pastors can demand money from their congregations in exchange for supposed miracles and blessings? Isn’t that a contradiction?

We have witnessed people being told to eat miracle bread or holy rice, supposedly to allow the power of the Holy Spirit to work through them. But how exactly does this work? How can a piece of bread or a handful of rice become a miraculous instrument on demand? And if these objects genuinely possess such healing powers, why aren’t these men of God taking them to hospitals for free to heal the sick who desperately need divine intervention?

If miracles are truly acts of God, why should access to them be tied to money? Why should the poor be persuaded to part with their hard earned savings in pursuit of healing and blessings that are supposedly freely given by God? If God’s power cannot be bought, why are some of His supposed servants behaving like miracle salesmen?

There is absolutely nothing wrong with questioning or exposing false prophets. The Bible itself warns against false prophets and false teachers. Exposing deception is not an attack on God; it is a challenge to those who invoke His name to justify their actions.

If these men genuinely perform miracles through the power of God, let them demonstrate that power without turning it into a commercial enterprise. Let them visit hospitals, help the sick and offer hope to the desperate without demanding payment or making financial contributions a condition for divine intervention.

A genuine servant of God should be concerned with serving people, not exploiting their desperation. Faith should not be a marketplace, and the pulpit should never become a platform for profiting from the suffering of the poor. If the miracles are real, let the evidence speak for itself. If they are not, then the public has every right to demand answers.

text:
Skydance says Paramount and Warner Bros. will remain separate creative studios. It also says they’ll keep buying from outside producers and selling programming to outside platforms.

Those commitments matter, but you also have to look at how the businesses actually operate.

If both studios want the same project, can they compete for it? Do they have independent budgets? Can each executive approve the deal, or does somebody above them decide which division gets it and what the company will pay?

That affects the negotiation before you ever get to a contract.

When I’m taking out a project, multiple interested buyers give me options on money, casting, creative control, ownership, distribution and how the project gets made.

One might offer more money. Another might have the filmmaker, release plan or role that makes more sense for the client. You need the ability to compare those offers and walk away from one.

When potential buyers end up under the same ownership, I want to know how much of that competition survives.

For independent producers, can you bring in a package and get a serious commitment? Is there room in the budget for outside projects? Is the studio willing to negotiate over rights?

And if you’re producing inside that company, can you take the show to the buyer that makes the most sense, even when that buyer is a competing platform?

Having studios, networks, streaming and distribution within one company can create opportunities. A project can have more places to go. But somebody needs the authority and the budget to move it forward.

Who can say yes, who can compete for the project and how many approvals does it take to close?

Then there’s what all of this means for individual talent.

With the wrestling clients I represent, I’m also looking at what these relationships can create across film, television, documentaries and other projects.

A performer can bring an audience, name recognition, physical ability, timing and years of experience working in front of a camera. Those are things you can build on.

Then you have to find the right material and do the work.

For somebody pursuing acting, that means getting in front of filmmakers, producers and casting directors, preparing for the role and showing what they can do. The wrestling audience gives a buyer something to consider. The performance has to work within the project.

The role matters, too. You want material that gives somebody an opportunity to show range and get considered for the next job.

There’s a practical side. Availability, preparation, shooting dates, travel, promotion. You have to work through those things early enough that an opportunity can turn into a deal.

That’s where executives who take an individual performer seriously can make a difference. Somebody reads the material, watches the tape, makes the introduction or helps resolve the issue holding everything up.

With Rice coming into Netflix and the changes across Skydance, I’m interested in who gets put in charge across the slate and how receptive those teams are to talent coming out of wrestling.

These companies have film studios, television operations, documentary teams and enormous distribution. They can develop projects around individual performers, cast them in existing projects and introduce them to different audiences.

Some talent want to act. Some want to produce. Some have a story they want to tell. The approach should reflect what that person wants and what they’re capable of doing.

From my side, that means identifying the opportunity, putting together something credible and getting it to the people who can move it forward.

The next rights deal matters to the wrestling company. 

I’m also looking at the next role, the next project and what gives an individual client more options over the course of their career.

text:
The 2026 United States midterm elections

These contests occur midway through President Donald Trump’s second term, on November 3 and will determine control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency. 
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are on the ballot, along with dozens of governorships and thousands of state and local offices. Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress.

What is at stake

Control of the House allows a party to set the legislative agenda, chair committees, control appropriations, and launch investigations or begin impeachment proceedings. The Senate confirms presidential nominees, including federal judges, and conducts any impeachment trials. 
A change in either chamber would limit Trump’s ability to advance legislation, although he retains veto power. 
Midterm elections have historically produced losses for the president’s party, and Trump’s approval ratings remain in the high 30s while the generic congressional ballot shows Democrats ahead by roughly seven to eight points.

Key candidates and competitive races

Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats to win a majority. 
Several races are tightly contested. In Texas, Democratic state Representative James Talarico leads Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in recent polling. In Maine, Troy Jackson holds a narrow edge over incumbent Senator Susan Collins. Iowa is essentially tied between Josh Turek and Ashley Hinson, while Minnesota shows Peggy Flanagan ahead of Michele Tafoya. North Carolina favors former Governor Roy Cooper over Michael Whatley, and Alaska remains close between Mary Peltola and Dan Sullivan. Incumbent Democrat Jon Ossoff leads in Georgia. Additional battlegrounds include Ohio, Michigan, and New Hampshire. 
In the House, Democrats are favored to win control and need only a modest net gain of seats.

Outlook and voting procedures

Most forecasting models give Democrats a strong chance of taking the House and a competitive chance of winning the Senate, though outcomes will depend on turnout and results in a small number of close races. 
Election Day falls on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November. Most states offer early in-person voting and mail ballots, with registration deadlines set by each state. Primaries have already concluded. 
After results are certified, the new Congress will convene in January 2027. 
The elections will shape the legislative environment and oversight of the executive branch through the remainder of the decade.
