text:
In 2021, Texas suffered the worst energy infrastructure failure in state history, following three severe winter storms in February. At least 246 people were killed as a result of the disruptions, which led to food, water, heat and electricity shortages.

If energy officials had had more time to prepare for the storms, for example by bringing in more trucks of natural gas to disrupted areas, damage from the event could have been mitigated. Unfortunately, weather forecasts beyond two weeks are notoriously unreliable, making for a tighter window for energy operators, farmers, and emergency response officials around the globe.

A new technique by a team including researchers at MIT significantly improves weather forecasting beyond two weeks. The researchers developed a machine-learning model that learns to correct errors in existing forecasting models to improve their output over the two-to-six-week time frame. When applied to a gold-standard forecasting model, it doubled forecasting accuracy over that time frame, placing first in a prominent international forecasting competition.

In a new paper in Nature, the researchers describe their approach and show how it enables forecasts that for the first time beat climatologic averages between two and six weeks.

“Not only does this do better on time averaged forecasts for this range, which is already very useful for farmers and members of the energy industry trying to match supply with demand, but it also improves predictions of extreme weather events, whether it’s flooding or cold spells or something else,” co-author and MIT Research Scientist Judah Cohen says. “It’s really important to predict both, but extreme events might be the most impactful part of this for society.” 

Joining Cohen on the paper are lead authors Hannah Guan, a Harvard College undergraduate; Soukayna Mouatadid, a University of Toronto postdoc; Genevieve Flaspohler SM ’18, PhD ’22; Paulo Orenstein, an associate professor at Brazil’s National Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics; Jeremy Berman of the data company DTN; Jakob Schloer and Joshua Talib, researchers with the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts; and Alex Lu, Haiyu Dong, Jonathan Weyn, Zekun Ni, and Lester Mackey, all researchers at Microsoft.

Longer forecasts

In the 1970s, longtime MIT Professor Edward Lorenz came up with the idea of chaos theory to describe how tiny changes in initial weather conditions lead to completely different outcomes.

“He came up with this theoretical two-week limit where beyond that, we just can’t predict weather because the noise in the system grows so much that it overwhelms any signal you start with,” Cohen says. “That had a strong influence on the field that may have held people back from exploring forecasting beyond the two-week range. I never really believed that completely. In theory the atmosphere can create an infinite number of patterns, but it likes to fall into these favorite patterns over and over again. Once one thing happens, I think you can predict the domino that will fall after that, and the domino that will fall after that.”

Today, the best weather forecasts come from either dynamical models, which numerically simulate how the atmosphere and oceans evolve over time, or artificial intelligence models, which learn to make predictions from historical weather data. AI models have shown improvements in predicting weather at short ranges, but they’re even worse than dynamical models at longer time ranges.

Cohen, who is based in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, focuses on forecasting weather two to six weeks in advance, which is known as subseasonal forecasting. “That range is referred to as the ‘predictability desert,’ because in the short range you can capitalize on the initial conditions in the climate system and the atmosphere, and on the longer term you have these slow, varying boundary forces, like the super El Niño everyone’s focused on this winter,” Cohen says. “The subseasonal range can’t take advantage of either of those. In most cases forecasting in the subseasonal ranges is no different than going to a casino and rolling the dice.”

Cohen credits his co-author Lester Mackey, whom he has been collaborating with for more than a decade, with the initial idea of using machine learning to reduce errors in forecasting models.

“We built this wrapper — Lester calls it postprocessing,” Cohen says. “We know AI models have a lot of errors, so we thought maybe we can quantify those errors and remove them.”

While other forecasting systems do more simplistic error correction, the research team’s postprocessing layer uses AI to learn from a forecasting system’s mistakes based on historic data and shifts its forecasts. In that time range, forecasters use so-called probabilistic forecasts, where the likelihood of a range of possibilities if given.

“As more forecasts and data become available, our model adaptively improves its correction,” Cohen says.

To build the model, the researchers used MIT Engaging, a supercomputing cluster hosted by MIT’s Office of Research Computing and Data, but the resulting model does not require a supercomputer to run.

To put their model to the test, last year the research team submitted three models that included their post-processing layer to the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which is considered the best forecasting center in the world. Each season ECMWF holds forecasting competitions between models.

The submission that won first place combined ECMWF’s forecasting model with another, and then applied the postprocessing correction on top. That approach ended up doubling the original model’s predictive power in the subseasonal range. For the first time, the model offered an improvement over relying on climatologic averages.

“Up until now, no one had been able to show a model predicts weather better than long term averages for these subseasonal forecasts,” Cohen says. “They’ve pretty much all been worse than that — you could literally flip a coin and do better. People have questioned if it’s even worth investing in models at all for this time range. We consistently beat climatology averages with our models.”

The model also showed a statistically significant improvement in the ability to predict extreme weather.

“That’s one of the more important findings, because it’s so difficult to accomplish,” Cohen says. “When the ECMWF developed their own, non-AI, error-correction to their model, it got worse at predicting extreme weather. I think that’s because traditional error, or bias, correction is always trying to get to the mean, whereas extreme weather is on the fringe of probabilities.”

Preparing for disaster

In the Nature paper, the team showed their technique could be used to improve land forecasts in most regions across the globe. They also applied their bias correction technique to other models and showed it improved those as well, putting even lesser models on par with the ECMWF’s forecasts.

“What’s nice about our model is it’s an add-on wrapper,” Cohen explains. “We used it with the ECMWF’s dynamical model because that was considered the best, but it can be used with any model. It even improves models that are already bias corrected using another AI algorithm. So it shows a robust improvement. And it’s open source and low cost.”

Cohen says the meteorological office for the Republic of Kenya has already reached out about implementing the model to improve forecasting of the annual monsoon season to improve agricultural yields this winter. He hopes other groups will also use the model.

“This could help you decide when to fertilize around rain, when there’s a freeze coming to protect crops during winter harvests, or help you avoid droughts,” Cohen says. “It could also be useful for energy and emergency management. I’ve talked to energy officials who say, ‘If I’m told two days before that an ice storm’s coming, I don’t have enough time, but if I had two weeks, that could be enough to make adequate preparations.”

The work was supported, in part, by the U.S. National Science Foundation, the Carlos Chagas Filho Foundation for Research Support, and the European Union.

Europe opened Friday where Asia left off. Frankfurt leads, London and Paris are flat, and the region is headed for a winning week, hours after Seoul finished its worst week since 2008.

The verdict at 4:20am ET: Europe is taking the relief from easing worries about interest rates and AI spending, but it is not paying extra for good news that comes with heavy new borrowing. Schneider Electric, the French maker of the power and cooling gear inside data centers, just reported the strongest quarter in its history, and its shares are lower. US index futures are up only about a fifth of a percent, a calm handoff rather than a strong one.

Europe so far, each from Thursday's close, as of 4:20am ET:

- DAX (Germany): 25,586, +204 points / +0.80%.
- FTSE 100 (UK): 10,839, -1.76 points / -0.02%.
- CAC 40 (France): 7,941.68, +6.98 points / +0.09%.

Frankfurt opened 0.4% higher and has built on it. The news agency dpa-AFX credited easing worries about rates and about how AI investment will be paid for, and noted that Frankfurt's index leans on older industries.

Some of the buying is coming out of safety. Across Europe, by industry group:

- Aerospace and defense: +1.5%.
- Carmakers: +1.5%.
- Tech: +0.9%.
- Health care: -0.5%.

Drug stocks were where US investors hid on Thursday. Europe is selling them on Friday.

Asia's Friday closes, each from Thursday's close:

- Nikkei 225 (Japan): 65,324, +898 points / +1.39%.
- KOSPI (South Korea): 5,668.05, +113.83 points / +2.05%.
- Taiex (Taiwan): 47,111.26, +141.39 points / +0.30%.
- Hang Seng (Hong Kong): 24,186.83, +124.11 points / +0.52%.
- Shanghai Composite (mainland China): 3,716.28, +8.81 points / +0.24%.

Every one finished below its best level of the day, and Seoul gave back more than half of a 4.6% gain (arithmetic).

The week is where the two regions part. From each market's last close of the week before (arithmetic):

- Seoul: -14.5%, its worst week since the one ending October 24, 2008.
- Tokyo: -5.4%.
- Taipei: -4.5%.
- Frankfurt: +2.0% so far.

The losses ran deepest where chipmakers carry the most weight, and Europe's big indexes hold far fewer of them. That is a reading of the prices; dpa made the same point about Frankfurt.

Now the exception:

Schneider Electric (SBGSY) at $57.49, -$0.87 / -1.49% on Thursday.

That New York price was set before the report. In Paris, its main listing, it opened 2.0% higher and turned lower inside the first hour. By about 4:20am ET it was at 254.55 euros, -3.45 euros / -1.34% from Thursday's close.

The July-September quarter, reported at 1:30am ET:

- Revenue, the money coming in the door: 11.46 billion euros vs 11.13 billion expected; +16.9% from a year earlier, leaving out currency swings and acquisitions.
- Data centers: demand more than doubled from a year earlier, the company said.
- 2026 forecast, raised for the second time this year: revenue growth 12%-14%, from 10%-13%.

Finance chief Nathan Fast called it "the strongest quarter in Schneider's history," Reuters reported. https://t.co/5Qgbvb82VL put the fade down to selling on the news and to lingering worry over a purchase still ahead:

PTC (PTC) at $193.15, -$0.49 / -0.25% on Thursday.

On October 5, Schneider agreed to pay $205 a share in cash, about $22.6B, for the US maker of software engineers use to design products. Yahoo Finance reported roughly $16B-$17B of that would be borrowed, the rest raised by selling new shares, and Friday's release said buybacks pause in 2027 and 2028.

Schneider fell about 10% the day the deal was announced and now sits 16.0% under its October 2 close in Paris (arithmetic). A record quarter has won none of that back. Its growth needs no borrowing; its purchase does, and the stock is trading on the purchase.

Schneider Electric is on none of the six Len5 watchlists: the nearest, Momentum, hunts stocks climbing to new highs, and its Paris shares are 18.2% under August 12's closing high of 311 euros (arithmetic). The Momentum Len5 is watching PTC at #18 of 30 because of its jump on Schneider's offer, not because of its own business.

US index futures, each since Thursday's close, as of 4:20am ET:

- S&P 500 futures: 7,806.50, +15.50 points / +0.20%.
- Nasdaq-100 futures: 30,184.50, +40.75 points / +0.14%.
- Dow futures: 52,543.00, +113 points / +0.22%.
- Russell 2000 futures: 2,790.20, +8.40 points / +0.30%.

All four are higher, and the contract built from the biggest US tech companies is the weakest. The 10-year Treasury yield, which sets borrowing costs across the US economy, sits at 5.09%, about where Thursday's drop left it. New York inherits Europe's calm, not a reason to rally, and moves this small before dawn often vanish by the 9:30am ET opening bell.

What would make this more than relief: Frankfurt holding its gain into New York's open, and Schneider climbing back above Thursday's close. What would show it fading: Europe giving back its morning the way Seoul did.

What comes next, Eastern time:

- 5am: final September inflation for the euro area from Eurostat, the EU's statistics agency. Early estimate: 3.8% from a year earlier, up from 3.2% in August.
- 8:30am: US import prices for September (Bureau of Labor Statistics), after +0.7% in August.
- 9:15am: the Federal Reserve's September industrial production, the output of factories, mines and utilities; forecasts near +0.4%, after a flat August.
- October 29: the European Central Bank's next rate decision.

The key risk: a euro-area figure revised above 3.8%, or a jump in US import prices, would revive the rate fears behind Thursday's selloff before New York opens.

Europe will pay for a rebound this morning. It will not yet pay full price for a record quarter that arrives with up to $17 billion of new debt.

text:
Fusion CX IPO closes today.

What the company does

Fusion CX is a Kolkata-based customer support and BPO company.

It handles calls, chats and back-office work for other companies. About 85% of its revenue comes from the US and Canada, and almost half comes from telecom and tech clients.

The offer

Price band: ₹275 to ₹289

Size: ₹702 cr (₹500 cr fresh, ₹202 cr sold by the promoters)

Listing date: 22 October

How the business is doing

FY26 revenue: ₹1,818 cr, up 37%

FY26 profit: ₹170 cr, vs ₹74 cr in FY25

EBITDA margin: 18%, vs 10.6% in FY24

Latest quarter (Apr-Jun 2026): ₹490 cr revenue, ₹56 cr profit

This is a real improvement and not just a one-year jump.

Valuation

At ₹289 it trades at about 24x FY26 earnings after counting the new shares. Listed peers in the RHP average around 27x. So the price is fair, not cheap.

What I like

Strong growth with rising margins
About ₹276 cr of the fresh issue goes to repay debt

Anchors came in at ₹289, the full top of the band

What worries me

The top 10 clients bring about 50% of revenue. Losing one big client would hurt.

Employee attrition is 31%, which is high.

A lot of the growth came from buying other companies, and part of the IPO money is for acquisitions not yet named.

FY26 tax was only about 10% of profit before tax. If that goes up, profit will look lower.

Anchor book

₹316 cr was raised from 19 anchors
About 78% came from 6 mutual funds

Biggest names: Kotak Multi Asset, ICICI Prudential Technology and Motilal Oswal Digital India
Kotak Life Insurance also took a share

It's a decent list, but mostly hybrid and thematic funds, so I wouldn't call it a very strong signal.

GMP and subscription

GMP was ₹55 on 9 Oct, ₹33 on 14 Oct, ₹22 on 15 Oct and ₹13 today
That's only about 4.5% above the cap price

Subscription: 0.43x on Day 1, 1.16x on Day 2, and 1.80x at 1 PM today
GMP has fallen every day, and demand has been slow.

My view

Good business, fair price, weak market interest. For listing gains, I'm not applying. 

A 4-5% GMP leaves almost no cushion once you count allotment risk and market mood.

Not advice. GMP is unofficial. Do your own research.

text:
✨The DURGA PUJA at the MRINMOYEE TEMPLE in BISHNUPUR, WEST BENGAL, is widely recognized as the OLDEST documented continuing DURGA PUJA in BENGAL. Celebrating its 1,030TH YEAR, this historic royal festival dates back to 997 CE when it was established by King Jagat Malla of the Malla dynasty.

✨Unlike the rest of Bengal where festivities traditionally gather steam around Mahalaya, the ritual calendar at this historic site extends for an extraordinary 15 to 18 days, beginning weeks earlier on Krishna Nabami/Jita Ashtami.

The Dynamic Rituals & Timeline:-
The Early Commencement: The rituals formally kick off on Krishna Nabami (the ninth lunar day of the waning moon). The official arrival is traditionally heralded by the firing of nine cannon shots from the nearby Murchchar Hill.

Sequential Arrival of Deities - The Three Thakuranis:-
The long-standing worship revolves around three distinct painted scrolls (Patachitras) representing three forms of the Goddess:
1. Boro Thakurani (The Elder Goddess - MahaKali): Enters the temple on Krishna-Navami, 15 days before the main Puja.
2. Mejo Thakurani (The Middle Goddess - MahaLaxmi): Arrives on Chaturthi.
3. Chhoto Thakurani (The Younger Goddess - MahaSaraswati): Arrives on Shasthi.
These are sequentially uncovered and worshipped after the ceremonial installation of the Ghata (sacred clay pot).

The Twilight Sandhi Puja: The absolute peak of the festival takes place during Sandhi Puja—the exact transition between Mahastami and Mahanavami. The precise auspicious moment is announced to the entire town by firing a royal cannon. Following this thunderous roar, symbolic vegetable sacrifices are carried out inside the temple complex.

Bijaya Dashami Rest: On the final day, the ritual shifts away from standard immersion. Instead, the permanent Idol is offered stale rice (panta bhaat) as a symbol of domestic simplicity and domestic peace before the festival concludes.

Secrets, Legends, and Hidden Truths:-
The Vision Under the Banyan Tree: According to the local administrative histories documented by the West Bengal Tourism Department, King Jagat Malla was hunting in a dense wilderness when he witnessed a strange omen—a tiny bird overpowering a massive hawk near a banyan tree. Shortly after, the Goddess appeared in a dream, ordering him to relocate the Malla capital from Pradyumnapur to this specific forested spot, which eventually became Bishnupur.

The Buried Face of Ganga Clay: The Goddess revealed that a small, naturally formed clay representation of Her face was buried beneath the earth at the banyan site. The king unearthed the sacred relic and incorporated it right into the core foundation of a larger statue sculpted from holy Ganga clay.

The Immortal Idol: While modern Durga idols are ritually immersed in water (visarjan) at the end of Dashami, the idol of Maa Mrinmoyee is never immersed. The original 10th-century sacred structure resides permanently inside the inner Sanctum, preserving a continuous, unbroken lineage of worship spanning over a millennium.

The Lost Bloodline Ritual: Historically, the Malla kings belonged to the Sakta sect, and the temple originally hosted intense esoteric rituals dedicated to the Chamunda form of the Goddess. However, when the royal house converted to Vaishnavism under King Veer Hambir in the late 16th century, animal sacrifices were strictly forbidden inside the main courtyard. Despite the shift, one secret custom remained: the hidden Mahamaarir Puja. Conducted in absolute privacy on the 9th night of Navaratri by direct descendants of the Malla line, this ritual uses highly restricted prayers designed to ward off deadly endemics and famines from the kingdom.

text:
As the verse states, मूलेन आवाहयेद्देवी श्रवणेन विसर्जयेत् (mūlena āvāhayeddevī śravaṇena visarjayet—Invoke Goddess Sarasvatī under the Mūla star and ceremonially conclude the pūjā under the Śravana star), on the day of the Mūlanakṣatra, Amman is invoked and welcomed. Just as we invite Varalakshmi Amman during the Varalakshmi Vratham, we invoke Sarasvatī Amman on the Mūla nakṣatra, and the pūjā continues until the Śravana nakṣatra. The Śravana nakṣatra is also significant for Lord Venkateswara Svāmī, Venkatachalapati of Tirupati. It is on the Śravana nakṣatra that the annual Brahmotsavam in Tirupati is observed, as indicated by the statement:
वरुषे वरुषे तु मासेस्मिन् कन्या राशि गते रवौ (varuṣe varuṣe tu māsesmin kanyā rāśi gate ravau). The Chakra Snānam and pūrṇāhuti of the Brahmotsavam also take place on the day of the Śravana nakṣatra. Similarly, the Sarasvatī Amman pūjā continues until the Śravana nakṣatra. The pūjā concludes with the mantra सर्वोपचारान समर्पयामि (sarvopacārāna samarpayāmi— I offer all forms of upacārā to the Goddess.)

When we perform worship for other deities, such as Pillaiyār, after completing the pūjā we say: शोभनार्थे क्षेमाय पुनरागमनाय च (śobhanārthe kṣemāya punarāgamanāya ca—For auspiciousness, well-being, and for Your return again, please come back) However, in   Sarasvatī pūjā, after offering all the upacārā, we conclude with sarvopacārāna samarpayāmi. Similarly, when offering dāna, such as coconuts, mangoes, silver, gold, land, rice, lentils, wheat, or the nine grains, one says:
ब्राह्मणाय तुभ्यमहं सम्प्रददे न मम।(brāhmaṇāya tubhyamahaṃ sampradade na mama): I give this to you; it is no longer mine. However, during Kanyādāna one stops by saying, I give. Similarly, during  Sarasvatī pūjā, one concludes with sarvopacārāna samarpayāmi. Hara Hara  Śaṅkarā Jaya Jaya Śaṅkarā    #kamakoti #JagadguruVacanam

THE TICKET THAT DELIVERS

He does not come alone. His running mate is Rotimi Amaechi. As Governor, Amaechi built over 300 model schools and about 180 health centres across Rivers State. As Minister of Transportation, he completed and put into service about 700 kilometres of standard gauge railway. That included the Itakpe to Warri line, unfinished since 1987. And on his watch Nigeria passed the first anti-piracy law in West and Central Africa. He builds and he finishes. That is the ticket.

WHY ONLY ATIKU

Look at the ballot honestly. One candidate has had his turn, and the nation is bleeding. The others have never sat at the head of a national economy. Only one man has done all of these things:

Chaired the National Economic Council.

Sat at the table when Nigeria cleared its Paris Club debt.

Published a plan for every wound before the vote.

Promised to do it in a single term.

He is not learning on the job. He has done the job.

Nigeria cannot afford another four years of trial and error. It cannot afford a leader who needs three years to discover that the nation is bleeding. It needs a man who already knows where the levers are, because he has pulled them before.

AWALOKAN

Awalokan is the cry of the suffering Nigerian masses: the mother in the market, the farmer in his burnt village, the graduate with a certificate and no job, the pensioner whose pension buys nothing. It is the voice of a people saying they have carried this country long enough. Now let a leader carry them.

The Waziri is ready to carry them.

EVERY NIGERIAN HAS A ROLE

The market woman can tell every customer what she paid for rice three years ago and what she pays today. She may be Iya Risi in Ibadan, Mama Chioma in Onitsha or Hajiya Binta in Kano.

The okada rider in Sokoto, the keke rider in Owerri and the danfo driver in Lagos can carry the message to every passenger.

The student can share this series in every group chat.

The pastor and the imam can preach the card.

The Nigerian abroad can call home every Sunday until election day.

The farmer can tell his cooperative what it costs him to plant under the eyes of bandits.

The pensioner can tell his grandchildren what Nigeria looked like when it walked out of the Paris Club.

Nobody is too small for this campaign. Every voice carries, and every vote counts.

Now the question belongs to you. Collect your card this week. Bring five people with you. Go out early on 16 January 2027. Stay until the result is counted and posted. Guard your vote with your eyes, not your fists, because a peaceful people in their millions cannot be rigged out of their own country.

They said Emilokan. Nigeria answers: Awalokan.

At Ise Grand Shrine in Japan, approximately 1,500 sacred ceremonies are held every year.

Among them, the most important is Kannamesai, a sacred festival in which the year’s first harvest of rice is offered to Amaterasu Omikami, the Sun Goddess, in gratitude.

For the Japanese people, rice has never been merely food.

It is a sacred blessing from the gods, a gift of nature, and a source of life.

And as rice ripens, its stalks bow lower under the weight of their grains.

【An Important Day Every Japanese Person Should Know About 🇯🇵】

Today, October 15, marks the beginning of Kannamesai, one of the most sacred festivals held at Ise Grand Shrine in Japan.

Approximately 1,500 ceremonies are performed at Ise Grand Shrine each year, but Kannamesai is considered the most important of them all.

During this sacred festival, the first harvest of the year, especially freshly harvested rice, is offered to Amaterasu Omikami, the Sun Goddess, as an expression of gratitude.

Since ancient times, the Japanese people have never taken nature’s blessings for granted. We have honored the divine and expressed our gratitude for the gifts of the earth.

Once again this year, golden rice fields have ripened under the sun. 🌾

And once again, we are blessed with rice on our tables every day.

But this is something we should never take for granted.

To the farmers who dedicate themselves to growing our rice.

To the abundance of nature.

And to the prayers and traditions that have been passed down through countless generations.

I offer my heartfelt gratitude. 🙏

That is why I share the significance of Kannamesai every year.

text:
🇸🇦🇾🇪 Yemen's Brave Resistance Exposes Zionist-Backed Saudi Weakness, IMEC Trade Corridor in Jeopardy as China Expands

Saudi Arabia was supposed to be the gateway to a new economic future. Instead, the war with Yemen is exposing Saudi Arabia’s military weaknesses, threatening its finances, and putting a major trade corridor to Israel at risk.

For Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), the consequences could reach far beyond the battlefield. His ambitious Vision 2030 is under growing pressure, and the future of the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, known as IMEC, is becoming increasingly uncertain.

The first warning came at Riyadh’s international airport.

This week, missiles launched by Yemen struck Terminals 3 and 4, killing and injuring people and exposing Saudi Arabia’s difficulties in protecting critical infrastructure. International airlines have already canceled flights to Riyadh as Yemen seeks to close Saudi airspace.

The economic outlook is adding to the pressure. The International Monetary Fund announced this week that Saudi Arabia’s gross domestic product is expected to contract by 3.3% this year.

The problem is not simply the damage caused by missile attacks. Saudi Arabia must now consider the enormous cost of defending its territory while continuing to finance a war it has struggled to win. That means more money for military equipment and air defense systems, and potentially less for the economic projects on which MBS has staked his future.

There is another weakness that advanced weapons cannot easily solve: the shortage of capable ground forces needed to conquer territory in Yemen. Decades of purchasing American military technology have not given Saudi Arabia the ability to achieve its objectives on the battlefield.

For a leadership that has spent years presenting Saudi Arabia as a rising regional power, the consequences could be severe. Its military limitations are becoming harder to conceal, while its economic ambitions are increasingly vulnerable to the costs of war.

And one of the biggest casualties could be a trade corridor designed to reshape the region.

The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor was announced in 2023 at the G20 summit in New Delhi as a strategic alternative to China’s Belt and Road Initiative, the vast infrastructure network launched by President Xi Jinping in 2013.

The plan calls for a continuous rail connection linking the United Arab Emirates to Saudi Arabia, then Jordan, Israel’s port of Haifa, and Europe. The United States, India, the Persian Gulf states, Israel, and European partners see the corridor as a way to strengthen trade and create a strategic counterweight to China.

But the route depends heavily on Saudi Arabia’s ability to finance and build the necessary infrastructure.

Under the original plan, Riyadh would need to invest tens of billions of dollars in new railway lines and upgrades to existing networks through its Saudi Land Bridge project. Now, mounting financial pressure and cuts to Vision 2030 development budgets threaten to delay the work further.

The war is therefore creating a problem that extends well beyond Saudi Arabia’s borders. Every delay makes it harder to turn IMEC from a strategic announcement into a functioning trade network.

Turkey is already promoting an alternative.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan wants to establish a route that bypasses Israel. His proposed Dry Canal would move goods from the United Arab Emirates and Qatar through Iraq to Turkish ports, where cargo could connect with Europe’s railway network.

Qatar could help finance the route alongside Iraq and Turkey, creating an alternative to the corridor planned through Haifa.

On paper, the Turkish proposal has clear advantages. It avoids Saudi Arabia, Israel, and the Suez Canal. But its geography creates another set of problems.

The route would pass through Iraq, where security threats and continuing tensions between Turkish forces and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) complicate the security picture.

Investors must weigh those risks against the commercial benefits. Even so, work under signed contracts has already begun on the Turkish route, while IMEC remains stalled, partly because of the war in Israel.

That leaves a striking possibility: the more the United States and its vassals struggle to establish an alternative trade network, the more room China has to expand its own.

Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative continues to offer a framework for infrastructure development and international trade. Meanwhile, the American effort to build a competing network is running into obstacles created by the very regional conflicts that Washington has struggled to contain.

Saudi Arabia’s difficulties are also weakening its position among its neighbors.

Since its establishment in 1981, the Gulf Cooperation Council has brought together Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Oman. Riyadh has long been viewed as a central security and political power within this group.

That position is now under pressure.

Saudi Arabia’s inability to reliably protect critical infrastructure has raised questions about its value as a regional security guarantor. The attack on Saudi Aramco’s oil facilities in 2019, involving unmanned aerial vehicles and cruise missiles, had already exposed serious vulnerabilities. The latest developments are reinforcing those concerns.

Saudi Arabia remains heavily dependent on external assistance, particularly from the United States under President Donald Trump, as well as on Israeli intelligence support and its developing relationships with regional powers such as Turkey and Pakistan.

Its neighbors are responding by looking more closely at their own security and foreign policy options. The United Arab Emirates, for example, receives overt military assistance from Israel.

The underlying economic problem is just as serious.

Saudi Arabia depends heavily on oil production and exports. Changes in global energy prices, the gradual shift toward alternative energy sources in Western markets, and the physical vulnerability of refining and transportation facilities all increase the risks associated with that dependence.

Diversifying the economy requires enormous investment. Defending Saudi Arabia requires more spending, too. As military costs rise, the money available for long-term economic transformation becomes harder to protect.

The figures tell the story.

According to the International Monetary Fund, Saudi economic growth is expected to fall to 1.7% this year, down from 4.6% last year. Growth could recover to 5.5% next year.

Non-oil growth is projected at 2.6% this year, compared with 4.2% last year, before rising to 4.5% next year.

The budget deficit is expected to reach 3.7% of GDP this year, improving from 5.8% last year, with a forecast of 3.1% next year. Meanwhile, the non-oil budget deficit is projected at 22.2% this year, compared with 23.3% last year, before reaching 20.9% next year.

These figures highlight the central challenge facing MBS. Despite years of promises to diversify the economy, Saudi Arabia remains deeply dependent on oil revenue to support its spending ambitions.

Foreign exchange reserves stand at $462 billion, up from $445 billion last year. But substantial reserves do not eliminate the difficult choices created by rising military costs, slowing growth, and expensive development projects.

Few projects better illustrate the scale of those ambitions than NEOM.

Located in northwestern Saudi Arabia, along the Red Sea and near the Strait of Tiran, NEOM was designed as the flagship project of Vision 2030. It was supposed to demonstrate that the kingdom could move beyond oil and become a global center for technology, innovation, clean energy, and luxury tourism.

Instead, the project has run into engineering challenges, enormous cost overruns, a difficult global economic environment, and regional military tensions.

The original vision included a 170-kilometer-long rectangular city in the desert, fully air-conditioned and designed to serve as a global tourism and innovation hub. That vision is now being sharply scaled back, with some components reduced in scope or partially halted.

The financial pressure is mounting elsewhere, too.

Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund, which plays a central role in financing Vision 2030, must spread its resources across a growing list of expensive commitments. These include real estate development in Riyadh and major investments in international sports and aviation.

The more money that flows into projects that fail to deliver their promised returns, the harder it becomes to sustain the entire development strategy.

Criticism is also growing among members of the traditional elite, including wealthy investors and major business interests. Their concern is that MBS’s grand ambitions have exposed Saudi Arabia to excessive financial risk.

The war with Yemen is making those risks more difficult to manage.

For Israel, this creates an opportunity to turn Saudi Arabia’s need for security assistance into a strategic bargain.

Israel’s proposal is straightforward: Israel should work with the United States to help strengthen Saudi Arabia’s defenses, but it should not provide military intelligence cooperation without securing concrete benefits in return.

Those benefits, according to this argument, should include Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords and making a public commitment that Haifa will remain the departure port for IMEC.

The terms should be transparent from the beginning. Israel would gain a formal place in the emerging trade network, while the Turkish alternative would face a stronger strategic obstacle.

The Israeli proposal also rejects the idea that Israel should provide extensive assistance to Saudi Arabia without receiving something substantial in return. Riyadh has already approached Israel through U.S. Central Command, making the question of what each side stands to gain especially important.

For MBS, the choices are becoming more difficult.

He can pursue closer cooperation with Israel and the United States, hoping to strengthen his security position and preserve his political future. Alternatively, he can face the consequences of continued military setbacks and financial pressure, both of which could weaken his position within the Saudi leadership.

The memory of the arrests he ordered at the Ritz-Carlton hotel in 2017 has not disappeared among Saudi Arabia’s elite. As confidence in his leadership erodes, the question of succession to King Salman bin Abdulaziz could become increasingly important.

No one can say with certainty how that struggle will unfold. But the combination of military setbacks, economic pressure, and dissatisfaction among influential figures creates a difficult environment for the man who promised to transform Saudi Arabia.

The stakes extend far beyond a bilateral agreement. If IMEC is to become a functioning trade corridor linking India with Europe, its planners must overcome the military and political obstacles threatening the route through Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Israel.

For Israel, allowing the Haifa connection to disappear would mean surrendering a potentially important strategic and economic position. For Saudi Arabia, the challenge is whether it can protect its infrastructure, finance its ambitions, and maintain its regional influence while the war continues.

MBS promised a new future for Saudi Arabia. Now, military setbacks and financial pressures are testing that promise.

As Riyadh struggles to keep its ambitions alive, the battle over the trade routes connecting Asia and Europe may determine who gains the most from the crisis: Israel, Turkey, or China.

text:
Your ZIP Code Shouldn’t Decide What You Can Afford to Buy

Find something online at a reasonable price, put it in your cart, and then watch the shipping charge wreck the deal. For rural Americans, that frustration raises a question Congress needs to answer: Why is the United States Postal Service making where you live an increasingly important factor in what you can afford to buy?

USPS holiday package increases took effect October 4. Another geographic pricing change is scheduled to reach some online shipping customers October 18, introducing three destination-based rate groups alongside standard rates. Families have barely started their Christmas shopping, and the postage rules are moving again.

Counting nationwide adjustments, rural ZIP code classifications, and changes documented by shipping platforms, there are at least eight separate change dates this year through October 18: January 18, February 23, April 26, July 12, July 15, September 19, October 4, and October 18. These were not eight increases on every package, nor did every change apply through every shipping provider. They were eight occasions when part of the system determining shipping costs changed or was scheduled to change.

Most buyers will never read those announcements. They will simply discover that a bargain is no longer a bargain once shipping appears.

For someone surrounded by stores, an expensive delivery charge might mean a short drive instead. For someone outside town, the alternative can mean a substantial trip, gasoline, and time away from work or family. For an older person who no longer drives, that alternative may not be practical at all. Online shopping provides access to products and prices that a person’s own community may not offer.

Think about a parent buying secondhand children’s clothes, a retiree looking for an inexpensive replacement part, or a family ordering a used book. These are ordinary purchases where a few extra dollars can determine whether the transaction makes sense. A shipping increase that barely registers on an expensive television can swallow much of the savings on a modest purchase.

The rural pricing problem is already visible. One shipping provider documented a July 15 adjustment moving eligible rural Ground Advantage packages weighing less than 12 ounces into a higher pricing band. The package did not become heavier. Its destination helped determine the price. Other shipping services also document separate USPS merchant and rural pricing tiers. This issue extends across online commerce.

The October geographic change adds another layer. An analysis by Value Added Resource found that more than 7,600 ZIP codes previously receiving standard pricing were assigned to the new groups in the rollout it examined. It also reported that the announcement supplied ZIP code assignments without actual rate cards or examples showing the resulting postage costs. That does not establish that every affected buyer will pay more. It does leave shoppers and sellers facing another change without a clear picture of the bill.

“Dynamic pricing” sounds considerably more impressive in a conference room than it does when you are trying to buy a ten-dollar item.

Buyers understandably question the seller when shipping looks ridiculous. Sometimes that charge deserves scrutiny. But when the underlying postage changes, the expense has to land somewhere: in the shipping charge, in the item’s price, or in whether the item remains economical to sell. “Free shipping” does not make the postal bill disappear.

For the customer, the consequence can be fewer affordable choices. Someone may find exactly the used part, discontinued item, collectible, or inexpensive household purchase they need. If postage makes the deal unreasonable, that option effectively disappears. The product remains on the screen while the buyer is priced out of buying it.

That is how a public postal system can become an arbiter of how rural Americans shop. It does not have to tell anyone which store to use. Its pricing can steer purchases toward retailers able to spread delivery costs across enormous volumes and away from individual bargains elsewhere. The customer’s freedom to choose remains, but the checkout total does the steering.

In practical terms, postal pricing can pick winners and losers—and the rural customer can wind up paying for the selection.

Congress has a direct responsibility here. The Constitution gives Congress the power to establish post offices and post roads. Today’s USPS was organized through legislation to carry out that public postal function. Federal postal policy specifically calls for effective, regular service to rural areas, communities, and small towns. Rural America is part of the mission.

Keeping an address on a delivery route is only part of the job. Congress should also ask whether ordinary people can afford to use the service that reaches it.

Where is that urgency?

Washington has found room for some remarkable calendar management. In February, Representative Andy Ogles introduced legislation to change the observance of Washington’s Birthday and establish Lincoln’s Birthday as a federal holiday. Earlier in this same Congress, Representative Claudia Tenney introduced legislation to make Trump’s Birthday and Flag Day a federal holiday. These are actual proposals. Apparently, Americans’ calendars require a level of attention their household shipping bills have yet to command.

Meanwhile, Senate Republicans are planning an accelerated postelection judicial-confirmation push, and House Democrats are preparing an agenda and investigations should they regain control. Washington can always find energy for the next struggle over power. Families stretching a paycheck deserve some of that energy directed toward the cost of everyday life.

Congress should demand clear prices before changes take effect, understandable explanations of geographic classifications, and a public accounting of what these policies mean for rural shoppers. If serving the entire country requires a different financial arrangement, lawmakers need to address it openly instead of letting the problem appear as another surprise at checkout.

Nobody expects postage to be free. People do have a right to expect that a public institution serving the whole country remembers those living beyond its busiest neighborhoods.

A ZIP code should be a delivery address, not an economic penalty. Rural Americans should not have to move closer to a shopping mall to get a fair chance at an affordable purchase—and they should not need a congressional holiday named after them before Washington notices.

text:
Thanks for that comprehensive reply. I can understand your views on the supposed inflexibility of the EU. Let me try to answer.

On your main points:

3) Responsibility for Brexit

The EU was not blameless, but Britain's deindustrialisation, regional inequality and overstretched public services were primarily failures of British governments.

On immigration, Britain could have controlled free movement much more effectively. Belgium, where I am, requires EU residents to register locally, conducts police residence checks and can require those without employment, genuine job prospects or sufficient resources to leave, subject to EU safeguards. Britain had similar powers but chose not to use them.

4) The Irish border

The Irish border was not an EU bargaining chip. It was the consequence of leaving the Single Market and Customs Union while promising to preserve an open border. Protecting the Good Friday Agreement was an obligation, not vindictiveness.

5) Your alternative deal

Why would 27 countries offer Britain better terms outside the EU than they enjoyed inside it? Britain already had full market access and substantial influence over the rules.

Sovereignty is not merely the freedom to say no. It is the power to shape decisions. Brexit exchanged influence over Europe's largest market for the illusion that its rules would no longer matter to us.

text:
Well, a few things.

1) I voted Remain.

2) Yes, Leave meant different things to different people, but the main reasons behind the Leave vote are clearly identifiable.

These included:

The Customs Union
Single Market rules, including state aid rules, EAW, ECJ and the silly Vat applications.
Free Movement of People (FOM). Ironically, for many people, including many Remain voters, the issue was not necessarily free movement itself, but the policies and obligations attached to it.
The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and Common Fisheries Policy (CFP).

3) The EU bears a significant share of the responsibility for Brexit.

The EU knew that its rules and policies were creating problems in parts of the UK, particularly in working-class communities. Rather than meaningfully addressing those concerns, it continued to double down on the existing arrangements. That failure to recognise and respond to legitimate grievances helped fuel support for Leave.

4) The negotiations only made matters worse.

Rather than taking a conciliatory approach and seeking a mutually beneficial agreement that respected the British people’s decision to leave, the EU doubled down again. The Irish border became a political bargaining chip, with the negotiations creating a situation that risked the Good Friday Agreement (GFA).

This only reinforced the perception among many Leave voters that the EU was more interested in protecting its own institutional interests than reaching a pragmatic settlement.

5) In 2016, a different approach might well have produced a different result.

Had the EU offered the UK something broadly equivalent to EFTA membership, but without free movement of people, with a veto over EU laws before they could apply in the UK, and with net-zero budget contributions, I suspect that proposal would have secured a Remain vote.

Of course, there is no way to know that for certain. But it would have addressed several of the principal concerns driving the Leave campaign while preserving many of the economic benefits of closer European cooperation.

And this brings us to the present day.

Even in 2026/2027, the EU continues to insist on the same approach to free movement, despite the fact that it remains one of the most divisive issues in British politics.

That position does little to bridge the divide created by Brexit. Instead, it risks perpetuating it, making it more likely that a future UK government will seek to reverse course once again.

Ultimately, my argument is this: Brexit was not inevitable. The EU had opportunities to address the concerns that drove the Leave vote, both before the referendum and during the negotiations. Its unwillingness to compromise helped turn a politically avoidable dispute into a lasting constitutional and economic divide.

To that point the UK is now better off outside the block until such time the EU puts forward a deal that takes the big 6 off the table so to speak.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner"

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

News

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner"

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
Former Nairobi Governor Mike Sonko has placed a serious allegation on the court record. He says two of the most expensive lawyers in Kenya were paid to abandon him at the exact moment he needed them most. The advocates are Cecil Miller(@CecilMillerJr) and George Kithi. The alleged paymaster is the State House of former President Uhuru Kenyatta. The moment was his impeachment fight in December 2020, when the Nairobi County Assembly vote threatened to end his tenure at City Hall.

The claim is not new in outline. It is new in venue. For years Sonko made the accusation on social media, in videos, in captions and in leaked audio. Recently he has carried it into a courtroom, where he testifies under oath, where recordings are played and where lawyers must answer questions about money. That shift is what makes this story harder to dismiss than a social media quarrel between a client and his former counsel.

Sonko has listed specific transfers that he says occurred between February and August 2021, the months that followed his removal from office and the collapse of his defence strategy. Those dates matter. They sit in the period when the legal team that had fronted his impeachment defence was no longer standing beside him, and when his position at City Hall had already been lost.

Neither advocate has issued a detailed public answer to the State House meeting claim or to the allegation that withdrawal was exchanged for payment. Earlier denials from the lawyers, made in a different season of the dispute, do not directly address the specific transfers Sonko has now listed. Whether bank records, the recordings or further testimony will substantiate the payment claim is a question that remains before the courts.
Cecil Miller and George Kithi were not peripheral figures in the Sonko saga. They were his lead counsel. When Sonko was arrested in Voi in 2019 and arraigned on corruption charges, it was Miller who stood in court and argued for his release. Sonko and seven officials in his administration denied nineteen counts over procurement tenders worth Sh357 million. The prosecution said the money was deposited into Sonko personal accounts across different banks and different parts of the country. Miller told the court that Sonko had been assaulted during his arrest, that he had chest pains and that his life was at risk. He also dismissed the idea that the governor was a flight risk, pointing out that Sonko was arrested while going about his business. He reminded the court that the Ethics and Anti Corruption Commission had previously cleared Sonko to run for Makadara MP, Nairobi Senator and governor.
That is the relationship the present allegation damages. A client who trusted his advocates with his liberty now says those same advocates were bought off when the Nairobi County Assembly moved against him. George Kithi stood beside Sonko in the early days of the impeachment fight, a senior advocate tasked with dismantling the vote and keeping the governor in office. Sonko now says the reason Kithi left was simple and transactional.

The public record shows that the two advocates did leave. Court reporting at the time recorded that Miller and Kithi abandoned Sonko in his Sh10 million corruption case on grounds that the trial magistrate was biased. Sonko also applied for the magistrate to recuse himself. When veteran lawyer John Khaminwa later took over and himself stormed out of court over a refusal to adjourn on health grounds, reporters noted that it was the second time Sonko lawyers had walked out of the same case. The first walkout belonged to Miller and Kithi.
The official reason for the exit was alleged magistrate bias. Sonko offers a different reason. He says the exit was bought. In his telling, the lawyers collected what he called stupendous sums under the guise of legal fees and then left him exposed at the height of his impeachment proceedings. He described them as the two beleaguered lawyers who duped him in his criminal case.

No separate human intermediary caste remains, because Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 7:27; 9:12; 10:10–14) and the finished work of tetelestai ended every residual temple order. 

Every believer, by direct access through Him, continuously proclaims and receives the life that the Father still brings forth from the earth.

text:
I think the better opportunity on @CantonNetwork sits in the app layer, not just in $CC

Here’s how the loop works.

Every time someone uses the network, they burn $CC to pay for Global Synchronizer traffic. The fee is set in dollars, but it is paid by burning $CC.

The network then mints new $CC and distributes it as rewards. A large and growing share of those rewards goes to the apps that generate the traffic.

→ The more real activity an app creates, the more $CC it can earn.

→ Idle tokenized assets create almost no traffic, so they earn almost nothing.

→ Collateral that gets borrowed and reused creates repeated transactions, interest, and traffic. Those apps capture more of the rewards.

Burn helps $CC, but a meaningful part of the value flows to the apps that actually put collateral to work. 

Here are some of notable projects shipping $CC value:

1/ @AlpendHQ - native money market

– Built natively for Canton’s selective disclosure model so individual positions stay private. Access is permissioned; integrated with Loop Wallet and BitSafe; Halborn-audited.

– Live isolated markets for CC, USDCx, and CBTC. Each asset has its own pool and parameters.

– ~$2.15M available TVL and ~$631k active loans. Total supplied is roughly $2.78M, which puts overall utilization around 22–23%.

– Alpend ONE (coming) is a CC-backed debt instrument geared to $1, intended to unlock dollar liquidity without selling the underlying CC.

2/ @Broadridge DLR - the repo platform running on Canton

– $7.5T in repo volume in sep 2026 with an average daily of ~$359B.

– Live on Canton since 2023, handling intraday and cross-border repo while expanding collateral eligibility from U.S. Treasuries toward G7 securities, and now sitting inside the broader DLX platform.

– The scale demonstrates that institutions are already moving real financing and collateral workflows onto Canton rails.

– Large notional volume still needs to be mapped to actual Global Synchronizer traffic and the resulting burn versus rewards minted.

3/ @Cantex_io and @temple_ny - liquidity layer

– Cantex has crossed $300M cumulative volume (up roughly $100M since its August). It offers atomic, self-custodial swaps with Canton’s privacy model.

– Temple has passed $1B cumulative volume as the first native institutional CLOB on Canton, with daily volumes recently in the $20M+ range.

– Collateral needs liquid markets and clear prices before it can be used at scale. Cantex and Temple provide that foundation for lending protocols.

– Temple previously reported crossing 1B CC burned in Sep.

4/ Others that still forming

– @Kintsu has opened a private beta (currently on testnet) with isolated, curator-driven markets, curated vaults, and CC staking.

– @Canborsa_DEX is testing a lending prototype on DevNet that lets users supply USDCx and borrow against CC or CBTC. It already uses CC as collateral for its RWA perps.

– @Rho_Labs offers funding-rate markets that use Canton for private settlement records while executing elsewhere.

A Guide to Independent Bookstores for Cozy Readers

A good independent bookstore has its own scent: paper, coffee, raincoats, and perhaps the faint perfume of a resident cat who considers the mystery shelf her office. This guide to independent bookstores is for readers who want more than a quick transaction. It is for the person looking for a bookshop that remembers a favorite detective, keeps a chair near the window, and understands why a clever mystery and a warm animal companion can improve an afternoon.

Independent bookstores are not all alike, which is part of their charm. One may specialize in signed first editions and local history; another may have a sunny children’s corner, a packed schedule of author events, and a staff member ready to recommend three small-town whodunits before you reach the register. Finding the right one takes a little curiosity, but the reward is a reading life with more surprises, better recommendations, and a real sense of community.

## Why Independent Bookstores Feel Personal

A large retailer can offer convenience and a huge selection. An independent bookstore often offers something harder to measure: attention. Booksellers build their shelves one title at a time, guided by their own reading, conversations with customers, and knowledge of the neighborhood. The result is a store with a point of view.

For cozy mystery readers, that point of view can be especially helpful. The genre has plenty of delightful choices, from culinary capers to seaside secrets, historical puzzles, and animal-centered sleuths. A good bookseller can distinguish between a gentle mystery with little violence and a darker story that happens to have a charming cover. They may know which series has a strong sense of place, which detective grows more interesting over several books, and which new release deserves to be carried home immediately.

There is also the pleasure of browsing without an algorithm nudging every choice. A handwritten shelf card can lead you from a familiar favorite to a new author. A display about Florida writers may send you looking for a mystery set near the coast. A staff pick can be the literary equivalent of a neighbor saying, “I think you’ll enjoy this.” For readers who love character, setting, and a fair clue or two, that kind of recommendation is worth a great deal.

## How to Find an Independent Bookstore You’ll Love

Start close to home, but do not stop there. Your town may have a long-established shop tucked beside a bakery, while a neighboring community may have a newer bookstore inside a former train depot or historic house. Independent bookstores often reflect their locations, so visiting a few can feel like a small road trip with a better souvenir than a magnet.

Before you go, look for clues about the store’s personality. Do they highlight mysteries, romance, children’s books, regional authors, or used and rare books? Do they host book clubs or signings? A busy event calendar usually means the shop is deeply connected to readers and writers. If you prefer a quiet browse, a smaller shop with curated shelves may suit you best. Neither is better. It depends on whether you are seeking conversation, discovery, or a peaceful hour among the stacks.

When you walk in, give yourself permission to wander. Notice the displays near the entrance, but also venture beyond them. The mystery section may be organized by author, subgenre, or staff favorites. Look for shelf talkers, those little handwritten notes that explain why someone loved a book. They are often more useful than a star rating because they tell you what kind of reading experience to expect.

Then ask a bookseller a specific question. “I love small-town mysteries with dogs. What should I try next?” will bring more useful answers than “What’s popular?” Mention a few authors or story elements you enjoy, such as a capable amateur sleuth, a Florida setting, light romance, recipes, historical details, or a mystery with no graphic scenes. Booksellers are skilled matchmakers, but even the best detective needs a few clues.

### Give the Bookseller a Few Clues

A helpful conversation does not need to be formal. Let the bookseller know whether you are buying a stand-alone novel for a weekend or beginning a series you hope will keep you company for months. Say if you prefer a brisk plot, a slower story with atmosphere, or a narrator with plenty of humor.

It also helps to mention what you do not want. Some readers enjoy a little spooky tension; others would rather avoid it. Some want an animal sidekick but not a story where an animal is endangered. There is no wrong preference. Reading should feel inviting, not like a test you have to pass.

If a title is not on the shelf, ask whether the store can order it. Most independent bookstores can obtain a wide range of new books, and placing an order through them is a practical way to support the shop while getting the book you actually want. It may take a few days rather than arriving at your door tomorrow morning, but anticipation has its pleasures. Daisy, the canine narrator of the Doc and Daisy Mysteries, would likely call it the waiting-and-sniffing stage of the investigation.

The Moon Pie began in the early twentieth century at the Chattanooga Bakery in Tennessee, which the Mountain City Flour Mill had established around 1902 to turn surplus flour into cookies, crackers, and other baked goods. In 1917, a company salesman named Earl Mitchell was working his route in Kentucky when local coal miners described the kind of snack they wanted for long shifts underground. They asked for something substantial enough to fill them up, built around graham crackers and marshmallow, and large enough to match the size of the moon. The bakery responded with a round sandwich of two soft graham cookies enclosing a thick marshmallow layer, all dipped in chocolate and sold for a nickel. The new item quickly proved practical for workers who needed an affordable, portable source of energy that would hold up in a lunch pail.

Within a few years the Moon Pie had become a steady seller across the South. Its low price and hearty size made it a common purchase for laborers and farm families, and it paired naturally with the equally inexpensive RC Cola, forming a combination that locals treated as a simple, satisfying meal. By the late 1920s the bakery was turning out hundreds of the pies each day, and the product's longer shelf life allowed it to travel farther than many other fresh baked goods of the era. The snack's reputation as honest, working-class fare took root in country stores and roadside stands, where it was valued more for reliability than for novelty.

The Second World War carried Moon Pies well beyond the region. Soldiers received them in care packages from home, and the familiar taste of chocolate, graham, and marshmallow offered a small reminder of ordinary life. After the war the same qualities that had appealed to miners and Gls made the pies popular with growing families during the baby boom. By the late 1950s the Chattanooga Bakery had narrowed its focus almost entirely to Moon Pies, dropping most of its earlier product lines. Demand for larger portions later led to the double-decker version, which stacked an extra cookie and another layer of filling, while new flavors such as vanilla and banana expanded the original chocolate offering.

More than a century after its introduction, the Moon Pie remains a family-owned product still made in Chattanooga. The company has added mini sizes, seasonal varieties, and limited editions while preserving the basic construction that first satisfied the Kentucky miners. What began as a practical answer to a practical request has settled into the landscape of Southern foodways, recognized both as an everyday snack and as a modest emblem of the region's industrial and rural past.

**Sara Adams’ visual poetry style** is defined by her ongoing **#poetryisrain** series, which combines original free-verse poetry with her photography (or related digital images) into single contemplative pieces. The approach prioritizes accessibility, emotional resonance, and integration with PresenceCognition themes of mindful presence and resilience.[](<https://t.co/pCKSRgBXZt>)

### Core Visual Approach
- **Photography as foundation**: Images from her personal archives (Oregon landscapes, nature, light/texture studies, everyday observational scenes, and occasional abstracts or symbolic motifs) serve as the base. These are typically straightforward, mindful captures rather than heavily stylized.
- **Text integration**: Original poems are layered directly onto or presented alongside the photographs using clean, intentional typography. Subtle overlays, effects, or compositional adjustments enhance emotional impact while keeping the work readable and contemplative.
- **Format**: Primarily individual Instagram posts or small series on @djdietpepsi. Some pieces are offered as digital downloads, wallpapers, or limited prints. Many include watermarks, copyright notices, or provenance seals consistent with her broader IP practices.

### Poetic Style
Poems are free-verse, image-driven, and compressed. They rely on extended metaphors (especially rain, but also fire, storms, chains, or zero-sum imagery), sensory language, rhetorical questions, and a tone that shifts between reflective/meditative, sensual, and confrontational. The central rain metaphor frames nourishment, renewal, and gentle persistence that coexists with hardship (drawing from her CRPS experience). Phoenix and rising imagery appear regularly as symbols of resilience that does not require the original difficulty to disappear first.[](<https://t.co/8XNXJSXwTH>)

Publicly shared examples illustrate the range:
- **“DANGEROUS PEOPLE”** — Confrontational free verse warning about those who “gorge on hate” and carve the world into zero-sum terms, using storm, acid-rain, and wildfire imagery.
- **“SINCE YOU’VE BEEN AROUND”** — Sensual piece employing summer-rain imagery for a presence that leaves the speaker “drenched” yet thirstier.

### Overall Character
The style functions as quiet, shareable visual meditations that blend observational photography with personal poetry. It emphasizes emotional accessibility and thematic continuity with PresenceCognition (grounded observation, pattern recognition in nature and experience, and creative agency amid constraint). Pieces are self-published across Instagram, X, and her Blogspot archives, often treated as protected creative assets. Descriptions and examples originate primarily from her own posts and related records.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner"

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
The History of Guitar Relicing - 1980s-2026

Guitar relicing began in vintage restoration, not as a factory option. Luthiers matched new lacquer, replacement parts and hardware to older instruments; fresh repairs otherwise stood out beside decades of checking, fading and oxidation. In 1982, Scott Baxendale showed J.W. Black an artificially aged 1952 Telecaster. Black later used similar methods at Roger Sadowsky’s New York shop.

Fender commercialized this craft. In 1994, Custom Shop builder J.W. Black, independent finishing specialist Vince Cunetto and director John Page developed deliberately aged new guitars. Prototypes displayed at Winter NAMM in January 1995 launched Fender’s Relic Series. Cunetto aged Fender parts in Missouri; final assembly took place in California. Instruments from 1995-1999 became known as Cunetto-era Relics.

In 1999 Fender moved aging in-house and introduced Time Machine categories: New Old Stock, essentially unworn; Closet Classic, lightly aged; and Relic, visibly worn. Later grades distinguished subtle checking from extensive finish loss and deteriorated hardware. The Mexican-made Road Worn Series extended relicing to more affordable guitars in 2009.

Gibson developed its approach through Tom Murphy, involved in its early-1990s Historic reissues. After leaving Gibson in 1994, Murphy refined aging techniques independently. Gibson offered Murphy-aged reissues from 1999. Its Murphy Lab, launched in 2021, standardized Ultra Light, Light, Heavy and Ultra Heavy treatments, coordinating lacquer checking, fading, finish wear and hardware aging.

Boutique builders followed. Nashguitars, founded in 2003, specialized in distressed vintage-inspired instruments; Dennis Fano and others applied aging to independent designs. By the 2020s, relicing reached both premium custom shops and affordable production lines.

Worldwide relic-specific revenue and sales volumes are not publicly reported in a reliable annual series. The graph instead depicts the broader global electric-guitar market:

2018 - $2.08 billion (baseline)
2019 - $2.34 billion (+12.5%)
2020 - $2.63 billion (+12.4%)
2021 - $2.97 billion (+12.9%)
2022 - $3.34 billion (+12.5%)
2023 - $3.75 billion (+12.3%)

These year-on-year percentages are calculated from the graphic’s rounded figures, not individually verified annual market totals. The Business Research Company reported a 12.57% compound annual growth rate for 2018-2023, with the global market reaching approximately $3.75 billion in 2023. The graph’s endpoints represent an 80.3% increase across five years. Its 2028 forecast was $6.11 billion.
