text:
St. Hedwig's Acceptance of the Will of God

“At the beginning of the thirteenth century, the plateau of Upper Asia poured down a fresh torrent of barbarians, more terrible than all their predecessors. The one fragile barrier, which the Graeco-Slavonian civilization could oppose to the Mongols had been swept away by the first wave of the invasion; not one of the States formed under the protection of the Byzantine Church had any prospect for the future. But beyond this Ruthania, which had fallen into dissolution before being conquered, the Roman Church had had time to form a brave and generous people: when the hour arrived, Poland was ready. The Mongols were already inundating Silesia when, in the plains of Liegnitz, they found themselves confronted by an army of thirty thousand warriors, headed by the Duke of Silesia, Henry the Pious. The encounter was terrible; the victory remained long undecided, until at length, by the odious treason of some Ruthanian princes, it turned in favor of the barbarians. Duke Henry and the flower of the Polish knighthood was left upon the battlefield. But their defeat was equal to a victory. The Mongols retired exhausted, for they had measured their strength with the soldiers of the Latin Christianity.

It is Poland’s happy lot that at each decisive epoch in its history a Saint appears to point out the road to the attainment of its glorious destiny. Over the battlefield of Liegnitz shines the gentle figure of St. Hedwige, mother of Duke Henry the Pious. She had retired, in her widowhood, into the Cistercian monastery of Trebnitz, founded by herself. Three years before the coming of the barbarians, she had had a revelation touching the future fate of her son. She offered her sacrifice in silence; and far from discouraging the young duke, she was the first to animate him to resistance.

The night following the battle, she awoke one of her companions, and said to her: “Demundis, know that I have lost my son. My beloved son has fled from me, like a bird on the wing; I shall never see my son again in this life.” Demundis endeavored to console her; no courier had arrived from the army, and her fears were vain. “It is but too true,” replied the duchess; “but mention it to no one.”

Three days later the fatal news was confirmed. “It is the will of God,” said Hedwige; “what God wills, and what pleases him, must please us also.” And rejoicing in the Lord: “I thank thee, O my God,” said she, raising her hands and eyes to heaven, “for having given me such a son. He loved me all his life, always treated me with great respect, and never grieved me. I much desired to have him with me on earth, but I congratulate him with my whole soul, for that by the shedding of his blood he is united with thee in heaven, with thee his Creator. I recommend his soul to thee, O Lord my God.” No less an example was needed to sustain Poland under the new task it had just accepted.

At Liegnitz it had raised up again the sword of Christendom, fallen from the feeble hands of Ruthenia. It became henceforth as a watchful sentinel, ever ready to defend Europe against the barbarians. Ninety-three times did the Tartars rush upon Christendom, thirsting for blood and rapine: ninety-three times Poland repulsed them at the edge of the sword, or had the grief to see the country laid waste, the towns burnt down, the flower of the nation carried into captivity. By these sacrifices it bore the brunt of the invasion, and deadened the blow for the rest of Europe. As long as blood and tears and victims were required, Poland gave them unstintedly; while the other European nations enjoyed the security purchased by this continual immolation. (Dom Guépin, S. Josaphat et Eglise grecque unie en Pologne, Introduction.)”

(The Liturgical Year, Reading for the feast of St. Hedwig of Silesia, 1841-1875, Dom Prosper Guéranger)

"Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

The least these families deserve is the security of their loved one having PIP, especially if the parents are only on a state pension.
These families have enough to worry about, what happens when they die.
At least having financial support in place means their child won't become homeless.

🚨🇧🇷 - CENSORSHIP IN BRAZIL: Is the American big tech company META promoting censorship?

Yes: American big tech Meta has been promoting censorship of political criticism and of those in power in Brazil, especially during an election year.

The case of actress and writer Katharina Zaparoli (@abobodacorte) and her Instagram account “A Bobo da Corte” is emblematic. In September and October 2026, she used verses, theater, and allegory (without directly naming individuals) to satirize the Master Case, STF decisions, and electoral interference. The account reached nearly 430,000 followers. On October 9 it was banned. She herself attributed the takedown to mass reporting after she posted screenshots of serious threats she had received (including wishes of rape and death directed at family members) and criticized the hypocrisy of those attacking her. Meta offered no public explanation. No specific judicial order has been identified. It was platform moderation—opaque and triggered by volume of reports—against satirical content criticizing constituted power.

This is not isolated. During the electoral period, Meta has removed content, restricted reach, applied shadow bans, and taken down accounts on a large scale and with little transparency. Surveys such as the one by CTRL+Z documented more than a thousand cases of restrictions on Instagram in October 2026—bans, drops in reach, and blocks without clear justification or effective appeal mechanisms. Brazil’s Federal Public Ministry opened an investigation precisely because of this. At the same time, the company complies with orders from the TSE and STF (including rules on AI-generated content and electoral decisions), under the threat of heavy fines. Meta’s own transparency reports record thousands of content restrictions in Brazil based on local laws and court orders. There is a documented history of extraterritorial orders and of blocks targeting critics of the STF in the context of the “fake news” inquiry.

The practical result is an environment in which criticism of authorities, satire, and debate about scandals or judicial decisions in an election year become risky. Meta, a private American company, applies its Community Standards in a selective and opaque manner while simultaneously bowing to often broad Brazilian judicial orders. When the TSE ordered (as it did on October 15, 2026) that Meta refrain from restricting the distribution of political content from either Lula or Flávio and guarantee equal treatment—under a daily fine of R$ 500,000—it was an implicit recognition that the platform interferes in the debate. Accusations of bias come from both sides, depending on the moment. The issue is not the political color of the victim: it is the principle.

A healthy democracy requires free public debate, including (and especially) sharp criticism of authorities, ministers, presidents, and institutions during election periods. Satire, allegory, and the exposure of facts of public interest cannot be treated as “guideline violations” or “disinformation” at the discretion of algorithms or mass-reporting campaigns. Meta is not a state body, but by controlling the circulation of political information in Brazil and by complying with censorship orders or applying opaque moderation that silences critics of power, it functions as an agent of restriction on freedom of expression. The lack of transparency, individualized justifications, and effective remedies makes the problem worse.

Free debate is not a threat to democracy; it is its precondition. When an American big tech company decides—alone or in collaboration with judicial orders—what may be said about constituted power in an election year, the sovereignty of public debate is compromised. Defending freedom of expression requires demanding transparency, clear criteria, robust protection for political criticism, and an end to practices that, in practice, amount to censorship.

Think about this:

"Hello, I am Palestinian. 📷
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

text:
To be fair, I live in the north of England, and much of our deindustrialisation was influenced by EEC/EU policies and directives. The UK government bears responsibility too, but the EU shouldn’t be absolved of its share.

3) Free movement and double standards

Yes, the UK didn’t always apply the rules correctly. But when Cameron sought retrospective changes, he was told he couldn’t restrict benefits for EU nationals without applying the same restrictions to Brits. Under EU rules, over a million EU nationals could potentially have been eligible for deportation in 2016. Does anyone seriously believe the EU would have accepted that?

I also know from personal family experience that, in 2016, an unskilled Austrian could move freely to the UK and access certain benefits and emergency accommodation, while an Australian who was a fully qualified Consultant in Emergency Medicine was denied a visa. She wanted to come here because her husband, a Brit, was still serving in the Army. That kind of double standard understandably angered people.

4) The Irish border

As someone born in an Irish border town(Dundalk), I disagree. Did you see the video of Barnier’s team discussing it? The volume of cross-border trade was relatively small, and practical solutions deserved serious consideration. More parcels enter the EU from China than many realise without individual physical inspections. Technology has advanced further since 2016, too.

The EU helped turn the border into a political obstacle rather than finding a pragmatic solution.

5) An alternative deal

The argument that the UK could retain meaningful influence falls down when you consider how Cameron was treated. Ironically, that treatment may have helped swing the referendum towards Leave.

I understand the other 27 countries protecting their interests. But to many people in the north and Midlands, the message was essentially: We know our rules disproportionately affect your communities, but you’ll have to live with it.

That only fuelled resentment.

6) The position in 2026/2027

The EU is pursuing an associative membership arrangement with Canada that would differ substantially from EU membership, without the same obligations regarding the CAP, CFP, free movement, Customs Union, Single Market and EU Laws.

So why couldn’t the EU have negotiated a comparable bespoke arrangement for the UK?

I accept the UK and Canada aren’t identical, but the principle remains: the EU can offer differentiated relationships when it chooses to.

Brexit wasn’t solely the result of British mistakes or voters being misled on both sides of the argument. The EU made choices too, and its unwillingness to address legitimate concerns helped produce the outcome it now struggles to manage.

If a bespoke relationship is possible for Canada, why was a more flexible arrangement for the UK treated as so unacceptable?

text:
MAA KATYAYANI: from Mahishasuramardini to Chhathi Maiya

शङ्खचक्रगदाशार्ङ्गगृहीतपरमायुधे।
प्रसीद वैष्णवीरूपे नारायणि नमोऽस्तु ते॥

“O Narayani, bearer of the Shankha, Chakra, Gada and Sharnga bow, be gracious in your Vaishnavi form. Salutations to you.”

— Devi Mahatmya, 11.15, Markandeya Purana

Mahishasura had defeated the gods and seized their dominion. From their combined radiance emerged the Divine Mother. Shiva gave her his Trishul, Vishnu his Sudarshan Chakra, Indra his Vajra, and Himavan, the king of the mountains, a lion.

She slayed Mahishasura. Thus we remember her as Mahishasuramardini, the slayer of the buffalo demon.

But how did she come to be known as Katyayani?

The Skanda Purana (Nagara Khanda, 120.12–13) offers one account:

कार्तिकेयस्य कोपेन कोपे मिश्रे दिवौकसाम्।
यस्माज्जातात्र सा कन्या तस्मात्कात्यायनी स्मृता॥

“Born from Kartikeya’s anger mingled with that of the celestial beings, the maiden came to be known as Katyayani.”

The Vamana Purana (Chapter 19) preserves another account, linking her manifestation to the divine radiance gathered at Sage Katyayana’s hermitage.

Different Puranas preserve different tellings of the Goddess’s manifestation, each offering another glimpse into her divine identity.

Then we travel to Braj.

In the Shrimad Bhagavatam (10.22.4), the gopis invoke Katyayani:

कात्यायनि महामाये महायोगिन्यधीश्वरि।
नन्दगोपसुतं देवि पतिं मे कुरु ते नमः॥

“O Katyayani, O Great Goddess, grant that the son of Nanda may become my husband.”

From the cosmic battlefield to the banks of the Yamuna, the Goddess is invoked in different narratives and forms of devotion.

And in Bihar, Chhath Puja brings devotees to rivers and ponds at sunset and sunrise, offering arghya to Surya Dev and worshipping Chhathi Maiya.

The Brahmavaivarta Purana (Prakriti Khanda, Chapter 43.57–58) preserves this invocation to Shashthi Devi:

नमो देव्यै महादेव्यै सिद्ध्यै शान्त्यै नमो नमः।
सुखादायै मोक्षदायै षष्ठीदेव्यै नमो नमः॥

वरदायै पुत्रदायै धनदायै नमो नमः।
सुखदायै मोक्षदायै षष्ठीदेव्यै नमो नमः॥

“Salutations to Shashthi Devi, who brings peace and happiness, grants boons, children and prosperity, and bestows liberation.”

From Mahishasuramardini to Katyayani of Braj and Shashthi Devi of the Puranas, these sacred narratives reveal the richness of India’s Goddess traditions.

She is the power that destroys the mightiest of demons, yet the mother to whom a child turns with the simplest of prayers. She is the courage that rises when all hope seems lost, the protection we seek in our helplessness, and the divine grace before which even the mightiest must bow. In her, we see both the terrible force that annihilates evil and the boundless compassion that nurtures life. We may speak of her glory, recount her victories and seek to understand her many forms but words will always fall short of her immeasurable greatness. At her feet, there is no pride, no pretence, no surrender too small. There is only devotion.

Maa Katyayani, Mahishasuramardini, Jagat Janani, at your feet, we bow. May your strength guide us, your grace protect us, and your blessings never leave us.

Jai Maa Katyayani. 🙏

text:
The most interesting question about a flying Roadster is what it might teach us to imagine next.

In a post dated October 16 Singapore time, Elon Musk shared a short video depicting a vehicle leaving the ground. Tesla's current Roadster page describes cold-gas thrusters, additional SpaceX components, and a single-seat Rocket configuration. The page also warns: "Not approved for public road use."

That is enough to make me curious. It is not enough to treat every performance claim as independently verified.

Briefly leaving the ground and becoming a practical flying car are different achievements. A demonstration is not mass production. Production is not the same as safe, affordable, everyday use.

Those distinctions matter. So does the willingness to explore something that does not yet fit our familiar categories.

The engineering question is fascinating: what happens when techniques associated with aerospace propulsion are applied to a car?

Tesla's own description explicitly connects the project with SpaceX components. Musk's involvement in both companies makes the possibility of transferring ideas, engineering knowledge, and experience especially interesting.

Other manufacturers can hire engineers, buy components, and collaborate with aerospace companies. None of this establishes an advantage that can never be copied. Nor does putting propulsion hardware into a car guarantee a successful product.

High-pressure storage, thrust distribution, structural loads, attitude control, and safe failure handling all raise difficult questions. The eventual answer might be that a particular approach is too expensive, too complex, or unsuitable for ordinary road vehicles.

Even then, exploring it could produce engineering knowledge that matters elsewhere.

But the question I care about most is not whether this Roadster is the most advanced car. It is why someone would choose to show such a machine, and how we should judge an idea whose practical use is still uncertain.

A car that can briefly leave the ground does not automatically solve school runs, grocery trips, or rush-hour traffic. I would not assume Musk needs to be reminded of that.

Its symbolic value may be much larger than its immediate usefulness.

First, it demonstrates an ambition to work outside the established frame.

The car industry competes on range, acceleration, driver assistance, manufacturing cost, and cabin comfort. These are valuable areas of progress. But much of that competition takes place inside a familiar set of assumptions.

One of those assumptions is that a car moves through the interaction between its tires and the ground.

An unusual propulsion system asks whether that assumption has to define every possible vehicle. The answer may ultimately be yes for most everyday uses. We learn more by investigating the question than by treating the answer as settled in advance.

Second, an extraordinary prototype can change what people believe a company is capable of attempting.

A dramatic machine attracts attention. It can help recruit ambitious engineers and influence how customers, partners, and investors imagine a company's future. That is a commercial incentive, and it deserves to be acknowledged.

A memorable presentation does not make an unfulfilled promise true. Marketing and technical exploration can exist in the same project. We still need evidence for the claims being made.

Third, Musk is effective at turning a technical ambition into a story that people can picture.

Reusable rockets. A journey to Mars. Humanoid robots. A car that leaves the ground.

These are very different projects, at different stages, with different records of success and uncertainty. Their shared power as stories does not give them the same technical credibility.

But a sufficiently ambitious goal can attract people who otherwise would not have joined the work. It can bring time, capital, and technical effort to a problem that previously seemed too remote to attempt.

The story opens a possibility. Engineering and real-world use must determine whether that possibility becomes valuable.

This brings me to two reactions that can coexist in any of us:

"I didn't know that was possible."

"What would anyone use it for?"

Both questions have a place. I worry when the second becomes an immediate veto on the first.

Does a new technology have to solve a mature commercial problem on the day it appears in order to deserve exploration?

The Wright brothers' first controlled, powered flights were very short. They did not immediately compete with trains on price or ships on cargo capacity. Their significance included establishing a capability that could then be developed.

Early electronic computers also had concrete purposes, including demanding scientific and military calculations. They were not useless machines. But those initial purposes did not exhaust what computing would eventually become.

The useful lesson is not that nobody understood those inventions. It is that an invention's first application may reveal only a small part of its eventual possibilities.

Sometimes a technical achievement first changes our understanding of what can be done. The surrounding uses, infrastructure, economics, and expectations develop afterward.

That possibility makes me think of Zhuangzi's story of the enormous gourd in the opening chapter of the Zhuangzi, often translated as "Free and Easy Wandering."

Huizi tells Zhuangzi that he grew an enormous gourd. He found it unsuitable for holding water and awkwardly large for a dipper. He judged it useless and destroyed it.

Zhuangzi's response is to question Huizi's way of using something so large. Why not make it into a flotation device and use it to wander on the water?

The gourd has not changed. The frame of reference has.

Huizi begins with the familiar job of a gourd. When this unusual gourd cannot perform that job conveniently, he concludes that it has no value.

Zhuangzi notices the unusual property itself: its size. What could that property make possible that an ordinary gourd could not do?

I see a useful parallel with the Roadster discussion.

If the only question is whether it makes today's commute cheaper or easier, a brief departure from the ground may offer very little. That is a reasonable conclusion about that particular use case.

It does not settle every question about what we might learn from building it, or where the underlying techniques could lead.

Why must every unusual machine first prove that it can do the familiar machine's job better?

There is an important limit to this analogy.

Zhuangzi's story does not prove that every apparently impractical invention will become useful. It certainly does not establish that every ambitious product claim should be believed.

The Roadster's propulsion approach could turn out to have little value outside a small, expensive niche. It could face costs, risks, maintenance requirements, or demand constraints that prevent wider use.

Curiosity does not remove those constraints. It gives us a reason to investigate them rather than assume we already know the result.

That is how I understand the "usefulness of the useless."

Sometimes the limitation lies in our current understanding of how to use something. A familiar definition of value can make an unfamiliar capability difficult to see.

Existing demand is essential when we build products for people who need something today. But it cannot be our only way of evaluating every experiment. Some possibilities become understandable only after a capability exists for people to encounter and adapt.

There is also a deeper question here: why do we feel such pressure to explain the usefulness of everything immediately?

Education should lead to a good job. A subject should lead to a marketable skill. Work should produce measurable returns. A startup should quickly explain its business model. Even a hobby is often asked to justify the time spent on it.

There are good reasons for this discipline.

A family with limited resources has to make choices. A company has obligations to employees and customers. Someone carrying real responsibilities cannot put every resource into an uncertain experiment.

I would never dismiss those constraints as a failure of imagination.

But if every person and institution applies the same immediate-return test to every activity, we narrow the kinds of progress we are willing to attempt.

We can become extremely good at improving established things: reducing the cost of a car, extending a phone's battery life, or making a software workflow more efficient.

Those improvements matter. They also differ from exploring a direction whose eventual application is still unclear.

Exploration often includes a long period in which the honest answer to "What is this for?" is incomplete.

Some experiments will fail. Some will remain specialized. Some may create tools or knowledge that become useful in ways their creators did not anticipate.

The fact that we cannot predict which outcome will occur is a reason to set appropriate budgets, milestones, and evidence requirements. It is not a reason to demand that every experiment already possess the certainty of a mature product.

We benefit today from earlier work whose full value could not be calculated at its beginning. That does not mean every speculative project deserves unlimited resources. It means uncertainty and worthlessness are different judgments.

This is why I think the Roadster is worth discussing even if it never becomes a successful everyday vehicle.

Its commercial promises should be tested. Its engineering should be scrutinized. Its safety claims deserve especially demanding evidence.

At the same time, I want to keep two questions separate:

"You say you achieved this. What exactly did you demonstrate, and what evidence supports it?"

"Even if you achieved it, what might it be useful for?"

The first is a question about facts. We should be rigorous about it.

The second is a question about possibilities and value. We should ask it seriously, with room for answers we do not yet have.

I can question a company's timetable, challenge a claim, or doubt a product's commercial prospects while still valuing the attempt to explore a new capability.

Finally, I come back to Zhuangzi.

One way to contrast Confucian and Zhuangzian concerns is that the former helps us think about responsibilities and relationships within society, while the latter invites us to question standards we have come to treat as obvious.

That is a simplified comparison. Confucian thought is not a rejection of imagination, and Zhuangzi was not a modern technology entrepreneur.

Still, as tools for thinking, both concerns matter. We need people who can solve the problems in front of us, and people willing to ask questions for which we do not yet have a practical answer.

A society cannot live on speculative possibilities alone. It also loses something if every possibility is judged only by the uses we already recognize.

Huizi looks at the enormous gourd and asks why it cannot serve as his familiar container.

Zhuangzi looks at the same gourd and asks what its unusual size might make possible.

The next time an unfamiliar technology appears, I want to leave room for a question alongside "What is it for?"

"I didn't know we could do that. What could come next?"

Sometimes an invention's first contribution is to show us that the world contains another possibility.

Avalanche of G.O.P. Cash Keeps the Party Competitive Despite Its Problems

16OCT2026
By Theodore Schleifer and Matt Zdun
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/RdrzfzpuXD

Republican Senate and House candidates are being out-raised by their Democratic rivals, but the party has received a huge boost from groups tied to Elon Musk and President Trump.

The political fund-raising picture in the final month of the midterm elections is something of a Rorschach test.

If you’re a Democrat, new election filings show many of the party’s Senate and House nominees raising more than their Republican rivals. This campaign cash is the most important money in politics, because candidates can control it directly and buy ads at cheaper rates.

If you’re a Republican, the same filings show that the G.O.P. has a significant advantage in money from super PACs and other outside groups tied to Elon Musk, President Trump and the party’s big donors. In many races, this edge has allowed the party to club Democrats with advertising even though Republican groups have to pay more for ads.

In fact, both of these perceptions are true. And for Republicans, the ability to hold their own — at least — in the midterm money fight is a rare bright spot as the party faces a gloomy political environment. This financial resilience has allowed Republicans to put up a robust defense of the Senate, in particular, as they try to keep control of Congress.

A bonanza of Federal Election Commission filings on Thursday offers a view of how much every federal candidate in the country raised and spent from July through September, as well as the finances of many of the outside groups supporting them. Even more filings for those groups will land next week.

Here are seven takeaways from the filings:
Democratic Senate contenders have raked in cash.
In eight of the Senate races expected to be most competitive in November, Democrats have raised more money this year through their main campaign committees than their Republican challengers, the filings show.

No Democrat raised money like James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas. His campaign hauled in a staggering $114 million from January through September, about $100 million more than his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, raised.

The Democratic edge was also striking in Kansas, a surprising Senate battleground. Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee, raised $13.4 million in the first nine months of the year, roughly six times as much as his Republican opponent, Senator Roger Marshall. (In just the third quarter, Mr. Hamilton brought in nearly $10 million, compared with Mr. Marshall’s roughly $800,000.)

The money will help Democrats’ effort to take back the chamber, but many of the seats the party needs to flip are in solidly red states — and Republicans have more money from outside groups.

Democratic House candidates also have an edge.

A similar story played out in the House, with Democrats out-raising Republicans in 38 of the 42 races currently considered competitive.

One of Democrats’ largest fund-raising advantages was in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, a tossup race that was thrown into turmoil when the incumbent Republican, Representative Chuck Edwards, dropped his re-election bid amid sexual harassment allegations. The Democratic nominee, Jamie Ager, raised about $4.6 million in the first nine months of the year, versus about $350,000 for the Republican nominee, Jennifer Balkcom.

But Republicans are winning with outside money.

Despite Democratic candidates’ fund-raising strength, party leaders have expressed profound concerns that Republicans hold a financial advantage.

Why? Because Republican super PACs and other outside groups have raised and spent far more than their Democratic counterparts.

That helps explain why Republicans are currently slated to have an advantage of about $650 million in general-election advertising, according to a review of past and future ad reservations across federal and state races by AdImpact, a media-tracking firm. (Ad reservations are fluid and are likely to change before Nov. 3.)

The main super PAC for Republican Senate candidates, the Senate Leadership Fund, out-raised its Democratic rival by about $122 million this quarter. The Republican group also revealed on Thursday that it had been the sole funder of super PACs backing several of the party’s battleground candidates: Mr. Paxton in Texas and Senators Pete Ricketts of Nebraska, Susan Collins of Maine and Dan Sullivan of Alaska.

The parties’ main House super PACs appear to be in a more competitive financial fight, according to advertising data. The main House Republican group raised $94 million in the last quarter, but its Democratic counterpart will not disclose its finances until Tuesday.

Nationally, some of the gap between Republicans and Democrats can be traced to three Trump-affiliated super PACs, which have combined to spend over $210 million on advertising, according to AdImpact. These groups’ finances will not be revealed until Tuesday, either.

If Paxton wins in Texas, he owes Elon Musk big time.

For weeks, it wasn’t quite clear how national Republicans were able to spend close to $160 million to help Mr. Paxton, who has long struggled to raise money and faces the single strongest Democratic midterm fund-raiser, Mr. Talarico.

The answer was Elon Musk.

The filings on Thursday suggested that the world’s richest person indirectly funded Texas PAC, the biggest-spending super PAC backing Mr. Paxton. He did it by sending enormous sums to the main Republican Senate super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, which had long resisted spending on behalf of Mr. Paxton. The group feared that doing so in a pricey state like Texas would divert resources from other competitive Senate races.

But Mr. Musk, the new filings show, made two huge donations to the Senate Leadership Fund: $75 million on Sept. 9 and $83 million on Sept. 23. After each one, the Senate Leadership Fund sent an identical amount the next day to Texas PAC — which had no other donors through Sept. 30.

So even as Republicans worry that Mr. Paxton could do the unthinkable and lose to a Democrat in Texas, Mr. Musk appears to have given him a better chance of hanging on.

Republican megadonors are still giving generously.

Democrats have their own big donors. Two super PACs funded by the Soros family entered October with about $174 million on hand. And two of the party’s biggest donors, the Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and his wife, Cari Tuna, put $16 million into the midterms fight, the new filings show.

But most of the biggest midterm donors are supporting Republicans.

Dick Uihlein, a Midwest-based billionaire industrialist, put a staggering $67 million more into his super PAC last quarter, which in turn gave $15 million to the anti-tax Club for Growth.

Jeff Yass, a hedge fund investor, gave $10 million more to a super PAC backing Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio. Mr. Yass has now spent $30 million backing Mr. Ramaswamy.

Mr. Yass and Mr. Uihlein have each now donated well over $100 million this cycle to federal political committees.

And then there’s Mr. Musk, who backed a few Republican groups beyond S.L.F., including about $89 million he gave to his own super PAC. In sum, Mr. Musk disclosed on Thursday a total of about $289 million in third-quarter contributions to federal committees, making him the biggest known midterm donor.

Mysterious dark-money groups are everywhere.

Several political groups made disclosures on Thursday that did not actually disclose much of anything about the true origins of their cash.

That is a reflection of the rise of dark money, with both parties relying more heavily on nonprofit groups that are not legally required to report the identities of their donors.

A lot of Democratic money traces its way back to super PACs with names like Government That Works PAC, Your Community PAC, and United Futures. Those groups, in turn, got their cash from a battery of liberal dark-money nonprofit groups.

The main Democratic Senate super PAC raised a majority of its money in the third quarter from dark-money groups, according to an analysis of its donors.

On the Republican side, a super PAC called Defend Us PAC, which is spending against Mr. Talarico in Texas, said it raised $8.3 million last quarter. Of that, $6 million came from a group called the American Prosperity Caucus Inc., which does not appear in state records in Georgia, where it says it is based.

And most of the money raised by a super PAC backing Senator Jon Husted of Ohio, $5 million, came from a dark-money nonprofit in Delaware nonprofit that was created in May.

There are plenty of other examples. Confused? In modern campaigns, that’s the point.

There were other revelations, too.

Here are a few other things that caught our attention in the third quarter:

Democrats are getting $38 million worth of digital help at the last minute from a new super PAC. That group, Lower Costs Now, received that much in late September.

Trump administration officials continue to be major donors to political causes even while serving in government. The ambassador to Britain, Warren Stephens, and the White House chief design officer, Joe Gebbia — both of whom are billionaires — each donated over $1 million to Republican efforts.

The Republican Governors Association seems particularly invested in electing Zach Lahn to lead Iowa. The group’s super PAC sent $12.5 million to his campaign, an investment it did not make for any other candidate.

A super PAC for the sports-betting industry, Win for America, has now raised $82 million this cycle, making it one of the wealthiest industry interest groups in the midterms. About half of that sum has come from the company DraftKings.

About the data

Fund-raising figures in the graphics include total contributions to each candidate’s main campaign committee, not including refunded contributions and contributions that candidates made to themselves. The totals also include transfers to the main campaign committee from other committees.

text:
Speech at the European Conference of Presidents of Parliament on "Renewing the rules-based international order: the role of parliaments in addressing and responding to contemporary crises"

The rules-based international order does not erode by itself. It erodes when international institutions that embody our shared values and rules are weakened. International institutions are only as strong as the trust and commitment behind them. Their authority stems from legitimacy: the belief that rules apply equally to all; that decisions rest on facts and fair procedure rather than political convenience; and that no one is above them.

When the legitimacy fades, no treaty text can restore it.

And whydo these institutions weaken when the international order continues to crumble before our eyes? Too often, they weaken because they are instrumentalized. The growing practice of leveraging international organizations and weaponizing them to advance politically motivated and perception-based positions is concerning. When some states and political groupings use institutions to advance narrowly defined political agendas, to pressure some members while shielding others, or to turn monitoring and assessment into political tools, they hollow out these institutions’ core meaning. An institution used as an instrument is no longer an institution; it is an extension of someone's interest.

PACE’s treatment of Georgia is a very good example of this. In October 2024, Georgia held parliamentary elections. OSCE/ODIHRassessed them in detail, found them competitive and generally expressing the will of the people. The OSCE / ODIHR Report describes strengths and weaknesses and offers a path forward. Meanwhile, the Council of Europe delegation, made up of members of PACE, chose a diametrically different course.

Disagreeingwith OSCE / ODIHR, PACE prepared a report that questioned the results of elections. Even though Georgia’s international partners, including the EU, emphasized that the OSCE/ODIHR report would be decisive in evaluating the elections, this promise was disregarded by some European governments and political groupings. Based on this near-fraudulent Report, PACE adopted a resolution that, as a matter of fact, rejected the recognition of a democratically elected Georgian Parliament. After almost two years, all allegations and pretenses advanced by PACE proved to be wrong, unfounded, and factually false. Nevertheless, PACE refuses to admit its deliberate mistake, while the process entered the impasse.

Thus,the organization that we joined for safeguarding our sovereignty and popular democracy, persists in violating Georgian people’s democratic will, and, thus its freedom. PACE should return to the very foundations of the international law, for the sake of which it is created to uphold. The situation where democracy, sovereignty, human rights, and freedom have become formal slogans only is not tolerable. The end result of this process is loss of trust and evisceration of the Organization.

Parliamentary diplomacy is an important tool that can contribute to the support of rules-based order but it is crucial to clearly differentiate dialogue from interference. Dialogue means exchanging views, sharing best practice and holding all states to common standards that all members have freely accepted. Restoring the rules-based order, therefore, begins with renewing the integrity of the institutions and organizations that sustain it. Georgia remains committed to this task.

text:
RC Cola, originally known as Royal Crown Cola, emerged in the early twentieth century as a distinctive challenger in the growing American soft drink market. Claud
A. Hatcher, a pharmacist in Columbus, Georgia, developed the formula in 1905 after a dispute with a Coca-Cola bottler left him seeking an independent alternative.
Initially marketed as Chero-Cola, the beverage gained a foothold through regional bottling agreements and a flavor profile that emphasized a slightly sweeter, less acidic taste compared to its larger rivals. By the 1920s and 1930s, the brand had shortened its name to RC Cola and expanded its distribution, building a reputation for quality and consistency that appealed particularly to consumers in the South.

The company distinguished itself through a series of practical innovations that reshaped packaging and product variety. RC Cola became the first major soft drink to be sold in aluminum cans during the 1950s, offering convenience that glass bottles could not match. It also introduced Diet Rite in 1958, one of the earliest nationally marketed diet colas, years before larger competitors followed suit. These advances reflected a willingness to experiment with both containers and formulations, helping the brand maintain relevance even as national advertising budgets for Coca-Cola and Pepsi grew far larger. The result was a product line that blended traditional cola character with forward-looking adjustments to consumer preferences for lighter options and portable packaging.

Despite never matching the scale of the two dominant brands, RC Cola cultivated a loyal following rooted in regional identity and value. In many Southern communities it remained a staple at gatherings, roadside stands, and family meals, often preferred for its bold sweetness and the sense that it offered an underdog alternative. The brand's marketing frequently leaned on straightforward appeals to taste and affordability rather than elaborate lifestyle campaigns. Over time this approach fostered a durable, if smaller, customer base that valued familiarity and local connections, allowing RC Cola to persist through decades of industry consolidation and shifting ownership.

Today RC Cola continues as a recognizable name under the umbrella of larger beverage companies, still available in many markets and occasionally revived in limited or nostalgic editions. Its history illustrates how a regional formula, timely packaging changes, and consistent flavor can sustain a brand for more than a century even without the resources of the industry's biggest players. The drink's endurance underscores the importance of early innovation and regional roots in an otherwise concentrated soft drink landscape.

text:
None of this $74.3M Navy order is Navy money.

Canada funded $38.4M and Japan $35.4M. The Coast Guard covered the last $0.5M. The Oct. 9 order is for production of SEWIP (V)6 electronic warfare systems from Lockheed Martin.

Both countries bought through Foreign Military Sales, where the US government does the buying for an ally. So their order went onto the Navy's own fixed-price contract. The work happens at 2 US sites. Liverpool, NY does 78% of it and Lansdale, PA does 22%. All of the allied money was committed at award.

Nine days earlier, on Sept. 30, the Navy put $209.0M of its own funds on that contract for the same systems. Across the two fall orders, roughly one dollar in four came from Canada and Japan. Both are expected to be completed by Sept. 2029.

Canada and Japan are funding part of the same US production line the Navy buys from.

Naval Sea Systems Command runs the contract. It dates to 2020, when it was open to any bidder and drew 2 offers. With options it could reach $1.71B.

Neither notice says how many systems either order buys or which ships get them.

text:
Warren Buffett traveled about 10 hours to a Harvard Business School interview near Chicago

It took 10 minutes. The interviewer looked at him and said forget it

Asked by David Rubenstein if he’s ever run into that man since, Buffett said no. He needs protection now

He hadn’t even wanted to go to college. His father did, and Buffett always wanted to please him. He wanted to quit Wharton after the first year, stayed a second only because his dad asked, then finished in Nebraska in three years. Harvard was his father’s idea too

The rejection sent him to a library in Omaha, leafing through catalogs. That’s where he noticed that Benjamin Graham and David Dodd, whose book he had read so many times he could recite it better than they could, were teaching at Columbia

He wrote to Dodd and told him he’d thought they were dead. Now that he knew they were alive, he’d really like to come. He got in. Later he offered to work for Graham for nothing, and eventually got to work for his hero

When he moved back to Omaha, he had about $175,000 and thought that was all he’d ever need. He even considered law school instead. His first partnership started with $105,000 from seven people, and $100 from him

Berkshire’s first annual meeting had 12 people, and that counted his aunt Katie and uncle Fred. Today about 40,000 show up

One 10-minute no from Harvard. And the rest of the story only happened because of where it sent him

He’s one of 10 people in the article below who almost didn’t make it. Son lost $70 billion. Schultz heard no 242 times. Jobs was pushed out of his own company

Persistence or luck? ↓

On 15th October, reports about a possible Tesla takeover quoted 0.7 SpaceX shares for every Tesla share. At that day’s closing prices, you would receive $104.03 for a share worth $362.44.

That is a 71% discount. Neither company has announced such an offer. 

SpaceX closed at $148.62. To match Tesla’s closing price, you would need about 2.44 SpaceX shares, before any takeover premium or change in share structure.

The 0.7 figure closely matches Tesla’s reported $1.5 trillion valuation divided by SpaceX’s $2.1 trillion. Those are the values of entire companies. SpaceX has more shares, so that calculation cannot tell you what one Tesla share should receive.

The reports attribute the scenario to Barclays. It remains unclear whether the bank used 0.7 as a per-share ratio or whether that wording entered through later coverage. 

Tesla’s Roadster demonstration in Texas that day already showed the companies working together. Production is targeted for 2028. A merger would have to add benefits beyond cooperation already happening. 

Any bid would need to explain how many SpaceX shares Tesla owners receive and why issuing them benefits existing SpaceX owners.

text:
If you hold Tesla $TSLA then a takeover should pay you more than the market does. This week's reports put a Barclays estimate at about 0.7 SpaceX shares per Tesla share, which would hand you $104 of SpaceX stock for a Tesla share that closed Thursday at $362.44.

HERE IS THE MATH 

@SpaceX closed at $148.62, so a swap at market prices takes 2.44 SpaceX shares per Tesla share, before any premium. The 0.7 divides company values instead. "The math follows the market caps," @unusual_whales writes, $1.5 trillion over $2.1 trillion. SpaceX is worth more, but each share costs less, because it has 13.18 billion shares to Tesla's 3.95 billion.

THE 40%

TradingKey says 0.7 would leave Tesla holders about 40% of the combined company, and Barclays puts Elon at about 37%. Both figures only work at market prices. At 0.7 per share, Tesla stockholders would own about 17%. I'm not sure whether Barclays wrote 0.7 per share or the reports did...

THE ROADSTER

Tesla's epic flying Roadster, shown Thursday at a SpaceX site in Texas, flips using thrusters built with SpaceX engineers. That took no merger. Elon says production begins in 2028, and Morningstar's Seth Goldstein calls it Tesla's new halo car but expects about 2,000 a year, against 1.6 million Teslas sold last year.

THE ODDS

Barclays sees a possible announcement before Tesla's annual meeting, expected by 6th December 2026. No deal has been announced or filed so far... @Polymarket puts an official announcement at about 25% by 31st December and 63% by the end of 2027.

The reports rightly call 0.7 an estimate, not an offer, and read per share, it would still value your share 71% below Thursday's close.

If SpaceX bids, should Tesla holders hold out for more than market value, or should SpaceX holders oppose any premium? thoughts? ...

text:
**Tesla’s Roadster Demo Is a Kitty Hawk Moment for Flying Cars**

On October 15, 2026, at a SpaceX facility in McGregor, Texas, Tesla’s second-generation Roadster did something no production car has done before. Using a fan suction system capable of pulling roughly 2 g and cold-gas thrusters fed by roughly 250 kg of compressed air stored in carbon-overwrapped pressure vessels, the car drove upside-down along a curved ramp, launched off the end, flipped in mid-air, and landed under thruster control. It also hopped over a line of @Tesla  vehicles, including a Semi. @elonmusk  and Tesla’s vehicle engineering lead called it proof that “flying cars are real.”

Critics immediately noted the obvious: these were short, staged hops and flips, not sustained flight. The demonstrator carried no driver, the tanks empty quickly, production is targeted for 2028 (after years of delay), and any real airborne use would face FAA classification and airspace rules. The base Performance version lacks thrusters entirely; only the invite-only Rocket variant is described as “air ready.”

That criticism misses the historical parallel. On December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk, Orville Wright flew the Flyer for 12 seconds and 120 feet—shorter than a modern airliner’s wingspan. The machine pitched, the landing was abrupt, and the day’s longest flight reached only 59 seconds and 852 feet. Contemporary observers could (and did) dismiss it as a brief hop rather than “real” flight. Yet it was the first time a heavier-than-air machine rose under its own power, stayed under control, and landed at the same altitude it started. That short, imperfect demonstration marked the before-and-after of aviation.

The Roadster’s demonstration is analogous. It proves a production-oriented electric car can leave the ground, reorient, and return safely using technology already proven in rocketry (SpaceX cold-gas thrusters) and motorsport (downforce fans). Steps in transportation have always been incremental: the Wright Flyer did not become a passenger airliner overnight, and this Roadster will not replace highways tomorrow. But the principle has been shown in hardware, not simulation. Once the concept works in a car-shaped vehicle that can also drive on roads, the path to practical vertical or short-hop mobility becomes an engineering and regulatory problem rather than a physics one.

Transportation has a clear before and after. Before Kitty Hawk, sustained powered flight was speculation. After it, the trajectory was set. The same logic applies here. Whether the 2028 production cars offer only brief thruster-assisted hops or evolve into longer flights, the October 15 demonstration moves “flying car” from pure concept to demonstrated hardware. Small steps, not giant leaps, are how transportation changes forever.

The Soul of Sound: How AI Challenges Human Expression in MusicIvan NikolicOct 29, 2025📷StableDiffusion

In This Article:
The Illusion of CreativityCopyright in CrisisThe Educational MirageWhy This Fight Matters5 Key Takeaways
In an age where artificial intelligence can mimic the voice of Freddie Mercury or reimagine pop hits as synthwave ballads, a new frontier has emerged — one that blurs the line between innovation and erosion. While AI offers undeniable benefits in technical domains, its intrusion into creative arts, especially music, raises urgent questions. Not just about copyright, but about culture, education, and the very soul of artistic expression.

📷        13 GIFs Every Music Major Will Relate To     

📷        Here's The Reason Why You Should Expand Your Music Taste     

The Illusion of Creativity
📷

AI-generated music is often marketed as “artistic” or “educational.” But what does it really teach?

That style can be replicated without understanding.
That emotion can be simulated without feeling.
That effort can be bypassed with a prompt.
For young creators, this sets a dangerous precedent. Why learn to play guitar when an algorithm can do it faster? Why study harmony when AI can generate chord progressions in seconds? The risk isn’t just laziness — it’s the loss of depth, discipline, and the tactile joy of creation.
I have listened to several AI-generated music covers. My initial reaction was one of considerable impressiveness, particularly regarding the reimagining of classic pop hits in diverse genres with novel arrangements. Here is one good example a-ha — Take On Me

However, after engaging with several such Ai generated song covers, a sense of emotional detachment emerged, attributable to the perceived absence of human artistry and genuine sentiment, resulting in a technically flawless yet ultimately soulless auditory experience.

Copyright in Crisis

📷

What does the copyright law say about AI generated music, especially in field of music covers. Who is liable for copyright in this case, AI developers, people who used AI to generate music or people who published it on music platforms?

Recent lawsuits show that the music industry is pushing back hard:
Universal, Sony, and Warner sued AI music platforms Suno and Udio in 2024 for allegedly training their models on copyrighted songs without permission Ars Technica The Lyon Firm.

They’re seeking up to $150,000 per infringed song, arguing that the AI outputs resemble famous tracks and voices (e.g., Mariah Carey, Michael Jackson).

These lawsuits target the developers of the AI tools — but they raise broader questions:The legal gray area is training data. Courts haven’t yet ruled definitively on whether using copyrighted songs to train AI counts as infringement or fair use Sites at USC.

But who’s liable?
Role
Legal Risk

Why

AI Developers
✅ High

For training on copyrighted material without licenses.
Users

⚠️ Moderate

If they intentionally recreate protected works.
Publishers/Platforms

✅ High
For distributing infringing content.

The grey area lies in training data. Courts haven’t yet ruled definitively on whether using copyrighted songs to train AI counts as infringement or fair use. Meanwhile, AI-generated works themselves aren’t eligible for copyright unless a human provides substantial creative input — leaving them in legal limbo.

The Educational Mirage
📷

Some argue that AI music helps people learn genres, production styles, or vocal techniques. But this “education” often lacks context. It’s like learning to paint by watching a printer — technically impressive, but creatively hollow.
True musical education involves:

Struggle and iteration: Learning through mistakes.
Emotional connection: Expressing what words can’t.

Cultural lineage: Understanding the roots of sound.

AI shortcuts bypass all of this. And in doing so, they risk flattening the rich terrain of human creativity into a sterile landscape of algorithmic mimicry.
Why This Fight Matters

This isn’t just about music. It’s about the future of art, storytelling, and human expression. If we allow machines to dominate creative spaces, we risk turning culture into content — optimized, monetized, and devoid of soul.

We must ask: Do we want a world where art is made by machines, or one where machines help humans make better art?

5 Key Takeaways
AI-generated music blurs the line between innovation and erosion in the creative arts
AI-generated music raises questions about copyright, culture, education, and artistic expression

AI-generated music can replicate style without understanding, simulate emotion without feeling, and bypass effort with a prompt
AI-generated music sets a dangerous precedent for young creators by potentially leading to a loss of depth, discipline, and joy of creation

text:
Your arguement relies on several standard logical fallacies.

1. Hasty generalization: You treat the current (perceived) failure of billionaires to "help people right now" as sufficient grounds to conclude they will never do so under future conditions of AI-driven abundance and robotics. This ignores the possibility that incentives, productive capacity, or political arrangements can and will change, in directions that we cannot predict or model.

2. Ad hominem (circumstantial) / poisoning the well: Rather than addressing the substance of arguments for technological abundance or "universal high income," you focuse on Musk’s alleged personal motives ("not going to care," "ultimate goal is to suck all the resources"). The source’s supposed character or interests are used to dismiss the idea itself. Which his ridiculous and casual flawed at best, and ignorant at worst. 

3. Straw man: You attribute to Musk the specific claim that UBI is merely a "carrot" offered so people "trust him and not uprise." When Musk’s own public statements have framed high income or abundance as a predicted byproduct of extreme productivity gains from AI and robotics, not as a political sop to suppress unrest. We don't live in Victorian France. 

4. Slippery slope: You chain unproven steps, robots + extreme wealth → indifference to the population → total resource extraction from Earth → permanent abandonment for a Mars colony populated only with "his tech." No necessary causal link is shown between successive stages. This is cognitive bias on your part and is ignoring all of the actual evidence in front of you to the opposite. 

5. Appeal to ignorance / argument from incredulity: "Nothing is in place right now" and the rhetorical question about which governments are actively implementing UBI are used to conclude that it "ain’t going to happen."

Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Absence of full-scale implementation today is treated as evidence of future impossibility, rather than as a status of current policy.

6. False dilemma: Your framing presents a binary (billionaires either help now or the future is bleak/abandonment) while excluding intermediate possibilities such as partial income supports, changing tax regimes, productivity gains that reduce scarcity, or multi-planetary settlement as risk mitigation rather than pure extraction and flight.

All of these combine to convert speculation about motives and timelines into an asserted conclusion, a conclusion that is highly cynical and devoid of any attempt allow others to pursue the potentials.

text:
Until recently, when a Massachusetts shellfish warden needed to know how much rain had fallen overnight before deciding whether to close a shellfishing area, the process might look something like this: call a local resident who happened to own a rain gauge, ask for the measurement, write it down, and use that number to make the call. Heavy rain may cause a closure due to stormwater runoff that can carry pollutants from land to water. If the area closed, the public found out the same low-tech way: a paper notice at the boat ramp, a phone call, or word passed along at the marina.

It’s a system built on trust between neighbors, but it doesn’t scale particularly well. According to the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries’ 2024 Annual Report, Massachusetts shellfisheries yielded an ex-vessel value of over $441 million. This number includes shellfish spread across 738 classified growing areas along the coast that fall under a tangle of overlapping state and municipal jurisdictions. Add in thousands of recreational permit holders, and the old system starts to show its age.

With support from MIT’s Abdul Latif Jameel Water and Food Systems Lab (J-WAFS), MIT Sea Grant researchers have spent the past several years trying to close the gap between the data that exist and the data people can actually use. The effort was proposed to J-WAFS by Michael Triantafyllou, the Henry L. and Grace Doherty Professor in Ocean Science and Engineering and director of MIT Sea Grant, under the title “Cloud-Based Data Applications for Streamlining Natural Resource Management.” 

The original aim of the proposal was to build a web-based system to help decision-making among managers and their stakeholders in order to support productivity of shellfisheries, safe human consumption, and vitality of coastal economies. The team wanted the platform to be scalable enough to serve the entire decision-making pipeline, from the state agency managing hundreds of growing areas down to an individual permit holder deciding whether it’s worth the drive to the water that day. 

The result is a platform called Seashell. The team describes it as sitting at the intersection of big data, natural resource management, and what’s often called the blue economy — the sustainable use of ocean and coastal resources for economic growth — a phrase increasingly common in state and federal policy circles, and one Massachusetts has staked real ground on. Food security is a large part of the equation too. Many of these towns don’t just issue permits for sport; these areas are open so residents have shellfish to eat. When permit holders can trust a platform to tell them, in real time, whether an area is safe to harvest, that’s not just convenience. It’s local food supply staying reliable.

An old bottleneck, a new pipeline

The project’s origins trace back to 2020, when MIT Sea Grant Research Scientist Carolina Bastidas and her colleagues built a shellfish restoration webpage and noticed that propagation data was scattered and often misrepresented. Propagation isn’t a minor detail; it’s how many coastal towns support food security for residents, a fact that came into sharper focus during the Covid-19 pandemic, when recreational shellfishing demand rose sharply enough that some towns limited permit sales just to protect their beds.

That early work led to an informal working group with the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries (DMF) and towns of Falmouth, Mashpee, and Nantucket well before any formal funding existed. “We already had engagement,” says Ben Bray, geospatial applications developer at MIT. “We already had a very real starting point.” 

By the time J-WAFS awarded the team a seed grant in 2022, letters of support from DMF and all three towns were already in hand, each describing the same underlying problem: a lack of an efficient, shared way to track and communicate shellfishing area status.

Bray’s path to this work goes back two decades. He joined MIT Sea Grant in 2005 to help build an internal grant management system, and the job pulled him toward an idea he’d recently encountered in Thomas Friedman’s book “The World Is Flat”: that data tend to sit stranded on disconnected “islands,” reachable only through the right application programming interface (API).

The underlying architecture reflects that same philosophy of connecting, rather than replacing, existing systems. Seashell runs on a PostgreSQL database and Amazon Web Services cloud infrastructure, designed from the outset to be exportable — towns or states that want to run it on their own servers can do so. Rather than asking DMF or municipalities to abandon the tools they already use, the system pulls in data through APIs from a long list of sources: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration tide stations, satellite feeds for sea surface temperature and chlorophyll-a, local weather networks, and DMF’s own geographic information system.

Built with towns, not for them

If Seashell has a defining trait, it’s that the towns using it had a hand in shaping nearly every piece of it. In 2023, the research team ran a regional assessment of the Massachusetts shellfishing community that drew responses from more than 312 people, 122 of whom volunteered for follow-up focus groups. In 2025, dedicated focus groups for both the public and administrative interfaces — described by Bastidas as involving anywhere from one to a handful of participants at a time — drove a final round of revisions before launch.

What the team learned sometimes cut against their own assumptions. “How little the end user wants to see and interact with” the data was the biggest surprise, Bray says. Focus group participants didn’t want a comprehensive dashboard of every growing area in the state; they wanted their own location, loaded automatically, with the fewest clicks possible. More simply, users wanted answers to questions such as: Is an area open? Is it high or low tide? What’s the water temperature? That preference reshaped the public interface around geolocation and minimal menu navigation, particularly for mobile use, allowing permit holders to check the system on their way out the door.

The towns themselves turned out to have sharply different needs, shaped largely by how many people they have on staff and who’s showing up at their docks. Many of these departments run on a skeleton crew with one or two staff, managing the entire permitting and enforcement operation. “All the organizations we work with are all understaffed,” Bray says. “I didn’t realize that going into this.”

That imbalance shaped something called the “Ways to Water” feature. Towns popular with seasonal and vacationing residents who buy a permit without knowing the local geography asked for a tool that could route users to the nearest shellfishing access points. They also wanted the tool to show parking availability, boat ramps, and travel time. This detail captures the blue economy dimension of the project well. Both tourism and traditional shellfishing for food security call for differing groups to share the same water and the same system, without necessarily sharing the same local knowledge.

Other requests were smaller, but no less telling. One shellfish officer asked simply whether the interface could be offered in different languages, a request the team is now addressing through built-in translation. It’s the kind of feature that doesn’t show up in a funding proposal’s list of objectives, but that turned out to matter a great deal to the people actually using the tool.

The relationship with DMF followed a different shape than the one with the towns. Where individual towns had fewer resources but could move quickly once they decided to adopt something, DMF moved more deliberately. “They had more ability than they had power,” Bray says of DMF staff, describing an agency with existing institutional constraints that limited the design approach the researchers could take. That distinction ultimately reshaped the project’s strategy: rather than building one system meant to unify DMF and every town under a single workflow, the team shifted toward treating towns and DMF as separate entities with distinct needs, while still syncing DMF’s official closure data into the platform automatically. Bray describes the process as investing effort where towns have the flexibility to adopt something new, rather than waiting on slower-moving state processes to catch up.

Rules, real-time data, and respecting jurisdiction

The system’s handling of jurisdiction is arguably its core technical achievement. DMF manages the baseline layer of the state’s 738 growing areas; individual towns manage sub-areas on top of that layer, closing sections for reasons ranging from water quality to family-designated harvesting zones reserved for local residents. Early on, the team assumed DMF would want to manage its polygons directly inside Seashell. DMF preferred to keep working in an existing ArcGIS system. So the MIT team adjusted, syncing Seashell to DMF’s existing records via API instead, and building in automatic alerts whenever DMF’s underlying data changed. It’s a small design decision with an outsized effect: DMF keeps full control of its own data while towns still benefit from updated, synced data.

The administrative interface goes a step further, pulling in real-time environmental data and using it to recommend closure decisions based on rules that towns configure themselves. It’s a direct stand-in for the old rain-gauge phone call, and it’s built to shrink the gap between when DMF issues a closure notice and when the public actually learns about it.

A rare bipartisan corner of ocean policy

Seashell officially launched at the 2026 Northeast Aquaculture Conference and Exposition in Portland, Maine, this past January. The team is scheduled to present at the Massachusetts Shellfish Officers Association’s meeting this October, betting that broader town-level adoption will reduce the confusion that crops up when neighboring towns operate on entirely different systems. Some towns’ shellfish officers are using Seashell while the next town over might still be working on paper.

Bray sees something durable in the subject matter itself, apart from the technology. “Shellfishing is one of the few things, in terms of the ocean, in terms of cultural communities, that is bipartisan,” he says. Bastidas points to the layered value of the resource, not just its economic footprint, but its role in food security and in traditions, including Indigenous shellfishing practices, that predate Massachusetts’ current regulatory system by centuries.

Looking ahead, the team is exploring an extension into commercial fisheries and landing-data reporting, building on related, town-driven effort. More broadly, the researchers see little about the underlying framework that’s specific to shellfishing. The same architecture, they argue, could serve any natural resource management problem with a geospatial and jurisdictional dimension: wildlife management, water quality, coastal permitting.

For Bray, who led his first funded research project through this J-WAFS grant, the work has doubled as a lesson in institutional collaboration as much as software design. The project helped him understand how fast and how much a large state agency can move versus a small town, and where to put the effort to balance both sides. “You have to figure out what an organization is capable of providing, and work within that,” he says, “while still trying to push things forward.”

text:
October 16, 1923. Los Angeles.
A four-page contract got signed in a Hollywood home, and a company was born.

Walt Disney, 21, had come west from Kansas City after his Laugh-O-Gram studio went bankrupt. He had one sample reel, Alice's Wonderland, and, as the story goes, $40. Margaret Winkler, one of film's first female distributors, offered $1,500 per short for a series of Alice Comedies.

In the middle of the night, Walt visited his brother Roy at the veterans' hospital, where Roy was recovering from tuberculosis, and asked him to go into business.

The first short was due in eight weeks, and their star, Virginia Davis, was still in Kansas City. They opened the Disney Brothers Cartoon Studio in the back of a real-estate office on Kingswell Avenue.
Five years later, a mouse showed up. Every film and park since traces back to one order and one stubborn idea: cartoons could be more than gags.

text:
When an autistic traveler collapsed from sensory overload at an airport, an airline employee didn't just rebook his ticket—he sat on the floor beside him and protected his dignity. 

Curled up behind a vacant ticket counter at Reno-Tahoe International Airport, Samuel Allen shook and hyperventilated as two consecutive days of flight delays pushed him into severe sensory overload.

An American Airlines customer service agent named David noticed the situation and approached the quiet corner. Crouching down beside Allen on the floor, David asked what was wrong. Through rapid breathing and muscle spasms, Allen explained that he had autism and was currently unable to think clearly.

Allen was scheduled to deliver a public speech on autism awareness the following day in Cincinnati, Ohio, but his missed connections had left him stranded. David reviewed the ticketing system and identified a late-night routing that could still get Allen to Cincinnati in time for his presentation. Recognizing that another flight inside a crowded cabin posed a daunting sensory hurdle, David offered Allen a slice of pizza for lunch and gave him ten minutes to consider his options

When David returned ten minutes later, he brought along the captain of the scheduled flight. The pilot reassured Allen, noting that his present experience only reinforced the value and authenticity of the advocacy message he was traveling to share.

To manage the sensory environment, David worked with the flight crew to clear out an entire row of seats so Allen would have dedicated personal space on board. David then arranged for early pre-boarding and walked beside Allen onto the aircraft. Before stepping back onto the jet bridge, David introduced Allen individually to each member of the flight crew. Allen took his seat in the reserved row and departed for Cincinnati.
