text:
America Is in Decline, and Trump Is Leading the Fall

[continued]

Video
14OCT2026
By Lydia Polgreen, Rahmane Idrissa, and Kaiser Kuo
Produced by Derek Arthur
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/amvHbzhdTO
The old world order is fraying. Who gets to shape the next one?

Polgreen: Yeah. Kaiser, I’m curious, how does this look from your vantage point?

Kuo: Well, when I think about the post-rupture moment, I go back to the late Joe Nye. In 2017, he came up with this idea of — and it was really kind of a challenge to this idea of the “Thucydides Trap,” which has, has gained a lot of currency. He said the more dangerous trap is the “Kindleberger Trap,” wherein an incumbent power either refuses to or is unable to provide those public goods any longer, and the rising power in the world is unable to step in and do that in its place.

So we are in such a trap right now, I think, where the United States has abdicated its traditional role of provision of public goods, and it’s unclear that China is willing to do all of that. In some areas, it clearly is. In development, in infrastructure lending, in provision of manufactured goods, in absorbing all the demand for commodities. There are a lot of things in which China has stepped up, but it’s clearly shown no appetite for much of the rest of it. Look at its relative absence of a role in the Iran crisis. It’s not going to step in. And the United States doesn’t want it to. The United States seems hellbent on preventing China from filling that role.

So we’re then stuck with this question: Can you unbundle all of these things? Can all of these different public goods come from a disparate set of actors? Can Brussels provide regulatory public goods, while China does what it’s good at doing, the manufactured goods? The United States is abdicating it at a very, very difficult time, where we face unprecedented challenges from the advent of A.I. and all these other things. So I think that the waters are going to be choppy for a while.

Polgreen: I’m curious, Rahmane, are there possibilities of something different and newer and perhaps more equitable coming out of this time of great rupture?

Idrissa: I think there is the possibility of an aspiration. It has to be cultivated, because this situation of hegemony is actually quite rare in history. Actually, the U.S. situation, from the end of the Cold War to the age of Trump, is the one example that I can really think of as a hegemony that we have known since the Roman Empire, basically.

What has tended to exist in the past is those competing big powers that created endless wars. And in fact, the problem that we’re facing here is that we do not want to go back to that situation. When you remove the kind of hegemonic system, what you might end up having is big powers with ambitions. Even if they don’t fight each other, they can create wars elsewhere. So I think the problem that sliding into this new cacophonous world might present us with is this dire return of international war and conflicts. So to me, the direction to go is how to save international law from the ambitions of the big powers, because the big powers don’t like international law.

The Soviet Union and the United States are the two countries that refused to adhere to the international justice system when it was being born in the late 1940s. They didn’t want to be tied to that. And whichever country is reluctant to accept or adhere to international law, you may be sure it has bad intentions. And it’s usually those big powers. So in our case, it’s China and the U.S. But, and I agree with Kaiser here, the U.S. is proving to be even the worst case in this situation. They are practically attacking the international justice system, trying to destroy it and undermining it.

I think there is an aspiration of reviving international law that kind of exists in very small groups in many countries. The problem is that this has not coalesced into a movement, and also this is being a bit checked and contained by the fact that what really sustains the growth of international law is the reality of domestic law. In international law you don’t have an army. There’s no force behind it. The force that is behind it is a commitment of states. So if you have states that have good domestic laws, then you can have this system of international law emerging.

And so, I think we should be worried by all these processes of democratic backsliding and things like that, because they are, by definition, anti-law. They destroy domestic law and destroy the commitment of states to international law. So I think going forward, I don’t know what will happen. I cannot predict it. But if we really want to avoid going back to the horrors of the past, we have to fight for international law, and it has to start within our own respective countries.

Polgreen: Kaiser?

Kuo: I think, if we look at what China says, at least ostensibly, it wants to lean into the extant U.N. system. It’s been a very vocal proponent of existing multilateral institutions. And it’s quite clear. I mean, they’ve made clear that China’s preferred outcome — from all of this, when the dust settles — is a genuinely multipolar order with poles including, of course, China and the United States, the E.U., Brazil, India certainly, Russia. And I think we need to look at what else is on offer right now. The United States’ vision — at the Busan talks, afterward, Donald Trump called it “G2.” He re-invoked this old, dead word.

China is at least on record as being adamantly opposed to that. I don’t know whether China, in fact, in its heart of hearts, really dislikes the idea as much as it says it does. I think that for the middle powers, this is the worst possible outcome. They want to hedge. They want to be able to play the two powers off against one another. They want a voice in how decisions are made. They certainly don’t want the two powers, in condominium, making decisions over their heads. So I think that’s probably a terrible outcome, and one in which China’s vision of a more genuinely multipolar order probably has some purchase. So we shall see.

Polgreen: Yeah. We keep adding numbers after the G and then taking them away, and I think that tells you a lot about the state of global affairs.

But just to wrap this up in just a sentence or two — I’d love to hear from both of you. What are the opportunities for these middle powers, as their governments assert themselves in the absence of U.S. hegemony and encounter the rise of China?

Kuo: I think that in a world where we have these two rival aspirants to the throne, it’s possible to play them off against one another to exact concessions from each, because they are the jury; they are the audience to which these two powers are ultimately playing. In an ideal world, that keeps them on their best behavior, and they have resources that both need — I mean, you look at a country, a country like Indonesia with its near monopoly, really, on nickel, which is so important for electric vehicle batteries and for so many other things, and it’s able to exert that.

I think that in this world of mutually assured disruption, people are coming into their own. They’re realizing the kinds of chokehold power that they have. I think that there are going to be ways in which their hold on certain necessary minerals, and on critical resources, will be able to help them in exacting the kind of leverage, and will help them to hedge more successfully into balance.

Polgreen: Rahmane?

Idrissa: Well, they probably have to engage the big powers anyway. I mean, there is nothing that can be done without China or the U.S. in the picture. I guess they should probably exploit the fact that they no longer have to be beholden to the U.S. to create a different pathway that could be an alternative to pure domination.

Because in the end, when you are dealing with these very, very large powers, the inequality is such that even if they do not want to crush you, they will tend to crush you just by the sheer physics of the relationship. Whereas with the middle powers, you do not actually have that amount of radical inequality. And also, it is with the middle powers that this return to international law is more feasible, not with China or the U.S., especially not with the U.S. as it is today.

Polgreen: Yeah. The U.S. might change, but the world has already changed, and I don’t think that we will soon be seeing a return to the restoration of even the rhetoric of what drove U.S. hegemony for all those decades.

Kuo: Well, a boy can hope.

Polgreen: Thank you for coming together across these time zones and distance to have this really important conversation with me. I really, really enjoyed it, and I’m sure that our listeners will too.

Idrissa: Thank you. Thank you, Lydia.

Kuo: Thank you, Lydia.

Great discussion. It strikes me that since the end of the Cold War, during which the world was ordered by dualism, we've entered a period increasingly ordered by pluralism, an arrangement in which power is spread among many diverse societies, each with its own strengths and weaknesses. The rise of authoritarianism is a logical reaction to this, adding alarm to the"cacophony" mentioned in the conversation. Although authoritarianism has hastened the end of the old order and is doing great damage, it's also running up against its limits (Trump in Iran, Putin in Ukraine). Thanks to drones and cyber-warfare, traditional military might has also come up short. China, the creeping giant, is quietly strengthening its hand in manufacturing, shipping, and cheap A.I., but its immense internal challenges will prevent its rise to the superpower level the U.S. has enjoyed - and squandered - since the 1990s. The age of pluralism will present a lot to sort out, but in the end it's the way the world is and, if managed properly (e.g. strengthening international law), the only way we can all survive.

“Who Fought You from Israel and America Inside Taiz?” Yemeni Army Officer Challenges Houthi Colonel's Claims

Another leaked conversation offers further insight into how the Houthis are conducting psychological operations (PSYOPs) against Yemen's National Army.

The recording reportedly captures Houthi Colonel Muhammad Sufyan al-Kamil speaking with Yemen National Army Lieutenant Colonel Saddam al-Maqlua, attempting to persuade him through a mixture of political arguments, assurances about security and stability, and familiar Houthi propaganda narratives.

One exchange particularly caught my attention. The Houthi colonel appears to suggest that Houthi forces have fought and killed Americans and Israelis during their recent military campaigns. When challenged to explain who these Americans and Israelis were and where they had fought inside Taiz, he struggles to provide a convincing answer.

There is no credible evidence that American or Israeli military personnel have been fighting alongside Yemeni government forces in Taiz, much less that the Houthis have killed them during their recent offensive.

The conversation also reveals how the Houthis are attempting to portray their military advances as an effort to restore security and stability rather than seize territory. The colonel urges his counterpart to maintain order, avoid chaos, and accept assurances that the country belongs to everyone.

What makes this exchange interesting is the difficulty the Houthi officer appears to have defending his own narrative when confronted with basic questions. The recording offers another example of how Houthi psychological operations rely on familiar ideological claims, exaggerated battlefield narratives, and promises of stability to influence opposing military officers.

"Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

               This study examines the historical value of the Iliad and Odyssey by asking not whether the Trojan War happened exactly as Homer describes, but how much genuine historical memory survives within the Homeric tradition. Drawing on archaeology, Hittite texts, Linear B tablets, comparative epic literature, and recent Homeric scholarship, it argues that the poems preserve overlapping memories of the Late Bronze Age, the Early Iron Age, and the mythic world of Greek epic.

Topics include the identification of Ahhiyawa and Wilusa in Hittite sources, the archaeology of Troy, oral-formulaic composition, the Homeric Question, Mycenaean political institutions, Bronze Age weaponry and elite culture, Early Iron Age funerary practices, the Catalogue of Ships, and the influence of Anatolian and Near Eastern literary traditions. Particular attention is given to how historical realities were transformed through centuries of oral transmission before reaching their extant form.

Rather than treating Homer as either a reliable historian or a creator of pure fiction, we suggest the Iliad and Odyssey are more like repositories of cultural memory, preserving authentic details from multiple historical periods while reshaping them into one of history's greatest epic traditions. The result is a synthesis of archaeology, ancient history, philology, and literary criticism that offers a new perspective on the relationship between myth, memory, and history in the ancient eastern Mediterranean.

                       Video Summary 
                  Some Takeaways 

                   video explores whether the Iliad and Odyssey function as historical records or mythic repositories, arguing that they act as a "time machine" preserving overlapping memories from three distinct eras: the Late Bronze Age, the Early Iron Age, and the mythic tradition of Greek epic (0:00-0:38).

Key Historical Context
Late Bronze Age Connections: While the Iliad does not describe a singular, accurate historical war, archaeology and Hittite texts (referencing Ahhiyawa and Wilusa) confirm consistent conflict in Western Anatolia between Mycenaean Greeks and local powers (2:22-6:56).
Literary Transmission: Homeric epics are rooted in an oral-formulaic tradition where poets utilized a repertoire of stock phrases and epithets to perform and adapt stories over centuries (12:20-13:42).
Mycenaean Heritage: The poems preserve genuine historical remnants, such as specific geographic sites (e.g., Pylos), political titles like wanax (king), and the use of boar-tusk helmets, which were obsolete by the Iron Age (20:00-26:57).
Early Iron Age Influence: Much of the social structure, feasting customs, and burial practices (specifically cremation and the construction of tumuli, similar to the findings at Lefkandi) reflect the post-collapse Iron Age, rather than the Bronze Age (27:46-32:45).

The Catalogue of Ships
This passage (Book 2 of the Iliad) is analyzed as a case study in blending history and myth. It likely contains authentic late Bronze Age geographical memories, but its composition was influenced by later Iron Age political needs and literary requirements (32:45-39:41).

Conclusion
The narrator concludes that Homer was a poet, not a historian. His value lies not in acting as a perfect chronicler of events, but in building an enduring world of words that preserved cultural memory through a dark age (39:41-42:15).connection between Ahhiyawa and Troy (referred to as Wilusa in Hittite texts) centers on repeated historical conflict in Western Anatolia during the Late Bronze Age (3:01-3:22, 6:39-6:56).

She shows up in Escanaba with Abdul El-Sayed to play progressive savior in Trump country, and what does she offer voters in the Upper Peninsula? A conspiracy theory so stupid it collapses the second you read the actual rule.

The Trump administration is not banning women from college. It is not "attacking women's ability to have an education." It implemented a loan reform under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that says if you want to borrow $200k+ in federal money for grad school, you should be in a field where you can pay it back. That's it. Professional degrees like medicine, law, dentistry get the higher cap. Graduate programs like education, social work, nursing — fields where the Department explicitly said students were being crushed by unpayable debt — get a lower cap.

You can agree or disagree with that tradeoff. But to twist a boring federal borrowing formula into "they don't want women to go to college, y'all" is pure demagoguery. It's AOC turning nurses and teachers into props because she knows her audience won't check the Federal Register.

text:
$GME Doomsday? @ryancohen 

Under §251(g), a Delaware corporation (like GameStop) can create a new holding company parent and merge itself into a wholly owned subsidiary of that parent. No shareholder vote is required if the conditions are met (identical rights, same directors, old company becomes a pure subsidiary, etc.). This is the exact mechanism Google used in 2015 to become a subsidiary of Alphabet.

On the effective date of the merger, three things happen simultaneously:

•  Common stock: Every outstanding GME share automatically converts 1-for-1 into a share of the new HoldCo. Shareholders wake up owning HoldCo stock instead of GME stock. The old GameStop entity becomes a subsidiary. The economic rights stay essentially the same, but the legal security and CUSIP change.

•  Convertible notes (~$2.8B remaining): Standard convertible indentures define a “fundamental change” (or “make-whole fundamental change”) to include mergers, consolidations, or changes in the underlying common stock. 

A 251(g) holdco reorg usually qualifies. When it triggers, noteholders typically get the right to put the notes back to the company for cash at 100% of principal, or to convert at an enhanced “make-whole” rate into the new HoldCo shares. 
Either way, the bond positions close or reprice. The arbitrage desks that had been long the convertible and short the stock (their delta hedge) suddenly lose the bond leg of the trade. With no new convertible offered to roll into, those short hedges have to be covered in the open market.

•  Warrants (GME WS): Warrant agreements and OCC (Options Clearing Corporation) rules almost always contain adjustment provisions for reorganizations, mergers, or changes in the common stock. 
The warrants adjust so that exercising them delivers whatever the common stockholders receive—in this case, HoldCo shares instead of GME shares. Settlement mechanics, the underlying, and sometimes the CUSIP change. Any short or hedge positions layered against the warrants get disrupted at the same moment.

Because the corporate action is a single event with one effective date, the common swap, the convertible fundamental-change trigger, and the warrant adjustment all occur together. Positions that were hedged across the three instruments (long convert + short stock + short warrant, or similar combinations) lose their matching legs at once and cannot easily cross-hedge the unwind using the other instruments. That is the mechanical basis for the “cascade” claim in the thesis.

In short: one statutory merger changes the underlying security for everything at the same time, and the standard contractual language in convertibles and warrants forces their holders (and the people hedged against them) to deal with the consequences on that same day. 

the idea is that a §251(g) holdco reorg would force many of the remaining delta-hedge shorts (the ones tied to the ~$2.8B convertibles) to cover because their matching long bond position disappears or changes when the fundamental-change provisions trigger. Some would likely start covering or adjusting right away if the bonds get put back for cash or converted, because those hedges would no longer have a clean counterpart.

However, not every short is a pure convertible arb hedge. Some are directional bets, some are hedged against the warrants or other positions, and some desks can temporarily re-hedge in other ways or wait for liquidity. Covering tends to happen in waves depending on price movement, available shares, and how aggressively the noteholders exercise their put/conversion rights.

text:
Met a girl in Austin who owes $200K on credit cards and hasn't paid a single dollar of interest in over 5 years…

Thought she was full of shit

She pulled up a color-coded Google Sheet and walked me through it. The math actually checks out. She might be the smartest person I've ever met or the most reckless. Probably both

She's been cycling balance transfers across banks in a loop that never ends

The play is stupid simple once you see it:

She takes $200K in 0% APR business cards. Uses the money for her real estate business. Month 10, before the 0% promo expires, she applies for a new round of 0% cards at different banks

Gets approved (because her score is 760+ since business cards don't report to personal credit)

Does a balance transfer from the old cards to the new ones. 0% clock resets for another 12-18 months

Old cards go to $0 balance. New cards hold the $200K. She hasn't paid a penny in interest

"But you can't balance transfer business cards"

Some banks allow it directly. For the ones that don't, she uses a workaround. She liquidates the new 0% cards into cash (2-3% fee through a payment processor), then uses that cash to pay off the old cards manually

Same result

Costs her about 4K-6K per cycle which she treats as a business expense

She's been doing this for 5 years straight. That's roughly $25K in total fees to maintain access to $200K in perpetual 0% capital

The interest on $200K at normal business loan rates (8-12%) would be 16K-24K per year. She's paying $5K per year instead. Over 5 years that's roughly 75K-95K in interest she just didn't pay

The spreadsheet tracks every card, every promo expiration date, every bank, every cycle. She has it planned out 18 months in advance. She knows exactly when to apply at which bank and in what order

text:
He had the Medal of Honor, a hometown parade, and a safe job selling war bonds. He asked to go back to the war anyway.

John Basilone was one of ten children, raised in Raritan, New Jersey. He served three years in the Army, much of it in the Philippines, and his buddies called him "Manila John." In 1940 he joined the Marines.

October 1942. Guadalcanal. Sgt. Basilone was in charge of two sections of heavy machine guns with the 1st Battalion, 7th Marines, when the enemy hit their line.

One of his sections was knocked out, leaving only 2 men able to fight. He moved an extra gun into place, repaired another and manned it himself. With ammunition running low and the supply lines cut, he fought his way through enemy lines and came back with shells for his gunners.

He was credited with killing at least 38 enemy soldiers with a machine gun and a pistol. He received the Medal of Honor.

Back home, Raritan threw him a parade that made LIFE magazine. He toured the country selling war bonds. The Marine Corps offered him a commission. He turned it down. He said he was just a plain soldier.

He kept asking to go back. Finally, the answer was yes. While training at Camp Pendleton, he married Lena Riggi, a sergeant in the Marine Corps Women's Reserve.

February 19, 1945. The first day on Iwo Jima. With his company pinned down by a Japanese blockhouse, he worked his way on top of it and destroyed it with grenades and demolitions. Later that day he guided a Marine tank out of a minefield under heavy fire.

He was killed at the edge of Airfield Number 1. He was 28.

He was awarded the Navy Cross. No other enlisted Marine in World War II received both it and the Medal of Honor. Lena never remarried.

Remember John Basilone.

text:
Few people have used the power of their personal story to challenge injustice as effectively as Olaudah Equiano. A writer, sailor, businessman and abolitionist, Equiano became one of the most influential voices in the campaign against the transatlantic slave trade, using his own experiences to expose the cruelty of slavery to the world.

Born 16 October 1745, Equiano was also known for much of his adult life as Gustavus Vassa. Although the exact details of his birth remain disputed, his life and writings have secured his place in the history of the struggle for freedom and human dignity.

In his autobiography, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, published in 1789, Equiano stated that he was born in Isseke community in Anambra state; southeastern Nigeria.

He described growing up in an African society with it's own traditions, customs, social structures and values. His account offered European readers a glimpse of African life beyond the negative stereotypes often used to justify slavery.

According to his account, Equiano was kidnapped as a child, around the age of 11, alongside his sister. The siblings were eventually separated, and he was sold into slavery.

His life changed dramatically as he passed between enslavers and was taken across the Atlantic. He experienced the harsh realities of enslavement in the Americas and learned seafaring skills while serving under British naval officer Michael Pascal, who gave him the name Gustavus Vassa.

Equiano was later sold to Robert King, a merchant who permitted him to engage in trading activities. Through hard work, business dealings and determination, he saved enough money to purchase his freedom in 1766.

As a free man, he travelled widely and eventually settled in Britain, where he became increasingly involved in the movement to abolish the slave trade. Rather than remain silent about the suffering he had witnessed, he turned his experiences into a powerful argument against human bondage.

Equiano's 1789 autobiography became one of the most significant published accounts associated with the abolitionist movement.

His work challenged the arguments used to defend slavery and helped mobilise public opinion against the transatlantic slave trade. At a time when the voices of enslaved and formerly enslaved Africans were frequently ignored, Equiano's testimony demanded attention.

He did not live to see the British Parliament abolish the British transatlantic slave trade in 1807. He died on March 31, 1797. Slavery itself continued in Britain's colonies until later legislation brought about its abolition in most of the British Empire in 1833, with implementation following in subsequent years.

In his autobiography, he identified Isseke, in Igboland, as his homeland. However, some historians have questioned this account because baptismal and naval records have been interpreted as indicating that he was born in South Carolina.

The debate remains unresolved, with scholars disagreeing over how the documentary evidence should be weighed against Equiano's own account.

For this reason, October 16, 1745, sometimes listed as his birthday, should not be treated as a confirmed date. Both his exact birth date and his claimed African birthplace remain subjects of historical discussion.

Olaudah Equiano's significance extends beyond his personal journey from enslavement to freedom. He demonstrated how storytelling, education and determined advocacy could challenge an unjust system and influence public debate.

For Nigerian and Igbo history, his account is especially valuable because it preserves his description of an African community before his enslavement, even as questions about his early life continue to attract scholarly attention.

The lesson of his legacy: One courageous voice can challenge a powerful system. Equiano used his life story to confront injustice, expose the cruelty of slavery and inspire generations to recognise the value of freedom and human equality.

"In 1845, Texas came incredibly close to rejecting US annexation to remain an independent republic. A razor-thin vote in the Texas Congress altered the map of North America forever."]

The incorporation of the Republic of Texas into the United States was far from a certainty and nearly collapsed due to deep local pride and foreign geopolitical intrigue. In 1845, the Lone Star Republic was on the verge of rejecting American annexation in favor of a sovereign empire supported by European powers.

After winning its independence from Mexico in 1836, Texas spent nearly a decade operating as an independent nation. During this era, British and French diplomats worked tirelessly to prevent Texas from joining the United States, offering to negotiate formal Mexican recognition of Texan sovereignty in exchange for Texas remaining forever independent.

Many prominent Texan leaders, including former President Sam Houston, seriously entertained this European offer. They envisioned a grand independent empire stretching to the Pacific, operating as a low-tariff agricultural nation that would rival the economic power of the northern United States.

When the annexation resolution finally came before the Texas Congress in July 1845, the debate was incredibly fierce. Anti-annexation factions argued that joining the Union would strip Texas of its hard-won freedom and entangle it in the growing American sectional conflict over slavery.

Ultimately, the desire for security against Mexico and financial stability won by a razor-thin margin. The Texas Congress accepted the annexation terms, leading to statehood in December 1845. Had the vote gone the other way, Texas would have remained a permanent geopolitical buffer state, changing the entire history of the American West.

$2.63. That is how much the UN Panel of Experts on Haiti found frozen in the account of a man the Security Council sanctioned last October. The Security Council renewed Haiti's sanctions regime on 14 October (Resolution 2831, 14-0-1, Russia abstaining). Renewing it was the easy part.

The Panel's 94-page final report (S/2026/714, dated 8 September, made public 7 October) covers October 2025 to July 2026. Its headline finding: "violent fractures" inside the Viv Ansanm gang alliance. Romain Le Cour of the Global Initiative told AP that each leader will now seek electoral arrangements on its own terms, trading territory, access to voters and security of the process.

The money and protection layer: the Panel names former officials it says financed, armed or shielded gangs. They include a former Arcahaie mayor alleged to have laundered funds through three Haiti-registered companies and tipped off gang leaders about police operations, and former legislators alleged to have armed groups in Kenscoff and Miragoâne. They deny the findings or did not respond; these are allegations, not convictions. The Panel also documents police officers selling ammunition out of the Saint-Marc area, and gang arsenals fed by traffickers abroad, inter-gang transfers and diversion from police stocks.

Enforcement is the weak link. One frozen account of sanctioned ex-lawmaker Prophane Victor holds $421. The Panel found $0 frozen at the central bank for several gang leaders, and $2.63 for Dimitri Hérard, designated in October 2025. In its words: "The meagre amounts of money frozen by banks do not correlate with the wealth accumulated by those individuals." Delays let assets move to third parties, and "the vast majority" of gang supporters remain undesignated.

Elections raise the stakes. The Panel says the lower Artibonite, Haiti's second-largest electoral district, has faced an "unprecedented level of coordinated gang violence" since March, and that child recruits are offered about $1,000 and a motorcycle.

Practitioner question: now that the Council has renewed the travel ban, asset freeze and arms embargo under Resolution 2831, will it add the financiers the Panel documented, or keep a list whose targets hold $2.63?

Primary: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2026/714; UNSC Resolution 2794 (17 Oct 2025); UNSC Resolution 2831 (14 Oct 2026); AP (7 Oct 2026); Miami Herald (6 Oct 2026).

text:
#RadioMoskva

Europe’s delusions risk starting a war with Russia

Europe is talking itself into war with Russia. The bust up between Ukraine and America in the last days has not only been the most dramatic split between the two since the famous Oval Office fracas in February last year, but is also pushing Europe into more and more extreme positions to protect and help its friend Ukraine.

But with no negotiations between Brussels and Moscow of any sort, the danger of escalating to the point when actual hostilities between Russia and Europe break out are growing alarmingly. The problem is European leaders are getting caught up in their own hyperbole and the chances of a mistake that sparks a major conflict are growing.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said that the US has “betrayed” Ukraine. He is right. And has been for at least two years, when it became too obvious to ignore.

Europe doesn’t want to hear it. “Some things are best not said out loud,” one MEP advised Zelenskiy after he let go in public during an EU summit yesterday.

One take on his outburst is that he has painted himself into a corner and now it’s clear no one is going to come and help Ukraine fend off a Russian winter onslaught that is already under way he has nothing to lose. As I argued yesterday, Trump’s “energy ceasefire” was probably the last chance this year to stop the war before Putin’s total war of destruction rains down on Ukraine.

The tone in Europe has changed remarkably in the last year. Ukraine’s extraordinary reliance and heroism in the first year of swashbuckling teams of three wielding US-made Javelinmissiles “popping the tops” of Russian tanks quickly led to the first Ramstein meeting on April 26 that year where the billions of dollars-worth of gear began to flow. But from the very beginning Nato Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg made it perfectly clear that the West’s number one priority was to “prevent WWIII” and that helping Ukraine was a distant second.

“Nato is not sending troops to be on the ground. We also have a responsibility to prevent this conflict from escalating beyond Ukraine, and become even more deadly, even more dangerous and destructive,” he said in April 2022.

That has changed now where European countries are actively setting up weapons factories on their own territory to arm Ukraine under the so-called Danish model, which has invited mounting hybrid attacks by Russia inside Europe proper. Ukraine is backed into the corner and the fighting talk has started again. But much of the rhetoric is delusional and Europe is running the danger of unintentionally starting the very third world war it has been trying to avoid for the last four and half years.

No peace talks: For all his faults, Trump did actively try to facilitate a peace deal that culminated in the 27-point peace plan (27PPP) during the Moscow meeting on December 3 carrying through from the Alaska summit on August 15. Admittedly, that deal was very Kremlin-friendly, but it was a workable deal along the lines of the Finlandisation of Ukraine. That initiative led to the Trump administration’s “final offer” offered at a London summit, which was rejected by Bankova thanks to the backing of the coalition of the willing in London in April last year.

No interlocutor: Since then, the White House took itself out of the talks completely following the start of the Iran war in February this year. The EU tried to step into the breach, but the effort to find a suitable interlocutor that could deal with the Kremlin rapidly descended into farce. Instead of coming up with someone that Putin would accept, the discussion descended into hot air statements of “increasing the pressure” on Putin.

There are now no talks with the Kremlin at all. Without a rapporteur there is no prospect of ending the war; in this set up there can only be escalation with Russia into a global conflict or defeat for Ukraine. A Ukrainian victory has been written off as an option by the West from the very beginning.

Schroeder so be it: the one European name Putin did suggest was ex-Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder, who was in Moscow on October 7 to celebrate Putin’s 74 birthday. That was widely seen as risible and dismissed out of hand. But I would argue that Trump is an even worse choice as intermediator as he is far more “pro-Putin” than Schoeder.

He has pushed the Kremlin’s agenda at every turn, as he clearly wants to go into business with Russia. Since taking office he has imposed only one set of oil sanctions on Lukoil and Rosneft. He just signed Lindsey Graham’s ‘hellish sanctions' that in theory could break Russia’s economic back, but within weeks the first thing he actually did was to ease diesel sanctions on Russia.

After the Miami meeting with the Dynamic Envoy Due the so-called Dmitriev package of deals worth an astonishing $12 trillion seems to be back in play and there is talk of more sanctions relief. Just this weekend the US suggested that part of the $300bn frozen in Europe should be handed over to the US to do joint venture investments with Russia as Kyiv faces its Battle of Britain moment of a non-stop missile barrage that is already turning out the lights and heat across Ukraine.

Yes, Schroeder is a very good friend of Putin’s but at least he is a proper politician with presumably some sense of duty to his fellow countrymen. Trump’s “energy ceasefire” tweet showed he is a rank amateur and incompetent to boot. Good relations with Putin is probably an advantage in talks. What is the alternative? Send EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who on paper should be the person to go, but is obviously a total non-starter. The bottom line is someone has to go to Moscow and if Schroeder is the only choice – so be it. If you don’t like his deal, then reject it.

US actively working for Ukraine’s defeat:Trump is now not only not supporting Ukraine, he seems to be actively working to facilitate its defeat. Today it was reported that Ukraine has officially run out of Patriot interceptor missiles completely. But the throttling of Starlink in the last two days took Ukraine’s vaulted drones offline too. That means that the AFU cannot even hit Russian troops inside their own country, let alone targets deep inside Russia.

The skies are wide open. Over the last two days Russian missiles have not only destroyed what was left of Kyiv’s power generation capacity, but are now actively targeting the substations that feed from the remaining nuclear power capacity. Trump has not only withdrawn what little support the US did supply but is also ordering Europe to curtail its Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) weapons supply programme for Ukraine.

Sanctions have failed: the only plan that the EU has is to “increase the pressure” on Russia with more sanctions. It just released the 21st and 22nd sanctions packages, but these are having almost no effect. The 21stsanctions package was supposed to be crushing but they were gutted by calving out Greek tankers which make up a fifth of the shadow fleet and carried a record amount of oil last month. Von der Leyen has just introduced some exemptions into the 22nd package for business reasons. Russia continues to be able to fund its war out of its cashflow, while Europe and Ukraine are racking up ever more debt.

Budget constraints: Nato General Secretary Mark Rutte likes to boast that the economic might of the EU can crush Russia’s war economy like a walnut, but he hasn’t done the math. While the size of Europe’s economy is much larger than Russia’s it has largely become a service economy. China and Russia between them remain global manufacturing powerhouses and in war it is industrial production, not wealth, that counts.

Russia’s economy is under pressure, but it is not under enough pressure to stop the war and won’t be for at least two more years, former oligarch Mikhail Khodorkovsky told IntelliNews this week. Indeed, Russia is already in a full-scale war but its factories are running three shifts 24/7. In contrast the dysfunctional European economy is slipping into crisis. Everyone in Europe is now spending more than the Welsh Nato summit recommended 2% of GDP, but only Poland and the Baltic states are near the 5% recommended at the Nato summit in the Hague. By comparison Russia’s 7.5% of GDP defence spending looks relatively restrained.

Russia’s debt will increase to around 21% of GDP this year whereas almost all of Europe is already well over the Maastricht maximum of 60% of GDP. Servicing that debt is becoming increasingly painful. Typically the government tries to hold debt servicing costs to 4% of government spending and Russia is already at 8%. But half of the rest of Europe is already well over the maximum 3% EU’s Excessive Deficit threshold mandate with France well over 5% and will probably need a Greek-style bail out by the ECB. The UK is at a whopping 10%, dubbed “Ponzi scheme” levels by economics commentator Liam Halligan. Most of Europe has already used up what little fiscal wiggle room  it had to fund a war.

Russia also has a growing budget deficit problem, which is on course to end this year at just under 4% of GDP, but when the US entered WWII its deficit immediately jumped to 22% of GDP and remained there for the duration; Russia’s budget deficit is not going to force Putin to stop the war, whereas Ukraine’s might if the EU stops funding it. Kyiv says that it is already short $28bn for this year and next year’s is expected to climb to $75bn – almost all of which is covered by external borrowing.

Legitimate military targets: Since the US stopped supplying weapons Brussels has promised to step into America’s shoes, but as IntelliNews reported, Europe has not been able to offset US arms supplies and European military supplies to Ukraine fell for the first time last year. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s €800bn ReArmprogramme to modernise Europe’s military has also only just gotten under way.

The work around has been to set up defence joint production on EU territory and dozens of projects have been launched. However, this is very risky as the Kremlin is arguing that this changes Europe from being a mere “supporter” of Ukraine to an “active participant” in the war with Russia. The issue came up with British-made Nyan drones that Ukraine is using to target the sensitive parts of Russian oil refineries that are manufactured in Wiltshire. The Kremlin has said that these factories are now “legitimate military targets.”

The assumption is that these EU-based factories are immune from Russian attack thanks to Nato’s Article 5 clause, but that is only true for as long as it is true. No one is expecting Russian missiles to start coming down in Wiltshire, but it is already clearing a rise in sabotage, arson and hybrid attacks on EU territory. That is a mistake waiting to happen.

Asymmetric war deficit: Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski boasted a week ago that EU forces would defeat Russia in “six weeks” thanks to its superior airpower, but that ignores Russia’s overwhelming advantage in drones and the new style of asymmetrical war that is now the norm. Russia is on course to produce about 1.5mn drones this year, whereas Europe’s entire production is estimated to be around 300,000. And the Kremlin has poured money into development and now operates one of the most technologically advanced fleets of drones in the world – currently it is ahead of even Ukraine. And it is streets ahead of Europe in both missile production and innovations.

Russia’s economic assets were all hard-topped already during the Cold War and since then it has deployed extensive air defences across the country, whereas Europe is largely unprotected. And Russia has deployed intermediate range missiles like the Oreshnikand the Iskander in Kaliningrad, The Crimea and Belarus that can hit most cities in Europe. Neither Ukraine nor America have any hypersonic missiles at all and are unable to stop them. What few Patriot systems Europe did have, have already been mostly donated to Ukraine.

More generally, simple things like supplying itself with diesel will be a major problem for Europe and no problem at all for Russia. The Polish drone incursion last September, underscored how thorough unprepared Europe is to fend off a thousand-strong Russian drone swarm attack. Plans for a “Drone wall” remain just that – a plan.

Nato in collapse: In the meantime Trump is also actively undermining the Nato guarantee. The new National Security Strategy (NSS) released last December was almost scathing about the EU and says that Europe is now responsible for its own protection. Russia is now a European, not American, problem. Moreover, US military leaders have told Europe that the US will pull out of many of its European functions in 2027. In particular, Nato European logistics is entirely under the command of one US general, but he will be withdrawn next year, and control of logistics will be given to a committee made up of all 27 members. In addition, this will require massive investment as the battle plan goes from a US force arriving on Europe’s coast two weeks after a Russian attack and moving east, to moving European material from southern Europe to northern Europe and much of the necessary infrastructure to do that is missing. Whether the US will come to Europe’s aid at all if Russia attacks remains an open question. For his part, Putin has repeatedly said that Russia has no intention of attacking Europe, for whatever that is worth.

EU Political chaos: Marianne Le Penn is on the way to take over from French President Emmanuel Macron next year and said yesterday if she wins the election she will cut off Ukraine’s funding. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has already opted out of the €90bn EU loan and said yesterday that Slovakia would not contribute to any future funding plans either. The AfD (Alternative für Deutschland) just took control of its first region ever, is now the most popular party in Germany, and has opened talks with Moscow to turn Russia’s gas supplies back on.

Right-wing populist parties are on the rise across the EU and already also control Italy, Finland, Czechia and Austria. At the same time the incumbent liberal-conservatives are in retreat. Macron is already almost a lame duck. With only a 10% approval rating, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government is close to collapse and he will be replaced in 2029. And even Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who replaced Putin’s biggest ally in Europe, Viktor Orban, is better described as a national popularist than a European team player; he has refused to cut off Russian supplies of gas.

An even bigger question would be if a war broke out would Europe’s citizens be willing to go to war and fight and die in the wheat fields of Ukraine? That remains an open question, but the rise of the right across the Continent suggests very strongly that they would not be. Milbloggers have dismissed the recent talk of an “imminent Russian attack on Nato” as nonsense as the bulk of the Russian equipment and men are bogged down in the Donbas, but Putin has yet to call for a general mobilisation and could up to another half a million men into the field very quickly. And as the Russian public have largely swallowed the Kremlin’s rhetoric that Russia is already fighting a proxy war with Nato, they probably would be willing to fight Europe.

text:
🇺🇸🗳️ 16-Oct North Carolina Early Voting Update: Day One, and It's Bad for Republicans 🗳️

In-person early voting opened yesterday. I've been saying early in-person voting where the real signal starts. It started, and it's bad for Republicans.

The DataRepublican NC map now defaults to all early voting (mail + in person) against the same point in 2022. It updates every morning.

Benchmark first: at this point in 2022, the early vote was D+13. It finished D+7, and Republicans still won every statewide race. A Democratic lead in the early vote is normal. What matters is how big the lead is compared with 2022.

Day 1 in person, against Day 1 in 2022:

🔵 D+27.6 (2022: D+6.0, 2024: D+1.5)
🔵 That's a 21.6-point shift toward Democrats

All early voting so far, mail + in person, against the same point in 2022 (19 days out):

🔴 R share: −9.1
🔵 D share: +5.1
🟡 I share: +4.0

Raw D–R margin: 🔵+14.2 shift toward Democrats (D+27.4, against D+13.2)
With independents split by each county's R/D ratio: 🔵+22.2 (D+40.8, against D+18.6)

Raw counts so far (2022 same point in brackets):

🔴 R : 46,341 [54,195]
🔵 D : 111,482 [79,117]
🟡 I : 79,716 [56,063]

🟡 I leaning 🔴 R: 23,954
🟡 I leaning 🔵 D: 55,762

Turnout is up 25% over 2022 overall and up 47% for in person alone. Republicans are the only group that went down. Republican in-person ballots fell 12% while Democratic ones rose 78%.

It isn't only blue counties:

🔴 R-registration counties (65): R+13.8 in 2022 → D+8.3 now
🔵 D-registration counties (35): D+26.8 → D+44.0
Republican raw count below 2022 in 62 of 98 counties. Margin moved toward Democrats in 89.

Who's voting:

⚫ Black share of in-person ballots: 26.1%, against 19.4% in 2022 and 21.3% in 2024. That's 56,057 Black early voters so far, up from 34,128.
⚪ White early voters: D+7.7, against R+5.8 in 2022. That's a 13.5-point swing among white voters. Republican white ballots are down 17%, and Democratic white ballots are up 27%.
👴 65+: 58.5%, against 59.6% in 2022. This isn't an older electorate than 2022. It's the same mix of ages with different people showing up.

Mail is a sideshow now. It's 36k ballots against 202k in person. On its own it's D+26.4, against D+32.1 in 2022, still a modest shift toward Republicans like last month.

Can Republicans explain this away?

• "Day 1 is always the most Democratic day." True, but statewide the drift is small. In 2022, in-person went from D+6.0 on Day 1 to D+5.5 at the end of early voting. In 2024 it went from D+1.5 to R+1.5. Even a drift twice as large as either year leaves 2026 about 15 points worse for Republicans.
• "Republicans are saving it for Election Day." That's the only real way out, and Day 1 data can't rule it out. But asking a midterm electorate to stay home until Election Day in a race this close is a bad bet.
• "Registration labels are stale." In the rural east, registration is moving away from Democrats, as old conservative white Democrats re-register R or unaffiliated. That makes a Democratic gain in labels harder to get, not easier. The few counties that shifted toward Republicans (Hyde, Gates, Anson, Duplin) are tiny, and the shift there is re-registration, not turnout.
• "Helene." That could explain some of the drop in western NC. It doesn't explain Wake or the R-registration counties in the east.

Caveats:
• It's one day. In 2022, NC cast about 2.2M early votes and 3.8M total.
• Party registration isn't a vote. Unaffiliated voters broke R in 2024. The independent split above assumes they break the way their county's D and R voters do, and so far that means Democratic.
• 2024 was a presidential year with far higher turnout, so the useful comparison to 2024 is the margin, not the counts.

Last time, I said the mail numbers neither ruled out a Democratic wave nor showed one. Day 1 in person looks like a Democratic wave. If Monday still comes in above D+20, this is no longer a Day 1 story.

What does this mean for other states? 

States like OH and GA have no true party label, so we've been estimating via demographics there. This NC D+22.2 advantage comes despite similar demographics as 2022. So OH and GA are not necessarily signals that this is isolated to NC. 

What we've been seeing is that Republicans are doing well in mail voting. Republicans did well in mail voting in NC, NV, PA, and FL, but that advantage got wiped out in the first day of IPEV. 

Clark County and Florida start their in-person early voting soon. We will see if these two states follow NC's steps.

text:
The tech has reached a point where local businesses must choose a path: McDonald's-style kiosks or real human service. The middle ground will disappear.

Square's new kiosk takes voice orders and answers allergy questions. It's fast, convenient, and great for getting complex orders right.

I've run a café since 2018. Here's who each path suits.

Kiosks fit high-volume, repeat, grab-and-go spots where customers want speed and accuracy. A line out the door is the problem you're solving.

Human service fits places where the visit is the product: regulars, recommendations, a barista who knows your order. Some customers pay extra for that.

The danger is the middle: a half-staffed counter plus a tablet nobody wants. It's slower than a kiosk and colder than a person.

One hybrid that can work is mobile ordering, because the customer chooses before they arrive. What fails is making them choose between a person and a screen when they walk in the door. Panera is one chain that offers both, and it just doesn't work.

text:
A minivan cruises along the corniche as waves rumble against the shore. A gust of wind brushes my face, and my seat rocks gently with every turn.

But no, I’m not in the minivan. I’m watching “Whalefall” in 4DX.

I’d heard about the tech before. If my memory serves me right, my first taste of 4D effects came during a family trip to Enchanted Kingdom some years ago, when I watched animated shorts in a small theater.

This time around, a press invitation to the new survival thriller gave me a chance to experience 4DX “more properly," at Greenbelt 3.

I came in blind. No research, no expectations. The curious cat in me had always wanted to try something new.

Before the movie began, I took a moment to inspect the seats. They sat higher than ordinary cinema chairs, with soft cushions and a footrest that could be raised or lowered. Unlike typical cinema seats, these didn’t fold up—something I especially appreciated after a few past “incidents” involving my bags or popcorn boxes.

Then a 4DX trailer gave me and the other invitees a preview of what was to come. The seats bucked and tilted, air rushed past us, strobe lights flashed, and puffs of smoke burst from below. For many of us who are presumably 4DX virgins, we found ourselves screaming and clapping as the effects happened.

Trailer pa lang, pelikula na, I thought. If the preview was already this wild, what would happen when the actual movie started?

"Whalefall," adapted from Daniel Kraus’ 2023 novel, follows scuba diver Jay (Austin Abrams), who is swallowed by a sperm whale while searching for his father’s remains (Josh Brolin). It was directed by Brian Duffield, who co-wrote the screenplay with Kraus.

The effects came in subtly enough as the movie progressed. When a vehicle turned right, drove off, or came to a sudden stop, my seat moved along with it. There were also the occasional vibrations.

During a motorboat scene, wind machines suspended from the ceiling sent powerful blasts of air our way, making the force and chill of the ride feel almost real.

The movie only got more intense, particularly during the sequences inside the whale. Amid Jay’s ordeal, our seats started jerking and tilting in different directions. Halos ibalibag na kami. It reminded me of my late-night jeepney rides with a kaskasero driver en route to SM Fairview or Cubao.

But the more the balibagan happened, the more I found myself gripping the seat and checking in on how I felt with every jolt. I even caught myself hoping things would let up, just so I could settle back into the movie.

To be sure, it wasn’t necessarily unpleasant. But instead of getting completely absorbed in the movie—as I would during any other big-screen viewing—I became more conscious of my own reactions.

The strobe lights, meanwhile, served a curious purpose. When Jay touched a bioluminescent jellyfish and got stung, a camera-like flash went off. Looking back, though, it felt less like a complement to the interaction and more like a distraction.

"Whalefall" ran for just under two hours, and everybody clapped as the credits rolled.

In writing this, I find myself thinking about how we all have different appetites for sensory experiences. Maybe it’s a little like sex: some want every physical sensation awakened. A lick of heat, a chill against the skin, fingernails trailing down one's back, maybe even being tossed around a little.

Others prefer to take it nice and slow, keep things quiet, and simply savor the feeling while it lasts, with dim lights or hazy music.

And then there are those who like to move between the gentle and the intense, depending on the mood.

The "Whalefall" screening in 4DX was quite the ride. It offered a little bit of everything, from the gentlest breeze to the wildest balibag.

I’m not sure whether I’d try it again, but I suspect I’ll remember this ride far better than my 4D experience in Santa Rosa.

(✍️: Nikko Miguel Garcia)

text:
350% up in ad spend while improving ROAS. 🔥

Lets dive into our holistic growth strategy approach that scaled New customer acquisition for a mid 7 figure brand. 

- Eliminate the 10% mindset. 

When we try to get a brand from 0-1 we dont EVER look at things to squeeze. 

We dont care if we dont accelerate in all things. 

This mindset comes from understanding the true levers of DR principles. 

Which is: 
''If your offer hits, your ad account should work with simple statics'' 

Not at every spend level, but at least you can still make your ad account work at a stable rhythm without trying to hard on your ads. 

Once you offer start making your cvr go ⬆️ you dive deeper into ads. 

I see a lot of brands with good products never testing their offer and pricing. 

This usually leads your ad account to be very seasonal dependent, and have a LOT of fluctuations. 

In essence, we dont look to squeeze everything at the early stages, all resources go to the elements that will make the spend show an increase of 100%  at least. 

- Media buying for pattern recognition 

Media buying is mostly for pattern recognition.

We do have our cbo's and ABO's, our scaling and testing campaigns (Depending on the brand) 

BUT 

We are not here to squeeze 5-10% from our media buying. 

We are looking at overall account spend allocation. 

-What takes spend 
-WHY 
-Can we get our iteration playbook to get more spend on our winning angle? 
-Did our loosing formats got executed the right way? 
 
Patterns are everything. 

Havent seen an LLM being very good with this regardless the context we feed it. Tread carefully. 

- Creative stages 

Most accounts are having a huge problem with TOF content. 

Most of them are seeing frequency and CPA to go up. 

True TOF content is something that will start taking spend at 1.03 frequency, and raise the entire daily spend bar of your ad account. 

This is the content you have to put your effort towards. 

Usually we play around 70% unaware (depending on the vertical) and 30% other awareness stages. 

For this you need: 

- Understand your mechanisms and apply the right ones.
- Hooks that opening your TAM (aka never start with your product) 
- Open loops 
-  Social proof 

Thats it

🇺🇦 Zelenskyy offers to halt strikes on Russian refineries if Ukraine receives missiles to defend its cities

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has presented Washington and its allies with a conditional proposal: if they want Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, they must provide the air-defense missiles needed to intercept Russian ballistic strikes.

“You decided that we shouldn’t attack Russian oil refineries. But they will keep attacking us. Then give us missiles so we can shoot down ballistic missiles,” Zelenskyy said.

The proposal comes amid a deepening dispute with President Donald Trump, who has demanded that Kyiv stop targeting Russian oil infrastructure and blamed those strikes for higher energy prices.

Zelenskyy argued that Ukraine cannot be expected to surrender one of its means of military and economic pressure while Russian missiles continue hitting Ukrainian cities and energy facilities.

“We were attacked. Our people were killed. It is perfectly reasonable that we have the right to defend ourselves,” he said.

He also disputed Trump's argument about energy prices, asserting that Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have no measurable effect on them. That economic claim has not been independently established.

Ukraine had previously offered a reciprocal energy ceasefire, under which Kyiv would halt refinery strikes if Moscow stopped attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. After Russia continued its attacks during the pause announced by Washington, Ukraine resumed operations against Russian refineries.

The latest proposal introduces another possible arrangement: replacing Ukraine's offensive pressure on Russia's oil industry with additional defensive capabilities against ballistic missiles.

It remains unclear whether Washington or European governments are prepared to provide the interceptors Ukraine is requesting.

A journalist in Brussels asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy whether Donald Trump was blaming him for problems of his own ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Zelenskyy paused, smiled and replied: “That is my answer.”

The exchange drew laughter from journalists at the press conference following his meeting with European Union leaders.

The moment came less than a day after Trump told Newsmax that Zelenskyy was “not a good guy for us to deal with,” accused him of resisting a peace settlement and said he found the Ukrainian president more difficult to negotiate with than Vladimir Putin.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have deteriorated amid disputes over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, U.S. sanctions relief for Russian diesel and restrictions affecting Ukraine's military satellite communications.

Zelenskyy offered no explicit endorsement of the journalist's suggestion. His brief response nevertheless became one of the most memorable moments of his visit to Brussels.

text:
Mining Is Not a Supply Chain | Guest Blogger, Watts Up With That?

On July 22, 2026, the Australian mining company Harena announced it had signed a Project Development Funding Agreement with the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) for up to $4.84 million. The money will fund permitting, environmental and social studies, laboratory work, and pilot-plant development at Ampasindava, a rare-earth deposit on the northwest coast of Madagascar. On paper, American capital backing a non-Chinese source of the minerals needed for everything from fighter jets to wind turbines is a great success, but zooming on the deal exposes critical oversights in Washington’s strategy.

The United States is increasingly backing African critical-mineral projects to reduce its dependence on China. But Ampasindava shows why securing access to ore is not the same as securing access to usable rare-earth materials. Washington is addressing the former much faster than the latter.

The Chokepoint Isn’t in the Ground

China’s dominance of rare earths is usually described as a mining problem when it’s actually a refining one. Although China controls roughly 60% of global rare-earth mining, it controls more than 91% of global refining and nearly 94% of permanent-magnet production.

China’s advantage is the industrial capacity that turns ore into usable components: separation, refining, alloy production, and magnet manufacturing. If African material must still pass through Chinese-controlled processing, Washington has diversified extraction without changing who controls the supply chain that defense, energy, automotive, and advanced-technology industries rely on.

What Ampasindava Actually Is

Ampasindava contains high concentrations of neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium, the elements needed to build the permanent magnets used in precision-guided munitions and fighter jets. Once complete, the mine is expected to produce about 4,000 metric tons of rare-earth oxides a year, including roughly 1,700 tons of the higher-value magnet rare earths neodymium-praseodymium and dysprosium and terbium.

Harena is targeting production in mid-2028 and is currently shopping the offtake around Europe and the United States. The project, as designed, covers mining only. There are no provisions yet for on-site separation, refining, or magnet-making. Madagascar’s ore would strengthen the upstream end of the Western supply chain but at the same time leave the specialized, high-value downstream steps untouched.

This is the pattern to watch elsewhere in Africa as well. Outside Ampasindava, U.S. investment in African rare earths has gone mainly to Malawi and South Africa, with mineral-processing frameworks secured in Kenya and Tanzania. The current approach is to fund extraction in countries not aligned with Beijing.

The Workforce Problem Nobody Is Pricing In

Even if Washington wanted to build the missing downstream capacity tomorrow, it would run into a second constraint: people. American firms have the capability to start building a Western rare-earth supply chain, but they face a shrinking mining pipeline, almost no domestic separation expertise, and no existing magnet-manufacturing workforce. Capital can be raised faster than metallurgists and process engineers can be trained.

This is also where Africa’s leverage comes in. African leaders are increasingly pushing foreign companies to conduct some processing locally, both for economic development and because purely extractive arrangements carry obvious post-colonial baggage. Zimbabwe, Tanzania, and Ghana have already banned raw lithium exports rather than continue shipping unprocessed ore abroad. As the scramble for critical minerals accelerates, African governments will realize they hold real policy leverage, and DFC investment offers should get ahead of that by proactively including local processing or capacity-building components.

France has already moved in this direction, committing to shift some mining-related processing back to Gabon by 2029. If Washington wants African partners on favorable terms over the long run, some renegotiation of how gains are split will be necessary. There is also a workforce opportunity buried in this trade-off. Training African miners and engineers, whether they eventually work in U.S. facilities or return home to build local manufacturing, either rebuilds the domestic rare earth elements (REE) workforce or seeds economic and soft-power gains that cut against Chinese influence. China already runs education and upskilling programs with its African partners; a comparable American offer would not be a novel idea, just a belated one.

Logistics Is the Quiet Third Problem

Getting the material out is a whole other issue that gets less attention than mining or processing. Through the Belt and Road Initiative, China controls much of the logistics infrastructure connecting mines to ports across Africa. Even if mining, processing, and magnet production all eventually happened in American or partner-nation facilities, the supply chain could still run through Chinese-controlled roads, rail, and ports. Extraction and processing are the visible chokepoints. Logistics is the one that can quietly undo progress on the other two.

Why This Is Also a Race

China has long dominated investment in Africa’s copper, cobalt, and lithium sectors and is well positioned to extend that position into rare earths. It already controls the downstream end of the REE supply chain; adding ownership stakes in African REE projects would let it close the loop from mine to finished component. In the first half of 2025 alone, Chinese state-owned banks issued $24.9 billion in Belt and Road-linked mining loans, and mining’s share of BRI engagement has been trending upward. If the United States treats African engagement as optional, it is ceding the field to competitors who clearly do not.

Nonetheless, Washington isn’t starting from zero on coordination either. Since 2022, the U.S. has belonged to the Minerals Security Partnership, a group of countries including the EU, Japan, Australia, and Canada that pools resources and coordinates on which mining and processing projects to back. In 2025 the G7 went further, launching a Critical Minerals Action Plan that called on member countries’ development banks, including the US government’s DFC, to coordinate their support instead of funding projects one at a time in isolation. The infrastructure to act as a bloc already exists. It just hasn’t been used at anywhere near the scale China’s numbers demand.

The stakes of inaction, however, have significant implications. Estimates show that a full Chinese export restriction on rare-earth metals could cost $6.5 trillion outside China, on top of severing the supply chains behind precision-guided missiles and other advanced defense platforms the United States has relied on for decades. Despite growing awareness of the problem, current investment is not close to sufficient: by 2035, existing and announced rare-earth projects are projected to supply less than half of global mining demand outside China, a quarter of refining demand, and less than a fifth of magnet-production demand. Closing that gap is estimated to require roughly $60 billion in investment over the next decade.

In 2010, China restricted its rare-earth exports, and prices spiked. Western companies rushed to take advantage, including reopening Mountain Pass, an old mine in California. Then China lifted the restrictions, prices collapsed back down, and by 2015 the company that reopened Mountain Pass, Molycorp, was bankrupt. Its stock had gone from $79 a share to 35 cents. China didn’t have to invade anyone or break any laws. It just let the market do the work, because it could set the price low enough to make new competitors unprofitable.

The Pentagon’s answer to this, so far, has been a deal with MP Materials, the company that now owns Mountain Pass. In 2025, the Department of Defense agreed to guarantee that MP Materials would get paid at least $110 for every kilogram of a key rare-earth material it sells, no matter what China does to the market price. If the market price falls below that, the government covers the difference. The government also promised to buy all the magnets from MP’s new factory for ten years. In plain terms: Washington removed the incentive for China to simply crash the price and wait for the American company to go under again.

What a Real Strategy Would Require

DFC financing should be tied to an integrated supply-chain strategy rather than treated as an end in itself. Mine finance should be paired with guaranteed non-Chinese processing and logistics, as well as direct investment in Western separation and magnet manufacturing. Long-term offtake agreements and price protections can give producers the certainty needed to survive market manipulation. African partners, meanwhile, should receive meaningful local processing and economic benefits rather than serving solely as sources of raw material.

Without these elements, individual mining investments remain commercially exposed, single-purpose bets rather than components of a secure supply chain. A mine with no refining outlet and no magnet buyer is still, functionally, a supplier to China.

Congress has already given DFC room to act. Its December 2025 reauthorization raised its lending and investment ceiling from $60 billion to $205 billion and created a critical-minerals exception allowing investment in Five Eyes countries. That matters because much of the missing separation, refining, and magnet capacity needs to be built in allied countries with advanced economies. With the money and authorization to fund a new supply chain, DFC now faces a choice rather than a legal obstacle.

The Bottom Line

In what amounts to a second great-power competition, the winners will not be the countries that own the most mines. They will be the ones that pair extraction with effective governance, resilient infrastructure, and integrated processing capacity. China’s 91% share of global refined rare-earth output and 94% share of magnet production make clear that mining investment alone will not deliver the supply-chain resilience the United States is after.

The United States should measure critical-mineral security by how much of the resulting supply chain can operate independently of China, not by how many foreign mines it has financed. Africa can be a genuine pillar of American rare-earth diversification, but only if Washington connects extraction to processing, purchasing, price protection, manufacturing, and local value creation. Absent that, the United States risks changing where rare earths come out of the ground without changing who controls them before they reach American industry.

text:
🚨🎮 SONY'S INTEGRITY IS ON TRIAL. GAMERS ARE BRINGING THE RECEIPTS! ⚖️

Let's talk about Sony's integrity for a sec. What we're witnessing today raises some uncomfortable questions about the direction PlayStation has taken over the last decade.

Remember when backwards compatibility was supposedly too difficult? When Sony executives questioned whether gamers even wanted to play their older games?

I do.

In 2017, former PlayStation executive Jim Ryan questioned why anyone would want to play those old PS1 and PS2 games.

Well, Jim, apparently quite a few people! 😂

Jump to 2026.

Independent developers and the homebrew community are demonstrating capabilities on jailbroken PS5 consoles that Sony never offered its customers. PS2 disc experiments, emulation, alternative operating systems, and even efforts to get PS3 games running.

Not everything works. Some projects are experimental. But the progress is real, and it doesn't appear to be slowing down.

Here's where I have a problem.

For years, gamers have been offered remasters, rereleases, subscriptions, and opportunities to purchase older titles again. Meanwhile, much of the original PlayStation library is inaccessible through native backwards compatibility on modern consoles.

Was that a technical limitation? A business decision? Or some combination of both?🤔

@Sony gamers deserve an answer.

When independent developers begin accomplishing things that a multibillion-dollar corporation won't provide, people are going to question that corporation's priorities.

Now. Ownership.

Sony can establish terms for accessing PlayStation Network and enforce its intellectual property rights. But Sony cannot physically move into your living room and dictate every modification you make to hardware you purchased.

There are legal limitations and consequences, of course. Circumventing technological protections can raise separate legal issues, and modifying a console can result in losing access to PlayStation services.

Let me be clear. I DO NOT condone piracy.

Copyrighted material deserves legal protection. Devs deserve compensation for their work. Jailbreaking and emulation are not automatically piracy, and neither gives anyone a free pass to distribute or download copyrighted games without authorization.

Gamers need to understand the risks involved.

But none of that excuses Sony from answering legitimate questions about consumer choice, game preservation, and the restrictions placed on hardware and software.

And the silence?

DEAFENING.

I'm beginning to wonder whether there's a run on blood pressure medication at PlayStation headquarters. I suspect a few executives are discovering what happens when gamers start asking questions they would rather not answer. 🤣

But seriously..

I'm just going to say it.

Sony, I think your refusal to openly confront these concerns is cowardly.

You've spent years building an ecosystem where you control the storefront, the services, and much of the customer's access to their purchases.

Now gamers find alternatives, and the company that once questioned the value of older games is watching enthusiasts demonstrate just how much that gaming history still matters.

Sony deserves credit for the backwards compatibility it has delivered, particularly with PS4 games on PS5. But that doesn't erase the generations left behind.

And when the chickens come home to roost?

Crickets. 🦗

Sony, we aren't asking for miracles. We're asking for honesty, transparency, and choices.

You can disagree with gamers. You can defend your business model. You can explain the technical challenges.

But you cannot expect people to stop asking questions simply because you refuse to answer them.👈

Sony, wake up! The barbarians are at the gates!
