National Liqueur Day🍒🥃⭐🥃🍹🍸🥃‧₊˚ 🥂⋅♡𓂃 ࣪ ִֶָ☾.

A unique category in the world of alcoholic beverages, liqueur is a distilled spirit. Though the name is similar (and it is sometimes even made from liquor), liqueur is different from liquor in that it is sweeter.

Liqueurs are mainly used as a flavoring agent in mixed drinks and they also may be enjoyed as after dinner drinks. National Liqueur Day offers a time to learn about and celebrate everything related to this delicious category of drinks!

Fortified spirits have a history that goes way back to at least 400 BC when the Egyptians would use distilled wine to produce beverages. Sometimes they were mixed with honey, which would produce mead in the same process that is still used today.

As it turns out, the word liqueur comes from the Latin word “liquifacere” which means to liquefy. Other names for liqueurs might include cordials or schnapps.

Today, in order to be categorized as a liqueur, the sugar content must reach a minimum of 2.5%, which is why it is often served as a dessert drink. Some of the most popular and well-known liqueurs of today include Kahlúa, Baileys Irish Cream, Amaretto, Crème de menthe, Angostura Bitters, Limoncello and many others.

Basilica of San Clemente stands in Rome, Italy. San Clemente is one of Rome’s most complete encounters with the layers of Christian memory. The present twelfth-century basilica stands above a fourth-century church, which itself rests over Roman buildings. A pilgrim can descend from living liturgy through early medieval frescoes toward the physical world in which Rome’s first Christian communities took shape. The basilica is also a major shrine of saints. The relics traditionally identified with Pope St. Clement I and St. Ignatius of Antioch are venerated beneath the high altar. In the lower basilica, pilgrims visit the traditional tomb of St. Cyril, the ninth-century missionary who, with his brother Methodius, brought Scripture and liturgy to the Slavic peoples in their own language. Cyril died in Rome in 869 and was buried here at Methodius’s request. His relics were removed for safekeeping during the French occupation and largely lost; a surviving fragment was solemnly returned in the twentieth century and is venerated in the upper church. The official basilica explains that Cyril and Methodius had earlier brought St. Clement’s relics from Crimea to Rome. An eleventh-century fresco in the lower church shows the solemn transfer. Nearby wall paintings form one of Rome’s richest surviving early-medieval cycles, while still deeper rooms preserve a Roman house, a Mithraic sanctuary, and flowing underground water. Come first for prayer, not archaeology alone. Honor Clement’s witness, Ignatius’s journey toward martyrdom, and Cyril’s missionary intelligence; then descend slowly enough to see how successive Christian generations built literally upon what they had received. Excavation access is ticketed and opening times differ from worship hours, so consult the basilica before travel. San Clemente is one of Rome’s most complete encounters with the layers of Christian memory. Its connection with Feast of Saints Cyril and Methodius gives pilgrims a specific reason to understand the people, prayer, history, and present-day community gathered here.

Each year, this place comes into sharper focus through Feast of Saints Cyril and Methodius on 02-14 and Feast of Saint Clement I on 11-23. The observance gives pilgrims a reason to return to the story and to the community that still keeps it. Anyone planning a visit should confirm the current program with the shrine, parish, or diocese, because Masses, processions, access routes, and crowd arrangements can change even when the annual commemoration remains the same.

The saints connected with this destination are St. Clement I — relics traditionally venerated beneath the high altar and patron of the basilica, St. Cyril — traditional tomb in the lower basilica and surviving relic fragment in the upper church, and St. Ignatius of Antioch — relics traditionally venerated beneath the high altar. Those relationships matter: a patron, founder, visitor, martyr, relic, and tomb do not tell the same story. Here the saint is not a name added to a building. A Christian life becomes visible through an altar, a road, a burial place, a community, or a landscape where faith was actually practiced.

It separately records Relics traditionally identified with St. Clement I and St. Ignatius of Antioch — Longstanding ecclesial tradition and Surviving relic fragment of St. Cyril — Ecclesiastically received and enshrined. That distinction matters. Church recognition, ecclesiastical custody, public devotion, local tradition, archaeology, and tourism promotion do not all answer the same question. Saying plainly what is known—and what remains a received tradition—protects the truth without taking the wonder out of the story.

Pray first in the living upper basilica, then descend through the fourth-century church to St. Cyril’s traditional tomb and the earliest layers of Christian Rome. The destination guide identifies St. Cyril’s traditional tomb: Honor the Apostle of the Slavs in the lower basilica where he was buried in 869., Clement and Ignatius at the high altar: Venerate the two early martyr-bishops traditionally associated with the basilica’s principal relics., The fresco of St. Clement’s translation: Read the eleventh-century image of Cyril, Methodius, and Pope Adrian II bringing Clement’s relics into the church., and Three levels of Roman memory: Descend from the medieval basilica through an early Christian church to Roman structures below.. A good visit does not treat these as boxes to check. Begin with the devotional or historical center, notice the details around it, and then leave room for worship or quiet reflection. A photograph can preserve the look of a moment; pilgrimage needs enough time for the meaning of the place to settle in.

For travelers who cannot come soon, the story still has value. Learning about Basilica of San Clemente can widen the mental map of the Church and make prayer less abstract. It reminds us that Catholic life is being lived in communities we may never see firsthand. That is not a substitute for local knowledge or for an eventual visit, but it is a beginning. Read the official source, remember the community by name, and let the destination become part of how you imagine the worldwide Church at prayer.

Excavations require a ticket and may use timed entry. Dress for a church, respect liturgies, and do not describe the surviving Cyril relic as his complete body. The official source should outrank an old itinerary, especially during feast days, restoration work, seasonal closures, or major pilgrimages. Entry to the main church also may not include every chapel, relic, museum room, or devotional area connected with its history.

Catholic sacred places hold time differently. At Basilica of San Clemente, the past is not preserved simply because it is old. Memory remains active when people continue to worship, keep a feast, tell the story carefully, and hand a place to the next generation. This is why current visitor information matters alongside history. A church is not a museum that happens to contain an altar, and a shrine is not scenery arranged for a traveler. The visitor enters an existing life of prayer. Respecting services, silence, local custom, and access rules is one way of acknowledging that living continuity.

For anyone who wants to go deeper, the source trail begins with https://t.co/zJGjUfeztc and was last reviewed on 2026-10-09. That matters because sacred places are living places. A custodian may change hours, clarify a tradition, restore a chapel, or publish better evidence. When that happens, the story should change too. Good research is not a badge placed on a finished post; it is a promise to keep listening to the people responsible for the place.

The geography matters. Rome, Italy is not a generic setting into which a Catholic story was dropped. Language, landscape, political history, local art, and the endurance of a particular community shape how the faith became visible here. A responsible story resists flattening those details into a universal postcard. Catholicity is universal precisely because it is received in actual cultures. The same Gospel takes root in mountain roads, crowded cities, coastal settlements, mission landscapes, and parish neighborhoods without making those places interchangeable.

Beautiful sites are especially vulnerable to being consumed quickly. At Basilica of San Clemente, the challenge is to let beauty perform its older work: not self-display, but direction. Stone, wood, paint, light, landscape, and ritual can direct attention toward mysteries they do not contain or control. Even when the artistic achievement is extraordinary, Christian art remains most intelligible in relation to worship. The pilgrim can admire the maker’s skill while asking what truth the work was meant to confess and what kind of life that confession invites.

Let Feast of Saints Cyril and Methodius lead beyond historical curiosity. Approach Basilica of San Clemente with gratitude, verify the current liturgical program before travel, and ask what concrete act of prayer, conversion, service, or remembrance this place invites. A feast can tell us when to remember, but it cannot do the remembering for us. Let the history become prayer, gratitude, repentance, service, or one concrete act of charity. Before leaving the story, choose one detail worth carrying with you and remember the living community behind it. If you share it, tell it with the same care you would hope a visitor would bring to a place you love: without exaggeration, without contempt for honest questions, and without losing sight of the people who still pray there. Whether the journey happens soon or remains a hope for later, pray for the people who keep this place and approach it with confidence and humility. The goal is not another saved location, but a deeper encounter with Christ and His Church.

text:
The Window Seat

Takumi had reserved seat 12A three weeks ago. It was the Tokyo-to-Kyoto trip, a Friday, and he had paid extra to pick the window. After a week of back-to-back client meetings, it was the one small thing he’d promised himself.

When he reached row 12, a man was already in it. Mid-thirties, tired eyes, a toddler asleep against his chest, one small shoe dangling off her foot. A woman beside him held a diaper bag and a half-eaten rice ball.

“That’s my seat,” Takumi said in English.

The man blinked. “?”

Great. He doesn’t even understand. “Do you have a ticket?”

The man looked at the number above the window, then at Takumi, then at his phone. “This is your seat,” he said slowly, in careful English. “Yes. I know. I am sorry.”

Then move. Takumi stood there with his bag on his shoulder, waiting.

The man didn’t move. He just looked at the sleeping girl, then at the aisle.

A younger man in the three-seat row across the aisle leaned over and pointed to an empty seat. “Excuse me. There is a free seat here, on the aisle. Maybe you could sit there?”

Takumi stared at it. An aisle seat, next to a stranger, in a group that was clearly all together. He could already picture the next two hours: polite small talk, shared snacks, someone’s elbow.

“No,” he said. “I want the window.”

Nobody argued. The man just nodded, very slightly, the way people do when they’ve decided a fight isn’t worth the energy, and began to shift. The girl stirred and whimpered. The woman reached over to steady her head. It took a full minute, and the whole car watched.

Takumi sat down by the window and pulled out his laptop. He had won.

Somewhere past Shizuoka, he glanced at the aisle. The father was now in the seat the younger man had offered, rigid, arm stretched out at an awkward angle so the girl could keep sleeping across two laps. His mother-in-law, or whoever she was, had taken the seat beside him, and the others had quietly rearranged themselves around the child like a small fence.

Takumi realized, slowly, what the seating chart had really looked like. They hadn’t been trying to steal a window. Whoever booked their tickets had been unable to get seven seats together, and the sleeping child had been moved to wherever she could rest on someone. The man had said “I am sorry” and “This is your seat.” He had never once said it was theirs.

And Takumi had heard “Do you have a ticket?” in his own voice, and the tone he’d used to say it.

He watched the fields slide by. The window was lovely: a flat gold light, a mountain with its top just hidden in cloud. He couldn’t enjoy it.

At Nagoya, the man stood to stretch his back. Takumi took off his headphones.

“Excuse me,” he said. The man turned, wary. “Your daughter. She can have this seat. For the rest of the way. Please.”

“No, no,” the man said. “It is your seat.”

“I know,” Takumi said. “That’s why I can give it.”

A pause. Then the man’s whole face changed, softened, and he said something in his own language to the woman, who covered her mouth. They moved the girl over carefully, still asleep, and she curled against the window with one hand on the glass.

Takumi took the aisle seat. The younger man from across the aisle, whose name turned out to be Marek, leaned over and offered him a small paper bag of pretzels without a word.

They did talk, a little. Not much. Takumi’s English was rusty and Marek’s Japanese was four phrases long. It was awkward, and it was fine.

When the train pulled into Kyoto, the girl woke up, rubbed her eyes, and waved at him with her whole arm.

He waved back.

What stayed with me:

Being in the right is not the same as being right to insist. A ticket gives you the claim to a seat. It doesn’t tell you what it costs the person you’re claiming it from, and sometimes the generous thing is to look at that cost before you decide how hard to hold on.

 assuming someone doesn’t understand you is often just a way of avoiding what they’re actually saying.

❤️ She Was Eating Stale Bread Because There Was No Flour Left. Then the Police Arrived…

In a remote village of Agra, an elderly woman named Bhuri Devi lives alone in a small hut on a farmer's land.

Her son works in Ahmedabad, while she struggles to meet her daily needs.

When ACP Imran Ahmed and the Dauki police team reached her hut under the Mission Shakti campaign, they discovered her difficult circumstances.

🏠 She had been surviving on stale bread because there was no flour left to prepare fresh food.

The officers brought her rations, vegetables and a new sari.

But what Bhuri Devi revealed next was heartbreaking.

🚔 When she first saw the police vehicle, she became frightened. She thought the officers had come to evict her from the hut.

She also recalled feeling ashamed after once drinking water at a police station, as though she had done something wrong.

ACP Imran Ahmed reassured her: “Don't worry, the police won't remove you.”

When she requested a small piece of land to build her own hut, he spoke to the village head and assured her that he would look into the matter.

He also promised to discuss arrangements for monthly wheat and rice supplies.

👮‍♂️ The visit was part of the Mission Shakti campaign being implemented across Agra's police stations on the instructions of Police Commissioner Deepak Kumar.

For Bhuri Devi, the officers brought more than food and clothing. They offered reassurance, listened to her concerns and showed that the police could be a source of support rather than fear.

Sometimes, the most meaningful act of public service begins with listening to someone who feels forgotten. ❤️

Every kanji is a tiny story.

休
A person (亻) leaning against a tree (木).
It means "rest."

America doesn't have kanji.
So I made some.
(Not real. Yet.)

車 + 口
car + mouth
= drive-thru
A car that eats.

火 + 肉 + 父
fire + meat + father
= backyard barbecue
Do not approach. Do not offer advice. He knows.

雪 + 手 + 隣
snow + hand + neighbor
= shoveling your neighbor's driveway before he wakes up
He will never find out who did it. He will do yours next week.

日 + 球 + 祭
sun + ball + festival
= Sunday
Church at 9. Kickoff at 1. Both are mandatory.

犬 + 門 + 心
dog + gate + heart
= the dog waiting at the door when you come home
English doesn't have a word for this. Now it has a kanji.

星 + 布 + 胸
star + cloth + chest
= the hand that goes over the heart when the flag passes by
Nobody teaches you this one. You just know.

And now, a real one.

In Japanese, the kanji for America is 米.

It means rice.

Not because of rice. A long time ago, Japan spelled "America" with sounds, and the "me" sound got this character. It stuck.

So officially, in my country, you are the Rice Country.

You're welcome. 🍚

text:
The expansion of the early United States to the Rocky Mountains was almost halted by a sudden bout of buyer's remorse from one of history's greatest military strategists. In the spring of 1803, Napoleon Bonaparte came close to tearing up the treaty that would double the territory of the American republic.

American envoys James Monroe and Robert Livingston had arrived in Paris with instructions only to purchase New Orleans and parts of Florida. To their absolute astonishment, Napoleon's ministers offered to sell the entire Louisiana Territory, a vast wilderness of over 800,000 square miles, because France was broke and facing an imminent war with Great Britain.

However, as the negotiation drafted toward its final days, Napoleon began to second-guess his decision. His brothers, Lucien and Joseph, desperately pleaded with him not to surrender France's empire in the New World. They even confronted Napoleon in his bath, sparking a furious argument where the leader splashed water all over his brothers in rage, refusing to back down.

Furthermore, the American negotiators faced a severe crisis of authority. President Thomas Jefferson had no constitutional permission to acquire such vast foreign territories, and federalist opponents in Congress strongly condemned the deal. Any delay in signing would have given Napoleon the perfect excuse to cancel the arrangement.

Livingston and Monroe decided to bypass the constitutional doubts and signed the landmark treaty on April 30, 1803, before France could change its mind. This bold initiative prevented the territory from returning to Spanish control or being conquered by the British fleet, permanently securing America's westward destiny.

text:
A very interesting short story: I showed my fiance's parents my family picture, then they told me the wedding is off

I (m, 24) met my fiance, Christina (f, 23) 2 years ago when I visited my mom's home country, the Philippines to spend time with my grand parents. We were in the same flight, started to talk about our lives and I found out that she was also going home for a 2-weeks vacation to see her parents living in the Philippines. I fell in love with her that day. That flight was the beginning of our perfect relationship that continued when we both got back in the States.

She was, in lack of a better word, a perfect partner. Shes beautiful, caring, and loving. Yes, we had disagreements but we never had any big arguments that she didn't talk to me about to fix before we end our day.

We both live in California, different cities but I decided to move in with her a year after we started dating since it is easier for me to find jobs because of my line of work.

Fast forward to 6 months ago, I decided I was going to propose to her. I've contacted her parents in the Philippines to ask for permission (I was close to them at this point as I've met them several times when they visited my fiance, and constantly talk to them whenever they call my fiance) and my STBMIL was so happy when she heard. They both gave me their blessings, their only condition is that they will take care of all wedding preparations and expenses to make sure their only daughter gets the wedding she deserves. I did not oppose to it.

I then planned to do the proposal and timed it to when her parents would be around for their annual visit. Her mom was crying when I asked Christina to marry me and she said yes. This was 2 months ago.

My fiance dreamed to have a fall wedding so we set the date for an october wedding. My parents live in Sedona, Arizona and owns an inn that could accommodate the number of people we plan to invite. As a wedding gift, they reserved 3 days for our wedding. They have met my fiance whenever we visited Sedona for the holidays and my mom loves her like her own daughter.

Last night while meeting her parents for dinner, I and my fiance told them that they do not have to worry about the location, that my parents offered their inn for 3 days as a gift. They then realized that they've never met my parents and asked when will they get to meet them? Apparently, traditionally, grooms parents are supposed to be around during proposal but my mother was sick and could not do long travels. I explained to them her medical situation and remembered I have my parents picture in my wallet and showed it to them.

My STBMIL looked confused and whispered to STBFIL "why does she look familiar?" pointing at my mom. And then her eyes got bigger and looked worried at my STBFIL. My STBFIL, at first I thought he was just expressionless, but then I saw anger in his eyes. He stood up, told my fiance there will be no more wedding, and walked away, STBMIL followed. I and fiance both were clueless and shocked at what happened.

Today she decided to go see them alone to talk to them and find out the reason why her father reacted that way. Its been a full day and I haven't heard from her since this morning. Talking to my best friend, he suggested our parents might have known each other, or they might have been lovers. I don't know. I'm so confused and don't know what to do.

text:
"Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸 (a poem)

And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.
Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.
I am Palestinian. 

I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

$SNDL CATALYST UPDATE: The Reverse Split Is Defeated, Record Free Cash Flow Hits, and Management Launches a C$50M Premium Tender Offer.

The October 15, 2026 shareholder meeting marks an official turning point for SNDL’s capital allocation strategy. Retail investors delivered an unmistakable message: fix the valuation through an aggressive return of real capital, not through artificial share consolidation.

Here is the objective breakdown of the regulatory mechanics, the SIB timeline, the earnings setup, and what this means for shareholders.

1. THE REVERSE SPLIT DEFEAT: SHAREHOLDERS TAKE THE REINS
Management proposed a special resolution for a share consolidation to address Nasdaq listing optics. Under Canadian corporate law, this required a 66.7% (two-thirds) supermajority. It received only 54.1%. 
The consolidation is officially dead. Instead of forcing paper engineering, CEO Zach George and the Board listened to the shareholder mandate: deploy the balance sheet to defend the stock price organically.

2. THE C$50M SUBSTANTIAL ISSUER BID (SIB) EXPLAINED
To accelerate value return, the Board directed management to pursue a Substantial Issuer Bid (tender offer) up to C$50M (~$35.5M USD) at a price up to C$1.92 CAD ($1.35 USD)—a 17.4% premium over the market price.
• Float Impact: With 243.8M shares outstanding, a full C$50M deployment at C$1.92 retires up to ~26.04M shares—erasing roughly 10.7% of the entire company float in a single corporate action.
• Cumulative Repurchases: This builds directly on the 21.8M shares (C$43.4M) SNDL already repurchased over the last 12 months. Together, SNDL is on track to eliminate nearly 48M shares (~20% of its float) in ~15 months.

3. THE REGULATORY TIMELINE: SEC & CANADIAN PROTOCOLS
Why can't the SIB launch tomorrow? Cross-border securities regulations dictate the timeline:
• The Earnings Gate: Under SEC Rule 13e-4 and Canadian NI 62-104, an issuer cannot launch a tender offer while in possession of Material Non-Public Information (MNPI). SNDL must report its official Q3 2026 earnings first to cleanse the market.
• Launch & Tender Window: Once Q3 results are filed, SNDL submits an Issuer Bid Circular on SEDAR+ and a Schedule TO with the SEC. Cross-border rules mandate the tender offer remain open for a minimum of 35 calendar days.
• Execution & Settlement: Shareholders tender their shares, the offer closes, and SNDL takes up and cancels the shares within 3-10 business days.
• Total Duration: Expect formal launch post-Q3 earnings, with completion requiring approximately 45 to 60 days.

4. PRELIMINARY Q3 EARNINGS & THE C$10.6M CASH SURGE
SNDL pre-announced expected Q3 Free Cash Flow of ~C$20M—the highest quarterly free cash flow in company history. 
• The Driver: FCF benefited from ~C$10.6M from unwinding the captive insurance structure (net of premiums), alongside operational working capital gains.
• Cash Flow vs. EPS Reality: Unwinding captive insurance releases restricted collateral back into operating cash. While this provides pure, unencumbered liquidity to easily fund the C$50M SIB without taking on debt, investors should note this is primarily a cash balance sheet enhancement rather than a pure recurring operating EPS gain. However, lower ongoing insurance overhead and cash generation provide substantial fundamental support.

5. STRATEGIC EXPANSION: PARALLEL & DOMESTIC OPTIMIZATION
While the buyback takes center stage, SNDL significantly strengthened its operational core:
• Parallel Ownership to 92%: Increased its indirect stake from 67% to 92% via a rights offering, funding a state-of-the-art Gainesville cultivation facility to feed 56 U.S. dispensaries ahead of federal medical integration.
• Ontario AGCO Settlement: Resolved outstanding regulatory issues for a minor $200k fine, transitioning to a franchise/third-party model that preserves net economics.
• Exiting Unprofitable Flower: Exiting low-margin domestic dried flower to focus strictly on high-margin retail and concentrates.

THE BOTTOM LINE
SNDL is a debt-free parent company generating record quarterly cash flow, buying back over 10% of its float at a 17.4% premium, and expanding its U.S. footprint to 92% ownership. The era of dilution is completely over. The era of aggressive capital return has begun.

text:
The highest ROI skill in business is financially exploiting people who are in a state of absolute panic.

It sounds evil, but it is exactly how my stores cleared over $1,000,000 last Q4 alone.

90% of beginners fail because they try to sell a $30 "Best Dad" coffee mug to a 50-year-old dad.

He doesn't care. He isn't buying it.

You don't sell to the end user. You sell to the Gift Buyer.

You sell that exact same mug to his 22-year-old daughter who is in a state of sheer panic 4 days before Father's Day because she forgot to buy a present.

When you do product research, you always have to think the second level: Who is actually pulling out their credit card?

1. Prove demand
I use Kalodata to find products selling 1,000+ units a month.

2. Read the 5-Star Reviews
Don't look at the product photos. Look at the buyer comments. "My husband laughed so hard" or "Got this for my boss." Now you know exactly who is panicking to buy this.

3. Limit the options
When you give customers too many options, they make none. Don't offer 14 colors. Offer black and white. Make the buying decision take under two minutes so they can relieve their panic immediately.

I don't reinvent the wheel. I just find out who is desperate for a gift, and put a better version right in front of them.

I'm breaking down exactly how I find these winning products on a free training this Tuesday. Link in bio.

text:
64 years ago today, President Kennedy sat down with his advisers over U-2 spy plane photos of Soviet nuclear missile sites going up in Cuba.

His advisers split. The State Department's historians say some, including all of the Joint Chiefs, argued for an air strike followed by an invasion, while others favored stern warnings. Kennedy kept them arguing in private for days. On Oct 22 he took a middle course and ordered a naval quarantine. The word was chosen on purpose. Legally, a blockade assumed a state of war and a quarantine did not, and that choice helped the U.S. get the backing of the Organization of American States, the group of governments across the Americas.

Firmness alone didn't end it. On Oct 27 an American U-2 was shot down over Cuba, and Kennedy's team prepared for an attack on Cuba within days while still searching for a diplomatic way out. Khrushchev had sent two messages. The first offered to remove the missiles in exchange for a promise not to invade Cuba. The second also demanded U.S. missiles out of Turkey. Kennedy chose to answer the first, pledging no invasion if the missiles came out under UN supervision. That night Robert Kennedy privately told the Soviet ambassador the U.S. was already planning to remove its missiles from Turkey soon, but that this could not be part of any public deal. Khrushchev agreed the next morning. The Turkey missiles came out the following April.

The State Department's historians also describe miscalculations and miscommunications during the crisis. My view is that good judgment alone didn't guarantee this ending. What Kennedy controlled was how he decided.

When someone says a problem has to be hit right now, ask how long you actually have, and use that time to hear the people who disagree. When the other side gives you more than one offer, answer the one you can live with, and leave them a way to step back.

text:
Okay Marketing people, it's time for some tough love.

52 cents.

That's what it could cost you to find 50 new target persona contact details at target companies that show signs of needing to buy what your company offers. (think right time for a call)

Literally 52 cents.

No LinkedIn Sales Navigator, ZoomInfo, Apollo, or Clay subscriptions.

There aren't excuses anymore for:

❌ Spending thousands of dollars on lists full of junk and lobbing them to sales
❌ Creating lists from a CRM where 60% of your data is bad
❌ Sending over un-enriched trade show lists and calling them "MQLs"
❌ Buying an over-priced subscription to put a band-aid on outdated GTM efforts

I don't care how big or small your company is. It's time to start evolving your thinking and understanding that you have the tools at your disposal to do this a different way. 

Example workflow. Build an AI agent system with Claude or ChatGPT to:

✅  Find a free complete roster, like a state license file or a federal registry. 
✅  Add a dated public signal, like a new hire, new location, or new license. 
✅  Then find the contact email and check it before anyone sends.

None of that needs a five-figure platform. This is GTM architecting or GTM engineering.

I found 250 valid contacts and emails for people at companies showing signs of being ready to buy for a customer yesterday from my Claude desktop app (with APIs) for under $10.

It's possible! 

Marketing's job is handing sales people who have a reason to buy now and an inbox that works.

What's one expensive GTM subscription you're paying for now that could be replaced?

text:
Elon Musk left South Africa at 17 years old and arrived in Canada with a small bag, a few hundred dollars, and the address of a relative he had never met. The relative was not at the address. The house was empty. His first night in the country he was supposed to build his life in began with a closed door and nowhere to sleep.

He had left South Africa to avoid mandatory military service in the apartheid era army. The choice was serve a government he considered morally bankrupt or leave everything and start over in a country where he knew almost no one. He left. At 17. Alone.

The first months in Canada were spent doing manual labor. He worked at a lumber yard. He shoveled grain. He cleaned boilers at a lumber mill. The boiler cleaning job was described by his cousin as "the most physically disgusting work available" because it involved climbing inside industrial boilers and scraping sludge in confined spaces. He was paid $18 per hour, which was the highest wage he could find, and he took it because the money mattered more than the conditions.

The distance between cleaning industrial boilers at 17 and running 6 companies at 53 is not a metaphor for the American dream. It is a literal account of what a 17 year old was willing to endure to escape a country that offered him nothing but violence at school, indifference at home, and conscription into an army he refused to serve.

He has rarely spoken about the Canada period in detail. The vulnerability is too raw. The story of a teenager arriving at an empty house in a foreign country with no plan except "not South Africa" does not fit the image of the calculated visionary. The visionary came later. The teenager was just surviving.

The man who calculates orbital trajectories began by calculating which Canadian city had the cheapest rent. The ambition scaled. The survival instinct that launched it did not come from a boardroom. It came from a boiler.

the German village of Salzeneck. The best quarters in the village were
assigned to cavalry-captain Denísov, the squadron commander, known
throughout the whole cavalry division as Váska Denísov. Cadet Rostóv,
ever since he had overtaken the regiment in Poland, had lived with the
squadron commander.

On October 11, the day when all was astir at headquarters over the news
of Mack’s defeat, the camp life of the officers of this squadron was
proceeding as usual. Denísov, who had been losing at cards all night,
had not yet come home when Rostóv rode back early in the morning from
a foraging expedition. Rostóv in his cadet uniform, with a jerk to his
horse, rode up to the porch, swung his leg over the saddle with a supple
youthful movement, stood for a moment in the stirrup as if loathe to
part from his horse, and at last sprang down and called to his orderly.

“Ah, Bondarénko, dear friend!” said he to the hussar who rushed up
headlong to the horse. “Walk him up and down, my dear fellow,” he
continued, with that gay brotherly cordiality which goodhearted young
people show to everyone when they are happy.

“Yes, your excellency,” answered the Ukrainian gaily, tossing his
head.

“Mind, walk him up and down well!”

Another hussar also rushed toward the horse, but Bondarénko had already
thrown the reins of the snaffle bridle over the horse’s head. It was
evident that the cadet was liberal with his tips and that it paid to
serve him. Rostóv patted the horse’s neck and then his flank, and
lingered for a moment.

“Splendid! What a horse he will be!” he thought with a smile, and
holding up his saber, his spurs jingling, he ran up the steps of the
porch. His landlord, who in a waistcoat and a pointed cap, pitchfork in
hand, was clearing manure from the cowhouse, looked out, and his face
immediately brightened on seeing Rostóv. “Schön gut Morgen! Schön
gut Morgen!” * he said winking with a merry smile, evidently pleased
to greet the young man.

    * “A very good morning! A very good morning!”

“Schon fleissig?” * said Rostóv with the same gay brotherly smile
which did not leave his eager face. “Hoch Oestreicher! Hoch Russen!
Kaiser Alexander hoch!” *(2) said he, quoting words often repeated by
the German landlord.

    * “Busy already?”

    * (2) “Hurrah for the Austrians! Hurrah for the Russians!
     Hurrah for Emperor Alexander!”

The German laughed, came out of the cowshed, pulled off his cap, and
waving it above his head cried:

“Und die ganze Welt hoch!” *

    * “And hurrah for the whole world!”

Rostóv waved his cap above his head like the German and cried laughing,
“Und vivat die ganze Welt!” Though neither the German cleaning his
cowshed nor Rostóv back with his platoon from foraging for hay had any
reason for rejoicing, they looked at each other with joyful delight and
brotherly love, wagged their heads in token of their mutual affection,
and parted smiling, the German returning to his cowshed and Rostóv
going to the cottage he occupied with Denísov.

“What about your master?” he asked Lavrúshka, Denísov’s orderly,
whom all the regiment knew for a rogue.

“Hasn’t been in since the evening. Must have been losing,”
answered Lavrúshka. “I know by now, if he wins he comes back early to
brag about it, but if he stays out till morning it means he’s lost and
will come back in a rage. Will you have coffee?”

“Yes, bring some.”

Ten minutes later Lavrúshka brought the coffee. “He’s coming!”
said he. “Now for trouble!” Rostóv looked out of the window and
saw Denísov coming home. Denísov was a small man with a red face,
sparkling black eyes, and black tousled mustache and hair. He wore an
unfastened cloak, wide breeches hanging down in creases, and a crumpled
shako on the back of his head. He came up to the porch gloomily, hanging
his head.

“Lavwúska!” he shouted loudly and angrily, “take it off,
blockhead!”

“Well, I am taking it off,” replied Lavrúshka’s voice.

“Ah, you’re up already,” said Denísov, entering the room.

“Long ago,” answered Rostóv, “I have already been for the hay,
and have seen Fräulein Mathilde.”

“Weally! And I’ve been losing, bwother. I lost yesterday like a
damned fool!” cried Denísov, not pronouncing his r’s. “Such ill
luck! Such ill luck. As soon as you left, it began and went on. Hullo
there! Tea!”

Puckering up his face though smiling, and showing his short strong
teeth, he began with stubby fingers of both hands to ruffle up his thick
tangled black hair.

“And what devil made me go to that wat?” (an officer nicknamed
“the rat”) he said, rubbing his forehead and whole face with both
hands. “Just fancy, he didn’t let me win a single cahd, not one
cahd.”

He took the lighted pipe that was offered to him, gripped it in his
fist, and tapped it on the floor, making the sparks fly, while he
continued to shout.

“He lets one win the singles and collahs it as soon as one doubles it;
gives the singles and snatches the doubles!”

He scattered the burning tobacco, smashed the pipe, and threw it away.
Then he remained silent for a while, and all at once looked cheerfully
with his glittering, black eyes at Rostóv.

“If at least we had some women here; but there’s nothing foh one
to do but dwink. If we could only get to fighting soon. Hullo, who’s
there?” he said, turning to the door as he heard a tread of heavy
boots and the clinking of spurs that came to a stop, and a respectful
cough.

“The squadron quartermaster!” said Lavrúshka.

Denísov’s face puckered still more.

“Wetched!” he muttered, throwing down a purse with some gold in it.
“Wostóv, deah fellow, just see how much there is left and shove the
purse undah the pillow,” he said, and went out to the quartermaster.

Rostóv took the money and, mechanically arranging the old and new coins
in separate piles, began counting them.

“Ah! Telyánin! How d’ye do? They plucked me last night,” came
Denísov’s voice from the next room.

“Where? At Bykov’s, at the rat’s... I knew it,” replied a piping
voice, and Lieutenant Telyánin, a small officer of the same squadron,
entered the room.

Rostóv thrust the purse under the pillow and shook the damp little hand
which was offered him. Telyánin for some reason had been transferred
from the Guards just before this campaign. He behaved very well in the
regiment but was not liked; Rostóv especially detested him and was
unable to overcome or conceal his groundless antipathy to the man.

“Well, young cavalryman, how is my Rook behaving?” he asked. (Rook
was a young horse Telyánin had sold to Rostóv.)

The lieutenant never looked the man he was speaking to straight in the
face; his eyes continually wandered from one object to another.

“I saw you riding this morning...” he added.

“Oh, he’s all right, a good horse,” answered Rostóv, though the
horse for which he had paid seven hundred rubbles was not worth half
that sum. “He’s begun to go a little lame on the left foreleg,” he
added.

“The hoof’s cracked! That’s nothing. I’ll teach you what to do
and show you what kind of rivet to use.”

“Yes, please do,” said Rostóv.

“I’ll show you, I’ll show you! It’s not a secret. And it’s a
horse you’ll thank me for.”

“Then I’ll have it brought round,” said Rostóv wishing to avoid
Telyánin, and he went out to give the order.

In the passage Denísov, with a pipe, was squatting on the threshold
facing the quartermaster who was reporting to him. On seeing Rostóv,
Denísov screwed up his face and pointing over his shoulder with his
thumb to the room where Telyánin was sitting, he frowned and gave a
shudder of disgust.

“Ugh! I don’t like that fellow,” he said, regardless of the
quartermaster’s presence.

Rostóv shrugged his shoulders as much as to say: “Nor do I, but
what’s one to do?” and, having given his order, he returned to
Telyánin.

Telyánin was sitting in the same indolent pose in which Rostóv had
left him, rubbing his small white hands.

“Well there certainly are disgusting people,” thought Rostóv as he
entered.

“Have you told them to bring the horse?” asked Telyánin, getting up
and looking carelessly about him.

“I have.”

“Let us go ourselves. I only came round to ask Denísov about
yesterday’s order. Have you got it, Denísov?”

“Not yet. But where are you off to?”

“I want to teach this young man how to shoe a horse,” said
Telyánin.

They went through the porch and into the stable. The lieutenant
explained how to rivet the hoof and went away to his own quarters.

When Rostóv went back there was a bottle of vodka and a sausage on the
table. Denísov was sitting there scratching with his pen on a sheet of
paper. He looked gloomily in Rostóv’s face and said: “I am witing
to her.”

He leaned his elbows on the table with his pen in his hand and,
evidently glad of a chance to say quicker in words what he wanted to
write, told Rostóv the contents of his letter.

“You see, my fwiend,” he said, “we sleep when we don’t love. We
are childwen of the dust... but one falls in love and one is a God, one
is pua’ as on the fihst day of cweation... Who’s that now? Send him
to the devil, I’m busy!” he shouted to Lavrúshka, who went up to
him not in the least abashed.

“Who should it be? You yourself told him to come. It’s the
quartermaster for the money.”

Denísov frowned and was about to shout some reply but stopped.

“Wetched business,” he muttered to himself. “How much is left in
the puhse?” he asked, turning to Rostóv.

“Seven new and three old imperials.”

“Oh, it’s wetched! Well, what are you standing there for, you
sca’cwow? Call the quahtehmasteh,” he shouted to Lavrúshka.

“Please, Denísov, let me lend you some: I have some, you know,”
said Rostóv, blushing.

“Don’t like bowwowing from my own fellows, I don’t,” growled
Denísov.

“But if you won’t accept money from me like a comrade, you will
offend me. Really I have some,” Rostóv repeated.

“No, I tell you.”

And Denísov went to the bed to get the purse from under the pillow.

“Where have you put it, Wostóv?”

“Under the lower pillow.”

“It’s not there.”

Denísov threw both pillows on the floor. The purse was not there.

“That’s a miwacle.”

“Wait, haven’t you dropped it?” said Rostóv, picking up the
pillows one at a time and shaking them.

He pulled off the quilt and shook it. The purse was not there.

“Dear me, can I have forgotten? No, I remember thinking that you kept
it under your head like a treasure,” said Rostóv. “I put it just
here. Where is it?” he asked, turning to Lavrúshka.

“I haven’t been in the room. It must be where you put it.”

“But it isn’t?...”

“You’re always like that; you thwow a thing down anywhere and forget
it. Feel in your pockets.”

“No, if I hadn’t thought of it being a treasure,” said Rostóv,
“but I remember putting it there.”

Lavrúshka turned all the bedding over, looked under the bed and under
the table, searched everywhere, and stood still in the middle of the
room.

Below is how each entry on the list is supported using Biblical scripture:

1. Prayers for the Dead (300 AD)
2 Maccabees 12:44–45: "For if he were not expecting that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have been superfluous and foolish to pray for the dead... Therefore he made atonement for the dead, that they might be delivered from their sin."

2. Making the Sign of the Cross (300 AD)
Ezekiel 9:4: God commands an angel to mark the foreheads of the faithful with a mark (Taw, which in ancient Hebrew was written as a cross + or X).

Revelation 7:3 & 14:1: The servants of God receive a seal or mark on their foreheads.

Galatians 6:14: "Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ."

3. Veneration of Angels and Saints (375 AD)
Joshua 5:14: Joshua falls on his face to the earth and worships/venerates the Commander of the Lord's Army (an angel).

Revelation 5:8 & 8:3–4: The elders and angels in Heaven offer the prayers of the saints on Earth before God's throne in golden bowls.

4. Use of Images in Worship (375 AD)
Exodus 25:18–20: God explicitly commands Moses: "And you shall make two cherubim of gold... on the two ends of the mercy seat."

Numbers 21:8–9: God orders the creation of a bronze serpent image to bring healing when looked upon.

1 Kings 6:23–29: Solomon fills the Holy of Holies with carved images of cherubim, palm trees, and flowers.

5. The Mass as a Daily Celebration (394 AD)
Acts 2:46: The early Christians continued "day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes."

Malachi 1:11: Prophesies that a pure sacrifice will be offered continuously among the Gentiles in every place, from the rising of the sun to its setting.

6. Mary as the "Mother of God" (Theotokos) (431 AD)
Luke 1:43: Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, asks: "And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" (Scripture explicitly calls Jesus "Lord" / God, making Mary the mother of Jesus who is God).

Isaiah 7:14 & Matthew 1:23: The Virgin shall bear Emmanuel ("God with us").

7. Extreme Unction / Anointing of the Sick (526 AD)
James 5:14–15: "Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord... and if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven."

Mark 6:13: The apostles "anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them."

8. Doctrine of Purgatory (593 AD / 1439 AD)
1 Corinthians 3:13–15: A person’s work is tested by fire: "If any man's work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire."

Matthew 12:32: Jesus implies sins can be forgiven in the age to come: "it will not be forgiven him, either in this age or in the age to come."

Matthew 5:25–26: Being cast into prison until paying the last penny.

9. Prayers to Mary and Saints (600 AD)
Revelation 5:8: Saints in heaven hold golden bowls of incense, "which are the prayers of the saints" on Earth.

Hebrews 12:1: Believers on Earth are surrounded by a "great cloud of witnesses" (the deceased saints in heaven).

10. Respect for Relics (786 AD)
2 Kings 13:21: A dead man comes back to life immediately upon touching the bones of the prophet Elisha.

Acts 19:11–12: Handkerchiefs or aprons touched by Paul are brought to the sick, curing diseases and casting out demons.

Matthew 9:20–22: A woman is healed merely by touching the fringe of Jesus' garment.

11. Canonization / Recognition of Saints (995 AD)
Hebrews 11: The Bible itself provides an official "canon" or list of holy and faithful heroes of faith.

Psalm 116:15: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints."

12. Celibacy of the Priesthood (1079 AD)
Matthew 19:12: Jesus talks about those who "have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven."

1 Corinthians 7:32–34: Paul advocates celibacy for ministers: "The unmarried man is anxious about the affairs of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly affairs..."

2 Timothy 2:3–4: "No soldier on service gets entangled in civilian pursuits."

13. The Rosary (1090 AD)
The Rosary consists almost entirely of direct Biblical passages:

The Lord’s Prayer (Our Father): Matthew 6:9–13.

The Hail Mary: Luke 1:28 ("Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you") + Luke 1:42 ("Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb").

Meditations: The mysteries focus on the life, death, and resurrection of Christ in the Gospels.

14. Indulgences (1090 AD)
Matthew 16:19 & 18:18: "Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven."

2 Corinthians 2:10: Paul remits temporal penalty in the presence/person of Christ ("what I have forgiven... I have forgiven for your sake in the presence of Christ").

15. Transubstantiation / Adoration of the Eucharist (1215 / 1220 AD)
John 6:53–56: Jesus says, "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you. For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink."

1 Corinthians 11:27–29: Paul warns against receiving unworthily: "Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of profaning the body and blood of the Lord."

16. Confession of Sins to a Priest (1215 AD)
John 20:22–23: Jesus breathes on the Apostles and says, "If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld."

James 5:16: "Therefore confess your sins to one another..."

2 Corinthians 5:18: God gave the apostles the "ministry of reconciliation."

17. "The Cup" / Communion Under One Kind (1416 AD)
1 Corinthians 11:27: "Whoever eats the bread OR drinks the cup..." (indicates receiving Christ in either form alone communicates the full Sacrament).

Luke 24:30–35: At Emmaus, Jesus breaks bread only before disappearing, yet He was fully present.

18. The Seven Sacraments (1439 AD)
All seven sacraments are instituted in the Bible:

Baptism: Matthew 28:19 / John 3:5

Confirmation: Acts 8:14–17

Eucharist: Matthew 26:26–28

Confession: John 20:23

Anointing of the Sick: James 5:14–15

Holy Orders: Luke 22:19 / 2 Timothy 1:6

Matrimony: Matthew 19:4–6 / Ephesians 5:31–32

19. Sacred Tradition Equal with Scripture (1545 AD)
2 Thessalonians 2:15: "So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter."

2 Thessalonians 3:6: "Keep away from any brother who is walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us."

1 Corinthians 11:2: "I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you."

20. "Apocrypha" / Deuterocanonical Books in the Bible (1546 AD)
Historical/Biblical Fact: The Old Testament used by Jesus and the Apostles was the Greek Septuagint (LXX), which contained these books.

Hebrews 11:35: Mentions martyrs being tortured and refusing release to gain a better resurrection—an explicit reference to 2 Maccabees 7, which is in the Deuterocanon.

21. Immaculate Conception of Mary (1854 AD)
Luke 1:28: The Angel Gabriel addresses Mary as Kecharitomene (Greek: "Having been completely filled with grace prior to this moment").

Genesis 3:15: Total enmity placed between the serpent and the woman.

22. Infallibility of the Pope (1870 AD)
Matthew 16:18–19: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church... I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven."

Luke 22:31–32: Jesus says to Peter, "I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers."

John 21:15–17: Jesus charges Peter uniquely: "Feed my lambs... Tend my sheep."

23. Bodily Assumption of Mary (1950 AD)
Revelation 12:1: "A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars."

Biblical Precedents: Enoch (Genesis 5:24) and Elijah (2 Kings 2:11) were assumed bodily into heaven; Saints were raised bodily in Matthew 27:52–53.

24. Mary Proclaimed "Mother of the Church" (1965 AD)
John 19:26–27: At the cross, Jesus says to the beloved disciple (representing all Christians): "Behold, your mother!"

Revelation 12:17: Defines Christians as Mary's children: "Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus."

text:
Imagine being told that a new treatment could help improve your vision by changing how your own cells behave. That is the promise behind an emerging field of research known as cell reprogramming, which scientists are investigating for a range of medical conditions. A report about a human trial describing improved vision after eight weeks has sparked interest because it suggests that changing cellular activity might offer new possibilities for people affected by certain forms of sight loss.

Cells follow biological instructions that influence their function, survival, and responses to their surroundings. Reprogramming techniques aim to alter those instructions or change a cell's behavior in a controlled way. In vision research, scientists are particularly interested in whether these approaches can protect vulnerable retinal cells, improve their function, or support recovery from damage. The retina contains specialized cells that convert light into signals the brain interprets as images. When these cells or their supporting structures are damaged, vision can deteriorate, and some forms of injury are difficult to reverse. The precise technique and diagnosis involved in this particular trial are essential to understanding what the reported improvement means.

There is an important distinction between an encouraging early result and a treatment that has been proven to work broadly. Researchers need to determine how large the improvement was, whether it lasted, what side effects occurred, and whether the benefits were greater than those seen with existing care. Human trials can provide valuable evidence, but their findings need to be confirmed in larger and more diverse groups. People experiencing vision loss should continue seeking advice from qualified eye specialists rather than relying on experimental treatments advertised online. The prospect of helping people see better is genuinely exciting, but the strongest medical breakthroughs are built on reproducible evidence, careful safety monitoring, and results that stand up over time. 👁️

💰 MY 2 CENTS — SCHWAB OPENS THE DOOR TO 40 MILLION ACCOUNTS, WHILE CRYPTO ETFs BLEED
October 16, 2026 | Distribution, flows and what it means for Bitcoin
 
Wall Street is building the biggest on-ramp to crypto in history, and in the same weeks institutional money is walking out of crypto ETFs. Both stories are true. Here is how they fit together, with the hype separated from the facts.
 
1️⃣ THE HEADLINE VS THE FACTS
"JUST IN: $13 trillion Charles Schwab fully launches Bitcoin & Ethereum trading to its 40 million eligible retail clients." The headline is broadly right, but it needs context. [Facts] Schwab announced spot BTC and ETH trading in April and began a phased rollout on May 13. With its third-quarter results on October 15, the company said Schwab Crypto is now available to all eligible clients and that crypto transfers in and out are being switched on gradually. Schwab manages about $13.3 trillion in client assets across roughly 40.3 million active brokerage accounts. [Context] Not all of those 40 million accounts can trade: residents of New York, Louisiana and U.S. territories are excluded, and so are international clients. The news is the completion of a rollout, not a surprise launch. It still matters.
 
2️⃣ WHAT SCHWAB ACTUALLY OFFERS
Clients open a Schwab Crypto account linked to their brokerage account and trade spot Bitcoin and Ether on https://t.co/CFe5jkDy8x, the mobile app and thinkorswim. The fee is 0.75% of the value of each trade, with a $1 minimum and a $2 million maximum per transaction. The custodian is Schwab's own bank, Charles Schwab Premier Bank, with Paxos providing sub-custody and execution. Transfers currently work only on the Bitcoin and Ethereum networks, and withdrawal addresses must be registered in advance. According to reports, Solana, Avalanche and Chainlink are planned before the end of 2026; Schwab itself has confirmed "three more coins" by year-end.
 
3️⃣ WHY IT MATTERS — SCALE AND TRUST
Schwab is not a crypto company trying to look like a bank. It is one of the largest brokers in the world, and it just reported a record quarter: revenue up 17% to $7.2 billion and $190 billion of core net new assets, up 38% on the year. According to its own estimates, Schwab clients already hold about 20% of all spot crypto ETPs. Until now they could buy exposure through a fund; now they can hold the asset directly, next to their stocks and bonds, inside an app they already trust. For a large part of the U.S. middle class, the step from "I have a Schwab account" to "I own Bitcoin" has become one click.
 
4️⃣ THE DISTRIBUTION WAR — BROKERS AND EXCHANGES ARE CONVERGING
Schwab is part of a broader shift. Morgan Stanley launched its own spot Bitcoin ETF in April. Goldman Sachs has filed for a Bitcoin-linked income ETF. Coinbase now offers stocks and ETFs, and Kraken has launched tokenised equity futures. Traditional brokers are adding crypto, crypto exchanges are adding stocks, and the client ends up in a single account for everything. [Inference] The competitive pressure falls on pure crypto platforms and on fees. At 0.75% per trade Schwab is not the cheapest option, but for its clients convenience and trust count more than a few basis points.
 
5️⃣ BITCOIN ETFs — A PAUSE, NOT A CAPITULATION
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs manage about $106 billion, with cumulative net inflows of about $56.9 billion since January 2024. October is negative so far by about $535–540 million, after inflows of $2.6 billion in September and $3.5 billion in August. Last week's outflows were close to $680 million. This week has been mixed: $175 million in on Monday, about $261 million out on Wednesday after the hot CPI, and a small inflow of about $5 million on Thursday. [Inference] That is a reduction of exposure, not panic. June's $4.5 billion of outflows, the worst month on record, was a real capitulation; October so far is not.
 
6️⃣ ETHER ETFs — THE WEAKEST LINK
Ether funds are under heavier pressure. Between October 5 and 9 they recorded about $542 million of net outflows, part of a run of nine consecutive sessions without inflows. Total assets fell from $17.7 billion to $15.7 billion, but only about 27% of that drop came from redemptions; the rest was the fall in the ETH price. Ether trades around $2,435, roughly 50% below its all-time high. [Inference] When institutions reduce risk, they cut the asset with the weakest relative momentum first, and today that is ETH.
 
7️⃣ ALTCOIN ETFs — SOLANA SLOWS, XRP KEEPS BUYING
Solana ETFs recorded about $24.8 million of outflows in the week to October 9, their largest weekly exit since launch, ending a 14-week run of inflows. Their assets fell to $1.73 billion. XRP ETFs are the exception: 13 consecutive weeks of inflows, a record $1.80 billion of cumulative net inflows and $1.57 billion in assets, now only about $160 million behind Solana. At the global level, CoinShares' latest weekly report shows about $434 million of outflows from digital-asset investment products. [Inference] Money is not leaving the sector all at once; it is rotating and becoming more selective.
 
8️⃣ THE PARADOX — THE DOORS OPEN WHILE THE MONEY WAITS
Why are flows weak just as access improves? Because access is structural and flows are cyclical. This week U.S. CPI rose to 3.7% and producer prices jumped 6.3%, the fastest since 2022. The odds of a Fed hike on October 28 touched about 50% before falling back to around 25–30%. AI credit stress is pushing investors toward Treasuries. In that environment, institutions reduce risk regardless of how easy it is to buy Bitcoin. [Inference] Schwab's launch does not change the next two weeks. It changes the size of the market that can respond when macro conditions improve.
 
9️⃣ THE COST MATH — DIRECT BITCOIN OR AN ETF?
A practical point for investors. At 0.75% per trade, buying and later selling costs about 1.5% in total. A spot Bitcoin ETF such as IBIT charges about 0.25% a year. For an active trader, the ETF inside a brokerage account remains cheaper. For a long-term holder who buys rarely, direct ownership has one decisive advantage: once transfers are enabled, the coins can be moved to self-custody, which an ETF never allows. [Assumption] Part of Schwab's direct crypto demand may come from investors who already hold crypto ETFs, so not every dollar will be new money.
 
🔟 MY 2 CENTS — STRUCTURALLY BULLISH, CYCLICALLY PATIENT
Main scenario: no immediate impact on price. The Schwab launch is a long-term structural positive, but in the short term flows will follow the Fed and the bond market. I expect mixed ETF flows and Bitcoin in a $78–84K range until the FOMC on October 28.
 
Bullish scenario: ETF flows turn consistently positive, the Fed avoids a hike and Bitcoin confirms Thursday's sweep below $80K with a daily close above $82.8K, then a reclaim of $83.7K. In that case new distribution channels like Schwab could amplify the recovery.
 
Bearish scenario: another hot data point or a Fed hike, ETF outflows extending into November and a daily close below $80.1K, opening the way to $78K and then $76–77K.
 
What I am monitoring: daily Bitcoin and Ether ETF flows, Schwab's first figures on crypto accounts and assets, the activation of transfers, the XRP vs Solana ETF race, the U.S. 10-year yield and Fed hike odds, and Bitcoin's daily close relative to $82.8K.
 
What would invalidate my view: several consecutive days of large ETF inflows before the Fed meeting, which would show that institutions are buying the dip regardless of macro.
 
The lesson: adoption is not a price signal for tomorrow; it is a bigger engine waiting for the right fuel. For long-term holders, BTC, ETH and SOL should continue to be assessed through disciplined DCA, separately from speculative trading.

Mary Phagan Case You Are There: Judge Hill Confirms That Roan Will Hear Leo Frank's New Trial Motion as a Witness Defends Juror Henslee

The Atlanta Journal, Friday, October 10, 1913, page 3, column 1, and page 5, column 2.

Judge Roan Will Finish the Frank Case

On Friday, October 10, 1913, The Atlanta Journal reported that Judge Benjamin Harvey Hill had cleared up the uncertainty over who would hear Leo Max Frank's request for a new trial. Judge Leonard Strickland Roan, who had presided over Frank's murder trial, would remain in his position long enough to finish the case.

Frank had been convicted on Monday, August 25, 1913, of murdering 13-year-old Mary Phagan. Judge Roan sentenced him to death the following day. Frank's lawyers were now trying to overturn the verdict, arguing that mistakes during the trial and accusations of prejudice against two jurors justified another trial.

The timing had created a problem. Georgia was making changes to several judgeships, and Roan was preparing to leave his position to join the Georgia Court of Appeals. If he moved too soon, someone else might have to deal with Frank's unfinished case.

Judge Hill put those concerns to rest. He explained that he and Roan would remain in their present jobs until they had finished their work.

Hill told the newspaper:

"I do not know just when I will forward my resignation from the court of appeals, but I presume that Judge Roan and I will continue in our present capacities until we have both disposed of all unfinished business."

That settled the immediate question. Roan would remain responsible for deciding whether Frank should receive another trial (The Atlanta Journal, 1).

Seventy Criminal Cases Were Waiting

Judge Hill had his own problems to deal with. About seventy criminal cases were scheduled for argument before the Georgia Court of Appeals on Monday, October 13. Hill believed the judges might be able to finish hearing those cases within a week, but he was not prepared to resign while the work remained unfinished.

The planned changes involved three judges. Benjamin Harvey Hill was expected to leave the Court of Appeals and become the fourth Superior Court judge in Atlanta. Leonard Strickland Roan would take Hill's place on the Court of Appeals, while Solicitor General Charles S. Reid would replace Roan as judge of the Stone Mountain Judicial Circuit.

The appointments had been announced by Governor John Marshall Slaton in September, but the judges needed time to finish their existing cases.

Meanwhile, Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey and his assistant, Ed Stephens, identified in other reports as E. A. Stephens, were spending their time preparing the state's answer to Frank's request for another trial.

With the prosecutors occupied and the judges waiting to move into their new positions, Atlanta's criminal court had little reason to begin another round of cases. The Frank proceedings were holding up ordinary court business (The Atlanta Journal, 1).

A Witness Steps Forward to Defend Juror Henslee

The more interesting report appeared on page 5, column 2, under the headline "Turner Defends Juror Henslee."

The article concerned Atticus Haygood Henslee, one of the twelve jurors who had convicted Frank. Henslee was a 36-year-old traveling salesman associated with the Franklin Buggy Company of Barnesville, Georgia.

Frank's attorneys accused Henslee of having decided Frank was guilty before the trial began. They were gathering statements from people who claimed to have heard him make remarks about the case while traveling through Georgia.

Henslee denied entering the jury with his mind already made up.

Now another man had written to The Atlanta Journal to defend him.

The newspaper identified the writer as S. W. Turner, an agent for the Jefferson-Standard Life Insurance Company who lived in Hawkinsville, Georgia. The article later called him Mr. Turney, leaving a small difference in the spelling of his surname.

Turner described something that happened at a hotel in Ocilla, Georgia, on Thursday, June 26, 1913, about a month before Frank's trial began.

The $100 Bet That Henslee Refused

According to Turner, he had been arguing with a Jewish traveling salesman about the Frank case. The salesman offered to bet him $100 that Frank would not be convicted.

Turner was apparently willing to accept the wager. He left the hotel with Henslee and suggested they return and take the other man up on his offer.

Henslee refused.

Turner explained that Henslee did not want to argue about Frank's case, and the matter ended there.

His account included this statement:

"I left the hotel with Mr. Henslee and asked him to go back with me and let's bet him the money, and he refused, stating that he did not care to argue the case at all, and no more was said in regard to the case."

Turner said he was speaking up because so much had been written about Henslee supposedly traveling around Georgia discussing Frank's guilt.

He wanted readers to know that, at least on this occasion, Henslee had declined an opportunity to argue about the case or place money on the outcome (The Atlanta Journal, 1).

What Turner's Statement Tells Us

Turner's letter is worth examining because it gives us a different picture of Henslee from the one presented by Frank's lawyers.

The defense was gathering accounts from people who claimed Henslee had expressed strong opinions about Frank's guilt. Turner described a specific occasion when Henslee refused to take part in an argument about the case.

The date is important. The incident supposedly occurred on Thursday, June 26, 1913, more than four weeks before jury selection began on Monday, July 28.

Turner's account, if accurate, shows Henslee declining to bet on Frank's conviction while the case was still awaiting trial. It does not prove Henslee never expressed an opinion on some other occasion. Turner could speak only about what he personally witnessed at the Ocilla hotel.

Still, his statement deserves consideration alongside the accusations against Henslee. A fair examination of the controversy should include both the people who accused the juror and those who defended him.

It is also worth remembering that Turner identified himself as Henslee's friend. That relationship is useful background when weighing his account, just as the circumstances surrounding the defense witnesses deserve examination.

The Fight Over the Two Jurors Continued

Henslee was not the only juror being accused of prejudice. Frank's lawyers also challenged Marcellus Johenning, claiming that he had expressed an opinion about Frank's guilt before the trial.

These accusations became an important part of the effort to overturn the verdict. The defense gathered statements against the two men, while Dorsey collected statements supporting the jurors and challenging the reliability of their accusers.

On Friday, October 31, 1913, Judge Roan denied Frank's request for a new trial. The defense continued its fight in the Supreme Court of Georgia, which upheld the conviction by a vote of four to two on Tuesday, February 17, 1914.

The dispute over Henslee and Johenning remained part of the larger battle over the fairness of Frank's trial.

October 10, 1913: A Date Worth Remembering

There is another reason this newspaper edition deserves attention.

Friday, October 10, 1913, was originally supposed to be the day Leo Frank was executed.

Judge Roan had set that date when he sentenced Frank on Tuesday, August 26. However, Frank's request for a new trial had stopped the execution from going forward while the courts considered his case.

Instead of reporting Frank's execution, The Atlanta Journal was reporting that the judge who sentenced him would remain in office long enough to hear his request for another trial.

On the same day, the newspaper published Turner's defense of Henslee, giving readers another account to consider in the growing fight over the jurors.

Taken together, these reports show how the case continued to develop after the August verdict. Frank's lawyers were trying to obtain another trial, prosecutors were defending the conviction, and witnesses on both sides were entering the public argument over whether the jury had been fair.

Turner's letter adds one small but useful piece to that history. It records a man who said he had personally witnessed Henslee refuse to argue or gamble over Frank's guilt before the trial. That account deserves a place beside the accusations, denials, and sworn statements that Judge Roan eventually had to consider.

References

The Atlanta Journal. (Friday, October 10, 1913). “Judge Hill's Statement Dispells All Doubt That Roan Will Preside” and “Turner Defends Juror Henslee.” Pages 3 and 5, columns 1 and 2, respectively.https://t.co/UJ1wS84h7d

The Atlanta Journal. (Tuesday, October 7, 1913). “Dorsey and Stephens Busy in Valdosta” and “Henslee Answers Perjury Charges of Frank Defense.” Page 7, columns 3–4.https://t.co/qbkBq1tSkC

The Atlanta Journal. (Sunday, September 14, 1913). “Three Judgeships Announced: Judge B. H. Hill Appointed to New Atlanta Judgeship.”https://t.co/tsEbNx6YDy

Nelson, B. (2026, October 15). Two jurors accused of bias after the Leo Frank verdict. Mary Phagan Kean Legacy Project.https://t.co/RLOLT9apXc

Transcript

The Atlanta Journal,

Friday, 10th October 1913,

PAGE 3, COLUMN 1.

Judge Hill's Statement Dispells All Doubt

That Roan Will

Preside Doubt that the Frank motion for a new trial would be heard by Judge L. S. Roan has been dispelled by a statement from Judge Ben H. Hill, of the court of appeals.

"I do not know just when I will forward my resignation from the court of appeals," Judge Hill said, "but I presume that Judge Roan and I will continue in our present capacities until we have both disposed of all unfinished business."

The hearing of the motion for a new trial for Leo M. Frank comes under the head of Judge Roan's "unfinished business," as he presided at the famous prisoner's trial.

Judge Hill was reminded that on Monday about seventy criminal cases are set for argument before the court of appeals.

"We can dispose of these cases possibly in a week," Judge Hill said.

Judge Hill said that he certainly would not resign from the court of appeals by next Monday, when it was generally supposed his resignation would be effective.

With Solicitor Dorsey and his assistant, E. A. Stephens, both spending all their time on the Frank motion, it would be useless for Judge Hill to take his seat as the fourth judge of the Atlanta circuit, a new position, Judge Roan succeeding to the court of appeals and Solicitor Reid taking Judge Roan's position as judge of the Stone Mountain circuit.

PAGE 5, COLUMN 2

TURNER DEFENDS JUROR HENSLEE S. W. Turner, agent of the Jefferson-Standard Life Insurance company, a resident of Hawkinsville, has written a card to The Journal, defending A. H. Henslee, the juror in the Frank case, who has been attacked in the defense's motion for a new trial as prejudiced.

In his statement Mr. Turney says:

"Owing to so much being said in the papers in regard to Mr. A. H. Henslee being biased in the Leo M. Frank trial, I think I ought to come to his rescue as a friend and state what transpired at the hotel in Ocilla, Ga., on June 26, 1913, when myself and a Jew travelling salesman had up an argument about the trial of Frank and the Jew wanted to bet me $100 that they would not convict Frank.

I left the hotel with Mr. Henslee and asked him to go back with me and let's bet him the money, and he refused, stating that he did not care to argue the case at all, and no more was said in regard to the case.

"I only ask you to publish this so that the public will know that he had not been discussing the case over the country prior to the trial at random."
