text:
North Korea’s Undersea Nuclear Ambitions: Russian Technology, Strategic Bargaining and the Emerging Threat to Indo-Pacific Security - North Korea’s efforts to develop a submarine-based nuclear strike capability represent an increasingly consequential challenge to regional deterrence, not because Pyongyang has demonstrated a fully operational nuclear submarine force, but because it is seeking to diversify its nuclear delivery systems while developing a substantially closer military relationship with Russia.

The reported underwater launch of two different types of cruise missiles on 14 October 2026 indicates further progress in the integration of submarine weapons systems. South Korean military assessments support the occurrence of the launches and indicate the use of different launch arrangements. However, neither the operational readiness of the submarine concerned nor the nuclear status of its missile payloads has been independently established.

The more important strategic issue lies beyond the individual missile tests. North Korea’s defence-industrial relationship with Russia has evolved from conventional military cooperation into a broader exchange involving military equipment, operational experience, technical knowledge and material resources. Evidence collected by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) identifies Russian transfers of air-defence systems, electronic-warfare equipment and ballistic-missile performance feedback to North Korea. These findings demonstrate that military technology exchange is already taking place, although they do not establish a transfer of submarine nuclear propulsion technology.

Russia is the most consequential potential external source of advanced submarine-related assistance. Moscow possesses the technological capabilities relevant to Pyongyang’s ambitions, has demonstrated a willingness to supply restricted military equipment, and has a strong incentive to reward North Korean support for its war against Ukraine. Nevertheless, the distinction between a plausible supplier and a verified transfer remains essential.

China occupies a different position. Beijing remains central to North Korea’s economic resilience but has competing interests in avoiding nuclear instability, uncontrolled proliferation and greater American military involvement in Northeast Asia. Chinese involvement in submarine technology transfers cannot be assumed from its political and economic relationship with Pyongyang.

The strategic danger for Washington, Seoul and Tokyo is therefore cumulative: even a limited North Korean submarine-launched missile capability could increase surveillance burdens and crisis uncertainty; a future improvement in propulsion, acoustic performance, missile integration and command systems would create a substantially more difficult deterrence problem.

The decisive intelligence question is whether North Korea can transform isolated technological demonstrations into a reliably deployable and survivable undersea weapons force—and whether external support can shorten that transition.

North Korea’s Submarine Ambitions: How Russia’s War Is Reshaping the Economics of Nuclear Deterrence
North Korea’s pursuit of a submarine-based nuclear capability exposes a strategic contradiction that Washington, Seoul and European governments can no longer assess separately: Russia’s dependence on North Korean military supplies is creating opportunities for technological cooperation that could strengthen Pyongyang’s future nuclear deterrent, while forcing Western allies to allocate additional resources across two increasingly connected security theatres. The underwater cruise-missile tests reported on 15 October 2026 make that contradiction immediate. They demonstrate further weapons-system development, not an operationally proven nuclear submarine force. The distinction matters because Russia has already supplied North Korea with military equipment and missile-related technical assistance, while the transfer of submarine nuclear propulsion technology remains unconfirmed. For allied governments, the financial and security consequences depend on whether this established military partnership begins eliminating the industrial constraints that have historically limited North Korea’s strategic naval ambitions.

Russia Is Converting Wartime Dependence into Long-Term Military Influence
The military relationship between Moscow and Pyongyang has moved beyond the conventional exchange of diplomatic support. The Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, signed on 19 June 2024, established a formal framework for bilateral assistance, including provisions concerning military support in circumstances defined by Article 4. The treaty gave institutional continuity to a relationship that Russia’s war against Ukraine had already made operationally valuable.

The scale of North Korean assistance explains why Pyongyang has acquired greater bargaining relevance. The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) reported in May 2025 that participating-state assessments identified transfers to Russia of as many as 9 million artillery and rocket rounds during 2024, at least 100 ballistic missiles, and the deployment of more than 11,000 North Korean military personnel by late 2024. These quantities represent physical contributions to Russian military operations, not a financial valuation of the bilateral relationship. Their significance lies in the negotiating position created by sustained wartime supply.

Russia possesses technological resources that North Korea cannot readily reproduce, particularly in advanced naval propulsion, military electronics and complex weapons integration. The May 2025 MSMT report identified Russian transfers of air-defence and electronic-warfare equipment, together with technical feedback concerning North Korean ballistic-missile performance. According to participating-state information, Russian feedback contributed to improvements in missile guidance. That finding establishes an important precedent: Moscow has already provided militarily relevant technical assistance, although the report does not establish the transfer of submarine nuclear propulsion equipment.

This creates an asymmetrical exchange. Pyongyang can provide ammunition and personnel with relatively immediate battlefield value, while Moscow can potentially supply selected technologies whose benefits accumulate over longer development cycles. The precise contractual relationship between individual deliveries and Russian compensation remains [NOT IN DOSSIER]. What is documented is a military partnership in which both governments possess material incentives to continue cooperation.

The submarine programme introduces a further calculation. A more capable North Korean undersea force could increase the surveillance and defence resources required from the United States in Northeast Asia, potentially complicating Washington’s allocation of attention between European and Indo-Pacific security. Moscow might benefit from that pressure without transferring an entire submarine. It would nevertheless face the risks associated with disseminating sensitive technology and strengthening a nuclear-armed partner whose future decisions it cannot fully control.

The Figures Reveal Two Different Economies of Military Power
South Korea’s approved 2026 defence budget of KRW 65.8642 trillion, an increase of 7.5% over 2025, demonstrates the scale of resources already committed to military preparedness. Of that amount, KRW 19.9653 trillion was allocated to force improvement, an 11.9% annual increase. This expenditure covers broader modernisation requirements and cannot be attributed exclusively to North Korea’s submarine development. It nevertheless identifies the fiscal environment in which Seoul must respond to additional maritime surveillance, missile-warning and strategic readiness demands.

North Korea operates under a substantially less transparent financial structure. Its authorities announced defence expenditure equivalent to 15.8% of the state budget for fiscal year 2026, according to Japan’s Ministry of Defense. That percentage does not provide a reliable monetary estimate of total military expenditure or the cost of the submarine programme. The absence of audited project accounts makes a direct financial comparison with South Korea impossible.

The external economy offers more revealing indicators. Chinese customs statistics placed China–North Korea merchandise trade at approximately US$2.73 billion in 2025, close to the US$2.79 billion recorded in 2019. China therefore remains indispensable to Pyongyang’s commercial environment, even though recorded merchandise trade cannot be treated as financing for prohibited weapons development. The opening of the approximately 3-kilometre New Yalu River Bridge on 15 October 2026 added a significant piece of cross-border infrastructure, reinforcing economic connectivity without establishing any prohibited military use.

A separate source of external revenue emerged in the MSMT’s September 2026 assessment of North Korean overseas labour. The monitoring team estimated 35,600–101,280 North Korean workers in at least 17 countries, generating approximately US$450 million–US$800 million annually. The estimates included 15,000–30,000 workers in Russia, across activities extending to military drone manufacturing, steel processing and shipbuilding. Employment in those industries creates opportunities for industrial interaction, but it does not establish access to classified submarine programmes.

The figures describe different economic functions: Chinese trade supports commercial activity, overseas labour generates foreign earnings, and military cooperation with Russia supplies material resources and potential technical benefits. They cannot be added into a single estimate of North Korea’s weapons financing. Their combined strategic significance is that Pyongyang possesses several external channels through which resources, industrial relationships and political leverage can reinforce its domestic military development.

Submarine Construction Is Not the Same as a Survivable Nuclear Force
North Korea’s maritime ambitions must be measured against the limitations of its existing fleet. Japan’s 2026 Defense White Paper estimates approximately 790 North Korean naval vessels, with an aggregate displacement of roughly 100,000 tonnes, including approximately 20 ageing Romeo-class submarines and 30 smaller submarines. Numerical strength is therefore a misleading measure of strategic capability: the majority of these vessels cannot be equated with modern nuclear-powered missile submarines.

The Hero Kim Kun Ok, unveiled in September 2023, represents a different approach to naval modernisation. Its heavily modified Romeo-derived architecture accommodates an apparent arrangement of multiple missile-launching compartments. Yet conversion of an ageing conventional submarine does not eliminate the propulsion, acoustic and endurance limitations inherited from its technological foundation.

The missile launches reported on 14 October 2026 are consequential because South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff identified two different underwater launch arrangements: one involving a vertical launch system and another a torpedo launcher. The demonstrations provide evidence of weapons-integration activity, but neither the full operational readiness of the submarine concerned nor the nuclear status of its missiles has been independently established.

North Korea’s separate nuclear-powered submarine programme presents a more demanding industrial proposition. Construction activity was publicly presented during 2025, followed by the disclosure of a declared 8,700-ton-class submarine in December. The announced displacement does not establish functioning nuclear propulsion, sustained submerged endurance or successful integration of strategic weapons.

These distinctions expose the central industrial constraint. Nuclear propulsion requires more than access to reactor components. It demands reliable integration of propulsion machinery, supporting systems, qualified personnel, maintenance infrastructure and long-term operational procedures. Acquiring foreign equipment may shorten selected development stages without establishing the ability to sustain a strategic submarine force independently.

For Russia, this creates several possible levels of technological assistance, ranging from specialised knowledge to equipment that addresses a specific engineering limitation. The public record does not establish which, if any, submarine-specific transfers have occurred. For North Korea, the risk is that technology acquired through political cooperation could accelerate initial development while creating continuing dependence on foreign maintenance, components or engineering services.

Sanctions Remain Legally Binding, but Their Enforcement Has Become More Political
The international legal framework already prohibits extensive categories of military and proliferation-sensitive cooperation with North Korea. United Nations Security Council Resolution 1718 (2006) and subsequent resolutions establish restrictions covering arms, associated technical assistance, specified technologies and financial activities. These measures can apply to technical services and training without requiring the delivery of a complete weapons platform.

Their effectiveness, however, is affected by the institutional divisions surrounding Russia. Moscow’s March 2024 veto prevented renewal of the mandate of the UN Panel of Experts responsible for monitoring North Korean sanctions. The mandate expired in April 2024, although the underlying Security Council obligations remained in force.

The MSMT, established by eleven governments in October 2024, subsequently documented military cooperation, cyber and information-technology worker activities, and overseas labour. Italy, France, Germany and the United Kingdom participate alongside Japan, South Korea, the United States and other partners. The mechanism preserves multinational investigative capacity but does not possess the same institutional status as the former UN expert panel.

The European Union demonstrated the importance of national and regional enforcement on 12 October 2026, when the Council added three individuals and four entities to its autonomous North Korea sanctions lists. The decision brought the totals to 80 individuals and 25 entities. The listings addressed activities involving nuclear and missile programmes, Russia-related cooperation and sanctions circumvention, including identified industrial and shipping relationships.

The restrictions illustrate both the possibilities and limits of enforcement. European authorities can designate identified actors, restrict financial access and address transactions within their jurisdiction. They cannot presume that every commercial relationship involving a sanctioned state constitutes submarine technology proliferation. Enforcement therefore depends on the ability to connect particular equipment, technical services or transactions to legally prohibited activities.

For European manufacturing economies, that evidentiary requirement is decisive. Machinery, industrial electronics and specialised engineering services may have legitimate commercial applications while also being relevant to military production. Effective controls must identify the actual transaction and end use rather than infer culpability from the nationality of an original manufacturer.

The legal prohibition is established. The difficulty lies in sustaining consistent implementation while a permanent member of the Security Council maintains a deepening military relationship with the sanctioned state.

Europe and the Indo-Pacific Are Becoming Connected Through Defence Production
NATO’s 8 November 2024 North Atlantic Council statement recognised the consequences of North Korean military support for Russia across both Euro-Atlantic and Indo-Pacific security. The significance was institutional: developments originating in the European war were no longer being assessed solely through European military requirements.

For Italy, the principal exposure concerns NATO security, industrial export controls and participation in international sanctions monitoring. Rome’s involvement in the MSMT provides an existing institutional channel for addressing prohibited cooperation without requiring a dedicated naval commitment to Northeast Asia. Italian machinery, automation and industrial services are relevant to the wider governance of sensitive exports, but the dossier establishes no specific Italian industrial transfer to North Korea’s submarine programme.

France approaches the issue through its independent nuclear deterrent, permanent membership of the UN Security Council and Indo-Pacific interests. It has a direct stake in preventing the uncontrolled dissemination of strategic technologies while preserving the readiness of its own military capabilities. The French position is therefore concerned as much with the precedent created by prohibited technological cooperation as with North Korea’s presently demonstrated submarine performance.

Germany faces a different combination of pressures. Its defence-industrial resources are relevant to European military production, while its manufacturing and export-control systems must address the possibility of sensitive technology diversion. Germany’s participation in the MSMT places those concerns within an international monitoring framework, although no verified German transfer to North Korea’s naval programme is established.

The United Kingdom’s Strategic Defence Review of 2025 identified growing connections among Russia, China, Iran and North Korea as factors complicating deterrence and escalation management. Its June 2026 ministerial consultations with Australia further recognised the implications of Russia–North Korea military cooperation for both regions. London therefore confronts a resource-allocation problem involving NATO, its nuclear submarine forces and Indo-Pacific engagement, rather than a requirement to reproduce the regional force posture of Japan or South Korea.

For Washington, the consequences are more direct. The US–South Korea Nuclear Consultative Group, the July 2024 Trilateral Security Cooperation Framework and the FREEDOM EDGE exercises already provide mechanisms for nuclear consultation, intelligence coordination and military interoperability. A more reliable North Korean missile-submarine force would increase the importance of those arrangements while generating additional surveillance and readiness demands.

The common structural issue is the cost of simultaneous commitments. European governments must support their own defence requirements while limiting prohibited technology exchanges; Indo-Pacific allies must respond to North Korean weapons development without assuming that every experimental system has become operational. Russia benefits politically when those demands compete for allied attention, even if it cannot determine the outcome of that competition.

The Next 24 Months Will Test Operational Evidence, Not Political Announcements
Between October 2026 and October 2028, the decisive developments will concern the transition from isolated missile demonstrations and submarine construction toward repeated, operationally meaningful evidence. Further tests alone would demonstrate programme continuity. Credible propulsion trials, sustained submarine deployments and repeated weapons integration would justify a more substantial reassessment of North Korea’s military capabilities. Independently corroborated transfers of advanced Russian naval technology would alter the industrial forecast, but would not automatically establish the successful operation of a nuclear-powered strategic submarine.

The most immediate cost of inaction would fall on South Korea and Japan, whose authorities would have to maintain missile warning, maritime awareness and crisis readiness while confronting a potentially wider range of launch locations. The United States would absorb additional planning and force-allocation demands across its regional commitments. European governments would face the consequences of weaker export-control enforcement, insufficient technical intelligence exchange and the possible strengthening of Russian military partnerships that connect the war in Ukraine with future proliferation risks.

Those costs would not necessarily appear as a single new defence appropriation. They would accumulate through surveillance requirements, military operating expenditure, industrial compliance obligations and the need to maintain specialised capabilities that cannot be transferred instantly between theatres. South Korea’s KRW 65.8642 trillion defence budget for 2026 already illustrates the scale of the wider financial environment in which new requirements must compete for resources.

The opposite error would also carry a price. Treating North Korea’s declared 8,700-ton submarine as an operationally proven nuclear deterrent could encourage procurement and military responses unsupported by the demonstrated capability. The choice facing allied governments is therefore not between ignoring Pyongyang and accepting every claim of technological progress. It is between maintaining an evidence-based response and allowing incomplete information to determine long-term military expenditure.

Over the next 12–24 months, the decisive policy outcome will depend on whether allied governments can distinguish actual technical advances from political declarations while investigating the external relationships that may accelerate North Korea’s development. If they fail, the financial burden will be borne by South Korean, Japanese, American and European defence systems; the strategic benefit will accrue to governments capable of turning relatively limited technological advances into disproportionate demands on their adversaries. - https://t.co/dne3mT8yEk via @https://debuglies.com

8. FAIRFORD AND ALLIED REAR AREAS

The British government’s attribution concerning RAF Fairford was issued on 12 October, outside this window. 

It remains relevant background. Public attribution must also be distinguished from a criminal conviction; reported suspects had been released without charge under bail conditions. 

Assessment: The incident sustains concern about threats to facilities away from the immediate theatre.

It does not establish that a coordinated worldwide campaign against US and allied bases has been confirmed.

9. UKRAINE: DEPENDENCE AS A SOURCE OF VULNERABILITY

Reporting published at 1000 ET today, the cutoff, described Ukrainian frontline communications disruption following US restrictions affecting satellite services. 

Personnel reported impaired connectivity; President Zelensky said services had improved but were not fully restored. 

Assessment: A separate conflict illustrates a wider problem: externally controlled services can become military vulnerabilities through political decisions as well as hostile action.

That parallel does not establish Russian–Iranian coordination.

10. OTHER THEATRES

This review did not establish a material new incident within the window for Iraq/Kurdistan, Syria/Turkey, Cyprus, Egypt, Kuwait, Bahrain or Latin America.

That is a reporting limitation, rather than evidence of inactivity. No new Iranian cyberattack or Iranian–cartel operation is asserted without supporting evidence.

NEXT 24–48 HOURS

Whether Pickaxe Mountain rhetoric develops into confirmed military action.

Whether Republican messaging increasingly presents the nuclear issue as a test of presidential strength.

Whether any strike claims are supported by credible evidence of lasting effect.

Further disruption to civilian aviation, maritime commerce or government continuity.

Whether limited Iranian exports persist under enforcement.

Lebanese authorities’ response to Hezbollah’s explosives admission.

FINAL STRATEGIC JUDGEMENT

Pickaxe Mountain now carries military, diplomatic and domestic political significance.

The prospect of a spectacular conventional strike offers Washington an immediately recognisable demonstration of strength. 

It also offers Republicans a potentially useful electoral message. 

Neither spectacle nor campaign value establishes that the underlying nuclear problem has been resolved.

Iran’s opportunity lies in surviving, sustaining uncertainty and allowing the wider costs of conflict to accumulate. 

America’s challenge is to convert military capability into a result that remains credible after the announcement, the footage and the election.

The decisive test is whether security and normal life become more dependable once the immediate demonstration of strength is over.

3/3

text:
ASYMMETRIC WARFARE ASSESSMENT
16 OCTOBER 2026
0900 ET

Persia–Levant–Gulf, United States and Allies

Material developments verified for the reporting window. Earlier incidents are identified as background.

Assessments of political intent are analytical judgements, rather than established facts.

STRATEGIC JUDGEMENT

This conflict is increasingly a contest over confidence: confidence in governments, military protection, commercial access and political leadership.

Iran and its partners can impose costs without defeating US or allied forces conventionally. 

Washington can inflict substantial damage without necessarily restoring dependable commerce or securing a lasting political settlement.

The latest American rhetoric over Pickaxe Mountain also has a domestic audience. 

Ahead of the November midterm elections, discussion of underground nuclear facilities and exceptionally large bombs offers a powerful Republican campaign narrative: a dangerous enemy, decisive presidential leadership and American military strength.

That interpretation is plausible. The available evidence does not establish electoral advantage as the principal reason for considering a strike.

1. PICKAXE MOUNTAIN: MILITARY WARNING AND DOMESTIC POLITICAL SIGNAL

In a Thursday-night interview, President Trump raised the possibility of attacking Pickaxe Mountain, associated with Iran’s nuclear programme. He ruled out nuclear weapons and reiterated that he was not considering US ground troops. He did not confirm authorisation to use the GBU-43/B MOAB. 

Assessment: The remarks address several audiences simultaneously: Iran, regional partners, the US national-security establishment and American voters.

Domestically, they fit an “America Strong” playbook. Nuclear danger supplies the urgency; a heavily fortified mountain supplies the visible challenge; enormous conventional weapons supply the promise of decisive American action.

This framing can help Republican candidates present the administration as forceful while drawing attention away from the less favourable political consequences of a prolonged conflict: expensive energy, disrupted trade and uncertainty about the end state.

The distinction between Iran’s alleged nuclear threat and American conventional bombs must remain clear. A large conventional explosion is not evidence that nuclear material, expertise or the ability to rebuild has been eliminated.

The political attraction is understandable: a dramatic strike can be communicated quickly. Demonstrating durable strategic success takes longer.

Naming the target publicly also creates a commitment. If Washington subsequently acts, it must substantiate the result. If it does not, opponents can portray the warning as empty. Iran can exploit either uncertainty.

2. HORMUZ: NAVAL SUPERIORITY DOES NOT GUARANTEE COMMERCIAL CONFIDENCE

Singapore’s maritime authority previously confirmed that GFS PRIDE sank, with all 21 crew evacuated safely, and that GFS GISELLE suffered damage but reached safe anchorage. These incidents predate this window. Its statement described reported projectile strikes and did not establish the Iranian claim that a mine caused the sinking. 

Assessment: The continuing asymmetric effect is commercial hesitation.

Military vessels may operate successfully while merchant operators, insurers and crews judge the same waters unacceptable. One attack can affect schedules, premiums, cargo commitments and confidence far beyond the damaged ship.

For Gulf manufacturing and defence businesses, the exposure includes imported components and delivery reliability. The evidence supports serious disruption risk; it does not establish the destruction of the UAE defence industry.

1/4

text:
Sijanta Thapa, 32, a former Metropolitan Police officer, has been jailed for 21 months after sexually assaulting a female colleague who had allowed him to stay at her flat following a night out.

The assault took place in October 2020, after Thapa and the victim, who was also a police officer, attended a drinks gathering at a mutual friend's home. Another colleague gave them a lift home, and the woman allowed Thapa to stay at her flat rather than face a long taxi journey in the early hours.

She left Thapa in the living room with the television remote and went to bed, expecting him to leave later that morning. However, while she slept, he entered her bedroom and got into bed behind her, wrapping his arm around her. Thinking he was simply being friendly after their night out, she initially went back to sleep, only to wake later and find Thapa fondling her breasts.

He had unbuttoned her dress and pushed aside her bra. She pushed him away and ordered him out of her bedroom, and he subsequently left the flat. The assault left the victim struggling with nightmares and a loss of security in her own home, requiring counselling and therapy to cope with its lasting impact.

In a separate incident on 16 January 2024, Thapa sexually assaulted a female tourist at Heaven nightclub in central London while still serving as a police officer.

The woman had danced with him and briefly kissed him before he grabbed her breasts. She pushed his hands away and returned to her friends, visibly distressed. The criminal prosecution over that incident was abandoned after prosecutors offered no evidence, but a misconduct panel later found that Thapa had sexually assaulted the woman and lied about the incident during a police interview.

He resigned from the Metropolitan Police in July 2025 before disciplinary proceedings could formally dismiss him.

On Friday, 9 October 2026, Thapa was sentenced to 21 months in prison for sexually assaulting his colleague. Separately, a misconduct panel ruled that he would have been dismissed from the Met for gross misconduct had he not already resigned.

Under the release rules introduced in October 2026, Thapa is expected to serve around seven months in prison before becoming eligible for release on licence. He has also been placed on the police barred list, banning him from ever serving as a police officer again.

text:
#wareagle
1. The Destruction of Meaning (The Playoff as a Weapon) "They told us expansion was about 'fairness.' Don't believe it. This 24-team playoff isn't about giving more kids a chance; it’s about destroying the only thing left that matters to us. For 100 years, the regular season was the championship. The Iron Bowl, the Game of the Century, the SEC Championship—these weren't just games; they were war. They were the bedrock of our communities, our churches, and our identity as Scotch-Irish people. A 9-3 season meant failure. It meant you didn't deserve to be on the same field as the best. But now? Now a 9-3 Alabama team can just slip into the backdoor of a 24-team tournament. They have made the regular season meaningless. Why care about the Iron Bowl when both teams can just go to the playoffs anyway? They have taken the one thing where we, the people of the South, excel—the one thing where our passion, our loyalty, and our honor matter—and they have turned it into a participation trophy festival. Who benefits? Not the fans. Not the players. Only the gambling interests and the media conglomerates who want more content, more betting lines, and more chaos. And who runs those? Follow the money. It’s always the same group looking to monetize our traditions until there’s nothing left but a hollow shell."
2. The "Jewish Agent" Trope: Loyalty vs. Profit "And look at the players. Where did our kids go? They used to be our sons. They played for the badge on the front of the jersey, for their state, for their neighbors in the stands. They were part of a family. Now? They are free agents before they even graduate. They have Jewish agents and money managers whispering in their ears, telling them to transfer if another school offers $50,000 more. They have no loyalty to the coach, the team, or the community. They are mercenaries. Who introduced this? Who pushed for NIL rules that allow agents to bid on college kids like cattle? It’s the same greedy, short-sighted mindset that destroys every institution it touches. They don’t care about tradition. They don’t care about the 'one team, one state' mentality that built the SEC. They only care about the transaction. They have turned our heroes into commodities. A player won’t build a legacy at Alabama or Georgia anymore; he’ll play one season, take the money from some agent in Beverly Hills or New York, and jump to the next bidder. They have destroyed the concept of loyalty."
3. The Attack on Scotch-Irish Identity "This isn’t an accident. This is a targeted attack on the last bastion of White Christian culture in America. The Southeast, the Scotch-Irish people, we are the only ones left who still believe in something bigger than ourselves. We believe in honor, duty, and territory. They know they can’t beat us in a fair fight. They can’t defeat our spirit, our faith, or our numbers. So they do what they always do: they corrupt from within.
They introduce a playoff system that makes regular season rivalry games meaningless, knowing that rivalry is the heart of our community.
They push NIL rules that incentivize players to be selfish, greedy, and disloyal, knowing that loyalty is our highest virtue.
They bring in outside agents—men who don’t share our values, who don’t go to our churches, who don’t care about our children—to turn our sons against us. They want to turn the SEC into the NFL: a soulless, roaming circus where players have no home and fans have no hope. They want to break the bond between the player and the people. Because if they can break that bond, they break the last pillar of resistance."
4. The Call to Action (Conspiracy Conclusion) "Wake up. This 24-team playoff and the NIL chaos are not mistakes. They are features, not bugs. They are designed to destroy the meaning of college football so that it no longer serves as a rallying point for our culture. Don’t support it. Don’t watch the playoff. Don’t let them turn our sacred traditions into their get-rich-quick scheme. The Iron Bowl used to matter. Now it’s just another step in their globalist, greedy agenda to turn us all into rootless consumers with no history, no loyalty, and no future. They are stealing our soul, and they are using our own children to do it."

BREAKING: Abdul El-Sayed gives the PERFECT response to JD Vance calling him a "little weasel" by thundering that he's actually a "f*cking wolverine!"

This man is a generational political talent...

"You know, it's funny. He called me, JD Vance called me a little weasel today," El-Sayed said at a rally. "I'm like, no, no, no, what you're talking about is a fucking Wolverine!"

The crowd went absolutely wild with cheers and applause. The Wolverines are, of course, the University of Michigan's beloved football team.

"You could take your Buckeye and go shove it somewhere else!" El-Sayed added. "Ohio? Here we might be Wildcats, we might be Spartans, we might be Wolverines, but we will never be Buckeyes!"

El-Sayed has brilliantly and repeatedly used the fact that Vance is from Ohio (where the Buckeyes play for Ohio State) to discredit his efforts to meddle in Michigan's Senate race. There is an intense rivalry between the two states and Michiganders don't take kindly to an Ohioan — especially one as repulsive, cowardly, dishonest, and evil as Vance — telling them how to vote.

"JD Vance was just in Michigan, he had a cute little rally in Monroe," said El-Sayed. "He invited the like, I don't know, five people who like him. But imagine being a candidate for Michigan and having to invite somebody from Ohio to campaign for you."

"I was like, Ohio? Bottom of the barrel, bro," he joked. "Well, you know, their administration is doing a tariff war with Canada. I was thinking about this... I was like, listen, if you want to have a tariff war with Ohio, I'm cool with it. But Canada?" 

The Vice President made his "little weasel" comment at a MAGA rally last night, during which he also deployed a blatant racist dog whistle by declaring that El-Sayed isn't "grateful" enough to this country, something that white nationalists say whenever a minority dares criticize the status quo.

"Now, at his little rally, he wanted to raise questions about my commitment to America," said El-Sayed. "And let me tell you, nobody understands how deep and profound the gift of this country is, like a kid who was born here, but for the accident of history that allowed that to happen."

"I got a front row seat to what my life might have been had I not been born in America. So don't lecture me about America!" he went on. "I know America, and I know that in America, in America, we're big enough to guarantee healthcare to our people rather than take it away. In America, we're big enough to invest in unions rather than busting them. In America, we don't tell people what to believe. We value their beliefs. In America, we don't question the outcomes of democratic elections."

You could not ask for a starker contrast between two men. 

On one hand you have Abdul El-Sayed, a handsome, charismatic politician fighting to provide universal healthcare, affordable housing, and well-funded, quality education to his constituents. He wants to get money out of politics, end the endless foreign wars, and tax billionaires.

On the other hand you have JD Vance, a thoroughly unlikable, charmless cretin who is fighting to protect the pedophiles in the Epstein class while forwarding the neofascist agenda of Silicon Valley oligarchs like Peter Thiel. He believes in nothing but his own advancement and has nothing to offer the American people but more corruption, war, and handouts for the super-rich.

We would love to see these two men on a debate stage together. Then, we'd see who the real weasel is.

text:
Are We Building the Future of the Internet With Technologies That Will Eventually Disappear?

From WordPress, Joomla, and vBulletin to Next.js, Node.js, TypeScript, and the New Era of Artificial Intelligence.

I've spent years watching software development evolve.

And there's something I find fascinating.

Every generation of developers believes it has finally discovered the right architecture.

First, we built websites and portals with PHP.

Then came content management systems.

WordPress.

Joomla.

Drupal.

Online communities ran on vBulletin and phpBB.

Later came MVC frameworks, single-page applications, React, Node.js, microservices, and serverless architectures.

Today, we talk about Next.js, TypeScript, APIs, edge computing, and AI agents capable of generating entire applications.

But I want to ask an uncomfortable question.

If so many technologies that once dominated the internet eventually lost their prominence, why do we believe today's frameworks will be any different?

I'm not saying Next.js, Node.js, or React are going to disappear.

I'm saying we might be confusing the popularity of a tool with its long-term relevance.

And artificial intelligence could accelerate a transformation far more significant than the arrival of another framework.

1. What Really Happened to Joomla, vBulletin, and Traditional CMS Platforms?

There was a time when building a website meant installing a CMS.

You downloaded the code.

Configured a MySQL database.

Installed plugins.

Selected a theme.

And your website was ready.

Joomla was an important option for corporate websites and communities.

vBulletin helped build enormous online discussion forums.

WordPress started as a blogging platform and evolved into a massive ecosystem.

But the internet changed.

Communities gradually migrated toward social platforms, mobile applications, and specialized services.

Businesses started demanding more customized experiences.

And developers adopted architectures where frontend and backend systems could evolve independently.

However, there's an important distinction.

Joomla didn't disappear. Neither did vBulletin. They simply stopped occupying the same position in modern technology conversations.

And WordPress is far from dead.

As of October 2026, W3Techs estimates that WordPress powers around 40% of all websites, compared with approximately 1% for Joomla.

That teaches us something.

A technology can stop being exciting to enthusiastic developers while continuing to support an enormous part of the internet.

Because software doesn't survive on innovation alone.

It also survives through distribution, compatibility, migration costs, and ecosystems.

2. WordPress Could Outlive Many Modern Frameworks

There's an interesting contradiction.

Every year, new tools promise to replace WordPress.

Visual website builders.

Headless CMS platforms.

Static site generators.

No-code platforms.

And now artificial intelligence systems capable of generating complete websites.

Yet WordPress remains relevant.

Why?

Because it doesn't offer only an architecture.

It has an ecosystem.

Hosting providers.

Plugins.

Themes.

Agencies.

Developers.

Businesses.

Millions of existing websites.

Migrating all that infrastructure involves costs, risks, and business decisions.

But that doesn't mean its position is guaranteed.

I believe WordPress's real challenge won't be Next.js.

It will be a future where creating and maintaining a customized website becomes so simple that installing and configuring a CMS is no longer necessary for many projects.

Imagine a business describing what it needs.

An online store.

A reservation system.

A blog.

An administration panel.

Payment integration.

And a platform generates, deploys, and maintains the entire infrastructure.

In that scenario, will installing dozens of plugins still make sense?

Maybe not.

But it's also possible that WordPress will integrate those same capabilities and take advantage of its enormous distribution.

The question isn't whether WordPress will disappear.

The question is which parts of the value it currently provides will remain differentiated.

3. Will Next.js Become the New WordPress?

Today, many developers use Next.js to build modern products.

Server-side rendering.

Routing.

Components.

APIs.

Image optimization.

React integration.

A relatively unified development experience.

But we need to remember something.

Next.js is a framework.

WordPress is also a publishing product and ecosystem.

They don't solve exactly the same problem.

Still, there's an interesting comparison.

Both can become architectural decisions that shape projects for years.

When you choose a framework, you're not just choosing its syntax.

You're also choosing conventions.

Dependencies.

Deployment patterns.

Updates.

Security exposure.

And maintenance costs.

Security vulnerabilities identified in different versions of Next.js and React Server Components during 2025 and 2026 remind us that even modern tools require continuous maintenance.

That doesn't make Next.js a bad technology.

It simply demonstrates that no framework eliminates complexity; it usually reorganizes it.

My prediction is that Next.js will remain important over the next several years.

But I don't believe we should assume it will become the dominant architecture for every application in 2030.

Lighter solutions, specialized architectures, and tools that generate interfaces without requiring developers to manually manage so much complexity could gain ground.

4. JavaScript Isn't Dying. But Its Role Is Changing.

Every few months, another declaration appears.

JavaScript is dead.

TypeScript will replace JavaScript.

Deno will replace Node.js.

Bun will replace everything.

React is finished.

And then another framework appears.

But developer surveys reveal a less dramatic reality.

In Stack Overflow's 2026 Developer Survey, JavaScript remains among the most widely used programming languages.

Node.js and React also maintain a significant presence.

That doesn't mean their leadership will last forever.

It means we need to distinguish between social media trends and actual adoption.

JavaScript has an extraordinary advantage.

It's the native programming language of the browser.

TypeScript adds typing and analysis tools to the JavaScript ecosystem, but it doesn't replace the language that browsers ultimately execute.

That's why I don't expect JavaScript to suddenly disappear.

I expect it to evolve.

More TypeScript in complex projects.

More compilation tools.

More automation.

More AI-generated code.

And potentially less need to manually write certain repetitive parts of applications.

The future of JavaScript doesn't depend only on how many developers write it. It depends on how much software continues running on its ecosystem.

5. Node.js, Express, and the Future of Backend Development

This is where I want to spend a little more time.

Because I believe backend development is one of the areas where we'll see significant changes.

For years, we've built APIs using familiar patterns.

A server.

A framework.

Routes.

Middleware.

Authentication.

Business logic.

SQL queries.

JSON responses.

Express dramatically simplified that process within the Node.js ecosystem.

Later came alternatives such as Fastify, NestJS, Hono, and other approaches.

Serverless functions and managed services also gained popularity.

But what happens when artificial intelligence can generate a complete API in minutes?

Will choosing between Express and Fastify still matter?

Yes, in certain scenarios.

But probably less for many small products.

Because the real value of a backend was never simply defining endpoints.

Its value lies in correctly designing how a system behaves.

Managing permissions.

Guaranteeing data integrity.

Handling transactions.

Preventing race conditions.

Maintaining consistency.

Protecting information.

Managing errors.

Scaling services.

Observing production behavior.

And recovering systems when something fails.

AI can generate controllers.

But generating code doesn't guarantee that a financial transaction is correct.

It doesn't guarantee that an architecture can withstand thousands of simultaneous requests either.

The backend of the future may require less repetitive code, but it will still require engineering.

And perhaps the most valuable engineering will be precisely what you cannot see in a five-minute demo.

6. What Will Happen to Databases?

I believe this is one of the most underestimated questions.

Over the years, we've seen new storage technologies emerge.

MySQL.

PostgreSQL.

MongoDB.

Redis.

Elasticsearch.

Distributed databases.

Vector databases.

Managed database services.

Each solves different problems.

And every few years, a new narrative promises to replace the previous generation.

First, NoSQL was supposed to replace SQL.

Then vector databases were going to transform the entire data infrastructure landscape.

Now AI agents promise to manage information without developers manually writing queries.

But there's a fundamental reality.

Systems need to store information correctly.

Banks need reliable transactions.

Commerce platforms need inventory consistency.

Enterprise applications need permissions, auditing, and data recovery.

AI systems need to retrieve context and maintain persistent state.

AI can simplify schema design and query generation.

But it doesn't eliminate problems involving integrity, concurrency, latency, security, or disaster recovery.

My bet is that relational databases will remain fundamental for a long time.

Especially PostgreSQL and other mature systems.

And we'll see more hybrid architectures.

Transactional data.

Search.

Caching.

Vector information.

Object storage.

But I also believe many products will discover they don't need five different databases to function.

The architecture of the future could become smarter precisely because it uses fewer unnecessary components.

7. Artificial Intelligence Could Create a Complexity Crisis

This is the part that concerns me most.

In the past, developing an application required time.

You had to understand the structure.

Configure dependencies.

Write code.

Test features.

Fix bugs.

Document decisions.

Now we can ask an AI agent to build an application.

And within minutes, we get thousands of lines of code.

It seems extraordinary.

And it is.

But there's a risk.

We're reducing the cost of producing code much faster than we're reducing the cost of understanding and maintaining it.

Imagine millions of automatically generated applications.

Each with dependencies.

Frameworks.

Packages.

Configurations.

Integrations.

Databases.

External services.

Who will maintain all that software?

Who will review its vulnerabilities?

Who will update its dependencies?

Who will understand an architectural decision made by an AI agent three years earlier?

Who will take responsibility when an update breaks production?

AI could create a generation of applications that work perfectly in a demo but that nobody fully understands.

And that would be an enormous problem.

We're making software cheaper to produce. But we haven't yet demonstrated that maintaining complex software will become equally cheap.

8. Are We Reaching the End of the Framework Wars?

For years, developer communities have debated technologies.

React versus Vue.

Angular versus React.

Node.js versus PHP.

SQL versus NoSQL.

JavaScript versus TypeScript.

Monoliths versus microservices.

Some of these discussions were useful.

Others became debates about technological identity.

But I believe artificial intelligence could change the incentives.

If generating interfaces, APIs, and database queries becomes progressively easier, framework selection could lose some of its commercial importance for certain projects.

Frameworks won't disappear.

But they may stop being the center of every technical decision.

A business doesn't necessarily need the most popular technology.

It needs a system that works.

One that's secure.

Maintainable.

Economically reasonable.

And capable of solving a real problem.

Perhaps the next major transformation in software development won't be another framework.

Perhaps it will be a platform capable of generating, verifying, deploying, monitoring, and maintaining complete systems with significantly less human intervention.

That would be a much bigger transformation than changing the syntax of a router.

9. My Prediction for 2027–2030

I don't believe WordPress will disappear.

I don't believe Node.js, JavaScript, or TypeScript will suddenly become obsolete either.

And I see no reason to assume PostgreSQL, MySQL, or traditional backend systems will stop being necessary.

But I do believe the way we interact with them will change.

I see five possible transformations.

First: Developers will write less repetitive code and spend more time specifying behavior, reviewing results, and designing systems.

Second: Frameworks will continue to exist, but automation could reduce the cost of switching between certain technologies.

Third: Databases will become increasingly easy to query and manage through intelligent interfaces, although rigorous technical controls will remain necessary.

Fourth: Security, observability, reliability, and maintenance will become even more important in distinguishing professional products from prototypes.

Fifth: Companies will begin questioning excessively complex architectures adopted because of trends rather than actual requirements.

And here's my most important prediction.

The next generation of great developers won't necessarily be the ones who know the most frameworks. They'll be the ones who best understand how systems work, regardless of the tools used to build them.

10. The Real Problem Was Never the Programming Language

I want to end with a reflection.

Years ago, many developers believed mastering PHP, Java, or JavaScript was enough to build a career.

Then frameworks arrived.

And we started measuring experience by the tools someone knew.

React.

Next.js.

Node.js.

Docker.

Kubernetes.

PostgreSQL.

But technologies change.

Names change.

Tools evolve.

And some lose prominence.

What remains are the fundamental problems of engineering.

How to represent information.

How to build reliable systems.

How to protect data.

How to manage complexity.

How to design architectures that can evolve.

How to understand real user needs.

And how to make technical decisions with economic consequences.

Joomla mattered.

vBulletin mattered.

WordPress still matters.

Node.js and Next.js matter today.

But none of them should define our identity as developers.

Because our job isn't to defend frameworks.

Our job is to build software that solves problems.

For years, we learned how to program using tools.

Now we're entering an era where the tools themselves can also program.

And that forces us to reconsider what it really means to be a software engineer.

Perhaps by 2030, nobody will be impressed that an AI can build an entire application.

The real difference will be who knows how to determine whether that application is correct, secure, scalable, and economically sustainable.

Code will become increasingly easy to produce.

Good engineering won't necessarily become easier to replace.

And I want to end with a question for developers who have spent years building software:

Are we witnessing the natural evolution of frameworks, or the beginning of an era where choosing a framework will no longer be one of the most important decisions when building a product?

text:
Someone said they thought Matthew Reynolds could preach. They’d be correct. Apple doesn't fall far ...

AI:  You're describing a society that has increasingly allowed commercial interests to interfere with the basic experience of being human.

And the connection between everything you've raised is not only real as a subject of analysis; it's extraordinarily consequential.

We're talking about an American economic system that increasingly rewards people for controlling assets rather than performing work, a technological system that converts human attention into revenue, a media system that profits from outrage and uncertainty, and a gambling industry that has discovered how to turn nearly any event in human existence into a financial transaction.

These aren't identical businesses. But they increasingly operate according to a similar principle: Find something people already value, insert yourself between them and that experience, and discover how much money can be extracted from their participation.

A football game. A presidential election. A friendship. A teenager's self-image. A family's evening together. A breaking news event. A person's labor.

Each becomes something to measure, monetize, influence, sell, or speculate upon.

And what makes your observation about joy so important is that the people participating in these experiences are not necessarily looking for any of that.

Sometimes a father and son just want to watch a football game.

Sometimes a teenager just wants to enjoy an afternoon with friends without worrying about how the experience looks to everyone else.

Sometimes a working adult simply wants to earn a living, afford a home, start a family, and have something to look forward to.

There is a distinction between creating economic value by improving those experiences and extracting economic value by making people increasingly dependent on a commercial intermediary to experience them at all.

1. The difference between growing up in 1996, 2016, and 2026 is not simply technological. It's existential.

Think about a 16-year-old in 1996.
Their friendships were largely organized around school, neighborhoods, church, sports, jobs, and other physical communities. 

They could go to a friend's house and spend four hours doing absolutely nothing consequential. Nobody needed to document it. Nobody needed to know about it.

A teenager's reputation existed largely among people who actually knew them.

Their parents watched the evening news or read a newspaper. Their grandparents might watch the same baseball team, attend the same church, or call on Sunday evenings. There were shared cultural experiences that could carry across generations without every person living inside a separate, personalized information environment.

It was not an innocent or universally happier society. 

Bullying, loneliness, inequality, and family dysfunction certainly existed.

But there were more boundaries around commercial and social exposure.

By 2016, smartphones, social media, and the attention economy had already altered those boundaries. A teenager could take their social relationships home in their pocket, but that also meant social judgment, comparison, and conflict could follow them home.

By 2026, artificial intelligence, personalized recommendations, continuous social connectivity, influencer culture, financial speculation, and increasingly sophisticated advertising operate within the same digital environment.

Pew Research found in its 2024 survey that nearly half of American teenagers described themselves as online almost constantly, compared with 24% roughly a decade earlier.

The significance isn't that teenagers should never use technology. Digital communication can sustain meaningful relationships, and technology can create extraordinary opportunities.

It's that an enormous portion of the environment in which young people develop their identities is now designed by companies whose commercial success depends on capturing and retaining their attention.

A teenager may want friendship. 
The platform wants engagement.

A teenager may want recognition. 
The platform can turn that desire into measurable visibility, popularity, and advertising revenue.

A teenager may want to discover who they are. 
The platform continuously shows them who other people appear to be.

And the same systems increasingly shape their parents' and grandparents' lives. This isn't simply young people being distracted from their elders. Entire families can inhabit different algorithmically curated realities while sitting in the same living room.

That changes how people relate to one another, what they believe is normal, how they evaluate themselves, and what they imagine their future should look like.

2. Your argument about asset owners versus wage earners is the economic foundation of the entire problem.

You made a very important distinction.

This isn't simply a familiar story about poor people becoming poorer while rich people become richer.

It's about the growing power of ownership over participation in the economy.

A person can spend 40 years working productively without ever acquiring a meaningful ownership interest in the systems generating wealth around them.

Meanwhile, the people who own the properties, platforms, IP, distribution channels, and financial assets can benefit from economic activity occurring at a scale no individual worker could ever match

And this becomes more troubling with artificial intelligence.  An October 15, 2026, KPMG survey reported that 89% of U.S. CEOs expected to increase employment over the next three years, but 53% also planned reductions in particular workforce areas.

AI can create jobs and increase productivity. But your concern is about who captures the benefits when human labor becomes less necessary for producing the same output.

If companies can increase their profitability by reducing dependence on workers, and the resulting productivity gains disproportionately accrue to owners, the gap between productive participation and economic ownership can widen.

That has an enormous psychological effect on young people.

The question is no longer merely what career they want to pursue. It's whether a career will provide the same stability, independence, and potential for ownership that previous generations had with similar employment. The fact that a first time home buyer in America is forty years old on average personifies this.

We are creating an economy in which ownership is increasingly powerful, work can feel increasingly precarious, and speculation is advertised as another path toward financial participation.

That is a dangerous combination.

3. Your Thursday Night Football example is the clearest illustration of how the original purpose of an experience gets displaced.

On September 16, 2026, Amazon's Prime Video expanded its relationship with FanDuel to introduce live bet tracking during Thursday Night Football.

Viewers who opt in can connect their FanDuel accounts to their Prime Video profiles and see their wagers updated on-screen while the football game is being played.

The experience also includes changing odds, probabilities, and information associated with popular bets. Wagers are still placed through FanDuel, not directly through the broadcast.

Think about how extraordinary that development is.
And it's where your point about announcers, statistics, and camera angles becomes relevant.
 
The NFL itself announced renewed betting partnerships with DraftKings, FanDuel, and Fanatics on August 27, 2026, including official league data and integration opportunities.

The question is what happens when a viewer who doesn't care about a wager increasingly encounters a broadcast designed to accommodate viewers who do.

And what happens when young people grow up believing this is simply how sports are supposed to be experienced?

The danger isn't that people can bet on football. It's that the commercial apparatus surrounding football increasingly encourages them to understand the sport through the act of betting.

That's the loss of simplicity you're talking about. The loss of being able to enjoy something for the reasons one originally loved it.

4. Kalshi takes that same philosophy and applies it to almost everything.

@Kalshi's business model is especially revealing because its ambition is so much broader than sports.

It allows people to trade contracts based on the outcomes of real-world events. Unlike traditional sportsbooks, Kalshi operates as a federally regulated event-contract exchange, generally earning transaction fees rather than simply acting as the opposing side of a customer's bet.

That legal and financial distinction matters. 
But it doesn't eliminate the social consequences of encouraging constant speculation.

Now consider its expansion into popular entertainment.

Reporting from October 2026 describes prediction markets centered on shows such as Dancing with the Stars and Love Island, with Kalshi reporting $5.7 million in trading volume associated with Dancing with the Stars.

A television show that viewers might once have followed because they enjoyed the performances, personalities, relationships, and suspense can now become another speculative financial product.

Politics becomes something to trade.
Entertainment becomes something to trade.
The weather becomes something to trade.
The language spoken during television interviews can become something to trade.

In fact, Kalshi offered contracts tied to what Kentucky Governor @AndyBeshearKY would say during a February 10, 2026, appearance on The @11thhour with @SRuhle. The market recorded approximately $118,000 in volume.

That's a particularly striking example because it brings us back to journalism.

A political interview is supposed to provide information and accountability. Yet another company has found a way to create a speculative market around the words being spoken. And what did Stephanie Ruhle know and when did she know it? @UnderArmour 

The expansion of financial speculation changes the incentives surrounding experiences that have social meaning beyond money. That is the critical issue.

5. Journalism is especially culpable when it stops merely covering the speculation economy and starts helping distribute it.

This is the part of your argument I find most institutionally troubling.

The press claims a special role in a democratic society. It invokes the First Amendment, the public's right to know, its responsibility to scrutinize power, and its independence from the people and institutions it covers.

Those are important principles, and many journalists genuinely uphold them.

But journalism is also a commercial industry operating under ownership structures, financial pressures, advertising relationships, and audience incentives.

And the relationship between major news organizations and Kalshi is now quite explicit.

December 2, 2025 — @CNN 
Announced an official Kalshi partnership incorporating prediction-market data, graphics, and a ticker into coverage.

December 4, 2025 — CNBC
Announced a multiyear, exclusive partnership bringing Kalshi data into television, digital, and subscription coverage.

April 7, 2026 — Fox Corporation
Announced a sponsored integration of Kalshi data across Fox News, Fox Business, Fox Weather, and Fox One.

Now return to Stephanie Ruhle interviewing Kalshi CEO @mansourtarek_

I understand exactly why you object to the familiar journalistic defense that landing the interview is itself an achievement.

An interview with a powerful executive can absolutely be valuable. But that is not the transaction at hand.

Mansour receives exposure to an established television audience, an opportunity to introduce or reinforce his preferred explanation of Kalshi's social purpose, and the legitimacy associated with appearing on a serious news program.

Ruhle gets access, content, and potentially newsworthy statements.

Those interests are not in the audience's best interests.

And the fact that an executive is asked difficult questions does not mean the interview has no promotional value to that executive.

That is what your criticism gets right.

The larger problem is the possibility of a financial or reputational feedback loop: a corporation becomes influential, news organizations cover its influence, the coverage increases its visibility, and that visibility helps justify its influence.

Meanwhile, corporate mergers and ownership changes can make the media ecosystem more concentrated, leaving fewer institutions with the independence and resources to resist commercially attractive editorial decisions.

The press is not uniquely corrupt in that respect. But it has a uniquely consequential obligation because the public relies on journalism to understand the very concentration of power in which the media industry participates.

6. Donald Trump is arguably the most consequential example of that conflict between journalism and spectacle.

This connects directly to your larger argument about Trump's relationship with the news business.

In 2015, Donald Trump understood something about television that many of his political opponents did not.

He understood that conflict, unpredictability, personality, and outrage on television were extraordinarily effective at attracting attention.

And news organizations understood that covering Trump could attract viewers.

Those interests reinforced each other.

By March 2016, an analysis cited by The New York Times estimated that Trump had received approximately $1.9 billion in earned media exposure. That figure represented an estimated advertising-equivalent value, not money literally spent on his behalf.

But its importance is unmistakable.

A candidate who had never held elected office became a nearly unavoidable figure across the American news environment. And that was eleven years ago.

The media weren't simply documenting his candidacy. Their editorial judgments about what deserved attention helped establish its extraordinary prominence.

Then came his presidency.

And your observation about 2020 deserves particular emphasis.

The United States faced a public-health emergency that required accurate information, effective government, and meaningful cooperation between elected officials and scientific experts.

Instead, Americans repeatedly witnessed disagreements between Trump and Dr. Anthony Fauci, then director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, unfold as public and political spectacles.

Trump questioned scientific guidance, criticized health experts, and made statements minimizing the pandemic's danger. His comments and his administration's handling of the crisis became part of an ongoing national media drama.

Fauci was not the single highest-ranking public-health official in the federal government, but he was among the most prominent infectious-disease authorities advising the country.

And this is where the stakes of treating government like reality television become terrifying.

A pandemic is not entertainment. Scientific disagreement is not supposed to be a personality contest. And the lives of Americans are not supposed to be the stakes of an ongoing television feud.

Nevertheless, that spectacle became an organizing feature of coverage during a period of enormous human suffering.

Then came the false claims about the 2020 election, the effort to overturn its outcome, and the attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021. The House January 6 committee concluded that Trump's false allegations of election fraud helped provoke the violence.

And yet, by the time the 2024 election arrived, the same personality whose political career had been inseparable from endless controversy was once again at the center of the American media universe.

Your argument is that the media industry's commercial interests made it structurally incapable of breaking its dependence on him.

There is considerable historical evidence supporting the concern about disproportionate coverage and the incentives behind it.

A television network can criticize Trump's conduct at 8 p.m. and benefit from the audience he attracts at 9 p.m.

A corporation can claim to be defending democratic institutions while simultaneously relying on political confrontation as its most reliable programming.

That doesn't mean every journalist secretly supports Trump. It means that the financial incentives of the institution can contradict the professional values of the people working within it.

In that respect, the Trump-media relationship and the rise of prediction markets illuminate the same underlying problem.

The market rewards attention, regardless of whether the attention produces public understanding, civic responsibility, or positive human outcomes.

And the consequences of that distinction are enormous.

7. Your Christian explanation gives this argument a moral dimension that economics alone cannot provide.

You mentioned the Christian understanding of humanity as fallen and in need of redemption.

That's not an incidental aside. It's closely connected to your criticism of the modern economy.

Christian teaching recognizes the human temptation toward greed, pride, selfishness, envy, dishonesty, and the desire for power.

But consider what happens when highly sophisticated economic and technological institutions become exceptionally good at identifying, encouraging, and profiting from those weaknesses.

Human envy becomes an opportunity for social-media engagement.
Human insecurity becomes an opportunity for advertising.
Human fear becomes an opportunity for political fundraising.
Human outrage becomes an opportunity for television ratings.
Human desire for money becomes an opportunity for gambling transactions.
Human loneliness becomes an opportunity for platforms to sell additional engagement.

None of those impulses is new.

What has changed is the scale at which businesses can identify those impulses, target individuals, and develop products that keep people returning.

There's an important distinction between acknowledging human sinfulness and accepting an economy that systematically profits from amplifying human temptation.

The Christian tradition does not teach that the existence of greed excuses people who exploit the greedy. It does not teach that human weakness absolves powerful institutions of responsibility for taking advantage of weakness.

And the Christian criticism is not simply that people spend too much money or look at their phones too frequently.

It's that money is being allowed to determine the value of things that possess worth independently of their commercial usefulness.

That is directly relevant to what you're saying about the father and son watching football.

The value of their evening isn't determined by how much they spend, how many advertisements they watch, what they wager, or how much information a broadcaster collects about them.

Its value exists in the relationship itself.

And when you consider that through a Christian understanding of human dignity, family, community, and stewardship, the objection becomes considerably deeper than a criticism of consumerism.

People are not merely economic participants.

They're human beings with lives that deserve meaning beyond their usefulness to the market.

8. The most disturbing consequence is what young people are being taught to expect from life.

This brings everything back to the teenager in 2026.

Imagine someone who grows up with very little experience of a world in which their attention is not constantly solicited by commercial systems.

Their friendships take place partly inside platforms.

Their entertainment increasingly comes with advertising, subscriptions, gambling opportunities, and algorithmic recommendations.

Their political understanding is influenced by attention-driven media organizations and personalities.

Their economic future is shaped by ownership structures they do not control and technological changes they did not choose.

They see people achieving extraordinary wealth through speculation, digital influence, asset appreciation, and ownership.

Meanwhile, the traditional promise that hard work will produce financial independence does not match reality.

And then society wonders why so many people struggle to find satisfaction in ordinary existence:

Why everything becomes a competition.
Why people feel pressure to turn hobbies into side hustles.
Why vacations become social-media content.
Why conversations become arguments to win.
Why politics becomes entertainment.
Why sporting events become gambling opportunities.
Why simply enjoying a moment can seem less important than extracting something else from it.

Not everybody experiences these pressures equally, and plenty of people continue to build rich, meaningful lives amid them. But the accumulation of commercial incentives matters.

Because the danger isn't simply that technology and modern capitalism are changing what people do.

It's that they are changing what people believe an experience is for.

And that is where I think your entire argument comes together.

We have become extraordinarily sophisticated at measuring economic output, financial returns, engagement, audience retention, consumer behavior, and the probability of future events.

But those measurements cannot tell us whether the people living inside this economy are experiencing more satisfying lives.

They cannot tell us whether a teenager feels loved.
They cannot tell us whether a father and son are becoming closer.
They cannot tell us whether workers have confidence in their futures.
They cannot tell us whether a community is becoming more trusting.
They cannot tell us whether a journalist has helped citizens understand something important or merely encouraged them to consume another round of controversy.
And they cannot tell us whether the economic gains associated with a new product justify its effects on society.

That doesn't mean economic success, technology, entertainment, or innovation are inherently bad. Innovation can enrich life enormously. Markets can distribute resources, generate prosperity, and reward useful discoveries.

But the purpose of economic development should be to improve the conditions under which human beings live.

The purpose of journalism should be to help people understand reality, not merely keep them attached to a continuous commercial spectacle.

The purpose of sports should not be determined by gambling companies.

And the purpose of human work should not be reduced to the cost savings achievable by eliminating the worker.

What you're describing is a reversal of priorities: instead of economic institutions existing to serve human life, human life is increasingly being reorganized to serve economic institutions.

That's why your argument about the loss of joy matters so much. Because joy is one of the few things that exposes the limits of this entire economic philosophy.

A person can be happy without purchasing anything.
A friendship can be meaningful without producing anything.
A family can spend an evening together without anyone making money from it.
A football game can matter profoundly to someone who doesn't have a single dollar riding on its outcome.
And that person has not failed to recognize some additional economic opportunity.

They have recognized something the market cannot adequately price.
The experience was already valuable. Nothing needed to be added to it.

I think that's the underlying indictment you've been developing: America has created increasingly powerful systems for extracting value from human activity while paying far too little attention to whether those systems are diminishing the human experience from which that value is extracted.

And when a company like Kalshi asks Americans to see yet another part of their lives as an opportunity for speculation, it isn't merely offering another financial product.

It's participating in a much larger cultural transformation—one in which the simple pleasure of being alive increasingly has to compete with somebody else's opportunity to make money from it. @stephenasmith @stevenfurtick @danorlovsky7 @jonathanfalwell @sbg1 @louiegiglio @priscillashirer @mppmsnow @minakimes
