text:
I think Mexico City is just a negotiation tactic and I still have near certainty that the Sonics will be back. Seattle spent years as the city the NBA could point to whenever another town needed convincing. This week the league started pointing somewhere else.

At last month’s board of governors meeting, Adam Silver left owners with the impression that Seattle is no longer a lock for an expansion team, ESPN’s Brian Windhorst reported Friday. Silver brought back Mexico City, where a local group has pitched the league’s bankers on a new team and a new arena district. Seattle’s offers are coming in well below a Las Vegas bidding war that could top $10 billion, and Windhorst reads the Mexico City talk as leverage to close that gap.

In 1999, economists James Quirk and Rodney Fort laid out how this works in a book called “Hard Ball.” Their argument is that pro leagues operate as monopolies and keep the number of teams low on purpose. They expand just enough to keep rival leagues out, but they leave enough good cities without a team that a threat to move one is believable. An empty market works as a bargaining chip.

Seattle was that chip. In 2013, a group led by Chris Hansen and Steve Ballmer had a deal to buy the Sacramento Kings and move them here as the SuperSonics. Sacramento answered with a plan for a $447 million arena, $258 million of it public money, and NBA owners voted 22-8 to keep the Kings where they were. The committee that recommended it was chaired by Clay Bennett, the man who moved the Sonics to Oklahoma City.

I am a Sonics fan when Bennett took them, and I watched my city spend the next decade as the NBA’s favorite threat. Now the league has found a new one to use against us. The Kings opened Golden 1 Center in 2016. Seattle hasn’t hosted a regular-season NBA game since 2008.

text:
The View from Oregon – 414
Re: Singleton Concepts in Formal Contexts
Friday 09 October 2026

Dear Friends,

Last week I considered the philosophical logic of singleton concepts, which is what I called concepts with only one entity falling under them. In discussing my examples of singleton concepts last week I used the concept, “Natural satellite of the third planet from the sun,” and I noted that terms in the intension of the concept could take different referents (say, if the moon no longer exists, or if Earth is no longer the third planet from the sun), with the modified referents of the intension of the concept translating into a modified extension of the concept. Planets and moons are corporeal bodies, and as such they are subject to change as are all material bodies. They come into being, change, and pass away. Any theoretical framework that remains fixed while the world to which it refers changes will end up playing the role of a function, yielding distinct values in its extension as the terms to which the intension refers take different arguments.

Also last week I said that I was interested to try to apply the distinction between idiographic and nomothetic concepts to formal concepts, presumably without reference to the changing world, which therefore offers a potential escape from the ambiguities of the actual world. A formal singleton concept could be something like, “Whole numbers greater than one and less than three.” One and only one entity falls under this concept, the number two. With numbers, there are no corporeal bodies to be subject to the vicissitudes of the world, and without such changes, the terms of the intension of the concept “Whole numbers greater than one and less than three” would not change over time. It’s obvious from this example that we can construct an infinitude of idiographic arithmetical concepts. We can also construct idiographic geometrical concepts.

“Triangles in Euclidean space with equal angles” is the concept that uniquely picks out equilateral triangles. We could define an infinitude of different kinds of space in which this concept no longer uniquely picks out equilateral triangles, which is why we specify “in Euclidean space.” In a fragmented space, no equilateral triangle would be possible, unless we re-defined an equilateral triangle, as indeed straight lines were re-defined as the shortest distance between two points, which allowed for a generalization away from Euclidean space that would also obtain in hyperbolic (space of constant positive curvature) and elliptical space (space of constant negative curvature).

An equilateral triangle on the surface of a sphere (a hyperbolic surface) can have interior angles up to 90 degrees, though if the triangle is made smaller its interior angles decrease, converging on 60 degrees as the triangle becomes infinitely small. Thus on the surface of a sphere the length of the side of the triangle (relative to the size of the sphere) matters, while it doesn’t matter in Euclidean space (assuming that the Euclidean plane is infinite). In this way, the length of the side of an abstract triangle relative to the size of the space in which it appears is relevant to the classification of the triangle, therefore relevant to the singleton concept that would capture such a triangle. Despite my attempt to escape from the vicissitudes of actuality by defining an abstract object and a singleton concept that uniquely would pick out this abstract object, we see that we can imagine circumstances in which the intension for the concept of some abstract object would have to be as complex as the intension of the concept of some concrete existent so as to uniquely pick out that abstract object.

If the size of a triangle mattered to whether or not that triangle was equilateral, then there would be an infinitude of equilateral triangles, and the concept “Triangles in Euclidean space with equal angles” would not pick out one and only one object, an abstract equilateral triangle that is identical to any other equilateral triangle (by Leibniz’s law of the identity of indiscernibles, because any equilateral triangle would have all its properties in common with any other equilateral triangle). But, as we’ve seen, in some spaces there could be an infinitude of distinct equilateral triangles, but we’ve already included “Euclidean space” in the intension of our concept so as to rule out these other spaces.

Consider some other non-Euclidean spaces. The surface of a cone could be infinitely extended, like Euclidean space, so that the size of a triangle constructed on a cone should be indifferent, but whether the triangle is constructed with the vertex of the cone inside or outside the triangle, or if one of the lines of the triangle passes through the vertex, will be relevant to the shape of the resulting triangle. Euclidean space shares many, but not all, properties with the surface of a cone, and it would be pretty easy to produce intuitive mappings of an infinite Euclidean place onto an infinitely extended cone. With an exhaustive mapping, any construction on one surface constitutes a mapping on the other surface, and vice versa, but that doesn’t make an equilateral triangle on a Euclidean plane into an equilateral triangle when it’s mapped onto a cone. The more imaginative our constructions become, the more they approximate an idiographic conception on a par with idiographic concepts that uniquely pick out individual entities in the actual world.

In any finite Euclidean space, any equilateral triangles that could not be constructed in that space without protruding beyond the boundaries of that finite space would be impossible, thus making the relative size of an equilateral triangle relevant to finite spaces in a way that size is not relevant to infinite Euclidean space. But a given Euclidean space could be infinite and still have a boundary (if infinitely extended away from the boundary), so that while an equilateral triangle could be constructed of any size, its placement in such a space would matter whether or not the construction could be made. Thus placement in space can be another variable along with the size of the space relative to the size of the construction. Earlier I wrote that objects of the actual world change over time—they come into being, change while existing, and then pass away—and it strikes me now that, while the constructions I’ve described with a triangle don’t involve changes over time, they do involve changes over space, where changes of space are the various possible locations for the construction of a triangle within a given space. In physics these changes in space are called translations in space, and symmetry with respect to translations in space is understood to be routine. However, depending upon the properties of which we must take into account (like the placement of an equilateral triangle within an infinite Euclidean plane with a boundary) this symmetry admits of exceptions in purely formal contexts. We can push this idea even farther.

There are geometrical constructions that involve an abstract kind of time, as when a moving point is said to describe a curve. The curve described by a point in the circumference of a circle as that circle makes one rotation is called a cycloid, and a cycloid is a special case of a trochoid. We could think of geometrical constructions like a cycloid curve as imaginatively assisted by the image of a moving point, but that once the construction is made, the imaginative construction in time is irrelevant. In other words, under this interpretation the moving point is merely what Daniel Dennett called an intuition pump. But we could just as well interpret constructions made with a moving point as the adding in of a component of actuality (viz. time) into an otherwise and previously purely abstract construction with no component of actuality whatsoever involved. That is to say, it becomes a property that we need to take into account.
Why would we want to employ such an interpretation? It is interesting because it displays a symmetry with thought experiments that involve idealization. The example of idealization that I usually trot out is that of a simple pendulum, which I discussed in newsletter 349. Idealizations employed in science begin with some actual feature or construction in the actual world, like the pendulum of a clock, and abstract from its physical properties one-by-one until we reach an abstract model of whatever it was that we started with. To get from a physical pendulum to a simple pendulum requires a number of steps as we attempt to control for material effects that we want to eliminate from our ideal model. Some of these steps are well known, like a frictionless fulcrum and a weightless string, and some are less well known, like a perfectly rigid frame and a uniform field of gravity, because a greater effort of thought is required to bring out the many presuppositions of a simple pendulum. Intuitively, we know what we want when we talk about a simple pendulum, but actually getting to an adequate model requires some effort.

How is this like my example of allowing time into mathematics through the use of a moving point? Some accounts of a cycloid curve include the provision that the circle must move without slipping—but once we add in something as material as slipping, we can imagine a great many other material conditions of a rolling circle that could result in the failure of a point on the circumference of a circle inscribing a perfect cycloid curve as the circle turns. Not only might the circle slip in its rotation, it might jump or bump or wiggle or any number of other real world imperfections that are precisely what we are abstracting away from when we construct an idealization. Thus with mathematical constructions we are starting with something completely abstract, and if we add to this properties from the actual world, the conception becomes less abstract. With idealizations, we start from some actuality and modify its properties so that it becomes more abstract. The two movements of thought, idealization and materialization, are complementary; they involve different directions of travel along the continuum from the abstract to the concrete. We can imagine the process of idealization employed in the construction of a simple pendulum meeting in the middle with the process of materialization employed in the construction of some mathematical construction into which we have added material components (like time). The continuum that stretches between an abstraction, characterized by pure idealization, and some actuality, characterized by pure materialization, has a place for every construction of any degree of abstraction, and the two complementary constructions of idealization and materialization can be shown to stand in relation to each other in this continuum.

Best wishes,

Nick

PS—Week before last, in newsletter 412, I said in a PS that I have long had it in mind to travel to a place and stay for a month. Now that I’ve had this experience I am going to find it rather difficult to go back to traveling in the conventional way, moving from place to place, living out of a suitcase. I’ve always favored longer stays and have avoided one night stays except when it was necessary to make a travel connection, usually to catch a flight. But, for me, a longer stay was several days or a week. For example, twice last year I traveled for three weeks, spending a week in three different places. Now my baseline is a month, and that substantially ups the ante. The problem is that I don’t have the money to spend a month in all the places I’d like to see at this leisurely pace. I’ve been looking into longer stays in Corsica and Menorca, and they were more than I’ve spent in Greece. And, in all honesty, I don’t have that much time either. I don’t have the strength to travel like I did ten or twenty or thirty years ago (exactly thirty years ago I stayed for two weeks in Paris, so even then I was pursing longer stays over moving around). My declining strength is one of the reasons that I chose this slow pace. Anything I do next will feel like a compromise, with time and cost defining the parameters of the compromise, as indeed it will feel like a compromise when I spend a week in Thessaloniki before I return to Oregon.

In a recent conversation it was suggested that I should see the St. Augustine sites of North Africa, and I would definitely like to do this. After visiting Pavia in 2019 I was chagrined to discover, after I left, that the tomb of St. Augustine is in Pavia (in the same church with the tomb of Boethius), but I didn’t visit it. I would like to correct that mistake and also spend some time in North Africa, and if I followed the trail of St. Augustine this would also take me to Milan and a few other places. This would be a perfect opportunity for a slow-paced visit to the places associated with St. Augustine, but that’s not the only travel project I have in mind.

Some years ago I said somewhere (I don’t recall if it was a newsletter or a blog post or both) that I would like to write a popular book about Hegel to be titled Travels with Hegel (following the model of Travels with Herodotus by Ryszard Kapuściński and Travels with Epicurus by Daniel Klein). I’ve been thinking about this a lot lately, even starting an outline for the project. This would require a lot of travel. If I followed the itinerary of Hegel’s life— Stuttgart 1770-1788, Tübingen 1788-1793, Berne 1793-1796, with summers at Tshugg at Landgut Steiger, Frankfurt 1797-1801, Jena 1801-1807, Bamberg 1807-1808, Nuremburg 1808-1816, Heidelberg 1816-1818, and Berlin 1818-1831 (and that’s not even including his trips to Weimar, Northern Netherlands, Leipzig, Vienna, Prague, and Paris)—and spent a week at each location, that would take two months. Obviously, it would be better to spend a month at each location, and that would require the better part of a year and money that I don’t have. I have to be careful in planning whatever years I have remaining, so should I prioritize Hegel or St. Augustine? I don’t yet have an answer to that. And it doesn’t end there.

I have another quasi-historical project that I would like to pursue which would be about the Transylvania Saxons. I say “quasi-historical” because I have no pretensions to being an historian. Sometimes I use history as a way to discuss philosophical ideas, and this is what I have in mind for the Hegel project mentioned above, and this is how I would approach the Transylvania Saxons. My working title for this project is Seven Weeks in the Seven Cities: The Transylvanian Saxons in the Siebenburgen, the seven cities being Sibiu (Hermannstadt) 20 December 1191, Bistrita (Bistritz), Brasov (Kronstadt), Cluj (Klausenburg), Medias (Mediasch), Sebes (Mühlbach), and Sighisoara (Schässburg). Secondarily there are the cities of Biertan, Câlnic, Copsa Mare, Crit, Prejmer, Harman, Richis, Rupea, Saschiz, Viscri, several of which cities are the sites of fortified churches, as with Biertan-Birthälm, Prejmer-Tartlau, Viscri-Weisskirch, Dârjiu-Székelyderzs, Saschiz-Keisd, Câlnic-Kelling, and Valea Viilor-Wurmloch.

This has been on my mind since I traveled to Romania in 2017 and saw several of the Siebenburgen and the fortified churches. Again, this would require a lot of travel, though the title suggests I could do it all in seven weeks. That would be the set up for the discussion (I think it’s a good title), but research would probably need to go beyond that seven weeks. The Saxons were invited into Transylvania by King Géza II of Hungary to promote industrial development in the region. The Saxons were an enterprising people and they went to work creating industries in Transylvania, but I find it especially interesting that despite their economic success, their long residency in Transylvania, and their remaining a coherent people among the many other peoples who lived in or passed through Transylvania, they never sought to declare a Saxon state in Transylvania. There was never a succession movement among the Saxons of Transylvania. At least one source called their attitude that of “ethno-corporatism,” which was sufficiently satisfied under the rule of a distant prince. I think a little more digging would reveal further dimensions to the story.

text:
National Teen Driver Safety Week is October 18-24

Teen driver safety depends on parent and guardian action

Safe driving starts long before anyone gets behind the wheel. This National Teen Driver Safety Week, Livermore Police encourages parents and guardians to discuss safe driving habits with their teens before handing over the keys.

Car crashes are a leading cause of death for teens (15-18 years old) in the United States. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, in 2024, there were 2,320 people killed in crashes involving a teen driver. That same year, 496 people were killed in crashes on California roads involving drivers aged 20 or younger.

Teens should understand the dangers of risky driving behaviors, like speeding, texting while driving, not wearing a seat belt and driving under the influence of alcohol and/or drugs.

“Meaningful conversations at home can help shape the choices teens make on the road,” Livermore Police Sergeant Harrison said. “Parents and guardians who talk about distractions, speeding and impairment give teens the tools to navigate real-world risks and steer them toward safer habits every time they drive.”

Teens are also encouraged to use free, mobile-friendly resources from the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV), including the free, mobile-friendly California Quick Reference Driver's Handbook, educational videos and the Teen Driver Roadmap, a step-by-step video guide for teens and their parents to help them prepare to get behind the wheel safely.

The Office of Traffic Safety offers the following tips to support teen drivers: 

▪️Learn about California’s provisional licensing law and Graduated Driver Licensing laws, which places restrictions on passengers and nighttime driving during the first year a teen has a license.

▪️Lead by example: Every time you're behind the wheel, it is a chance to model safe driving habits and talk about it with your teen.

▪️Establish safe driving behaviors that are not only expected, but also the law. This includes no phone use while driving, eliminating distractions from friends, always following the posted speed limit and always buckling up. · Friends, family members, parents and guardians can create a teen driving contract to outline specific driving guidelines.

▪️Speak up for safety: Encourage your teen to say something as a passenger if the driver is speeding, distracted, not wearing their seat belt or otherwise driving unsafely.

Teens, parents, educators, mentors and California drivers can also practice safe driving behaviors in realistic situations on the new, free, web-based driving simulation, The Road Ahead, at https://t.co/TY9vnV8Glj. Additionally, there is a user guide that provides an overview for how to get started and how to facilitate discussions about the game experience. The user guide is available online.

Funding for this program was provided by a grant from the California Office of Traffic Safety, through the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.

text:
Commemoration.

Martyr Longinus the Centurion
This is the Centurion who stood at the Cross of Christ and, seeing Him breathe his last, cried out “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matthew 27:54). From that day forth he was a believer, and was soon baptized. According to some accounts, he was one of the guard at the Tomb of Christ, and was one of those whom the Judaean leaders sought to bribe not to tell the news of the Resurrection. But Longinus would not be bribed, so the leaders plotted to kill him. He left the army and went to his homeland of Cappadocia, where he boldly preached Christ. He was beheaded at the instigation of Pontius Pilate.

Our Venerable Father Gall, Enlightener of Switzerland (640)
He was born in Ireland to wealthy parents, who sent him to be educated at the Monastery of Bangor. There he embraced the ascetical life and became a monk. He was one of the twelve monks who traveled with his spiritual father St Columbanus (November 23) as missionaries to Gaul. In time some of the group traveled into pagan lands, up the Rhine river to Lake Zurich. The monks settled on Lake Constance around a chapel dedicated to St Aurelia, which had been taken by the pagans as a shrine; they cleansed and reconsecrated the chapel, which became the center of their new monastery. Saint Gall lived as a hermit, serving the brethren by making nets and catching fish. In 612 St Columbanus went on to Italy with most of his disciples, leaving St Gall and a few others to continue their life. When St Gall delivered Frideburga, the daughter of a local duke, from a demon, he offered the saint a tract of land on the shores of Lake Constance; here was founded the monastery that in later times bore St Gall’s name.

At various times, the holy Gall refused calls to become a bishop, or to take over the abbacy of the great monastery at Luxeuil. To all such requests he answered that he would rather serve than command. He continued living in his isolated monastic community until he reposed in peace in 640, at the age of ninety-nine. In later years, and continuing well into the middle ages, the Monastery of St Gall became famed for the holiness of its monks and for its library.

The Venerable Longinus, the Lover of Labor
Longinus was a monk of the Monastery of the Kiev Caves in the fourteenth century. He was the gatekeeper of the monastery, and had such a pure and grace-filled heart that he always knew the thoughts of those who were entering the monastery and of those who were leaving the monastery. The miracle-working relics of Longinus repose in the Cave of St. Theodosius.

𝟮𝟬 𝗙𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀, 𝟵𝟯 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀, 𝟭𝟵 𝗣𝗮𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀. 𝗚𝗲𝘁 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗼 𝗣𝗮𝘀𝘀 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆.

On 25 September, FounderWise [@Founder_Wise] opened MVP Studio to the Uganda cohort at AVODA Institute of Entrepreneurship [@AvodaBiz]. Twenty founders used it.

Three weeks on, those 20 founders have logged 93 customer conversations, and 19 customers have paid them. 9 of those payments were deposits. 10 were full or repeat payments. 7 founders now have payments on the record.

From today, 16 October, any founder or program can get into the Studios. Every price is further down. First, what the cohort did, and the research behind the one rule they all followed.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝟮𝟬 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗸𝘀

Most founder programs measure what is easy to count: sessions attended, workbooks handed in, a pitch on the last day. Those programs teach a lot. They still leave the hardest question open, which is whether a customer will pay.

Steve Blank [@sgblank] put the starting point bluntly in October 2009: "There are no facts inside the building so get the heck outside". A few months later he wrote down what founders find once they do: "Most of the time the darn customers don't behave as you predicted."

MVP Studio is built for that trip outside. A founder brings one idea. The Studio takes it to a first version with a price on it, and then the founder tests that price with real people.

The cohort's record after three weeks:

20 founders

93 customer conversations, logged

19 paying customers: 9 deposits and 10 full or repeat payments

7 founders with payments recorded

Across the cohort, that is about one paying customer for every five logged conversations. It is a cohort-wide figure, and it will not hold for every founder.

The deposits matter most to me. Rob Fitzpatrick [@robfitz], author of The Mom Test, warned in a March 2019 SaaS Club interview about "bad data, which is most commonly compliments and opinions." His advice: "just ask them for something that they'll only give you if they're serious." With consumers, he added, "it's more common that they'll give you like a pre order or deposit".

Alberto Savoia, who worked at Google, made the same point in a March 2019 Stanford talk: "I'd rather have a one page business plan, an outline, with four checks stapled to it than a 30 page highly detailed business plan with all kinds of charts." Nine deposits are nine of those checks.

That leaves 13 founders with no payment recorded yet. For each of them, the record shows the conversations so far and how far they still are from the line they set.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝘂𝗹𝗲: 𝘄𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗻𝗰𝗵

Before launch, every founder wrote down a pass line. It is the number customers have to hit for the idea to go on. For some founders it was a count of deposits. For others it was signed contracts naming a fee, or payments received.

Hit the line and the idea goes on. Miss it, and you change the offer before you put more money into it.

Annie Duke [@AnnieDuke] described the same discipline on the podcast People I (Mostly) Admire in November 2022: "So the best kill criteria contain a state and a date. If I am not in this state by this date, I must quit." A pass line is that idea pointed toward going on: the state and the date that earn the idea more of your time and money.

Timing is why the line gets written first. After two weeks of building, a founder wants the idea to work, and every kind word from a customer starts to sound like evidence. Duke told First Round Review in October 2022 to write the criteria down and share them "so you can actually act on them."

Savoia gives the line a grammar. He calls it the XYZ hypothesis, "X percent of Y will Z", and says the format "forces you to write your idea in numbers."

The line also has to match how the business really gets paid. One founder in the cohort runs a property-management business. Landlords pay that business a percentage fee at the end of each month. A pass line that only counted cash in hand this week would have scored a working business as a failure.

So for that founder, a signed contract that names the fee counts now. The cash follows at month end.

I want founders making that call before launch, while they can still be honest about it.

𝗦𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲

You can do this tonight, before you open anything.

Start by writing down how a customer actually pays you. Some pay up front. Some put down a deposit and settle the balance later. Some sign a contract and pay a fee at month end.

Then count the evidence that matches. Customers who pay up front mean you count payments. Deposits mean you count deposits. Contracts paid later mean you count signed contracts that name your fee.

Add a number and a date. "Five deposits by the end of the month" is a pass line. "Good interest from customers" is a hope with no date on it.

Last, show the line to one person who will hold you to it, and do that before you launch.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗳 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘆

In March 2026, CB Insights [@CBinsights] published the reasons behind 385 VC-backed startups that shut down since 2023. 43% of them failed on poor product-market fit, and two-thirds of those were early-stage companies "that never found a market." Running out of capital topped the list at 70%, and the report calls it "almost always the final cause of death, not the root problem."

Those companies had investors. An early founder in Uganda is raising in a market where small checks are getting harder to find. Africa: The Big Deal [@AfricaTBD] counted $3.2 billion raised by African startups in 2025, with Uganda 13th by amount at $22m. In its 13 October 2026 update, the number of startups raising between $100k and $1m in the first nine months of the year fell from 220 to 171, "another record low."

So founders here mostly pay for their own first try. Uganda's National Household Survey 2023/24, published by UBOS in July 2025, found that 31 percent of households run a non-crop-farming household enterprise, and that 77 percent of people running one used their own savings as their main startup capital. The UBOS Labour Market Survey 2025 puts informal employment outside agriculture at 87.6 percent.

When the first money in a business is the founder's own savings, the pass line is what protects it. Deposits by the date tell you to keep spending. No deposits by the date tell you to change the offer while there is still something left to change it with.

𝗧𝘄𝗼 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗼𝘀, 𝘁𝘄𝗼 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

MVP Studio takes one idea to a priced, tested first version. It is the Studio the cohort used.

GTM Studio starts from the money a founder needs each month. It works back to the number of sales, and the number of conversations, it takes to get there. Then it checks in with you every week.

The bar further up the ladder looks familiar. Sam Altman's Startup Playbook says Y Combinator asks enterprise founders whether they have "a letter of intent from a customer saying they'll buy what you're building," and asks B2B founders, "do you have at least 10 paying customers?"

If you are still finding out whether anyone will pay, start with MVP Studio. If people already pay and the question is how many more you need, and by when, GTM Studio is the one.

𝗪𝗮𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝗼𝗻𝗲: 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹, 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿

The first 14 days are free. Invite 3 founders who sign up, and you get 7 more days.

After that you buy a pass. You pay once, and it never renews.

One Studio for 30 days: $19

One Studio for 90 days: $39

Both Studios for 90 days: $59

You pay by card at checkout. When a pass ends, your plan and your evidence stay readable, so the record you built is still there when you come back.

A pass ends on the date it says. A founder watching every dollar should never find a surprise renewal on a card statement for a tool they stopped opening.

𝗪𝗮𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝘄𝗼: 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗺, 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿, 𝗵𝘂𝗯 𝗼𝗿 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿

If you run a cohort, use Program. Your founders pay nothing. You pay per cohort of up to 30 founders, by invoice.

East Africa prices, per cohort:

MVP Studio or GTM Studio alone: $1,000

MVP + GTM + a funder report: $1,500

All of that plus the Brief for 90 days: $2,000

Year terms for the same three levels are $2,800, $4,000 and $5,500. Outside East Africa, prices are double.

A free pilot is available, so you can run it with one intake before you commit a budget line to it.

Programs do move the numbers. GALI, the research initiative co-led by the Aspen Network of Development Entrepreneurs (ANDE) [@AspenANDE] and Emory University, followed 2,455 ventures that applied to 43 programs in 9 countries. In emerging markets, accelerated ventures added $15,090 more revenue in a year than the applicants the programs turned down. That is May 2017 data, from programs run through 2016.

Measuring that is hard for the programs themselves. GALI's November 2020 study of accelerators and incubators in East Africa listed the delivery problems as "time-constrained staff, evaluating program outcomes, and identifying and maintaining funding sources."

A program gets a record for each founder of what happened with customers: conversations logged, deposits taken, payments received, all measured against a pass line the founder set before launch.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗸

If you are a founder, open the Studio today and write your pass line before you build anything. Use the 14 free days for your first conversations. By day 14 you will know whether to buy a pass, and which one.

If you run a program, tell me when your next intake starts. We will set up the pilot before it begins.

Passes and prices: https://t.co/Pm1Y0flCkX

Book a call about a pilot: https://t.co/ZsS6d5KfGO

Sources: Steve Blank, https://t.co/V99CBz4aUB (8 Oct 2009, 25 Jan 2010); Rob Fitzpatrick, SaaS Club podcast (26 Mar 2019); Alberto Savoia, Stanford eCorner (13 Mar 2019); Annie Duke, People I (Mostly) Admire (26 Nov 2022) and First Round Review (11 Oct 2022); CB Insights, top reasons startups fail (5 Mar 2026); Africa: The Big Deal (7 Jan, 13 Jan and 13 Oct 2026); UBOS, National Household Survey 2023/24 (Jul 2025) and Labour Market Survey 2025; Sam Altman, Startup Playbook; GALI (May 2017, Nov 2020).

Joshua Pi'Rwot. Country Director, AVODA Institute of Entrepreneurship. Founder, FounderWise.

So which will it be this week: your pass line, written down, or the start date of your next cohort?

text:
NHPC Limited (NSE: NHPC), originally incorporated as National Hydroelectric Power Corporation, is a premier Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE) under the Ministry of Power, Government of India. Established in 1975 and recently accorded the prestigious "Navratna" status, it is the largest organization for hydropower development in India.

Here is an overview of NHPC's key business segments and operations:

1. Hydroelectric Power Generation (Core Business)
This is the primary revenue driver for NHPC. The company is responsible for planning, developing, and operating massive hydroelectric power stations across the country.

Asset Footprint: NHPC operates numerous dams and power stations, predominantly in the northern and Himalayan regions (such as Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and Sikkim).
Strategic Role: Hydropower is crucial for grid stability, providing essential "peaking power" to balance out the intermittent nature of other renewable sources like solar and wind.

2. Renewable Energy (Solar & Wind)
To align with India's broader green energy goals, NHPC is aggressively diversifying its portfolio beyond traditional hydro projects.

Projects: The company is developing utility-scale solar and wind farms, including massive floating solar projects (such as the 88 MW project in Omkareshwar, Madhya Pradesh).
Future Tech: They are also exploring pilot projects in green hydrogen energy solutions.

3. Consultancy and Project Management
Leveraging decades of specialized civil engineering and hydro-infrastructure expertise, NHPC offers consultancy services.

Services: They provide end-to-end project management, design, engineering, and construction services for domestic and international power projects.
International Reach: The company is expanding its footprint by undertaking survey, investigation, and development stages for projects in neighboring countries like Nepal.

4. Power Trading
NHPC sells the bulk power it generates directly to State Electricity Boards (SEBs), state departments, and power distribution companies (Discoms) under long-term Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs).

Market Context:
As a state-backed, large-cap utility company, NHPC is known in the Indian stock market for its stable cash flows, high promoter holding (Government of India), and consistent dividend yields. Its long-term growth is heavily tied to India's transition to clean energy and the massive capital expenditure pipeline required to build out the nation's hydro and renewable capacity.

text:
Signing off from the Waldorf Jerusalem for 25+ hours of family time away from all ringing, pinging, tweeting devices! Best time of the week!

This week, we read the second portion of the Torah, the portion of Noah, in which we learn about one of the most famous biblical stories ever, the story of Noah’s ark.

The portion begins, “This is the line of Noah. Noah was a righteous man; he was blameless in his age; Noah walked with God.”

All the commentators ask a very obvious question. Why does the verse have to say “in his age”?

It says Noah was a righteous man and he was blameless. What do the words “in his age” add? 

We know the Torah doesn’t waste space and that every word in the Torah is there to teach us something.

So what are we to learn from the words “in his age”?

Famously, the commentator Rashi explains that there is a debate among the rabbis about whether those words are meant to praise Noah, that despite the world being so corrupt, he was still righteous, or the opposite, that he was righteous in his generation, but if he had lived in the generation of Abraham, he would not have been considered righteous.

As Rabbi Goldberg pointed out, this is like the debate about Michael Jordan. Was he great in his time because the NBA was softer back then, or was he truly the GOAT, and even in today’s NBA, he’d still be Michael Jordan?

A funny and pretty spot-on analogy.

So what is really behind this debate? It’s not just a historical or descriptive verse that’s here to tell us that Noah was righteous. What is this debate really about?

Well, perhaps to shed some light on this, let’s go back to the first few words of the portion.

“This is the line of Noah. Noah was a righteous man…”

The portion begins by telling us that it’s about to list Noah’s offspring, but then it seemingly changes course and tells us about Noah, not his offspring. Why?

It should say, “This is the line of Noah,” and then proceed to tell us the names of Noah’s kids, which it does in the next verse. But why the break?

Rabbi Goldberg explains beautifully that before parents can educate their kids, before they can expect greatness from their children, they need to first work on themselves and make sure they are good role models.

If parents behave immorally, you can’t expect their kids to behave morally.

Who was Noah’s first child? Himself. Not literally, but before the Torah tells us about Noah’s kids and how he raised them, it says, “These are the offspring of Noah, Noah…”

Noah, first and foremost, worked on himself.

Great. That’s what makes him righteous.

The difference is that Abraham didn’t only work on himself; he also inspired the whole generation.

In fact, when God told Abraham that He was going to destroy Sedom, unlike Noah, who just accepted that God was going to destroy the world, Abraham fought back and asked God not to destroy Sedom.

Sure, Noah was a righteous man, but he was not the leader Abraham was. He built his ark and saved himself in it. He did not try to change those around him like Abraham did.

This reminds me of one of my favorite quotes.

“When I speak to managers, I feel like they’re important. When I speak to leaders, I feel like I am important.”

Good leaders don’t only take care of themselves. Good leaders empower others.

So yes, Noah was a righteous man, but he lacked the leadership abilities possessed by Abraham and our other leaders, including Moses, who cared more about the nation than he cared about himself.

Some more quotes about this idea:

“Leadership is unlocking people’s potential to become better.” — Bill Bradley

“A leader is best when people barely know he exists. When his work is done, his aim fulfilled, they will say: We did it ourselves.” — Lao Tzu

“As we look ahead into the next century, leaders will be those who empower others.” — Bill Gates

“The greatest leader is not necessarily the one who does the greatest things. He is the one that gets the people to do the greatest things.” — Ronald Reagan

Noah was righteous, but his generation wasn’t. They were corrupt. Instead of asking God to have mercy on them, he accepted their fate, built himself an ark, and put walls around himself instead of influencing others to be better.

That’s why the Torah uses the words “in his generation…”

Because in regard to his generation, he wasn’t a leader, unlike Abraham.

Noah was righteous, but he wasn’t a leader.

A few verses later, the Torah says, “The earth became corrupt before God; the earth was filled with lawlessness.”

The word the Torah uses for lawlessness is, wait for it… Hamas.

Yep, that’s right. God believed that once there was Hamas, there was no saving the world. It had gone too far, it had become too morally bankrupt, and there was no coming back.

If you drill down on that verse, you’ll notice a nice idea I never thought of before.

What was their sin? It says they became corrupt and the world was chaotic, but why? What was their mistake that led to all of that immorality?

The verse says the words “Haaretz Lifnei Haelokim,” the land before God.

Their problem was that they put earthly matters before God, before spirituality.

They put their own comfort, their own greed, before God.

When a generation does that, when they put their own materialistic interests before they put God, what happens is chaos.

If there is no God, there are no boundaries. When there are no boundaries, everything is allowed.

They put “earth” before God, and that was their fundamental mistake.

OK, so why did God punish them with a flood? Now we understand why.

They had no boundaries. They had no problem stealing, for example, because if they had no God, they had nothing stopping them from doing whatever they wanted.

So God says, “OK, you lived without boundaries? I will remove My boundaries too.”

We have beaches. We have sand. We have the shore. The water doesn’t usually flow freely onto the land. If it did, we’d all be dead.

But God put boundaries into nature. As soon as they removed boundaries from society, God punished them with the appropriate punishment of removing boundaries in nature.

And now to an even more fundamental idea.

Why an ark? If God was going to destroy the world and He wanted Noah to survive, why not just perform a miracle so that the water wouldn’t reach Noah? Why not just save Noah without the need for so much construction of this ark?

What was the point of God telling Noah to construct an ark? Why not just perform the miracle and save Noah?

The commentators offer one answer, and I’d like to offer another.

The commentators on the Torah explain that God asked Noah to build the ark so that those around him would ask him what he was building and why.

He’d then explain to them that God was going to destroy the world due to their corrupt ways, and hopefully, that would scare them enough that they’d repent.

That’s why God asked Noah to build the ark, so others around him would potentially change their ways.

To me, that answer doesn’t really address the question.

If God wanted the people to repent, why not just perform a miracle and have them repent? Why the need for this ark?

I think the idea is even deeper.

I think God is teaching us, yet again, how He runs the world.

Sure, He performs miracles, and He looks after His children, but not before His children make the first move.

God is, in essence, saying to Noah, “You want Me to save you? Sure, but first, get to work. Build the ark.”

As I have said many times, my favorite verse in the entire Torah takes place when the Israelites approached the Red Sea and were seemingly stuck.

In front of them was the terrifying darkness of the sea, and behind them were the chariots of the world’s strongest empire, Egypt.

They were stuck.

So they did the natural thing and asked Moses why he had taken them out of Egypt to die there on the shore.

Moses then relays that question to God and asks God why He told him to take them out of Egypt, only for them to die there on the shore.

Now, if you stop and think about that, you might expect God to instruct Moses to tell the people to pray. Or maybe to do good deeds. Maybe God would tell them to love their neighbor.

However, God says none of those things.

God’s response is, “Why are you yelling at Me, Moses? Tell the Israelites to jump in and go!”

As soon as Nachshon jumped in, only then did God split the sea.

God is perhaps teaching us here that He can perform miracles, He can save Noah, but first, God requires Noah to demonstrate his faith, to take that first step, and then God can perform His miracle.

Generally speaking, God performs miracles within nature, at least in today’s modern world. Today, we don’t have miracles like the splitting of the sea or the 10 plagues.

Today, God performs miracles for us through nature, but He requires us to take that first step.

He needs us to build an army, an economy, a society, and then, and only then, does He perform His miracles and make Israel into a miraculous state.

The same is, of course, true for Aliyah.

You want to make Aliyah successfully? You need to jump in.

Sure, God will perform miracles so that you can build an incredible life for yourself in Israel, but He requires you to take that first step.

It’s a scary step, just like the step into the Red Sea was a scary step, but if you want God to take care of you and help you build a successful life in the State of Israel, you need to demonstrate to God that you are willing to take that first step, get on a plane, and do your part.

God told Noah to build the ark so that Noah would do his part. Noah would take that first step so that God could then step into the ring and do His thing.

In Judaism, we call that Hishtadlut, translated as “effort.”

We know God runs the world, so why even work? Why even do anything if God decides our fate? The answer is that we have to do our part, and if we do, God will do the rest, but we can’t just sit back and wait for God’s miracles.

We can’t just sit back in the diaspora and wait for God to bring Mashiach so we can all come back to Israel. God is waiting for US to come back SO THAT He can bring Mashiach.

Back to Noah’s leadership, or lack thereof, God instructs Noah to build the ark and gives him exact dimensions.

One of God’s instructions to Noah is to build a window into the ark. Why? Why is that important?

Now that we know that Noah was righteous but not a leader, perhaps God is saying to Noah, “Listen, you’re righteous, and that’s why I’m saving you, but be a leader. Put that window into the ark so you can see the suffering of those around you. Don’t just worry about yourself. Be more like Abraham. For that, you need a window so you can look out of the ark and see how the world is being destroyed around you.”

Maybe He’s even telling him to build a window as a rebuke. “You saved yourself by being righteous, but look around you. Look at this missed opportunity. You could have prevented all this suffering, all this destruction, if only you had been a leader like Abraham.”

Now, skipping ahead to the end of the portion, we have another famous story, the story of the Tower of Babel.

The Torah says, “Everyone on earth had the same language and the same words. And as they migrated from the east, they came upon a valley in the land of Shinar and settled there.

They said to one another, ‘Come, let us make bricks and burn them hard.’ Brick served them as stone, and bitumen served them as mortar.

And they said, ‘Come, let us build us a city, and a tower with its top in the sky, to make a name for ourselves; else we shall be scattered all over the world.’”

In other words, these sinners tried to build a tower to the heavens to be like God.

So what did they do wrong exactly, and how does God react?

“GOD came down to look at the city and tower that the mortals had built, and GOD said, ‘If, as one people with one language for all, this is how they have begun to act, then nothing that they may propose to do will be out of their reach. Let us, then, go down and confound their speech there, so that they shall not understand one another’s speech.’”

There are two words here that need explaining.

“Came down…”

God “came down” to see the tower?

He couldn’t see it from the heavens? He had to come down to see it? What’s that about?

God here is also teaching us an incredibly important lesson that is more relevant today than ever.

God, before judging and punishing the people for building the tower, had to “come down” to see their circumstances, to put Himself in their shoes.

God is teaching us that before we judge anyone, even if we think they are dead wrong, we need to first understand who they are, what their circumstances are, and we need to put ourselves in their shoes.

This is true for people, and it is true for nations.

If only the world would ask itself the question, “What would we do if we were in Israel’s shoes?” Everything would be very different.

One of the most glaring questions surrounding this war and that dark day on which it began is: All those criticizing Israel, what would they do if their country were attacked the way Israel was attacked?

It’s very easy to sit “in the heavens” and look down and judge others, but instead, even God “comes down” and puts Himself in their shoes before reaching any conclusions.

If only humans behaved this way, the world would be an infinitely better place.

And finally, there is one more lesson from those words “came down.”

Unlike other religions that believe in abstaining from the pleasures of this world, Judaism believes and teaches something else.

God does not want us up in the heavens. In fact, there is even an actual verse in the Torah itself that says “Lo Bashamayim Hi,” which means that the Torah and the commandments are not in the heavens, but rather, they are in our hearts, and they are accessible and attainable to those who pursue them.

God doesn’t want us disconnecting from this world and acting like angels. God created us as humans, and He created the world for us to live in it and enjoy it.

What God DOES expect from us is to bring Him down into our lives.

In Judaism, we have the opportunity to inject Godliness into literally everything we do. We believe in bringing God down to us, not us going up to Him.

We bless God when we open our eyes. We bless God when we wash our hands in the morning. We bless God when we go to the bathroom. We bless God when we eat. We thank God for letting us live another day. We bless God when we see beauty in nature. We bless God when we see lightning.

The list is very long, but the idea is that God wants us to live and enjoy life, but He also wants us to bring Him down into our lives and sanctify even the most mundane things by injecting spirituality into everything we do.

God “came down” to earth to, first and foremost, understand the people before judging them for their sin. But He also “came down” to teach us how He expects us to live, as holy creatures who were created in His image and who are to emulate His ways by sanctifying the world around us.

Shabbat shalom.

text:
The settlement of the remote Pacific by the ancestors of the Polynesians was one of the great feats of human migration. Over roughly two thousand years, voyagers in double-hulled canoes reached nearly every habitable island inside a vast triangle marked by Hawaiʻi, Aotearoa New Zealand, and Rapa Nui.

The movement began with the Lapita culture, named for a pottery site in New Caledonia. Around 3,000 years ago Lapita communities sailed east and reached Fiji, Tonga, and Samoa. A long pause followed. A 2011 radiocarbon study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences dated the settlement of the Society Islands to about 1025 to 1120 CE. Within roughly two centuries, colonists reached the most distant islands of East Polynesia, including Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui, and New Zealand. Canoes carried families, dogs, pigs, chickens, and crop plants such as taro and breadfruit, so each new island could be farmed much like the last. The sweet potato, a plant native to South America, also spread through East Polynesia, which suggests that some voyagers reached the Americas and returned.

Scholars offer several reasons for leaving islands that seemed well supplied. Small islands could feed only limited populations. Chiefly succession often favored elder sons, which gave younger siblings motives to seek land of their own. Conflict, drought, and the prestige of discovery also played roles. Navigators read stars, ocean swells, birds, and clouds without instruments. Much of that knowledge was nearly lost after European contact. In 1976 the Polynesian Voyaging Society sailed the double canoe Hōkūleʻa from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti, guided by Mau Piailug, a master navigator from Satawal in Micronesia. More than 17,000 people met the canoe at Papeʻete, and the voyage revived traditional wayfinding across the Pacific.

text:
Oregon already has gun control…like:

Oregon has several state-level gun control and safety laws, though some of its strictest recent ballot measures face ongoing legal battles.

Background Checks & Purchasing

• Background Checks: Oregon requires background checks for all firearm sales, including private and dealer transactions, processed through the Oregon State Police.
• Minimum Age: You must be at least 21 years old to purchase a handgun, and at least 18 years old to purchase a rifle or shotgun.
• Measure 114 (Permit-to-Purchase & Magazines): Approved by voters in 2022, this law requires a permit, safety training, and completed background checks to buy a firearm, and bans magazines holding more than 10 rounds. Following legal challenges, implementation has been delayed by the legislature until March 2028.

Carrying & Public Spaces

• Concealed Carry: Carrying a concealed handgun in public requires an Oregon Concealed Handgun License (CHL), available to residents aged 21 and older who pass competency training. Oregon does not offer reciprocity for out-of-state CHL permits.
• Open Carry: Open carry is legal statewide, but local cities and counties (such as Portland and Multnomah County) can ban the open carry of loaded firearms in public places (though CHL holders are exempt).
• Prohibited Locations: Firearms are banned in public buildings and facilities listed under state law, including the State Capitol, court facilities, and restricted areas of airports. Public schools and universities may also adopt policies prohibiting firearms on their grounds.

Storage & Safety Laws

• Safe Storage: Gun owners are legally required to securely store firearms when they are not in their immediate control, particularly to keep them out of reach of children.
• Lost or Stolen Reporting: Owners must report lost or stolen firearms to law enforcement (typically within 48 hours in jurisdictions like Portland).

Red Flag & Restriction Laws

• Extreme Risk Protection Orders (ERPOs): Oregon has a "red flag" law allowing law enforcement or family members to petition a court to temporarily remove firearms from individuals considered a danger to themselves or others.
• Ghost Guns & Rapid-Fire Devices: Oregon bans untraceable ghost guns and 3D-printed firearms, as well as rapid-fire conversion devices.

text:
Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary

FRIDAY

Morning Prayer
God, come to my assistance.
- Lord, make haste to help me

Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit
as it was in the beginning, is now, and will be forever.  Amen.

Virgin of virgins,
I choose you today
as my sovereign, my queen, my empress,
and I declare myself, as I am in fact,
your servant and your slave.
I invoke your royal name of Mary,
that is, sovereign Lady,
and beg of you with all my heart
to admit me into the privileged circle¡
of your family
as one of your servants,
to do your will
as a humble slave and a loving child.
As a sign of your acceptance
engrave on my heart
with the fire of your love,
not the brand of an unwilling slave,
but those two gracious words of the angel:
Ave Maria.
As long as I draw breath
may your burning love ensure
that I bear these words
in my heart and in my memory,
and that until my dying breath
my will may be always on fire
with my great desire to serve you,
my sovereign and my queen,
glorious in your majesty.
Though I am in every way unworthy
of so honorable a title,
I resolve sincerely to be your slave,
to serve you wholeheartedly,
to protect your name,
and that of your Son,
against every insult,
as far as it may rest with me,
and never to allow anyone in my charge
to offend your Son in any way.
By your tender love for your Son,
by the glories you have received
from the Most Holy Trinity,
do not reject me from your service
but as my sovereign and my queen
preside over all my actions,
command whatever you will,
direct all my work,
remedy all its defects.
During my whole life
rule over me
as your servant and slave.
At the hour of my death,
as I hope for
at the end of my loving servitude
among the privileged members of your family,
receive my soul and escort it
into the presence of God.

St Bartolome de Los Rios(1580-1652)

PSALMODY

Ant.1 My soul clings to you, Lord Jesus Christ.

Psalm 51
O God, have mercy on me
Your inmost being must be renewed, and you must put on the new man. (Eph 4:23-24)
Have mercy on me, God, in your kindness.
In your compassion blot out my offense.
O wash me more and more from my guilt
and cleanse me from my sin.
My offenses truly I know them;
my sin is always before me
Against you, you alone, have I sinned;
what is evil in your sight I have done.
That you may be justified when you give sentence
and be without reproach when you judge,
O see, in guilt I was born,
a sinner was I conceived.
Indeed you love truth in the heart;
then in the secret of my heart teach me wisdom.
O purify me, then I shall be clean;
O wash me, I shall be whiter than snow.
Make me hear rejoicing and gladness,
that the bones you have crushed may thrill.
From my sins turn away your face
and blot out all my guilt.
A pure heart create for me, O God,
put a steadfast spirit within me.
Do not cast me away from your presence,
nor deprive me of your holy spirit.
Give me again the joy of your help;
with a spirit of fervor sustain me,
that I may teach transgressors your ways
and sinners may return to you.
O rescue me, God, my helper,
and my tongue shall ring out your goodness.
O Lord, open my lips
and my mouth shall declare your praise.
For in sacrifice you take no delight,
burnt offering from me you would refuse,
my sacrifice, a contrite spirit,
a humbled, contrite heart you will not spurn.
In your goodness, show favor to Zion:
rebuild the walls of Jerusalem.
Then you will be pleased with lawful sacrifice,
(burnt offerings wholly consumed),

text:
Ten. That's how many men on the product were analysed in the one placebo-controlled exosome hair trial I could read in full, followed for 16 weeks. Clinics already use exosome injections on thinning scalps, and the FDA says no exosome product is approved.

The trial (Amini and colleagues, Life, 2025) randomised 24 men with early pattern loss at a Malaysian university to a commercial exosome product with two plant extracts, or saline, injected into the scalp under local anaesthetic in four sessions about two weeks apart. Twenty were analysed.

On the product, the median gain was 9.5 hairs in a 0.5 cm² patch against 1.5 on saline (p=0.006). The spread was wide, two men had mild scalp irritation, and the authors call their sample small and follow-up short. The paper doesn't say where the exosomes came from. The company that supported the research materials also prepared the coded group labels, and the trial was registered a week after the paper was accepted.

That trial sits near the top of a thin pile. A 2025 review (Al Ameer and colleagues, Clin Cosmet Investig Dermatol) found 11 studies of exosomes for hair loss:
- 2 randomised trials
- 3 single-group studies
- 3 look-backs at clinic records
- 1 case series
- 2 case reports

All reported improvement and none reported serious side effects, but the nine without random allocation can't show what would have happened anyway. The review's authors call exosomes promising and still ask for well-standardised, high-quality randomised trials.

The FDA adds that exosome products meant to treat a condition need its approval, and in 2019 it warned of serious adverse events in Nebraska patients given unapproved ones (that alert doesn't mention hair).

That leaves the evidence for exosomes in pattern hair loss weak, though clinics offer them now.

With exosomes drawn from six different stem-cell sources plus a plant-extract product, and no standard dose or schedule, a result for one product says little about the next.

text:
The profanation of the Last Supper during the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympic Games did shock me. 

But what shocked me more was something else: the spectacle of Marie Antoinette, decapitated, holding her own severed head.

That grotesque image of a woman’s execution was offered to the world as a proud national story, as if murder were glory.

Today, October 16th, marks the anniversary of her execution in 1793. Two hundred and thirty-three years have passed since the French Republic sent a 37-year-old woman to the guillotine. Her husband had already been executed. Her children were taken from her. She was humiliated, imprisoned, and dragged before a court whose verdict was never truly in doubt.

Her accusers even stooped to the grotesque allegation of incest with her own son, an accusation of extraordinary cruelty meant to destroy not only a queen but a mother.

Marie Antoinette was not a saint, but that changes nothing essential: **she did not deserve to die.** She was a human being, a wife, a mother, and ultimately a defenceless prisoner.

What makes this especially horrifying is that those who killed her believed themselves righteous. They spoke the language of liberty and humanity while committing cruelty.

And she was one among thousands. Aristocrats, priests, ordinary people, opponents, and eventually revolutionaries themselves were consumed by political violence presented as virtue.

Yet what disturbs me almost as much as the crime itself is how easily modern France can fold that violence into celebration.

This is a country of immense cultural and intellectual achievement. But brilliance is not the same as moral maturity.

A civilization must be able to say plainly: **what was done to this human being was wrong**, without hiding behind myths of progress. If it cannot, something essential is missing from its claim to greatness.

On this anniversary, I feel sorrow for Marie Antoinette, horror at the cruelty inflicted on her, and deep disappointment that a nation capable of so much still struggles to confront that suffering with the seriousness it deserves.

text:
@bismil_prasad 

A Lecture for Aashish Joshi: Kaccha Badam, the Collegium and the Meaning of a Polyvocal Judiciary

Dear Aashish Joshi Sir,

This lecture is offered because your understanding of the Collegium appears incomplete. The purpose is not to insult you, but to invite you to examine judicial appointments beyond political slogans, famous surnames and the narrow opposition between “merit” and “representation.”

1. The constitutional meaning of Kaccha Badam

The peanut seller is not an object of pity. Selling peanuts is neither illegal nor undignified. The real question is why elite society notices the vendor as entertainment but rarely accepts him as a producer of culture, knowledge or political thought.

Bhuban Badyakar’s Kacha Badam travelled across the world without Bollywood’s studios or established stars. Viral democracy heard his voice directly. Yet cultural power and economic reward continued to remain concentrated elsewhere.

Shah Rukh Khan represents the extraordinary outsider who entered Bollywood and conquered its star system. Bhuban Badyakar represents another outsider whose creation conquered the public without giving him comparable institutional power. This is the dichotomy: one outsider becomes the institution, while another is consumed by it.

The same problem appears in law. The judicial system may celebrate social diversity symbolically while continuing to decide whose voice possesses authority.

2. From the peanut seller to the Collegium

The Collegium is not merely a committee recommending names. It is a constitutional mechanism situated between two dangers:

executive control over judicial appointments; and
oligarchic reproduction within the Bar and Bench.

Judicial independence requires protection from political capture. But independence cannot mean that a small professional circle continuously appoints people drawn from familiar families, chambers, communities and social networks.

A judiciary can be independent of the executive and still remain socially unrepresentative. That is the central contradiction of the Collegium.

3. Professor G. Mohan Gopal’s argument

Professor G. Mohan Gopal’s position should not be reduced to the statement that “the Supreme Court is an oligarchy.” His deeper argument is that oligarchic power begins within the Bar, where a few social groups frequently dominate professional opportunity, visibility and eventual access to the Bench.

At the same time, he has defended the Collegium against greater executive control under present political conditions. His position therefore contains an important constitutional tension: protect the Collegium as a safeguard of independence, but reform it so that independence does not become inherited privilege.

Representation is not opposed to merit. If access to legal education, chambers, reported cases, senior designation and professional recognition is unequal, the prevailing definition of “merit” may simply reward those who already possess institutional advantage.

4. What is a polyvocal judiciary?

A polyvocal judiciary is a court containing multiple constitutional voices, social experiences and methods of reasoning. It does not speak in one inherited language of class, caste, region or professional pedigree.

Polyvocality requires more than demographic photographs. Different backgrounds must be permitted to influence how judges understand liberty, poverty, disability, caste, gender, criminal justice and state power.

It also does not mean that every judge from an underrepresented group will deliver “progressive” judgments. That assumption reduces judges to their identities. Genuine representation permits a judge to remain intellectually independent—including the freedom to disappoint those who welcomed the appointment.

5. Justice J.B. Pardiwala and accountability without permanent exile

Justice J.B. Pardiwala’s journey presents one of the most difficult examples of a polyvocal appointment.

In 2015, controversial observations concerning reservation in an order connected with Hardik Patel led 58 Rajya Sabha members to submit a notice seeking his removal. The disputed observations were subsequently expunged, and the removal process was not pursued. Therefore, it is accurate to speak of an impeachment or removal controversy, not an accomplished impeachment.

His later elevation to the Supreme Court raises a serious institutional question: can a judge be publicly criticised, correct the formal record, continue to develop and later contribute meaningfully to constitutional law?

The answer cannot be automatic absolution. Appointment after controversy does not itself prove transformation. That must be assessed through a careful comparison of earlier and later judgments.

But one controversial episode should not necessarily become permanent intellectual exile. Accountability must preserve the possibility of learning. Otherwise, constitutional criticism becomes punishment rather than correction.

Justice Pardiwala’s elevation is therefore significant because it contains contradiction: controversy and confidence, criticism and continuation, institutional memory and the possibility of development. This is the Pardiwala paradox.

6. Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah as an innovative appointment

Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah is among the finest examples of an innovative post-2014 Collegium appointment. His elevation brought together judicial experience, social representation, constitutional sensitivity and a distinctive practical voice.

Calling his appointment innovative does not mean that the Collegium performed an act of charity. Representation is not a relaxation of merit. A socially diverse Bench can perceive facts, injuries and institutional realities that an enclosed professional class may overlook.

An innovative judge does not invent law according to personal preference. An innovative judge discovers neglected possibilities already present within the Constitution and applies settled legal principles with sensitivity to lived reality.

Justice Amanullah’s appointment did not resolve the structural problem of representation. No individual appointment could. But it changed the terms of the debate: judicial diversity could no longer be dismissed as inconsistent with excellence.

7. The contribution of those who raised representation

Professor Arvind Kumar, Professor Dilip Mandal, Dr Ratan Lal and Waman Meshram must be remembered as voices that repeatedly drew attention to the gap between India’s constitutional diversity and the composition of its higher judiciary.

Justice Amanullah’s appointment should not be used to silence these critics. One appointment cannot become evidence that every representational deficit has disappeared.

The better conclusion is that sustained public criticism made an institutional absence visible, while the appointment demonstrated how representation could enrich the Court. Tokenism closes the conversation; a meaningful appointment deepens it.

8. The Chandrachud-era question

The Chandrachud period should not be assessed only through individual judgments, speeches or family legacy. It must also be examined through the appointments, elevations and institutional possibilities associated with that era.

The question is whether the Collegium widened the constitutional imagination of the Court. Did it identify judges with different social histories and jurisprudential approaches? Did it recognise voices that the conventional networks of the Bar might have overlooked? Did it explain its choices adequately?

Justice Amanullah offers a strong affirmative example. Justice Pardiwala presents a more complicated example involving controversy, correction and institutional confidence. Together, they demonstrate that polyvocality is not ideological uniformity. It includes voices that cannot be placed comfortably within “progressive” and “conservative” boxes.

9. Khushwant Singh, irreverence and judicial morality

Khushwant Singh represents irreverence—the ability to puncture public hypocrisy without claiming saintliness. The moral professor represents disciplined theory and institutional criticism.

Law requires both qualities. Without moral seriousness, irreverence becomes mere performance. Without irreverence, legal morality can become self-righteous and detached from ordinary life.

The satirical expression “Professor of Immoral Traffic” should therefore be understood as a criticism of the way morality circulates through law and politics—not as an allegation of personal criminal conduct. Law sometimes scrutinises the morality of vulnerable citizens more intensely than it examines institutional power.

A judge’s technical arbitration decisions, visible emotions and willingness to work in a Vacation Bench may reveal different parts of the same judicial personality. Human complexity should neither prevent criticism nor be erased by it.

10. The final connection

The peanut seller and the Supreme Court judge appear to inhabit entirely different worlds, but the same problem connects them: elite institutions interpret both before allowing either to speak in an independent voice.

The vendor is reduced to a viral song. The judge is reduced either to a controversy, a surname, a community or institutional prestige. In both cases, complexity disappears.

A genuinely polyvocal democracy must recognise the peanut seller as a creator and examine the judge as a developing constitutional actor. It must not romanticise the vendor, absolve the judge or treat representation as decoration.

Therefore, Aashish Joshi Sir, the proper question is not whether the Collegium is wholly virtuous or entirely oligarchic. The real inquiry is whether it can defend judicial independence, confront its own social exclusivity, recognise constitutional talent beyond familiar networks, preserve accountability and still permit intellectual transformation.

That is the meaning of a polyvocal judiciary. It is not a Bench on which everyone agrees. It is a Bench on which India’s disagreements can finally be heard?

text:
Indian constitutionalism, the rule of law, and Parsi legal culture
Mitra Sharafi

The Real Test of a Polyvocal Judiciary: Dr Abhinav Chandrachud. Sir, is Dr Abhinav Chandrachud—not merely another celebrated surname—the real test of whether India truly wants a polyvocal judiciary? His lectures on the CAA and NRC, his historical writings, and even his elegant argument concerning whether criticism of Hinduism can legally amount to defamation reveal both an inherited familiarity with law and an independent constitutional mind.
But the deeper post-2014 question concerns appointment, elevation and resignation. If the Collegium repeatedly overlooks jurists merely because their scholarship, family history or public reasoning creates discomfort, will the judiciary not lose an important voice—and with it one of the most productive dichotomies in Indian law: inheritance alongside independence, tradition alongside criticism, and constitutional office alongside intellectual freedom?
The Indian Constitution was not shaped by barristers alone. It emerged from many languages, social struggles, memories and cultural traditions. Even during difficult political times, that constitutional culture survives in unexpected persons and institutions. Smriti Irani, too, must be included in this discussion—not as a decorative political reference, but as a reminder that education, authority and constitutional participation cannot be monopolised by one profession, university, dynasty or ideological class.
The real question, therefore, is not whether someone belongs to the Chandrachud family, supports the government, criticises Hinduism or comes from outside the legal elite. The question is whether our institutions possess enough confidence to accommodate contradictory voices. If they do not, “polyvocality” will remain merely an attractive academic word—and the Collegium will continue reproducing the very oligarchy that it was expected to transcend? @bismil_prasad
