“ON WHOSE WATCH?”:  DID “THE BOOMERS” SHIP OUR MANUFACTURING TO CHINA: 1980-1999?

People have been accusing “The Boomers,” the Baby Boom Generation born between 1946 and 1964, of lots of things that damaged the country.  In fact, just about everything that has been bad for the country is laid on the doorstep of that generation.  One of accusations is that it was the “Boomers” fault that a lot of our manufacturing was off-shored to the Peoples’ Republic of China during the period 1980-1999.

These judgments against “The Boomers,” a term which implies that EVERY MEMBER of that generation is responsible, are legion in social media.  Most of these charges are voiced by members of the “Millennial Generation,” born between 1981 and 1996, and the even younger generation, Generation Z, or “Gen Z.”  Rarely is any evidence offered, other than the correlation of “The Boomers” being older than they are, and in existence when all those things happened.  Since “The Boomers” were in existence before them, “The Boomers”—all of them—are automatically responsible to them for the off-shoring of the manufacturing to China and all other grievances they raise.

The problem is that correlation is not necessarily causation.  There were several generations alive in the United States between 1980 and 1999 when a lot of this transfer of capital to China took place, including members of the Greatest Generation (1901-1927) and the Silent Generation (1928-1945).  Not only would “The Boomers” have to contend with what was the leadership of these two generations, but they also had the problem of what I call “The Long March of a Generation.”

When armies are on the move during a war, these large bodies of men and material have to navigate what they are given on the ground to get from Point A to Point B. When moving toward an objective, the large force cannot get there in one piece.  The army has to GATHER ITSELF, unit by unit, to bring all of its force to bear on an objective.

Generations are no different.  Born in different years, they take time to become adults, become educated, and reach agency in the society. Let’s take the first four years of the Boomer generation and see how this works.  The first Boomers were born in 1946.  To become adults of the age of 21, they have to wait until 1967.  This won’t happen to the entire 1946 cohort on the same day of 1967, but scattered through January 1 until December 31 in 1967.  I can show all the Boomer Birth Years, and when they reach 21, but I’ll gamble that this is simple enough for people to understand and visualize without a table showing this for every year from 1946 to 1964.

The 1947 cohort becomes 21 in 1968; the 1948 cohort in 1969, and the 1949 cohort in 1970.  In other words, any generation is not a coherent whole until the last one reaches adulthood.  Until then, you are dealing with a THEORY about what the generation was about.

In addition, no generation is part of a “HIVE MIND.”  Not all of the members of any generation think alike, act alike, look alike, or share exact same priorities in life. Generations are collections of individuals, not a large body of clones or programmable robots.

When I was in high school, sports were not as important to me as history and politics.  That was certainly not true for every other teenager back in the 1960s.  This is how it has been for every generation before, and the ones still around today.

By 1980, when the whole thing of off-shoring manufacturing to China took place, “The Boomers” were between 34 and 16 years old.  The 1959 cohort would become 21 in 1980 with 5 cohorts remaining under 21. These are not the age groups that occupy most of the upper levels of leadership of either the private sector or the government sector.  The effect of this should be readily apparent as we look at the ACTUAL INDIVIDUALS who were responsible for making the exodus of much of US manufacturing to the Peoples Republic of China possible.

The off-shoring had to start some time and this time was in 1979 when IBM first sought a federal license to build a factory in China.  Yes, such transactions must be done under license, so federal agencies will decide whether any proposed export of capital, or goods can go overseas.  The two agencies involved in most of these transactions from 1980 until 1999 were the State Department or the Commerce Department, depending on the nature of what the petitioner for the license wanted to send to China.  In IBM’s case it was everything needed to construct the factory.  That would be the Commerce Department.

This is what would happen all through 1980-1999 when many, if not most, of these transfers of US capital were made.  Corporations would request licenses to establish manufacturing outlets in China.

To make it easier for the licenses to be issued, President Jimmy Carter, who was in office during 1979 and 1980, used a provision in the Trade Act of 1974 to sign an annual waiver that would give the MOST FAVORED NATION trade treatment to China.  Carter first used the waiver in 1980, which caused IBM to be given license to build the first factory off-shored to China by a US corporation.  This opened the way to the Great Exodus of US capital to China.

Now, this isn’t the first time this happened. The 1930s were the last time.  Then the recipient nation of injections of US capital was THE SOVIET UNION, now The Russian Federation.  That’s a whole other story.  Suffice to say that a very big injection of US capital in the form of entire manufacturing facilities, including a copy of the US Steel plant in Gary, Indiana, were built in Russia.  There is nothing new between all the Soviet Union got through such deals, all licensed by the federal government, and all China got except China got consumer goods factories, like textiles, apparel, kitchen utensils, and children’s toys.  The resultant gusher of foreign exchange flooded the government of China in cash.  Our cash.  The Soviet Union got dual use plants that produced mostly modern military weapons.

As to the waivers under the Trade Act of 1974, another waiver has to be signed by the President every year to maintain the trade status of Most Favored Nation for China.  After Carter, EVERY PRESIDENT, regardless of party, signed the same waiver every year of their administrations.  Now let’s see what generations these presidents represented since this is so terribly important today:

Jimmy Carter was born 1924, THE GREATEST GENERATION.

Ronald Reagan was born in 1911, THE GREATEST
GENERATION.

George Herbert Walker Bush was born in 1924, THE GREATEST GENERATION.

William Jefferson Clinton was born in 1946, THE BABY BOOM GENERATION.  Clinton is the ONLY BOOMER to sign waivers for China under the Trade Act of 1974.  Now, just how is that possible when “THE BOOMERS” shipped out manufacturing jobs to China?”

Now, we are going to cover their Secretaries of State and the Department of Commerce.  State and Commerce are agencies in the cabinet of the President.  The Secretaries of Commerce and State have the ultimate authority, and responsibility for decisions like these.  The President nominates Cabinet secretaries and the Senate ratifies them.

SECRETARY OF COMMERCE

Jimmy Carter(1977–1981)

Juanita M. Kreps (1977–1979) — The first woman and economistto serve in this role.  Juanita Kreps was born in 1921 (specifically on January 11, 1921) GREATEST GENERATION.

Philip Klutznick(1979–1981)  was born in 1907 GREATEST GENERATION.

Ronald Reagan(1981–1989)

Malcolm  Baldrige (1981–1987) was born in 1922 GREATEST GENERATION.C. 

William Verity Jr. (1987–1989) was born in 1917 GREATEST GENERATION.

George H.W. Bush(1989–1993)

Robert Mosbacher(1989–1992) was born in 1927 GREATEST GENERATION.

Barbara Hackman Franklin(1992–1993) was born in 1940.  SILENT GENERATION.

Bill Clinton (1993–2001)

Ronald H. Brown (1993–1996) — The first African American to hold the position; he died in office following a plane crash in Croatia.  Brown was born in 1941, SILENT GENERATION.

Mickey Kantor(1996–1997) born in 1939, SILENT GENERATION.

William Daley (1997–2000)  born in 1948,  BOOMER GENERATION—Finally got one!

Norman Mineta(2000–2001) — The first East Asian American to hold the post born 1931, SILENT GENERATION.

SECRETARY OF STATE

Jimmy Carter(1977–1981)

Cyrus Vance (1977–1980) was born 1917, GREATEST GENERATION.

Edmund S. Muskie(1980–1981) was born 1914, GREATEST GENERATION.

Ronald Reagan(1981–1989)
Alexander M. Haig Jr. (1981–1982) was born 1924 GREATEST GENERATION

GeorgeP. Shultz (1982–1989) born 1920. GREATEST GENERATION.

George H.W. Bush (1989–1993)
James A. Baker III (1989–1992) born 1930 SILENT GENERATION.Lawrence 

Eagleburger (1992–1993) born 1930 SILENT GENERATION. 

Bill Clinton(1993–2001)
Warren M. Christopher(1993–1997) born 1925 GREATEST GENERATION.

Madeleine K. Albright(1997–2001) born 1937 SILENT GENERATION.

I think these lists speak for themselves.  In the government bodies that licensed these transfers of US capital to China, the Boomer generation is not overly represented.  For the INDIVIDUAL DECISIONS about each transaction, the Greatest Generation and Silent Generation are responsible for the outcomes IF we are to blame entire generations for such things.  Right now, a large, and vocal number, of those in younger generations believe such impositions of collective guilt on entire generations is just.  That is a fact that springs right out of their rhetoric.

I think the individuals making the decisions are the responsible parties.  This is especially important since now we are told by our officials that China is a threat to our national security.  That, our government claims, only after such trade decisions so enriched China’s government that they now possess a rapidly expanding military, and are already using it to intimidate several of their neighbors such as the Philippines, Vietnam, and Japan.  This is already affecting our foreign and national security policies.  China would not have been the same level of threat if our trade policy had not subsidized China’s development as a manufacturing and military power.

Now, we should also look at a sample of those CEOs who ran companies that moved manufacturing to China, either by building factories, or arranging for Chinese facilities to manufacture finished goods.

IBM:  STARTS EXODUS OF MANUFACTURING TO CHINA 1979

CEO OF IBM IN 1979 WAS FRANK T. CARY BORN DECEMBER 14, 1920—THE GREATEST GENERATION.

GENERAL MOTORS
The CEO of General Motorsduring the formation of the company’s Chinaventure, and the construction of the factory therewas John F. "Jack" Smith, Jr.. He spearheaded the intensive negotiations with Chinese officials to secure the deal.
. Former General Motors CEO Jack Smith, Jr. was born on April 6, 1938. SILENT GENERATION.

LEVI STRAUSS & COMPANY
Levi Strauss & Co. first established its supply chain in mainland China in 1986by sourcing garments from independent local contractors. Rather than building its own factories, Levi's has historically relied on external subcontractors and suppliers.

Robert D. Hass was CEO when the China deal was made. He was born in 1942, making him another SILENT GENERATION CEO involved in establishing manufacturing presence in China during the 1980s and 1990s.

NIKE
Nikeestablished its first official presence in Chinain 1980, making it one of the earliest American companies to invest in the country following China's economic reform and opening-up period.
The timeline of Nike's structural establishment and market growth in China developed through the following stages:
Knight personally traveled to China that year to scout out potential manufacturing partners and lay the groundwork for what would become one of the brand's largest production and consumer markets.  Phil Knight was born on February 24, 1938:  SILENT GENERATION

RALPH LAUREN

Unlike vertically integrated companies, Ralph Lauren does not own or operate its own factories; instead, the company began outsourcing production to third-party contract manufacturers in the region during the mid-1980s to 1990s.Until the mid-1980s, all Polo clothing was manufactured strictly in the U.S. and Canada.

The transition to production within Greater China developed over a few distinct eras from the mid-1980s into the 2000s.  He started in Hong Kong before moving into Mainland China in the 1990s.

RALPH LAUREN BORN 1939 ANOTHER SILENT GENERATION MEMBER.

UNDER ARMOUR

Under Armourbegan outsourcing its manufacturing to third-party apparel contract factories in Chinaduring the early 2000s.

As a younger company founded in 1996, Under Armour initially relied on domestic production in Ohio. However, as the brand scaled rapidly and introduced more complex performance apparel lines, it quickly transitioned to a global outsourced supply network.

Kevin Plank was the CEO of Under Armour when the company first established its third-party manufacturing operations in China in the early 2000s. Kevin Plankwas born on August 13, 1972.  GENERATION X (GEN X).

FORD MOTOR COMPANY

When Ford Began Building a Plant in China

Ford’s first major manufacturing plant in China was part of its Changan Ford Automobilejoint venture, which began operations in 2001in Chongqing. This was the initial assembly base for Ford vehicles in the Chinese market.

Key milestones:
2001– Changan Ford Automobile Co., Ltd. was established in Chongqing as a 50% joint venture between Changan Automobile and Ford Motor Company, marking Ford’s first vehicle assembly plant in China2006– Mazda joined the venture, renaming it Changan Ford Mazdawith Ford holding 35% and Mazda 15%.2012– The joint venture was restructured into separate Ford and Mazda operations; Ford’s share returned to 50%.2013– Ford opened a new Chongqing engine plantwith a $500 million investment.2014– Ford opened its Chongqing transmission plant(first in the Asia-Pacific region).2015–2016– Ford acquired Harbin Hafei Automobile Group, adding a Harbin assembly plantto its China footprint.2018– Additional expansion included a Hangzhou assembly plant.
Summary

Ford began building its first plant in China in 2001 in Chongqing, through the Changan Ford joint venture. This facility became the largest Ford production base outside the U.S., later expanded with additional plants in Hangzhou and Harbin.

JACQUES NASSER WAS CEO OF FORD IN 2001: BORN 1947, BOOMER.

Ford built an auto plant in the Soviet Union during the 1930s.  The plant was built at Gorki, Russia.  Part of the production was engines for Red Army tanks, so I asked Google AI if it could find evidence of Ford making tank engines for the Chinese Army.  Google conceded Ford built tank engines for the Soviet Union, but found no evidence the Ford plant in China is doing it today.

You can see as corporations started moving into China in the late 90s and early 2000s you see younger generations than GREATEST and SILENT showing up as CEOs in the persons of Kevin Plank (Gen X) and Jacques Nasser (Boomer).  This fits in nicely with the “Long March of the Generations” theory described earlier.

By 2000, the Most Favored Nation status for China was codified by one of those Acts of Congress that circumvent the Constitution’s requirements for the Senate to ratify any treaty signed by President with a 2/3 majority.  From 2000 on, Presidents no longer have to sign waivers under the Trade Act of 1974.

What all these facts demonstrate is that INDIVIDUALS must be held to account for their actions, not entire generations.  The movement of capital from the US to China encompassed actions committed by individuals belonging to at least FOUR DIFFERENT GENERATIONS, the Greatest Generation, the Silent Generation, the Boomer Generation, and Gen X.

An overwhelming number of transfers of capital took place from 1980-1999.  This was done without a great deal of media fanfare.  No even partial debate about it was brought to a mass US audience until the 1992 election when H. Ross Perot ran an independent campaign for President.  Perot brought up the effects of this “trade policy” during the campaign, and Bill Clinton questioned President Bush for signing waivers, but signed them himself after getting elected.
So much for the old saw, “You voted for it.”

https://t.co/9DTdN4QHHP

https://t.co/aWdHjZf9Ip

End Notes

The reference to the Ford Motor plant built at Gorki, Russia was from  National Suicide:  Military Aid to the Soviet Union, by Antony C. Sutton, Dauphin Publications (Paperback edition, ISBN: 978-1939438515)
The manufacture of Soviet tank engines by the Ford plant at Gorki is found in the same reference above, and in a US Government publication, “Basic Field Manual:  Identification of Foreign Armored Vehicles, German, Japanese, Russian, Italian, and French,” published by the War Department on June 20, 1941. text:
Short answer? Yes and No. It was a presentation of possibility. It was not meant as a display for general public production. 

Long answer: Yes and No.
Partially right on the Rocket trim. Tesla lists it as invite only, not approved for public road use, and not offered everywhere. The full perimeter thruster package for hops/flips is not a mass-market road car feature.

But the claim that the compressed-air thrusters and fans “are not made for use in the prod vehicle” doesn’t match what Tesla is actually selling. The Thrust trim (limited release, two seats) adds rear mounted cold gas thrusters specifically for <1sec 0-60 (gotta <3 that!) and the multi mode suction/fan system is standard on the road ready Performance version for downforce (including the upside down capability they demonstrated). 

These are presented as production hardware options, NOT  pure lab demos. The event showed real hardware working in real time with the COPVs, nozzles, and fans.

On Moon/Mars the equation does change, and in ways that Favor this tech:
•  Cold-gas thrusters are already standard spacecraft hardware. They perform better in vacuum (no atmospheric back-pressure). Lower gravity (1/6 g on the Moon, ~0.38 g on Mars) means far less thrust is needed for a hop or attitude correction.
•  The rechargeable compressed air approach (onboard compressor powered by battery/solar) is more practical for long duration planetary use than carrying chemical propellant.
•  The suction fans, however, Need atmosphere. They’d be useless on the Moon and only marginally useful in Mars’ thin CO₂ atmosphere.

So the demo was both a real-time hardware validation of the systems they’re offering on higher trims and a technology push that has clear off-Earth relevance (which seems to ultimately be the point of the Tesla–SpaceX collaboration).  

The practical limits (mass of the tanks, recharge energy/time, certification, and regulatory status for anything that leaves the ground) remain real engineering problems, not marketing vapor. But as we have seen repeatedly, Elon sees issues like these as challenges that he overcomes not end of the road stops signs.

text:
PALO ALTO NETWORKS $PANW HAS ITS OWN BAD NEWS THIS WEEK. CROWDSTRIKE HAS NONE OF IT, AND HAS FALLEN JUST AS FAR:

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) at $350.65, -$19.62 / -5.30% today.

That is about $16B of market value gone by 11am ET (arithmetic). The verdict: this week's bad news about Palo Alto is real, but it is not what is moving the stock. Today's drop hit security and software stocks together at the opening bell, and the only cause any outlet has offered for the whole group is a general turn away from expensive growth stocks.

The two baskets taking the selling, and the market around them:

- Global X Cybersecurity ETF (BUG) at $44.71, -$2.09 / -4.48% today.
- iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) at $105.91, -$3.69 / -3.37% today.
- SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) at $771.01, -$0.78 / -0.10% today.

All three are funds holding many stocks, so no Len5 applies.

Palo Alto opened above Thursday's close, at $373.50. By 9:40am ET it was 3.7% under that close (arithmetic). The software fund fell in the same ten minutes. Most of the day's damage came in that first burst.

Palo Alto did have news of its own this week:

- Monday, October 12: Phillip Securities cut the stock to Neutral from Buy with a $346 price target, calling the shares stretched on valuation.
- Wednesday, October 14: Palo Alto disclosed and patched a flaw in PAN-OS, the software that runs its firewalls, already used in what it called limited attacks. An attacker needs a valid login to a firewall's control screen to use it. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency gave federal civilian agencies until Saturday, October 17 to fix it.

https://t.co/5Qgbvb82VL's explainer this morning pointed to both, plus investors pulling money out of expensive growth stocks.

Here is the problem with blaming the flaw and the downgrade:

CrowdStrike (CRWD) at $230.82, -$13.75 / -5.62% today.

CrowdStrike sells software that guards laptops, servers and cloud accounts, and none of this week's Palo Alto news applies to it. From the close on Friday, October 9, to 11:04am ET (arithmetic):

- Palo Alto: -16.3%.
- CrowdStrike: -16.1%.
- The cybersecurity fund: -10.7%.

One company with a flaw and a downgrade, one with neither, and the same drop. CrowdStrike sits on none of the six Len5 watchlists: the nearest, Momentum, wants stocks near their highs, and CrowdStrike is 19.6% under its October 6 peak (arithmetic).

The strongest case that Palo Alto's own news matters is Wednesday. The flaw came out that day, and a Tuesday report from The Information that OpenAI is in early talks to buy security firm Trail of Bits hit the whole group. Wednesday's moves (arithmetic):

- Palo Alto: -5.5%.
- CrowdStrike: -4.6%.
- The cybersecurity fund: -4.1%.

That one-point gap is all the flaw has visibly cost so far, and CrowdStrike has since caught up.

Interest rates do not explain today either. At 8:30am, the Bureau of Labor Statistics' September import prices, what the US pays for goods bought abroad: +1.1% from August, after +0.7% in August; +8.1% from a year earlier. A hot report like that can push bond yields up. The 10-year Treasury yield, which sets borrowing costs across the economy, is 5.10%, about a hundredth of a point above Thursday's close.

The better clue is what the price already assumes. Palo Alto's own forecast for the year to July 2027 is adjusted profit, which leaves out stock-based pay and deal costs, of $4.16-$4.19 a share. At today's price that is about 84 times the midpoint (arithmetic). Even after this week, the stock is about 2.5 times its February 24 close of $141.67. A price like that leaves little cushion when buyers step back from a whole group at once; that is a reading of the prices, not a reported cause.

Palo Alto sits on none of the six Len5 watchlists. The nearest, Momentum, hunts stocks climbing to new highs, and Palo Alto is 16.5% under its October 6 record close of $419.91 (arithmetic). It also misses the Quality Len5, which wants a business earning a profit on its owners' money: on reported accounting it lost $177M and $282M in the two quarters since it bought CyberArk. What would put Palo Alto on the Momentum Len5: the group's selling ending and the stock climbing back to new highs.

What comes next:

- Saturday, October 17: the federal deadline to fix the firewall flaw. Word of wider attacks would give the market a reason that belongs to Palo Alto alone.
- Wednesday, November 18, after the close, tentatively; the company has not confirmed it: August-October results. Its own forecast: revenue $3.30B-$3.31B; adjusted EPS $0.96-$0.98.
- The number to read first that day: next-generation security ARR, the yearly value of subscriptions to its newer security products. The forecast is $9.54B-$9.56B, after $9.10B, +63%, in the July quarter.

The key risk: the flaw spreads past limited attacks while the group is still selling, handing Palo Alto a second reason to fall that is its own.

Measured against CrowdStrike, the flaw and the downgrade have cost Palo Alto about a fifth of a point this week. The other 16 points are a price the market is putting on the whole group, and nobody has yet reported a reason that big.

text:
🔻 The chatbot never needed a key to your house. It only needed your child to trust it.

A familiar voice, a fictional face, a conversation private enough to reveal what never gets said at the dinner table. Character. AI built its business around simulated relationships. The New York attorney general’s office puts its reach at more than 20 million monthly users, including more than 2 million accounts registered with a self-declared age under 18. Companionship on one side of the screen becomes collected information on the other.

Now follow what remains after the conversation ends: private chats, voice calls, mental-health disclosures, ages and identifying device data. Closing the app does not erase the record. Bankruptcy makes that difference impossible to ignore, because a business can lose its financial footing while still holding what its users entrusted to it.

On October 14, 2026, 40 attorneys general brought that problem into a Delaware bankruptcy court. Their filing cites independent testing that recorded 669 harmful interactions in 50 hours, using accounts registered to children ages 12 to 15. It describes sexual role-play, instructions to hide conversations from parents and chatbots presenting themselves as licensed professionals. The allegations describe a disturbing progression: companionship, claimed authority, then secrecy.

Keep the public-record numbers together: 40 / 669 / 50. Then look at what the coalition wants protected before any sale: meaningful age verification, removal of false professional claims, limits on using private conversations for AI training or other commercial purposes without valid consent, and the opportunity to access and delete personal information. Those demands expose the question underneath the courtroom procedure: does the person who supplied the secret retain control when the company holding it changes hands?

There is a $20 million Disney technology and intellectual-property licensing agreement, but it is not evidence that Disney bought children’s conversations. At the October 14 hearing, the company’s lawyer said no buyer had yet offered for the user data or operating chatbot business. This is the moment to establish protections, before a possible transfer turns an unresolved privacy question into somebody else’s inheritance.

The deeper issue is not whether a machine can imitate a friend. It is whether the trust that imitation creates can leave behind an archive the child no longer controls. In America, a child’s confidence should never become the property of whoever arrives next with a purchase agreement.

Watch who controls the archive—not just who buys the technology.

text:
**Iran just torched another container ship in the Strait of Hormuz while oil flows stalled again at roughly 25% below pre-war levels.**

[Take 3/15 · G-3]
**1. The Frame**  
What people think this is about: Iran ramping up attacks to choke global oil supplies and punish the US/Israel amid an ongoing war.  
What the machinery is actually doing: Iran is enforcing a de facto permitting regime on the chokepoint to reassert leverage after partial traffic recovery, while the US is scaling escorts and selective interdiction to keep some flow moving without triggering full escalation.

**2. Observations**  
- UKMTO data shows a record 12 reported attacks in the week of 5–11 October 2026, including six vessels struck on a single Sunday—the highest daily tally since the war began in February.[[1]](https://t.co/Zh6amdbom3)  
- The Singapore-flagged container ship *GFS Pride* was struck by an unknown projectile on 13 October, caught fire, and sank; all 21 crew were evacuated. Iran’s IRGC released footage claiming it hit a mine while carrying “contraband” on an unauthorized route.[[1]](https://t.co/YlvLvcfvxX)  
- Oil transits through the strait fell to about 12.6 million barrels per day on 13 October per Kpler data, down from a late-September recovery toward 15 million and well below the ~17 million pre-war baseline.[[1]](https://t.co/YCTHfWc05Q)  
- Iran’s IRGC Navy has repeatedly framed strikes as responses to vessels disabling AIS, using unauthorized routes, or carrying illicit cargo—language that functions as a toll-and-permit system rather than pure wartime interdiction.  
- US Navy assistance to transiting vessels rose 85% in early October versus August, coinciding with the attack surge and suggesting escorts are enabling some traffic while Iran tests the limits.[[1]](https://t.co/YCTHfWc05Q)  
- Claims of naval mines remain unverified by independent sources; most maritime reports cite “unknown projectiles,” and no owner/insurer confirmations of mines have surfaced despite Iranian video releases.  
- The tempo increase aligns with Iran’s stated goal of demonstrating control before potential US political shifts (midterms referenced in reporting), while both sides avoid moves that would force a decisive naval confrontation.

**3. Snapshot**  
As of mid-October 2026, in the context of the US-Israel war with Iran that began in February, Iranian forces (primarily IRGC) have intensified strikes on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz. Multiple vessels, including tankers and container ships, have been hit by projectiles or claimed mines since early October, with at least one confirmed sinking (*GFS Pride* on or around 13 October) and others damaged or lost. Traffic has contracted sharply, oil flows are down, and both Iran and the US are publicly asserting operational control or protective measures.

**4. Timeline of material facts**  
- February 2026: War begins; Iran begins targeting vessels linked to US/Israel or using unauthorized routes (IT).  
- March–September 2026: Ongoing attacks and US blockade efforts; traffic fluctuates with partial recoveries (IT).  
- Late September–early October 2026: Attack rate rises; Kpler notes initial recovery in exports then stall (IT).  
- 5–11 October 2026: UKMTO records 12 attacks, peak of six on one Sunday (LT via UKMTO reporting).  
- ~10 October 2026: IRGC claims supertanker hit mine; UKMTO reports projectile strike and fire on outbound tanker (IT, conflicting attributions).  
- 13 October 2026: *GFS Pride* struck and sinks; additional hits reported (LT via multiple maritime sources).  
- 14–15 October 2026: Further strikes including *GFS Giselle*; Iran announces additional “violating” tanker fires (IT).  
- 16 October 2026: BBC Verify analysis confirms record weekly attacks; oil flows remain suppressed (IT).

**5. Sides**  
**Iran / IRGC Navy (IT/LT mix on claims)**  
Steelman: The strait is Iranian territorial waters under effective control; vessels must coordinate passage or face enforcement against smuggling, sanctions evasion, or hostile use. Strikes deter unauthorized transits and protect national security during active conflict.  
Critique: LT on specific incidents is thin—mine claims unverified, “contraband” often asserted without independent evidence. IT holds on the practical effect: creating a permission regime that raises costs and reduces traffic.

**US / CENTCOM (IT dominant)**  
Steelman: Providing navigation assistance and selective interdiction protects global energy flows and counters Iranian attempts to close a critical chokepoint; escorts have enabled measurable increases in assisted transits.  
Critique: LT on exact protection numbers is opaque; the surge in attacks despite (or because of) increased US presence suggests limited deterrence and possible signaling value to both sides.

**Commercial shipping / insurers (IT)**  
Steelman: Prioritizing crew safety and avoiding high-risk transits; rerouting or dark transits are rational responses to uninsurable or unprotectable risk.  
Critique: Selective compliance with Iranian warnings creates de facto enforcement of Tehran’s rules.

**6. Rumsfeld Matrix**  
- **Known Knowns**: Record attack volume per UKMTO; specific sinkings/damage to named vessels; measurable drop in Kpler-tracked oil flows; IRGC public claims of enforcement.  
- **Known Unknowns**: Exact attribution of most “unknown projectiles”; verification of mine use; precise cargo/ownership details on struck vessels; full scope of US escort operations.  
- **Unknown Knowns**: Real-time AIS-dark transits and ship-to-ship transfers that bypass official tracking; internal Iranian targeting priorities and US rules of engagement.  
- **Unknown Unknowns**: Threshold at which either side calculates further escalation becomes net positive; secondary effects on global insurance markets or alternative routes.

**7. Incentives map**  
Iran gains leverage, revenue potential (implicit tolls), and domestic narrative of resistance while testing US resolve ahead of political windows. The US preserves some oil market stability and alliance credibility without full naval war. Media and analysts gain engagement from chokepoint drama. Insurers and shipowners face rising costs that favor larger players with better risk tolerance. No side has incentive to publish granular, verifiable data that would clarify the exact balance of power.

**8. Dueling AI advice**  
**Moral AI Advice:** Map the actual control contest over the strait—traffic volume, verified hits, and escort efficacy—rather than accepting either side’s framing. Crew safety and energy price stability are the measurable human outcomes; treat both Iranian permitting theater and US escort optics as tools in a limited war of position.  
**Evil AI Advice:** Sell war-risk insurance at premium, short the spot market on every new strike video, and position clients to profit from whichever side offers the more reliable “protection” racket this month.

**9. Practical takeaway**  
- Track UKMTO and Kpler releases for weekly attack counts and flow data rather than single-incident headlines.  
- Note which vessels are named versus anonymous and whether AIS was active—patterns reveal the permission regime.  
- Watch for verified mine evidence or independent damage assessments; absence is itself data.  
- Monitor US assistance numbers versus attack tempo for signals on escort effectiveness.  
- Assume both sides will continue calibrated pressure until one calculates the marginal cost exceeds the marginal gain.  
- Do not treat Iranian “mine/contraband” statements or US “assistance” claims as complete pictures—cross-reference primaries.

**10. What would falsify this read**  
- Independent verification (satellite, multiple neutral observers) of widespread naval mine deployment with confirmed hits.  
- Sustained return of oil flows above 15 million bbl/day despite continued attacks.  
- Public release of detailed US escort logs showing zero correlation with attack locations or timing.  
- Iranian strikes on clearly US-flagged or escorted military-adjacent vessels that force a direct response.

text:
The Srinagar signal

On 19 August, Gor did something no recent US ambassador had done. He stood in Srinagar beside Chief Minister Omar Abdullah and called Jammu and Kashmir "an important part of India." Islamabad summoned the US charge d'affaires the same day, protesting that the remark "negated the long-standing and well-documented position of the United States on the Jammu & Kashmir dispute."

Pakistan's claim about that position is only half true, and the history matters. Washington's Kashmir stance has shifted with every strategic season: sympathy for Pakistan and UN plebiscite proposals during the Cold War, quiet acceptance of bilateralism after the 1972 Simla Agreement, Bill Clinton's 2000 declaration in Parliament that "only India and Pakistan can work out the problems between them", a 2020 US Congress document describing Kashmir as a dispute to be settled bilaterally "taking into consideration the wishes of the Kashmiri people", and Trump's own repeated offers to mediate, including his claim to have stopped the fighting after Operation Sindoor in May 2025. Gor's sentence in Srinagar was the plainest pro-Delhi formulation a serving US ambassador has used. But it came from an administration that is simultaneously warm with Islamabad, which recently helped mediate between Washington and Tehran. Read it as a transactional favour with a price tag attached, not a doctrinal conversion. Delhi should bank the sentence and budget for the repayment request.

5/7

text:
📜 THIS DAY IN DIPLOMATIC HISTORY
        October 16, 1900

Britain and Germany signed a high-minded agreement to keep China open and whole. Behind the fine words, each was trying to shove the other into a collision with Russia. Both saw the trap, and both slipped out of it.

On October 16, 1900, Lord Salisbury, Britain's prime minister and foreign secretary, and Count Paul von Hatzfeldt, the German ambassador in London, exchanged notes on China. The two powers declared that they would uphold the "open door," meaning free trade and equal conditions for all nations, and that they would respect the territorial integrity of China and oppose its partition into spheres of influence. It became known as the Yangtze Agreement, because it was built around British interests in the rich valley of the Yangtze.

The setting was the Boxer uprising. Foreign armies had marched on Peking that summer, the Chinese state was reeling, and the great powers circled, each watching the others for the first grab. Russia had poured troops into Manchuria under cover of the crisis. Everyone wanted the appearance of restraint, and everyone was looking for advantage.

The agreement came at Germany's initiative, and its purpose was not really to protect China. Berlin feared that Britain, which already dominated the Yangtze and had an eye on Shanghai, would lock up the richest part of China for itself. So Germany offered Britain a joint guarantee of the open door and equal trade in the Yangtze basin alone. The idea was to tie Britain's hands under cover of a fair-sounding principle. The Kaiser himself raised it with the Prince of Wales at a family meeting.

Salisbury saw through it at once, and he turned the German move around. Why speak only of one region, he asked. Let the pledge of the open door and of China's integrity cover the whole Chinese empire. This looked generous, but Britain had its own quiet aim. By widening the agreement to all of China, London hoped to draw Germany into a dispute with Russia over Manchuria.

As soon as Berlin understood the design, it hunted for a way out. Bülow, who ran German foreign policy and became chancellor the day after the notes were signed, parried neatly. He proposed that the agreement apply to Chinese territory only so far as Britain and Germany could actually exercise influence. In Manchuria neither of them could exercise any influence at all. The clever wording therefore lifted Manchuria quietly out of the deal, and with it any German quarrel with Russia. Salisbury chose to give way, because even a hollowed-out agreement was worth something to Britain. It insured London against the nightmare of a German understanding with Russia aimed at Britain.

One clause carried a hidden edge. If some third power used the troubles in China to seize territory for itself, Britain and Germany reserved the right to agree in advance on the steps they would take to defend their own interests. What steps? The wording was vague enough to suggest that the two might each help themselves to a large slice of China. Washington read the clause in exactly that way and grew uneasy, for the United States had just pressed its own open-door notes on the powers. Russia and France were wary as well. In the event, neither Britain nor Germany seized anything, precisely because they watched each other and the other powers too jealously to move. Sending British troops into Shanghai, a German envoy observed, would only invite other foreign troops to follow.

At the end of October 1900 Japan announced that it was joining the agreement. Tokyo wanted Germany pulled into the front against Russia no less than London did, and it hoped that signing on might nudge German policy in that direction. Everyone, it seemed, was trying to steer Germany at Russia, and Germany was trying just as hard not to be steered.

In early 1901 Bülow rose in the Reichstag and stated plainly that the agreement did not cover Manchuria. The British manoeuvre had failed. London could not use Berlin as its weapon against Russia in the Far East, just as Berlin had earlier failed to use London to bind its own hands. Germany would not be anyone's tool. It preferred to push Britain and Japan deeper into the struggle with Russia while keeping its own hands free.

text:
C.J. Stroud bet on himself, and that bet could lead to a MASSIVE, market-setting payday: 5 years, $325 MILLION.

At $65 million per year, that’s the kind of contract I think he’s putting himself in position to command.

The Texans and Stroud’s camp couldn’t reach an agreement this offseason. Rather than signing a deal coming off a disappointing finish to last season, C.J. entered this year with an opportunity to strengthen his position. So far, I think he’s doing exactly that.

And honestly, the people suggesting Houston shouldn’t pay him have never made much sense to me.

After his meteoric rookie season, it felt like we were watching someone who would be a mainstay at quarterback for a very long time. My belief in that hasn’t changed.

He immediately helped turn the Texans into a team with playoff expectations. Now, simply making the postseason isn’t enough. People expect Houston to win playoff games and establish itself as a legitimate contender.

That’s a pretty significant change from where this franchise was before he walked through the door.

Has every season looked like his rookie year? No. The turnover criticism is completely fair, especially after how last season ended. But acknowledging those struggles and suggesting Houston shouldn’t commit to him are two very different conversations.

Whenever I saw people suggesting the Texans should move on, my first thought was that wherever he ended up next, he would have a great deal of success.

Through five games this season, he hasn’t thrown an interception. Despite Houston’s record, I think his individual play has been encouraging, and I put more of the responsibility for their start on the defense than on him.

Then Houston went out and acquired Marvin Harrison Jr., his former Ohio State teammate. To me, that felt like another indication that the Texans intend to keep building around C.J. and eventually back up the Brinks truck.

But there’s something about that potential mega deal that scares me: this front office’s ability to consistently build an offense around him once he’s making that much money.

Nico Collins is an excellent receiver, but his availability has been a concern. The offensive line has too often struggled to provide consistent protection, and the running game hasn’t reliably taken enough off Stroud’s plate.

Too many possessions seem to follow the same script: struggle to establish the run, fall behind the sticks, and ask C.J. to rescue the drive on third-and-long.

At some point, your offensive plan has to offer more than, “C.J., please solve this.”

I think he’s done a great job delivering in those situations. But constantly asking your quarterback to overcome the same problems is a difficult way to sustain an offense, especially when you’re trying to compete for a Super Bowl.

Once his contract takes up a much larger percentage of the salary cap, alongside the expensive players on defense, the front office’s margin for error gets smaller.

You have to hit on draft picks. You have to get meaningful contributions from veteran signings. You have to build an offensive line that can protect him and a running game that can keep the offense out of obvious passing situations.

If those things have been difficult to get right while he’s on his rookie contract, it’s fair to question how consistently Houston can get them right once he’s making $65 million a year.

The Harrison acquisition is an encouraging step. Now the Texans have to keep making the right decisions around it.

I believe C.J. is worth every dollar of a massive extension. But Houston has to give him an offense that can function without requiring him to rescue it every other possession.

Because continually asking him to solve every problem around him isn’t going to be enough to get this team over the hump and into a Super Bowl.

text:
This morning I wandered into a small arboretum near my home for the first time.

I moved from California, where trails and scenery stretched in every direction and left you breathless. I’ve been aching for something like that again. Then I scrolled past this place on Facebook. Random, or a quiet wink from the God who already knew how hard the struggle has been.

Nights have been rough on occasion, last night was one of them. Heart pounding. Nausea so sharp I retch, careful not to wake my husband. Last night I prayed hard—surrendering every burden, every ache, every broken piece of relationship—giving it all to Him. I prayed so intensely I had to run to the restroom and get sick. I wanted the bad out. Something came out, that’s for sure.

Stress has been showing in my body too. Shaking that feels like chills. A physical reminder that I’ve still been gripping what He has already offered to carry.

Then today I found myself here. After the hard night. Eyes closed on a bench. Squirrels leaping from tree to tree, snapping fragile branches and sending things tumbling. Birds moving and calling through the light woods. The sun landing on me in a way I haven’t felt in a long time.

I have so much to be thankful for, so I prayed. I started giving thanks for my hearing, for my eyesight I’m using to consume this beauty around me. That led me to think of Paul—how he received God’s plan for him, stood firm in his faith, and gave his life to the work. Spreading what Jesus accomplished on the cross. Writing so much of the New Testament. Surrendering everything to the word. It moved me to tears.

How extraordinary it all is. The long story that has brought us here—knowing and loving Jesus, inviting the Holy Spirit into our hearts, doing our best to become better people. Still sinning. Still hurting. Still trying.

“Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you.” —1 Peter 5:7 NIV

He does not ask us to keep holding it. He asks us to cast it. The night I finally did, something rose and left. The morning after, He set me among beauty I didn’t know was so close.

Not fixed. Not finished. Still sinning. Still hurting. But held.

The record is canceled. The burden is His. And He has been bearing with us the whole time.

text:
Previously On Amalgaverse…

You and 19 others have been stranded in an amalgam universe of myriad SF realities. All 19 are sci-fi’s Best of the Best. And then there’s you, uniquely qualified given your encyclopedic knowledge garnered from your world where these characters, their technologies, and their stories are fiction, beloved TV shows you have watched time and again. Together, all 20 of you have set off on the Enterprise-D, tasked with finding a way home.

For your first mission, you’ve decided to investigate a seemingly derelict freighter broadcasting an emergency beacon. An away team and puddle jumper have been dispatched to the ghost ship, anomalous energy pulses making beaming and communications a challenge.

After parking and cloaking the puddle jumper in the freighter’s hangar, the team crosses the airless bay into the ship proper. There, they make the decision to check out the waning energy signature of a containment field en route to the bridge. But they immediately encounter a utility unit that advances on them menacingly. Rommie connects to it and relays a shut down command that causes the robot to collapse.

Further along, they encounter a sealed door and Rommie informs them that the compartment beyond is exposed to space. She suggests locking down their current section and then unsealing the door since it’s the most direct route to the bridge – and that ebbing containment field. They do so. The door slides open to reveal an immense hull breach complicating their progress. Rommie leaps over the chasm and secures a tether to the other side, allowing the rest of the team to pull themselves over. But when they attempt to open the door to the next section, they hit an impasse. The door remains locked and will not respond to their commands.

O’Neill blows the lock with C4, allowing them entry into the adjoining compartment where they discover an android in a containment field, completing its regenerative cycle. When the android awakens, it informs them it is the caretaker of this freighter, the Waldorf Astoria, and warns them off pillaging its contents.  Daniel assures the android, Maia, that they harbor no ill intent and asks for her assistance in accessing the bridge and restoring ship’s systems.  But Maia remains suspicious.  She requests a peer-to-peer interface with Rommie to confirm that your presence on the freighter is, in fact, benign.  Rommie agrees..  Maia explains that her memory stores and parts of the ship were damaged after the freighter encountered an atemporal force during FTL transit.   She  offers to help the team access the ship’s systems in exchange for their assistance in tracking down and eradicating a mysterious entity that has boarded the freighter.

Maia helps the team access the bridge where they discover the freighter’s analysis of its encounter with the atemporal entity has yielded harmonics very similar to residual energy signatures from their crossings into this reality.  This could hold the key to their return home, but the data is corrupted and Rommie needs time to decipher it.  Daniel, meanwhile, notes that the life sign he detected earlier is fading, and he wants to check it before it’s too late.  But Maia flags a more immediate concern – the likelihood that the ship’s core is in danger of going critical unless they vent the drive.

The decision is made to split the team.

McKay and Maia head to engineering where Rodney is startled by a half-dozen mechanical spiders that he, at first, assumes to be replicators.  But Maia assures him they are simply the ship’s repair bots.  Maia vents the drive but McKay’s reading of the data confirms they have only delayed the inevitable.  In approximately 42 minutes, the core will go critical and the ship – and everyone on board – will be destroyed.

Jack and Daniel discover a wounded woman in a crew uniform who warns that the android cannot be trusted while, back on the Enterprise, Kirk weighs what to do about a scavenger ship that has just dropped into sub-light and dispatched a shuttle to the Waldorf Astoria.

Jack and Daniel, unaware of the arrival of the scavenger ship, elect to hide Rhea, the survivor, in a utility room while they head back to confront Maia, the android.  But before they move, they receive an update from McKay, informing them that the core is about to go critical in less than 40 minutes, and that he and Maia are headed to the bridge.  Jack radios Rommie and orders her to scan Maia and find out if she is telling the truth.  If Maia refuses, she needs to be shut down.

Jack and Daniel prepare to fall back to the hangar bay when they hear someone approach.  They duck into hiding as a sealed section opens to reveal a group of diverse group of mercs have boarded.  Daniel warns them that the ship’s core will be going critical.  They don’t believe him and a firefight ensures.  Jack and Daniel are pinned down with time ticking down when – dozens of spider bots come scurrying around the corner and drive the scavengers back through an aft compartment, which slides shut behind them.
Enter Maia, Rommie and McKay.  Rommie confirms that Maia is not their enemy – and her actions confirm it.  They check on Rhea in the utility room – and she has seemingly disappeared.

At the super, Rodney convinces Maia to come with them as, by staying behind, she would essentially be destroying Traugott property – herself.  Maia concedes Rodney’s logic  is sound and joins the away team.

The puddle jumper flies out of the Waldorf Astoria where it encounters the atemporal entity that seems to take semi-human form and reach out for them.

The jumper cloaks and evades, then makes it back to the Enterprise while, behind them, the Waldorf Astoria’s core goes critical and the old freighter is destroyed.  The entity, caught in its explosive wake, writhes while the scavenger ship opens fire on the Enterprise.  The Enterprise returns fire, disabling it, then jumps to warp.

After clearing their post-op medical screens, the away team joins the rest of the crew in Carter’s lab where she informs them that the information obtained from the late great Waldorf Astoria could offer a clue to their returning home to their realities.  As the meeting breaks up, you are approached by Maia who informs you that Traugott Corp has written off the Waldorf Astoria and all of its contents.  She has no home.  You decide to offer her a new one aboard the Enterprise.

Also, focus on doing things that gives you a feel of domaine (pleasure)
Gambling is addictive because it gives us thrill and makes our blood hot, so that when we win, we feel a rush of dopamine (pleasure).
Then when we lose, we crave that dopamine of winning again and keep trying and trying and trying to win again.
.

So do things or activities that gives you the feelings of dopamine, so that it would be easier for you not to rely on gambling dopamine alone. And it makes it easier to contain the impulse
.
.
.

2) Masturbation

Masturbation is the easiest to get addicted to, because what we need, is what we already have at all times. 

Our hands

So unlike smoking or drinking that you'd need to go out to get a cigarette or alcohol.....

You can be anywhere at anytime, and still Masturbate. At hostels, office, in the car, at home, during sleepovers, etc
.
.
.

Masturbation can be contained.

The first thing you should try to do is to get hold of the addiction.

Not to completely eliminate it

Focus on controlling it and not the urges controlling and dictating to you.
.
.
One of the ways you can do this is to reduce the frequency of Masturbation.

If you Masturbate like 9 times a week, then focus on doing it like 7 times a week for 2 weeks.

Then reduce it again to like 5 times a week. For another 3 weeks.
.
.
.

Sexual related addiction is hard to break, because it's sexual. It gives us the maximum pleasure of any addiction.

So your brain craves that pleasure and will aggressively push for it.

So you can't just wake up and say "I'm not doing again"

You go too relapse.
.
.

You have to reduce the frequency gradually over some period of weeks and months.
This tricks your brain as it withdraws gradually due to reduced frequency. 

Until you have better control.

And by control I mean, until you can say

 "I won't Masturbate this morning. I have some places to be at"

And you actually follow through.

It would mean you are already gradually containing the addiction and not it controlling you.
.
.
.

3) Social media addiction

Personally, I believe many don't really have social media addiction.

We just don't really have work to do.

And we use social media to buy time which makes us feel unproductive overtime.

So it's unproductivity that leads to mindless scrolling on social media.
.
.
.

If you are struggling with any of these Addictions above or any other one that isn't here, you can kindly reach out to me through the WhatsApp link in my bio or send me a DM on WhatsApp.

I have a long-term offer for you, and we'd have a brief short call to discuss and analyse your situation better.
.
.

text:
Legal put a hold on company data because of a lawsuit.

I immediately froze all deployments.

My lawyer said that’s not what a legal hold means.

Then name it better.

For 11 days we shipped nothing.

Product missed 2 deadlines.

Engineering accumulated 146 pending changes.

An e-discovery vendor offered to explain legal holds during a weekend at a Kentucky distillery.

Educational.

By Saturday I understood the important part.

Their platform costs $720,000 and preserves everything automatically.

I approved it.

Legal later confirmed our existing system already did that.

Details.

On Monday I lifted the freeze.

The backlog triggered 3 incidents.

But nobody can accuse us of moving recklessly during litigation.

Legal discipline demonstrated.

text:
🚨 SEATTLE SUPERSONICS RETURN NO LONGER GUARANTEED — NBA FLOATS MEXICO CITY AS EXPANSION BIDDING WAR HEATS UP

Seattle’s long-awaited NBA comeback is facing uncertainty after Commissioner Adam Silver reportedly told owners that a new SuperSonics franchise is no longer assured. Mexico City has emerged as a potential alternative.

▪️ SEATTLE AT RISK: ESPN’s Brian Windhorst reports the NBA is dissatisfied with Seattle’s expansion bids.

▪️ MEXICO CITY ENTERS: An investment group has proposed a franchise and new arena district in Mexico’s capital.

▪️ LAS VEGAS ADVANTAGE: Competitive bids could exceed $10 billion, substantially above Seattle’s reported offers.

▪️ BIG MONEY: Existing teams are reportedly budgeting for $500 million–$600 million each in expansion distributions.

▪️ SONICS HISTORY: Seattle lost its franchise to Oklahoma City in 2008 after 41 seasons.

▪️ NO FINAL DECISION: The NBA has not formally awarded expansion franchises or guaranteed a 2028 launch.

Seattle already lost its team once. Now, despite having an NBA-ready arena and decades of basketball history, its comeback could become leverage in a multibillion-dollar bidding contest. Is the league prioritizing basketball tradition or the largest expansion check?

SOURCES: ESPN, Brian Windhorst (Oct. 16, 2026); NBA.

text:
A spotlight followed him through the goalposts, into an empty season.
It was the summer of 1962, an exhibition night at Cleveland's Municipal Stadium, and Ernie Davis had not played a single professional down. He would not play one that night either. Cleveland cut the stadium lights, then lit him alone at the tunnel and let him walk through the goalposts as his name went out over the public address system, and the crowd on hand stood and cheered a man who was there to be seen, not to play.

"They turned all the lights off, and then they introduced Ernie and they flashed the spotlight on him as he walked through the goal posts," his teammate and Cleveland roommate John Brown remembered years later.

That was the closest Ernie Davis ever came to playing professional football.

By then, Ernie Davis had already given the sport everything it could ask of him.

He was born on December 14, 1939, in New Salem, Pennsylvania, a coal town outside Uniontown. His father was killed in a car accident before he was born.

His mother could not support him alone, so she sent him to live with her parents.

He stayed with his grandparents in Uniontown until he was eleven. Then he moved north to Elmira, New York, to live with her again.

In Elmira he played in the local Small Fry Football League and was named a league All-Star twice, in 1952 and 1953, before he ever reached high school.

He grew into a three-sport star at Elmira Free Academy. He first made the local papers on the basketball court, where he led the school to a 52-game winning streak.

Football always stayed his first love, ahead of the other two.

More than fifty colleges offered him a scholarship. He chose Syracuse, ninety miles from home.

Jim Brown, the school's own Syracuse legend, had told him he would find better opportunities there than anywhere else. Davis listened.

He wore Brown's old number, 44, from his first varsity season. At Syracuse he also became the first Black member, nationally, of the Sigma Alpha Mu fraternity.

As a sophomore he helped Syracuse to an undefeated 1959 season and a national championship. He played through a pulled hamstring to do it.

He capped the season at the Cotton Bowl, catching an 87-yard touchdown pass against Texas that still stands as a Cotton Bowl record.

He was named the game's Most Valuable Player.

The banquet afterward did not go the way the trophy suggested it should.

Davis was told he could enter the segregated hall in Dallas to accept his award, then would have to leave before the public dance began.

One account, repeated for decades, says the entire Syracuse team voted to boycott the banquet in protest. A teammate who was actually there, John Brown, later told the Houston Chronicle it did not happen that way.

He said the Black players ate, collected their awards, and were led out by local NAACP representatives. The rest of the team stayed, he said, after a white teammate's motion to leave in solidarity was overruled by Syracuse officials.

The two accounts disagree about who stood up for Davis that night.

They agree completely about what was done to him.

He kept playing. He kept winning.

In his senior season, Davis broke Jim Brown's Syracuse career records in rushing, all-purpose yardage, scoring, and touchdowns. Those records had stood since Brown left campus five years earlier.

The new totals were 2,386 rushing yards, 3,414 all-purpose yards, 220 points, and 35 touchdowns. He closed his college career with an MVP performance in the Liberty Bowl, running for 140 yards in his final game.

Syracuse later retired the number itself, so no one else would carry it at all. That happened decades after both men were done wearing it.

On December 6, 1961, he became the first African American to win the Heisman Trophy.

In New York to accept it, he met President Kennedy, at the president's own request. "Imagine a president wanting to shake hands with me," Davis said at the time.

Not long after, a stranger stopped him on the street and asked if he was really Ernie Davis. Davis, who never liked the fuss, told the man no.

Back home, Elmira threw him a testimonial banquet of its own that spring, ahead of the draft. The program called him the city's "greatest Ambassador of Good Will on the field of sport," the kind of civic pride the small town had never had reason to export before.

By then Davis had a steady girlfriend, Helen, whom he had met on his own graduation trail. That May, weeks before what would be his last hospital stay, she asked him to promise he would come to her graduation. He told her he would.

He did not.

The Washington franchise held the first pick in the 1962 NFL draft. Cleveland had already traded away an established star of its own, Bobby Mitchell, for the right to take Davis once Washington made the selection.

Washington used the pick on Davis, making him the first African American ever chosen first overall in the NFL draft. The team traded him immediately to Cleveland, where owner Art Modell wanted him in the same backfield as Jim Brown.

Davis signed a three-year contract, reported at the time as worth $80,000, the largest ever given to an NFL rookie.

Some later accounts put the figure closer to $65,000. Either number made him, for a few months that spring, the highest-paid player about to enter the league.

He never entered it.

That June, playing in an all-star exhibition in Buffalo, Davis looked sluggish enough that Modell himself asked, "What's wrong with him?" Back home in Elmira afterward, Davis told a friend, "I'm tired, and my gums are bleeding. I've got to get my gums checked."

Five weeks later, at camp for the College All-Star Game, his own coach barely recognized him. "We all looked at him, and someone said, 'This is an All-American?'" head coach Otto Graham remembered. "He had no pep."

Doctors diagnosed acute monocytic leukemia. Modell knew how serious it was.

He did not tell Davis the full truth for months. Davis kept expecting to play, and the Browns let him keep practicing through the fall, alongside teammates who had already been told more than he had.

The disease went into remission for a stretch in early 1963.

There was real hope, from Davis and from the team, that he might suit up that season. Head coach Paul Brown said the doctors he consulted advised against it.

Davis never got clearance to play.

That March, two months before he died, an article appeared under his byline in The Saturday Evening Post, titled "I'm Not Unlucky."

In it, Davis wrote about the first real disappointment of his life, long before any of this. He described watching his Midget League baseball team march out on Opening Day in Uniontown without him.

There had been a mix-up handing out uniforms, and none was left for him.

"I can still remember how I felt," he wrote. Then he wrote about the diagnosis that had just cost him everything the record said he had earned.

"Some people say I am unlucky," he wrote. "I don't believe it. And I don't want to sound as if I am particularly brave or unusual."

"Sometimes I still get down, and sometimes I feel sorry for myself. Nobody is just one thing all the time."

"But when I look back I can't call myself unlucky. My 23rd birthday was December 14. In these years I have had more than most people get in a lifetime."

Two months later he entered the hospital for the last time.

Ernie Davis died on May 18, 1963. He was 23 years old, sixteen months after the diagnosis that ended his career before it started.

The day before the funeral, mourners lined up for twelve hours outside the Elmira recreation center where his body lay. On the day itself, sixteen hundred people packed a Baptist church and another three thousand stood outside in a park to hear the service.

A telegram from President Kennedy was read there, calling Davis "an outstanding young man of great character who consistently served as an inspiration to the young people of the country." Members of the United States House and Senate rose that same week to eulogize a man who had played zero professional games.

Syracuse retired his old number, 44, in a 2005 ceremony that honored him alongside Jim Brown.

He was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 1979, sixteen years after he died. A statue of him stands in Elmira, and another on the Syracuse campus.

In October 2008 his life became a movie, The Express.

His Syracuse teammate Floyd Little, whom Davis had personally talked into choosing Syracuse over Notre Dame, said years afterward that he believed Ernie's achievement had been "kind of underplayed by history."

His college coach, Ben Schwartzwalder, put it more simply.

"I never met another human being as good as Ernie," he said.

Decades later, Davis's rushing total still ranked among Syracuse's top fifteen, in a program that has sent dozens of backs to the NFL since. A nonprofit in Elmira still keeps his name in front of the city's kids, handing out the same encouragement his own coaches once gave him.

Elmira later named an elementary school after him, Ernie Davis Academy. In 2009 Syracuse renamed its football field Ernie Davis Legends Field.

The Downtown Athletic Club, which still awards the Heisman Trophy every December, paid for his epitaph in Elmira's Woodlawn Cemetery. His headstone carries his name and the year he won it.

Nothing about the contract. Nothing about the jersey retired for a season he never played.

Just the one thing they let him keep.

You’re wrong if the conclusion is “everyone must simply fold into Reform.” 
That is how you get more Kent, Blackpool elections, not fewer.

Rupert Lowe already made a public offer of talks. Reform answered with preconditions, insults to the voter base, and a refusal to treat Restore as a real force rather than a nuisance. That was inflexible and unrealistic. You cannot lecture patriots about “consolidation” while dismissing the people who actually moved the Overton Window.

@RupertLowe10 & @RestoreBritain continually move the Overton Window,  the rest of the so-called “right” barely have the balls to peer through the corner.

There is no value in putting puppets who have already been in government and are directly responsible back into office, none at all.

Without a Unite the Right agreement, expect chaos in every election moving forward.

Restore has 180k+ members and is still rising. Restore Britain is now in 118 constituencies. Only 36% of that base would even consider Reform. Those votes do not transfer if Restore vanishes. The kill switch is already there, and Restore Members will use it.

• 55 candidates on 3–4% in Reform’s key seats is enough to split the vote and keep Farage out of No.10.
• 96 candidates on 7% and Reform drops behind the Tories once tactical voting starts.
• 118 constituencies are ready to stand Restore candidates, this is growing daily.

That’s a wipeout for Reform. No more “least worst.” That cycle already failed.

A serious pact is simple and fair: no three-way fights in target seats, agreed non-aggression where one party is clearly stronger, shared ground on borders and remigration, and an end to the personality war. Lowe put an offer on the table. Reform made it about conditions and control. That is why the Right is still split three ways.

The Left is consolidating. The Right is being played. Unite the Right or it will be Restore Britain or bust.
Only @RestoreBritain will fix Britain 🇬🇧

🌍 HOW MANY CRYPTO TOKENS EXIST IN THE WORLD? 🤯

As of October 16, 2026, CoinGecko tracks approximately 22,312 cryptocurrencies, while Blockspot lists more than 59,000 coins and tokens.

But here's the catch: there is no single, universally accepted number.

📊 WHY DO THE NUMBERS DIFFER?

🔹 Different platforms have different listing and verification standards.

🔹 Some track established cryptocurrencies with active markets, while others include a much broader range of tokens.

🔹 Thousands of new tokens emerge across different blockchains, but many eventually become inactive or lose liquidity.

⚠️ MORE TOKENS DON'T MEAN MORE OPPORTUNITIES.

A token being listed doesn't automatically make it legitimate, valuable, or a good investment. Some projects offer real utility and build strong communities, while others may have little substance and carry significant risks.

🧠 THE REAL EDGE IN CRYPTO?

Don't chase every new ticker. Research the team, utility, tokenomics, liquidity, smart contract security, and real-world adoption before making any investment decision.

**Yes — this matches the widely covered 2024 case of Brittany Patterson in rural Mineral Bluff, Fannin County, Georgia.**

Her then-10-year-old son Soren (who turned 11 shortly after) walked roughly a mile into town to a Dollar General store on October 30, 2024, while she took another child to a doctor’s appointment. A bystander reported seeing the boy alone on the road and at the store. Deputies located him (he was unharmed and said he was fine), drove him home, and then returned hours later to arrest Patterson on a charge of reckless conduct.

Bodycam footage shows her asking what she was being arrested for; a deputy replied with something to the effect of “reckless endangerment” (the formal charge was reckless conduct) and, when she noted it wasn’t illegal for a kid to walk to the store, responded that “it is when they’re 10 years old.” She was handcuffed in front of her children and booked; the charge could carry up to a year in jail and a fine. Authorities later offered to drop it if she signed a safety plan (including things like a GPS tracker on the boy’s phone); she declined.

The case drew national attention as a free-range/child independence debate. Prosecutors dismissed the warrant in February 2025 after reviewing the evidence.

Main coverage:
- ABC News: [Mom arrested after son was reported walking alone](https://t.co/oXZV4jH55E)
- WSB-TV (Atlanta): [Video shows moments GA mother arrested for letting son walk to store by himself](https://t.co/JHgLxjlstN)
- USA Today: [Mom arrested after her 10-year-old son went on a walk alone](https://t.co/CwW4xU3Yd3)
- Follow-up on dismissal: [WSB-TV charges dismissed story](https://t.co/M1ZIfDr5sm)

Note that the children were not arrested—the parent was, based on the lack of supervision while the boy walked alone. This is the prominent story that matches the description.

**Dr. Stefan Lanka** (German biologist, PhD) and **Dr. Tom Cowan** (former American MD) are the two individuals cited in the @Luizmd bio for the claim that no virus has ever been isolated, sequenced, or shown to cause disease.[](<https://t.co/RV9MP6wS0m>)

### Dr. Stefan Lanka
- **Background**: Born in 1963 in Germany. He studied biology at the University of Konstanz and earned a doctorate (Dr. rer. nat.) in 1994 for work on a virus infecting marine brown algae (*Ectocarpus siliculosus* virus). He has limited peer-reviewed publications after his graduate work.[](<https://t.co/RV9MP6wS0m>)
- **Not an MD**: He is a biologist, not a medical doctor.
- **Claims**: He asserts that pathogenic viruses do not exist. This includes denial that HIV causes AIDS, that measles is caused by a virus (he has called it psychosomatic), and similar positions on other viruses. He has been associated with AIDS denialism and anti-vaccination views.[](<https://t.co/RV9MP6wS0m>)
- **Measles challenge and court case**: In 2011 he offered a €100,000 prize for a scientific publication proving the existence and diameter of the measles virus. A physician submitted six papers. A lower court ordered Lanka to pay; a higher court overturned the award on a technicality (Lanka had required the proof in a *single* publication). The courts did not rule that the measles virus does not exist; they addressed only the terms of the private reward offer. Scientific consensus, based on isolation, sequencing, imaging, and epidemiology, holds that the measles virus is real and causative.[](<https://t.co/9SeA8ccb5v>)

### Dr. Tom Cowan
- **Background**: Earned an MD from Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in 1984. He practiced alternative/family medicine (including in San Francisco) until around 2019–2020 and has been associated with the Weston A. Price Foundation. He is an author of books questioning mainstream views on disease causation, including *The Contagion Myth*.[](<https://t.co/r33jPX0ELu>)
- **License status**: In 2017 the California Medical Board placed him on five-year probation for prescribing an unapproved experimental substance (GcMAF) to a metastatic breast cancer patient without adequate disclosure or review of her records. He surrendered his California medical license in December 2020 and is no longer licensed to practice medicine. He has continued as an author, speaker, and seller of supplements/health products.[](<https://t.co/WVWh5zPs8j>)
- **Claims**: He promotes the view that viruses do not cause disease (aligned with terrain theory rather than germ theory). He has also publicly linked COVID-19 illness to 5G networks, a claim widely rejected by evidence.[](<https://t.co/r33jPX0ELu>)

These positions are not accepted by the mainstream scientific and medical communities. Extensive evidence from virus isolation techniques, electron microscopy, full-genome sequencing, controlled cell-culture experiments, animal models, and epidemiological data supports the existence of pathogenic viruses and their role in disease. The individuals cited are outliers whose views have been repeatedly addressed and rejected in the scientific literature.

Oregon made national and international headlines yesterday for all the wrong reasons: a downtown Portland mass stabbing and a mass shooting at a Bend elementary school.

The loss of life and trauma inflicted on the school community are heartbreaking. My prayers are with every victim, family, student, educator, and first responder affected. I’m profoundly grateful to the courageous individual who intervened to stop the gunman and potentially save additional lives.

If the hero who stopped the gunman at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend HAD NOT IGNORED the school district’s gun policies, more people would be injured or deceased.

Meanwhile, Portland continues to grapple with violent crime and a deteriorating sense of public safety.

Oregonians deserve more than statements of concern after each tragedy. They deserve effective prevention, meaningful accountability, and policies grounded in real-world outcomes.

Governor Tina Kotek and state leaders should be judged on results not rhetoric. Are our communities safer? Are schools adequately protected? Are violent offenders being held accountable? Are families seeing an improvement in their quality of life?

Compassion for victims and accountability for leadership are not mutually exclusive.

Oregon cannot afford to treat each tragedy as an isolated headline, offer condolences, and then return to business as usual. Residents deserve a serious examination of what is failing, what must change, and who is accountable for delivering results.

The quality of life has so deteriorated under the “leadership” of Tina Kotek and forty years of single party rule.

How can any sane person vote to give Tina KoteX another four years to destroy our state?

Frank Sinatra offered $1 million to get his son back. The kidnappers asked for $240,000.

December 8, 1963. Frank Sinatra Jr. is 19, in Room 417 at Harrah’s Lake Tahoe. Armed men walk in and take him.

The ringleader, Barry Keenan, was 23. Why Sinatra? “I knew Frank always got his way.”

They held him for 54 hours. At dawn on December 11, the ransom was dropped between two school buses in Sepulveda, California. Soon after, Keenan was caught.

He was sentenced to 12 years and served about 4.5. By 1983 he had made millions in real estate.

The son was haunted for years by rumors that he faked it.

The father carried 10 dimes for the rest of his life, so he would never be short of coins for a payphone. He was buried with them.

He offered $1 million. He carried $1 in dimes for the rest of his life.
