TRUMP WANTS THE MIDTERMS TO BE A REFERENDUM ON HIM.

HIS OWN CANDIDATES ARE RUNNING AGAINST THE COST OF HIS TARIFFS.

In Michigan, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers now says Canada is not the enemy and wants the tariff war ended.

In New Hampshire, John Sununu says the tariffs should be struck down to reduce living costs.

In Maine, Susan Collins emphasizes that she opposed Trump’s tariffs on Canada.

In Colorado, Representative Jeff Hurd voted against them—and was attacked by the president for doing so.

These are not anti-Trump Republicans.

They are candidates who still need Trump’s voters but can no longer defend the economic consequences of one of his signature policies.

That tension is defining the midterms.

Trump wants Republican candidates to run on loyalty.

Competitive districts are forcing them to run on affordability.

US inflation reached 3.7% in September.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 78% of Americans blame Trump’s policies—including tariffs and the Iran conflict—for prices rising faster than wages.

Democrats understand the opportunity.

Since September 1, Democratic campaigns and allied groups have spent more than $163 million on television advertising that mentions Trump.

Republicans have spent only $11 million on comparable ads.

Trump wants his name on the ballot.

Many Republican candidates appear to want his voters without his economic record.

The immediate question is who controls Congress after November 3.

The second-order consequence concerns who controls American trade policy afterward.

If Republicans in battleground states survive by openly opposing tariffs, they will return to Washington with evidence that breaking with Trump works.

That could produce a congressional bloc demanding exemptions, limits on presidential tariff authority or an end to the dispute with Canada.

If they lose, the conclusion may be even more damaging to Trump’s trade agenda: tariffs protected neither American purchasing power nor Republican majorities.

Canada and Mexico are watching the same calculation.

They now have a reason to delay major concessions until after the election, when a weaker White House or a different Congress may offer better terms.

The midterms are therefore becoming more than a referendum on Trump.

They are becoming a market test for economic nationalism.

Republican candidates are discovering that protectionism sounds national in Washington.

Its costs remain local—in Michigan factories, Maine ports, border businesses and household bills.

Trump transformed tariffs into a test of party loyalty.

Voters may transform them into a test of political survival.

Tracking second-order effects.

text:
“It’s actually the Lagos Coastal Highway; don’t call it Lagos-Calabar. It will not get there… We have the largest number of poor people in the world. We have the largest number of out-of-school kids in the world, then you turn around and say you are the largest economy in Africa.”

— Governor Donald Duke

I concur with Governor Duke’s argument✅. At a time when Nigerians are struggling with the cost of living, inadequate healthcare, poor education and deteriorating infrastructure, public expenditure must be guided by rigorous economic appraisal, measurable benefits and the greatest possible public value.

Furthermore, projects of this scale demand careful consideration of their financing structure and long-term fiscal implications. Where infrastructure is financed through government-backed loans, the repayment burden ultimately falls on public finances, potentially limiting the resources available for other national priorities.

Nigeria should therefore explore commercially viable public-private partnerships and Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) concessions where they offer better value for money. Such arrangements can enable private investors to mobilise long-term capital, develop and operate infrastructure, and recover their investments under transparent contractual terms, while allocating risks appropriately.

Dubai and other infrastructure-driven economies offer useful lessons in mobilising private capital for major infrastructure development. Nigeria should strengthen its concession framework, deepen its capital markets and create the conditions for institutional investors and infrastructure funds to participate in bankable projects. These models should be adapted to Nigeria’s economic realities and pursued where they offer demonstrable value for money.

The objective should be simple: use scarce public resources where government intervention is most urgently needed, while mobilising private capital where the market can efficiently finance viable infrastructure.

That is how we maximise public value and ensure that development is driven not merely by the scale of projects, but by the needs of the people.

text:
🔴 The Same Script, Next Page: From "Lending a Hand" to the Abraham Accords. Saudi Arabia Is Being Locked into the Same Cage

October 16, 2026 | Washington

A reporter stood up and asked a second question.

"Are the Abraham Accords and Saudi Arabia back on the table?"

Trump replied without hesitation, without a pause, and without any need to weigh his words.

"Yes, I think so. Perhaps more than ever before. Saudi Arabia is very happy to have the support of Israel and our support."

This is the second script. The same pattern. The same objective. Only the question has changed.

💥 What "Back on the Table" Really Means: It Never Left

The very phrase "back on the table" is a lie.

The Abraham Accords never left the table; they were simply covered by a cloth, a cloth labeled "Palestinian Statehood." Saudi Arabia needed this cloth. It needed a way to explain to the Arab world, the Muslim world, and its own people: "We have not yet recognized Israel; we are still waiting for a Palestinian state to be established."

But beneath that cloth, nothing on the table was ever removed.

Intelligence sharing between Saudi Arabia and Israel; air defense coordination; Israeli-made helmets worn by pilots in Saudi F-15s; Israeli data flowing into Saudi command centers; the opening of Saudi airspace to Israeli flights, none of these are things that are "returning" to the table. They are things that have been on the table and in operation all along.

When Trump says "back on the table," what he really means is: it is time to remove the cloth.

🎯 What "More Than Ever Before" Means

This is not mere rhetoric; it is a precise statement.

Why "more than ever before"? Because Ansarallah is winning this war.

Saudi airports have been shut down. Operations at King Khalid International Airport have been suspended. Air navigation at Abha Airport has been halted. Residents of Riyadh have been killed or wounded in drone attacks.  The office tower at Saudi Aramco’s headquarters was struck by a missile, setting the top three floors including the level housing the CEO’s office ablaze.

American protection has proven to be a sham. U.S. aircraft carriers have been forced to retreat from the Red Sea. American Patriot missile systems have failed to intercept Iranian ballistic missiles, and the U.S. THAAD system has proven incapable of safeguarding Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure.

Saudi Arabia requires a protector that is actually capable of fighting. The United States cannot but Israel can.

However, Israel’s assistance does not come for free. The price is recognition not merely in terms of military or intelligence cooperation, but formal political recognition. It entails the official signing of the Abraham Accords, the opening of embassies, an end to Saudi votes against Israel at the United Nations, and a cessation of Saudi efforts to block Israel’s entry into the Arab League.

The phrase "more than ever before" implies that Ansarallah has left Saudi Arabia with no other choice.

⚔️ "Very happy" these two words are the cruelest part of the entire statement.

Trump remarked, "Saudi Arabia is very happy to have Israel’s support and our support."

"Very happy." This is not the language of diplomacy; it is the language used to describe a child receiving a gift, a beggar receiving alms, or a dependent expressing gratitude to a benefactor.

Saudi Arabia is not merely a "very happy" recipient. It is a sovereign state, the custodian of Mecca and Medina, a leader of the Arab world, and the cornerstone of OPEC. It possesses a population of 35 million and the world’s largest oil reserves.

Yet, Trump describes it as "very happy."

This is not a description of Saudi Arabia; it is a redefinition of it recasting a sovereign state as a beneficiary, a protector as a protected party, and a provider as a mere recipient.

The term "very happy" conveys a message to Saudi Arabia: You are now a dependent. Dependents have no standing to set conditions, no right to discuss the issue of Palestine, and no basis to demand East Jerusalem. A dependent’s only role is to say, "Thank you."

📜 Why now?

Because Ansarallah’s missiles are landing on Saudi airports.  Drones fly across the skies of Riyadh. The towers at the Aramco headquarters are ablaze. Saudi Arabia’s air defense systems have failed to stop them.

The Saudi Crown Prince faces a choice: continue to rely on the United States, a protector that has proven incapable of shielding him or turn toward Israel, a protector already operating within his own war rooms.

Trump’s playbook offers a clear directive: turn to Israel. The price? The Abraham Accords. The price? Recognition. The price? Abandoning the Palestinians.

This is not a "return to the negotiating table." It is being forced onto the table.

🔻 Palestine, Sold Out Once Again

1993: The Oslo Accords. Palestinians were told: recognize Israel, and you shall have a state. They recognized Israel. They received no state.

2020: The Abraham Accords. The UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan were told: recognize Israel, and you shall gain economic benefits and security guarantees. They recognized Israel. They received Israeli spyware and American weaponry. The Palestinians received no state.

2026: Saudi Arabia is told: recognize Israel, and you shall gain Israeli air defense systems and intelligence support. Will Saudi Arabia agree? Trump says yes.

Each time, "recognizing Israel" has been packaged as "peace." Each time, the price of this "peace" has been Palestine. Each time, the Palestinians have been told: wait a little longer. Make one more concession. Give up a little more.

This time, the betrayal of Palestine would come from the Custodian of Mecca and Medina the leader of the Arab world, the guardian of the holiest lands in the Islamic faith.

This is not diplomacy. It is betrayal, a betrayal of the deepest kind.

The Next Page in the Playbook

The first playbook addressed Israeli assistance to Saudi Arabia. The second addressed the Abraham Accords. And there is a third playbook. And a fourth.  The next question might be: "Is Saudi Arabia prepared to establish formal diplomatic relations with Israel?" Trump’s response could be: "Yes, I think so. Perhaps more than ever before. Saudi Arabia is very happy to have Israel as a friend."

Each question is a continuation of the one before it. Each answer serves as a confirmation of the previous one. This is not an interview; it is a staged announcement. Every "question-and-answer" exchange is a brick laid into the same wall and behind that wall lies the grave of Palestine.

Long live Palestine. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

Who was she, and why does she matter?

In 1673, Jesus began appearing to St. Margaret Mary Alacoque, a French nun. He showed her His Sacred Heart burning with love for humanity, surrounded by thorns because of our sins.

Jesus asked her to spread devotion to His Sacred Heart, encouraging Catholics to receive Holy Communion, make reparation for sins, and grow closer to Him.

Through these revelations, Jesus also gave her the Nine First Fridays devotion, which is still practiced today.

How to practice it:

Receive Holy Communion on the First Friday of nine consecutive months, in a state of grace. Go to Confession if needed, and offer each Communion in reparation to the Sacred Heart of Jesus.

St. Margaret Mary dedicated her life to reminding the world how much Jesus loves us and desires our love in return.

text:
A letter from "Palestine".    
"Hello, I am Palestinian. 📷
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.
1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.
1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.
1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.
Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.
Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.
Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.
Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.
Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.
Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.
Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.
Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.
I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.
So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.
And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

text:
I asked Grok to unpack every point where lawyers shaped that path. Full breakdown below.

The live performance you’re pointing to is Foster the People doing “Pumped Up Kicks” on The Late Show with David Letterman (CBS) around late October 2011, tied to their Live on Letterman webcast from the Ed Sullivan Theater. It is a usefully specific moment to stress-test the “AI will replace lawyers” line, because almost none of what made that stage possible is the kind of discrete, document-generating task that current models handle well. It is a chain of multi-party negotiations, power imbalances, incomplete information, human judgment under pressure, and ongoing relationship management.

Here’s the functional (and sometimes emotional) scaffolding that had to be in place for three guys who started playing together in late 2009 to stand on that CBS stage roughly two years later, playing a song that had gone from free website download to radio and TV ubiquity.

Band formation and internal structure (late 2009). Mark Foster, Mark Pontius, and Cubbie Fink started playing together. Without written agreements covering song ownership splits, decision-making, profit participation, and what happens if someone leaves, bands routinely blow up over exactly these issues once money appears. Lawyers (or at least competent counsel) draft or negotiate the partnership/LLC operating agreement that prevents the later “I wrote the hit so I own everything” or “you’re not a real member” fights. Foster controlled publishing in North America through his Smims Coffee and Tea Music Publishing entity; that control had to be locked down early so the label deal didn’t swallow it.

Name clearance and trademark. The name evolved from “Foster & the People” after people kept mishearing it. Before anyone invests heavily in logos, merch, or promotion, someone runs clearance searches and, if clear, files for trademark protection (live performances in Class 41, clothing/merch in Class 25, etc.). Skipping this is how bands later get cease-and-desist letters or lose the name. The emotional piece here is counseling the artists not to fall in love with a name that has latent conflicts.

The viral moment and the panic call (early 2010). Foster posted “Pumped Up Kicks” as a free download. It exploded. He called manager Brent Kredel in a state of overwhelm: “Everyone is calling me and e-mailing me—what do I do? Who are the good guys, who are the bad guys?” That is not a contract-drafting problem. It is triage, reputation assessment, and strategic filtering while the inbox fills with offers. Managers and their lawyers spent weeks sorting legitimate interest from noise. The same period produced an oral-management claim from Brandon Dorsky (who also claimed he named the band). That dispute became a 2011 lawsuit for breach of oral contract and was settled. Oral deals and informal arrangements are exactly what generate expensive fights later; the emotional value of counsel is the calm “don’t sign anything and don’t agree to anything until we paper this” conversation when the artist is euphoric and exhausted.

The record deal (May 2010). Meetings with Warner Bros., Atlantic, Columbia, Universal Republic. They signed a multi-album deal with Columbia’s Startime International imprint that notably did not include ancillary rights (merch and touring). In 2010 that was unusually artist-friendly. Publishing outside North America went to Sony/ATV; Foster kept North America. Lawyers negotiate the advance structure, royalty rates, creative control and delivery requirements, option periods, and reversion language. They also flag when a “great” deal is actually a short-term cash grab that handicaps the next five years. Managers later described turning down endorsements and placements that would have paid immediately but damaged the long-term trajectory. That filtering is judgment, not form-filling.

Copyright, publishing, and licensing infrastructure. “Pumped Up Kicks” was written and recorded by Foster (mostly alone at Mophonics while he was still doing commercial jingles). Registration, chain-of-title confirmation, and PRO affiliation (ASCAP/BMI) had to be handled so the song could generate performance royalties and so sync licenses could be granted cleanly. The song was licensed into Entourage and other shows before the album even existed. Each sync requires separate licenses for the composition and the master, negotiated fees, territory, term, and media scope. For a live television performance the issues are different but still contractual: the network’s appearance agreement, clearances for the live performance of the composition, any reuse of the taped performance, publicity rights, and liability allocation.

Booking, early touring, and the TV appearance itself. Booking agent Tom Windish (Windish Agency) put them on small club dates so they could develop as a live act before the big rooms. Those are performance contracts with venues or promoters covering fees, riders, cancellation, insurance, and indemnity. The Letterman/Live on Letterman booking is a network appearance agreement (CBS, under the then-prevailing AFTRA/network code rules for musical performers). It covers compensation, performance obligations, technical requirements, rights granted in the recording of the performance, and various releases. A lawyer reviews it so the band does not inadvertently grant the network overly broad rights in the performance or accept unfavorable liability language. Union rules and scale payments also enter the picture.

Ongoing protection and the “say no” function. Once the band was moving, the team (managers, label, lawyers) spent real time declining offers that looked lucrative in the moment but were bad for the brand or the catalog. That is not glamorous work, but it is how artists avoid the classic “we signed everything away and now we can’t tour or merch under our own name” outcome.

None of this is primarily about generating perfect boilerplate. It is about negotiating against counterparties with more experience and leverage, spotting when a deal term will hurt the artist two or three albums later, mediating internal band dynamics before they become litigation, and giving a client who is suddenly fielding hundreds of emails a framework for deciding who to trust. AI can draft a first-pass management agreement or flag missing clauses in a record deal term sheet. It does not currently replace the judgment calls, the relationship reading, the emotional ballast during the chaotic early rise, or the willingness to sit across the table and push back on a label or network when the artist’s long-term interests diverge from the short-term cash. The Letterman stage was the visible result of that invisible scaffolding. Without it, the band either never reaches the stage or reaches it under terms that make the rest of the career much harder.

While people often use the terms interchangeably in everyday conversation, a technical difference exists based on licensing and courtroom authority. 

Lawyer

Definition: Someone who has completed law school and earned a law degree, such as a Juris Doctor (J.D.).
Licensing: Has not necessarily passed a state bar exam.
What they do: Can offer legal research, education, policy advice, or consulting, but cannot legally represent clients in court or file lawsuits without a license. 

Attorney (Attorney at Law)

Definition: A lawyer who has passed a state bar exam and holds an active license to practice law in a specific jurisdiction.
Licensing: Officially admitted to practice by a state bar association.
What they do: Can represent clients in court, negotiate legal settlements, draft binding legal documents, and offer formal legal representation.

text:
A Chicago packing house refused to hire Black women, so the Negro Labor Relations League waited for chitterling season and took the company apart in the one month it could not afford to lose a customer. Agar did not just start hiring Black women on the packing floor. It hired them into the front office. You are looking at the same outfit that handed the man in this photograph his sign.

The man in the photograph has no name.

He is standing on a Chicago sidewalk in July of 1941, shirt white, collar buttoned, tie knotted at the throat in summer heat. On his shoulder he carries a plank of wood the way a soldier carries a rifle at rest.

The sign is hand-lettered. It reads: If Negro men can carry guns for Uncle Sam surely they can drive milk wagons for Bowman Dairy.

A federal photographer named John Vachon made the picture that month, and the print is in a New York museum now, catalogued and credited and measured to the eighth of an inch. Nobody wrote down who the man was.

But he did not make that board by himself, and he was not out there on a feeling.

The people who put him on that sidewalk had a name, an office, a newspaper, and a method. And a few months before this, that same method had broken a packing house in half.

Start there, because it tells you exactly who you are looking at.
The Agar Packing Company in Chicago had a hiring rule, and it was not written in code.

No Black women wanted.

That was the whole policy. A Black woman could walk into Agar with twenty years of packing experience and she would not be hired to sweep the floor, and everybody on the South Side knew it, and for years nothing happened about it.

The Negro Labor Relations League did not go pound on Agar's door in July.
They waited for chitterling season.

Understand what that means, because if you did not grow up with it you will miss the whole blade of this. Chitterlings were a cold weather food, a winter food, the thing that came out of the pot when the money was thin and the family was large and the house needed to smell like somebody loved it.

Which means a Chicago packing house that sold chitterlings made a serious share of its year in a few cold months. And it made that money almost entirely out of Black kitchens.

Agar had built a business on Black women's grocery dollars while refusing to let a Black woman touch a paycheck, so the League let the calendar come around.

When the cold hit and the demand rose and the orders started stacking up, the Crusader went to press against Agar, hard, and it kept printing. And Black Chicago quit buying.

Not for a week. Through the season, through the one window a chitterling packer cannot afford to lose, in a city with a Black population big enough to make that decision felt in an accountant's ledger by the second week.

Agar broke.

And it did not break halfway, which is the part that should raise the hair on your arms. The company did not just start hiring Black women onto the packing floor, it hired them into the front office.

Front office. Desks, telephones, payroll, the rooms where Black women had never been allowed to sit down in that building.

That was not luck and it was not a moral awakening at Agar. That was a group of people who had studied a company's calendar until they found the exact week it could be hurt.

Now you know what kind of outfit handed a man a plank of wood outside a dairy.
The Negro Labor Relations League was organized in Chicago in 1937 to break the color line in hiring, and it ran on two men who could not have looked less alike on paper.

Joseph H. Jefferson was a South Side native who owned a wrecking company. He knew how to take a building down, which is a useful cast of mind.

Jefferson never ran for office in his life, and he was arrested again and again for the demonstrations he organized.

Sit with that sentence a second. Not arrested once, as a young man, in a burst of nerve.

Arrested repeatedly, across years, as a business owner with something to lose, and then out on the sidewalk again the next time. A man who has been booked once and quits is ordinary and forgivable.

A Chicago packing house refused to hire Black women, so the Negro Labor Relations League waited for chitterling season and took the company apart in the one month it could not afford to lose a customer. Agar did not just start hiring Black women on the packing floor. It hired them into the front office. You are looking at the same outfit that handed the man in this photograph his sign.

A man who has been booked five times and shows up for the sixth is a different animal.

Balm L. Leavell Jr. was born in Louisville, Kentucky, went to Fisk, and intended to be a doctor. He came to Chicago in 1930 instead, about twenty years old, and went to work in the liquor and beverage trade.

By 1938 he was organizing the Dining Car Waiters Union. He spent his days with men who fed white passengers across the country and came home to a city that would not hire them to drive a truck.

That is the year the two of them met.

Together they went after the motion picture operators' unions and the local theaters. They went after the Milk Wagon Drivers union, the city's dairies, and several of the major daily newspapers.

That list is not my summary of their work. It is Jefferson's own accounting, written in a column he published the week after Leavell died.

They pushed the Pabst Brewing Company until Black men were driving its trucks on the South Side. They got Black men onto beer trucks and bread trucks and buses.

They went after the pawnbrokers who had been quietly bleeding people who could not read a contract closely. They walked out of that negotiation with an agreement that changed how the whole trade dealt with Black customers.

Both men were threatened for it, and neither one of them stopped.

And in June of 1940, a year before that photograph, the two of them started a newspaper because nobody else was going to write any of this down.
It was one page.

They ran it out of an apartment in the Ida B. Wells Homes on the South Side, and Jefferson said plainly what they wanted it for. They wanted a house organ that would cover the League's work completely and sincerely.

There was a hole where that coverage should have been. The Chicago Defender's founder, Robert S. Abbott, had died four months earlier, and his paper was locked in a succession fight that would end in court.

So two men with a job to do put out one sheet of paper about Black people getting hired.
And they gave it away free for seventeen years.

Do that math with a business eye. Seventeen years of paper, ink, and labor, handed out on street corners for nothing, because the point was never the paper.

The point was that when the League leaned on a company, twenty thousand people had to know why by Saturday.
That single sheet became the Chicago Crusader, which is still publishing today, and it is the reason we can say with certainty that the man outside Bowman Dairy was not a lone soul with a grievance.

Now the job he was standing there for, because it was a real job and he knew exactly what it paid.

Bowman was the biggest prize in the city. It was the largest fluid-milk distributor in Chicago, employing more than three thousand people in the Chicago area by the middle of the 1930s.

And it had built its big bottling plants on the South Side.

The plants stood in and beside the Black Belt. The bottles came out of those plants, rode to Black kitchens, went up Black front steps, and were paid for out of Black pockets, carried by a white man in a Bowman uniform.

A Chicago milkman's day started at four forty-five in the morning, the earliest hour the union contract would allow, which tells you men had once been made to start earlier than that.
He loaded at the plant door and rolled out after five fifteen.

Then a hundred and fifty stops, twenty-two miles out and back, in the dark for the first hours of it. He solicited the trade, sold the product, billed the customer, collected the money, and settled every argument about a short quart personally, at the door, before six in the morning.

At the end of it he came back, wrote his tickets for the empties, handed his cash to the cashier, and ordered tomorrow. Then he either filled his gasoline tank or unhitched his horse, because in Chicago in 1941 it could still be a horse.

Nine-hour day on paper, and fifty-six in the actual telling of the men who did it.

And the basic union wage for that work was forty-eight dollars a week, guaranteed, before commissions, in a trade where drivers were averaging around fifty-two.
Put that number in a kitchen and see what it buys.

Forty-eight dollars a week is a family that pays rent on the first without a conversation about it. It is shoes that fit, coal in February, a doctor when the baby's chest rattles, and a Sunday where nobody counts.

For a household that had come north on a train to get out from under Mississippi wages, that job was not a job. It was the whole reason for the train.

Which brings us to the wall.

Federal investigators surveyed Chicago drivers that same winter and found the typical man on a milk route was about forty-two years old. He had been driving milk for nearly fifteen years and had been with the same dairy more than eleven.

The government's own analysts explained why. The industry had barely hired anybody in a decade.

So this was not a wide field with a color bar at the gate. It was a nearly frozen field with a color bar at the gate, and the rare opening that did come went to a white man who then held it for fifteen years.

Meanwhile the men locked out of it took what Chicago handed them. The killing floors of the stockyards, the heat of the mills, red caps, porters, elevator work, and other people's kitchens.

Now hold that forty-eight dollars a week against what the country was offering him that same month.

The first peacetime draft in American history had been signed the previous September, and Black men across Chicago went down and registered like everybody else. The Army took them, into segregated units, under white officers, and it sorted the overwhelming majority into labor and service battalions rather than combat arms.

Which means the Army had already decided what a Black man was for. It decided he was for loading, hauling, digging, cooking, and driving trucks.

Read that last one twice.

The Army would put him behind a wheel and point him at a war. Bowman would not put him behind a wheel and point him at Sixty-Third Street.

And an Army private in July of 1941 started at twenty-one dollars a month.

Twenty-one a month with a rifle. Forty-eight a week with a milk bottle, and he could not have the milk bottle.

That is the arithmetic he was carrying on his shoulder, and he had every legal right to carry it, which is its own buried story.

On March 28, 1938, the Supreme Court decided New Negro Alliance against Sanitary Grocery. The facts were almost absurdly small.

A Black civic group asked a grocery chain to hire Black clerks in stores whose customers were Black. The company ignored them, so the group put one person in front of one store on one day with a placard.

One person, one sign, one day.

The placard said the company employed no Negroes, and a lower court ruled that this was not a labor dispute at all and shut the picketing down.
Two Black lawyers, Belford V. Lawson Jr. and Thurman L. Dodson, took it to the Supreme Court of the United States and won it six to two.

Justice Roberts wrote that this was a labor dispute, that the Norris-LaGuardia Act reached it, and that the information on the placard was true. That ruling is the reason a man could stand outside a Chicago dairy three years later with a homemade board and not be dragged off for it.

Now look at the union he was asking to join.

The Milk Wagon Drivers' Union of Chicago, Local 753, had carried its own picketing fight all the way to the Supreme Court and lost it on February 10, 1941. Five months before this photograph, the milk drivers of Chicago were in Washington arguing that their right to walk a line was close to sacred.

Five months later a Black man was walking a line for permission to become one of them.

And the union and the dairy were not strangers to each other: in November of 1938 a federal grand jury indicted the whole Chicago milk market for restraint of trade. Bowman Dairy and Local 753 both sat on that defendant list, and they settled together in September of 1940.

The company and the union could find each other in a courtroom. Neither one could find him on the sidewalk.

One more thing had happened, one month before Vachon lifted his camera, and it is the reason this photograph should sting.

A. Philip Randolph told the White House that a hundred thousand Black people would march on the capital on July 1, 1941, demanding an end to discrimination in defense hiring and in the armed forces. Roosevelt met him and Walter White on June 18 and tried to talk him out of it.

The President said he could not issue an order for one group, because then there would be "no end to other groups coming in here" asking for theirs.
Randolph did not move.

On June 25, 1941, Roosevelt signed Executive Order 8802, declaring there would be no discrimination in the employment of workers in defense industries and in government because of race, creed, color, or national origin. It was the first presidential directive on race since Reconstruction, and Randolph called off the march.

And then, in July, a man walked out onto a Chicago sidewalk with a plank of wood, because a dairy is not a defense plant.

That is the buried thing inside this picture. The order reached federal agencies and companies doing war work, and milk carried up a back staircase on the South Side was neither.

He was standing in the gap the order left behind, days after the most celebrated civil rights document in seventy years had been signed without reaching him. He knew that, and he went out anyway.

We never learn how it ended for him. Nobody recorded whether Bowman gave in, or whether he ever drove one of those wagons.

But we know what it cost the men who sent him, because that part is written down.
Jefferson kept getting arrested and kept going back out, all the way through, and he lived until 1984 and died at seventy-six.

Balm Leavell did not get that long.

Sometime around 1959, a teenage girl from Pine Bluff, Arkansas went to see Lorraine Hansberry's A Raisin in the Sun. Afterward a man offered her and her friend a ride home.

In the car she talked the whole way about the newspaper job she was going to get and everything she meant to do once she had it. She had no idea she was talking to the publisher.

When her friend told her afterward who had been driving, Dorothy said she almost died. She went to the interview anyway, which is the sentence that explains the rest of her life.

Two people had called in sick at the Crusader that day and Balm Leavell needed hands. He hired her at thirty-five dollars a week to keep the books.

Two people out sick. That is how thin the thread was.

They married in 1963. They had five years.

In July of 1968 Balm went into Michael Reese Hospital for exploratory surgery, and the surgeons found stage four pancreatic cancer.

He was awake on October 23 for his wife's twenty-fourth birthday. The next day he slipped into a coma, and on Friday, October 25, 1968, he died with her beside him.

She was twenty-four years old. She had a three-year-old, a two-year-old, and two newspapers.

According to the Crusader's own account of that week, Balm's children from an earlier marriage tried to keep her from his bedside while he was dying. They made threats to her at the funeral and in the days after.

Twenty-four, widowed, two babies, and threatened over the body.

There was a twenty-four-hour wake at First Deliverance Church in Bronzeville, and nearly a hundred floral arrangements around the casket. She wore black with a veil and led the mourners out to Lincoln Cemetery, where her husband was laid in a mausoleum a short distance from Robert Abbott.

Then the children went to court for the estate.

And Joseph Jefferson, made executor by Judge Richard Gumbel, held a majority interest in the company and could have taken the whole thing. Instead he put his weight behind the twenty-four-year-old widow and made her publisher.

He had spent thirty years fighting people who kept Black folks out of rooms. He was not about to start doing it himself at the end.

Dorothy R. Leavell has run those papers ever since, from 1968 to right now, and in all that time the Crusader has never missed an issue.

Not one, through the assassinations, the riots, the collapse of American newspapers, a pandemic. Fifty-eight years of getting a paper out on time for a readership that other publishers decided was not worth the postage.

In October of 2016 the city of Chicago finally did something for the two men who started it.

There was a small ceremony in a parking lot half a block from the Crusader office on King Drive. Alderman, historian, former alderman, family, a few dozen people standing around in the fall.

Then somebody pulled a cover off a street sign.

It is brown, rectangular, and sixteen inches long. It hangs on the pole underneath the sign that says Martin Luther King Jr. Drive.

Sixteen inches of painted metal for the men who put Black women in Agar's front office, Black drivers on Pabst's trucks, and a man in a pressed white shirt outside the largest dairy in Chicago.
Dorothy Leavell stood there and said she was excited and very pleased, and that the men being honored were legends.

She was seventy-one. She had been waiting since she was twenty-four.

Now go back to the photograph one last time, and look at what got kept and what got thrown away.

Bowman Dairy was bought out in 1966, and its old bottles turn up on collector sites now, the glass with the arrow through the B, and people pay real money for them. The company's name is preserved in a business encyclopedia, on shelves in antique shops, and, more permanently than either, on a picket sign hanging in a museum.

John Vachon's name is preserved. It is under the photograph, in the surveys of Depression-era photographers, in the credit line every time the image runs.

Every word on that board is preserved, down to the punctuation, in two archives and a Smithsonian exhibit.
The month is preserved, the city, the dimensions of the print in inches, and the year a museum bought it.

The man is not.

He is the only person in the frame and the only thing in it without a name, and he stood there in July heat asking for a job that started at four forty-five in the morning. Somebody with a camera was standing directly in front of him and never asked him who he was.

So here is the smallest honest repair available to us, eighty-five years late.

Stop calling him a man with a sign. He was a member of an organization, carrying an argument worked out in meetings by men who went to jail for it and got up and went back.

And when you tell somebody about this picture, do not stop at the picture. Tell them about the packing house that got broken in the middle of chitterling season, and the one-page paper handed out free for seventeen years, and the twenty-four-year-old in the veil who never missed an issue.

That crowd made him. He is what they looked like on an ordinary Tuesday.

And he asked for a milk route, and he said surely.

The man in this photograph never left us his name, but the movement around him changed Chicago forever. I research forgotten stories like his because the people who fought quietly for progress deserve to be remembered.

On 25 June 2026 the Army announced conditional lease awards for domestic critical-mineral processing on four installations, under a brand-new program it calls Strategic Capital Initiatives (SCI). The legal instrument is an Enhanced Use Lease under 10 U.S.C. § 2667 — "Leases: non-excess property of military departments and Defense Agencies." The solicitation was RFP No. DACA27-1-26-204.

So the rare-earth piece — the actual REE — went to Tooele, Utah, not Anniston. Anniston's is graphite. Worth being precise about, because that distinction will come up.

Utah fascinating as well. 

NOTE: opinion if I was looking at it all in totality minus some of the more confusing pieces I would say Obama, Biden, Clinton, Bush, and others all tried to destroy the United States so other nations could rise while getting very rich along the way. And now we are actually trying to reverse all that damage. BUT the zero accountability and justice thing for anyone previously involved, the War in Iran, the endless support of Israel over our own interests are all things that greatly confuse me. 

Then it advanced. On 7 October 2026 — nine days ago — Titan and the Army signed a term sheet setting the principal commercial terms for the Anniston EUL:

•~97 acres of "underutilized Army property at Anniston Army Depot."

•50-year initial term, plus two 25-year renewals exercisable by both parties — up to 100 years of tenure.

•Products: Purified Micronized Graphite (PMG) first, then Coated Spherical Purified Graphite (CSPG) after customer qualification. CSPG is lithium-ion battery anode material.

•Army right of first offer on uncommitted PMG and CSPG, capped at 10% of annual facility production.

•Rent at or above fair market value, with the Army stating a preference for consideration "to be provided through qualifying in-kind infrastructure improvements" — i.e., the company pays its rent by building things on the depot. That's § 2667(c)(1) in action.

•Title stays with the United States. It's a leasehold, not a sale. The lessee finances, designs, builds, operates, secures and decommissions at its own cost, against a mandatory decommissioning bond.

•Lessee must be U.S.-organized, majority domestic ownership and control. In-kind improvements must meet Davis-Bacon prevailing wage and the Buy American Act.

•Nothing is built until NEPA and the rest of the environmental and regulatory review is done. Development "may begin as early as 2027," with Initial Operating Capability targeted for 2028 or sooner.

•Still conditional: subject to the definitive EUL, development and energy operating plans, appraisal, financing, Titan board approval, and "applicable Army and Congressional processes."

•Pine Bluff Arsenal (~245 acres, the larger site) and Fort Drum, New York remain under diligence.

Two quotes you'll want. Titan's CEO Rita Adiani: "For the first time in American history, a critical minerals processing facility will be built on U.S. defense soil." And Dr. Jeff Waksman, Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment: "The ability to process critical minerals on U.S. soil is a national-defense priority" — and, in the October release, that it's being done "without putting any taxpayer dollars at risk."

text:
Case of Mary Phagan: Dorsey Prepares to Defend the Frank Verdict as Judge Roan Delays the Hearing Another Week

The Atlanta Journal, Saturday, October 11, 1913, pages 1, 2, and 3.

Dorsey and Stephens Continue Their Work in Valdosta

On Saturday, October 11, 1913, The Atlanta Journal reported that Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey and his assistant, Stephens, were still working in Valdosta, Georgia, preparing to fight Leo Max Frank's request for a new trial.

Frank had been convicted of murdering 13-year-old Mary Phagan on Monday, August 25, 1913. Judge Leonard Strickland Roan sentenced him to death the following day. His lawyers were now trying to overturn the verdict and obtain another trial.

Dorsey and Stephens had traveled to Valdosta so they could work without the daily interruptions of their Atlanta offices. They were studying the complaints raised by Frank's lawyers, reviewing the trial evidence, and preparing the state's arguments.

The newspaper reported that the two prosecutors expected to finish their written legal argument that Saturday evening. They hoped to finish reviewing Frank's request by Tuesday, October 14, leaving the rest of the week to study the law and evidence.

They also needed to collect sworn written statements from jurors and other witnesses who could help answer the defense's accusations.

Dorsey hoped to have everything ready by Saturday, October 18, although the newspaper suggested that another week's work might be needed.

Juror Henslee Expected to Visit the Prosecutors

One interesting detail concerned Atticus Haygood Henslee, one of the twelve jurors who had convicted Frank.

Henslee was expected to visit Valdosta on Sunday, October 12, to see his brother-in-law. While in town, he also planned to meet with Dorsey and Stephens.

The meeting was important because Frank's lawyers had accused Henslee of having decided Frank was guilty before the trial began.

Several people claimed they had heard Henslee discussing Frank's guilt while traveling around Georgia. The defense argued that he should never have been allowed to serve on the jury.

Henslee denied those accusations. He insisted that he had entered the jury box without having already decided the case.

Dorsey and Stephens were gathering statements to defend Henslee and challenge the accounts offered by Frank's lawyers.

The October 11 newspaper does not tell us whether Henslee actually met with the prosecutors the following Sunday. It does show that they expected to speak with him while preparing their answer to the defense.

Judge Roan Postpones the Hearing

Back in Atlanta, Judge Leonard Strickland Roan formally postponed Frank's new trial hearing until Saturday, October 18, 1913.

Dorsey was still in Valdosta, so Deputy Newt Garner, who worked in the prosecutor's office, appeared in court to request the delay on his behalf.

Judge Roan agreed.

He also made it clear that Frank's execution would remain on hold until the court had finished considering his request for another trial.

That was an important detail. Frank had originally been scheduled for execution on Friday, October 10, the day before this newspaper report appeared.

The delay meant that Frank would remain alive while his lawyers continued their attempt to overturn the conviction.

The newspaper explained that Dorsey could ask for even more time if he needed it. The October 18 hearing date was therefore not necessarily final.

Rumors Spread About a Third Juror

The newspaper also reported another development in the growing controversy over Frank's jury.

His lawyers had already accused two jurors, Atticus Haygood Henslee and Marcellus Johenning, of having formed opinions about Frank's guilt before hearing the trial evidence.

Now rumors were circulating that the defense might accuse a third juror of prejudice.

The newspaper said people had been expecting another sworn statement attacking a juror, but nothing new had been filed with the court that Saturday.

This is worth remembering when reading these old reports. A newspaper rumor about an accusation is not the same as an accusation formally presented to a judge.

As of Saturday, October 11, the supposed challenge to a third juror was still only a rumor.

Mayor Woodward Orders a Construction Fence Removed

While the Frank case occupied the courts, another argument was taking place in downtown Atlanta.

Mayor James G. Woodward was angry about a construction fence at the corner of Broad and Alabama streets.

The fence had been erected for remodeling work on a building owned by the estate of A. W. Calhoun. The owners had permission to block the sidewalk during construction, but the fence extended well beyond the sidewalk and nearly reached the streetcar tracks.

That left little room for traffic to pass.

Woodward had received several complaints about the obstruction. He had also seen the fence himself and believed the owners had gone too far.

After checking the permission granted by the City Council, he learned that the owners had been allowed to use only the sidewalk.

He immediately instructed Police Chief James L. Beavers to have the fence moved back and the street reopened.

Woodward told the newspaper:

"It is outrageous that traffic would be obstructed every time somebody wants to do a little moving around."

The mayor was also unhappy with the city's building permit rules. He questioned whether the City Council should have the power to allow contractors to block public sidewalks at all.

He believed that allowing construction fences to extend into the streets was even harder to justify.

Woodward also suspected that the fence had been erected before the owners received permission.

He wanted it moved and the street reopened to traffic.

Atlanta Was Dealing With Two Different Problems

These reports give us a picture of Atlanta on Saturday, October 11, 1913.

In Valdosta, Dorsey and Stephens were preparing to defend Frank's conviction and collecting statements to answer the accusations against the jurors.

In Atlanta, Judge Roan had postponed the hearing another week, while rumors continued about the possibility of a third juror being accused of prejudice.

Meanwhile, Mayor Woodward and Police Chief Beavers were dealing with a more ordinary problem: a construction fence blocking traffic in the middle of downtown Atlanta.

The report about Henslee is especially interesting because it places him in direct contact with the prosecutors while they were preparing to answer the defense's accusations.

It raises questions worth investigating. Did Henslee visit Valdosta on Sunday, October 12? Did he give Dorsey and Stephens another sworn statement? What evidence did the prosecutors gather to answer the claims against him?

Those questions take us directly into the arguments over the two accused jurors and Judge Roan's eventual decision to deny Frank another trial on Friday, October 31, 1913.

References

The Atlanta Journal. (Saturday, October 11, 1913). “They Hope to Have Their Case Ready by Next Saturday.” Page 1, column 2.

The Atlanta Journal. (Saturday, October 11, 1913). “Declares Fences at Broad and Alabama Streets Obstruct Traffic.” Page 2, column 6.

The Atlanta Journal. (Saturday, October 11, 1913). “Judge Roan Continues Frank Motion for Week.” Page 3, column 1.

The Atlanta Journal. (Tuesday, October 7, 1913). “Dorsey and Stephens Busy in Valdosta” and “Henslee Answers Perjury Charges of Frank Defense.” Page 7, columns 3–4.

text:
The world needs more wind energy. But anyone designing new wind turbines or trying to squeeze more power out of existing ones faces a stiff challenge testing new approaches. That’s because the atmosphere is a tough place for a controlled experiment.

Some researchers use wind tunnels to conduct tests, but scaled-down wind turbines in traditional wind tunnels can differ widely from conditions in the field. (Wind turbines are the largest rotating machines ever made.) The problem hampers not only development of better wind turbines, but also our understanding of basic questions like how much power to expect from a turbine when winds change direction.

In a new open access paper published in PNAS Nexus, researchers closed the gap between experiments in the field and the lab by using a wind tunnel that features high pressurization to simulate the flow physics in the atmosphere. With this approach, the researchers determined how the alignment of the turbine and its tip speed relative to the wind influence the power it generates, offering new insights into how to get more power from existing wind farms.

They also used the approach to validate a computationally lightweight model that engineers can use to test different turbine designs and wind farm control strategies.

Together, the researchers estimate that optimizing the turbine alignment relative to wind, the blade pitch angles, which control the airfoil’s angle of attack, and the tip speed relative to the wind could potentially result in tens of thousands of dollars per turbine every year in additional revenue.

“The immediate impact of this study is that we’ve now both improved and validated models that go into wind turbine control protocols for existing farms,” says Michael Howland, MIT’s Jeffrey Cheah Career Development Professor. “The bigger, medium-term impact, with a much larger upside, is this new experimental paradigm to rapidly prototype, validate simulation models, and test hypotheses about better designs and control strategies much faster than has been possible before.”

Joining Howland on the paper are first author John Kurelek, an assistant professor at Queen’s University; MIT PhD candidates Ilan Upfal and Kirby Heck; Queen’s University postdoc Supun Pieris; Penn State University researcher Alexander Piqué; and Princeton University Professor Marcus Hultmark.

Answers in the wind

Howland has spent years developing models to simulate wind farm performance and developing new techniques to increase their power output. In 2022, he showed that accounting for the wake of individual turbines when controlling the entire wind farm could significantly increase power output.

But that work required his research team to first conduct a lengthy field experiment that temporarily resulted in lowering a real wind farm’s power output by intentionally misaligning turbines from the wind for months to better understand their performance in misalignment.

“Wind energy is a uniquely challenging problem to study experimentally,” Howland says. “We want to test the effect of a certain change in isolation, but wind farms operate in chaotic, turbulent environments where the weather is constantly evolving. Wind turbines have to react to weather conditions that we have no control over, and that introduces complexities in identifying the impact of the imposed change we are studying. The field sits at this unique intersection between environmental flow, mechanics, aerodynamics, and meteorology.”

The difficulty of running experiments at real wind farms has left researchers and engineers unsure of how changes in the alignment between the wind and turbine or factors like the turbine’s tip speed relative to the wind change power output.

In fact, the researchers say many predictive models people use are built on the assumption that turbines are always perfectly perpendicular to the wind. That’s rarely the case in the real world, even with modern turbines that gradually adjust their angle in response to the wind’s rapid directional changes.

“People have been debating which models are best for understanding the output from these wind farms, but if you have nothing to compare them against, it’s very difficult to advance the field,” Hultmark says. “This paper tries to do both of those things.”

Hultmark’s research lab at Princeton has pioneered the study of scaled-down wind turbines in pressurized wind tunnels, which, as previous studies have shown, better reproduce large-scale turbines in the atmosphere because pressure makes air more dense, resulting in more inertia within the scaled laboratory environment. For the new study, the researchers used a turbine measuring 15 centimeters in diameter at varying pressures of up to 240 atmospheres.

“By pressurizing the chamber, we’re testing a turbine that is, all else being equal, 15 to 20 meters in diameter, with the ability to go up to 35 meters in diameter,” lead-author Kurelek explains. “That’s because we’re increasing the density by a factor of 100 to 220 times,” 

Kurelek sent the dimensions of the wind tunnel and wind turbine setup to Howland, who used them to calculate the aerodynamics, forces, and power production using a newly developed unified wind turbine model, which builds on previous work that developed a more general aerodynamic theory for wind turbines. The new model enables the researchers to simulate wind turbine performance across operating conditions without relying on empirical corrections that have historically been used in wind power models.

The researchers then ran a series of experiments in the tunnel over the course of several weeks, testing the turbine’s performance at different wind alignments and with different control strategies, to isolate how each factor affects performance.

They found power output could be significantly increased by adjusting the turbine’s tip speed based on its misalignment angle with the wind — a control strategy that is rarely employed in wind farms today but could offer a way to boost performance with minimal added costs.

“The big output of the experiments was clearly showing that new power maximums can be achieved when the turbine becomes misaligned with the wind through only changes to the tip speed,” Kurelek says.

Scaling the approach

The study served as validation for Howland’s model, which is fast enough to be run by engineers designing and operating wind turbines around the world using regular laptop computers.

“What we really want to know is if the turbines are always operating in some degree of misalignment with the wind, how should we control the turbine to get the maximum achievable power production?” Howland explains. “Our unified momentum model was able to make predictions of how to do this control a few years ago, and this is the first time we’e able to experimentally validate that model.”

Howland says validating models is only one part of the paper’s potential impact.

“This study also shows the huge opportunity to perform these high-throughput, controlled experiments in the pressurized facilities that Marcus and John work with, enabling us to achieve the right physics but in a time efficient and low-cost manner,” Howland says. “Right now, there’s a massive gap between idealized theoretical and simulation models and full-scale testing in extremely complicated field environments. Nothing is filling that gap except for these pressurized experiments. I hope this can be an enabler to investigate a huge range of unanswered wind energy questions in controlled environments.”

The work was supported in part by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada; the National Science Foundation; and the MIT-GE Vernova Alliance.

A New Governance Model for the Post-Industrial Era: Why Steve Hilton’s California Blueprint is Key to Unlocking Advanced Capitalist Economies (Part 3 to 5)

III. Working-Class Entrepreneurship and Restructuring Society Beyond Government Dependency

One of the most transformative dimensions of Steve Hilton’s governance approach is the democratization of entrepreneurship and skills training in underprivileged communities.

In the poorest and most overlooked neighborhoods, governance should not consist of endless government handouts, which often breed apathy and institutional dependency. 

Instead, through targeted education, regulatory simplification, and resource pairing, working-class families and low-income individuals can be empowered to create wealth through their own hands and initiative. 

Imagine a low-income community long accustomed to relying on government welfare: the moment a few successful businesses take root, they naturally attract further investment and hire locals to work for them. Through hands-on experience, these residents learn how to operate businesses themselves rather than depending on state aid.

This transformation does far more than restore dignity and happiness through honest work—it catalyzes an upward surge of social momentum, passing the rewards of one generation's perseverance down to the next, cementing the value created within the community, and lifting surrounding families out of poverty. 

Naturally, this shift continually reduces government welfare expenditures. As local productivity flourishes and more jobs are generated, workers get to keep what they earn—especially under Steve Hilton's platform, where the first $150,000 of income is entirely tax-free, ensuring that every dollar earned goes straight into their own pockets.

This environment is further reinforced by Steve Hilton's small business and economic policies, which include:
 * Abolishing the $800 small business tax
 * Cutting California’s regulations by more than half
 * Ending shakedown lawsuits
 * Eliminating the 2.1% unemployment debt surcharge
 * Cutting workers’ compensation costs by 25%

This not only generates new economic vitality out of thin air, but fundamentally alters social structures and mindsets—shifting communities away from passive government reliance toward self-worth, dignity, and upward mobility.

Simultaneously, by cutting through red tape and artificial market distortions, housing and daily living can once again become affordable for young people and working families in states like California. When California regains competitive parity with places like Texas in terms of cost of living and job opportunities, it establishes a true "Post-Industrial Governance Model."

IV. Transcending Partisan Polarization: A High-Dimensional "Partner Government"

Steve Hilton’s governance philosophy possesses an inherent trans-partisan appeal, synthesizing the core strengths of both the political Left and Right:
 
From the Right: A commitment to market efficiency, radical reduction of bureaucratic bloat, lower tax and regulatory burdens on individuals and businesses, respect for family values, and belief in individual agency.
 
From the Left: A commitment to social mobility, empowerment of marginalized communities, equal opportunity through accessible education, environmental/human safeguards, and using the state to lift people out of poverty.

This fusion directly heals the deep political polarization gripping modern Western democracies. Instead of forcing citizens to make a false choice between a heavy-handed nanny state and cold, unfettered capitalism, it redefines government as an empowering platform and ecosystem builder—one that reduces burdens, provides infrastructure, and then steps back to let individuals, families, and businesses flourish in harmony.

V. Conclusion: The Blueprint for Global Mature Economies

Respecting the family, honoring individual effort, and creatively reducing government burdens to restore human happiness—this is not just a California issue; it is the defining challenge for all mature economies worldwide.

If this new governance model—built on lean administration, AI-empowered education, living research labs, working-class entrepreneurship, and trans-partisan synthesis—can be successfully executed in a high-difficulty environment like California, its impact will be global:

 For the United States: It will offer an actionable roadmap for mature East Coast states (such as New York, Massachusetts, New Jersey, and Connecticut) struggling with bureaucratic paralysis and high costs.

 For Global Western Allies: It will serve as a vital blueprint for mature economies in Europe (UK, France, Germany) and Asia (Japan, South Korea) facing low growth, aging populations, and entrenched administrative sclerosis—showing them how to re-ignite productivity, restore social cohesion, and rebuild genuine civic prosperity.

Study abroad is more than a change of location; it’s a chance to notice which habits feel “normal” and how they shape listening, judgment, and professional relationships.

Comparative learning asks curiosity about another legal system; cross-cultural learning starts one step earlier—with the willingness to examine our own.

text:
Paxton in Texas midterms has a lot of baggage. Republicans have spent about 240 million for his campaign so far.

That’s Ken Paxton, Texas attorney general and now a Senate candidate. The core story is the Nate Paul affair. In twenty twenty, eight of Paxton’s top deputies went to the FBI saying he was using the office to help Paul, an Austin developer and donor — halting foreclosures on Paul’s properties, handing over sealed FBI documents, even hiring an outside lawyer Paul effectively directed. That produced twenty articles of impeachment in May twenty twenty-three, passed one twenty-one to twenty-three with sixty Republicans voting yes. The Senate acquitted him sixteen to fourteen that September, but a Travis County judge later ruled the firings were retaliation and ordered six point six million in damages.
Separately, Paxton took a securities-fraud plea in twenty fifteen — three hundred thousand in restitution, community service, ethics training — over a company called Servergy where investors said he hid his own compensation. Then there’s the Dubai video from New Year’s Eve twenty twenty-four: Paxton partying with two federal fraud fugitives, one of whom had given him a hundred ninety thousand dollars, including twenty-five thousand days after his indictment. His wife filed for divorce in twenty twenty-five citing adultery, and ProPublica found he took at least seventeen taxpayer-funded trips during the three months he was barred from official business after impeachment — resorts in Park City and Vail, with state troopers along every time.
He denies all of it and calls it political persecution. Worth noting no criminal conviction has stuck, which is exactly the argument his defenders lean on.
One angle that doesn’t get enough airtime: his office offered a child-abuse defendant a plea deal with one day in jail, no sex-offender registration. The judge rejected it and imposed sixty days. That’s not corruption in the financial sense, but it tells you something about how the office weighs victims

The Ghan: Australia’s Legendary Luxury Train Across the Red Heart

Few rail journeys in the world capture the imagination quite like The Ghan. Stretching from Adelaide in South Australia to Darwin in the Northern Territory, this iconic train crosses nearly the entire Australian continent, traversing some of the most remote, dramatic, and culturally significant landscapes on Earth. More than simply a means of transportation, The Ghan is a luxury expedition that combines fine dining, elegant accommodations, attentive service, and immersive excursions into Australia's Outback.

The History of The Ghan

The Ghan's story is deeply connected to the pioneering days of Australia's interior exploration. The train takes its name from the Afghan cameleers who arrived in Australia during the 19th century. These skilled transport workers used camel caravans to carry supplies through Australia's harsh interior long before modern roads and railways existed. Their efforts played a crucial role in opening the Outback to settlement and commerce.

Rail service into the Australian interior began in stages during the late 1800s. The original route was far less reliable than today's modern railway and often suffered from flooding and washouts. Over decades, improvements, rerouting, and modernization culminated in the completion of the Adelaide-to-Darwin rail connection in 2004, finally linking Australia's southern and northern coasts by rail. Today, The Ghan operates as one of the world's great luxury rail journeys.

The Route: Through the Heart of Australia

The classic northbound journey covers approximately 1,850 miles (2,979 km) over three days and two nights.

Adelaide

The journey begins in Adelaide, South Australia's elegant capital. Passengers depart the vineyards and coastal landscapes of the south before heading toward the interior.

Flinders Ranges

Shortly after departure, passengers witness the ancient and rugged Flinders Ranges, among the oldest mountain ranges in the world. Their dramatic ridgelines signal the transition into Australia's Outback.

Marla

During the northbound journey, guests stop at the remote outpost of Marla, where an unforgettable sunrise experience introduces travelers to the colors and vastness of the desert landscape.

Alice Springs

Located in Australia's Red Centre, Alice Springs is one of the nation's most iconic Outback towns. Surrounded by the magnificent MacDonnell Ranges, it offers insight into Indigenous culture, pioneering history, and the realities of life in the Australian interior.

Katherine and Nitmiluk Gorge

In the tropical north, passengers experience Katherine and often enjoy excursions to Nitmiluk Gorge, renowned for its towering sandstone cliffs, Aboriginal rock art, and the culture of the Jawoyn people.

Darwin

The journey concludes in Darwin, Australia's gateway to Asia and the tropics. Palm trees, warm weather, and multicultural influences provide a dramatic contrast to the desert landscapes left behind.

The Luxury Experience

The Ghan is frequently compared with luxury trains such as the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express and South Africa's Rovos Rail.

Dining

Dining is a centerpiece of the experience.

Guests enjoy:

Regionally inspired menus
Premium Australian wines
Craft beers and spirits
Fresh local produce
Multi-course lunches and dinners

Specialties frequently feature Australian ingredients such as barramundi, kangaroo, native herbs, and seasonal regional produce. Meals are included within the fare.

Lounge Cars

The various lounges serve as social hubs where travelers enjoy cocktails, wine tastings, coffee, and conversation while watching the Australian landscape roll by.

Staff Service

Service aboard The Ghan ranks among the finest in Australian tourism. Cabins are serviced daily, beds are turned down each evening, and staff develop remarkably personal relationships with guests during the journey. Platinum guests enjoy an even more elevated service level with transfers, premium amenities, and exclusive access areas.

Accommodation Categories
Gold Service

Gold Service remains the most popular option.

Features include:

Private sleeper accommodations
Shared or compact ensuite options depending on cabin category
Access to the Outback Explorer Lounge
Included meals and beverages
Off-train excursions

Available as:

Gold Twin
Gold Single
Accessible Gold Cabins
Gold Premium

Gold Premium bridges the gap between Gold and Platinum.

Features include:

Larger contemporary cabins
Private compact ensuite
Exclusive Gold Premium Lounge
Dedicated Gold Premium Dining Car
Premium beverage selection
Priority luggage service
Platinum Service

For many travelers, Platinum represents the ultimate way to experience The Ghan.

Features include:

Cabins nearly twice the size of Gold cabins
Full private ensuite with separate shower
Panoramic windows
Exclusive Platinum Club carriage
Premium Champagne and amenities
Personalized transfers
Double or twin-bed configuration
Australis and Aurora Suites

Beginning in 2026, The Ghan introduces even more luxurious accommodation categories:

Aurora Suites
Australis Suites

These represent the highest level of accommodation available on the train.

Dress Code

The Ghan does not maintain an overly formal dress code.

Daytime

Most guests dress in:

Smart casual attire
Polo shirts or collared shirts
Khakis or travel slacks
Comfortable footwear
Evening

Fine dining encourages:

Business casual
Resort elegant
Jacket optional for gentlemen
Cocktail-style attire for ladies

Formal wear is unnecessary, but most passengers enjoy dressing up slightly for dinner. Cargo shorts, athletic wear, and flip-flops are generally avoided in dining venues.

How Far in Advance Should You Book?

For couples, especially those seeking Platinum or premium suite accommodations:

Recommended Booking Windows
Platinum: 9-12 months ahead
Gold Premium: 6-9 months ahead
Gold Service: 4-6 months ahead

The train often sells out during Australia's peak travel season. Premium accommodations are particularly limited.

Best Time to Travel

The Ghan generally operates from February through November, with the most popular season running from March through November.

Best Overall Months

April through September

Advantages:

Pleasant temperatures
Clear skies
Comfortable touring conditions
Ideal photography opportunities
Peak Luxury Season

May through August

This period delivers the most comfortable Outback weather but also commands the highest fares.

Final Thoughts

The Ghan is not merely a train ride. It is one of the world's great travel experiences, combining five-star hospitality with a journey through landscapes that few international visitors ever see. From the vineyards of South Australia to the tropical north of Darwin, passengers cross a continent in extraordinary comfort while experiencing the rich history, Indigenous culture, immense distances, and stunning natural beauty that define Australia itself. For couples seeking a bucket-list rail adventure, The Ghan stands among the finest luxury train journeys on Earth.

💜 DOMESTIC VIOLENCE AWARENESS NIGHT | MESA, ARIZONA 💜

Last night, Missing In America Network had the honor of participating in the City of Mesa's Domestic Violence Awareness Night at The Post.
It was a privilege to stand alongside so many incredible organizations dedicated to supporting survivors of domestic violence and their families. We were especially moved by the powerful story shared by keynote speaker Crystal James, whose message of resilience, healing, and hope was truly inspiring.

💜 The connection between domestic violence and missing persons is something we see firsthand.

At Missing In America Network, we often work with families whose missing loved ones have experienced domestic violence. These situations can be incredibly complex, and families need more than awareness. They need support, guidance, and access to the right resources.
One of the most valuable parts of last night's event was connecting with organizations that specialize in domestic violence services. These new relationships will help us better support the families who turn to us during some of the most difficult moments of their lives.

text:
From the Booth to the Front Office? It Might Be Time, Troy.
Troy Aikman is going to be a free agent. The Hall of Fame quarterback said Thursday that he’ll call this season for ESPN, including the network’s first Super Bowl on February 14, 2027, and then “see what happens” about “where my next landing spot might be.”
The timing tells you a lot. Joe Buck, his partner of 25 years, signed a new six-year deal with ESPN in September. Aikman reportedly hasn’t gotten a formal offer. Front Office Sports reported that the two argued about it before last Monday’s Rams-Bills game. On Dallas radio, Aikman didn’t deny it: “I don’t know that it’s hard to figure out kind of what’s happened.”
So why not go to the front office? Aikman has openly talked about wanting to be a GM, and he’s already gotten a taste of it. This year the Dolphins brought him in as a consultant on their GM search. He sat in on interviews, was one of the biggest supporters of eventual hire Jon-Eric Sullivan, and said he’d keep working with Miami “in some capacity.” “I thoroughly enjoyed it and felt like I was of some help,” Aikman said.
He has the résumé for it. He won three Super Bowls as the Cowboys’ quarterback, and he’s spent years breaking down NFL rosters every week. He has relationships all over the league. Plenty of former players have tried to jump to running a team, but few have been as well prepared as Aikman.
TV will still want him. CBS’s top booth could be open after it parted ways with Tony Romo. At 59, though, Aikman could decide that instead of analyzing other people’s roster decisions, it’s time to make his own.
Beep! beep! Somebody hand Troy a GM job.
