text:
Levi P. Morton was America's 22nd Vice President, and he once turned down a job that would have made him President.

He was born in Vermont in 1824, the son of a minister, and never went to college. He started as a store clerk and built a successful dry goods business in New York. When the Civil War broke out in 1861, his Southern customers stopped paying their debts and the business went bankrupt. Years later, after he'd made a fortune, he paid back every creditor in full, with interest, even though he legally didn't have to.

He made that fortune in banking. His firm helped the federal government refinance its war debt and handled the massive payment Britain made to the U.S. for damage done by Confederate warships built in British shipyards.

In 1880, James Garfield's camp offered him the vice presidential nomination. Morton asked his political boss, Roscoe Conkling, who told him to say no. He did. The spot went to Chester Arthur instead. A year later Garfield was assassinated and Arthur became President.

Morton got appointed minister to France instead, and he ended up in the middle of one of the most famous projects in American history. In 1881, in a Paris workshop, he drove the first rivet into the Statue of Liberty. It went into the big toe.

He finally became Vice President under Benjamin Harrison in 1889. When Republicans tried to pass a bill protecting Black voting rights in the South, Southern Democrats filibustered it. Republicans wanted Morton to use his power in the chair to break the filibuster. He refused, saying it wasn't his place. The bill died, and Harrison dumped him from the ticket in 1892.

He went on to become governor of New York.

Then he outlived almost everyone. Morton died on May 16, 1920. It was his 96th birthday.

text:
In the end, God wins. ✝️

Everett, WA school district forced elementary kids to hide their Bibles in sealed envelopes, and now they owe $275K and a public apology.

LifeWise Academy offers voluntary, parent-permission, off-campus Bible instruction during school hours. It’s legal under decades-old Supreme Court precedent. That didn’t stop Everett Public Schools from targeting it.

- Required students to seal Bibles and materials in envelopes and stuff them in backpacks so other kids wouldn’t “be exposed” to them.

- Demanded weekly hand-delivered permission slips.

- Barred LifeWise from school fairs and flyer boards open to everyone else.

A board member openly admitted he held “animus” toward the program, calling it “homophobic bullies” pushing an “authoritarian theocracy.”

A federal judge slapped them with a preliminary injunction for viewpoint discrimination. Facing a trial, the district settled: $275,000 in legal fees, mandatory religious liberty training for the board, policy changes, and a public apology posted on the district website for six months.

This is what it looks like when activists on a school board try to drive out a Christian program that parents actually want. They lost. Religious liberty still matters in public schools, even in Washington.

2. THE CAUSES OF REBELLION
53:2.1 (602.4) Lucifer and his first assistant, Satan, had reigned on Jerusem for more than five hundred thousand years when in their hearts they began to array themselves against the Universal Father and his then vicegerent Son, Michael.

53:2.2 (602.5) There were no peculiar or special conditions in the system of Satania which suggested or favored rebellion. It is our belief that the idea took origin and form in Lucifer’s mind, and that he might have instigated such a rebellion no matter where he might have been stationed. Lucifer first announced his plans to Satan, but it required several months to corrupt the mind of his able and brilliant associate. However, when once converted to the rebel theories, he became a bold and earnest advocate of “self-assertion and liberty.”

53:2.3 (602.6) No one ever suggested rebellion to Lucifer. The idea of self-assertion in opposition to the will of Michael and to the plans of the Universal Father, as they are represented in Michael, had its origin in his own mind. His relations with the Creator Son had been intimate and always cordial. At no time prior to the exaltation of his own mind did Lucifer openly express dissatisfaction about the universe administration. Notwithstanding his silence, for more than one hundred years of standard time the Union of Days on Salvington had been reflectivating to Uversa that all was not at peace in Lucifer’s mind. This information was also communicated to the Creator Son and the Constellation Fathers of Norlatiadek.

53:2.4 (602.7) Throughout this period Lucifer became increasingly critical of the entire plan of universe administration but always professed wholehearted loyalty to the Supreme Rulers. His first outspoken disloyalty was manifested on the occasion of a visit of Gabriel to Jerusem just a few days before the open proclamation of the Lucifer Declaration of Liberty. Gabriel was so profoundly impressed with the certainty of the impending outbreak that he went direct to Edentia to confer with the Constellation Fathers regarding the measures to be employed in case of open rebellion.

53:2.5 (603.1) It is very difficult to point out the exact cause or causes which finally culminated in the Lucifer rebellion. We are certain of only one thing, and that is: Whatever these first beginnings were, they had their origin in Lucifer’s mind. There must have been a pride of self that nourished itself to the point of self-deception, so that Lucifer for a time really persuaded himself that his contemplation of rebellion was actually for the good of the system, if not of the universe. By the time his plans had developed to the point of disillusionment, no doubt he had gone too far for his original and mischief-making pride to permit him to stop. At some point in this experience he became insincere, and evil evolved into deliberate and willful sin. That this happened is proved by the subsequent conduct of this brilliant executive. He was long offered opportunity for repentance, but only some of his subordinates ever accepted the proffered mercy. The Faithful of Days of Edentia, on the request of the Constellation Fathers, in person presented the plan of Michael for the saving of these flagrant rebels, but always was the mercy of the Creator Son rejected and rejected with increasing contempt and disdain.
~Urantia Book

text:
Support and responsibility: the panel’s shared thesis.

Konstantin Kisin, Francis Foster, Winston Marshall and Tom Slater connect topics that are usually debated separately—French unrest, civic identity, neurodevelopmental diagnoses and the Cornell case—through a common institutional thesis.

They argue that institutions become unstable when they remove responsibility without replacing it with a credible framework for belonging and judgment. In France, they see weak integration and an anti-national education culture leaving young people vulnerable to competing identities. In healthcare and education, they worry that expanded support can drift into the medicalisation of ordinary difficulty. In campus discipline, they question whether protection has been separated from consistent procedures.

Their proposed response is not simply harsher punishment. Schools should teach history with context while offering a positive civic identity. Integration should involve participation in shared civic life. Mental-health services should prioritise people with substantial impairment while improving diagnostic precision. Universities should protect students through reliable, proportionate systems that distinguish coercion, incapacity, regret and consensual conduct.

That is the episode’s most coherent practical idea: compassion and accountability are not opposites. Support becomes more credible when standards are clear, and responsibility becomes more legitimate when institutions offer people a real place within a shared community.

Which institution most urgently needs to rebuild the link between support and responsibility?

What do you make of this point?

text:
TANTRA’S ANCIENT SEX RITUALS

Sexuality was never merely carnal. It was a deliberate, consecrated act of cosmic remembrance—an alchemical fire in which the dualities of form and formlessness, self and other, matter and spirit were ritually dissolved.

The ancient practitioners understood the body as a living temple and the sexual current as the most potent vehicle for awakening the coiled serpent of kundalini. Through carefully guarded rituals of maithuna (sacred union), the male principle (Shiva, pure consciousness) and the female principle (Shakti, dynamic energy) were not “used” for pleasure alone but invoked, worshipped, and consciously merged. The partners became living deities. Every breath, gaze, and touch was offered as mantra. Orgasm was not the goal; it was a gateway that could be held, transmuted, and directed upward so that the finite body might taste the infinite.

These were not casual encounters. They were liturgies performed within precise geometric yantras, under the watch of fierce protectors and benevolent wisdom deities. The left-hand path worked with the raw, unrefined energies of the body and the world; the right-hand path sublimated the same forces into pure devotion and visualization. In both, the central revelation was identical: when two become one without remainder, the ordinary mind collapses into non-dual awareness. What remains is the silent, luminous ground from which all dualities arise.

Tantra’s ancient sex rituals were therefore never about indulgence. They were technologies of liberation—dangerous, precise, and ultimately aimed at the same summit sought by every mystical tradition: the recognition that the divine has never been elsewhere. It has only ever been here, pulsing in the very flesh we so often refuse to honor.

Navratri’s most powerful window is arriving — and it lasts only 48 minutes.
This is Sandhi Kaal — the sacred transition between Ashtami ending and Navami beginning.

In 2026 it falls on Monday, 19th October from 10:27 AM to 11:15 AM.

⚔️ Why This Time Is Divine
According to tradition, this is the exact moment when Goddess Durga manifested as Maa Chamunda to destroy the demons Chanda and Munda.

That is why Sandhi Puja is performed only during these 48 minutes — the peak of divine energy in Navratri.

🪔 Simple Home Ritual During Sandhi Kaal

You do not need a temple. A sincere home puja is enough:
• Light a single diya in front of Maa Durga’s idol or photo 🪔
• Offer red flowers (lotus or hibiscus) and a red fruit 🍎🌺
• Chant the Chamunda mantra 108 times:
🕉️ ॐ ऐं ह्रीं क्लीं चामुण्डायै विच्चे॥
Om Aim Hreem Kleem Chamundayai Vicche
While chanting, pray from the heart:
“Maa, keep my entire family safe, healthy, and happy. Thank you.” 🙏

🛡️ What Maa Chamunda Protects Against
• Repeated illness in the family
• Legal troubles or court cases
• Negative energies and obstacles
Maa Chamunda removes fear and destroys barriers for her devotees.

text:
AMRISH PURI vs RAGHUVARAN: WHO WAS THE BETTER VILLAIN? 

Purely from an acting point of view, I believe Amrish Puri was miles ahead of most contemporaries.

But comparing him with Raghuvaran is fascinating, especially since both played the same character in Mudhalvan and Nayak.

Amrish Puri was much more than a villain. Remembering him only as Mogambo does injustice to his legacy.

Look at his performances in Aakrosh, Ardh Satya, Party, Arohan, Sooraj Ka Satvan Ghoda, Gardish, Ghatak and Virasat. A regular in Shyam Benegal's films, he effortlessly moved between positive, negative and comic roles. Jhooth Bole Kauwa Kaate and Chachi 420 showcased his versatility.

He was equally impressive in regional cinema. His performance in Kaalapani was menacing, and he worked across several languages, including acclaimed films like Kaadu and Shantata! Court Chalu Aahe. His international recognition through Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, where he played Mola Ram, cemented his reputation as an unforgettable antagonist.

Raghuvaran had a completely different screen presence. A handsome, charismatic actor who could have succeeded as a leading man, he showcased his dramatic abilities in films like Anjali.

As a villain, Raghuvaran often relied on intelligence, manipulation and psychological intimidation rather than physical power. He could make a character threatening without raising his voice.

Comparing them is difficult. Raghuvaran died far too young, in his 40s, while Amrish Puri began his film career in his 40s. Raghuvaran often played younger characters, while Amrish Puri was cast in more mature roles.

Their performances as the Chief Minister in Mudhalvan and its Hindi remake Nayak offer an interesting comparison. Both delivered memorable performances, though Tamil audiences often prefer Raghuvaran, while Hindi audiences favour Amrish Puri.

Personally, I found Raghuvaran's prosthetics and artificial hair in Nayak somewhat distracting. Amrish Puri seemed naturally suited to the character.

I must admit my bias. My initial exposure to Raghuvaran was through Hindi films like Rakshak and Laal Badshah, where I wasn't impressed. I felt his performance in Rakshak weakened the film's dramatic impact.

Discovering his work in South Indian cinema changed my perspective. I began to understand his immense contribution to Indian cinema.

Both actors could carry films, overshadow co-stars and command the screen with their extraordinary voices. Both appeared in commercial cinema as well as critically acclaimed films.

My pick is Amrish Puri. His range across languages, genres and character types gives him the edge.

Raghuvaran was phenomenal, and his career ended far too soon. But Amrish Puri's versatility and extraordinary body of work make him the more accomplished performer in my eyes.

Who would you choose: Amrish Puri or Raghuvaran?

text:
Hi Mariana. These books came out of several years of research. I had a particularly interesting, and in some ways tragic, conversion to Christianity. Trying to understand my own experience led me into a deep dive through Christian theology and history, then into ancient history more broadly—the Book of Enoch, Second Temple literature, Jewish history and theology, and the myths of cultures around the world.
I wanted to reintroduce people to the biblical narrative without flattening it the way the modern West has. Evangelical culture has often accepted basic supernatural events while discarding the rich story that actually illuminates the text. It’s hard to tell a young man why he should avoid gratuitous sex and easy money if you can’t show him why that avoidance matters. That lesson lands differently when it comes with a cosmology that demonstrates why righteousness matters in the grand scheme of reality.
Many modern Christian traditions have grown close to power and, as a result, have made their peace with greed and intolerance. The true calling of a Christian life reaches well beyond them.
These books were painstaking to write, and I can justify everything in the stories by the ancient works that inspired them. I offer them as $0.99 ebooks not because I think they lack value, but because I want as many people as possible to read them. If I could give them away for free on Amazon, I would. I run free promotions as often as the platform allows.
The stories work at face value, but I was careful to give them real theological weight. I worked with some excellent scholars on that. There’s another way of seeing the world and our place in it than the one modern Christian storytelling usually offers. I’m trying to reclaim that for a new generation. In a world of UAP and seemingly endless war, people need to understand how the old world saw things. It wasn’t all sin and love. It certainly was not accepting hatred of certain groups (lgbtqia, Muslims, etc) as righteous, as many Christians have in modern times. We are to seek to restore people, not turn them over to the world with a clear concious.

Big Pharma led the S&P 500 on a generally down day for the market as the three major indexes traded in the red...The rally wasn’t driven by a company-specific catalyst; rather, it was triggered by September’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) reading...The resulting risk-off sentiment sent investors piling back into healthcare. Historically, the sector has acted as a defensive haven during broader market volatility and a primary destination for anti-tech rotations—a trend that has gained traction in recent months."

In July, I published a report on "The Medical Innovation Inflection" (https://t.co/MLWyx9pR04). Since, the XLV has significantly outperformed the QQQ. I wrote the report when I did because I believed market participants were neglecting that across all three fronts of care—biomedical science, patient care, and health systems—medical innovation has been accelerating and now, AI is poised to supercharge that acceleration. I also wrote it because I believed healthcare was an AI trade risk mitigator. As I wrote at the time:

"All year, we have made an effort  to present investment convictions that can mitigate the risk of excessive concentration in the AI trade. That concern certainly played a role in why we wrote this report now. To our mind, the medical innovation inflection offers an opportunity to capitalize on AI’s potential while mitigating the risk of a sustained dip in AI sentiment. Healthcare stocks are relatively uncorrelated to tech stocks. To quote Blackrock from May: “Over the longer term, healthcare and tech have exhibited low to moderate correlation, suggesting the two can provide offsetting risk/reward characteristics in a portfolio. In recent years, as the market narrative has been dominated by the AI mega force, this correlation has hovered around its lowest in two decades.”

Big Express Entry update — effective November 3, 2026.

IRCC is refocusing CRS points on high-wage talent and Canadian work experience. 

Starting Nov 3:

•New Labour Market Integration factor awards extra points for eligible Canadian work experience or a qualifying job offer in a high-wage occupation (median wage ≥ 1.3× the national median — think engineers, electricians, many health, tech, trades, and education roles).

•Work-experience route: +20 / +40 / +70 points depending on the wage tier (on top of existing Canadian experience points).

•Job-offer route: 50 / 70 / 100 points by wage tier.

•You get the higher of the two — not both.

•LMIA no longer required for these qualifying job offers to earn the new points or meet FSW/FST job-offer eligibility. Officers still assess genuineness.

Scores for existing profiles will be recalculated automatically (draws paused for up to two weeks). 

Anyone seeking job-offer points must update their profile before November 3.

text:
Good day, Money Market!

Money went into three sleeves of the portfolio today.

Dividend Growth: Caterpillar $CAT, McDonald’s $MCD, and NextEra Energy $NEE.

Blue Ocean: Axon Enterprise $AXON, Beam Therapeutics $BEAM, BYD Company $BYDDY, Figma $FIG, Grab Holdings $GRAB, Mobileye $MBLY, Planet Labs $PL, and Ubtech Robotics $UBTRF.

Quantigence: International Business Machines $IBM, Lockheed Martin $LMT, Lowe's $LOW, Novo Nordisk $NVO, PepsiCo $PEP, RTX Corporation $RTX, and Stryker $SYK.

Each name sits under the 200-day moving average on the one-year chart, with RSI and Bollinger bands in a zone that favors dollar-cost-average accumulation. Remember, we are playing the long game. This is not a chase.

In stock talk, two separate items drove the day's topics: a launch delay at Rocket Lab $RKLB that produced an intraday swing of up to 15%, and an exit from Trulieve $TRLV after three years of flat results among multi-state cannabis operators. Rocket Lab $RKLB provides launch services for payloads smaller than those handled by SpaceX $SPCX, while the cannabis group continues to trade at low simple valuation ratios amid federal restrictions. Neither development rewrites a long-term case on its own, yet both highlight how premium or policy-sensitive names react when execution or growth stalls.

The operating machine at Rocket Lab $RKLB is booking and completing flights for customers who need capacity that's short of what the largest providers offer. The figure that frames the current price is a simple valuation ratio of 34, well above the Nanalyze Tech Stock Catalog average of roughly 8. Names carrying that kind of premium tend to react sharply to any delay or setback, and investors have grown uneasy after repeated slips. The postponement of the first Neutron launch came from a safety issue that has already been fixed, though the reusable vehicle has seen prior delays since its 2021 announcement. Space stands as the highest-risk theme under coverage, and further positive or negative items are likely in the years ahead. The delay itself does not rewrite the longer-term case, yet the elevated level leaves limited cushion for additional friction. The name remains preferred only at lower valuations. Holders are better served by filtering short-term noise and applying fixed rules for adding, cutting, or exiting, along with a cap on position size.

Cannabis coverage began roughly a decade ago, driven by sector hype rather than any claim of disruptive technology. The largest multi-state operators now show market capitalizations of $2.34 billion for Curaleaf, $1.95 billion for Trulieve $TRLV, $1.40 billion for Green Thumb, $0.38 billion for Verano, and $0.36 billion for Glass House against FY2025 revenues of $1.27 billion, $1.18 billion, $1.18 billion, $0.82 billion, and $0.18 billion. Those figures produce an average simple valuation ratio near 1.4 after years of declines. The low readings are cheap for a reason: they track stalled growth and the continued federal ban on the product in the United States. Steps toward wider legalization continue, but neither the schedule nor the final result is known. Trulieve $TRLV has posted flat revenue for three straight years while overall U.S. cannabis retail sales have also leveled off. Staying in the name solely on the chance of a legalization-driven re-rating now looks more like speculation than an investment in current operations. The stake has been closed, and a replacement will be named soon.

Under the base path for Rocket Lab $RKLB, the resolved safety item allows the Neutron schedule to move forward without major new slips, preserving the launch franchise at the current premium. Under the miss path, further delays or shortfalls in the high-risk sector compress the valuation ratio. For cannabis operators, the base case requires visible federal progress that restarts sales growth. In contrast, the miss case is prolonged flat results and legal uncertainty that keep the ratios low for structural reasons. The next test for Rocket Lab $RKLB is the actual Neutron launch date and any revised timeline. For the cannabis exit, the next test is the specific replacement name and the associated operating case.

U.S. company Shield AI has delivered its first V-BAT unmanned aerial system (UAS) to Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration (CGA).

Working with Taiwan-based partner Aerospace Industrial Development Corporation (AIDC), Shield AI plans to deliver a total of 12 V-BAT systems to the coast guard in the coming months. The CGA selected the system through its shipborne UAV program. The contract value and total number of aircraft to be acquired have not been disclosed.

The V-BAT is a Group 3 vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) UAV featuring a ducted-fan design and a heavy-fuel engine. According to Shield AI, it offers more than 12 hours of endurance and is designed to operate in contested electronic-warfare environments.

The CGA plans to use the system for ship-based maritime surveillance, coastal patrols and law-enforcement operations, providing intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities across the Taiwan Strait and surrounding maritime areas.

Shield AI and AIDC will also provide training for coast guard operators and maintenance personnel and establish local support capabilities in Taiwan.

text:
Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access is not an attempt to challenge Eritrea’s sovereignty or lay claim to its territory. It is a matter of Ethiopia’s legitimate national interest and strategic necessity, one that can be addressed through peaceful negotiations and mutually beneficial arrangements.
When Ethiopia reached an agreement with Somaliland to secure access to the sea, Eritrea opposed it. Its position on Red Sea affairs, including its insistence that governance of the Red Sea should be restricted to coastal states, raises a fundamental question: On what principle does Eritrea oppose Ethiopia’s legitimate aspiration to secure sea access?
If Eritrea’s position offers no viable alternative for Ethiopia and instead focuses on preventing Ethiopia from securing access to the sea through peaceful means, such a stance contradicts the principles of good neighbourliness, regional cooperation, and shared development.
Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access should not be treated as a justification for territorial conflict with Eritrea. However, just as Eritrea expects its own sovereignty to be respected, it must also refrain from policies that undermine Ethiopia’s legitimate national interests. The future stability of the region will not be secured by one country denying another its legitimate interests, but by pursuing solutions through dialogue, mutual understanding, and mutually beneficial cooperation.

The pattern groups into three document types — **11 invoices**, **12 ledger entries**, and **11 checks** — all allegedly falsified to disguise reimbursements to Michael Cohen as legal fees, concealing the underlying hush-money payment to Stormy Daniels.
The records were falsified for two interlocking reasons:
**What made them false:** The reimbursements Trump made to Michael Cohen were recorded in Trump Organization books as "legal expenses" under a retainer agreement. Prosecutors proved that **no such retainer agreement existed** and Cohen was not being paid for legal services in 2017. The true purpose of the payments was to reimburse Cohen for the $130,000 he had paid Stormy Daniels to buy her silence about an alleged sexual encounter shortly before the 2016 election.
**Why it mattered legally (felony vs. misdemeanor):** Under New York Penal Law § 175.10, falsifying business records is only a **felony** when the falsification is done with "intent to commit another crime or to aid or conceal the commission thereof." Prosecutors argued the records were falsified specifically to **conceal a violation of New York election law** (Penal Law § 215.00), which criminalizes promoting a candidate's election through "unlawful means." By disguising the hush-money reimbursement as legal fees, the scheme was designed to keep the payment hidden from voters and to prevent it from being disclosed as a campaign-related expenditure.
In short: the records were falsified to make a covert political payoff look like a routine legal bill, thereby concealing what prosecutors characterized as an attempt to unlawfully influence the 2016 election.
I need to correct my earlier answer: the specific statute was **New York Election Law § 17-152**, not Penal Law § 215.00.
## The Statute
**N.Y. Election Law § 17-152** — *Conspiracy to promote or prevent election*:
> "Any two or more persons who conspire to promote or prevent the election of any person to a public office by **unlawful means** and which conspiracy is acted upon by one or more of the parties thereto, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor."
It's a misdemeanor on its own, but it served as the "underlying crime" that elevated falsifying business records from a misdemeanor to a **Class E felony**.
## The Three "Unlawful Means" Theories
Prosecutors offered the jury three possible "unlawful means" that the conspiracy used to promote Trump's election. The jury was instructed that it **did not need to agree** on which one(s) applied:
| # | Unlawful Means | Theory |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Federal campaign finance violation** (FECA) | The $130,000 payment to Daniels constituted an undisclosed campaign contribution exceeding the federal cap on individual contributions. |
| 2 | **Falsification of bank records** | The reimbursement checks and trust records were false entries in banking/financial records. |
| 3 | **Tax law violation** | Mischaracterizing the hush-money reimbursements as "legal fees" on tax returns constituted a tax fraud. |
## Why It Mattered Structurally
The legal chain was:
1. **Falsifying business records** (Penal Law § 175.10) — normally a misdemeanor
2. …done with **intent to commit or conceal another crime** — elevates it to a felony
3. That "other crime" = **Election Law § 17-152** (conspiracy to promote election by unlawful means)
4. The "unlawful means" = one of the three theories above
This nesting was the central legal controversy of the case. Critics called it a "twisty" theory, and the law was described as having never before been used in a prosecution. Two judges (Merchan and Hellerstein) upheld its use before and during trial.
Essentially no. The statute has been on the books since at least the mid-1970s, but it has virtually never been prosecuted:
- **Two prior charges, both dropped.** In 2011, Aron Wieder (vice president of the East Ramapo school board) was charged under § 17-152 for assisting voters who had been told they couldn't bring baby strollers inside a polling place. The same year, Clement Campana (former city council president in Troy, N.Y.) was charged with both a felony count of falsifying business records **and** a misdemeanor count of election conspiracy under § 17-152 in connection with a mayoral bid. Both cases were dropped before trial.
- **No successful prosecutions.** Multiple election law experts — including a former state senator with 53 years of election law practice and two law professors — stated they could not recall the statute ever being used in a successful prosecution.
- **First use as an "object offense."** The Trump case was the first time § 17-152 was used specifically as the underlying crime to elevate falsifying business records from a misdemeanor to a felony, and the first time it went to a full trial.
So while the statute technically has two prior (dropped) charges, the specific legal architecture prosecutors used — nesting § 17-152 as the predicate for felony falsification, with three alternative "unlawful means" theories — was entirely novel.

text:
East Arkansas Paramedic
·  
Only in EMS can a man be so sick he can barely suck air, still have enough wind to cuss you, bump his chest into you three times, roll hisself down a hill, then holler you assaulted him.
Had a patient get riled up with me the other day.

Now this fella was sick. Weak. Breathing hard as a bellows with a hole in it. I honestly figured getting that worked up might kill him before whatever was already wrong with him got around to it.
But he was bound and determined to get in my face.
Puffed up. Started bumping me in the chest.
I just stood there.
Wasn’t standing there trying to prove I was some kinda tough guy. From where I was standing, he barely had enough in him to stay on his feet, much less hurt anybody. I was more worried he was fixin’ to wear hisself slap out.
First bump.
Second bump.
Third bump, he stumbled backward and went rollin’ down the hill.
Then he started hollerin’.
“You assaulted me!”
I looked at him.
You have GOT to be kiddin’ me.
“I never laid a hand on you! You walked up here and got in my face.”
“You pushed me! You assaulted me!”
Apparently, standin’ still had turned into a contact sport.
I offered to call the police. Reminded him who walked up and started puttin’ his chest into who.
He told me to go fuck myself.
Well, we sure weren’t makin’ much headway with the therapeutic relationship.
Then, before we could get him loaded up or get much of anything done, he just got up and walked off.
Sick as a dog. Bent on fightin’. Rolled down a hill. Accused me of assault. Then walked off like he had somewhere else to be.
The part that bothered me was watchin’ a man who needed help spend what little energy he had tryin’ to start somethin’ with the person there to help him.
I wasn’t worried about losin’ a fight. I was worried he was gonna make hisself worse.
And that puts an EMS crew in a hell of a spot.
You’re tryin’ to figure out what’s wrong, what needs doin’, and how to get somebody cared for. Meanwhile, they’ve decided you’re the enemy, and now you’ve got to work around that, too.
I can tell this particular story with some dry humor because of how ridiculous it was. But I don’t want the point gettin’ lost just because this fella was too weak to do much.
Paramedics and EMTs ought to be able to help people without gettin’ threatened, shoved, hit, or spit on.
Being able to tolerate somethin’ don’t make it acceptable.
And before somebody says, “Well, they’re sick,” I know. I was standin’ there lookin’ at him.
Sick people need care. Sometimes they’re scared or confused. Sometimes there’s more goin’ on than we can understand right then. We’ve got to use judgment.
But “use your judgment” ought to mean the service trusts you to look at the situation and backs you when you need help.
It shouldn’t mean, “Handle whatever happens, and please don’t generate any paperwork.”
Lord knows an ambulance service can survive three busted recliners and a coffee pot growin’ its own ecosystem. Somehow, an incident report is what brings the whole operation to its knees.
This encounter didn’t scare me. It aggravated me. I wanted to help the man, and he was makin’ that harder on both of us.
The next crew’s encounter may be a whole different deal. We need to listen when they tell us that.
EMS folks, how do y’all handle somebody who needs your help but is bound and determined to fight you over givin’ it? Non-EMS folks, you ever had somebody take their worst day out on you while you was tryin’ to help?
Share this with your crew, and follow East Arkansas Paramedic. I know I ain’t the only one who’s come back with a story like this.
Some days, gettin’ folks to let you help ’em will flat wear you out.
-- East Arkansas Paramedic

1SG 🫡 WOGBTC EVENING ORDER — October 16, 2026
TSE Training • KNOWN BY THE FATHER—FREE TO STAND

1 — THE ORDER

“Do not fear therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows.”
— Luke 12:7, NKJV

Morning’s promise: Known, valued, and remembered.
Tonight’s training: Let the Father’s care give you courage to obey.

Battle Line: My Father knows me completely; I will trust His care and obey His Son.

Read Luke 12:1–12. Jesus gives this assurance while preparing His disciples for opposition. He knows they will face pressure, rejection, and danger.

The Father’s care remains true through those circumstances. Difficulty does not mean you have been forgotten.

2 — THE TRAINING

Warrior Doctrine — Being known by God frees you to live honestly and faithfully.

A. KNOWN: Bring your actual concern to Him.

Jesus begins this passage by warning against hypocrisy. The Father who numbers your hairs also knows what troubles your heart.

You can pray plainly: “Father, this is what I fear. Help me obey You here.”

Honest prayer puts your concern before the One who already understands it.

B. VALUED: You can withstand human disapproval.

In Luke 12:8–9, Jesus speaks about acknowledging Him before others. The Father’s care gives His disciples courage to identify with Christ when doing so becomes costly.

Your assignment is to speak truth with humility, respond patiently, and remain faithful to Jesus. Another person’s reaction does not determine your worth before God.

C. REMEMBERED: His care continues during hardship.

Jesus prepares His followers for hostile questioning in verses 11–12 and promises the Holy Spirit’s help in that setting.

God’s care does not guarantee that obedience will feel comfortable. It gives you reason to trust Him while you obey.

D. LOVED: The cross gives your trust a firm foundation.

Romans 8:32 points to the Father giving His own Son as grounds for confidence in His gracious purpose.

That connects with today’s discussion about Jesus’ blood: His completed sacrifice gives you access to God. Hebrews 4:14–16 calls us to approach the throne of grace through our great High Priest, seeking mercy and help.

You are welcome to bring your need to Him.

Armor Fit

Belt of truth: Separate what happened from what you fear might happen.
Breastplate of righteousness: Choose the response that honors Christ.
Shield of faith: Answer “God has forgotten me” with Luke 12:6–7.
Helmet of salvation: Remember the hope secured by your Savior.
Sword of the Spirit: Read the whole passage before applying the promise.
Boots of peace: Take your next step with gentleness and courage.

Train the Trainer

Ask someone: “What was Jesus preparing His disciples to face—and how would knowing the Father cared help them?”

Teach this principle: God’s care strengthens faithful witness, including when obedience costs us.

3 — THE EXECUTION

Commander’s Orders — One Concern, One Prayer, One Step

Before bed:

Read Luke 12:1–12 slowly.
Write: “Father, my concern is ______.”
Write: “Your Word reminds me ______.”
Write: “By tomorrow evening, I will ______.”

Choose one specific action within your responsibility: make a needed call, offer an apology, complete a neglected task, or check on someone who may feel overlooked.

Mission standard: Complete that action by tomorrow evening. Record what you learned about responding faithfully.

Prayer of Deployment

Father, You know me completely, and You have not forgotten me. Thank You for giving Your Son and welcoming me through Him. Bring my fears into the light of Your truth. Help me receive Your care, acknowledge Jesus with courage, and treat others with patience. By Your Spirit, lead me in the next faithful step. I entrust what I cannot control to You. In Jesus’ name, amen.

Evening Review: Where did fear influence my response today? What faithful step will I take tomorrow?

TRAIN • STAND • EXECUTE

Ryan McBeth’s geopolitical argument does not depend on Russian shipments solving America’s diesel problem. The reported volumes would cover only a temporary share of the estimated U.S. shortfall. In his reading, however, even a limited offer could connect Ukrainian refinery attacks, fuel prices, and U.S. policy.

Trump may favor additional Russian supply because lower global diesel prices could have domestic political value before the midterm elections. Putin, meanwhile, may be pursuing a broader objective: pressuring Washington to reduce support for Ukraine, particularly if Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries continue.

That pressure could involve encouraging Trump to restrain Ukraine or potentially limit intelligence sharing. Russia could present diesel exports as a path to price relief while encouraging the United States to view Ukrainian operations as an economic liability.

This would make the fuel a bargaining instrument rather than simply a commodity. The proposal could serve both sides’ immediate interests: Trump could seek lower prices, while Putin could seek a change in U.S. policy toward Ukraine. McBeth emphasizes that this is an inference, not confirmed evidence.

The theory would weaken if deliveries fail to materialize, remain too small to influence prices, or occur without any corresponding policy change. The key test is whether the offer leads to pressure on Ukraine, limits on intelligence sharing, or another shift in Washington’s position.

text:
Patty Murray’s post quotes the Seattle Times item but does not engage its specific content. The Seattle Times post states a factual detail: three of the five initial experts on her Public Health for America Working Group are from Washington state. Her reply ignores that detail entirely and instead offers a general assertion that public health is as important as national defense, must be “trusted and grounded in science,” and that she is building something “that can’t be broken again” after Trump and RFK Jr. “broke” it.

This is a common rhetorical pattern rather than a direct response. Quote-tweeting media coverage lets her amplify her preferred framing (the need for a more resilient, “politics-proof” system) while sidestepping the concrete point the article highlighted about the group’s composition. The underlying Seattle Times piece is largely descriptive of her initiative and the experts’ backgrounds; it does not strongly criticize the Washington-heavy makeup, but the headline/post isolates that fact, which she does not address.

Her language relies on loaded premises and elevation without engagement. Asserting that Trump and RFK Jr. “broke” public health functions as an unargued premise in the post itself. Comparing public health to national defense is an appeal that raises its priority rhetorically but does not examine trade-offs, evidence of prior system performance, or the specific geographic concentration in her working group. The net effect is deflection: the quoted article’s detail is treated as a prompt for a broader narrative rather than something requiring a response.

text:
HOUSTON WE HAVE A FCKGN PROBLEM 

THE GREAT BANKING TRICK
YOU PROVIDE THE SIGNATURE; WE PROVIDE THE NUMBERS

I. THE MANAGERIAL PIGGY BANK

As a child, I was told: “The bank keeps your savings and lends them to someone who wants to produce something.”

How beautiful! A community piggy bank with air conditioning.

Then I discovered that the explanation was about as complete as the instructions for assembling furniture: the important pieces were missing, and there was an extra guy charging me.

II. LET THERE BE MONEY

When a bank grants a loan, it typically creates a deposit in your account and records your debt as one of its assets.

New numbers appear!

I write one hundred thousand dollars on a napkin, and the waiter calls security. The bank writes it on a screen and offers me a mortgage.

Of course, it has capital, liquidity, regulatory, and risk requirements. It cannot create unlimited amounts of money. Even magic needs accounting… and a department that calls you during lunch.

III. YOUR MONEY IS HERE… ACCOUNTING-WISE

Your balance does not mean there is a little box containing your bills, your name, and a red ribbon.

It is an obligation the bank has to you: it owes you that amount.

You walked in thinking you were renting a vault and walked out as a creditor of a corporation.

Congratulations! You have been promoted to financier without an interview, without a desk, and while paying maintenance fees.

IV. THE MIRACULOUS SIGNATURE

You sign the contract and, when applicable, a promissory note documenting your commitment to repay the money.

That does not mean every signature creates wealth or that the loan is a secret sale of your autograph.

But admit it: the show is impressive.

They record the loan in seconds. You need twenty years, two jobs, and a new knee to pay it off.

How efficient technology becomes when someone else is responsible for the obligation!

V. THE FINAL DISAPPEARANCE

When you repay the principal, that bank-created money is extinguished. Interest is a separate matter.

Wonderful! The money enters through an accounting entry and leaves after you have hauled boxes, sold empanadas, or endured meetings that could have been an email.

The number disappears. Your back pain keeps every decimal place.

VI. TRUST, WITH FEES

A large share of modern money consists of bank deposits. The proportion depends on the country and on how it is measured.

The mechanism is legal. What is extraordinary is that we live with it without almost anyone explaining it clearly.

For a toaster, they give you forty pages of warnings. To put you in debt for thirty years, they give you a smile and a pen attached to a chain.

Because they can trust you with a half-million-dollar mortgage…

BUT THE PEN STAYS!

NOTHING CAN STOP WHAT IS COMING.

Except, apparently, a calendar. Why Houston? 

The problem isn't just the problem. The problem is nobody put a FCKNG DATE on it.

text:
❤️🧸 “DADDY, IF I FALL ASLEEP, WILL YOU WAKE ME WHEN IT'S MY TURN?”

Andrew stopped typing and listened.

His six-year-old daughter stood beside his desk in her pyjamas. She held a tiny pink teacup in both hands, and one sleeve had slipped over her fingers.

“Your turn for what, sweetheart?”

“To play with you.”

He glanced at the clock. Nearly eight. He had told her he would come downstairs after dinner. That had been almost an hour ago.

“Just ten more minutes, Grace.”

She nodded and leaned against the doorframe.

“That's why I'm asking. Sometimes your ten minutes takes until I'm asleep.”

There was no anger in her voice. She was explaining a problem she hoped he could help her solve.

Andrew looked past her into the living room. The little table was set. Rosie, her pink teddy bear, occupied one chair. Another had been pulled out for him.

On it sat a cushion from the sofa.

“What's the cushion for?”

“Your back. You said that chair hurt your back.”

He couldn't remember saying it.

Grace had remembered. She had found a way to make him comfortable, poured his imaginary tea, and waited while it grew dark outside.

“I thought you could stay longer if it didn't hurt.”

Andrew put his hands in his lap.

He had spent the evening adjusting a website he was afraid to show anyone. In the next room, his daughter had been adjusting a chair so he would want to stay.

“You don't have to wait until you're asleep,” he said.

She looked at the laptop.

“But you haven't finished.”

He saved the page, closed the screen, and stood.

“I've finished for tonight.”

Grace searched his face before offering him her hand.

“Really?”

“Really. Show me my seat.”

She took him down the hallway, calling ahead to her bear.

“Rosie! You can pour it now!”

🐾

Seven months earlier, Andrew had come home with an idea he could hardly wait to tell his wife.

He was forty-one, worked full-time, and had begun measuring too many weeks by what remained in the bank after the bills came out. Their home was comfortable, but every unexpected expense seemed to arrive carrying another one behind it.

A car repair. A school trip. A washing machine that had started making a noise neither of them wanted to investigate.

Andrew and Hannah managed. They talked things through at the kitchen table and found ways to stretch what they had. Yet Andrew carried an old fear that managing could become struggling very quickly.

He remembered his own parents lowering their voices when money was discussed. He remembered saying he didn't want to go on a trip because he had overheard what it cost. He wanted his children to feel secure asking for ordinary things.

Their son, Ethan, was nine. He loved football, building things from cardboard, and explaining facts he had learned at school with the authority of a university lecturer.

Grace was six. She carried a teddy bear called Rosie through most of the house and believed a biscuit tasted better if everyone at the table had one.

Andrew loved the noise they made. He loved hearing them argue about whose turn it was to choose a film. He even loved the shoes in the hallway, though he complained about them whenever he tripped.

He wanted to protect that life.

So when he began learning how to build websites for small businesses, he saw a possibility. He could work on something of his own, earn additional income, and perhaps eventually reduce the hours he spent in a job that left him exhausted.

“Imagine being able to pick them up from school,” he told Hannah. “Without having to ask someone for permission every time.”

Hannah smiled. “That would be lovely.”

“And we could take a holiday without spending the whole journey worrying about what we'd spent.”

She reached across the table and squeezed his hand.

“Let's work out how to give it a proper chance.”

They made a small budget. They agreed he would study in the evenings. Andrew bought a notebook and wrote down what he hoped the business could make possible.

Near the top, above the figures and the practical goals, he wrote: MORE TIME WITH THE FAMILY.

At first, that sentence helped him keep going.

Later, he stopped seeing it.

💻

There was so much to learn that Andrew struggled to decide where learning should end and doing should begin.

One lesson explained how to choose a niche. Another warned against choosing too quickly. Someone recommended a particular website builder; someone else said serious businesses needed something entirely different.

Andrew took notes on all of it.

He watched tutorials after the children were asleep. He listened to interviews during his lunch break. He collected examples of successful websites and saved articles he intended to read when he had time.

His folders became organised. His bookmarks became extensive. His confidence rose after a good lesson and fell whenever he discovered another thing he hadn't considered.

He built a website for his own service, then rebuilt it after seeing one he liked more. He changed his prices before anyone had asked what they were. He wrote an introduction so many times that Hannah could recognise the opening sentence from across the room.

“I think that version sounds like you,” she said one evening.

Andrew frowned at the screen. “Do you think it sounds professional enough?”

“I think someone could understand what you're offering.”

He read it again, still uncertain.

He cared about doing good work. He also feared finding out that he couldn't.

While the offer stayed on his screen, he could keep improving it. Sending it to a real person meant giving someone the chance to say no.

He knew rejection would happen. Knowing that didn't make the first message easier to send.

So he found another lesson.

Another checklist.

Another reason to begin on Monday.

The work gradually spread beyond the time he and Hannah had planned for it. A lesson ran late. An evening became a Saturday morning. A quick change to the website followed him into Sunday afternoon.

Andrew always believed he was close to finishing.

The family began hearing that belief in different forms.

“Nearly done.”

“Just this last bit.”

“Once I've sorted this, things will be easier.”

🧸

Grace's tea parties usually began after dinner.

She put Rosie in one chair and a smaller rabbit in another. Ethan occasionally joined, provided he was allowed to give his character an elaborate name and a suspicious accent.

There were rules. Everyone received a cup. The teapot had to go around twice. Rosie needed help holding hers because, as Grace explained patiently, she had paws.

Andrew used to pretend the tea was too hot. Grace would tell him to blow on it, then collapse into laughter when he blew hard enough to knock over a plastic spoon.

Sometimes he arrived wearing an imaginary hat and asked whether the restaurant accepted very important visitors.

Grace always answered, “Only if they're polite.”

As work filled more evenings, she began carrying his invitation into the little room where he kept his computer.

“Your tea is ready, Daddy.”

Andrew would smile. “Bring me a cup, sweetheart.”

“You have to sit at the table.”

“In a minute, then.”

She trusted that answer at first. She went back to arrange the spoons, straighten Rosie's dress, and explain to Ethan that Daddy would be coming soon.

Sometimes he did come. Those evenings kept her asking.

Sometimes the tea party ended with his chair empty.

Hannah would help put the cups away, and Grace would carry the cushion back to the sofa without saying much.

Andrew usually found out later, when he stepped into a tidy living room and asked whether the children were already in bed.

He felt disappointed with himself. Then he tried to finish more quickly the following evening, and the same pattern returned.

Ethan adapted differently.

He stopped asking Andrew to inspect every cardboard invention and began leaving them outside the office door. A bridge. A football stadium. A vehicle with bottle-top wheels that didn't quite turn.

Andrew admired them on his way to bed.

He often meant to ask Ethan how he had made them. By breakfast, everyone was looking for school shoes, and the question slipped away.

One morning, Ethan carried a model towards the recycling bin.

“You're throwing that out?” Andrew asked. “I thought it was brilliant.”

Ethan paused. “You saw it?”

“Of course.”

“Oh.” His son looked down at the model. “I thought you hadn't.”

Andrew wished he had said something sooner.

🏠

Hannah noticed the changes before Andrew understood them.

She saw Grace pause outside the office, listening for the sound of a call. She heard Ethan say, “Daddy's working,” when a friend asked whether his father could help set up the goal in the garden.

She also saw Andrew trying.

She knew he was tired. She knew the figures on the kitchen table frightened him. She had watched him fall asleep with a course still playing and wake with an apology already on his lips.

One evening, after the children were asleep, she brought two mugs into the kitchen.

“Can we talk about our evenings?” she asked.

Andrew rubbed his eyes. “Have I missed something?”

“I miss you.”

He looked at her then.

She sat opposite him. “I know you're here in the house. I know why you're working. But I feel as though we're all waiting for the moment when you can finally stop.”

“I'm trying to get us out of worrying about money all the time.”

“I know. I'm worried too.”

There was no accusation in her voice. That made it easier for him to listen.

“I want this business to work,” she continued. “And I need us to talk about how much time we're giving it, and what it's actually moving us towards.”

Andrew stared into his tea.

“You think I'm wasting my time.”

“I think you're frightened of getting it wrong.”

He didn't answer immediately.

Hannah waited.

Eventually, he said, “What if I put everything into it and nobody wants what I make?”

“Then we'll know something we don't know today,” she said. “And we can decide what to do with that information.”

Andrew nodded, though the fear remained.

Before they went upstairs, Hannah touched his arm.

“The children still want to show you everything. I hope we can make a little more room for that.”

He promised they would.

He meant it.

🌙

That Thursday, Andrew came home determined to finish one particular lesson and then spend the evening with the children.

After dinner, Grace appeared with the pink teacup.

He told her ten minutes.

Then the lesson mentioned a setting he hadn't checked. He opened his website. A message appeared. He answered it. One change led to another, and the time he had promised disappeared into the time he hadn't noticed.

Until Grace stood beside his desk asking whether he would wake her when it was her turn.

Until he realised she was trying to stay awake for time he kept promising her.

Until he saw that she had remembered his aching back and saved him the comfortable seat.

When he finally took her hand, Grace led him down the hallway as though he might need directions to a place she knew by heart.

“Rosie! He's coming!”

Hannah looked up from the sofa.

Andrew met her eyes. “Apparently, I've kept everyone waiting for their tea.”

Grace pulled out his chair. “You're next to Rosie. She likes you.”

He lowered himself carefully onto the little cushion.

“That's a relief. I was hoping we were still friends.”

Grace placed a cup in his hands. “You have to ask her how she's been.”

Andrew turned solemnly towards the bear.

“How have you been, Rosie?”

Grace answered in a very small voice. “I've been quite busy.”

Hannah smiled into her mug.

Andrew nodded. “I understand. Me too.”

“But I have time for tea,” the small voice added.

He looked at his daughter.

She was concentrating on pouring from an empty teapot, entirely absorbed in making sure he received enough.

“I'm glad,” he said quietly. “So do I.”

For the next fifteen minutes, Andrew drank imaginary tea, accepted an invisible cake, and listened to an account of Rosie's difficult day at work.

Grace laughed when he tried to eat the cake with a spoon that was apparently reserved for sugar.

Ethan appeared in the doorway, watched for a moment, then asked whether the restaurant needed a waiter.

Within minutes, he was carrying a tea towel over one arm and announcing that the kitchen had run out of everything except biscuits.

The house filled with the ordinary noise Andrew had missed while sitting only a few steps away.

❤️

At bedtime, Andrew helped Grace put the cups into their box.

She handed him the cushion.

“You can leave it there if you want.”

“Would you like another tea party?”

“Yes. But you don't have to promise tomorrow if you can't.”

Andrew crouched beside her.

“You're right,” he said. “I have been promising things and then keeping you waiting. I'm sorry.”

Grace rubbed a finger along the edge of the box.

“I thought perhaps tea parties were a bit boring for grown-ups.”

He felt the sting of that, but he kept his voice gentle.

“I like being with you. I've been having trouble stopping my work when I say I will. That's something for me to sort out.”

She looked up. “I can help you close the computer.”

He smiled. “You can remind me sometimes. But it's my job to remember too.”

He didn't ask her to tell him everything was all right. He helped carry the box upstairs, listened while she chose a story, and stayed when she wanted to explain why the rabbit in the picture looked worried.

As he turned out the light, she called him back.

“Daddy?”

“Yes?”

“Rosie says thank you for coming.”

Andrew kissed her forehead.

“Tell her I had a lovely time.”

Downstairs, Hannah had left the lamp on.

Andrew sat beside her and let out a long breath.

“I don't want tonight to become another thing I do once and then talk about for months,” he said.

Hannah leaned against his shoulder.

“Then let's make a plan we can actually live with.”

📝

They talked for an hour.

There were no grand promises about never working late again. Andrew still had a job. Hannah still had her own responsibilities. The bills would arrive whether or not they had enjoyed a lovely evening.

They needed a schedule that could survive an ordinary difficult week.

They looked at the calendar together and chose specific evenings for business work. On other evenings, the laptop would stay closed until the children were asleep, or remain closed altogether.

They protected dinner where their working hours allowed it. They agreed that an unexpected busy period needed a conversation, rather than an assumption that Hannah would quietly manage everything.

Andrew asked what time she needed for herself too.

Hannah looked relieved by the question.

They made room for that on the calendar.

For the business, Andrew wrote three tasks for the following week: speak to potential customers, listen carefully, and make one clear offer he could deliver well.

He put the longer list of website improvements into a separate folder.

Then he opened the notebook to the first page and moved the sentence about family time somewhere he would see it every day.

The following morning, he sent his first message before he could find another reason to rewrite it.

It was polite, brief, and specific. He had noticed a practical problem on a local business website and asked whether the owner would be interested in discussing it.

After sending it, he stared at the screen.

Nothing happened.

No immediate reply. No sudden proof that he had chosen the right path.

He sent a second message, then a third.

At his scheduled stopping time, he wrote down what he would do next and closed the computer.

The uncertainty came with him into the living room.

So did he.

🌱

The changes were smaller and less tidy than Andrew had imagined.

He still reached for his phone when a notification sounded. Sometimes he caught himself thinking about a customer while Ethan was speaking. Occasionally, he needed a reminder that dinner was ready.

He began leaving the phone on a shelf during the time they had set aside together.

When his mind wandered, he tried to come back honestly.

“Sorry, I missed that last part. Tell me again.”

Ethan usually did, especially if the subject involved how a goalkeeper should stand during a penalty.

One Saturday, Andrew asked to see the cardboard stadium that had almost gone into the recycling.

Ethan fetched it from behind his wardrobe.

“I kept it,” he said, sounding a little embarrassed.

Andrew sat at the kitchen table while his son explained the tunnel, the stands, and the ingenious but unreliable roof.

“What's this part?” Andrew asked.

“Where the commentators sit.”

“They've got a good view.”

Ethan nodded, then began telling him how he had worked out the angle.

Andrew listened long enough to hear the explanation become more confident. They found some spare cardboard, adjusted the roof, and spent twenty minutes making it slightly less likely to fall on the imaginary crowd.

Later, Ethan asked whether they could try building floodlights.

“We can work out what we'd need,” Andrew said. “Let's write it down together.”

He was learning that his son needed invitations too. Ethan's requests had simply become easier to miss because they arrived more quietly.

Grace continued setting out the cups, but she checked the calendar now.

“Is this a computer evening?”

If it was, Andrew told her when he would be available and avoided promising a game he couldn't fit in. If it wasn't, she knew where to put his cushion.

Trust returned through those ordinary answers, followed by ordinary evenings when he did what he had said.

🌧️

There were difficult evenings as well.

One potential customer arranged a call at the only time they could manage it, during the hour Andrew had planned to spend with the children.

The old version of him would have accepted immediately and explained later.

This time, he asked whether another time was possible. When it wasn't, he spoke with Hannah before confirming.

They adjusted the evening together. Andrew told the children what was happening and gave them a specific time for the activity they would miss.

Grace looked disappointed.

He let her be disappointed without asking her to feel excited about a business call.

“I wanted you tonight,” she said.

“I know. I'm sorry we have to change it.”

He sat with her for a few minutes before going to work. The following afternoon, he kept the new arrangement.

Another week, the car repair cost more than expected. Andrew lay awake calculating figures he had already calculated twice.

He wanted to open the laptop and work until he felt less afraid.

Instead, he told Hannah what was happening in his head.

They looked at the figures together in the morning. The problem remained difficult, but it became something they could discuss in daylight.

Andrew was beginning to recognise how often worry dressed itself up as one more urgent task.

He still needed to earn money. He also needed sleep, clear decisions, and people he could speak to when he was frightened.

Some nights, the most useful thing he did for the next working day was go to bed.

📩

Three weeks after the tea party, a business owner replied to one of Andrew's messages.

They had a small project. Their existing website made it difficult for customers to find basic information, and updating it had become a source of frustration.

Andrew arranged a conversation, asked questions, and listened without trying to prove how much he knew.

He heard what mattered to them: clear information, a simple enquiry process, and someone who would answer when they needed help.

He prepared a modest proposal. He described what he could deliver, what it would cost, and how long he expected it to take. Where he needed clarification, he asked for it.

When the acceptance arrived, he read the email three times.

His first customer.

He stood in the kitchen with the phone in his hand, smiling before he had managed to tell Hannah why.

She read the message and hugged him.

“You did it.”

“I've got to do the work now,” he said, laughing nervously.

“Yes,” she replied. “And you've given yourself something real to work on.”

The payment would help. It would not solve every financial concern, and Andrew knew that. He had expenses to account for, work to complete, and a customer whose trust he needed to earn.

Still, something had changed.

For months, he had been imagining what somebody might need. Now he had a person to listen to and a clear piece of work to finish.

He broke the project into stages and put them on the calendar.

Alongside them were dinner, Ethan's match, and a small drawing of a teacup Grace had added to Saturday afternoon.

He left the drawing where it was.

He soon began putting small appointments with the children in his diary. They looked unremarkable beside meetings and deadlines, but he was learning to give them the same careful attention.

🌷

If you are reading this after a long shift, during a brief break, or beside a pile of work you cannot simply put aside, I hope you hear some kindness in it.

Providing for a family can be exhausting. Financial pressure is real. Some parents work hours they would change immediately if they could. Some are studying, caring for relatives, travelling for work, or raising children without the support they need.

Love exists in those efforts too.

A packed lunch prepared before sunrise. A bill paid after a difficult month. A tired parent remembering which school shirt needs washing. A voice message sent across a time zone so a child can hear a familiar goodnight.

Children receive care in many forms. No family has the same amount of time, money, flexibility, or help.

Andrew's story offers a question you can consider within your own circumstances: where is there a small, realistic space for connection that you might be able to protect?

Perhaps it is the walk from the car to the front door. Perhaps it is a few minutes before bed, a conversation over breakfast, or a regular call when working away.

It might mean asking your child to show you the game they keep talking about. Listening to the explanation of a drawing. Remembering to ask how something important turned out.

Sometimes it means telling them honestly when you are available, then keeping that small appointment as carefully as you can.

And when plans change, you can explain. You can apologise. You can choose another time and try again.

You are allowed to be a loving parent who gets tired. You are allowed to need rest and help. Your children can know that work matters, that responsibilities exist, and that they have a place in your life alongside them.

If the distance between you has grown, a conversation may be a beginning.

“I've missed spending time with you.”

“What have you been wanting to show me?”

“When can we do something together?”

Leave room for their answer. An older child may need time before accepting an invitation. A younger one may arrive immediately with a toy. Either response deserves patience.

There is no need to make the moment impressive. A familiar activity, repeated with care, can give you both somewhere comfortable to meet.

🧸

One night, as Andrew helped Grace tidy the living room, she handed him the cushion again.

“Shall I put this on the sofa?” he asked.

She considered it.

“Leave it on your chair.”

“My chair?”

She pointed towards the little table.

“That one. Next to Rosie.”

Andrew looked at the place she had kept for him through so many evenings.

He straightened the cushion and tucked the chair beneath the table.

“All ready, then.”

Grace took his hand on the way upstairs.

“I like it when you come,” she said.

He squeezed her hand gently.

“I like it too, sweetheart.”

There were still things he wanted to build. There were still bills to pay, lessons to learn, and mornings when he woke worried about how everything would work out.

But when Grace looked for him at her little table, she was beginning to expect that he would be there.

And Andrew was beginning to understand how much it meant to have a place someone was happy to save for him.

💬 What is one ordinary moment with your family that you still remember clearly?

Perhaps someone walked you to school, sat through a game, listened while you talked, or made a familiar meal after a difficult day. Perhaps your memory is of a parent who worked long hours and still found a small way to let you know you mattered.

You are welcome to share that memory here. It may give another family a simple idea they can make their own.

And if you know someone carrying the pressure of providing, consider sending this with a few words of encouragement. Tell them you see their effort. Ask how they are doing. Offer something practical if you can.

Sometimes the person who needs an invitation to sit down is the parent who has spent all day making sure everyone else has what they need.

Save them a comfortable seat too. ❤️🧸

text:
I’ve barely been trading lately.

Lost a shit ton of money over the past few months, and honestly, I needed to take a step back and ask myself what the fuck I’m even doing here anymore.

I’ve been in crypto long enough to remember why I fell in love with this industry in the first place.

Finding projects nobody was paying attention to. Digging into tech, finding an edge, backing teams building something new. Being early to a narrative before everyone and their mother started talking about it.

There was a reason to spend hours researching. There was something to figure out. You could actually get ahead by knowing more than the next guy.

Now what?

You buy a coin and pray it does a 10x before the dev dumps, insiders rotate out, or the next shiny ticker steals everyone’s attention.

You lose? You rotate into another coin.

Lose again? Chase the next meta.

Catch a runner? Roundtrip it because you think there’s another 10x in the tank.

Rinse and repeat until your wallet is fucking drained.

There’s no edge, no conviction, no reason to hold anything. Just an endless casino where everyone thinks they’re the one who’s going to beat the odds.

And the worst part is that we keep convincing ourselves we’re actually playing a game we can win.

I’ve spent countless hours in the trenches. I’ve made money, lost money, and watched entire metas come and go. But lately, it feels like none of that experience even matters anymore. You can do your research, find something genuinely interesting, and still get completely fucked because attention moved somewhere else overnight.

I’m not saying there’s no money to be made. Obviously there is.

I’m saying that making money and being good at crypto are becoming two completely different things.

And I’m tired of pretending that’s fine.

This isn’t the industry a lot of us OGs fell in love with.

Crypto was supposed to be about building an alternative financial system, experimenting with new technology, creating things that didn’t exist before, and finding opportunities the traditional world couldn’t offer.

Now we’re gambling against each other for scraps of liquidity while insiders and people with better access play a completely different game.

Maybe I’m just burned out. Maybe the market will change again.

But for now, I’m stepping back.

I don’t want to spend every waking hour chasing candles, refreshing charts, and trying to outplay a casino that gets more efficient at taking our money every single cycle.

I got into crypto because I believed in what it could become.

I don’t want to wake up one day and realize I spent years of my life gambling on fucking cartoon coins.

And if you’ve been feeling the same way lately, you’re probably not alone.

Take a step back if you need to. There’s more to life than the next 100x.

Because right now, it feels like the house is winning, and most of us are too addicted to the game to walk away.

text:
Romance in the Little Things:

1. The next time you go to a store, look for those small candy sticks or balls that fit into your palm when closed. You can find some for as cheap as 70 naira a piece. When you get home, keep one in your pocket and unwrap the other. Conceal the wrapped one in a closed fist and present both fists to your spouse. Ask him/her to guess which fist has the surprise. If they guess right, stick it into their mouth. If not, stick it in yours quickly. Allow the despair from the loss to sink in a bit before presenting the second one as compensation.

2. When you get home, for those with a car, stop just before driving into the house. Call your wife to come outside. When she comes, while you are standing over the car looking down from the driver's seat, tell her how much you have missed her all day. Remind her of memories from when your love story started. "Do you remember those days...." Ask her to get in the car. Chat for a few minutes. Switch on the AC and keep it at max for a more romantic ambience. Then drive into the house...

3. Offer to comb her hair. It’s a very simple task but good for bonding. Please be gentle. Their hair is not like ours. You can also offer to put finishing touches to his outfit when he is done dressing up.  Straighten out the faintest crease, dust away imaginary dirts, set his (traditional) cap so it aligns well with his glabella, sing praises of him so he feels emboldened as he steps out. "My King, my Odogwu. You look so handsome, so presidential!". Trust me, the first people he sees when he walks out will temporarily appear like his subjects.

4. When you pack his breakfast for work, leave a note in the pack: "I hope you enjoy it as much as you enjoy me."

5. Irrespective of your marital age and the number of children you have, do not stop eating together.

6. Take baths together. Not pre-planned, but somewhat accidental. Wait till he/she has started bathing, then barge in unannounced. Make sure your bathroom is clean and slip-proof. Bathroom accidents can be fatal! Before you try this, please consider the nature of your spouse. Some people aren't comfortable with this.

7. Wake up at night and pray together. When you are done, let her lie on your thigh or vice versa and make du'aa: "May Allah bless you as you have made me happy in this marriage." "May Allah never leave you to your affairs as you have never left us to ours."

8. Take evening strolls together. As long as you avoid unnecessary PDA, it is very healthy for both of you.

9. Exchange gifts, however little the item is. It is the intention that counts.

10. Think of anything within your reality and circumstances that will make your spouse feel special. It counts too as romance.

May Allah bless our homes.

Abu Imran

text:
My daughter-in-law showed up at my new cabin with four suitcases and announced that she and my son were moving in. She hadn’t even asked if they could stay. 

She just smiled and said, “We thought it was time we started taking care of you.”

My son stood behind her, looking at the floor.

I was sixty-eight years old, not dead. But judging by the way Deborah was already looking around my house, she’d decided those were practically the same thing.

I stepped aside and let them in.

What they didn’t know was that my lawyer was sitting in the living room, waiting for them.

I spent thirty-two years building a restaurant business from one small kitchen into a chain of restaurants across three states. I missed birthdays, worked through Christmases, and burned my arms often enough that my wife used to joke I should come with a warning label.

When I finally sold the business, I had enough money to stop working.

So I bought a cabin outside Aspen, somewhere I could wake up to snow on the mountains instead of a phone ringing before sunrise.

I wanted a quiet life. I wanted to cook when I felt like it, read the old cookbooks I’d collected over the years, and spend my evenings by the fireplace without worrying about payroll.

For the first time in decades, nobody needed anything from me.

Or so I thought.

My son, Trenton, was forty-one. When he was younger, he used to follow me around the restaurant, asking questions about everything. He could tell when a sauce was wrong before the chef admitted it. I thought he’d take over the business one day.

But after he married Deborah, something changed.

He started calling less. When he visited, he spent half the time checking his phone. Deborah was always polite enough in front of me, but there was something about the way she looked at my belongings that made me uncomfortable.

She didn’t look at my home the way a guest would.

She looked at it the way a buyer looks at a property before making an offer.

The first time I cooked dinner for them, she took two bites and said, “It’s good, Harold. I just prefer something a little more refined.”

Trenton laughed.

I didn’t say anything. I’d spent too many years in a professional kitchen to be offended by somebody’s taste in food.

But I remembered that laugh.

A few weeks later, I discovered something that bothered me far more.

I was in my kitchen when my phone rang. I answered it, but the connection was poor, so I set the phone on the counter while I finished washing my hands.

Then I heard Deborah’s voice.

“Do you think he’s going to live in that place alone forever?”

There was a pause.

My son’s voice followed.

“I don’t know, Deb. He’s healthy. He does everything himself.”

She sighed.

“That’s not what I’m asking.”

I picked up the phone, but neither of them knew I was listening.

Then Trenton said something I’ll never forget.

“We’ll figure it out eventually.”

The call ended a moment later.

🇺🇸🇮🇷 I had a deeply unsettling conversation with Professor Peter Kuznick about the possibility of nuclear weapons entering the conflict with Iran.

What worries him most isn't necessarily a deliberate decision to start a global nuclear war.

It's the growing belief among some military strategists that nuclear weapons can be used in a limited conflict without triggering something much worse.

Kuznick argues that this is a dangerously flawed assumption.

A tactical nuclear strike might be intended to force an adversary into submission. But the country being attacked could interpret it as the beginning of a much larger offensive and retaliate accordingly.

Suddenly, leaders are making decisions involving millions of lives with incomplete information and only minutes to respond.

We discussed the American president's authority to order a nuclear strike, the modernization of nuclear arsenals and the possibility that Iran's surviving nuclear infrastructure is buried beyond the reach of conventional American bombs.

Kuznick fears that another failed attempt to destroy those facilities could increase pressure for more extreme military options.

But he also raised something that deserves more attention.

The danger isn't confined to Washington or Tehran. A confrontation involving Russia, China or North Korea could create similar pressures, especially if leaders begin to believe they can eliminate an opponent's ability to retaliate.

Kuznick is now appealing to Pope Leo XIV to convene an emergency summit between the major nuclear powers.

I don't think nuclear escalation is inevitable, and the discussion offered no evidence that Trump has decided to use a nuclear weapon against Iran.

But Kuznick's central warning stayed with me.

The most dangerous nuclear war may begin with someone convinced they're starting a limited one.
