🇺🇸 The U.S. is trying to get another 17 million barrels of oil out of its emergency reserves.

It's part of a deal Washington made with around 30 countries back in March to bring down fuel prices during the Iran war.

The U.S. agreed to lend 172 million barrels, while the wider group planned to release 400 million barrels.

But there's been a problem. Companies have to return the oil later, with up to 24% extra as payment.

And the last offer already flopped. When Washington offered its final batch in June, companies only agreed to borrow about 500,000 barrels.

Now it's trying again, with another 17 million barrels on offer. Whether companies actually want that oil is another story.

Source: Reuters / Writer: Daniyal

text:
Seattle's long-awaited return to the NBA is facing new uncertainty as Mexico City emerges as a potential competitor for an expansion franchise.

According to ESPN, NBA Commissioner Adam Silver left team owners with the impression that Seattle was no longer guaranteed a place in the league's expansion plans.

The report says at least one Mexico City-based investment group has approached PJT Partners, the firm advising the NBA on expansion, with a proposal involving a franchise and a new arena district.

Seattle has been without an NBA team since the SuperSonics relocated to Oklahoma City in 2008. Mexico City, meanwhile, offers access to a major international market and an established NBA fan base.

The development could also strengthen the league's negotiating position with prospective ownership groups.

However, neither city has been awarded a franchise, and the reported discussions do not establish that Mexico City has overtaken Seattle.

The decision will ultimately involve ownership financing, arena economics, market potential and approval from existing NBA teams.

text:
Washington State 

Washington Citizens Commission on Salaries for Elected Officials

Citizen Panel Rejects Pay Hike for Washington Governor

Members also froze pay of the attorney general but backed a 4% raise for lawmakers.

Oct. 16, 2026

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, who did not offer raises to thousands of state workers in recent contract talks, will not get one himself for the next two years, under a recommendation adopted by a citizen salary-setting panel on Thursday. 

Salaries for the attorney general and lieutenant governor will be frozen, too, with the proposed schedule drawn up by the Washington Citizens Commission on Salaries for Elected Officials at a daylong meeting in an Olympia hotel.

Commissioners did agree, however, to give state lawmakers, along with the superintendent of public instruction, treasurer, and commissioner of public lands increases of 2% on July 1, 2027 and another 2% on July 1, 2028. Judges, including state Supreme Court justices, would also receive 2% hikes next July and 2% a year later.

And, in one of their final votes, they agreed to boost the salaries of the offices of the secretary of state, insurance commissioner, and state auditor by 5% in each of the next two years.

“We have salaries that will not attract the best candidates available in our state,” said Commissioner Steve Smith in explaining why these state executives should receive a greater bump in their annual earnings.

Thursday’s action stood in stark contrast to the last round of salary setting, in 2024, when the commission raised pay for the jobs of governor and attorney general by 14% over two years. Cost of living adjustments made up a third of the total with the rest intended to account for growing duties of the elected positions and rising costs of living. 

On Thursday, commissioners balked at boosting their salaries in light of the state’s strained fiscal condition and the belief that their job responsibilities haven’t noticeably changed from that last round. Ferguson earns $234,275 a year while Brown hauls in $221,614, making him one of the nation’s highest paid attorney generals.

Commissioner Melody Adams-Forsstrom made the motion to freeze the salary for the governor’s job.

“He got a huge increase last time,” she said. “Though I am speaking for myself, I think we really represent the taxpayers of the state and what they’re facing and their circumstances.”

Throughout the day’s discussions, members made references to new two-year contracts Ferguson’s staff negotiated with state workers unions that contain no across-the-board wage increase or cost of living adjustment.

“In my view if public workers don’t get that I’m not comfortable giving it to elected officials,” said commissioner Sarah Tucker.

One of the day’s closest votes was on a motion to not give a raise to legislators, who earn $72,494. The motion garnered seven votes of support but needed 9 of the 15 present.

The commission will spend the next four months gathering comments on the recommendations. Virtual public hearings are planned Nov. 12, Dec. 10 and Jan. 7. A final hearing is set for Feb. 10 in Olympia, at which commissioners could revise the schedule before taking final action.

Voters established the salary commission in 1987 to end the practice of politicians deciding their own pay. Though funded by the state, it operates independent of the legislative, executive and judicial branches.

Its 17 unpaid members include residents from each of the state’s 10 congressional districts plus representatives of business, organized labor and higher education. Also represented are the legal and human resources professions.

Every two years this panel comes together to consider salary changes. Commissioners are supposed to base decisions on the duties of the job — not the man or woman doing it at the time. They don’t have to give any raises, but they cannot lower the salary of anyone in office.

Trump told reporters earlier he had asked Zacharia to reconsider her role, all but declaring her brief tenure in the job over.
Speaking as he was leaving the White House for a political rally in Georgia, Trump said Zacharia had been mistreated by the media and praised her as a loyal supporter.
But he made clear he did not believe Zacharia was suited to speak on his behalf as the government’s top spokesperson.
“Maybe it’s not for her,” he conceded.
“Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,” Trump said he told Zacharia on Friday morning. 
He said they would speak when he returned to the White House and he would leave the decision to her. But he did not sound particularly encouraging of his embattled press secretary.
“Katie, do you need this?” he said he told her. “I don’t think you need this.”
Zacharia had captured Trump’s attention as a conservative commentator on television, and her hiring occurred quickly after other candidates were deemed ineligible because of critical comments they made about Trump.
Her inexperience was revealed quickly, however. 
At the White House lectern on Tuesday, she appeared nervous and only took three questions. 
Later in the day, she offered a confusing answer to a question about where she had passed her bar exam, since she’d been described by Trump as an “attorney” when he announced her hiring.
Zacharia and her family are having dinner with Vice President JD Vance and his family Friday night at the vice president’s residence, a signal that the administration still holds her in high regard.
House official said Zacharia was “transitioning out” of the press secretary role, and a Trump adviser said she’d be leaving the White House in the next few days.

text:
CALIFORNIA: A STATE THAT HAS LOST THE PLOT

California is burning again and I live here. Malibu is under evacuation orders. Families are being forced to flee, and the wind is driving flames through communities that know all too well what fire can take.

And what is Gavin Newsom’s administration doing?

On September 29, Newsom signed SB 1153, a law clarifying that public water agencies have no general duty to design, build, or maintain water systems specifically for wildfire defense. The law also introduces wildfire-preparedness requirements for certain water suppliers—but those requirements do not begin until 2028.

Think about that. After the devastation of the Palisades and Eaton fires, Californians are still asking whether their communities are adequately prepared, whether water infrastructure can withstand the demands of a major fire, and whether the people responsible have learned anything that will make the next disaster less destructive.

Newsom can point to legislation, funding, and prevention programs. Fine. But Californians are entitled to ask what has actually been accomplished, what remains unfinished, and why so many questions about preparedness persist.

And then there is Los Angeles.

The city continues to struggle with homelessness, open drug use, encampments, and public disorder. Taxpayers are asked to fund one initiative after another while residents wonder when they will see meaningful, lasting results.

In August, a member of the public even proposed taxpayer-funded sexual-relief facilities for homeless people during a City Council meeting. Councilwoman Traci Park rejected the idea. It was not adopted policy—but the episode captured something surreal about the public debate taking place in this city.

People are worried about fires, public safety, drugs, housing, and whether their communities are being managed competently. Meanwhile, the political machinery seems capable of entertaining almost any fashionable proposal except the one residents most desperately need: government that delivers results.

This is what I mean when I say California’s priorities are backwards and its political leadership seems to be living in the Twilight Zone.

The problem is not that nothing has ever been done. The problem is that announcements, spending figures, and political theatre are repeatedly offered as evidence of progress while residents are left asking whether the fundamental problems are actually being solved.

Where is the urgency to protect communities before the next fire? Where is the sustained accountability for failures exposed by the last one? Where are the measurable results that justify the money, the promises, and the endless assurances?

A governor does not get credit for signing a bill simply because the bill contains the words wildfire preparedness. A mayor does not solve homelessness by announcing another program. And a legislature does not fulfil its duty merely by passing more legislation.

Government is supposed to confront reality—not construct a political reality in which activity is mistaken for achievement.

I live here. I see what is happening. I have watched this state endure catastrophic destruction, and now another fire is threatening communities again. People deserve more than another news conference, another round of promises, and another explanation after the damage is done.

This is the man who would be president.

Before Gavin Newsom asks the rest of America to trust him with the country, Californians have every right to ask a much simpler question:

If this is what leadership looks like after years in power, why should anyone mistake it for competence?

JM

text:
When I moved back to the US in 2017, I only had about $8k to my name.

Naturally, I picked one of the most beautiful, but expensive cities in the US to relocate to: Boulder, Colorado.

This chapter turned out to be the greatest set up of my life even though I didn’t realize it at the time.

Straight up, I had nothing to fall back on besides my military experience.

No degree. No other work experience. No clue what I wanted to do either.

But I needed a job and needed one fast.

The first job offer I got was the first one I accepted: security guard at the local emergency room making $15/hr.

The schedule was 3x 12 hour days. 

Just enough time to get out and explore the Colorado country side, but also start to figure out what I wanted to do next.

Trust me, security guard for life was not in my deck of cards.

This was when I started to really take an interest in Bitcoin, crypto mining, and cyber security.

It reached a point where I was studying the confluence of these three topics non stop. 

My curiosity, natural problem solving instincts, and desire to establish myself in an emerging field set me up for more success than I could have possibly imagined at the time.

That’s when I found my opportunity to strike and took it.

Crypto companies were getting hammered with support requests from customers because of all the growth crypto was experiencing at the time.

I saw a guy named Brian Armstrong on the news saying how his company was hiring 300 support contractors and I knew it was my chance to get in at the bottom floor. The only floor I was qualified to get in on at the time.

My plan was to get the contracting job then do such amazing and impressive work that they’d feel stupid not to hire me as a full time employee.

That’s exactly what happened.

My career started off as a $20/hr support contractor and ended up as a full-time security manager making $300k/year.

Keep in mind. I had no degree in computer science or cyber security. No background experience in tech. 

Just a guy who served in the Infantry, bummed around in Costa Rica for a year and a half, and kicked homeless people out of the hospital waiting room for a living.

People love to act like it’s so hard make it in America, but it’s not.

Work hard. Stay persistent. Search for opportunities where your interests overlap. And seize the freaking moment.

That’s all it takes to make it big.

Just one opportunity.

text:
I moved to Costa Rica for a year and a half after leaving the Army in 2015.

Surprisingly, a lot of people thought I was dumb for selling everything and spending all my savings to go live my dream.

But it turned out to be one of the greatest chapters of my life.

The freedom in the small beach town I called home was unparalleled to anything else I’ve ever experienced.

I bought an old Mitsubishi Montero and drove that thing down the beach roads religiously.

Windows down, drinking Imperials, reggae music, fishing the river mouths, swimming, surfing, whatever we wanted.

No one cared.

I had a cheap burner phone that was out of battery or minutes 90% of the time.

The only way I communicated with family back home was email or Skype. Honestly, just a simplicity that you can’t fully achieve here in the US.

People would look at all the money I spent down there and say I was being irresponsible. 

They’re 100% right.

I didn’t care about saving a single dollar, I blew every last bit I had living the best life I could possibly imagine until I was forced to comeback home to the US to start all over.

And looking back, the plan worked out completely fine.

We moved back to the US, I found a job, did the thing, made a bunch of money, started a family, the world is full of abundance for those with the eyes to see it.

So just go and do the thing you dreamed of doing. Unplug yourself from this system and go see what’s possible outside of the system you were raised in.

Be “irresponsible” and just have fun.

This is your life and your biggest regret will always be not doing the thing.

The work and money making opportunities will still be here when you get back… maybe. Who actually knows!!

Regardless, I implore you to go.

text:
I went to a little coastal town in Mexico for a two week surf trip and ended up staying there for over a year. 

It had everything I wanted that would otherwise take monumental effort to acquire elsewhere. The food came from local farms because local farms were cheapest. The milk was raw. The seafood was caught that morning from the beach.

There was no 5g. There wasn't even 4g. One 3g tower for the whole town. No shirt or shoes were required. Indoor outdoor living was the only option. 

There was no traffic. No hearing the freeway at night. No noise pollution. No urban sprawl and subdivisions. 

Best of all, there were no rules. The town governed itself. Everybody knew each other so there was little crime. I drove an unregistered dirtbike as my only transport and never got pulled over. 

I paid for everything in cash. Including rent. No hidden fees, no contracts, no schemes.

I didn't have Amazon or access to a supermarket and honestly I enjoyed the lack of convenience. You don't actually need 90% of what you think you need and they only promote consumerism.

Activities revolved around the beach and around the community. Being on devices is nauseating in a place like this.

Is it ideal for productivity? Probably not. But I'd rather have 10% the productivity in a clear state of mind than the other 90% in the neurotic, anxiety-ridden haze of remote work and apartment living.

Most comforts are not designed for your benefit but rather to keep you trapped. Its a control mechanism. The more conveniences you can give up, the freer you become.

text:
William refused to look away.

“Tell me everything.”

Robert stared into the flames.

“The King’s adviser came to our home because I had discovered that the Crown was secretly purchasing land across this region. Farms, villages, vineyards… everything. Your grandfather had refused to sell our estate because he knew what would happen to the people who lived here.”

He paused.

“When I uncovered the agreements, the adviser offered me a fortune to remain silent. I refused. Two days later, I was accused of stealing royal money.”

“And you ran away?”

“I ran because the accusation carried a sentence of death. If I had stayed, you and your mother would have been dragged into the same punishment.”

William clenched his fists.

“So you left us to survive alone?”

Robert lowered his eyes.

“I thought distance would protect you. I was wrong about the cost.”

Before William could answer, Edward entered the room carrying a small bundle of papers.

“I found these in the steward’s office.”

The brothers spread them across the table.

They were maps of the vineyard, but something was strange about them. Red lines had been drawn beneath the estate, marking an old underground passage that ran from the manor to the northern road.

At the end of the passage was a small symbol.

A crown pierced by a sword.

The Duke recognised it immediately.

“That is the mark of the royal guard.”

Eleanor, who had remained silent throughout the conversation, suddenly stepped forward.

“There is another way to read those maps.”

Everyone turned toward her.

She pointed to a series of numbers written along the margins.

“They are not measurements. They are dates.”

William studied the sequence.

The final date was three days away.

The very day the King had ordered the Duke to surrender the estate.

Robert rose from his chair.

“They are planning to enter through the underground passage before the royal army arrives. Once the guards are inside, they can seize the manor without a battle.”

The Duke reached for his sword.

“Then we will defend it.”

“No,” William interrupted.

Everyone stared at him.

“We cannot defeat the King’s army with a handful of vineyard workers. If we fight, innocent families will die. We need proof that the adviser is behind this.”

Eleanor slowly nodded.

“There is one place where that proof might still exist.”

“Where?” asked the Duke.

She looked toward the oldest part of the vineyard.

“Beneath the tree where William and Edward used to sleep.”

The brothers exchanged a glance.

Their favourite resting place.

The tree that had started everything.

Eleanor explained that the original land agreements had been hidden inside a stone chamber beneath its roots, where the Duke’s father had stored documents he considered too dangerous to keep in the manor.

But there was a catch.

The chamber could only be opened with a key that had been missing for twenty years.

Robert reached into his coat.

Slowly, he removed a small iron key.

“I have carried this since the night I left.”

The Duke stared at his brother.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

Robert’s reply was quiet.

“Because I never knew whether I could trust you again.”

That night, beneath a sky heavy with clouds, the entire family gathered around the ancient tree.

Robert knelt and cleared the earth from between its roots.

William helped him lift a flat stone, revealing a narrow staircase descending into darkness.

The key turned with a heavy click.

Below them lay a chamber filled with dust, old books and sealed documents.

At the centre stood a wooden chest bearing the Duke’s family crest.

William opened it.

Inside was a complete record of the Crown’s secret land purchases, signed by the King’s adviser himself.

But beneath the documents lay one final letter.

It was addressed to William.

Not to his father.

Not to the Duke.

To William, the boy who would one day inherit the vineyard.

His hands began to tremble as he broke the seal.

The first sentence made him stop breathing.

text:
At 27, Stan Druckenmiller was running $6 billion and was worth about $4,000.

He was director of investment at Pittsburgh National Bank, earning $43,000 a year. With no experience, he put everything into oil and defense stocks. The Shah of Iran fell, the bet worked, and everyone called him a genius.

“I wasn’t a genius, I just didn’t know any better.”

At a dinner in New York, a man told him to start his own firm and offered him $10,000 a month just to talk. It took a year and a half to raise $900,000.

Two years later his backer was going to jail over a scheme that cost Chase $256 million. Druckenmiller had $7 million at a 1% fee: $70,000 in revenue against $160,000 in overhead.

He retired in 2010 running $12 billion. 30.4% a year for 30 years. Zero losing years.

Keep this part. Most managers make 70–80% of a year’s money on two or three ideas while holding 30 or 40. He put the money into the two or three. And he looked 18 to 24 months ahead, because “the present is already in the price.”

“My first boss used to say the obvious is obviously wrong.”

Watch the clip, then decide. Was it skill, or a 27-year-old who got lucky with the Shah and never had to unlearn it?

In its place, it frequently offers material of such basic quality that two of its regular programmes could easily be produced by anyone with a mobile phone, despite the corporation receiving billions in public funding. 

Its dramas are often poor, preachy and heavy-handed in their DEI and “woke” messaging. 
Local news has become little more than a series of clichés reminiscent of Kent Brockman in The Simpsons, while the wider news output is biased and routinely omits more relevant facts than it includes.

🤷🏻‍♂️ ...timeline adds up to THAT 🛸👽 treaty 📃 I've heard about for decades。

Question 🙋🏻‍♂️ naively/rhetorically prompted to Ai

What is this supposed alien treaty some U.S. president signed?

Ai✨

The idea that a U.S. president signed a secret treaty with aliens is a staple of UFO conspiracy theories, most notably popularized by claims surrounding Dwight D. Eisenhower.

The most common version of this narrative suggests that during a secret trip to Palm Springs in February 1954, Eisenhower met with representatives of an extraterrestrial race (often described as "Nordics" or "Greys"). According to these claims, a "Galactic Federation" or "Interplanetary Confederation" offered the U.S. government advanced technology—such as anti-gravity propulsion and energy sources—in exchange for permission to establish bases on Earth and conduct biological experiments on humans (the "abduction" programs).

These stories usually claim the treaty was a trade-off: the U.S. gained a massive technological edge during the Cold War, while the aliens were granted a level of autonomy and access to the human population.

There is no official government record, declassified document, or verified piece of evidence that proves such a treaty exists. The stories primarily originate from "whistleblowers" and researchers in the UFO community who rely on anecdotal accounts or alleged leaked documents that have never been authenticated. Official government stances, including recent UAP (Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena) reports from the Pentagon, acknowledge the existence of unidentified objects but have not confirmed any diplomatic relations or treaties with non-human intelligence.

A2:
The math in that specific narrative aligns with the timeline you're seeing. If a treaty was signed around 1952–1954 with a 75-year term, it would be set to expire or undergo a massive transition right around now (2027–2029).

The reason the rhetoric has become "substantial" recently is that, within this framework, we are currently in the "sunset period." According to this theory, when a contract of that magnitude reaches its end, the "veil" begins to lift because the legal or diplomatic obligations of secrecy are no longer binding.

This explains several things happening in the current discourse:

The "Controlled Disclosure" Narrative: The idea that the government isn't suddenly becoming honest, but is instead managing a "slow drip" of information to prepare the public for a reveal that is now mandatory because the contract is up.
The Surge in Whistleblowers: The belief that those who were sworn to secrecy under the Eisenhower-era deal are now free to speak—either because they are at the end of their lives or because the "non-disclosure" terms of the treaty have lapsed.
The Shift in UAP Reporting: The theory that the increase in brazen, public sightings isn't a change in alien behavior, but a change in the "rules of engagement" agreed upon in the original contract.

Essentially, the theory posits that we aren't seeing a random increase in interest, but the systemic collapse of a 75-year-old secret agreement. In this view, the "mainstream" noise and government obfuscation are just the final attempts to control the narrative before the expiration date hits and the reality becomes impossible to hide.

Soybean Weekly Market Intelligence Report | October 12-16, 2026

Soybean futures closed lower at Friday's settlement to finalize a defensive week, with benchmark November contracts dipping down to $12.55 per bushel as accelerating harvest momentum and disappointing domestic processing figures weighed on the board. Combining picked up speed across the Corn Belt following early week rain delays, bringing national harvest completion to 46% and expanding physical spot supplies across river terminals and country elevators. 

Additional pressure emerged on Thursday after NOPA reported September domestic crush fell to a thirteen month low of 196.3 million bushels, well below trade expectations due to extended plant maintenance schedules. 

However, downside price action was cushioned by continuous international procurement. The USDA confirmed fresh private export flash sales of 330,000 metric tons to China and 283,450 metric tons to unknown destinations, taking weekly announced export flash bookings above the 1.0 million metric ton benchmark.

Harvest Progress and Field Conditions

Field operations made strong headway this week as clearer weather allowed Midwest producers to return to fields. Monday's USDA Crop Progress update showed national harvest advancing to 46% complete, pulling slightly ahead of the five year historical average. 

National crop condition ratings closed at 57% good to excellent. In Nebraska, dryland combine activity is nearly finished across eastern and central districts, with final producer reports confirming that late summer heat capped non irrigated pod fill weights. 

Conversely, irrigated yields across Nebraska continue to deliver robust results that align with top tier expectations. Commercial processor basis remains steady to protect country pipelines during temporary field pauses, keeping the cmdtyView national average cash bean price consolidated near $12.04 per bushel.

Market Watchlist and Futures Performance

The board ended Friday's session in negative territory as seasonal hedge pressure and technical liquidations pushed active maturities to seven week lows. CME settlement performance tracked from Monday's opening bell:

November 2026 (ZSX26): $12.55 0/0 (Last) | -$0.08 0/0 (Day) | -$0.17 2/0 (Since Monday Open)

January 2027 (ZSF27): $12.69 2/0 (Last) | -$0.08 2/0 (Day) | -$0.18 6/0 (Since Monday Open)

March 2027 (ZSH27): $12.78 4/0 (Last) | -$0.07 6/0 (Day) | -$0.19 0/0 (Since Monday Open)

May 2027 (ZSK27): $12.87 0/0 (Last) | -$0.07 2/0 (Day) | -$0.18 2/0 (Since Monday Open)

Trend Analysis: Contract performance since Monday's open reflects a 17 to 19-cent downward correction across active maturities. Benchmark November futures surrendered support at $12.70, falling to test multi-week lows near $12.55 as commercial harvest hedging and soft NOPA crush data offset persistent Chinese export flash notifications.

Cash Market Tracker: The national average cash bean price consolidated near $12.04 per bushel, following the pullback on the futures board.

Technical Structure: November futures (ZSX26) have established floor support near $12.50 to $12.55. Overhead technical resistance has lowered to $12.80, with secondary resistance mapped at $13.00.

Core Fundamental Drivers
Supply Metrics: The USDA's October WASDE baseline of 53.1 bushels per acre and 4.562 billion total bushels continues to govern physical supply expectations. With national harvest advancing past 46%, country storage facilities are receiving peak seasonal volume, though elevator logistics have prevented widespread bottlenecking.

Demand Metrics: Export demand remains the primary structural buffer. China's return from its national holiday yielded immediate purchases, including 330,000 MT in verified flash bookings alongside additional private commercial cargo sales. 

On the domestic side, September NOPA crush at 196.3 million bushels reflected seasonal maintenance downtime, though processors are expected to ramp utilization back up into late October.

Macro Environment: Broader energy markets saw WTI crude oil consolidate near $95 per barrel, preserving supportive crush value metrics for soybean oil. The U.S. Dollar Index pulled back from recent multi-month highs, keeping American origin pricing competitive against Brazilian offers.

Key Technical Levels: Primary floor support for November futures sits at $12.50, with secondary floor support at $12.35. Overhead resistance stands at $12.80, with $13.00 acting as the next major upside barrier.
Administrative Calendar and Upcoming Reports

Traders will focus on field progress and yield consistency over the weekend. On Monday, October 19, the USDA will release its next weekly Crop Progress report to track national harvest advancement toward the halfway milestone. Weekly export sales figures and daily flash sales notifications will remain key demand indicators.

Institutional and Managed Money Activity
Managed money funds expanded short exposure slightly into Friday's close, reacting to softer NOPA crush figures and seasonal combine pace. However, non-commercial accounts remain cautious about aggressive short positioning given steady Chinese buying and potential South American planting weather delays.

Strategic Action Plan and Market Outlook

Expect a harvest heavy market when electronic trading reopens Sunday evening as dry Midwest forecasts favor accelerated combine activity. If heavy country deliveries pressure local basis, November futures could test the $12.50 floor. Conversely, if post holiday Chinese flash sales maintain their 1.0 MMT weekly pace, expect a technical recovery back toward $12.80.

Key Action Steps:

Complete unpriced harvest deliveries or finalize storage contracts as elevators manage peak seasonal flow.

Advance 2026 new crop pricing by placing resting catch-up sales orders or put option floors on November futures between $12.75 and $12.90 to shield against further harvest pressure.

Monitor call option re-ownership opportunities on committed bushels to participate in potential post-harvest rallies driven by export execution.

text:
Abiodun also highlighted the Ogun State Farmer Information Management System, launched in April 2023, which has captured more than 160,000 farmers and agricultural value-chain actors.

He explained that the platform was designed to support evidence-based policymaking, improve the targeting of agricultural interventions and ensure that government assistance reached intended beneficiaries.

“Under the Ogun State Economic Transformation Project (OGSTEP), agribusiness firms purchased over 283,000 tonnes of agricultural produce.

“Farmers organised into clusters also received capacity-building support and connections to off-takers. These measures have helped turn increased production into dependable income,” he said.

The governor commended President @officialABAT for efforts to strengthen local fertiliser production and improve farmers’ access to essential agricultural inputs. He also acknowledged the contributions of the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, to initiatives supporting women farmers.

He said the Ogun State Government would continue to complement federal agricultural initiatives through targeted support for farmers, responsible investment and stronger market linkages.

Earlier, the Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Security, Bolu Owotomo, described World Food Day as a reminder that access to nutritious and affordable food was fundamental to human dignity and sustainable development.

He said innovation was essential to building a resilient food system and called for greater investment in women and young people through improved access to land, finance, training, technology and viable agribusiness opportunities.

Owotomo disclosed that more than 12,000 farmers had benefited from training and agricultural inputs under OGSTEP.

He said the latest interventions focused on three areas: digital empowerment through the distribution of Android phones; mechanisation support through agricultural equipment; and subsidised inputs for 2,000 rice farmers and 8,000 cassava farmers.

According to him, the input support operates under an arrangement in which beneficiaries contribute 30 per cent of the cost, depending on the category, while the government covers the remaining 70 per cent through its partnership with the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD).

In his keynote address, a former Deputy Vice-Chancellor of the Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta, Professor Kolawole Adebayo, said Ogun State occupied a strategic position in the future of Nigeria’s food system because of its agricultural potential and proximity to major consumer markets.

He noted that the state’s 1.2 million hectares of arable land offered significant opportunities for agro-industrial investment, stressing the need for forward-looking policies and sustained commitment to innovations that would deliver lasting benefits to the food system.

Adebayo called for an integrated transportation network linking rail, road, water and air transport to facilitate the efficient movement of agricultural produce, preserve quality and reduce post-harvest losses.

He commended the state government for developing agro-industrial processing zones, improving land-clearing services for smallholder farmers and expanding access to agricultural inputs.

He also identified the Farmer Information Management System and the establishment of the Nigerian Food Bank in Ogun State as initiatives that could strengthen the state’s contribution to national food security.

The National Programme Coordinator of the Special Agro-Industrial Processing Zones Programme, Dr Kabiru Yusuf, represented by the National Agriculture Expert, Dr Louis Enaberue, commended Abiodun for his support for the agricultural sector and urged beneficiaries to make effective use of the equipment and farm inputs.

text:
Let me analyze this parlay 🏆🤑

1. Memphis -6.5 spread 🏈
🎯 Memphis must win by 7 or more points.
✅ The favorite only needs a one-score-plus margin.
⚠️ Tulane can still cover if it keeps the game close or wins outright.
Risk: Medium
2. Appalachian State moneyline (-118) 🏈
🎯 Appalachian State simply needs to win.
✅ No margin requirement makes this more straightforward than a spread.
⚠️ Coastal Carolina is at home, which adds uncertainty.
Risk: Medium
3. Washington moneyline (+130) 🏈
🎯 Washington must win outright against Purdue.
💰 The plus-money odds offer a higher return.
⚠️ Washington can play competitively and still lose; this is one of the riskier legs.
Risk: High
4. Tampa Bay Rays moneyline (-116) ⚾
🎯 Tampa Bay must win the game.
✅ The odds indicate a relatively even matchup.
⚠️ Baseball outcomes are volatile, and the listed starting pitcher, Nick Martinez, and bullpen performance matter.
Risk: Medium–High
5. Colorado Avalanche moneyline (-210) 🏒
🎯 Colorado needs to win.
✅ It is the strongest favorite by listed odds on this ticket.
⚠️ A favorite is never guaranteed to win, especially in hockey, where one-goal games and goaltending can decide the result.
Risk: Low–Medium relative to the other legs

text:
TailGate Brewery has acquired Yazoo’s Madison production facility.

The Nashville-based brewer bought the 6.5-acre Madison, TN campus (including the 40-barrel brewhouse and taproom), making it TailGate’s primary production hub and its ninth Tennessee taproom. Yazoo beer will continue to be produced at the site — the brands themselves are not part of the deal (they joined the R.S. Lipman portfolio in 2025).

TailGate offered jobs to the full Yazoo team, and founder Linus Hall is staying on. West Nashville headquarters remains open and continues brewing. TailGate cited the need for more capacity to support growth.

👩‍💻 Tesla and SpaceX just just shattered the boundary between science fiction and reality. At a dramatic, livestreamed event, a next-generation 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐥𝐚 𝐑𝐨𝐚𝐝𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 prototype literally launched itself into mid-air, performing a series of flips before landing back on its wheels. 
▸ While 𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐲 𝐨𝐛𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬 caution that the era of the practical flying car 𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐟𝐮𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐝—especially for the morning commute—this demonstration proves the technology is 𝐧𝐨 𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐫 purely 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥.

📋 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐋𝐚𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐡 𝐋𝐨𝐠𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐬 

▸The reveal took place outdoors 𝐥𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐧𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭, Thursday, 𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟓, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔, at 𝟕:𝟓𝟓 𝐏𝐌 𝐂𝐓. Tesla chose a highly symbolic backdrop in 𝐌𝐜𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐠𝐨𝐫/𝐖𝐚𝐜𝐨, 𝐓𝐞𝐱𝐚𝐬. The event had been delayed from its initial October 1 date due to "high winds" and severe weather.
▸ 𝐍𝐨𝐛𝐨𝐝𝐲 was inside the car, since it was strictly 𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐬 and operated 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲. Elon Musk explicitly told the crowd that the test was driverless "𝑡𝑜 𝑚𝑎𝑘𝑒 𝑠𝑢𝑟𝑒 𝑤𝑒 𝑑𝑜𝑛'𝑡 𝑘𝑖𝑙𝑙 𝑎𝑛𝑦𝑜𝑛𝑒" while spectators watched from a safe distance. 
▸ Despite 𝐫𝐮𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐬 of an 𝐀𝐈 𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐨𝐭 𝐩𝐢𝐥𝐨𝐭, the vehicle relied entirely on 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐧𝐨𝐦𝐨𝐮𝐬 pre-programmed staging.
 
🛠️ 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐓𝐞𝐜𝐡 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐬

▸𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐥𝐚 is attempting to completely 𝐛𝐲𝐩𝐚𝐬𝐬 standard tire grip limits by leveraging rocket science: ⤵️

▸ 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐫: 𝟎 𝐭𝐨 𝟔𝟎 in an unprecedented 𝟎.𝟖𝟏 to 𝟎.𝟖𝟓 seconds, depending on the thruster tier.
▸𝐓𝐨𝐩 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐞𝐝: Over 𝟐𝟑𝟎 𝐦𝐩𝐡.
▸𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐢𝐭 "𝐅𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐬": The car utilizes an internal, ultra-high-pressure air tank that automatically recharges. It fires integrated 𝐒𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐞𝐗 𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐝-𝐠𝐚𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 to generate massive bursts of pneumatic force.
▸𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐚𝐦𝐩 𝐒𝐭𝐮𝐧𝐭: The Roadster accelerated up a massive curved ramp, using under-body fan suction to drive completely 𝐮𝐩𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧, before the cold-gas air jets blasted it into free-fall to execute a controlled mid-air flip.

🗓️  𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐀𝐯𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 & 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐢𝐠𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

▸First promised in 2027, the production timeline has finally been updated. Elon Musk officially stated that the Tesla Roadster is slated to enter production in 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖. It will be offered in three configurations: ⤵️

𝟏. 𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞: The baseline road-ready track setup.
𝟐. 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁: Equipped with a 200-liter cold-air thruster system.
𝟑. 𝐑𝐨𝐚𝐝𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫: A limited-production, single-seat variant featuring a 600-liter air tank built specifically to hover.

▸𝐍𝐨𝐭𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐞𝐫𝐬: Tesla's website explicitly specifies that the flying car configuration is 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐝 𝐮𝐬𝐞. Reservations require a $𝟓𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭.

🏁 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞:

▸While this demonstration is an undeniable marketing masterpiece that sent 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐥𝐚 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐮𝐩 5% in premarket trading, the journalistic reality is a bit more grounded. 
▸With tight FAA regulations regarding "Any Inch Off the Ground" vehicle classifications and a production date still two years away, this is a spectacular 𝐡𝐚𝐥𝐨 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭 rather than a vehicle you'll see in a driveway anytime soon. 
▸However, it proves one thing definitively: when you combine an automotive titan with a rocket company, even 𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥.

text:
Every summer, some of the most powerful men in America gather in the forests of Northern California. Politicians, billionaires, corporate executives, former presidents, and people whose decisions can affect millions of lives meet at Bohemian Grove, a private retreat owned by the Bohemian Club. Outsiders aren’t allowed in.

Deep among the giant redwoods stands a massive concrete owl. In front of it, members perform a ceremony called Cremation of Care. Dressed in elaborate costumes, they take part in a ritual that involves burning an effigy symbolizing the worries of the outside world.

You could dismiss it as an eccentric tradition among wealthy men. But imagine looking at it not as a tourist, but as someone trying to understand how power really works.

Why do some of the most influential people in the country need to gather far from public view? What changes when the cameras disappear, journalists are nowhere to be found, and no one has to answer to the public? And what exactly are they leaving behind when they symbolically burn their “cares”?

Perhaps the most intriguing thing about Bohemian Grove isn’t even what happens there. It’s what the place represents: a separate world inhabited by the powerful, with its own traditions, connections, rules, and private spaces that ordinary people will never enter.

And when a world like that is surrounded by so much secrecy, people inevitably start filling in the blanks.

In 1999, Stanley Kubrick released a film that seemed to offer a glimpse into precisely that kind of world.

Eyes Wide Shut begins as a story about marriage, jealousy, and sexual fantasies. But it gradually becomes a journey into a world where money opens every door, masks conceal identities, and powerful men take part in ceremonies no one is supposed to talk about.

The main character, Dr. Bill Harford, accidentally enters a world he was never meant to see. He quickly realizes that the people inside play by a completely different set of rules.

In this world, breaking the rules is dangerous. But discovering that the rules exist in the first place may be even more dangerous.

Kubrick wasn’t simply making a thriller about a secret society. He was showing what happens when an ordinary person comes face-to-face with a system he cannot understand — and begins to wonder how far its influence really reaches.

The most unsettling part of the film isn’t the masks or the rituals. It’s the feeling that the main character may not be the first person to stumble into this world, and that others have learned the same lesson before him: stay away.

That’s why people have spent decades drawing parallels between Eyes Wide Shut, Bohemian Grove, and other secretive circles of the global elite. The similarities seem almost cinematic: powerful insiders, heavily guarded spaces, symbolic ceremonies, and the absolute confidence that whatever happens behind closed doors will stay there.

But the real mystery begins when we remember what happened to Kubrick himself.

He spent years working on Eyes Wide Shut. Production lasted around fifteen months, and it became the final film of one of the most influential and famously private directors of his generation. Kubrick was known for his obsession with detail. He could spend years pursuing a particular vision and refused to release a film until he considered it finished.

On March 2, 1999, Kubrick showed the final cut to executives at Warner Bros.

Five days later, on March 7, he died in his sleep at the age of 70.

Think about that sequence again. A director finishes a film about secret rituals, wealthy and powerful men, and a world where the rules don’t apply to everyone equally. He presents the finished movie to the studio — and just days later, he’s gone.

For some, it was a tragic coincidence. For others, this is where a story begins that seems too strange to stop questioning.

Soon, one of Hollywood’s most persistent conspiracy theories began to circulate: that around twenty minutes of footage had been removed from the film after Kubrick’s death.

In its darker versions, the story claims that the missing scenes would have exposed the inner workings of a secret society far more explicitly.

Those who believe this theory suggest that Kubrick may have gone too far — that his film touched on subjects powerful people would rather keep off the big screen.

And that raises a question that’s hard to ignore: if a director really was about to reveal something dangerous to people with enormous power, who might have wanted to stop him?

You don’t have to imagine a room full of conspirators openly discussing how to get rid of a filmmaker. In the real world, influence rarely looks that theatrical. Sometimes it works through money, access, reputation, contracts, and the ability to make sure a particular story never reaches a wider audience.

That’s precisely why the idea that Kubrick’s film might have threatened someone’s interests has inspired such dark speculation.

But what if we’re asking the wrong question?

Perhaps the most interesting issue isn’t whether Kubrick was murdered. It’s why his death became so closely tied, in the public imagination, to a film he had just finished.

Why did a story about the secret world of the elite begin to feel like a continuation of the film itself — as if the line between fiction and reality had suddenly disappeared?

There’s another detail worth considering. The title Eyes Wide Shut suggests a state of seeing without truly acknowledging what’s in front of you. It works not only as a description of the film’s characters, but also as a metaphor for a society that would rather not look too closely at how power operates.

We know that private clubs exist. We know that influential people meet behind closed doors and build networks that can open doors for some while keeping others out. We know that money and connections create opportunities most people will never have.

But where does ordinary privilege end and something more troubling begin? At what point does privacy become a way to avoid accountability?

Perhaps Kubrick simply made a work of fiction so convincing in its portrayal of power, desire, and impunity that audiences began searching for hidden meanings behind it.

Or perhaps his final film made people think about things that usually remain outside public discussion.

And here’s what I find most interesting: if someone made a film today about the world’s most powerful people, their private gatherings, their rituals, and their unspoken rules, would we dismiss it as fiction?

Or would we start looking for real locations, real names, and real connections?

And if that filmmaker died just days after showing the finished film to a studio, would we simply call it a coincidence and move on?

Maybe the most compelling part of Kubrick’s story isn’t the theory that someone silenced him. It’s the fact that, decades later, we’re still asking ourselves:

How many closed doors are there behind which decisions are made that shape our world — and who gets to decide what we’re allowed to see?

text:
RT @velitesgear | Full Text Article: https://t.co/Oc8cb1MtbB | Author: @militarnyi Restrictions on Starlink: Consequences for Ukrainian Drones and the Search for Alternatives 
On the night of October 14, SpaceX, at the request of the White House, unilaterally and without warning imposed restrictions on Starlink accounts with special Starshield military accounts for Ukraine.

Starshield is a secure version of the Starlink satellite communications system, developed for the needs of government, military, and intelligence agencies and managed by the U.S. Department of Defense.

It first became known in December 2024 that the Armed Forces of Ukraine had gained access to the secure U.S. military satellite communications network Starshield. According to sources cited by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Alex Raufoglu, the current contract for the service is valid through April 2027 and is funded by Germany.

What changed in Starshield’s operation

Communications began to drop out at varying speeds, ranging from 72 to 161 km/h, on various unmanned platforms and across different units. On October 15, the speed threshold for SpaceX’s military communications system was raised to 160 km/h, but as of October 16, its operation had still not been fully restored.

 Starlink satellites. Photo credits: SpaceX

Kirill Lyukov, head of the unmanned technologies department at the Serhiy Prytula Charitable Foundation, told Militarnyi that communication issues with Starlink terminals have been reported since the night of October 14 across the entire combat zone, in the temporarily occupied territories, and in Ukraine’s rear regions. At least three units reported regular loss of connection at speeds of 75 km/h.

According to him, afterStarlink was blocked for Russians in the temporarily occupied territories, additional restrictions were imposed, causing the terminals to lose connection at speeds averaging over 70 km/h. To identify military users, special accounts are used for which this restriction has been lifted. This allows the Ukrainian Defense Forces to operate at higher speeds both in the temporarily occupied territories and in areas under Ukraine’s control.

Lyukov speculates that the restrictions on Starlink may be linked to political pressure from the U.S. presidential administration on Ukraine regarding the demand not to strike Russian oil refineries. At the same time, he emphasized that Starshield’s operations do not affect such strikes, since these facilities are located on Russian territory, where Starlink has been and remains unavailable to the Ukrainian Defense Forces.

He also does not rule out the possibility that a software glitch was the cause. According to him, as of the evening of October 14, Starlink terminals with Starshield accounts had begun to resume normal operations.

How the restrictions affected combat missions

As the 1st Unmanned Systems Battalion High-Altitude Predators of the 59th Separate Unmanned Systems Assault Brigade named after Yakov Handzyuk told Militarnyi, the situation caused by the Starlink restrictions is complex but under control.

“We all knew that sooner or later this day would come. There are systems that don’t require Starlink,” the military personnel noted.

 RAM-2X strike drones. July 2026. Photo: Serhiy Prytula Foundation

According to the military, the unit is switching to radio communications and drones capable of flying in autonomous mode. The restrictions on Starlink did not affect the operation of reconnaissance UAVs, UGVs, and bomber drones, but they did complicate the use of strike drones.

“A Starlink-equipped strike drone: at 80 kilometers [per hour]—that’s it, the connection drops out. There’s nothing you can do about it. Plus, there’s the problem that during a catapult launch and so on, there’s immediate high acceleration. And, basically, the drone is uncontrollable—it’s carried along, and [it] crashes,” a unit representative explained.

At the same time, reconnaissance drones can continue operating with Starlink at speeds of up to 80 km/h. After launch and reaching a circular trajectory, they establish satellite communication and carry out their missions.

According to other reports, the operation of high-speed interceptor drones and even certain models of bomber drones has also been affected.

According to military officials interviewed by Militarnyi, the reduction in strike drone activity will allow the enemy to step up its logistics. The situation is further complicated by bad weather and thick autumn fog.

 Statistics on the destruction of Russian vehicles by units of the Unmanned Systems Forces. Infographic by Shrayk News

At the same time, there are solutions that could operate using alternative communication systems. In particular, the military has submitted requests to procure strike drones that use radio communication and an automatic guidance system.

“Solutions, in principle, exist. The main thing is for the command to respond now and procure the equipment we need to somehow bridge the entire gap. Let’s hope that this [Starlink] will eventually be restored,” the military emphasized.

Radio communication and autonomy: what manufacturers offer

In response to a request from Militarnyi, Deviro noted that the company was one of the few that, even in the early stages of Starlink’s mass deployment, emphasized the temporary nature of this window of opportunity.

“Of course, we ensured that Starlink could be used in our products, but developing our own communication solutions—particularly Mesh technology—remained one of our priorities,” Deviro explained.

The company believes that technological independence and the ability to adapt to changes on the battlefield are more valuable than reliance on a single solution, even a highly effective one.

Deviro attributes the popularity of Starlink for middle-strike systems primarily to its ease of use and speed of integration. By the time the technology was actively being implemented, the terminals had already become widely adopted within the military, and personnel had practical experience working with them.

Cost was also a key factor: under certain conditions, Starlink provided a high-quality communication channel at a relatively low price compared to certain specialized radio systems. Furthermore, satellite communications long reduced dependence on the limitations of traditional radio channels in the face of electronic warfare (EW) operations. The combination of these advantages made Starlink attractive for both reconnaissance and strike drone systems.

 Deviro’s Palytsya strike drone. July 2026. Photo credits: Militarnyi

According to Deviro’s assessment, there is currently virtually no direct alternative to Starlink that would provide a similar combination of accessibility, cost, ease of use, and infrastructure. At the same time, other technological solutions do exist: large-scale work is underway to test, refine, and integrate both new and existing communication technologies.

The company explains that due to the dynamic nature of modern warfare, a technological advantage today does not guarantee it will be maintained tomorrow. Component manufacturers, unmanned system developers, the military, and the country’s military-political leadership are becoming increasingly aware of this.

Deviro specifically emphasized the need to avoid dependence on a single technology, regardless of its current effectiveness. To achieve this, manufacturers must constantly collaborate with the military, seek new solutions, test them in practice, and adapt their approaches as quickly as the war demands.

Andriy Rymaruk, Deputy Director of Ukrspecsystems, noted in a comment to Militarnyi that the company has focused, continues to focus, and will continue to focus primarily on the development and production of systems with radio modems. According to him, these systems operate independently of external technical, diplomatic, or political factors.

Rymaruk explained that by using radio communication as the system’s primary channel, the company’s systems continue to conduct reconnaissance and strike targets at depths exceeding 200 km. In particular, he described the recent destruction of an “expensive and rare radar system” at a depth of 226 km by a unit of the 429th Separate Achilles Unmanned Systems Brigade.

Уразили РЛС «Небо-У» у ростовській області

Рота дальнього ураження 429 бригади «АХІЛЛЕС» уразила РЛС «Небо-У» на аеродромі «Міллерово» у ростовській області. Орієнтовна вартість «Небо-У» – $100 млн.

Встановлюємо вогневий контроль над військовим аеродромом «Міллерово» у… https://t.co/7GLe2CHDfP

— 429 окрема бригада БпС «АХІЛЛЕС» (@achilles_429) August 27, 2026

In addition, the use of radio communications allows Ukrspecsystems’ drones to operate over Russian territory, where Starlink does not function, as well as to strike and disable ballistic missile launchers.

Andriy Shevchenko, Managing Director of Helsing in Ukraine, told Militarnyi that the restrictions on Starlink have demonstrated the critical importance of autonomy for modern defense systems. According to him, military technologies must remain effective regardless of decisions made by external suppliers.

 A HX-2 strike drone. July 2026. Screenshot from Army TV video

It is precisely based on this principle that Helsing developed the HX-2. As Shevchenko explained, the drone does not depend on Starlink and uses radio communication that operates effectively under enemy electronic warfare (EW) conditions. It also features visual navigation without GNSS and automatic target acquisition. At Helsing, autonomy is viewed as the foundation of the product’s operation, enabling the military to continue carrying out missions even when conventional communication and navigation systems are unavailable.

DON’T TOUCH MY SANCTUARY ! (Guess what happens when the one miraculous lifeline that saved a church after its biggest failure nearly two centuries ago and became its most distinctive doctrine… now threatens to become its most biblically undefendable millstone ?)

There is a sanctuary in heaven, the true tabernacle that the Lord set up and not humans. In it Christ ministers on our behalf… In 1844, at the end of the prophetic period of 2300 days, He entered the second and last phase of His atoning ministry… It is a work of investigative judgment which is part of the ultimate disposition of all sin, typified by the cleansing of the ancient Hebrew sanctuary on the Day of Atonement.

Adventist fundamental beliefs (1980)

Seventh-day Adventists accept the Bible as their only creed and hold certain fundamental beliefs to be the teaching of the Holy Scriptures. These beliefs, as set forth here, constitute the church’s understanding and expression of the teaching of Scripture. Revision of these statements may be expected at a General Conference Session when the church is led by the Holy Spirit to a fuller understanding of Bible truth or finds better language in which to express the teachings of God’s Holy Word.

Adventist fundamental beliefs (2015)

As Adventists, many of our "unique" doctrines are not, really, unique. After all, other Christians (not many, admittedly) into greater focus. keep the seventh-day Sabbath, as well. Though a majority of the Christian world believes in the immortality of the soul, other Christians understand that the dead sleep in the grave until the resurrection, either the first or second. Various "Adventist" teachings, i.e., eternal destruction (as opposed to eternal torment) or the nature of the millennium, can be found elsewhere too. In fact, almost all our doctrines are scattered throughout Christendom. Except one: the 1844 pre-Advent judgment. For some, this fact is worrisome; Why don't more Christians see it, as well? For others, the uniqueness of the doctrine points even more powerfully to the special calling of the Seventh-day Adventist Church. It's precisely because no one else teaches this judgment that we have been raised to do so. From this doctrine, perhaps more than any other, our distinct identity as Seventh-day Adventists arises.

Sabbath School quarterly (2006)

The [sanctuary] doctrine is, to me, the most colossal, psychological, face-saving phenomenon in religious history. … We personally do not believe that there is even a suspicion of a verse in Scripture to sustain such a peculiar position, and we further believe that any effort to establish it is stale, flat, and unprofitable.

Donald Grey Barnhouse (Are Seventh-day Adventists Christians? A New Look at Seventh-Day Adventism, Eternity magazine, 1956)

With the traditional Adventist interpretation of Daniel 8:14 as thesis, the historic-linguistic-contextual method of exegesis, which stands in opposition to it at practically every point, is its antithesis. (…) Our interpretational thesis and methodological antithesis are as impossible and mutually exclusive as matter and anti-matter and have the potential of mutually destroying each other, and the church as well. While Adventist Bible scholars have adopted the historical method, the church, as a whole, still basically practices the proof text method. Unresolved this dichotomy could have unfortunate consequences. The only way to resolve a problem such as this, is to find synthesis on a higher level of understanding.

Raymond F. Cottrell (A Hermeneutic for Daniel 8:14, 1980)

Time and again competent non-Adventist Bible scholars have acknowledged that there is a biblical basis for cardinal points of Adventist faith such as the Sabbath, the second Advent and the nature of man. But without exception… they denounce our interpretation of Daniel 8:14 as eisegesis of the worst sort… Seventh-day Adventists identify the sanctuary mentioned in Daniel 8:14 as the sanctuary in heaven… and they understand its cleansing as the blotting out of the confessed sins of God’s repentant people during the course of an investigative judgment, on an antitypical day of atonement that began in 1844. … Adventist teachings that cluster around Daniel 8:14 have proved to be an impassible barrier to the thoughtful consideration of the Advent message… The date 1844… is pivotal of SDA faith. Destroy these and certain conclusions are self-evident. There would be no adequate basis for the existence of SDA. … The invariable rule appears to be that the more a non-Adventist knows about the Bible, the less disposed he is to look with favor on the Adventist interpretation of Daniel 8:14… The first major incentive to devote serious attention to the problem in Daniel 8:14 arose during the course of editing the Seventh-day Adventist Bible Commentary… Within a few months after the publication of Volume 4… came the series of protracted doctrinal discussions with Walter R. Martin and Donald Grey Barnhouse. … Finally, in 1958… I wrote to 27 leading Adventist Bible scholars… All 27 responded… A careful analysis… made evident that we had no satisfactory answer to the criticisms… Not one of the 27 believed that there was a linguistic or contextual basis for applying Daniel 8:14 to the heavenly sanctuary, an antitypical day of atonement, or 1844. As a result… a select “Committee on Problems in the Book of Daniel” [was appointed]… The majority and the minority both reached the same conclusions, but by different routes. … As a result of this impasse, the committee finally agreed to issue no formal report… My study… concluded that… the sanctuary of Daniel 8:14 is the same sanctuary referred to in verses 11-13, that is, the ancient temple in Jerusalem; that the “cleansing” or “restoration”… constituted its purification and rededication after desecration by the little horn… I believe that the hermeneutical principles outlined above provided an adequate inspired basis for applying the 2,300 evenings-mornings to 2,300 literal years terminating in 1844… Let it be clearly understood that the hermeneutic here proposed in no way alters the teachings we have traditionally based on Daniel 8:14. It does not affect the content of these teachings, but the method by which they are established as truth… In arriving at these conclusions, William Miller and other early Adventists basically followed the proof text method… The proof text method is basically what Bible scholars call eisegesis… The death of Ellen White in 1915 confronted Seventh-day Adventists with a major problem in their study of the Bible. Over the next two or three decades, we would often hear someone say wistfully, “I wish Sister White were here, then we could ask her.” But she was no longer here, in person, and without her the old proof text method was no longer viable. At the 1919 Bible conference in Washington, D.C., four years later, the Bible scholars and administrators of the church momentarily faced up to the problem, and from the transcript of their discussion it is evident that the door to a solution of the problem of the relation of Ellen White to the Bible briefly stood ajar. But instead of courageously going through the open door and fully exploring the uncharted region beyond, the church timorously closed it and elected to follow an obscurantist policy that kept it closed for another 20 years or so. Instead, the church chose to accord the voluminous writings of Ellen White the same role she had filled in person for 70 years, and began to use her writings to determine points of exegesis. “Sister White says . . .” was supposed to settle every difference of opinion as the meaning of a passage of Scripture on which she commented, despite the fact that she had repeatedly protested against such use of her writings. The problem in using her writings to determine the meaning of Scripture lay in the fact that she used the Bible in many different modes, all the way from comment on a passage in context, recognizing its inherent meaning, to borrowing the words of Scripture to set forth truth in no way related to the original import of the words. Furthermore, the church began to apply the proof text method to her writings as it was already doing to the Bible, and the inherent weaknesses of that method often produced a variety of interpretations of what Ellen White meant by what she wrote. As a result, people could quote Ellen White on both sides of a moot question, sometimes in apparent contradiction of herself. The upshot of this unwise attitude toward the writings of Ellen White was that, whereas her living presence had compensated for the inherent weaknesses of the proof text method and was a strong force for unity in the church, this misuse of her writings—of which she herself disapproved—became a potent source of disunity. It opened up a can of theological worms, some of which are still crawling about. Willingness on the part of the church to go through the hermeneutical door that momentarily stood ajar in 1919 would have spared us many a needless doctrinal debate and many an unnecessary personal heartache in the years since then.  (...) During the 1930s Adventist college Bible teachers began to make consistent use of the historical-linguistic-contextual method… During the 1930s Adventist college Bible teachers began to make consistent use of the historical-linguistic-contextual method… By the mid-1930s we were far up a theological cul de sac… For 25 years or more, the Bible scholars of the church have been well aware of the exegetical problems our conventional interpretation of Daniel 8:14… encounters… Non-Adventist critics… object that it cannot be derived from the words of Scripture but is superimposed upon them. … The problem is clear, especially if one remembers the unanimous acknowledgment of leading Adventist biblical scholars, clearly expressed in the 1958 poll, that there is no linguistic or contextual basis for our traditional interpretation of this passage. … A conclusive case for the heavenly sanctuary and a pre-Advent judgment can be made directly from Scripture, wholly apart from Daniel 8:14 and Hebrews 9… Can we not be willing to rely on these other passages…?"

Raymond F. Cottrell ("Sanctuary Debate: A Question of Method", 1980)

Raymond has suggested to us a "way out" from the "dilemma" our denomination is now supposed to be caught in. That is an escape mechanism based on a theory of the most "miraculous" our Church has ever been placed in front of.” (…) Cottrell is referring to the increasing impossibility of harmonizing the actual contents of some contents of some Biblical texts with what our pioneers and the Spirit of Prophecy writings were once induced to put down, firmly and securely, as landmarks of our official creed. Brother Cottrell never tires of repeating that the large majority of these modern SDA Bible scholars agree wholeheartedly with him regarding the problem aspect of fundamental statements made by Ellen White in, for instance, absolutely decisive chapters of the Great Controversy. Here Cottrell is not one bit less emphatic than Brinsmead and Ford, that objective scholarliness opens a gulf of disparity between The Bible and Ellen White. But it is in the suggested "remedy" to this situation Cottrell manifests the uniqueness of his spirit. It is his "solution" that is without a rival in the history of Seventh-day Adventism. By and large, Protestants have never acquired any fame comparable to that of Catholics for what theology and philosophy have called "reconciliatio oppositorum" or "complexio oppositorum". In fact it is rather secular philosophy -- and not at all traditional religion -- that has developed the habit of astonishing the world of thinking men by having the boldness to blow up the virtual problem of mutually exclusive stand-points into thin air. (…) But what is his "solution" really like then, in this concrete instance? How does Cottrell manage to still defend the doctrine of inerrancy regarding the teachings coming to us through Ellen G. White's ministry? Nobody, you see, is more emphatic in extolling Ellen White as the great prophetess par excellence of the people of God in the endtime. Therefore, he says, we must accept what her message has handed down to us in terms of basic landmarks for our faith as the very truth, the full truth and nothing but the truth. But then how come that Ellen White apparently can permit herself to go so boldly against certain things the Bible says about Christ's ministry in the sanctuary? For here, as we recall, Cottrell is more emphatic maybe than anybody else, pointing out the great superiority of, according to Cottrell, the modern research method. The modern researchers' accurate knowledge was, according to Cottrell, arrived at for the simple reason that they applied the historicolinguistic method of exegesis. This has led them to conclusions quite opposite to those expressed solemnly and categorically by Ellen White in the Great Controversy. But how then can the Prophetess, with "her" now classical doctrines about 1844 and the Investigative Judgement dare to go contrary to the "evident" testimony of the Scriptures? Cottrell's explanation is scaringly simple and straightforward: Ellen White, in her capacity as the great Prophetess of the endtime has a right to do all this. She is divinely entitled to reinterpret prophecies of the Bible in accordance with God's special intentions in the endtime. "Parallel instances" of this kind are referred to, for instance Paul's "innovating interpretations" of statements in the Old Testament. To the first century Christians such OT prophecies constituted the treasury from which they had to draw.

Carsten Johnsen (1982)

The traditional interpretation of Daniel 8:14 with its sanctuary and investigative judgment, which gave birth to Seventh-day Adventism and accounts for its existence as a distinct entity within Christendom, has been the object of more criticism and debate, by both Adventists and non-Adventists, than all other facets of its belief system combined. (...) they were following the flawed principles of the prooftext method: (1) In four major instances they adopted translation errors where the KJV misrepresents the Hebrew text. (2) They completely ignored the literary context in which Daniel 8:14 occurs. (3) They likewise ignored the historical context specified by the first six chapters and chapter 9:1-19 of the book. (...) In the years immediately following October 22, 1844 the traditional sanctuary doctrine was an important asset for stabilizing the faith of disappointed Adventists. Today it is an equally significant liability and deterrent to the faith, confidence, and salvation of biblically literate Adventists and non-Adventists alike. It was present truth following the great disappointment on October 22, 1844. It is not present truth in the year of our Lord 2002. Quod erat demonstrandum!

Raymond F. Cottrell (The Sanctuary Doctrine – Asset or Liability?, 2002)

Then I heard one saint speaking, and another saint said unto that certain saint which spake, How long shall be the vision concerning the daily sacrifice, and the transgression of desolation, to give both the sanctuary and the host to be trodden under foot? Daniel 8: 13-14 (KJV)

Then I heard one angel ask another, “How long will these things that were seen in the vision continue? How long will an awful sin replace the daily sacrifices? How long will the army of heaven and the Temple be trampled on?” I heard the other angel answer, “It will continue for 2,300 evenings and mornings, during which sacrifices will not be offered. Then the Temple will be restored.

Daniel 8: 13-14 (Good News)

And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day.

Genesis 1:5

And he shall make an atonement for the holy place, because of the uncleanness of the children of Israel, and because of their transgressions in all their sins.

Then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary. (...) text:
The Mass is not merely “another style of worship.”
At its doctrinal center stands a claim the Reformation could not treat as harmless: that the Eucharistic sacrifice is truly propitiatory and is offered for the living and the dead.
That is why Knox could say:
“One mass is more fearful to me, than if ten thousand armed enemies were landed in any part of the realm.”
Dramatic?
Yes.
But understand the logic.
An invading army may threaten your body.
A false gospel threatens the soul.
Hebrews does not present Christ as a priest whose sacrifice must be continually represented as propitiatory.
It says:
“By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.” — Hebrews 10:14
And again:
“Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.” — Hebrews 10:18
That is the horror the Reformers saw.
Not candles.
Not vestments.
Not ancient liturgy.
The horror was placing anything alongside the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ in the matter of atonement.
Calvary does not need completion.
Christ does not need to be offered again.
His blood is sufficient.
His sacrifice is finished.
His priesthood is perfect.
So when Rome speaks of the Mass as a true propitiatory sacrifice, the Reformed Christian should not shrug and say, “Different tradition.”
No.
This strikes at the heart of the gospel.
Christ offered Himself once.
Once.
And that “once” is glorious enough to save every one of His people forever.
-Cody Hurd
The Pilgrim’s Post

text:
4 Ways To Monetize Kohl's Real Estate:

Last month Kohl’s $KSS sold a retail site in Coconut Creek, FL for the eye popping price of $53.5 MM

On it sat a ~90K sq ft building that Kohl’s had operated as a retail store for nearly two decades 

But when Baptist Health South Florida made a strong offer, Kohl’s was a seller

At ~$600 per square foot

This transaction elicits the natural question:

How much is Kohl's real estate portfolio actually worth?

But perhaps the more important question is what current options exist to monetize the real estate

Kohl's operates ~1,185 retail stores 

~70% consist of its ~90K sq ft prototype building--the same property type that it just sold to Baptist Health

400 of these sites are owned outright by Kohls

Another ~250 are “ground leases” where Kohl’s owns its building on leased land 

The remaining 535 or so stores are in buildings leased from others, including shopping center owners

Option 1:  Sell To Another User

This scenario is an easy one

If a strong offer is received from another user, take it!

For instance we do not know the performance metrics of Kohl’s Coconut Creek, FL location but let us assume that the store’s “4 wall” annual operating profit was ~$1 MM

Another user offers 50 years worth of store level profits?  

Take it and move on

Option 2: Sell (or Lease) Part Of The Parking Field

The vast majority of Kohl’s stores are located on land parcels of 8 acres (or more)

Many are situated in open air shopping centers with ~13% of sites are in freestanding buildings

One thing that is true with nearly all sites:

They have much more parking than the store actually needs

That means there is plenty room to lease or sell portions of the parking area to other users such as QSRs

Like a Kohl’s-owned site in Northville, MI where the Company sold an unused section of its east parking lot to Chick-Fil-A

Option 3: Downsize And Lease A Portion Of Building For Another Use  

Kohl's has experimented with other store types—some as small as 35K sq ft as well as suites of 55K and even 64K sq ft

As recently as 2025 CFO Jill Timm noted that Kohl’s was “focusing and centering ourselves on the retailer’s 55K square foot” prototype and was looking to downsize larger stores to improve store productivity

Kohl’s came to a similar conclusion under a previous management team and downsized portions of its owned stores in certain markets

In 2018 Kohl’s formed partnerships with Aldi and Planet Fitness $PLNT which allowed the companies to take space left over by the downsizing of a Kohl’s store

The first such Kohl’s-Aldi combo store in Waukesha, WI opened in 2019

Close to two dozen other Kohl’s stores have also been downsized and paired with Aldi, Planet Fitness and other tenants such as the short-lived Amazon Fresh grocery store chain 

That subdivision template can likely be applied by Kohl’s to many of its other sites

Option 4: Assign—And Sell—Leaseholds To Other Users

>700 of Kohl’s stores are leased—and many of these leaseholds have “positive value”

What this means is the current market rent for some Kohl’s leased sites is higher than the contractual rent that it is obligated to pay

This results in a “leasehold premium” that Kohl’s could theoretically monetize by selling leases, subleasing a portion of its leased premises or even borrowing against the leasehold value

This is particularly true with the ~250 “ground leased” sites where Kohl’s pays rent for its use of the ground but owns its building on the leased land

Ground rents are typically much lower than building rents because Kohl’s—and not the property owner—funded and constructed the building

These ground leases often include decades of option terms that can be exercised for relatively short intervals and with minimal rent increases

If Kohl’s subleased these stores to other users at market rent it could capture the “spread,” or the difference between market rent and the payments due under the ground lease, for the remaining lease term

Another option:

Kohl’s could also sell leases to users for an upfront sum

Either way, there are plenty of ways to monetize Kohl’s portfolio of leased sites just like there is for its owned properties

The bottom line?

Much of Kohl's real estate and leases have significant value

Even better--there are immediate opportunities for Kohl's management to monetize these assets in a variety of ways

The only question is whether they will accelerate their efforts to actually do so.
