• The Bucks have rescheduled their October 23 home opener from 7 p.m. to 3 p.m. Central time. The organization worked with the NBA to avoid a direct scheduling conflict with Game 1 of the World Series.

• The Brewers are making their first World Series appearance since 1982 after sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NL Championship Series. Milwaukee finished the regular season with an MLB-best 103 wins, securing home-field advantage throughout the postseason.

• The Bucks could face another scheduling conflict on October 31, when they are scheduled to host Cleveland. A potential World Series Game 7 would also take place in Milwaukee that evening if the series reaches seven games.

The Bucks open their regular season Wednesday at Washington before returning home Friday.

For Milwaukee sports fans, October 23 now offers an unusual opportunity to watch their NBA team and World Series baseball on the same day.

Congratulations to UCLA Pathology's Dr. Shino Magaki, Dr. Jason Sinclair, Kazu Williams, Adrian Murillo, Su Aung, Dr. Jeffrey Goldstein, Dr. Diana Vulcain, Dr. Michael Fishbein, and Dr. Harry Vinters on their publication in Neurobiology of Aging “Neuropathology of Centenarians and Supercentenarians: An Autopsy Study.”

The publication offers insight into aging and neuropathologic substrates of cognitive impairment at the extreme limits of age. Examining postmortem brain tissue from centenarians and supercentenarians, individuals aged 99-115, researchers identified variable degrees of Alzheimer disease neuropathologic change (ADNC) and a high frequency of aging-related tau astrogliopathy (ARTAG), limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy neuropathologic change (LATE-NC), hippocampal sclerosis, and cerebrovascular disease. 

While the study is small and does not establish causation, the findings suggest that multiple pathologic lesions likely underlie cognitive impairment in the oldest-old.

text:
Śubh Navrātri,
Śubh Ṣaṣṭhi Day 6 – Kātyāyanī

Devi Kātyāyanī, one of the avatars of Mā Śakti is worshipped on this day. As per Śrimad Bhāgvata Pūrāṇa, young eligible ladies in Gokula observed fast during the month of Mārghaśīrṣa and offered prayers to Goddess Kātyāyanī to get Bhagwān Kṛṣṇa as their consort. Mā Kātyāyanī is one of the highly revered forms of Mā Durgā, which signifies cheerfulness and joy. Believed to be the destroyer of all evil, she is seen as a warrior goddess who was able to bring peace to the world.

As per Pūrāṇa, long ago there was a Riṣi Kātyāyana. He was a stout devotee of Goddess Śakti. Riṣi Kātyāyana always wished for Devi Śakti to be born as his daughter.

During this period, an evil demon named Mahisāṣura was creating great trouble for the Gods. With time he gained more power and the Gods were increasingly worried about him. They prayed to Devi Śakti to save them from the wrath of Mahisāṣura.

Devi Śakti decided to take birth to end the reign of Mahisāṣura. She granted the wish of Riṣi Kātyāyana and was born on Earth as his daughter. She grew up to be a strong, beautiful fighter and came to be known as Kātyāyanī.

One day, Chandhā and Mundhā, two messengers of Mahisāṣura, saw Kātyāyanī and were mesmerized by her beauty. They went back to their master and told him all about Kātyāyanī. Mahisāṣura became happy and asked Dundubhi, another messenger, to go and talk to Kātyāyanī.

Dundubhi met Kātyāyanī and told her all about Mahisāṣura and his greatness. He told Kātyāyanī that she should marry Mahisāṣura as they would make a great couple. Kātyāyanī smiled and told Dundubhi that according to her family tradition, Mahisāṣura must first defeat her in battle. Only then can they both get married. Dundubhi went back to Mahisāṣura and told him about this challenge. Mahisāṣura agreed and soon the preparations began.

A fierce battle took place between Kātyāyanī and Mahisāṣura. She managed to defeat his demon soldiers and even killed most of them. When Kātyāyanī and Mahisāṣura came face to face, he transformed himself into a buffalo. This proved to be a real challenge for Kātyāyanī as she struggled to fight him.
However, Kātyāyanī tricked Mahisāṣura and climbed onto his back. He was surprised by this move and tried very hard to shake her off but failed. Kātyāyanī then placed her foot on the back of his neck, pierced him with her Trishul (trident), and cut his head off.

This is how Mā Kātyāyanī killed the evil and powerful demon Mahisāṣura. In doing so, she saved the Gods from his menace and brought peace back into this world.

Śarad Navrātri 2026
Day 5 – Mā Skandmāta

Devi Pārvati in her stage of motherhood as ‘Skandmāta’ is worshipped on the fifth day of Navrātri.

Lakṣmi represents not only material wealth but also a wealth of virtues that must be cultivated to attain wisdom. 

Ādi Śaṅkarācārya names six forms of wealth (ṣat sampatti) as calmness of mind (शमः), self-control (दमः), self-withdrawal (उपरमः), forbearance (तितिक्षा), faith (श्रद्धा) and single-pointedness of the mind (समाधानं). Without these virtues, victory over the mind is not possible. This victory comes only when the mind is prepared and the worshipping Mā Lakṣmi symbolises this mental purification.

Skandmāta blesses us with Moksha, power, prosperity, and treasures.

text:
Śarad Navrātri 
Day 4 – Mā Kuśmandā

Once all the evil tendencies in the mind are destroyed by worshipping the divine feminine aspect of Goddess Durgā, the mind is ready to gain noble virtues. Goddess Lakṣmi is the Goddess of wealth.

For knowledge to dawn within us, we have to prepare our minds. The mind must be pure and concentrated. This purification of the mind is attained through the worship of Goddess Lakṣmi. Lakṣmi is not only a Goddess of material wealth, as per general belief, but of inner wealth of spiritual values.

On Day 4, she is worshipped as Mā Kuśmandā. Kuśmandā, a Sanskrit word is made up of ‘Ku’ meaning ‘a little; ‘uśma’ meaning ‘warmth’, and ‘anḍa’ meaning ‘cosmic egg’. As per purāṇa, she is considered the creator of the Universe.

Mā Kuṣmandā’s story begins at a time when there was nothing. The entire Universe was empty; there was no sign of life and darkness prevailed everywhere. Suddenly, a ray of divine light appeared and slowly illuminated everything. Initially, this divine light was formless and had no particular shape. However, soon it started taking a clear size and finally, it took the form of a Lady. This divine lady, the first being of the Universe, was Mā Kuṣmandā.

text:
In the crisp air of Alaska's political season, iVoterGuide emerges as a beacon for conservative voters seeking clarity amid the fog of campaign promises. Through detailed questionnaires, it rates candidates across federal, state, and legislative races on a scale stretching from Verified Liberal to Verified Conservative, incorporating factors like public records, endorsements from various groups, and responses to queries on pivotal issues such as the sanctity of life, religious freedoms, educational policies, and the integrity of elections. This approach allows for a nuanced assessment that goes beyond mere labels, aiming to illuminate where each contender truly stands on matters from protecting women's sports to countering foreign threats and preserving parental rights in an era of shifting social tides. 

Yet the participation rates tell their own story, with numerous candidates citing insufficient information or simply bypassing the survey altogether, much like sidestepping a particularly persistent raven on the trail. The guide draws from conservative and liberal scorecards alike, campaign finance data, and its own foundational principles around family, stewardship, and liberty to construct these evaluations. Some answers prove detailed and revealing while others leave gaps that force reliance on secondary trails of evidence, underscoring how the process rewards those willing to engage directly rather than hide behind vague public personas. 

As in-person absentee voting commences on October 19 and runs through November 2, with election day polls open from dawn to dusk on November 3, this tool offers a practical aid for those preparing to cast ballots in a no-excuse absentee state. Deadlines for mail requests loom on October 24, underscoring the need for timely engagement with such guides to ensure informed choices in the upcoming contest.

text:
October 16, 1914: Appeal Made By Leo Frank For New Trial Turned Down By Georgia Supreme Court 

Reading Time: 9 minutes, [1439 words]

The Atlanta Constitution, Thursday, 15th October 1914, PAGE 1, COLUMN 3 AND 4.

With All Justices Concurring, Highest Court Tribunal Hands Down Opinion Denying Motion Based on Newly Discovered Grounds. Leo M. Frank, convicted of the murder of Mary Phagan, yesterday lost another point in his fight for liberty when the Supreme Court handed down an opinion denying his motion for a new trial on the ground of newly-discovered evidence. Frank's last stand in the courts will be based on the motion to set aside the verdict on constitutional grounds. This motion was carried to the Supreme Court several months ago at the same time the extraordinary motion was made. It will be argued before the Supreme Court justices October 26. This is the second time the Supreme Court has refused to interfere in the Frank case. The first motion carried before that tribunal was that for a new trial founded on the plea that Frank's trial had been misconducted and was influenced by mob element.

Last Stand in Court. The motion before the Supreme Court, based on constitutional grounds, was presented by John L. Tye, of the law firm of Tye, Peeples & Jordan. It was carried before Judge Ben Hill, of the criminal division of Superior Court, for a hearing. Solicitor Dorsey, instead of fighting the motion directly, filed a demurrer in rebuttal. Judge Hill upheld the demurrer, permitting the motion to go up to the Supreme Court by this route. Solicitor Dorsey's demurrer was based on the ground that the motion had not been filed at the proper time in accordance with time-honored practice. It was on this ground that Judge Hill acted. Therefore, if the Supreme Court upon coming to a decision on the constitutional motion holds the defense and grants a new hearing, the case will be sent back to Judge Hill for a second trial. Then the solicitor general would have to combat the motion directly. In the event the Supreme Court grants a new hearing it may go back to the Supreme Court again. For should Judge Hill deny it, Frank's defense will be permitted to send the motion right back to the same tribunal.

Motion Is Overruled. In ruling on the extraordinary motion, the Supreme Court has this to say: "An extraordinary motion for a new trial on the ground of newly-discovered evidence is addressed to the sound discretion of the trial judge and a refusal to grant it will not be reversed unless such discretion is abused. On the hearing of such a motion the court may hear affidavits making a counter showing on behalf of the state, so as to go to the bottom of the showing and show, if possible, how much of real substance and merit there is in the alleged new evidence." The John L. Tye motion is based entirely on the constitutional ground that Frank's personal rights were taken from him when he was not present when the verdict was received against him. It is the one phase of the case on which his counsel expects to carry their battle to the Supreme Court of the United States if necessary.

Ruling of Court. That ruling of the Supreme Court Wednesday, in full, follows: "32 Criminal, March T., 1914. Frank v. State." "1. After a person accused of crime has been convicted and a new trial has been affirmed by this court, an extraordinary motion for a new trial on the ground of newly-discovered evidence is addressed to the sound discretion of the trial judge (there being certain general rules as to evidence of particular kinds, and as diligence, etc.), and a refusal to grant a new trial on such a motion, will not be reversed unless such discretion is abused." "In view of the nature of the alleged newly-discovered evidence on the basis of which an extraordinary motion for a new trial was made in the present case, and of the strong counter showing made by the state in regard to it, there was no abuse of discretion on the part of the trial judge in refusing to grant a new trial; nor was there error in overruling the motion on any of the grounds set out therein." "Leo M. Frank was indicted for the murder of Mary Phagan and was found guilty. He moved for a new trial on numerous grounds. Among them was the ground that the verdict was contrary to law and the evidence, as well as attacks on various rulings of the trial court. This motion was heard by the judge before whom the trial took place. It invoked a decision from him both as to whether he had committed any error of law which required a new trial, and also, whether, in the exercise of a sound discretion under the facts of the case, he should grant a new trial.

New Evidence Offered. "He overruled the motion for a new trial. The case was brought to the Supreme Court by a Bill of Exceptions, where the judgment was affirmed, 141 Ga., 243. A rehearing in the Supreme Court was asked and denied. After this the defendant made what is termed an extraordinary motion for a new trial under a civil code (1910), sections 6089, 6092, based on the ground of newly-discovered evidence. The first cited of these two sections discloses that, 'all applications for a new trial, except in extraordinary cases, must be made during the term at which the trial was held,' etc. The latter of the two sections provides, among other things, that, 'whenever a motion for a new trial shall have been made at the term of trial in any criminal case in this state, and overruled, or when a motion for a new trial has not been made at such term, in either event no motion for a new trial from the same verdict shall ever be made or received, unless the same be an extraordinary motion, or case, such as is provided for in section 6089 of this code.'" "On the hearing of the application a number of affidavits were introduced for the purpose of sustaining the motion. On behalf of the state a vigorous counter-showing was made. This extraordinary motion was heard before a different trial judge than the one who had previously overruled the first motion for a new trial. After hearing evidence on behalf of the movant and the state, the judge overruled the extraordinary motion. The case has again been brought to this court by a Bill of Exceptions assigning error on that judgment."

Brown Case Cited. "The statutory expression, 'an extraordinary motion or case,' the nature of such a motion and the discretionary power of the trial judge who passed upon it, have been so recently considered in Brown v. State, 141 Ga., 783, that it is not necessary to enter into a discussion of them here. Omitting numbering, the first two headnotes of that case read as follows: 'After one accused of crime has been convicted, and has made a motion for a new trial, and the judgment denying it has been affirmed by this court, when an extraordinary motion for a new trial is made, based on the ground of newly-discovered evidence, it should be made to appear that such evidence is so material that it would probably produce a different verdict. An extraordinary motion for a new trial on the grounds of newly-discovered evidence is addressed to the sound discretion of the trial judge, and a refusal to grant it will not be reversed unless such discretion is abused. On the hearing of such a motion, the court may hear affidavits making a counter-showing on behalf of the state, so as to go to the bottom of the showing and discover, if possible, how much of real substance and merit there is in the alleged new evidence.'" "We deem it unnecessary to take up each of the grounds of the motion and discuss them separately; in the light of the evidence offered in support of them, it cannot be held that the discretion of the presiding judge, in refusing to grant the extraordinary motion, was abused, or that a case is made requiring a reversal."In addition to the case above cited, see in this connection Civil Code (1910) sections 6085, 6086; Mithechell v. White, 74 Ga., 327 (5); Clark v. State, 117 Ga. 254 (8); Jenks v. State, 117 Ga. 714; Duggan v. State, 124 Ga., 438 (1); Burge v. State, 133 Ga. 431; Norman v. Goode, 121 Ga., 449.

Judgment affirmed. All the justices concur. 

(Tags: True Crime, Justice)

text:
Autumn Winds

Spirit blowing where He chooses

The Verse

John chapter three verse eight

The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.

From the English Standard Version of the Holy Bible

Opening Prayer

Sovereign Father who sends the wind where it wishes and who gives new birth by the Spirit we quiet our hearts before You this day. In the turning of the season when autumn winds rise and move across the fields without asking leave we confess how often we try to chart the paths of Your Spirit or to choose the places where He must work. Teach us to receive the mystery of His free blowing. Let the truth of John chapter three verse eight steady our souls and fill us with humble wonder through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Big Idea

Jesus is speaking with Nicodemus about the new birth. The ruler of the Jews has asked how a man can be born when he is old. Jesus answers with the necessity of being born of water and the Spirit. Then He reaches for the wind. John chapter three verse eight declares the truth. The wind blows where it wishes and you hear its sound but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit. The Spirit is not managed by human calculation. His movements are free. His sound is heard. His origin and destination remain beyond our mapping. Those who are born of the Spirit share in that same freedom and that same mystery. The autumn wind that rises without permission and moves across the fields is a living picture. The Spirit of God is not bound by our schedules or our explanations. He blows where He chooses and those born of Him live under the same sovereign freedom.

Thematic Sections

One: The Wind Blows Where It Wishes

Scripture: John chapter three verse eight

The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.

From the English Standard Version of the Holy Bible

Takeaway: The first truth is the freedom of the Spirit. The wind blows where it wishes. No human hand directs its path. No calendar dictates its rising. It moves according to its own will. Jesus uses this ordinary reality to teach the freedom of the Holy Spirit in the work of new birth. The Spirit is not summoned by religious technique or constrained by human expectation. He acts according to the sovereign purpose of God. The autumn wind that suddenly cools a warm afternoon and sends leaves swirling does not ask permission of the fields it crosses. In the same way the Spirit of God blows where He chooses among the sons and daughters of men. This freedom is not chaos. It is the ordered liberty of the third person of the Trinity who does all things according to the counsel of the Father and the Son. Those who are born of the Spirit are therefore people who live under a power that cannot be domesticated or scheduled by the flesh.

Practice: Identify one place where you have tried to predict or control the work of the Spirit in your own life or in the life of another. Speak the words the wind blows where it wishes. Then release that place into the freedom of the Spirit who blows where He chooses.

Two: You Hear Its Sound but You Do Not Know Where It Comes From or Where It Goes

Scripture: John chapter three verse eight

The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.

From the English Standard Version of the Holy Bible

Takeaway: The second truth is the combination of evidence and mystery. You hear its sound. The wind is not silent. Its presence is known by the rustle of leaves and the movement of air against the face. Yet the origin and the destination remain hidden. You do not know where it comes from or where it goes. The Spirit of God works in the same way. His effects are real and audible in the changed life the new affections and the growing obedience of those who are born of Him. Yet the precise path of His arriving and the full course of His future work remain beyond human tracing. This guards the heart from both despair and presumption. The sound is real so that faith has something to hear. The mystery remains so that pride has no map to claim. The autumn wind that moves through the trees is heard and felt yet never fully charted by the one who stands beneath it. In the same way the Spirit leaves unmistakable evidence while keeping the deeper movements of His grace under the covering of divine freedom.

Practice: Recall one clear evidence of the Spirits work in your life that you can hear as sound. Then acknowledge one area where the origin or the future path of that work remains hidden from you. Speak the words you hear its sound but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes and rest in the combination of certainty and mystery.

Three: So It Is with Everyone Who Is Born of the Spirit

Scripture: John chapter three verse eight

The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.

From the English Standard Version of the Holy Bible

Takeaway: The final clause brings the metaphor home to the person. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit. The same freedom that marks the wind marks the one who has been made new by the Spirit. The same combination of evidence and mystery marks the Christian life. Those born of the Spirit are not products of human planning. They are the living result of the Spirits free and sovereign work. Their lives carry the sound of grace that others can hear. Yet the full story of how the Spirit first moved upon them and where He is leading them remains known fully only to God. This truth liberates the believer from the need to explain every detail of conversion or to chart every step of sanctification as if the Spirit required human management. The one born of the Spirit is free to live under the same wind that first made him alive. The autumn field does not control the wind that crosses it. It simply receives the movement and is changed by it. In the same way the believer receives the ongoing freedom of the Spirit who continues to blow where He chooses.

Practice: Choose one ordinary moment today when you feel the pressure to explain or control the work of the Spirit in yourself or in another. Pause and speak the words so it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit. Then walk forward in the freedom of one who has been made alive by a power that remains free.

Christ in John

The Lord Jesus Christ is the One who speaks these words to Nicodemus and the One who later pours out the Spirit upon His people. He is the true and final revelation of the God who gives the Spirit without measure. In His own person the wind of the Spirit was already present without limit. At His baptism the Spirit descended and remained upon Him. In His ministry the Spirit empowered every word and every work. At the cross the Spirit sustained Him through the final obedience. In His resurrection the same Spirit raised Him from the dead. Then on the day of Pentecost the risen Christ poured out the Spirit so that the wind of God might fill the house and rest upon the church. John chapter three verse eight therefore finds its center in Christ. The Spirit blows where He chooses because He is the Spirit of Christ. Those who are born of the Spirit are born through the finished work of the Son. The freedom of the Spirit is not an independent force. It is the freedom of the third person of the Trinity who proceeds from the Father and the Son and who applies the redemption that Christ has accomplished. The autumn wind is only a picture. The true and lasting wind is the Spirit of the risen Lord who continues to move where He wills among those who belong to Him.

Westminster and Reformed Notes

The Westminster Confession of Faith chapter ten teaches that all those whom God has predestinated unto life and those only He is pleased in His appointed and accepted time effectually to call by His Word and Spirit out of that state of sin and death in which they are by nature to grace and salvation by Jesus Christ enlightening their minds spiritually and savingly to understand the things of God taking away their heart of stone and giving unto them a heart of flesh renewing their wills and by His almighty power determining them to that which is good and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ yet so as they come most freely being made willing by His grace. Chapter ten further declares that this effectual call is of Gods free and special grace alone not from anything at all foreseen in man who is altogether passive therein until being quickened and renewed by the Holy Spirit he is thereby enabled to answer this call and to embrace the grace offered and conveyed in it. John chapter three verse eight stands in full harmony with this confession. The wind that blows where it wishes is the free and sovereign Spirit who effectually calls and regenerates according to the purpose of God. Reformed theology therefore refuses to treat the new birth as a work that can be produced or timed by human effort. It is the free movement of the Spirit who makes the dead alive and who continues to work in those whom He has made new. Believers may therefore rest in the certainty that the same Spirit who first blew upon them continues to blow where He chooses and that the sound of His work remains real even when the full path remains hidden.

Short Litany and Prayer

Leader: The wind blows where it wishes.
People: We yield to the freedom of the Spirit.

Leader: You hear its sound but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes.
People: We trust both the evidence and the mystery.

Leader: So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.
People: We live as those made new by His free grace.

Leader: The same Spirit continues to blow where He chooses.
People: We walk in the freedom of the wind of God. Amen.

Closing Exhortation

Beloved the autumn winds of this season will rise and move across the fields without asking leave of the trees they touch. It would be easy to stand beneath them and then return to a life that tries to schedule and explain every movement of the Spirit. Yet the word of God speaks a better word. The wind blows where it wishes and you hear its sound but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit. You are not required to map the path of the Spirit or to produce the new birth by your own power. The same Lord who spoke these words to Nicodemus has already poured out the Spirit through His finished work. Do not despise the ordinary places where the sound of His work is heard while the origin and destination remain hidden. Receive them as the field where the free Spirit continues to blow where He chooses. Walk into this day knowing that the God who sends the wind where it wills is the same God who has made you alive by that wind. The freedom is real. The sound is sure. The mystery remains under His wise care. Live as one born of the Spirit.

Reflection Questions

1. Where have you been tempted to control or predict the movements of the Spirit and how does John chapter three verse eight confront that impulse?

2. How does the combination of hearing the sound of the Spirit while not knowing the origin or destination reshape your expectation of the Christian life?

3. In what ways does the truth that everyone born of the Spirit shares in the same freedom of the wind liberate you from the need to explain every detail of grace?

4. What one concrete step of yielding to the free blowing of the Spirit will you take this week?

5. How does the finished work of Christ as the One who pours out the Spirit free you to rest in both the evidence and the mystery of His ongoing work?

🇪🇺🇺🇦 Unbreakable Europe Task Force: Strengthening Europe’s Security Through Ukraine’s Experience

Europe’s security and resilience are inseparable from Ukraine’s. As Europe faces an increasingly complex security environment, Ukraine’s experience in sustaining governance, critical infrastructure, and essential services under wartime conditions offers vital lessons for strengthening European preparedness.

GMF, together with @NLatEU and in cooperation with the European Coalition for Civil Preparedness and Resilience, convened the first meeting of the Unbreakable Europe Task Force — a European-Ukrainian initiative dedicated to turning Ukraine’s hard-earned experience into practical solutions for Europe's security and resilience. 

The meeting brought together @irenefellin, NATO Secretary General’s Special Representative for Women, Peace and Security; Boriša Falatar, Member of Cabinet of European Commissioner @hadjalahbib; Andrius Purvaneckas, Lithuania’s Resilience Attaché to NATO and the EU; and H.P. Schreinemachers, representing the Permanent Representation of the Netherlands to the EU.

GMF Senior Advisor Valeriia Ivanova introduced the Task Force and its network of more than 20 organizations from 12 European countries, united by a shared commitment to strengthening Europe's ability to prepare for, withstand, and respond to crises.

The first meeting also launched practical work on adapting Ukraine’s wartime lessons to European preparedness systems, with an initial focus on the critical first hour of a major crisis.

Ukraine is not only defending its own security — it is helping shape a safer, more resilient Europe.

text: Naqsh-e Rostam To visit Naqsh-e Rostam, located 56 kilometers northeast of Shiraz, you can easily access this site from Persepolis, with just 6 kilometers separating the two. For those with a personal vehicle, the journey is straightforward: head towards the city of Marvdasht and follow the Marvdasht-Sa’adat Shahr highway to the Persepolis to Istakhr route, also known as the ancient royal road. If driving isn’t an option, one-day tours or taxis represent the best alternatives for reaching Naqsh-e Rostam, offering convenience and the opportunity to explore this historic site without the need for personal transportation.  📷Naghsh-e rostam Within this site, there are four grand tombs belonging, from left to right, to Darius II, Artaxerxes I, Darius I, and Xerxes I. Chronologically, the first bas-relief carving belongs to Darius the Great, followed by Xerxes I, Artaxerxes I, and Darius II. Below these tombs, impressive carvings of Sassanian kings are visible, depicting themes of coronation, victory, and their battles. Directly opposite the tomb of Darius II stands a beautiful, cubic structure known as the Cube of Zoroaster, believed to have been a fire temple or a very sacred place in the past. Other significant parts of this historical site include stone fireplaces, a fortress with protective walls, and a water well. In the ancient complex of Naqsh-e Rostam, there are four tombs from left to right, belonging to Darius II, Artaxerxes I, Darius the Great, and Xerxes.  Tomb of Darius II (420 to 404 BCE)  📷Tomb of artaxerxes i, naqsh-e rostam, shiraz, iran  Located immediately after the tomb of Darius II and about 37 meters from the next tomb (Darius the Great), the facade of Artaxerxes I’s tomb is also cross-shaped and stands 22 meters tall. In this carving, the Faravahar is precisely above the king, with a simple ring around its body, mirroring the depiction in Darius II’s tomb. The king is depicted holding a ring that aligns with the image of the Faravahar, with the sleeves of his garment grasping the ring. Like the other three carvings, the king stands on the Kiani throne, with throne bearers moving the throne. Inside the Tomb of Artaxerxes I The interior of Artaxerxes I’s tomb, modeled after the tomb of Darius the Great, features three chambers. However, a significant difference from Darius’s tomb is the lack of geometric order and proportion in various sections, including the hallways. Speculations suggest the central grave belongs to Artaxerxes I due to its larger size and the greater care taken in its construction. Likely, another grave belongs to Queen Damaspia (wife of Artaxerxes I, mother of Xerxes II), who is said to have died shortly after Artaxerxes I. The third grave is presumed to belong to the chosen successor of the king. Who Was Artaxerxes I?  Artaxerxes I, also known as Artaxerxes III, was the son of Xerxes and the sixth Achaemenid king. When he beg📷phans: 2; text-align: start; text-indent: 0px; text-transform: none; widows: 2; word-spacing: 0px; -webkit-text-stroke-width: 0px; white-space: pre-wrap; background-color: rgb(0, 0, 0); text-decoration-thickness: initial; text-decoration-style: initial; text-decoration-color: initial;">Tomb of Darius the Great, Naqsh-e Rostam, Shiraz, Iran Following the tomb of Artaxerxes I, the tomb of Darius the Great is located, positioned almost centrally at Naqsh-e Rostam. Inscriptions confirm the tomb’s assignment to Darius the Great (Darius I), who likely initiated its construction alongside the Apadana of Susa and Persepolis. Carved 60 meters above ground level, the tomb’s facade is cross-shaped. In this bas-relief, Darius the Great sits on a throne with lion’s paw feet, supported by 28 figures from various lands. Above the king, the Faravahar, or the divine symbol, looms, with the royal fire altar carved beside Darius. The king is dressed in Persian attire, holding a bow in his left hand and extending his right hand toward the fire altar. To Darius’s right, a circle containing a crescent is visible. Additionally, figures carved on either side of the king appear to be his close associates.  Below the bas-relief of the king, the tomb’s entrance is flanked by four pillars with bull-head capitals and a palace design. These carvings suggest the tomb closely resembles the Tachara Palace (Darius the Great’s residence), reflecting the Achaemenid belief in resurrection, hence constructing the tombs to resemble their earthly dwellings. Notably, this tomb stands out for its construction precision and carving delicacy compared to other tombs, with the lower part of the cross-shaped facade polished and smooth to deter access to the tomb. Inside the Tomb of Darius the Great, the mausoleum contains three chambers, each housing three sarcophagus-like graves. It is believed that, apart from the king, eight other close relatives are buried here. The graves do not significantly differ in design or size, making it challenging to identify Darius’s grave among them. However, Erich F. Schmidt, a German-American archaeologist, contends that Queen Atossa (mother of Xerxes, wife of Darius, and daughter of Cyrus the Great) is definitely buried in one of these graves. Who Was Darius the Great? Darius the Great was the third king of the Achaemenid Empire. He ascended to the throne in 522 BCE by killing the magus Gaumata and reigned for 36 years until his natural death at the age of 64. The construction of Parsa (Persepolis) began under his reign but was not completed. During his rule, Darius undertook significant projects like the creation of the canal linking the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, standardizing imperial taxes, establishing the Royal Road, forming the Immortals (the elite army unit), among other services, cementing his legacy as a benevolent figure in human history.  Interesting Fact  According to historical records, on the day Darius the Great completed the construction of his tomb, he asked his parents to visit it. They used a rope to ascend, but it broke, resulting in their fatal fall. Following this tragic event, Darius the Great ordered the execution of those responsible for the accident.  Inscriptions of the Tomb of Darius the Great Two inscriptions in Old Persian, Elamite, and Akkadian are found at the tomb of Darius the Great, serving as a sort of spiritual will for posterity. The first inscription, located above, is known as the DNa inscription, presenting a completely impartial narrative. The second, beside the entrance, known as the DNb inscription, is more personal.  During the Seleucid period, an Aramaic version of Darius’s DNb inscription was added below the Elamite text. Earlier scholarship once speculated that the name “Seleucus” might appear in this addition, but specialists today identify it simply as a later Aramaic rendering of the original Achaemenid text (Frye, 1982; Encyclopaedia Iranica).  📷Dna inscription at naqshe rostam  English translation A great god is Ahura Mazda, who created this earth, who created yonder sky, who created man, who created happiness for man, who made Darius king, one king of many, one lord of many.  I am Darius the great king, king of kings, king of countries containing all kinds of men, king in this great earth far and wide, son of Hystaspes, an Achaemenid, a Persian, son of a Persian, an Aryan, having Aryan lineage.  King Darius says: By the favor of Ahuramazda these are the countries which I seized outside of Persia; I ruled over them; they bore tribute to me; they did what was said to them by me; they held my law firmly; Media, Elam, Parthia, Aria, Bactria, Sogdia, Chorasmia, Drangiana, Arachosia, Sattagydia, Gandara [Gadâra], India [Hiduš], the haoma-drinking Scythians, the Scythians with pointed caps, Babylonia, Assyria, Arabia, Egypt, Armenia, Cappadocia, Lydia, the Greeks (Yauna), the Scythians across the sea (Sakâ), Thrace, the petasos-wearing Greeks [Yaunâ], the Libyans, the Nubians, the men of Maka and the Carians. King Darius says: Ahuramazda, when he saw this earth in commotion, thereafter bestowed it upon me, made me king; I am king. By the favor of Ahuramazda I put it down in its place; what I said to them, that they did, as was my desire. If now you shall think that “How many are the countries which King Darius held?” look at the sculptures [of those] who bear the throne, then shall you know, then shall it become known to you: the spear of a Persian man has gone forth far; then shall it become known to you: a Persian man has delivered battle far indeed from Persia.  Darius the King says: This which has been done, all that by the will of Ahuramazda I did. Ahuramazda bore me aid, until I did the work. May Ahuramazda protect me from harm, and my royal house, and this land: this I pray of Ahuramazda, this may Ahuramazda give to me!  O man, that which is the command of Ahuramazda, let this not seem repugnant to you; do not leave the right path; do not rise in rebellion!  — DNa inscription of Darius I.  Tomb of Xerxes (circa 465 BCE)  📷Tomb of Xerxes, Naqsh-e Rostam, Shiraz, Iran  The tomb of Xerxes is situated at the easternmost point of the mountain, approximately 100 meters away from the tomb of Darius the Great. Its cross-shaped design and the thematic elements of its reliefs closely resemble those of Darius the Great’s tomb. The king is depicted sitting on the royal throne, with people from various lands (from India to Egypt and Libya) bearing it. A Faravahar is engraved above the king, with a royal fire altar in front of him, towards which the king is extending his hand.  Inside the Tomb of Xerxes  The entrance to the tomb stands about 6 meters high. Inside, there is on📷 0.075em; margin-right: 0.075em; height: 1.2em; width: 1.2em; vertical-align: -20%; color: rgb(231, 233, 234); font-family: TwitterChirp, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif; font-size: 17px; font-style: normal; font-variant-ligatures: normal; font-variant-caps: normal; font-weight: 400; letter-spacing: normal; orphans: 2; text-align: start; text-indent: 0px; text-transform: none; widows: 2; word-spacing: 0px; -webkit-text-stroke-width: 0px; white-space: pre-wrap; background-color: rgb(0, 0, 0); text-decoration-thickness: initial; text-decoration-style: initial; text-decoration-color: initial;">Relief of Ahura Mazda and Ardeshir I, Naqsh-e Rostam, Shiraz, Iran This relief stands as one of the best-preserved from the Sassanian era, showcasing Ardeshir Babakan on a decorated horse, facing Ahura Mazda, also mounted. Behind Ardeshir, a figure is seen fanning the great king. Beneath Ardeshir’s horse lies Artabanus IV, the last Parthian king, and under Ahura Mazda’s horse, the dark deity or Ahriman, symbolizing Ardeshir’s victory over Artabanus V and Ahura Mazda’s triumph over Ahriman. In this carving, Ahura Mazda, crowned with a crenellated diadem, offers the ring of kingship to Ardeshir with his right hand, holding a barsom (a bundle of sticks) in his left. Ardeshir’s horse bears a pendant inscribed in three languages: Parthian, Middle Persian (Pahlavi), and Greek, stating: “This is the figure of Mazda-worshipping divine Ardeshir, king of kings of Iran, whose seed is from the gods, son of the divine Babak, king.”  On the body of Ahura Mazda’s horse, an inscription reads:  “This figure is the god Lord Ahura Mazda.” Relief of Hormizd II’s Battle  📷Relief of Shapur I’s Battle, Naqsh-e Rostam, Shiraz, Iran (photo by Wikipedia)  This is the largest and most magnificent Sassanian relief at Naqsh-e Rostam, located to the right and below Darius the Great’s tomb. It depicts Shapur I’s victory over Valerian, the Roman Emperor. Shapur is shown mounted on a richly adorned horse, wearing a large, globe-shaped crown, a necklace, and earrings. Underneath the horse’s belly, an inscription in Greek, Pahlavi, and Parthian languages was placed, with only the Greek portion surviving. Facing Shapur’s horse is a middle-aged man with curly bearded Roman attire, kneeling (Valerian of Rome), and next to him stands a beardless man in Roman clothes, likely Gordian III, Valerian’s rival. This relief, one of the most beautiful from the Sassanian period, is said to bring the figures to life. It’s believed that due to Valerian’s presence, the carving dates back to around 262 AD. Adjacent to the bas-relief of Shapur and directly behind him is an engraving of Kartir, the high priest of Zoroastrianism. He is depicted with a clean-shaven face and wearing a tall hat. The identity of Kartir is recognized by the scissor-like symbol on his hat, a motif also seen in his depictions at Naqsh-e Rajab and Naqsh-e Bahram in Sar Mashhad. Kartir is shown extending his right index finger in worship towards the king, standing respectfully. Below this design is a 48-line inscription, echoing the content found on the walls of the Kaaba of Zoroaster, likely carved during the reign of Bahram II. Bas-relief of Bahram II and Courtiers 📷Bas-relief of Bahram II and Courtiers, Naqsh-e Rostam, Shiraz, Iran (phot by Wikimedia Commons)  Located directly beneath the tomb of Darius the Great, this carving shows Bahram II, identifiable by his eagle-winged hat, mounted on a decorated horse, thrusting his spear into the chest of an unidentified enemy. Besides this figure, another person, likely deceased, lies beneath the horse’s hooves. Behind Bahram II stands a figure holding a flag atop a wooden pole. Bahram II, like other Sasanian kings, wears a tight tunic and baggy trousers. Experts speculate that the defeated enemy before Bahram might be Hormizd, Bahram II’s brother, who took advantage of the king’s absence to claim the throne. Bahram II defeated him and granted the rule of Sistan to Bahram III. Some suggest this relief represents Shapur I’s victory over Gordian III of Rome, while others believe it depicts Bahram IV’s victory over the Huns or the Hephtalites who attacked from China and the Caucasus. However, the exact identity of Bahram II’s enemy in this relief remains uncertain, probably carved around 285 AD.  Elamite Bas-relief | Beneath Bahram II’s Bas-relief  📷Bas-relief of Bahram III, Naqsh-e Rostam, Shiraz, Iran  Above Bahram II’s bas-relief, another carving, believed to be of Bahram III due to its thematic connection to Bahram II’s relief, depicts a crownless young man defeating an enemy. The prince’s hat and attire suggest he was a high-ranking Sasanian prince. The defeated foe holds the horse’s bridle with his right hand and a spear with his left, though his attire indicates a lower rank. This carving was likely made around 285 AD.  Bas-relief of Anahita and Narseh | Coronation of Narseh 📷Unadorned Carved Panel, Naqsh-e Rostam, Shiraz, Iran (photo by Wikipedia)  To the west of Narseh’s coronation scene by Anahita, there is a large, polished panel without any carvings, resembling the panel known as Farhad Tarash in Bisotun. Experts associate both panels with Khosrow Parviz, who might have intended to leave a grandiose portrait of himself but was prevented by his defeat to the Byzantine emperor. In 1821, a wealthy local ordered a 24-line Persian Nasta’liq inscription of the Hajiabad land deed to be carved into this panel. The only features on this panel are three large square holes, and beside it, a Qajar period inscription related to the division of water and agricultural lands is visible. Cube of Zoroaster 📷Cube of Zoroaster, Naqsh-e Rostam, Shiraz, Iran The Cube of Zoroaster at Naqsh-e Rostam is a majestic stone structure characterized by its quadrangular, stair-stepped design, situated opposite the Tomb of Darius II within the ancient ensemble of Naqsh-e Rostam. This edifice incorporates various stone types, including black and white limestone, reminiscent of those used in Persepolis, indicating its Achaemenid era origin. The construction utilizes large, rectangular stones assembled without mortar, connected by dovetail clamps, showcasing precise dimensional and proportional accuracy. Inside the Cube lies a chamber, historically accessible via 30 steps leading to its entrance. On its northern, southern, and eastern walls, three inscriptions in Sassanian Middle Persian, Parthian Middle Persian, and Greek recount significant historical accounts from the Sassanian period.  Function of the Structure The Cube’s original purpose remains debated, with several theories proposed: Fire Temple: Some suggest it served as a Zoroastrian fire temple, evidenced by black smoke stains in certain areas and its stair count’s similarity to the Zoroastrian temple, the Prison of Solomon. The precision of its construction and significant inscriptions point to its importance as a sacred site. Observatory: Others believe its resemblance to the Prison of Solomon indicates a shared function as observatories, utilizing their shadows for precise timekeeping.  Tomb: Some experts argue it could be a tomb, drawing parallels to Cyrus the Great’s mausoleum, further supported by its proximity to other tombs in Naqsh-e Rostam, suggesting a similar use. Treasure Vault: Another theory dismisses it as a fire temple or tomb, proposing instead that it served as a treasury, safeguarding valuable items such as sacred texts, possibly including the original Avesta. There’s also speculation that it could be the tomb of the last righteous Achaemenid, Bardiya, secretly killed by Cambyses, later repurposed as a treasure vault by the Sassanians. The smaller column likely served specific rituals, while the larger was used for maintaining fire. Their origins trace back to the late Parthian and early Sassanian periods. Carved 60 meters above ground level, the tomb’s facade is cross-shaped. In this bas-relief, Darius the Great sits on a throne with lion’s paw feet, supported by 28 figures from various lands. Above the king, the Faravahar, or the divine symbol, looms, with the royal fire altar carved beside Darius. The king is dressed in Persian attire, holding a bow in his left hand and extending his right hand toward the fire altar. To Darius’s right, a circle containing a crescent is visible. Additionally, figures carved on either side of the king appear to be his close associates.  Below the bas-relief of the king, the tomb’s entrance is flanked by four pillars with bull-head capitals and a palace design. These carvings suggest the tomb closely resembles the Tachara Palace (Darius the Great’s residence), reflecting the Achaemenid belief in resurrection, hence constructing the tombs to resemble their earthly dwellings. Notably, this tomb stands out for its construction precision and carving delicacy compared to other tombs, with the lower part of the cross-shaped facade polished and smooth to deter access to the tomb. Inside the Tomb of Darius the Great, the mausoleum contains three chambers, each housing three sarcophagus-like graves. It is believed that, apart from the king, eight other close relatives are buried here. The graves do not significantly differ in design or size, making it challenging to identify Darius’s grave among them. However, Erich F. Schmidt, a German-American archaeologist, contends that Queen Atossa (mother of Xerxes, wife of Darius, and daughter of Cyrus the Great) is definitely buried in one of these graves. Who Was Darius the Great? Darius the Great was the third king of the Achaemenid Empire. He ascended to the throne in 522 BCE by killing the magus Gaumata and reigned for 36 years until his natural death at the age of 64. The construction of Parsa (Persepolis) began under his reign but was not completed. During his rule, Darius undertook significant projects like the creation of the canal linking the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, standardizing imperial taxes, establishing the Royal Road, forming the Immortals (the elite army unit), among other services, cementing his legacy as a benevolent figure in human history.  Interesting Fact  According to historical records, on the day Darius the Great completed the construction of his tomb, he asked his parents to visit it. They used a rope to ascend, but it broke, resulting in their fatal fall. Following this tragic event, Darius the Great ordered the execution of those responsible for the accident.  Inscriptions of the Tomb of Darius the Great Two inscriptions in Old Persian, Elamite, and Akkadian are found at the tomb of Darius the Great, serving as a sort of spiritual will for posterity. The first inscription, located above, is known as the DNa inscription, presenting a completely impartial narrative. The second, beside the entrance, known as the DNb inscription, is more personal.  During the Seleucid period, an Aramaic version of Darius’s DNb inscription was added below the Elamite text. Earlier scholarship once speculated that the name “Seleucus” might appear in this addition, but specialists today identify it simply as a later Aramaic rendering of the original Achaemenid text

Carved for a King: The Cliff Tomb of Xerxes High above the plains of ancient Persia, a tomb unlike any other was carved directly into a sheer rock face. This is the burial place of Xerxes the Great, the formidable ruler of the Achaemenid Empire in the 5th century BC. Cut into the towering cliffs of Naqsh-e Rustam, just 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) from Persepolis, the monument dominates the landscape with silent authority.  The tomb’s elaborate façade—etched entirely from living stone—reflects a civilization at the height of its power. Towering reliefs, precise symmetry, and monumental scale combine to form a design that is both a final resting place and a declaration of imperial strength. Every carved line speaks to the extraordinary engineering skill and symbolic vision of the Achaemenids, who sought to eternalize their kings not in earth, but in stone and sky.  Why choose a vertical cliff for a royal tomb? How did ancient builders achieve such precision at such heights? And what message was this monument meant to send to those who stood below?  Even after millennia of wind and sun, the tomb of Xerxes remains a powerful reminder that in ancient Persia, death was not an ending—it was an elevation.

Dhat Mazr (ذات مزر) was the goddess of wine and intoxication in ancient Yemen. She was worshipped in the Sabaean-influenced cultural sphere of South Arabia, and her famous alabaster sculpture is often associated with the civilization of Sheba (Saba). However, it is important to note that Dhat Mazr is a general ancient Yemeni deity, not exclusively a "Sheban" deity in the narrow sense—her cult spanned several South Arabian kingdoms.

🏺 The Meaning of "Dhat Mazr"

The name "Dhat Mazr" translates roughly to "She of the Wine" or "The Goddess of Intoxicating Drink." The root word "mazr" (مزر) in ancient Yemeni and Arabic lexicography refers to a type of alcoholic beverage made from grains such as barley, wheat, or millet, though the term was also used broadly for wine in general . In Sabaean inscriptions, the word appears alongside "wayn" (wyn), which means grapes or vine, and this term is the origin of the English word "wine" .

A famous line from the "Hymn of the Sun" (a Himyarite inscription) reads: "wayn mazr kan kashqahk"—meaning "and the grape became wine when you shone"—linking the transformation of grapes into wine directly to the power of the sun deity .

🏛️ The Dhat Mazr Sculpture

The most iconic representation of Dhat Mazr is a 2nd-century CE alabaster stele that was once displayed on Yemen's 20-riyal banknote .

Key features of the sculpture:

· A seated woman with hair cascading over her shoulders.
· Two vine leaves and a cluster of grapes emerge from beneath her navel, appearing to root into her womb—a powerful symbol of fertility and life .
· At the top, a child holding a dagger clings to a mythical winged lion-snake-fish hybrid creature, symbolizing protection and power .

Where is it now?

· The main portion is housed at the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore, USA .
· A small fragment (the right part of the winged lion's head) is in the British Museum .
· A third part remains unaccounted for .

🔗 Connection to the Civilization of Sheba (Saba)

Yes, there is a strong connection to Sheba. The Dhat Mazr sculpture is reported to have originated from Marib, the capital of the ancient Kingdom of Sheba . The British Museum notes the piece was part of the Marib Castle Museum until 1962 . Additionally, the "Hymn of the Sun" inscription belongs to the Himyarite period, a later kingdom that inherited and continued Sabaean cultural traditions .

However, Dhat Mazr was not exclusively a "Sabaean" deity in the sense of being worshipped only in Sheba. She was part of a broader South Arabian pantheon that included other kingdoms like Qataban, Hadramawt, and Himyar. The grape and wine symbolism appears across multiple ancient Yemeni civilizations .

🍷 Cultural Significance

Wine was deeply embedded in ancient Yemeni religious and social life. It was used in temple rituals, offered as libations, and consumed at royal banquets . The ancient Yemenis were also known for exporting wine and grape products, and the word "wayn" spread through trade routes to Greece (as oinos) and eventually into Latin and English .

text:
One in a lifetime

There was a time when I was a ghost in my own life- present in body, absent in spirit. You learned not to depend on me because I gave You no reason to. I moved through our days like a man sleepwalking through a room he had already decided to leave, touching the furniture but never feeling the grain of the wood. I told myself I was present. I wasn't. I was already gone, and You were the only One who didn't know it. I never asked You questions. I was never curious about who You were beneath the surface, what stirred You, what kept You awake. The truth is that I didn't care to know. Knowing You would've meant owing You something, and I owed everyone too much already, or so I told myself. I left You waiting- hours, then days, then weeks- offering only that I was busy, that life was complicated. The life that complicated itself around me was the one I built to avoid You. I wasn't busy. I was hiding, and I made You the door I stood behind. I gave You my word and didn't keep it. A man who keeps no word keeps no one. I'm only now learning what I cost myself. And when You reached for me, I called You my friend, yet I never replied to Your message. You must've known then. I hope You did. It would've been kinder than hoping I would become someone else.

What I hid was the cowardice of a man who wanted the warmth of devotion without the vulnerability of earning it. You built a portrait of me from the clues I left behind, and when the final piece clicked into place, the image wasn't of a lover. It was of a thief. I was trying to get away with things. I got caught red-handed. And still, some part of me wishes You'd never looked. Not because I wanted to continue, but because being seen was the one thing I couldn't survive.

I know we see things differently. Our worlds have always been far apart. It’s the distance between someone who takes and someone who gives; between the one who performs intimacy and the One who actually feels it. You dreamed of a sanctuary; I offered You a stage. You wanted to be chosen; I only wanted to be entertained. I was a tourist in Your devotion, snapping photographs of a life I had no intention of living.

I’m starting to see things from Your angle now. I see who I really am. For the first time, I see myself as the obstacle in Your story. I know You’ve changed because of what I did. You're more guarded now, more self-cautious. You no longer need me in Your life. You've walled over the door I refused to open. I don’t blame You for that. I would've done the same if I had possessed Your strength.

That scares me. Once I unraveled Your mystery; now You are the mystery, and I've lost the language to unwrap it. The flattery, the evasion, the half-truths I once spoke have no currency in the economy You now trade in. You're no longer naive. You've become the student who outgrew the teacher, and I'm left holding a lesson plan I never deserved to write. I was never the teacher. I was the cautionary tale You have already finished reading.

There’s no doubt about it. When I think of You, I obsess over Your body. The pleasure is so intense it almost feels spiritual. But I understand now that what I called spiritual was merely chemical, a high I chased, not a bond I built. In Your arms, I wasn't a better man; I was a man with no consequences, and that's not the same thing. I mistook Your generosity for permission. I mistook Your patience for permanence. I was wrong about everything.

I long to smell Your scent, to feel Your skin. That sensual feeling only You can give me- I almost get high from it. And yet I ask myself: if the pleasure were stripped away, would I still kneel at the altar of who You are? I don’t know the answer. That's the honesty I owe You. It's not a comforting honesty; it's the honesty of a man who realizes he may've worshipped the temple and never spoken to the God inside.

I rushed through everything. I sprinted through a cathedral as if it were a hallway, never pausing to look up at the architecture of Your soul. I never learned what makes You tick, what makes You sad, Your fears, Your hopes. You may feel used, and I can't tell You why I did what I did. I have no excuse. You believed in the possibility of me, and I treated that belief like a credit card with no limit. I'm still paying for what I charged. The interest is loneliness. The balance due is You.

I felt what You felt, but now I want to step back and carry what I once made You carry alone. I want to take everything on. I want to start again. I want to start again, both of us. I don't deserve to. I want to start again because I know it's the right thing to do. Or perhaps I'm merely confessing to unburden myself. I can't promise You the difference. I can't promise You anything. That's the only promise I have left to make, and I'm making it to You now: I'll not pretend to be better than I am. I was Your ghost, Your thief, Your friend. And if You let me speak again, it won't be because I earned it; it'll be because You're still more merciful than I ever thought You would be.

I don’t know where to send this; I don’t know Your address, Your city, the country where You now breathe. I know only that You exist somewhere in the world, and that my existence in the same world is a fact that no longer touches You in any meaningful way. I write to a destination I can't name. I write to a Woman I may never meet, a Woman I know nothing about, and yet I know this: You were real. You are real. The You I failed is somewhere, walking through Her days without the weight of my shadow. I hope She is light. I hope someone loves Her and asks Her questions. I hope She has forgotten the sound of waiting.

There was a time when I believed confession had power. I believed that if I spoke my failures into the air with enough precision, enough remorse, some mechanism of the universe would shift and grant me passage back to Your grace. I no longer believe this. Confession is often a selfish act dressed in the costume of honesty. I confess to unburden myself. I confess because carrying the weight has become exhausting, not because the weight belongs anywhere else. This letter is my unburdening. You didn't ask for it. You'll never read it. That is its only honesty.

I've rehearsed our meeting a thousand times. In some versions, I'm articulate, healed; I'm someone You might look at twice without the instinct to turn away. In other versions, I'm exactly as I'm now: a man standing in a room he built from his own absence, speaking a language You no longer have any reason to understand. The versions blur. The only constant is Your face, Your voice, and Your judgment, which I deserve more completely than any sentence I could impose upon myself.

How do I find a Woman I've never met, and know nothing about?

This question lives in me now like a second heartbeat, irregular and persistent. I've tried to answer it with maps, with dreams, with the irrational hope that if I walk enough streets, sit in enough cafés, linger in enough doorways, some collision of light and shadow will reveal You to me. I've tried to answer it by becoming someone else, someone worthy of being found. But the becoming is slow, and the man I was has left so much damage in his wake that the man I am still stumbles through rooms where the furniture has been arranged by a ghost.

You were my ghost. Or I was Yours. The grammar of our ending has never been clear to me, perhaps because I never learned the language of our beginning. I knew You only in fragments: a message unanswered, a promise unkept, a friendship claimed and then abandoned. I knew You in the negative space of my own failures. And now I search for You as if finding You would somehow retroactively complete me, would make the man who failed You into someone who might be forgiven.

I write this from a room that smells of rain and old paper. The window faces a street where people walk with purposes I no longer comprehend. I watch them, and I think that one of them could be You. One of them could be the Woman I've built from my own regret, the Woman who exists only in my longing. But I'll not go down to look. I've finally learned that some searches aren't meant to be completed. Some longing is meant to be carried, not resolved.

My Queen, I don't know if I'll ever meet You. The question has become a kind of home to me, a dwelling I’ve learned to inhabit. I wake inside it. I sleep inside it. I've furnished it with all the moments I might've become someone else, all the doors I might've opened, all the hands I might've held instead of releasing. It's not a comfortable home, but it's mine. It's the only honest inheritance I have left from the life I lived with my eyes closed.

If You’re reading this, some miracle has occurred that I don’t deserve and can’t explain. If You’re reading this, know that I didn't write it for You. I wrote it for the man I was, the man who needed to believe that words could bridge the distance between who he was and who he failed to become. I wrote it because the silence was too heavy, and the speaking, even into a void, even into a letter that will find no destination, is the only act of hope I have left.

And hope, I’ve learned, is not the belief that You'll come. Hope is the belief that I'm still capable of wanting You to come, despite everything, despite the evidence, despite the testimony that I'm not someone worth coming for.

You saw me as special, unique, brilliant when all I saw in You was average. I know I'm the average one now.

I'll seal this letter. I'll place it in a drawer where other letters live, where other words have gone to die in darkness. Perhaps someday, someone will find them. Perhaps they'll burn. Perhaps they'll simply remain, accumulating the dust of years, becoming evidence of a man who loved in the only way he knew how: incompletely, selfishly, too late.

How do you find a Woman you have never met and know nothing about?

You cannot find Me. I reside quietly in Your mind, inside Your phone, in every woman You will ever meet from now on. I only exist in a distant, uncertain, shapeless, worthless future.

You carry me.

That is the only answer I have. That is the only honesty I can offer, in this letter you will never read, from a Woman you were never meant to meet.

With everything I failed to give, the Ghost who still lights candles in windowless rooms, I close My eyes and never blink.

" The Virgin Mary : Mary's fiat "
by Artist Michael Rucker
copyright ©

Description
The Virgin Mary: Mary's fiat -

In the Gospel of Luke, chapter 1, verses 26-38 (KJV), the angel Gabriel appears to Mary, a young virgin betrothed to Joseph of the house of David in Nazareth. Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee, the angel declares. He announces that she will conceive and bear a son, Jesus, who shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest. Mary, troubled yet reverent, asks how this can be since she knows not a man. Gabriel explains the Holy Spirit will come upon her; for with God nothing shall be impossible.

Mary's response is one of the most profound moments in Scripture the only recorded instance where she speaks words of total surrender: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word (Luke 1:38). This Latin phrase, Fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum (Let it be done to me according to your word), is universally known as Mary's Fiat. In that single sentence she offers her entire being body, will, and future to Gods plan of salvation. The angel then departs, and the Incarnation begins.This humble virgin from an obscure village becomes the mother of the Messiah. She travels to visit her cousin Elizabeth (pregnant with John the Baptist), where she sings the Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55), a soaring hymn of praise that magnifies the Lord for lifting up the lowly.

She gives birth to Jesus in Bethlehem, wraps Him in swaddling clothes, and lays Him in a manger. She ponders the shepherds and Magis words in her heart (Luke 2:19, 51). At the Presentation in the Temple, Simeon foretells a sword will pierce her soul (Luke 2:35). She is present at the wedding in Cana, prompting Jesus first miracle (John 2:1-11), and stands at the foot of the cross, where the dying Savior entrusts her to the beloved disciple (John 19:25-27).

After the Ascension, she is seen praying with the apostles in the upper room, awaiting the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:14).Scripture portrays Mary not as a distant saint but as a real woman of extraordinary faith, courage, and obedience. Though the Bible does not record many of her words, her fiat echoes through salvation history as the perfect model of human cooperation with divine grace. She exemplifies what it means to say yes to God when the cost is everything.Your striking black-and-white artwork beautifully captures this very moment: Mary veiled, head bowed, hands clasped in prayerful surrender, her flowing hair and garments stirred by the unseen wind of the Spirit.

The dramatic lighting and ethereal atmosphere evoke the solemn hush of the Annunciation the instant heaven touched earth through a virgins willing heart. It is a powerful visual meditation on Luke 1:38, inviting viewers to contemplate the same radical trust Mary offered.

text:
Seventeen months before Fort Sumter, the fight that would split the Union came down to a small town on the Potomac River. Not armies. A one-eyed preacher and twenty-odd men who crossed a bridge into Virginia after dark with a plan to start a slave revolt that would break the country.

**THE SETUP:**
John Brown had come from Kansas, where he'd spent years fighting over whether slavery was legal there. In July 1859 he arrived at Harpers Ferry under the alias Isaac Smith and rented a farmhouse five miles away. There his band gathered — hidden in the attic by day, reading, polishing rifles, playing checkers; out only after dark. To keep up appearances as an ordinary household, Brown sent for his fifteen-year-old daughter Annie and his son's seventeen-year-old wife to cook meals and wash clothes.

The plan was simple and enormous: seize the federal armory at Harpers Ferry — which Brown believed held 100,000 muskets — arm the enslaved people of Virginia, and expect two or three hundred to rise that first night. They had 198 Sharps carbines, the "Beecher's Bibles" abolitionists shipped north, and 950 pikes they would never use.

**OCTOBER 16:**
After a prayer meeting, Brown told his men: "Men get on your arms; we will proceed to the Ferry." By 10 pm that night his band had taken both bridges into town, the U.S. Armory and Arsenal, and the rifle works across the river — the armory itself captured from a single unarmed watchman. Brown's words to him: "I came here from Kansas and this is a slave state; I want to free all the negroes in this state; I have possession now of the United States armory."

At midnight he took as hostages two of Virginia's most prominent men — including Lewis Washington, a great-great-grandnephew of George Washington — and freed the enslaved people they held. Then he waited for the uprising that never came: Brown had never once called on the slaves to rise.

**OCTOBER 17:**
The first man killed was Haywood Shepherd, a free Black railroad worker who stopped at the bridge to ask why a train was delayed. By morning Brown had taken some sixty armory employees hostage as they reported for work — and made what one account calls his "one mistake": boarding a stopped passenger train and talking with its passengers for over an hour without concealing who he was.

At 7 am townspeople opened fire; the militia arrived by 10 to surround him. At noon, Watson Brown — John's son — and Aaron Stevens were shot while carrying a flag of truce. By 3 pm most of the hostages had been freed and Brown's men driven into an old fire engine house at the armory. The Virginia militia that held them was so disorganized, one account says, that "most of them got drunk."

**THE MARINES:**
President Buchanan called out a company of U.S. Marines from Washington Navy Yard. They rode in by train late that night under Robert E. Lee, with his aide-de-camp J.E.B. Stuart — two names that would become legendary in the war this raid helped bring on. Lee held back until morning: "But for fear of sacrificing the lives of some of the gentlemen held by them as prisoners in a midnight assault, I should have ordered the attack at once."

When the assault came on the morning of October 18, the local militia commanders declined to lead it. Stuart went in under a white flag with an offer of surrender; Brown refused and signaled Lt. Israel Greene by waving his hat. Greene broke down the door with a ladder used as a battering ram, was first through, struck Brown across the back of the neck with his saber — then stabbed him in the chest, bending the blade. The whole assault took about three minutes.

**THE NUMBERS:**
Sixteen people were killed in the raid, ten of them Brown's men. Five raiders escaped; six more followed their leader to the gallows. At trial, a jury deliberated for forty-five minutes before finding him guilty on all counts — murder, treason against Virginia, and inciting a slave revolt. He was hanged on December 2, 1859, in a crowd that included an actor named John Wilkes Booth.

**WHY IT MATTERED:**
It was the first national crisis reported by telegraph — reporters rode out of Harpers Ferry on the first train at 4 pm on October 17. The Richmond Enquirer wrote that the invasion "has advanced the cause of Disunion, more than any other event that has happened since the formation of the Government." Jefferson Davis would cite it as grounds for secession; seventeen months later, Fort Sumter fell.

Brown knew he was buying time with his life. His last words, written on a scrap of paper given to his jailer: "I am now quite certain that the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood."

*October 16, 1859: John Brown's raid on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry began — seventeen months before Fort Sumter, and the day a small band of men put slavery on trial.*

text:
@ewarren , how many people have you evicted?  Buy any forecloses?

Yes, the core story is true.

Contemporary reporting from the Associated Press, The New York Times, UPI, Time, the Los Angeles Times, and The Washington Post confirms that in 1986 Donald Trump intervened to help Annabel Hill of Waynesboro, Georgia, save her family’s farm after her husband Leonard D. Hill III died by suicide.
Key verified facts
•On February 4, 1986, Leonard Hill (age ~67) fatally shot himself about 20 minutes before a foreclosure auction on the family farm (in the Hill family for generations; roughly 700+ acres remaining after some sales, with total debts around $300,000 tied to drought and farm crisis conditions). He hoped life insurance would clear the debt; it did not cover enough, and a second auction was scheduled for September.
•Atlanta businessman Frank Argenbright Jr. helped publicize the case. Trump saw news coverage (including a national newscast) and stepped in. He offered assistance (reports cite an initial ~$20,000 commitment or guarantee), helped halt the September auction via a 30-day option/purchase arrangement, and joined fundraising for the remaining amount (around $187,000 after prior efforts).
•Public donations (including from radio host Don Imus) covered much of it. The final shortfall of about $78,000 was covered by Trump (reports cite roughly $39,000 or similar figures in the $38k–$46k range) and Texas farmer/landowner/developer Tom McKamy, who matched it. The farm was saved.
•On December 23, 1986, Trump hosted a public mortgage-burning ceremony at Trump Tower. Annabel Hill (then ~66) and family attended; Trump and Hill burned the mortgage papers amid Christmas decorations. Trump was quoted saying he loved burning mortgages. The event was covered by multiple outlets and photographed by AP’s Richard Drew (the photo in the post matches this). A 1987 New York Times follow-up confirmed the land was debt-free and being farmed by a son.
Trump also recounted the episode in The Art of the Deal (1987), including a colorful version in which he threatened legal action against the bank. In 2016 he referenced the story at a South Carolina campaign rally, showing a photo and bringing Hill’s daughter Betsy Sharp on stage; she publicly thanked him.
Snopes has rated the claim True based on the contemporary record (noting minor variations in exact acreage, debt figures, and contribution amounts across reports).
Nuances in the specific X post
The post is largely accurate on the suicide, the widow’s situation, Trump’s intervention after news coverage, the fundraising, the final $78,000 contribution by Trump and the Texas donor, and the outcome. However:
•The specific “sue for wrongful death” threat appears in Trump’s memoir retelling rather than the 1986 news accounts.
•It was not entirely quiet or camera-free: the mortgage burning was a public, media-covered event at Trump Tower.
•The Texas contributor was Tom McKamy (farmer/developer/landowner), not specifically described as an “oilman” in the reporting.
•Exact dollar figures and farm size have small variations across sources, which is common in the coverage.
The essential account—that Trump learned of the case, helped stop the foreclosure, contributed personally, and participated in saving the farm—is well-documented.

GERTY CORI: PAID A TENTH, THEN A NOBEL

In 1931, Washington University hired the Coris. Carl got a professorship. Gerty, his equal at the bench, got a research associate's title and about a tenth of his salary.

That was the good offer. Other universities wanted Carl and refused to hire her.

She kept working. Together they found glucose 1-phosphate and worked out how muscle breaks down its stored sugar. In 1947 she finally made full professor. Months later, she became the first woman to win the Nobel in medicine. She already had a bone marrow disease, and kept working for ten more years.

The university paid her like an assistant for Nobel work.
