text:
AI IS JUST A PRODUCT/TOOL ON THE MARKET: The team behind ArtCraft—a project offering free alternatives to Adobe applications—has introduced a new suite of tools that mimic Microsoft Office. Leveraging artificial intelligence, the developers have created versions of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. These are distributed for free and are open-source.

Earlier in October, the team garnered attention with ArtCraft, a suite of applications developed by reverse-engineering Adobe Photoshop, Lightroom, and Premiere. This approach involves analyzing the behavior and functions of existing software to build an alternative that replicates its operation.

The project utilizes Anthropic’s AI model, Claude. According to ArtCraft co-founder Michael Cafrey, the results of the initial development phase were so impressive that the team decided to release the applications as open-source software.

"We were surprised by how well they actually worked, which is why we decided to make them open-source," Cafrey told Futurism. He criticized Adobe for past controversial practices, adding that the team was surprised not only by the quality of the alternative but also by the fact that such a product hadn't appeared sooner.

Developer Brandon Thomas is now expanding the project with three new applications: GridCraft, an alternative to Excel; DeckCraft, which mimics PowerPoint; and WordCraft, which replicates the functionality of Word. All three are available for free via the ArtCraft website.

The project also offers additional credits for generating images and video using artificial intelligence. These features utilize Google’s "Nano Banana Pro" and offer developers an opportunity for additional revenue.

Images of the applications show interfaces that closely resemble the original Microsoft programs. For comparison, purchasing Office directly from the company can cost anywhere from $19.99 to $199.99 per year, depending on the specific product and subscription plan.

Critics of Microsoft and Adobe argue that software prices have risen over the years, while subscription models impose increasingly restrictive requirements—such as mandatory registration, license activation, and the need for periodic internet connectivity. Both companies have also faced criticism for integrating generative artificial intelligence into features that not all users wish to utilize.

ArtCraft holds one advantage over Google’s free office suite—Docs, Sheets, and Slides: these new tools function as standalone applications that do not require an internet connection. Consequently, users are not dependent on constant access to an online service, nor are they vulnerable to potential future changes in its pricing model.

It remains unclear, however, how long this project can continue without encountering legal challenges. Reverse-engineering popular applications to create alternatives that closely mimic the originals could provoke a response from Microsoft and Adobe. At present, there is no indication that either company has taken specific action against these new applications.

For the developers, this initiative also serves as a way to support the open-source software community. For years, independent programmers and creators have relied on tools whose pricing and terms are dictated by major technology corporations. "The tech industry has relied on the open-source software community for decades to keep its companies running," Kafri commented to Futurism. "Now, models are being trained on open-source code. So, it’s a bit like cosmic karma—open source is striking back."

text:
🇺🇸 WEEKLY MARKET CLOSING COMMENT

The week was defined by the AI trade cracking under ROI skepticism. 

The S&P 500 finished down 2.06% at 7,649. 
Nasdaq-100 dropped 5.49% to 29,188, its worst weekly performance in months. 
Russell 2000 shed 3.20%. 
The Dow was the lone bright spot among major indexes, up 0.67%, helped by its lighter tech weighting.

Chipmakers logged an eighth consecutive day of losses, a streak not seen since 2008. Investors questioned whether the pace of AI capital expenditure has outrun the ability of firms to generate returns on those investments. Nasdaq-100 fell an additional 2.5% on Friday alone. VIX surged 37.3% on the week to close at 20.38.

The sector picture is the clearest story. 10 of 11 S&P 500 sectors finished positive. The damage was entirely concentrated in Information Technology, down 6.54%. Money rotated into defensives and cyclicals with less AI exposure. 
Consumer Staples led at +4.07%. Materials +3.08%. 
Energy +2.47%. 
Health Care +2.27%. 
Utilities +1.79%. 
Real Estate +0.97%. 
Financials +0.67%.

Q3 bank earnings were mixed. $JPM equities S&T revenue came in at $4.95B versus $4.47B estimated. $GS equities posted $6.44B, well above expectations, though FICC disappointed at $3.47B versus $3.72B. $C FICC delivered its best Q3 in at least a decade at $4.4B, beating the $4.3B consensus. $WFC beat across the board as resilient consumers kept loan losses in check. $BAC was the laggard. Trading revenue missed and the bank absorbed a $1.2B charge tied to regulatory penalties. Shares fell as much as 8.7% on Wednesday. The KBW Bank Index is on pace for its worst weekly losing streak since the 2008 crisis, down roughly 1.1% on the week and about 13% off its August record.

On the macro side, September industrial production rose 0.7% m/m, well above the 0.4% consensus. BofA card spending data pointed to continued consumer resilience.

Rates provided some relief by the end of the week. The 10-year dropped 16.1 bp to 5.081%. The 30-year fell 16.8 bp to 5.431%. The 2-year declined 7.4 bp to 4.717%. The week’s CPI print came in hotter than expected and initially sent yields higher. By Friday the AI-driven equity selloff generated some safe-haven demand for duration and pulled long-end yields off their post-CPI peaks. Barkin acknowledged the data was higher than he would have hoped but stopped short of pre-committing to a hike. Warsh, speaking at the IMF meetings, offered no new policy signals and reiterated the commitment to price stability. Markets read that as consistent with a hold at the October meeting. The energy shock continues to complicate the Fed’s task as businesses pass along rising costs in airfares, logistics and delivery services.

AI cracked. The rest of the market held up. 10 of 11 sectors green says this is a sector-specific repricing, not a broad risk-off event.

The mass annihilation of the Company Man path by millennial nihilism has constituted a society-wide Agency Shredder. We tore the institutional application of creativity and intelligence away from youth with aptitude. The competency crisis is downstream of the fact that social mores deny outright earnest commitment to a goal larger than oneself. Moralist envyism is a mindvirus training people to hide their talents. Meanwhile, for 20th century America, The Company was God. You showed up everyday to advance a view of the world — you hastened the arrival of some heaven on Earth. But the millennial killed God and every substitute on offer. Now all you can do is lament student debt, "email job", dating app unromance, and idpol socialist pastiche. All you believe in is the vacuity of life. And you are surprised you are listless?

Silicon Valley deserves much of the scorn it receives but for the wrong reasons. So many hate that "tech bros" believe in anything at all. Futurists are the last in America to still carry out any work worth believing in. The issue with tech is that they remain godless millennials (though rebuking Secular AGI is for another post). They so tragically squander the greatest sums in history for tastelessness. The Future is enough to lead the horse to water, but not enough to save our society. No one even attempts it.

The Remilia Corporation is the last corporation left. The last company carrying the embers of the once mighty American capitalist torch, leading the way as it dragged the world into the postwar economic miracles. That Mandate of Heaven which once blessed entire industries has fallen to a single company. It's up to one postcancelled proana corpo-cult. text:
Hermes yesterday: race day, and the bugs lost. One pull request hunted down 27 race conditions, the kind where two writers grab the same file and one of them quietly loses. Meanwhile the installer stopped handing new users unreleased code, and the shared gateway learned to come back after a restart. 227 commits landed on main; here are the 10 that matter.

1️⃣ New installs land on the latest stable release

Before: hermes update has followed stable releases on official checkouts for a while, but https://t.co/N55KRzrRfk, install.ps1 and Hermes-Setup still cloned the tip of main, so every new user started on unreleased code and only reached stable at the next release. After: a fresh install of the official repository looks up the latest vX.Y.Z release (GitHub API, then the releases redirect, then the repository's own tags) and checks it out, which today is v0.22.2. If no release can be reached, a fresh install stops with a retryable error instead of falling back to main. --channel main, -Channel main or HERMES_INSTALL_CHANNEL=main installs main's tip and saves that choice for later updates. Who gets it: this is already live, because the hosted one-liners serve the script from main, and Hermes-Setup downloads it at install time. A rerun over an existing main checkout keeps it where it is and leaves the move to hermes update and its downgrade guard; forks, mirrors, other branches and --commit pins are unchanged.

2️⃣ Allowlist edits take effect without a restart

Before: on the shared gateway, command_allowlist was read once at startup, so a pattern you removed from config.yaml by hand stayed auto-approved until a gateway restart (rm -rf build ran with no prompt), and a pattern you added was ignored. Desktop requests could also still reach a disabled plugin's /api/plugins routes. After: every approval check applies what changed on disk, so a removed pattern prompts again and an added one matches; always approvals the gateway made but could not save are kept, and a pending always-save can no longer write a removed entry back. A malformed allowlist counts as empty, so commands prompt. Desktop requests to a disabled plugin get 404 like every other caller. In review: the same plugin gate for WebSocket connections and for every profile the gateway serves.

3️⃣ The gateway comes back after a restart, and the CLI with it

Before: hermes gateway restart on a gateway you or a client started by hand waited for a supervisor that did not exist, exited 1 and left no gateway running, so cron and bots stayed down. The classic CLI never re-attached afterwards and blamed every prompt on the model. API callers queued behind a running turn got a 503 with Retry-After, so the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs resent work that was going to run anyway. After an unclean exit, every local client hung while state.db was checked: 41 to 76 seconds on a 5.3 GB store. After: restart stops the gateway and starts a new one; the CLI redials on the next call and resumes its open sessions, and a turn cut off by the restart is reported as unknown and never resent; queued API callers are told their input is saved and must not be resent (x-should-retry: false, and /v1/runs reports them queued); and the database check runs in the background on WAL stores, with a 30 minute bound, and is skipped with one warning on rollback-journal stores.

4️⃣ Bots stop answering Sorry, I encountered an error

Before: on a gateway serving several profiles (this turns on by itself once a named profile has its own bot credentials), every message to a profile running a plugin that rewrites incoming text was refused with RuntimeStoreError invalid_params, and so was every /retry from Telegram, Discord or any other platform. On Mattermost, every plain text post without an attachment was refused the same way. After: rewritten messages keep the provenance of the message they came from, /retry re-runs the last turn, and text-only posts pass admission on every platform. A refusal now names the failed check in gateway.log, and the chat reply names it only when it is about the content, never a trust check. Not covered: a /retry that is still refused (a paused session, for one) leaves the last turn removed from the transcript; that is tracked in an open issue. The Mattermost fix was not run against a live server.

5️⃣ Background jobs report back on Discord and Telegram

Before: when a background process finished, its completion wake on Discord or Telegram was refused because it carried no message id while the chat's stored source did, and it was retried every 5 seconds until the process was pruned 30 minutes later, so the agent never got the result. On Telegram DM topics the reply failed even once admitted. After: the wake is admitted and answers in the right topic; if a refusal persists, the watcher retries 8 times over about five minutes and then sends the plain completion notice. Not covered: in a shared thread where a different user started the job, the wake is still refused and falls back to that plain notice. In review: Discord threads whose title changed after creation.

6️⃣ The real browser profile stops breaking the browser tool

Before: with browser.use_real_profile on, every browser call failed when the profile could not be copied: Chrome running on macOS or Linux (it locks the saved-password and autofill files), Windows with Chrome open, a non-Chromium default browser, a bad pin or a launch failure. After: with Chrome running, Hermes copies the cookies and skips the locked password and autofill files, so you stay signed in; when the profile cannot load at all, the session gets a fresh browser without your logins and the first result tells the model why, so it says it is signed out instead of failing. browser_exec with local=true falls back to a fresh local browser, never the cloud one.

7️⃣ The classic CLI catches up with the shared gateway

Before: the classic CLI now drives a session on the shared gateway, and several commands still looked at its own empty process: /model, /refine, /review and /moa did not reach the session, /agents showed 0 running processes, /diff session crashed or said checkpoints were off, /stop mid-turn froze input until every job exited, a stale toolset left in config refused every hermes chat with invalid_params, and @file and @folder references resolved against the gateway's folder instead of yours. After: those commands run on the gateway session; -s skills and the other launch flags are carried in, and resuming with a different flag is refused by name instead of silently ignored; and when the last window closes, the session's memory is committed on the gateway, once. Not changed: nothing runs those end-of-session hooks after a gateway crash. In review: /resume or /sessions as the first action of a fresh CLI is refused at the next prompt.

8️⃣ Editors over ACP get their commands back

Before: editors talking to Hermes over ACP went through a gateway client that dropped most of what the old in-process server returned: no model picker or modes, no slash commands, empty replies to /model and /compress, no usage updates, and a load with a changed MCP server list failed with acp_mcp_policy_conflict. After: the model picker, modes, slash commands (/help, /tools, /context, /reset, /steer, /queue, /version, /usage, /status), usage and title updates are back; the gateway owns each session's editor MCP servers, applies a changed list on load and keeps them connected while the session has a viewer; tool names keep the server name; and /steer only redirects this editor's own turn. Not yet: the Accept Edits and Don't Ask modes are not offered.

9️⃣ /loop counts down to its next wakeup

Before: a running /loop printed a one-time next in 45m line in the CLI that never moved, showed nothing in the TUI, and sat frozen in Desktop. After: the CLI's live-work dock gets a loop row with cadence, run count and a countdown (per minute, seconds in the last one), the TUI shows a loop bar under the goal bar, and Desktop counts down by the second and says due, waiting for idle when it is overdue; all three show running now during a wakeup and the reason when paused.

🔟 1 new plugin in the catalog

One new entry, and it is official: REA reverse-engineers native binaries, .NET assemblies, Electron and JavaScript apps, Android packages and firmware through its MCP server; it needs Node.js 22.19 or newer and your own Ghidra, Hopper or IDA for native decompilation. Heads-up: a few REA tools run a command, drive an app, change a connected Android device or overwrite a file without a Hermes prompt; its bundled skill tells the agent to ask first. Its first pin could not install on v0.22.2 because of a manifest key that release did not know; the catalog was re-pinned the same day, and on main a plugin with a newer manifest key now installs with a warning instead of failing. Catalog entries do not wait for a release: they go live once the published catalog refreshes.

• Reverse engineering: rea

━━━━━━━━━━

⚙️ Meanwhile, in the engine room

Dozens of fixes landed yesterday that most users will never see, and the biggest share came from that race-condition hunt: files rewritten while another process read them, caches saved over each other, and timers that counted a sleeping laptop as idle.

• Windows Desktop attaches again to a gateway running as a Scheduled Task, which hermes gateway ensure refused for every task the installer registered
• On macOS, Desktop no longer hangs at startup when the home path's letter case differs from the disk, and symlinked profiles get their tickets
• Desktop's own UI tools (preview, focus pane and the rest) work again on sessions the shared gateway owns, instead of saying they only run in the Desktop app
• A successful hermes update is no longer reported as failed because the gateway read its exit-code file mid-write

text:
Self help, too late.
Chokingonyourownhypocrisy Syndrome: A Field Guide For The Afflicted
By Chloe Trapanotto
Leftists, are you having trouble breathing, swallowing, or forming a coherent sentence? You may be suffering from Chokingonyourownhypocrisy Syndrome.

For many of you, it’s sadly incurable. Treatment would require summoning your frontal lobe to produce a single consistent moral or rational thought across any two topics, and that lobe, I’m told, was surgically removed sometime around 2016.

I myself am suffering from whiplash, struggling to keep pace with the antonymous thoughts, feelings, and hot takes being churned out and choked on by you guys and gals.

For instance, earlier this week, I was reliably informed that commenting on what women wear is NOT okay. Period. Ever! Especially when it comes to women’s gym clothing. Comedian Shane Gillis committed the unforgivable sin of doing exactly that, in colorful language, and was promptly told to kill himself and rot in hell. (Though we all secretly know the gym women who photograph themselves in tight, neon short-shorts that are being swallowed whole by their own buttcracks. Nobody asked the shorts for consent.)

Then yesterday, REVERSE! The media overlords collectively forgot that, mere days earlier, they had cried misogyny over a man’s comment on a woman’s clothing. Instead, they cheerfully began dragging the (now former) White House press secretary for her every physical characteristic!

Perhaps their collective memory now rivals a goldfish’s.

Vanity Fair’s style correspondent, José Criales-Unzueta, who dresses like a button-eyed character from “Coraline,” wrote this about Katie Zacharias’s first-day look:

Going by Zacharias’s look at her press briefing yesterday, she fits the bill. Her long hair was parted to the side in cascading waves and was paired with a white pussy-bow blouse done up inexplicably sans bow — perhaps to deliberately avoid any inevitable “grab ’em by the pussy” jokes — under a navy double-breasted skirt suit with wide shoulders and golden buttons, naval-style. A study of Zacharia’s personal social media reveals that she is more often than not wearing head-to-toe black or white, or black and white, in various kinds of tailoring styles, be that a vest-cut dress or a variety of suits. There’s also the occasional short A-line dress — Christian sorority-girl style — in pastel shades or, of course, MAGA red.

Cute. Criticism for thee, but not for me!

So which is it, leftists? Can we comment on clothing, or can we not? I’m fine with either. Just make up your ever-hating minds. 

Speaking of what women wear, it’s NFL season, baby, which means the WAGs (Wives and Girlfriends) of NFL players are out dressing to impress. Several have engineered their popularity into thriving businesses, crafting creative, artistic game-day wear for their men on the field and for every woman in the stands. Kristin Juszczyk, wife of San Francisco 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk, famously upcycles jerseys into custom puffer vests, tops, and coats. Her designs went viral after Taylor Swift wore one to a playoff game, and they eventually grew into a licensed NFL fashion line. Being a WAG has become a sweet career path in its own right, and people are hungry to know what it’s like.

But, as with everything good and fun in life, Chokingonyourownhypocrisy Syndrome takes hold if you haven’t been properly mentally vaccinated.

A chronic patient, Michelle Obama, had Kylie Kelce, wife of retired Eagles center Jason Kelce, on her truly awful podcast, “In My Opinion,” to ask her the hard-hitting questions. 

“Were you ever a WAG?” Michelle, the acronym stands for wives and girlfriends…so duh. But I digress. If this is the level of rigor your show offers, Hillary’s podcast may soon snatch the crown from yours in the Former First Ladies’ Garbage Podcast Division.

“Yes, I was a terrible WAG,” Kelce responded. “I felt like the term WAG itself reduced the women to being defined by the role that their husband held. I was fortunate on the Eagles; we had women who were lawyers, nurses, educators. We had these women who were seriously accomplished in their own right. And I’m like, ‘Don’t reduce yourself to get in line with him. You have your own stuff going on.’ And I was always really excited about the women with the Eagles, and never wanted them to be diminished.”

Wow! I’m shocked she managed to garble all that out with such hypocrisy lodged in her windpipe.

First of all, she is blatantly diminishing women who don’t hold law or health degrees, and she treats motherhood, entrepreneurship, and simply supporting one’s husband as lesser accomplishments. Marriage isn’t about shrinking your worth because you support your partner. It is the merging of two lives, two flesh becoming one, in which a wife’s accomplishment becomes her husband’s and vice versa. It is a partnership, not a competition. Just because the roles don’t look the same doesn’t mean the two aren’t equal, Kylie.

But secondly, come on.

Are we seriously watching two women, who are relevant to the media world solely because of their husbands, lecture us on how women shouldn’t be defined by the roles their husbands hold? Roles, and I’m just spitballing here, like president of the United States or a well-known NFL player?

Side effects of Chokingonyourownhypocrisy may include idiocy.

I don’t know whether this disease can be cured in certain women. TrumpRx offers the treatment at no cost to patients, but, alas, we can’t mandate that they take it.

But they need it. For months, patients have reported sympathy for a woman who strangled her three babies to death (and blamed hormones), while simultaneously insisting that women can run the world. For months, patients have declared that women have the right to do absolutely whatever they want with their bodies, while screaming that Sydney Sweeney using her assets to advertise a betting website is whorish and unbefitting. And for months, patients have preached that sexual freedom is the most important thing a woman can have and that nobody should ever judge what happens in a bedroom, while shrieking that consent while drunk doesn’t actually count and that sexual take-backs are perfectly fine!

Too bad they’ll never get the treatment they need. Side effects of the medication would include common sense, more respect from others, and the miraculous reattachment of that frontal lobe.

Sigh. One can dream. Until then, pray for those suffering from Chokingonyourownhypocrisy Syndrome.

✈️💥 Neptune strike on Borisoglebsk: six Su-34M hit — result still being confirmed
On the night of 15 October, the Ukrainian Navy struck Borisoglebsk airfield in Voronezh Oblast with the Neptune coastal missile system. The Navy reported a large fire, secondary detonations, and the destruction of flight-support equipment.
▶️ Important context on the airfield itself. Borisoglebsk has been attacked repeatedly: August and October 2024, July 2025, and July 2026. As of July 2026 there were no permanently based combat aircraft, and satellite imagery in recent months showed minimal activity — likely because of its proximity to the border. The presence of six Su-34M therefore indicates they had only recently been redeployed there.
The main Su-34 base is elsewhere. Borisoglebsk hosts a training centre and mixed units of an aviation division. Russia appears to have used it as a reserve parking area, assuming distance offered protection.
🚀 The key shift: earlier airfield strikes were mostly by drones carrying relatively small warheads that hit warehouses, hangars and parking spots. A Neptune missile is different — larger warhead, higher speed, less reaction time for air defence. For aircraft sitting in the open this is far more dangerous.
🛫 The production dimension matters. Open estimates put Russian Su-34 output at roughly 30 aircraft a year. If six machines are confirmed destroyed, that is about two and a half months of total production — and they cannot be replaced quickly. The Su-34 remains the primary carrier of KABs; its numbers directly affect the intensity of Russian glide-bomb strikes. Even partial damage means repairs and downtime, and the repair base is limited.
❗️ Dispersing aircraft to reserve airfields no longer guarantees safety once they can be reached by missiles from depth. Meaningful protection will require hardened shelters for each aircraft — expensive and slow to build.

A projected 2027 NFL broadcasting lineup featuring Jim Nantz and J.J. Watt, Joe Buck and Greg Olsen, Ian Eagle and Troy Aikman, and Joe Davis and Drew Brees could give each network a distinct identity by combining experienced play-by-play announcers with analysts who offer complementary perspectives.

On CBS, Jim Nantz and J.J. Watt would blend traditional broadcasting excellence with elite defensive insight. Nantz’s polished delivery and talent for storytelling would pair with Watt’s knowledge of pass-rush techniques, blocking schemes, and defensive strategy. Together, they could create a prestigious, big-game presentation with a greater emphasis on the battles in the trenches.

On ESPN and ABC, Joe Buck and Greg Olsen would offer a balance of major-game drama and detailed football analysis. Buck’s authoritative calls and sense of timing would complement Olsen’s ability to explain route combinations, coverage adjustments, and coaching decisions in an accessible way. Their booth could be conversational, intelligent, and engaging without losing the excitement of Monday Night Football.

On Amazon Prime Video, Ian Eagle and Troy Aikman could deliver a confident, modern broadcast built around sharp play-by-play and candid analysis. Eagle’s versatility and verbal agility would complement Aikman’s direct assessments of quarterback decisions, offensive execution, and game management. Their challenge would be maintaining a natural rhythm that allows Aikman to provide meaningful insight without interrupting the flow of the game.

On FOX, Joe Davis and Drew Brees could establish a more technical, quarterback-focused booth. Davis’s clear, energetic delivery would pair with Brees’s expertise in pre-snap reads, defensive recognition, pocket movement, and passing concepts. Davis could help translate Brees’s detailed football knowledge into concise explanations that appeal to both dedicated fans and casual viewers.

Ultimately, the strength of these four pairings would lie in their differences. Watt would emphasize defensive line play, Olsen would explain broader offensive and defensive strategy, Aikman would focus on quarterback judgment and game management, and Brees would reveal how quarterbacks process the game. If each analyst developed a concise, natural broadcasting style, these hypothetical partnerships could offer NFL viewers four distinct presentations, each combining football expertise with storytelling and entertainment.

This was one of the more difficult talks for me to hear in 2015. The Sabbath felt too busy to be a delight. I had meetings at 7 a.m. Brooke was getting young kids ready without me, we showed up a little late to 3 hours of church, we had meetings after, and by the end, I felt accomplished, but I wouldn't have called it a delight. I'm happy to do it all, but now I have to try and make it "delightful" too?!

​Well, 11 years later, my Sundays are arguably harder. A few weeks ago, I flew in from Florida on the 7 a.m. flight. I landed at 9:35 a.m., went home and changed for church, had meetings afterwards, visited a family in need and another after that, and offered blessings. As I was driving home exhausted, a thought came to my head that today had been a delight. I argued with myself! "How dare you think that! Today was hard!"

​I started to think about what God had given me that day. He gave me opportunities all day to hear Him, see Him, feel Him, serve Him, and serve His children. If that's not a delightful Sabbath, I don't know what is.

text:
THE PRICE OF PROGRESS: WHAT HAPPENED TO THE AMERICAN FAMILY?
Over the last fifty years, Americans have repeatedly been promised that the next great change would make their lives better. Greater independence, reorganized schools, global commerce—each arrived with confident assurances of progress.There were gains. But who counted the costs to the family, the neighborhood, and the working person?My perspective begins before those fifty years. In 1968, I was developing a Montessori and childcare enterprise in Kentucky. Bankers questioned whether mothers would pay forty dollars a week. Our first five academies eventually served six hundred children, with another six hundred waiting.I prospered by recognizing a change that established lenders underestimated. Yet making money from a social transformation does not oblige me to believe that everything about it was good.What I witnessed was bigger than mothers taking jobs. The relatives who traditionally helped care for children were entering the workforce too. Grandmother, sister, aunt, and cousin were becoming less available. A family arrangement built upon generations of mutual assistance was giving way to purchased services.Women deserved opportunity, equal treatment, and the freedom to choose their work. But respect for that freedom should have included respect for women who chose to raise children at home. In my experience, that work was increasingly dismissed, as though a paycheck were the only reliable measure of contribution...and a woman’s value!We learned to count paid childcare as economic activity. We were less attentive to the value of the family care it replaced.Schools underwent their own upheaval. Court-ordered busing sought to remedy an undeniable wrong: children had been denied equal educational opportunity because of race. That wrong required https://t.co/GCZcX3QcAO criticism concerns the remedy’s limitations. Transporting children could change school enrollment without resolving unequal housing, poverty, or differences in school resources. Where families withdrew or moved beyond district boundaries, the promise of lasting integration became harder to fulfill. Research documents how white flight could undermine that objective.I regard busing as a failure wherever officials treated moving children as a sufficient substitute for building excellent, durable schools and communities. But an honest assessment must acknowledge that desegregation also produced substantial educational and economic benefits for many Black students, particularly in the South. Calling every desegregation effort a failure would erase those achievements.The question should have remained practical: Did children receive a better education, and could those improvements endure? The answer is no...bussing was a failure. I was in the midst in Louisville working for the County Judge Executive. We argued that the solution was to integrate the neighborhoods but the black community did not embrace the concept!Then came the promises of global trade.NAFTA became a defining symbol of the bargain offered to blue-collar America: accept greater international competition, and broader prosperity would follow.For families whose livelihoods depended on vulnerable industries, that bargain could be a backbreaker. Research by economists Shushanik Hakobyan and John McLaren found sharply reduced wage growth among blue-collar workers in the industries and communities most exposed to NAFTA. The effects reached local service workers whose jobs did not directly compete with imports.A factory’s troubles do not stop at its gate. A smaller payroll means fewer customers for nearby businesses, less security for households, and fewer reasons for young people to stay.NAFTA did not cause every factory closing. Manufacturing employment was also affected by technological change, other international competition, and recessions. Assigning every lost job to one agreement would obscure the larger failure to protect communities through economic change.But national averages offer little comfort to a displaced worker. The Congressional Budget Office has described trade agreements as producing small overall economic benefits while acknowledging that individual workers can suffer lower earnings or prolonged unemployment—and that some losses can be permanent.That distinction belongs at the center of the argument. A country can report an economic gain while particular towns and families sustain devastating losses.Across these decades, I see a recurring mistake: leaders measured what changed more readily than they measured what people https://t.co/VvJCudqYKy care had value before anyone charged for it. A neighborhood school had obligations beyond meeting an enrollment formula. A manufacturing job supported more than the worker standing at a machine.We cannot recreate the past, and we should not romanticize its injustices. We can demand a better standard for the future.Respect the parent who stays home. Make every neighborhood school worthy of its children. Judge trade policy partly by the livelihoods and communities it leaves behind. Give workers a credible path forward before asking them to surrender the one they have.I built a successful business by seeing a need others missed. That experience taught me to listen carefully when ordinary families describe their circumstances.America’s next fifty years should begin by doing the same, and remembering not to repeat the failures of the past, like the overbuilt, overpriced housing scandal of 2008 which saw the banks bailed out by the American taxpayer! Are we now witnessing that same mistake?
Welby Cox: Professor of Historical FunkCiting: ChatGPT with editing assistance

On Tuesday, Mississippi Transportation Commission Chairman Willie Simmons presented William G. "Bill" Yates, Jr., Executive Chairman of The Yates Companies, Inc., with the Dick Hall Excellence in Transportation Award. This award recognizes those in Mississippi who have demonstrated exceptional leadership and a dedication to our state's transportation system. Mr. Yates co-founded W.G. text:
So I opened the file and turned to page 14.

It was a table of adverse events from a heart medication trial. Dozens of rows, each with a subject number, an age, a site, and an outcome. Most were marked "resolved."

Eleven rows near the bottom were marked "deceased." Next to every one was the same cause: "unrelated, pre-existing condition."

That was odd, but audits are full of odd. I kept reading.

Every one of the eleven had been reclassified after the original report. The dates were stamped in a different font from the rest of the table, as if the changes had been made later, in bulk.

Then I got to row nine.

Subject 0412. Male, 58. Site: Fresno.

My father had lived in Fresno. He was fifty-eight when he died.

I told myself it was a coincidence. Fresno is a big city. Fifty-eight is a common age. My father had also told me, a few months before he died, that he was "helping test a new heart pill." I remembered him laughing about it and saying he'd gotten a free checkup out of the deal.

I checked the enrollment date and the date of death. Both matched.

Then I read the original, unaltered cause of death in the margin, in faded pencil.

"Probable drug-related arrhythmia."

Someone had crossed it out, and someone had written "unrelated" above it.

I stopped asking why Martin deleted his emails. I started asking what I had misunderstood about the last seven years of my own life.

My father had died on a Tuesday, alone in his kitchen. The doctors told us it was his heart, and that it was always going to happen. I believed them.

And a month later, a man I had never met offered me a job, with no real interview.

I went to Martin's office. The door was unlocked, and the desk was bare except for one item in the center. It was a plain white envelope with my name on it.

I opened it with my hands shaking.

Inside was a single index card, in Martin's neat handwriting.

"I flagged page 14 seven years ago, and the firm told me to drop it. So I waited. I hired the one person who would never accept 'unrelated' as an answer, and I erased everything so no one could say I told you where to look. This had to be found by your hands, Nadia. It's the only way it counts."

text:
grok says - Yes, the core of this story is true, based on contemporaneous reporting from the Associated Press, United Press International, The New York Times, Time, the Chicago Tribune, and others, plus a recent Snopes fact-check that rates the claim True.
In February 1986, Georgia farmer Leonard (or L.D./Lenard) Hill III, of Waynesboro in Burke County, died by suicide about 20 minutes before a scheduled foreclosure auction of his roughly 700-acre family farm. He hoped life insurance would cover roughly $300,000 in debt (tied to drought and low crop prices). It did not—the insurance fell short (reports cite a net around $175,000, with issues such as a lapsed policy), and the bank rescheduled the auction for September 2.
Atlanta businessman Frank Argenbright Jr. organized help and took a 30-day option to buy time. Donald Trump, then a 40-year-old New York developer, learned of the situation via news coverage. His spokesperson said he phoned the auction process, stopped it, offered about $20,000 upfront, and pledged to help raise the rest. Public donations followed (including from radio host Don Imus). After those, a roughly $78,000 shortfall remained; Trump covered half (figures cited around $39,000–$46,000) and Texas farmer/developer/landowner Tom McKamy covered the other half. The total raised was about $180,000–$187,000.
In December 1986, there was a public mortgage-burning ceremony at Trump Tower with Annabel Hill (then about 66) present; media covered it and AP photos exist. Trump later recounted in The Art of the Deal that he threatened a lawsuit (describing it in terms of the bank’s actions contributing to the death) to get them to back down. Annabel Hill and family members expressed gratitude; reports indicate the farm (or the bulk of it) stayed with the family, with a son continuing to farm it. Later accounts, including from the family, confirm the farm remained in family hands.
Nuances in the viral version:

It was not entirely secret or without cameras/press. Contemporary outlets reported it, Trump held related press events, and the mortgage burning was public. Coverage was substantial at the time but faded.
The Texas contributor is consistently identified as Tom McKamy (farmer/developer), not specifically an “oilman.”
Exact debt, acreage, and contribution figures vary slightly across reports, but the overall sequence is consistent.
Trump’s “wrongful death”/lawsuit threat matches his own later account more than the initial wire reports, which emphasized the phone intervention and guarantee.

Snopes and the period reporting confirm Trump’s role in stopping the sale and helping close the funding gap so the family could keep the land. The story is a documented 1986 episode, not a later invention.

1986. Georgia farmer Leonard Hill walked out of his house 20 minutes before the bank auctioned his family’s five-generation farm. He never came back.

He took his own life, hoping insurance would cover $300,000 in drought debt. It didn’t. His 66-year-old widow Annabel was left to face the auction alone.

An Atlanta businessman started making calls. One reached a 40-year-old New York developer named Donald Trump.

Trump called the bank himself. When they said the foreclosure was happening, he told them he’d sue for wrongful death if they proceeded. The bank backed down.

Americans sent checks. It still wasn’t enough. Trump and a Texas oilman quietly covered the last $78,000. No press release. No cameras.

Annabel’s family still lives on that farm today.

The media never tells you this side of Trump.

A widow with no lobbyist got a phone call and $78,000 she never had to repay.

Remember that the next time they claim they already know everything about the man.

text:
OREGON

ROCK BOTTOM 

If Oregon has ‘hit bottom,’ which political party can bring us back from the brink?

Oct. 16, 2026

In addiction recovery, “hitting bottom” does not mean things cannot get worse. It means the consequences have become painful enough that staying the course is harder to justify than changing it.

Oregon may be nearing that point.

Last month, I examined a dispute over whether homelessness is primarily a housing problem or is also driven by addiction and serious mental illness. A similar tension now runs through the Oregon gubernatorial race between Tina Kotek and Christine Drazan.

Oregon’s unemployment rate is tied for the highest of any U.S. state. 

More than 27,000 people are unhoused across the state. 

Oregon’s 2024 fourth grade reading and eighth grade math scores were well below national averages and among the nation’s lowest. 

Federal estimates also rank Oregon highest among the states for adult mental-illness prevalence and among the highest for substance-use disorder.

No governor caused all of this, and no party controls every force behind it. But governing is ultimately judged by results as well as intentions. When failures accumulate across housing, schools, behavioral health and the economy, voters are entitled to ask what those in power prioritized, what they tried — and what they are prepared to change.

Every Oregon governor since 1987 has been a Democrat, and Democrats have controlled both legislative chambers since 2013. Tina Kotek spent nine years as House speaker — the longest tenure in state history — and helped enact major policies on housing, education, labor and taxes before becoming governor.

That makes November’s election a referendum not just on Kotek’s four years as governor, but on the record of a central figure in Oregon’s Democratic governing establishment.

Her own Prosperity Council sets a useful standard. It says Oregon is at an “inflection point,” cites weak employment growth and above-average unemployment, and says Oregonians want “bold action, not incremental change.” Its recommendations span taxes, permitting, regulation, site readiness and workforce policy.

Kotek has responded with housing and permitting reforms, infrastructure financing and new school-accountability measures. The question is whether those changes match the scale her own council says Oregon needs.

Housing makes that question concrete.

ProPublica reported this summer that Oregon has given affordable-housing developers $1.4 billion since 2021, while the average cost of developing a subsidized apartment nearly doubled, to about $540,000. ** Yet state law shields key project financial records from disclosure, making those costs harder to scrutinize.

California offers one clue to a possible cost driver. Research there has associated ** prevailing-wage requirements with higher affordable-housing development costs. Oregon lawmakers this year considered exempting some affordable-housing projects from prevailing-wage requirements, but the proposal died in committee.

That dispute gives context to what the Oregon Journalism Project called a $10 million “mystery check” from a California-based carpenters union to an Oregon political committee that has already supported Kotek. The union says the money is for multiple candidates and measures. But union official Ron Rowlett explicitly linked its political support to policy: the carpenters back officials who support their priorities on “jobs, wages and benefits.” Carpentry groups have given Kotek $650,000 this year.

That does not establish a quid pro quo, but it does highlight the political conflict: If lowering subsidized-housing costs eventually requires changing labor rules important to one of Kotek’s significant allies, how far would she go?

Portland shows why the cost question matters.

text:
My heartfelt prayers are with the families, friends, and everyone impacted by the shooting in Oregon. It’s heartbreaking and deeply unsettling when violence erupts in our communities without warning. It’s difficult to understand, and even harder to accept.

When a 16‑year‑old decides to shoot and kill elementary school children and their teacher, it reflects not only a profound lapse in judgment and emotional stability, but also signals something much deeper. What causes a young person to lose faith in the very community that raised them? What leads them to plan such a violent act, access a firearm at home, and carry out a crime against innocent children and their teacher?

We may never fully comprehend the silent motivations within this young mind. But what we can do — and must do — is stay connected to the young people around us. Talk to them. Listen to them. Pay attention to their struggles, their friendships, their isolation, their online world, and their emotional health. Ensure they feel supported, valued, and engaged in their schools and communities. Above all, help them stay safe, healthy, motivated, and hopeful.

Because when young minds believe they have a place in the community, the ability to make a positive impact, and a path toward a better future, they do not turn toward violence.

Let us each do our part. Mentor a young person. Reach out to someone who seems alone. Offer guidance, encouragement, and presence. A small act of care today may prevent another tragedy tomorrow.

text:
In 1984, Michael Jordan did not want Nike. He wanted Adidas. His mother put him on the plane anyway, and that flight became worth over $1.3 billion.

He was a rookie, not a legend yet. Converse and Adidas already had their stars and saw him as just another draft pick. Nike was the underdog, desperate to sign one.

Jordan refused to even take the meeting. Deloris Jordan, his mother, made him go listen.

What Nike offered, no rookie had ever seen. Not a flat fee, but his own signature shoe and a cut of every pair sold.

> Summer 1984, Beaverton, Oregon. Nike puts $500,000 a year on the table for five years. Triple the richest sneaker deal of the era.

> His mother adds one clause: royalties on every pair sold.

> Nike projects $3 million in Air Jordan sales over four years.

> Year one alone does $126 million.

> The NBA bans the shoe. Nike pays the $5,000 fine every game and turns the ban into an ad.

Today Jordan Brand clears over $5 billion a year for Nike. Jordan himself has pulled an estimated $1.3 billion from a $500,000 deal.

The talent was his. A paycheck pays you once. A percentage pays you forever.

text:
Danielle Lei, a 13-year-old Girl Scout from San Francisco, sold 117 boxes of cookies in two hours after setting up her sales table outside The Green Cross, a medical marijuana dispensary on Mission Street, with her mother’s blessing.

Lei set up on a Monday over Presidents’ Day weekend, stocking Tagalongs, Samoas and Dulce de Leche cookies. Demand was so strong she sold out within 45 minutes and had to call for backup inventory. According to Holli Bert, a spokesperson for The Green Cross, “her mother was quoted as saying that she sold about 117 boxes in two hours.” Bert noted the dispensary saw the pairing as a natural fit, saying “it’s no secret that cannabis is a powerful appetite stimulant, so we knew this would be a very beneficial endeavor for the girls.”

Lei’s mother, Carol, told local station KPIX the choice of location was not meant as a political statement but a chance to show her daughters different parts of the city and to start a conversation about drug use. She later told Mashable that Danielle sold roughly 37 more boxes outside the dispensary than she did during the same two-hour window outside a Safeway the following day. Danielle herself offered a simpler explanation for the demand, noting that customers “get very hungry after.”

The sale drew national attention after The Green Cross posted photos to its Facebook page, and the dispensary said Lei would return that Saturday due to popular demand, with half of those proceeds going to Alzheimer’s-related charities. Her local council, Girl Scouts of Northern California, said it does not dictate where troops can sell and issued a statement saying the decision “is not intended to be an endorsement or statement of any kind.” Not every council agreed: Girl Scouts of Colorado publicly objected around the same time, stating it does not allow scouts to sell cookies in front of marijuana shops, liquor stores or bars.

text:
The CEO of one of the largest cannabinoid suppliers in the country emailed me today. He sent a catalog. In that catalog were THCP, THC-O, HHC — chemically converted and semi-synthetic cannabinoids, offered for sale by the kilogram. Out of curiosity I called the number and met a representative for Bret Worley, not Bret himself. Tyler told me Bret founded HIFA, the organization that has spent millions lobbying Congress and the White House to keep chemical conversion alive.

Here’s what makes that call extraordinary. Bret Worley is not just any industry executive. NBC News reported in August that that he is the son-in-law of White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles — married to her youngest daughter. Republican senators have complained directly to their leadership about the White House’s push to delay the hemp ban, Susie Wiles’ office. The same White House that asked Congress for “fair treatment of hemp products” is connected, by marriage, to the man selling Schedule I-adjacent product out of a Colorado warehouse.

THCP is already Schedule I. It always has been. The DEA’s May 2026 rule put chemically converted cannabinoids on the synthetic side of the line. And under the law Congress passed, cannabinoids the plant cannot naturally produce lose hemp status on November 12 — not December 11. The December date only covers what the plant can make. THCP is not something the plant makes. It is something a lab makes from CBD.

So the picture is this: a company whose CEO has a family tie to the top of the White House is circulating a wholesale catalog of products that federal organizations have classified as controlled substances. The farmer  who tests a tenth of a percent over the threshold gets his crop destroyed, his license revoked, and in some cases loses everything. The converter gets White House access, a catalog, and from what I’ve been hearing a 2 year runway to get through all of their stockpiles of what I can only assume are imported from other countries. 

There are legislative documents circulating right now that would put guardrails on the hemp industry while still allowing naturally occurring cannabinoids. HIFA and the Hemp Roundtable continually block them from going forward if they don’t include conversions, because their business model relies on converting cannabinoids and keeping raw material providers like the American farmer out of the equation and useful only as precursor growers who take all the risk and reap none of the reqard. If the hemp industry, the medicinal marijuana industry, and the recreational marijuana industry all grouped together and pointed out the obvious … That chemical conversion companies should not be allowed to participate in cannabis and should stay in the pharmaceutical realm, which is what they are most closely adjacent to.  We could get something across the finish line. But no one is going to agree when we’ve got people like this man saying he represents us, because he does not. Just because he’s found a way to extract money by selling what I personally believe are already Schedule I drugs, converted, and therefore unable to take the hemp exemption…  he has taken that money and used it to lobby Congress and even state-level lawmakers to continue doing exactly this. This is an obvious abuse of the American farmer, and anyone who doesn’t appreciate that is being ignorant of the facts in exchange for money. If you didn’t know that, now you do. Now do something about it.

This is not a eulogy for hemp. Hemp has a real future in American agriculture as a rotation crop, a fiber source, a building material, a feed ingredient, and yes, as a source of naturally occurring cannabinoids grown under the rules. That future is worth fighting for. What I am saying is that the people currently negotiating the terms of that future are the same people who spent eight years exploiting the loopholes that destroyed it. They parade farmers at hearings and in press releases as proof they care. They don’t.

text:
An older Black woman climbed down into a hole in a Houston street and lay flat on her back in the dirt, because it was the only way left to stop the digging. Her name is Dorris Ellis Robinson, and the gap she was lying in was exactly forty-five bricks wide, which happens to be the size of a grave. Those bricks were paid for and laid by hand by freed families after the city told them no for seven straight years.

The hole in the road was forty-five bricks wide.

That is not a figure of speech. A crew had lifted exactly forty-five of them out of Andrews Street in Houston's Fourth Ward, and the gap they left behind was roughly the length and width of a grave.

An older woman stood at the edge of it and looked down. Her name is Dorris Ellis Robinson, and she had spent years by then trying to keep machines off that particular stretch of pavement.

She had gotten a restraining order once. She had sat in meetings and written letters and stood in front of the city council, and none of it had worked, because the digging had started again that morning and it was still going.

She asked them to stop and they kept going, so she asked again.

"They didn't stop digging," she said later. "I mean, they were adamant."

Then she got down on her hands and knees at the edge of the hole, and lowered herself into it, and lay flat on her back in the dirt where the bricks used to be.

Forty-five bricks was just enough room for a woman's body.

That photograph now hangs at the entrance of an exhibit at the African American Library at the Gregory School, so it is the first thing a visitor sees walking in. A Black woman lying full length in a Houston street, staring up at the sky, surrounded by pavement that people keep trying to take.

"So I did whatever it took to save them," is how she put it. To understand why a woman would lie down in a road, you have to know what those forty-five bricks cost the first time.

Emancipation reached Texas on June 19, 1865, and within months the walking started. Freed families came up out of the Brazos River plantations along San Felipe Road, which ran straight into Houston from the southwest, and about a thousand of them stopped on the swampy south bank of Buffalo Bayou just west of downtown.

One formerly enslaved man remembered his owner, Charles Longcope, gathering everyone in June 1865 and reading them the proclamation from the doorway of his mansion. Then Longcope offered each of them a building lot out in the Fourth Ward, which tells you precisely what he thought that land was worth.

It flooded.

That was the whole reason it was available to Black people at all.

They took it and built on it anyway, and they named it Freedmen's Town. Within fifteen years it held the overwhelming majority of Black Houston, and by the 1930s it had produced more than four hundred Black-owned businesses.

People there still call it the Mother Ward, because Third Ward and Fifth Ward were poured out of it. One of the men who came was a Virginia-born preacher named Jack Yates, who had been enslaved and who reached Houston after the war.

In 1869 he bought a lot on Andrews Street, and in 1870 he built his house on it. Hold onto Andrews Street, because every single thing in this story happens on Andrews Street.

Three years after he laid his foundation, Yates did something they should teach in every school in Texas. On July 10, 1872, he and Richard Allen and Richard Brock and the Reverend Elias Dibble, all four of them formerly enslaved, closed on ten acres of land in Third Ward, bought from the Wellborn heirs for eight hundred dollars scraped together out of two congregations.

They bought it so Black Houston would have one piece of ground to hold Juneteenth on that nobody could put them off of.

They named it Emancipation Park, and it is still there.

Seven years out of bondage, and they were buying real estate for a holiday.

Now understand what those same families were living with underfoot. There was no pavement on their streets and there never had been, because the city of Houston did not pave Black neighborhoods.

When it rained, and in that part of Houston it rains, the road turned to standing mud. Catherine Roberts of the Rutherford B. H. Yates Museum has described the ordinary daily consequence of that, and it is the detail that stays with me.

Women in long skirts and petticoats had to step down off the walk and into the mud to reach the trolley.

Picture that on a Sunday morning.

Your good clothes, the ones you paid for and pressed, and you are ankle-deep in filthy water before you have gone twenty feet from your own door. In a neighborhood that flooded, that was a health problem before it was ever an indignity.

So they asked the city to pave the street. They asked in 1907.

They asked again in 1908, and in 1909, and in 1910, and the answer came back the same way every time.

No.

Six or seven years of petitions, from a community that by then had thirteen blacksmiths and thirty-four brick makers and installers living inside its own boundaries. These were not people who lacked the skill.

They lacked the permission. The city finally relented around 1914, and it attached a condition.

The work had to be given to a white contractor. Then the white contractor read the address and refused the job.

His reasoning is the part that should be printed on a wall somewhere. There were still unpaved streets in white Houston neighborhoods, and he was not going to be the man who handed Black residents something white residents did not have yet.

So the permit went out with a white-owned firm's name on it, Eureka Paving. And Eureka turned around and hired the brick men who already lived in Freedmen's Town, the same men whose neighbors had been petitioning for seven years, and charged the community a steep price for the work.

Sit with that arrangement, because it is the whole American arithmetic in one sentence.

They were not allowed to pave their own street until a white company was paid to hire them to pave their own street.

Some of the brick came out of a works owned by the Reverend Ned Pullum, a Fourth Ward minister who built a fortune on Pullum Standard Brick. A Black-owned brickyard, supplying a Black neighborhood, for a road the city refused to build.

They paid for it out of their own pockets. Then they went out after their own workdays and laid it themselves, by hand, one brick at a time.

Because they were the ones installing it, they got to decide how it went down. The families have always said the pattern set into that pavement came from home, carried across the water and pressed into a Texas road by people whose parents had been somebody's property.

Here the record deserves honesty instead of drama, because the sources disagree about which tradition it was. Roberts has described it as Yoruba, while others have pointed toward BaKongo cross designs out of West Central Africa.

The archaeologist Carol McDavid, who has worked in Freedmen's Town for years, has taken the position that the question deserves serious study before anybody tears the street up rather than after. Which is a careful scholar's way of saying the question is real and nobody has bothered to answer it.

What nobody disputes is whose hands were in the dirt.

For a stretch of decades that street was the center of everything Black Houston had. Then the twentieth century came for it, and it came in pieces, and every single piece was a decision made by somebody sitting in an office.

In the 1930s, land was cleared for the City Hall complex and Black residents were moved off it. In 1944 the housing authority opened San Felipe Courts, a thousand units of public housing for white families only, built on top of blocks of the oldest part of Freedmen's Town.

They sited it next to the city incinerator. It did not admit a single Black family until 1968.

In the 1950s the freeway came through and cut what was left of the ward in half. Then the arithmetic did the rest, and none of the arithmetic is disputed.

The Fourth Ward held nearly seventeen thousand people in 1910. By 1980 the remaining residential strip was down to fewer than 4,400.

Almost half of them were living below the poverty line. Only five percent owned the roof over their heads.

That is the neighborhood a young photographer walked into in 1970 with a camera he had bought himself.

Earlie Hudnall Jr. was born in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, in 1946. His father took pictures of the family, but it was his grandmother Bonnie Jean who made him what he became.

She sat out on the porch in the summer with a can of Garrett snuff and told stories out of the family album. That book was not just birthdays.

She kept obituaries in it. She kept newspaper clippings in it, and two of those clippings never left him.

One was about a Navy flyer shot down in Korea, which was Jesse L. Brown, out of Hattiesburg. The other was about a man taken out of a jail in Poplarville, Mississippi, by a mob in 1959.

He was ten years old when his parents sat him down and told him what had happened to Emmett Till.

Those clippings and his father's pictures, he has said, taught him young that somebody had to write down what happened to their own people. Then he added four words about it.

"That was the start."

He carried a small camera into Vietnam as a Marine. When his tour ended he wanted to reenlist and his mother refused to hear it, so he applied to the art program at Texas Southern University instead, hopped the Greyhound, and rode across the South to Houston at twenty-two.

At TSU he found the muralist John Biggers, who became his mentor and gave him a three-word instruction he has been repeating for fifty years. Art is life, Biggers told him, so draw on your own family and your own community and what we are all about.

Then a dean named Thomas Freeman came looking for a photographer. Freeman was running the local end of the Model Cities Program, part of the War on Poverty, and he needed somebody to go out on Tuesday and Thursday evenings and photograph how people in Houston actually lived.

Hudnall took the job for the money and stayed sixty years. It put him on foot in the Third Ward and the Fourth Ward and the Fifth Ward, in Sunnyside and South Park, at the exact moment every planning document in the city was writing those neighborhoods off.

He did not see a problem to be solved.

He saw Hattiesburg.

"It was a kindred kind of connection," is how he described walking into the Fourth Ward the first time. He talks about the clapboard houses, the kids playing in the road, the porches in the evening, and the sound of people laughing at each other from across a street.

When the federal contract ran out, nothing changed. He kept going back on his own time and his own film for the next five decades, with nobody paying him a dollar to do it.

Which brings us to an afternoon in 1983. He was walking the Fourth Ward with the camera the way he had walked it a thousand times, and there were people out on the sidewalk on an ordinary day on their own block.

And a boy decided to flip.

He went up off the pavement and turned over in the air, upside down, arms out, and Hudnall got him at the top of it.

Look at what is in that frame besides the child. There are neighbors watching from the walk, and there is the road under him, and rising up behind all of it, filling the whole top of the picture, is the skyline of downtown Houston.

Hudnall did not arrange that.

The boy went up and the city was already standing there.

In 1983 nobody official had yet decided the Fourth Ward was worth keeping. That took two more years.

On January 17, 1985, Freedmen's Town was added to the National Register of Historic Places, and the survey counted 530 historic structures standing on sixty-four acres. Fewer than thirty of them are standing today.

Roughly seventy-nine percent of the historic fabric of Freedmen's Town has come down since the day the federal government certified that it mattered. Of nineteen churches, eight remain.

The listing stopped federal money from paying for demolition. It did nothing whatsoever about private money, and private money never stopped coming.

So Hudnall was not photographing a neighborhood that afternoon. He was photographing the last of one, two years ahead of the paperwork and four decades ahead of the townhouses.

The picture is called Flipping Boy. The Smithsonian bought a print in 1994, a Houston Chronicle essay later called it the definitive photograph of the city, and it hangs today in Washington and in the Museum of Fine Arts Houston.

Nobody has ever printed the boy's name.

He is a man past fifty now, somewhere, and the label under his body says Flipping Boy, 1983, and not one word more. Which brings us back to Andrews Street, and to a woman who was watching all of this happen from inside her own house.

Gladys House-El is the fifth generation of the families who planned and developed Freedmen's Town. Her people were there for the mud and the petitions and the bricks.

"My family sold blocks of ice on the back of a horse-drawn buggy," she has said.

She was the fourth of fourteen children, four boys and ten girls, in a neighborhood where everybody's mother could correct anybody's child. She started fighting the city over this land when she was fourteen years old.

She still lives in the building her family's business ran out of. So on November 21, 2016, when the sound of heavy equipment came up Andrews Street, she did not need anybody to explain to her what was being torn out of the ground.

A resident named Rodney Jones saw it first, in the 1600 block, and got on the phone to the community. House-El heard the machine from inside her house and did not wait to get dressed properly.

She came out into the street in her housecoat with her phone already recording. Then she stood in front of a running excavator and told the operator he was in violation of federal as well as state law.

Think about what that takes. An older woman in a housecoat, alone in the road at first, filming a man on a machine and quoting statute at him until he shuts it off.

He shut it off.

By then roughly forty feet of the street was gone.

The mayor was in Mexico City for a football game and put out word that the work had never been authorized and that no one should have touched Andrews Street without him. The construction firm's general partner wrote him a letter conceding the company had made a serious mistake in removing pavers installed by the original residents of Freedmen's Town.

A month later a plumbing crew hit Andrews Street again, at the other end, also without permission. "To disrupt the sacred heritage of our brick streets is just overwhelming," House-El said.

She has also said, plainly, that her people have been on that ground since the beginning of time. By January 2018 she estimated seven thousand bricks were still out of the earth.

That March, city contractors began setting 3,610 of them back in, over a fresh leveling pad poured at Genesee and Andrews so the returned bricks would sit flush with the ones that had survived. The neighborhood held a celebration.

It lasted seven years.

On June 3, 2025, weeks before Juneteenth, a contractor working the corner of Andrews and Wilson damaged twenty-two more of them. Charonda Johnson, a fifth-generation resident and one of the two women the city designates to be notified before anyone touches that pavement, happened to be standing right there and stopped the work herself.

"I don't want to think about her not being there to stop it," the conservancy's director said afterward. In February of this year it happened again, a crew connecting water meters without telling either monitor, which is the exact thing the protocol exists to prevent.

Then on March 25 of this year, the Houston City Council voted unanimously to hand over the bricks the city had been keeping in a warehouse, so they can finally come home to the Fourth Ward. Dozens of pallets of them, cataloged over weeks by archaeologists working alongside neighborhood teenagers.

The conservancy and a museum are putting up $19,304 out of their own budgets to move them and build something to hold them. Under the agreement, the city does not have to pay for any of it.

So the community is paying to bring its own street home. That is the second time in a hundred and ten years that Black Houston has had to buy this road.

Here is the last thing, and it is the part that will not leave me alone. Jack Yates built his house on Andrews Street in 1870.

In 1994 that house was lifted off its lot and hauled a mile downtown to a heritage park, because moving it was the only way to keep a bulldozer off it. The house survived by leaving.

The street had to stay and take it.

And there are now two photographs of Andrews Street that matter, and they ought to be hung facing each other. In one of them, from 1983, a Black boy is upside down in the air over that road with the whole downtown skyline standing behind his head, and nobody has ever recorded his name.

In the other one, a Black woman is lying flat on her back in that same road, in a hole exactly forty-five bricks wide, because that was the only tool she had left.

One of them going up. One of them lying down.

Both of them on the same street, and both of them still waiting on the rest of us to finish what their great-grandparents started paying for in 1907.

Freedmen’s Town was built by people who had just walked out of slavery and decided they would build something of their own. I research forgotten stories like this because the communities that carried history deserve to have their names and places remembered. If you want to support this work:
https://t.co/Vm6JEQzdIW
Every coffee helps me keep creating.
