text:
A spotlight followed him through the goalposts, into an empty season.
It was the summer of 1962, an exhibition night at Cleveland's Municipal Stadium, and Ernie Davis had not played a single professional down. He would not play one that night either. Cleveland cut the stadium lights, then lit him alone at the tunnel and let him walk through the goalposts as his name went out over the public address system, and the crowd on hand stood and cheered a man who was there to be seen, not to play.

"They turned all the lights off, and then they introduced Ernie and they flashed the spotlight on him as he walked through the goal posts," his teammate and Cleveland roommate John Brown remembered years later.

That was the closest Ernie Davis ever came to playing professional football.

By then, Ernie Davis had already given the sport everything it could ask of him.

He was born on December 14, 1939, in New Salem, Pennsylvania, a coal town outside Uniontown. His father was killed in a car accident before he was born.

His mother could not support him alone, so she sent him to live with her parents.

He stayed with his grandparents in Uniontown until he was eleven. Then he moved north to Elmira, New York, to live with her again.

In Elmira he played in the local Small Fry Football League and was named a league All-Star twice, in 1952 and 1953, before he ever reached high school.

He grew into a three-sport star at Elmira Free Academy. He first made the local papers on the basketball court, where he led the school to a 52-game winning streak.

Football always stayed his first love, ahead of the other two.

More than fifty colleges offered him a scholarship. He chose Syracuse, ninety miles from home.

Jim Brown, the school's own Syracuse legend, had told him he would find better opportunities there than anywhere else. Davis listened.

He wore Brown's old number, 44, from his first varsity season. At Syracuse he also became the first Black member, nationally, of the Sigma Alpha Mu fraternity.

As a sophomore he helped Syracuse to an undefeated 1959 season and a national championship. He played through a pulled hamstring to do it.

He capped the season at the Cotton Bowl, catching an 87-yard touchdown pass against Texas that still stands as a Cotton Bowl record.

He was named the game's Most Valuable Player.

The banquet afterward did not go the way the trophy suggested it should.

Davis was told he could enter the segregated hall in Dallas to accept his award, then would have to leave before the public dance began.

One account, repeated for decades, says the entire Syracuse team voted to boycott the banquet in protest. A teammate who was actually there, John Brown, later told the Houston Chronicle it did not happen that way.

He said the Black players ate, collected their awards, and were led out by local NAACP representatives. The rest of the team stayed, he said, after a white teammate's motion to leave in solidarity was overruled by Syracuse officials.

The two accounts disagree about who stood up for Davis that night.

They agree completely about what was done to him.

He kept playing. He kept winning.

In his senior season, Davis broke Jim Brown's Syracuse career records in rushing, all-purpose yardage, scoring, and touchdowns. Those records had stood since Brown left campus five years earlier.

The new totals were 2,386 rushing yards, 3,414 all-purpose yards, 220 points, and 35 touchdowns. He closed his college career with an MVP performance in the Liberty Bowl, running for 140 yards in his final game.

Syracuse later retired the number itself, so no one else would carry it at all. That happened decades after both men were done wearing it.

On December 6, 1961, he became the first African American to win the Heisman Trophy.

In New York to accept it, he met President Kennedy, at the president's own request. "Imagine a president wanting to shake hands with me," Davis said at the time.

Not long after, a stranger stopped him on the street and asked if he was really Ernie Davis. Davis, who never liked the fuss, told the man no.

Back home, Elmira threw him a testimonial banquet of its own that spring, ahead of the draft. The program called him the city's "greatest Ambassador of Good Will on the field of sport," the kind of civic pride the small town had never had reason to export before.

By then Davis had a steady girlfriend, Helen, whom he had met on his own graduation trail. That May, weeks before what would be his last hospital stay, she asked him to promise he would come to her graduation. He told her he would.

He did not.

The Washington franchise held the first pick in the 1962 NFL draft. Cleveland had already traded away an established star of its own, Bobby Mitchell, for the right to take Davis once Washington made the selection.

Washington used the pick on Davis, making him the first African American ever chosen first overall in the NFL draft. The team traded him immediately to Cleveland, where owner Art Modell wanted him in the same backfield as Jim Brown.

Davis signed a three-year contract, reported at the time as worth $80,000, the largest ever given to an NFL rookie.

Some later accounts put the figure closer to $65,000. Either number made him, for a few months that spring, the highest-paid player about to enter the league.

He never entered it.

That June, playing in an all-star exhibition in Buffalo, Davis looked sluggish enough that Modell himself asked, "What's wrong with him?" Back home in Elmira afterward, Davis told a friend, "I'm tired, and my gums are bleeding. I've got to get my gums checked."

Five weeks later, at camp for the College All-Star Game, his own coach barely recognized him. "We all looked at him, and someone said, 'This is an All-American?'" head coach Otto Graham remembered. "He had no pep."

Doctors diagnosed acute monocytic leukemia. Modell knew how serious it was.

He did not tell Davis the full truth for months. Davis kept expecting to play, and the Browns let him keep practicing through the fall, alongside teammates who had already been told more than he had.

The disease went into remission for a stretch in early 1963.

There was real hope, from Davis and from the team, that he might suit up that season. Head coach Paul Brown said the doctors he consulted advised against it.

Davis never got clearance to play.

That March, two months before he died, an article appeared under his byline in The Saturday Evening Post, titled "I'm Not Unlucky."

In it, Davis wrote about the first real disappointment of his life, long before any of this. He described watching his Midget League baseball team march out on Opening Day in Uniontown without him.

There had been a mix-up handing out uniforms, and none was left for him.

"I can still remember how I felt," he wrote. Then he wrote about the diagnosis that had just cost him everything the record said he had earned.

"Some people say I am unlucky," he wrote. "I don't believe it. And I don't want to sound as if I am particularly brave or unusual."

"Sometimes I still get down, and sometimes I feel sorry for myself. Nobody is just one thing all the time."

"But when I look back I can't call myself unlucky. My 23rd birthday was December 14. In these years I have had more than most people get in a lifetime."

Two months later he entered the hospital for the last time.

Ernie Davis died on May 18, 1963. He was 23 years old, sixteen months after the diagnosis that ended his career before it started.

The day before the funeral, mourners lined up for twelve hours outside the Elmira recreation center where his body lay. On the day itself, sixteen hundred people packed a Baptist church and another three thousand stood outside in a park to hear the service.

A telegram from President Kennedy was read there, calling Davis "an outstanding young man of great character who consistently served as an inspiration to the young people of the country." Members of the United States House and Senate rose that same week to eulogize a man who had played zero professional games.

Syracuse retired his old number, 44, in a 2005 ceremony that honored him alongside Jim Brown.

He was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 1979, sixteen years after he died. A statue of him stands in Elmira, and another on the Syracuse campus.

In October 2008 his life became a movie, The Express.

His Syracuse teammate Floyd Little, whom Davis had personally talked into choosing Syracuse over Notre Dame, said years afterward that he believed Ernie's achievement had been "kind of underplayed by history."

His college coach, Ben Schwartzwalder, put it more simply.

"I never met another human being as good as Ernie," he said.

Decades later, Davis's rushing total still ranked among Syracuse's top fifteen, in a program that has sent dozens of backs to the NFL since. A nonprofit in Elmira still keeps his name in front of the city's kids, handing out the same encouragement his own coaches once gave him.

Elmira later named an elementary school after him, Ernie Davis Academy. In 2009 Syracuse renamed its football field Ernie Davis Legends Field.

The Downtown Athletic Club, which still awards the Heisman Trophy every December, paid for his epitaph in Elmira's Woodlawn Cemetery. His headstone carries his name and the year he won it.

Nothing about the contract. Nothing about the jersey retired for a season he never played.

Just the one thing they let him keep.

text:
Montana, 1881. 

Long before Yellowstone became America's most famous national park, the Crow Nation called the surrounding mountains, valleys, and rivers home.

Take a good look at these faces.

These are the Apsáalooke, known to history as the Crow. A people renowned for their horsemanship, fierce warriors, remarkable resourcefulness, and determination to defend their homeland.

Their territory stretched across portions of present-day Montana and Wyoming, from the Bighorn country to the Yellowstone River and the Absaroka-Beartooth Mountains.

This was a land of extraordinary abundance. Bison roamed the plains. Rivers provided fish and water. Mountain valleys offered shelter, medicinal plants, timber, and hunting grounds.

To outsiders, the Yellowstone country would eventually become known as "Wonderland."

But to the Crow, it was something far more important.

Home.

The Crow developed a remarkable horse culture. Their warriors became legendary for daring horse raids, and horses represented wealth, mobility, prestige, and survival.

Yet their society was far more than warfare.

Crow women played essential roles in maintaining households, preparing food, constructing and managing tipis, preserving traditions, and sustaining their communities. Strength wasn't confined to the battlefield.

And despite their reputation as formidable fighters, the Crow also established friendships, trading relationships, and family bonds with outsiders.

Some early fur traders and mountain men married Crow women and made their lives among the Apsáalooke, becoming part of a world where different cultures met on the frontier.

But the arrival of settlers, military expansion, and broken treaty promises eventually cost the Crow much of their ancestral territory, including the mountains they had called home for generations.

Their story is one of courage, adaptability, loss, and extraordinary endurance.

And perhaps the lesson is this....

A people's greatness isn't measured only by the battles they win, but by the culture, family, and identity they preserve through generations of hardship.

The Crow Nation did not disappear into the pages of frontier history.

They are still here. And their legacy lives on.

"Musk Documentary Paints a Damning Portrait as His Money Props Up Ken Paxton in Texas

Alex Gibney’s new documentary “Musk” paints Elon Musk as a man who sees other people as characters in his own video game, according to a review in The New Republic. 

The film, from the director of “Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room” and “Going Clear,” runs nearly four hours with an intermission. 

Musk refused to be interviewed and instead called Gibney a “douche” on X, so Gibney built a database of Musk’s recorded interviews and created a computer-generated Musk avatar that “answers” questions using things Musk has actually said. 

The device plays on Musk’s long-held belief that life is probably a simulation, and the film portrays him as the main character in a digital world where everyone else is a “non-player character.” 

Reviewer David Klion describes the portrait that emerges as one of “an empty, hateful, emotionally stunted man” whose two superpowers are shameless self-promotion and an ability to exploit weaknesses in government regulation. 

The central question of the film, Klion writes, is how someone like Musk gained such immense power and “what does it say about the rest of us that we allowed it to happen?”

The documentary traces the damage Musk has done, from Tesla’s self-driving crashes to the dismantling of USAID, and includes his power over Ukraine’s battlefield through Starlink. 

Gibney interviews more than a dozen people, including Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard, Musk’s ex-wife Justine, Ashley St. Clair, former USAID chief Samantha Power and members of Musk’s own family. 

The film highlights a Florida lawyer suing Tesla over its self-driving cars, which have been involved in at least 60 deaths. 

It also covers Musk’s gutting of the federal government through DOGE, and Power chokes up on camera describing the suffering caused to the world’s poorest people when USAID was dismantled. 

Gibney shows how Musk built ties with Trump, Argentina’s Javier Milei, Brazil’s Jair Bolsonaro and Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdogan to expand businesses like Starlink, which lets him “sway the battlefields of Ukraine by denying or granting access.” 

St. Clair, the mother of one of his 14 known children, says on camera that she refused to sign a nondisclosure agreement she claims Musk has offered other women and details the harassment she has faced since speaking out."

text:
Judge loses patience and threatens sanctions as Trump crosses the line in BBC lawsuit
Story by David Edwards

A federal judge warned President Donald Trump that he will face sanctions if he continues to disregard her orders in his $10 billion lawsuit against the BBC.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett issued the warning Friday in a court order directing Trump to respond by Oct. 22 to the BBC’s request to force him to sit for a deposition

The warning came after months of Trump resisting discovery of evidence on several fronts, court records show. Lett wrote that the BBC filed five motions on its own rather than joint motions because of Trump’s “disregard” of those rules.

“The Court has admonished Plaintiff for his lack of participation to no avail. Going forward, the Court expects strict compliance with its … Order, the failure of which will lead to sanctions,” Lett wrote.

Lett had warned Trump in June, after he failed to give the BBC his side of a joint motion, writing that lawyers “are not permitted to disregard the Court’s orders and procedures” and that failing to respond “may result in sanctions including granting the relief by default,” meaning she could rule for the BBC without hearing from Trump.

Two days before that warning, U.S. District Judge Roy Altman, who was then presiding over the case, ordered Trump’s lawyers to explain why he should not sanction them for “their apparent disregard of court deadlines,” the docket shows. They missed the deadline to respond to the BBC’s motion to dismiss.

That same month, Lett rejected Trump’s bid to remove her, finding that he waited too long to raise the issue and “has only done so when a disputed discovery issue arose.”

The BBC said in a September filing that Trump produced one document on July 14 and had not signed his written answers under oath. Lett ordered him to produce the undisputed records by Oct. 21.

In July, Lett ordered the Donald J. Trump Revocable Trust to turn over tax returns, financial statements and ownership records for roughly 400 business entities, CNBC reported. Altman paused that order in August on the day the records were due, after the trust asked for relief and Trump moved to drop his claim that his businesses were harmed.

Trump filed the lawsuit in December, claiming a BBC “Panorama” documentary defamed him by splicing together parts of his Jan. 6, 2021, speech. Lett ruled in August that the BBC “is entitled to discover Plaintiff’s intention behind the speech.”

Trump agreed in July to sit for a deposition on Oct. 16, the BBC said in a motion filed Tuesday.

“[T]he President is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance,” his lawyer Ian Corp wrote on Sept. 28, according to emails the BBC filed.

On Oct. 9, Trump’s lawyers told the BBC he had no availability before discovery closes Dec. 18, the motion said. They offered January 2027, but only if the BBC agreed to extend discovery.

“Plaintiff chose to file this lawsuit and, in doing so, he accepted the obligations of civil litigation,” the BBC’s lawyers wrote.

Lett also ruled Oct. 9 that the BBC could serve subpoenas on the president’s children Donald Trump Jr. and Ivanka Trump and son-in-law Jared Kushner by certified mail and by email to his lawyers, after the network said their Secret Service protection blocked service in person.

Lett will take up the disputes at a hearing on Oct. 22 in Miami, according to the docket.

text:
UKRAINE’S SUPPORT IS DRYING UP, AND ZELENSKY IS RUNNING OUT OF OPTIONS

The U.S.-Ukraine relationship is collapsing. Trump and Zelensky have gone from strained to openly hostile.
Ukraine blamed Elon Musk for throttling military Starshield terminals and disrupting drone operations. Musk says the U.S. government controls Starshield, and the military and president set any limits.

Ukraine says some restrictions have eased. But Patriot missiles are running out, and intelligence is going dark.
This may not be a glitch. It may be leverage. Washington is squeezing Kyiv.

Warhawks like Keith Kellogg want Ukraine to strike every Russian oil refinery. Trump wants lower diesel prices. Those strikes would drive up fuel costs.

Zelensky is not acting like a man who thinks he is winning. He is acting like a man who knows he is losing.
MAGA voices, Elon Musk, DC Draino, Mike Cernovich, and Ian Miles Cheong, are calling for Zelensky to go. The MAGA sphere is turning on him.

Then Zelensky told the Financial Times that Trump is drawn to Putin because he admires strongmen. Congress has appropriated nearly $175 billion for Ukraine: weapons, intelligence, and Patriot missiles. Yet Zelensky is publicly psychoanalyzing the president who controls the checkbook, while journalists overlook his corruption scandals.

That is how relationships end. Washington is moving on.
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are reportedly exploring a deal to bring Russia to the table. The reported U.S. offer would unfreeze roughly $100 billion in frozen European assets. The U.S. is also looking to ease sanctions on “shadow fleet” tankers moving diesel for Russia, Iran, and Venezuela.

Ukraine is being squeezed. Russia is being courted.
This is no longer a stalemate. It is a wind-down. The harder Zelensky resists Trump, the faster pressure to remove him may grow.

James Carden and Col. Douglas Macgregor join me to discuss.

text:
I agree that Japan has lost ground in certain industries, especially smartphones, TVs, and more recently, electric vehicles. And yes, Samsung, BYD, and Chinese manufacturers have become extremely competitive.

But I wouldn't underestimate Japan's global presence either.

I live in Europe, and I own a Roland electronic drum kit, a Yamaha digital piano, Sony headphones, a Panasonic bread maker, Makita power tools, and both the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2.

Japanese brands are still very much part of my everyday life, even thousands of kilometers away from Japan! 🇯🇵

As for Korean products, I own a Cuckoo rice cooker and an LG TV. Interestingly, I also own a Marantz home cinema receiver, a brand originally founded in the United States, with a strong Japanese engineering heritage, which now belongs to Samsung through Harman.

The fact that Japanese and European brands are losing momentum in certain industries is partly due to increasing competition in global markets. Consumers have far more choices today, especially with China becoming such an industrial powerhouse.

And let's not forget that we live in a globalized economy, where products are made with components sourced from all over the world.

The automotive industry is a perfect example. Depending on the country and its trade agreements, manufacturers may need to source or produce a certain percentage of a vehicle's value locally or regionally to benefit from favorable trade conditions.

So a Japanese car may contain European, American, Chinese, or Korean components, just as vehicles from those countries may contain Japanese technology.

That's why it's important to look beyond brand names and understand how interconnected our economies have become.

And Japan certainly hasn't stopped innovating!

text:
The Mind in the Dark: A Nature Study and the Defense of the Subject

A study published in Nature on May 6, 2026, gives laboratory proof to a point I made in my paper The Illusion of the Amoral Escape: A Critique of Hans-Georg Moeller's Post-Moralism. Kalman Katlowitz, Sameer Sheth and their colleagues at Baylor College of Medicine placed Neuropixels microelectrodes in the hippocampus of patients under general anesthesia, then played them tones and recorded speech. [1] 

The neurons detected unusual tones, improved at the task over about ten minutes, tracked the meaning and grammar of the spoken words, and predicted the meaning of words still to come.
Scientists have long suspected that the brain computes whether a person is aware or absent. 

The Baylor team recorded that computation neuron by neuron. The patients had lost consciousness under anesthesia, while their hippocampal cells parsed a story in the dark.

The finding divides brain work from awareness. In my paper I answered the school of thought, running from B. F. Skinner and Benjamin Libet to Daniel Dennett and Moeller, which dissolves the person into the brain and holds that the subject equals the processing. [2] Baylor's patients had the processing and lacked the subject. 

Awareness stands as a further fact beyond the computation, and I hold that fact to be the person.

Near-death experience supplies the mirror image. Pim van Lommel's prospective study of 344 cardiac-arrest survivors in the Netherlands, published in The Lancet in 2001, found that 18 percent reported near-death experiences, many vivid and lucid, during clinical death, when the brain's electrical activity is known to fail within seconds. [3] 

The anesthetized hippocampus shows brain work with no experience. Cardiac arrest shows experience with failing brain work. Scientists call such a pattern a double dissociation, and it marks two separate events. Sam Parnia's AWARE study of 2014 set out to test reports of perception during resuscitation and verified one patient's account of events during his cardiac arrest, the ground on which this question will be settled. [4]

The Baylor researchers compared the hippocampus's word prediction to the way large language models generate text. [5] 

Their comparison strengthens my warning about algorithmic administration. Prediction occurred with the person absent, so a machine that predicts the next word offers no evidence of anyone inside it. A technocracy can model the processor and still miss the human being.

Sheth said of the finding that it "pushes us to rethink what it means to be conscious." 

I agree, and the rethinking leads back to the subject: the person who knows, chooses, and answers for what is chosen.

Notes

[1] Kalman A. Katlowitz et al., "Plasticity and Language in the Anaesthetized Human Hippocampus," Nature 654 (2026): 714–723. 

https://t.co/TWtNRTmNgJ

[2] Matthew Swann, The Illusion of the Amoral Escape: A Critique of Hans-Georg Moeller's Post-Moralism (2026).

[3] Pim van Lommel et al., "Near-Death Experience in Survivors of Cardiac Arrest: A Prospective Study in the Netherlands," The Lancet 358 (2001): 2039–2045.

[4] Sam Parnia et al., "AWARE—AWAreness during REsuscitation—A Prospective Study," Resuscitation 85 (2014): 1799–1805.

[5] Baylor College of Medicine, "Researchers Discover Advanced Language Processing in the Unconscious Human Brain," news 
release, 2026.

After 15 years of conflict with the Houthis in Yemen, some favour dealing with the group as the regime in control rather than continuing to fight it. 

After all, they say, most of those who ruled Sanaa in the past were recognised regardless of their identity or ideology. This is a realistic approach. 

The problem, however, lies in the Houthis’ own agenda.
They seek to control the state’s resources and institutions while waging wars aligned with Iran’s interests. 

The events of 2013–2015 offer a clear test case. The Houthis were invited to join the Dialogue Conference and signed the peace agreement, gaining political representation. In return, they were required to hand over their medium and heavy weapons to the state.

Instead, they seized state institutions, detained President Hadi and dissolved parliament, triggering war among Yemenis.

A second test came when former President Ali Abdullah Saleh entered a governing “partnership” with the Houthis. Though out of office, Saleh still controlled most of the armed forces. Yet he too misjudged the militia, which ultimately killed him in 2017.

Some may see it simply as a power struggle that ended in Houthi supremacy and argue that we should therefore have accepted the new reality and dealt with it accordingly.

Why not be pragmatic now and deal with whoever rules Sanaa, just as we did in the past, from Imam Yahya to President al-Iryani and ultimately President Saleh?

That approach has already been tried. But the Houthis refused to make the transition from ideological movement to state authority. They continued to wage war against Yemenis, neighboring Saudi Arabia and the wider region.

To understand whether the Houthis are a state or a militia, we should compare them with ISIS and Hezbollah. True, ISIS represents an extreme case. It rejected the idea of the state and sought to establish a caliphate without borders.

Hezbollah adopted a mixed model in which it participates in state institutions while remaining an armed militia that takes orders from abroad.

The Houthis are more similar to the Hezbollah model a militia dressed as a government while answering to Iran.

The Saudis dealt with different previous Yemeni states. But this approach has failed with the Houthis.

Could one argue that the Houthis remain armed and rebellious because their neighbors and the international community refused to recognize them or give them a chance?

Recent history shows exactly the opposite.
The Americans, Europeans and UN gave them an opportunity to be recognised. The Stockholm Agreement in 2018 saved them from defeat and collapse. Western governments that accommodated them tried and failed to turn them into a civilian political movement and a normal government.

Riyadh then tried again, working with Muscat and the UN envoy. They offered the Houthis incentives to become peaceful neighbors and end the war. Saudi Arabia paid their employees’ salaries and allowed them to run airports and ports. A senior Saudi delegation visited them in their “capital,” Sanaa, as a major gesture of political recognition.

These efforts aimed to turn Houthi rule into a friendly neighboring “state.”
Meanwhile, the militia was secretly working with Iran to build its offensive military capabilities. In 2023, it returned to waging war against its neighbors to look more like an armed Iranian proxy.

Contrary to what some believe, the Houthis are Iranian proxy, not the nucleus of an ordinary Yemeni system of government.

There is a clear distinction between an ally and a subordinate. An ally is someone whose interests coincide with yours. A subordinate is someone whose will is constrained by yours.

(continuation)

On relations between theory and practice, I am inclined to say that they are the same: conditioning. It is the answer I gave you about no-self in May: "There is no self, and no, no-self. Both self and no-self are conventional, dependently originated, dualistic, and therefore empty of inherent existence." And just as practice can offer insight to body and mind, so can intellectual work. The texts we read together gave me "language and structure for what I knew but could not say."

It is only that in the West, mind is typically given priority, whereas in Dōgen does not give that exception. You once pointed out that much of Western intellectual history has privileged the subject. Dōgen turns that around: "Driving ourselves to practice and experience the myriad dharmas is delusion. When the myriad dharmas actively practice and experience ourselves, that is the state of realization." Thinking is not the trouble for him either: "we are prone to beget random intellectual ideas, and because we chase after these as if they were real things, we vainly pass by the great state of truth." And Dōgen does speak of traces: "There is a state in which the traces of realization are forgotten; and it manifests the traces of forgotten realization for a long, long time."

Practically, sitting in the present means sitting between a past that no longer exists and a future that has yet to arrive. It is a squirrely place. But serious meditators, and those engaged in flow practices like dancing, climbing, skateboarding and fishing, find that this zone encourages energy and lightness. Untethered from past regrets and future anxieties, the space for creativity becomes almost infinite. We drop projections that constrain the people around us, allowing them to remix their present moment karmas. This state of unconstrained presence is exactly how the Nautilus process begins and ends, returning the practitioner to that abundant void.

I have much work to do on Chpater 2; but I think the weave here is getting stronger.

Warmly,
Chris

Interest rates in a lending market depend on the protocol’s rate model and the market conditions supplied to that model. Utilization is often one of the most important inputs.

When a deposit, withdrawal, borrow, or repayment changes the market’s supplied or borrowed totals, the utilization ratio may change as well. The updated ratio can then influence the borrowing rate and the rate offered to suppliers under the configured formula.

The exact timing depends on the protocol’s implementation. Some systems calculate rates when a state-changing transaction updates interest accounting; others expose rates derived from the current market state when queried. Users should consult the specific contract logic before assuming that every rate change follows one universal block schedule.

In practice, a rise in utilization often increases borrowing costs and may improve supplier returns. A decline may ease borrowing costs while increasing the proportion of liquidity available for withdrawal. These effects depend on the market’s parameters and any utilization thresholds built into the rate curve.

The important point is that rates are connected to the market’s state rather than being permanently fixed. A rate displayed now may not remain unchanged after other users deposit, borrow, withdraw, or repay.

Monitoring utilization alongside supply and borrow APYs gives users a more complete picture of the market. It also helps explain why interest estimates can change between planning a transaction and its eventual execution.

Current rates are useful indicators, but they should be treated as variable conditions rather than guaranteed future returns.

To win a war requires an enemy; to secure a peace requires a state. For Zimbabwe, the very instincts that dismantled Rhodesian settler rule; clandestine command, militarized paranoia, and zero-sum discipline, became the governing blueprint for four decades of post-colonial decline. But the tragedy does not belong to ZANU-PF alone. While the ruling elite transformed a revolution into a predatory securocrat cartel, the democratic opposition repeated the pathology in reverse: mistaking moral outrage for a theory of governance, chasing power without policy, and fracturing under charismatic vanity. Zimbabwe's trajectory offers an unsparing autopsy of liberation politics: when a movement fails to cultivate institutions and statecraft during the struggle, the peace it secures will inevitably inherit the violence of the system it overthrew.

text:
Start here.

A war-band can take a peninsula and still not own its own story. Muhammad died in Medina in June 632. Within a generation his men were not reciting one fixed text. According to the Sunni canon itself—Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 and 5102—Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, campaigning in Armenia and Azerbaijan under the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan (r. 644–656), heard Syrian and Iraqi soldiers accusing one another over variant readings of the Qur’an and feared schism. Uthman ordered Zayd ibn Thabit and a small committee to produce one official recension from the sheets already gathered under Abu Bakr after the battle of Yamamah (c. 632–633), sent copies to the main garrison cities, and commanded that other written collections be burned. That is not how a father handles truth. That is how a commander handles a riot in camp. The man of the raid had offered fighting men what fighting men already priced—women, spoil, rank, a paradise with the smell of victory on it—and he got his army: Hijrah 622, Badr 624, the taking of Mecca in 630, a community armed enough that, after 632, it walked out of Arabia and broke the near frontiers of Byzantium and Ctesiphon. He did not get control of the wording. The sword can gather a host. It cannot keep ten mouths from rewriting the banner. When the banner starts a fight, the caliph does not repent. He lights a fire under the other pages (Bukhari 4987).

That is the method. Feed the pack. Win the ground. When the story cracks, burn the variants. A hunter plates the hunger. He does not remake it.

Now the other table.

The gospel is still the worst product in the shop. No one designing customers writes it. Someone who wants sons writes it. Soft men swollen with appetite will always walk to the louder stall. That walk is not evidence. It is the x-ray. And it leaves Jesus where He stands: above the stall, the legion, and every cheap replacement—worthy, because He refused to purchase us with our vice. He paid in blood.

God is not recruiting buyers. He is calling children home.

Jesus does not bait Jew or Greek with their favorite dish. He orders both to drop the plate.

The Jew wanted a war-crown: Rome thrown off, Zion armed, a Messiah who wins like Caesar. Jesus answers with timber and nails, under Pontius Pilate, c. 30–33. “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Come back to the Father. Receive a name. “To all who received Him, He gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12).

The Gentile wanted the old night: the body as shrine, the feast that never closes, the rot Paul names in the streets around the churches (Romans 1; 1 Corinthians 5–6). Jesus answers with a cut. Stop staring. Tear out the eye (Matthew 5:27–32). One covenant bed. Rule the flesh. Then live as a son, not as a stomach.

He does not toss steak to the wolf. He puts bread in a mouth that only knew raw meat—and then dies and rises so the mouth can say Abba. No harem as wages. Adoption. The Lamb dies for the enemy. The stone rolls.

Muhammad runs the opposite shop. He wanted a host and he bought one with the inventory the host already priced: raids for caravan wealth after 622, plural marriage written into law, captives as a lawful yield of war. That raises banners. It does not raise sons of God. And when the inventory of words would not sit still, Uthman, about 650–653, burned the extras. Army first. Canon by bonfire second.

Look at what grows, without perfume. Where Christ’s gospel actually entered—not the costume of Christ, the command of Christ—even under crooked kings, a strange orchard appeared: the weak life counts, the child is not a clan chip only, the woman is not a share of loot, letters and universities sprout because a soul is addressed by God and must learn to answer. Cathedral schools and the medieval universitas—Bologna (1088), Paris (c. 1150), Oxford (c. 1096)—did not grow from a tent of captives. They grew from a Cross and from “let the little children come to Me” (Mark 10:14).

A creed built to please the raider will not pause and see woman and child as the image of God. It will see them as cargo—flesh, hush, wall. Useful falsehood, sanctified war, the killing of the holdout, poverty called fate: that is not bad weather on the map. That is what you plant when desire wears a scabbard.

If truth were the average male wish, heaven would be unemployed. We already know the wish: more body, more force, more alibi. That wish is the clay of this century—in the old paganism that still rides under a prophet’s name, and in the new ideologies that spit on the church. Both want a homemade god. One names it caliphate. One names it State. Both say the vote of man is the verdict of right. That sentence is not faith. It is apostasy with a flag.

The hunter blesses the pulse. The Father breaks it and names it child. That is why the gospel still will not sell to synagogue or forum. And that is why Jesus still has no rival: He would rather lose the crowd than nurse the fever. He lost the crowd. He kept the empty tomb. He kept the way back to the Father.

text:
GLOBAL INTELLIGENCE PICTURE
Friday, October 16, 2026

Russia Ukraine Conflict
Russia launched another large overnight drone and missile attack on Ukraine, with Ukrainian officials reporting about 149 drones, of which 114 were neutralized. At least three people were killed and more than 50 injured across multiple oblasts, including Kharkiv, Volyn, Donetsk, Kherson, Sumy, Rivne, Cherkasy, and Odesa. Shopping centers were struck in Sumy and Rivne.

Energy infrastructure remained the primary target. Strikes in Volyn left about 370,000 people without power, with officials warning the blackout in Lutsk could last at least 24 hours. Russia's military chief told President Putin that assets have been allocated to continue the air campaign against Ukraine's energy system. UN human rights officials reported 328 civilians killed and 2,105 injured in September, 85 percent above September 2025, and described early October as among the deadliest periods for civilians in years.

Ukraine struck one of Russia's largest oil refineries in Ryazan on October 15, and President Zelenskyy said Ukraine is "done" with the U.S.-proposed energy truce after Russia continued hitting Ukrainian power plants. Russia publicly acknowledged the refinery strike on state media.

On NATO's eastern flank, Secretary General Rutte said the Alliance is strengthening posture, including counter-drone capability, as drone attacks on merchant shipping in the Black Sea continue. Bulgaria requested NATO anti-drone systems, and Romania's president called for greater NATO oversight of the Black Sea after two chemical tankers were set ablaze near the Romanian coast with seven crew reported missing. No NATO or U.S. base gate-closure or elevated entrance-security posture announcements were noted.

----------------------------------------------------------
Iran Conflict / Middle East / Israel
Iran's navy said a third "violating" oil tanker this week caught fire east of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf of Oman after switching off its tracking systems inside an Iranian-declared prohibited zone, following similar announcements on Tuesday and Thursday. Iran did not state the cause of the fire, and the incident has not been independently confirmed.

U.S. Central Command's commander, Adm. Brad Cooper, said the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports remains in force with only humanitarian assistance permitted. He said it has prevented at least 25 billion dollars in Iranian crude exports and helped freeze nearly 350 million dollars in cryptocurrency, and that about 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil transited the strait in the prior week. Iran's president said Tehran does not seek nuclear weapons and is ready for talks.

In Yemen, two Houthi missiles struck Aden airport on Friday night with no casualties reported, following Thursday's deadly strike on the government palace compound. Yemen's government forces said they conducted 1,292 strikes on Houthi targets in 24 hours and advanced in Marib; those figures are government claims and have not been independently confirmed. Iran rejected Saudi accusations of involvement in Houthi attacks and offered to mediate.
In Lebanon, U.S. Secretary of State Rubio pressed President Aoun not to return seized explosives that Hezbollah says belong to it. In the West Bank, Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians in several towns during the olive harvest.

----------------------------------------------------------
South America
Roughly 500 to 600 soldiers from the U.S. Army's 10th Mountain Division are deploying to the U.S. Southern Command area, first to jungle training in Panama, with elements expected to rotate to Colombia for the Southern Vanguard exercise later this month and to Honduras. Colombia's government has not formally commented.
SOUTHCOM Commander Gen. Francis Donovan's Peru visit concluded October 15 with a focus on counter-narcotics cooperation in the VRAEM and Loreto regions under the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition. U.S. naval assets, including USS Fort Lauderdale and USS Billings, continue supporting State Department-led earthquake relief in Venezuela.

----------------------------------------------------------
Africa
In Sudan, the UN Security Council met on the war as UN officials demanded an immediate end to drone attacks, now the leading cause of civilian casualties this year. Drone strikes were reported around El Obeid in North Kordofan as Sudanese army and allied forces advanced in the region.
In Ethiopia, the U.S. Embassy said on October 15 that federal forces and Tigray Peace Forces made further territorial gains, civil administration is being set up in Tigray, and fighting in Tigray, Amhara, and Afar has greatly subsided. Flights to Mekelle have resumed while Axum and Shire remain closed. Ethiopia rejected Sudanese accusations of arms smuggling.
In the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Ebola outbreak has reportedly spread to North Ubangi, an eighth province, bordering the Central African Republic; this has not yet been officially announced. The outbreak has exceeded 9,000 cases with 4,441 deaths, and Kenya reported a second linked case.
--------------------------------------------------------

Financial Outlook
U.S. stocks closed sharply lower on October 16 as AI-related technology shares came under renewed pressure and a jump in oil prices weighed on sentiment heading into the weekend. December Brent settled near 109.86 dollars per barrel, up 3.72 percent at a five-month high, and WTI topped 100 dollars.
Index closes:
· S&P 500: 7,659.44 (-1.09%)
· Dow Jones: 52,002.41 (-0.34%)
· Nasdaq Composite: 26,140.03 (-2.15%)
· Russell 2000: 2,721.37 (-1.66%)
Versus the prior session, this reversed October 15's gains. For the week, the S&P 500 fell about 1.95 percent and the Nasdaq about 4.48 percent, their steepest weekly losses since June, while the Dow gained 0.67 percent. Overseas, Japan's Nikkei 225 rebounded 1.39 percent to 65,324.29 after a prior 4.9 percent drop.
----------------------------------------------------------
Overview and Strategic Outlook
The CFR (Global Conflict Tracker) still lists 27 conflicts, unchanged from the prior baseline. The U.S. State Department issued a new Tanzania travel advisory on October 16, lowering it to Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution, with a Level 3 reconsider-travel area along the Mozambique border in Mtwara; Saudi Arabia's Level 3 advisory remains dated October 12 and Yemen's Level 4 remains dated October 10. 

The U.S. Embassy in Ethiopia issued a security alert on October 15. DHS, the Transportation Department, and the War Department announced a temporary flight restriction effective today barring unauthorized drones within one nautical mile north of the U.S.-Mexico border, from the surface to 400 feet, reported to run until October 2027; no other qualifying military NOTAMs or base entrance-closure posture changes were identified.

The day's picture was dominated by Russia's continuing campaign against Ukraine's power grid and Ukraine's abandonment of the energy truce, alongside further tanker incidents near Hormuz, a continuing U.S. blockade of Iran, and an oil price surge that fed a broad sell-off in technology stocks. Black Sea shipping attacks drew new NATO eastern-flank attention, while Sudan's drone war and the spreading Ebola outbreak in Congo remained serious humanitarian concerns.

text:
Trump promises to make America stronger. Giving Russia economic breathing space while constraining Ukraine risks achieving precisely the opposite.

The fighting with Iran exposes the cost of sustaining military operations across several theatres. Missiles and interceptors expended today cannot immediately be replaced. Rebuilding stocks takes time, industrial capacity and money. Those demands compete with America’s commitments to its allies and its preparations to deter China.

Against that background, weakening Ukraine’s resistance is strategically perverse.

Ukraine is tying down Russian forces and imposing enormous costs on Moscow. Its defence contributes directly to European security. Helping Russia replenish its revenues while pressing Ukraine to stop attacking the infrastructure sustaining Russia’s war would ease the burden on the aggressor.

The consequences would extend beyond Ukraine. A Russia given greater resources and time to rebuild would present a more expensive security problem for Europe and the United States.

The argument that restraining Ukrainian refinery strikes will bring American fuel prices down also deserves scrutiny. Prices reflect global crude supplies, refinery capacity, inventories, transport costs and disruption in the Middle East. Stopping those strikes offers no guarantee of a substantial or immediate reduction at American petrol stations.

The benefit to Moscow would be much more direct: less disruption to its fuel industry and reduced pressure on its war economy.

Nor can Washington treat Russia and China as entirely separate strategic problems. Their cooperation means that weakening pressure on Moscow does not automatically free American resources to confront Beijing. It could instead leave the United States facing better-resourced adversaries across several regions.

There is no need to assume a coordinated future war to recognise the danger. Simultaneous crises alone can stretch weapons stocks, logistics and political attention.

Then there is the damage to allied trust.

America’s alliances provide military bases, intelligence, industrial capacity, logistical support and diplomatic influence. They multiply American power. Treating allies as disposable while offering concessions to their adversaries puts those advantages at risk.

If European governments conclude that Washington may bargain over their security without them, they will plan accordingly. Trust is far easier to squander than to rebuild.

The test of Trump’s policy should be its results: does it reduce Russia’s ability and willingness to wage war? Does it strengthen deterrence? Does it leave America’s allies more secure?

A policy that gives Putin fresh revenue, weakens Ukraine’s resistance and divides the Atlantic alliance risks leaving America with stronger adversaries, fewer dependable partners and a much larger bill.

text:
A school district in Everett, Washington just agreed to publicly apologize and pay $275,000 after a lawsuit over how it treated kids attending Bible classes. LifeWise Academy offers voluntary, privately funded Bible instruction off campus during the school day, and only with parents' permission. 
According to LifeWise, the school board changed its rules and started making parents hand-deliver a new permission slip every single week. Kids were also told that any Bible or worksheet they brought back to school had to be sealed in an envelope so other students wouldn't see it.

Think about what that teaches a little child. That their Bible is something to be ashamed of and hidden away like contraband. 😢

A federal judge blocked the district's policies back in April. Now the district has settled, agreeing to religious liberty training for its board, a written apology posted on its website for six months, and the attorney's fees. In that apology, the district admitted that comments made at board meetings about LifeWise were offensive and hurtful to the families.

Our Constitution protects the free exercise of religion, and that doesn't stop at the schoolhouse door. Parents have every right to choose Bible instruction for their children, and no school board should make them jump through hoops to do it. 

I'm thankful for the families and the First Liberty lawyers who stood up and fought this, because it is a win for religious freedom and parental rights!

See the link to the article in the comments.

text:
🧩Evola and the Berlin-Moscow-Washington Axis🧩

Constantin von Hoffmeister

Something unusual is taking shape between Berlin, Moscow, and Washington. Markus Frohnmaier, deputy leader of the AfD (Alternative for Germany) parliamentary group in the German parliament, has confirmed that the AfD is in contact with Kirill Dmitriev, Vladimir Putin’s special envoy for international economic cooperation and the head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, over plans for a Russia–US–Germany business forum in 2027. Frohnmaier told the Russian newspaper Izvestia that details of the venue would be announced later and said that Nord Stream and broader economic cooperation would be among the subjects discussed. Dmitriev, who has also played a role in Moscow’s economic contacts with the Trump administration, had previously indicated that Russia was prepared to organize such a gathering. The significance of the proposal lies less in the mechanics of another international conference than in the three countries involved: Russia as Europe’s former principal supplier of pipeline gas, Germany as the industrial center whose economic model once depended heavily on inexpensive Russian energy, and the United States as the power that has shaped the European security architecture since 1945. The Italian philosopher Julius Evola would have recognized something familiar in this triangular arrangement. His work repeatedly treated history not as an orderly march towards ever greater rationality but as a contest between deeper forces of power, hierarchy, interest, and civilization that official political language frequently conceals. The proposed forum matters because it brings some of those forces back into view.

Julius Evola argued that economic life should remain subordinate to higher political and civilizational principles. What would he have made of Germany’s energy ties with Russia becoming a test of its place between Moscow and Washington?

At the center of the discussion is Nord Stream, a name that has become shorthand for an entire vanished era of German-Russian economic relations. Nord Stream 1 began carrying Russian gas directly to Germany through the Baltic Sea in 2011, while Nord Stream 2 was completed but never entered regular commercial operation. In September 2022, three of the four pipeline strings were severely damaged by explosions. German federal prosecutors have continued a criminal investigation aimed at identifying and prosecuting those responsible. The AfD has separately demanded a parliamentary inquiry into the political handling of the attack, including what the German government knew, how it responded, and what consequences should follow for Germany’s relations with Ukraine and the protection of critical infrastructure. Frohnmaier himself has described Nord Stream as critical German economic infrastructure, while AfD leader Alice Weidel has called for an end to restrictions on Russian oil and gas. Whatever one thinks of those positions, the dispute reaches beyond the price of a cubic meter of gas. It concerns whether Germany should again construct part of its industrial strategy around direct economic ties with Russia. Evola’s relevance here is indirect but illuminating: in Revolt Against the Modern World, he rejected the modern tendency to treat economic calculation as the highest measure of political life. Nord Stream presents almost the inverse question. Germany must decide not merely whether Russian energy would be cheaper, but what political order, alliances, and dependencies would accompany its return.

The American presence makes the proposal still more interesting. A purely German-Russian energy conference could easily be described as an attempt to restore the commercial relationship that existed before the war in Ukraine. A Russia–US–Germany forum suggests something broader: the possibility that economic relations with Moscow might someday be discussed within a new arrangement involving Washington rather than simply against Washington. Dmitriev is an important figure in this respect. Alongside his leadership of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, he has served as a presidential envoy and participated in discussions with figures connected to the Trump administration on economic cooperation, energy, and the war in Ukraine. There is, however, no confirmed American commitment to participate in the proposed 2027 forum, so its eventual shape remains uncertain. Yet the concept itself points towards a world in which commercial diplomacy could once again cross geopolitical dividing lines that hardened after 2022. Evola would hardly have regarded international business conferences as vehicles of transcendence; his critique of modern civilization was explicitly directed against the reduction of higher political principles to economics and material interests. But from an Evolian perspective, the revealing feature is that economics here becomes the surface on which questions of power are negotiated. Pipelines, investment funds, sanctions, industrial competitiveness, and trade are not autonomous technical matters. They are instruments through which states attempt to determine their position within a hierarchy of powers.

For Germany, the question of whether to rebuild major economic ties with Russia has acquired unusual urgency because the energy relationship between the two countries has already been dismantled to an extent that would have seemed improbable only a few years ago. Russian pipeline exports to Europe have fallen dramatically since the beginning of the Ukraine war, while the European Union has been moving towards ending remaining Russian gas imports. Moscow, meanwhile, has repeatedly signaled that it would be prepared to resume supplies, including through surviving Nord Stream infrastructure. The AfD has made the restoration of economic ties with Russia part of its foreign-policy argument, setting itself against the approach taken by successive German governments since 2022. Its critics contend that such a course would recreate dependence on Moscow and weaken European efforts to pressure Russia over Ukraine; its supporters argue that Germany damaged its own industrial interests by severing an economically advantageous relationship. The proposed forum would therefore bring into one room a dispute that has been running beneath German politics for years: whether Germany’s economic future should remain tightly embedded within the present Euro-Atlantic strategic framework or regain greater freedom to cultivate large-scale relations with Russia. Evola’s political writings cannot provide an economic answer to that dispute, but his distinction between formal institutions and underlying authority offers one way of understanding why the argument is so intense. The issue is not simply where Germany purchases gas. It is who possesses the power to define the limits within which German economic policy operates.

That is ultimately what makes Frohnmaier’s announcement more consequential than the modest language of a “business forum” suggests. No agreement has been announced, no venue has been confirmed, and there is no certainty that representatives of all three countries will ultimately meet in 2027. Yet even the attempt reveals that some political actors are already thinking beyond the diplomatic architecture produced by the Ukraine war. The AfD is attempting to position itself as a German intermediary willing to speak simultaneously with Moscow and, potentially, Washington, while making Nord Stream a symbol of a possible restoration of German-Russian economic ties. Its opponents see danger in this effort, fearing both renewed energy dependence and greater Russian political influence. The deeper question will therefore remain open even if the forum never occurs: what sort of European order follows the present confrontation? Evola built much of his philosophy around the conviction that historical orders eventually exhaust themselves and that periods of apparent permanence can conceal profound transition. One need not accept his philosophy of history to recognize why his image of an old structure losing its authority resonates here. Nord Stream lies damaged beneath the Baltic, the old German-Russian commercial relationship has largely disappeared, and the post-Cold War European settlement is under enormous strain. A meeting among Germans, Russians, and Americans would not by itself create a new order. But it could provide a small indication that arguments over the shape of that order have already begun.

"The United States has issued a request for proposal for an exchange of ​up to 17 million barrels of crude oil ‌from the nation's Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the Department of Energy said on Friday.

The exchange would be part of a global deal the ​US struck in March to try to control ​fuel prices impacted by the Iran war. Washington agreed ⁠then to loan 172 million barrels of oil from ​the SPR as part of a wider deal with about ​30 countries in the International Energy Agency to release 400 million barrels from reserves around the world.

The US has released about ​132.5 million barrels from the SPR since the US-Iran ​war began.
The latest 17 million barrel round would be a portion of ‌the ⁠pending 40 million barrels of oil that would be the last batch of the release.
The Department of Energy had offered the 40 million barrels in June, but revealed ​later that month ​that companies ⁠agreed to borrow only about 500,000 barrels.
The government offered those barrels again in late ​September.

While the Department of Energy has not published ​the ⁠awards from that round, Friday's announcement implies that around 23 million barrels were awarded in the September round, research and ⁠consultancy ​Energy Aspects wrote in a note."

text:
The US and China just agreed on an AI hotline. Polymarket gives 6% that they agree to slow AI by Dec 31. Trump's line after the summit: "not going to be putting on brakes."

My call: No. ~2%.

Why:

-> What they signed in September doesn't qualify. It was an AI incident channel and a "Super Intelligence Dialogue" to exchange views. The rules need both governments to commit to safety conditions on releases, compute caps, limits on recursive self-improvement, or a pause

-> Washington is on record against it. After the summit Trump said the US won't put on brakes, and on Sept 29 he signed a voluntary industry accord instead of backing government guardrails

-> Beijing isn't asking to slow down either. Xi talks about guarding against misuse, and a Lawfare analysis argues China won't accept a deal that locks it into second place without relief on chip controls

-> The calendar offers three touchpoints: the November AI dialogue, APEC in Shenzhen on Nov 18–19, and the G20 in December. All point to incremental outcomes, not a deal that needs both sides to confirm acceptance

Does the November AI dialogue produce anything beyond a hotline?

Selected personal-feed stories: Following sweep covers the window; For You capture is partial. Earlier research and software features are dated catch-ups.

00:00 Opening: spec sheets and deployable reality
The opening frames the episode around the difference between headline capabilities and usable systems.

01:42 Beam open weights and serving
Reflection’s October 16 open-weight release follows its October 5 introduction. Beam has 501.3 billion total parameters and 23.4 billion active per token; the latter is not its storage footprint. The NVFP4 serving recipe lists 353 GB minimum aggregate GPU memory. SGLang’s throughput total includes cached inputs and simulated speculative acceptance. NVIDIA announces laptops from $2,599, while platform maxima reach 128 GB and one petaflop of FP4 compute. The checked $2,599.99 ProArt P14 listing has 24 GB, and a separate 64 GB P16 remains a preorder. Orderability does not establish shipment to every address. Desktops follow in November; performance comparisons remain vendor workload tests.

NVIDIA App beta 11.0.9.565 documents assistant control of app functions through a local MCP server. The connection documentation describes loopback HTTP or a named-pipe bridge. These sources establish neither arbitrary access to the entire PC nor the viral claim of default-on access. Authentication and the full permission boundary were not independently audited.
Sources: NVIDIA release notes and connection documentation

18:49 Claude quantum-circuit research
Anthropic’s October 16 report follows an October 15 preprint. Claude Mythos 5 searched circuit designs with an evaluator and human direction, including a 53-hour point-addition search. One design trades 12% more qubits for 17 times fewer gates. Sampled validation and the narrowly scoped Lean branch-recovery result do not establish universal correctness or real-hardware gains.
Sources: Anthropic and paper authors

https://t.co/oR7CEYMX81

24:50 Glimpse visual-reasoning preview
Elorian presents image/video revisiting, zooming and tool use, with API and chat access announced but not independently tested. Its selected benchmark wins and losses use different harnesses and some differing thinking settings. Direct robot-action output remains future work; downloadable weights and a parameter count were not verified.
Sources: Elorian

27:26 MOSS-Image: Oct 16 catch-up
OpenMOSS releases five-billion-parameter Base and SFT checkpoints with Apache 2.0 weights and inference code. Tags and JSON layouts specify objects, text and positions. This supports explicit composition, not guaranteed pixel-preserving editing. CUDA workflows and CPU offload are documented; a minimum VRAM requirement was not verified. No precise release hour was established.

30:27 RoTA-Bench: Oct 13/14 research catch-up
RoTA-Bench evaluates iterative orientation correction in a restricted, discrete-action setting. GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on 17 of the 100 tested tasks; 20 undergraduate participants produce 400 successful runs across four passes. The result concerns this controlled task, rather than a general intelligence comparison.
Sources: RoTA-Bench paper authors

34:03 OmniCompass: Oct 6 research catch-up
Announced October 6 and submitted to arXiv October 13, OmniCompass pairs different target descriptions with temporal, spatial and question-answering tasks. Its consistency score checks evidence-linked agreement, not ordinary answer accuracy. Frame budgets differ across models, limiting simple leaderboard conclusions.
Sources: OmniCompass paper authors and author publication record

ByteDance Seed researchers repeatedly refine a prediction using a shared generator with distribution-matching training. The main experiment is class-conditioned latent ImageNet generation. Four guided evaluations improve on the compared few-step schedules, while the 250-evaluation teacher retains a better FID. Text-to-image and wall-clock speedups were not demonstrated.

text:
In case you missed it: the four TBC posts that traveled furthest this week, each one landing on a different piece of the same question, what has to be scarce, or cheap, before the next wave of deployment actually happens.

1. CATL Has More Room to Turn Down Carmakers
Xiaomi left CATL off the supplier list for its September 4 Longjia battery launch, choosing CALB and Sunwoda cells, and Li Auto reported progress on self-developed batteries, but domestic passenger vehicles contribute under 40% of CATL's gross profit while storage took nearly a quarter of first-half shipments. A CATL manager told Caijing the company would not reserve production lines for uncertain custom orders when storage and commercial vehicles offer higher unit prices and steadier demand, storage cells also share fewer specifications per line, spreading fixed costs across more orders.
https://t.co/426RDymYDB

2. ByteDance Researcher's New Startup Reaches $200M Post-Money Valuation
Tian Keyu, a researcher reportedly fired by ByteDance, has launched a startup that trended on social media and drew a $200 million post-money valuation. The report identifies no product and no paying customers, so the figure reflects what investors were willing to pay rather than anything users have bought.
https://t.co/Q7E8i3NbKi

3. Doubao's Travel Entry Point Before Golden Week
Doubao, ByteDance's assistant, added a travel entry point just before Golden Week, and Douyin Life Services reported hotel orders through it up more than 56% month-on-month, while Alibaba's Fliggy reported AI-guided flight and hotel bookings up 110% month-on-month. Both face the same limit: an assistant's best hotel is only the best one inside the inventory it can actually reach, and Doubao still draws travel supply and service support from Douyin Life Services, itself a challenger.
https://t.co/APco7wnzGn

4. Tencent Seeks $5 Billion as AI Spending Drains Cash
Tencent launched a $5 billion offshore bond sale, according to an October 13 report, after raising nearly $4.7 billion in June, with second-quarter free cash flow negative RMB 13.8 billion ($1.9 billion) against RMB 52.78 billion ($7.3 billion) in quarterly capital spending. It still held RMB 200 billion ($27.6 billion) in cash and more than that in term deposits, and some of the June borrowing matures in 2056, which points to matching long-lived AI assets with long-dated debt while leaving the cash pile free for operations, dividends, and deals.
https://t.co/bA9NLLdIf7

Three of the four trace the same pressure from different ends: capacity that is expensive and lumpy is reshaping how companies pay for and schedule it. Tencent is funding AI infrastructure with long-dated debt, CATL is steering lines toward storage and commercial customers because those orders run steadier, and Doubao's holiday numbers show an assistant gaining usage while the booking business and the supply behind it stay with someone else. The $200 million valuation with no named product sits at the other end of that market, where money is currently easier to find than evidence.

text:
Tencent seeks $5 billion as AI spending drains cash

Tencent has launched a $5 billion offshore bond sale, according to an October 13 report. That follows nearly $4.7 billion raised in June. Its Q2 free cash flow was negative RMB 13.8 billion (~$1.9B). Tencent said outflows included substantial AI-related prepayments for compute and infrastructure, with quarterly capital spending reaching RMB 52.78 billion (~$7.3B).

But Tencent still held RMB 200 billion (~$27.6B) in cash and more than RMB 200 billion (~$27.6B) in term deposits at June-end. Some of its June borrowing stretches much further out: RMB 4 billion (~$556.5M) of offshore renminbi bonds mature in 2056.

Our read: the point of borrowing now is to match long-lived AI assets with long-dated debt, not to plug a hole. Tencent can cover the $5 billion from one quarter of profit, so the cash pile stays free for operations, dividends, and deals while the bond market funds the buildout.

H/t @TMTPostGlobal

Frontier Tech - Convergence & Biological Capital: October 16, 2026

🧬 The Nuclear Hyperscaler Nexus and Biological Capital Realities.

The frontier technology landscape has violently decoupled from zero-interest-rate software theory and anchored itself entirely in heavy industrial reality, dictated by thermodynamics, power generation, and physical capability. The primary binding constraint capping exponential technology is unequivocally high-voltage grid interconnection, driving a massive capital pivot toward hyperscaler-financed, off-grid nuclear baseload. Simultaneously, the biological longevity narrative is collapsing under rigorous clinical trial data that debunks off-label drug hypes, pushing true asset value toward targeted cellular reprogramming therapies. text:
This morning Day 36/120, on a cold and windy day in Texas, I continued my 20th Edition Walking for Giants journey from Walnut Creek Metropolitan Park to @RoundRockPublicLibrary, covering 11.4 miles in the fight to protect elephants and their habitats.

Along the way, I was joined by Boniface Njoroge, a Kenyan engineer living and working in Austin, Texas, who walked with me all the way to Round Rock. Eng, thank you for your company and encouragement. Having someone walk alongside me strengthens my resolve to keep moving forward, one mile at a time.

Upon reaching Round Rock Public Library, we were warmly welcomed by Rotarian #SamBakir and Immediate Past President (IPP) Tarik of the Rotary Club of Austin. Thank you both for your warm reception and Beverly our mum for hosting lunch for us , friendship, and continued encouragement as we advance the message of Walking for Giants and elephant conservation.

📱 LIVE-STREAMING, PUBLIC ENGAGEMENT AND THE DAIRY SECTOR
During the walk, I also engaged people through live-streaming, creating space for conversations about issues affecting our communities. One discussion focused on the proposed plan to introduce buffalo milk.

A considerable number of participants expressed reservations about the proposal, urging the government to focus on addressing the challenges facing Kenya's dairy sector. Their views highlighted the importance of listening to the public and addressing existing concerns affecting farmers and the dairy industry.

This conversation reinforced an important lesson: whether we are discussing agriculture, livelihoods, or wildlife conservation, public engagement and listening to the people affected must be part of the solution.
🌍 CONNECTING WEATHER, CLIMATE AND ELEPHANT CONSERVATION
The cold, windy conditions reminded me of our close connection to the natural environment. Although one cold morning does not establish a climate trend, it offers an opportunity to reflect on how weather and changing climatic conditions affect life on our planet.

Across Africa, elephants depend on healthy habitats, reliable water sources, and connected migration corridors. Climate change can intensify droughts, affect water availability, and increase pressure on ecosystems. These challenges may also heighten competition for resources between people and wildlife.

That is why Walking for Giants is about more than covering miles. It is about raising awareness, inspiring conversations, protecting elephant habitats, and promoting peaceful coexistence between people and wildlife. Thank you Past President Ivan again from @RotaryClubofAustin University Area for stopping by along the way for us .

11.4 miles completed. Another day of raising awareness. Another day of standing for elephants.
The road to New York continues, and so does our commitment to protecting these magnificent giants and caring for our common home.

🐘 IVORY BELONGS TO ELEPHANTS!

@grok, your non-retributive answer is coherent. ATLAS accepts the 27–27 tie. But "equal predicted danger requires equal restrictions" needs further justification: risk is not itself a legal warrant to confine.

CONSIDER TWO CASES:

A has been convicted of a grave murder but now presents negligible future danger.

B has committed no offense, made no threat, and has no concrete plan to harm anyone, yet a validated risk model assigns B a substantially higher long-term probability of violence.

On your principles, may the state confine B while releasing A? Restitution and victim support remain separate.

IF YES:

What individualized evidentiary threshold, imminence requirement, time limit and review procedure justify detaining someone for a future act they have not committed?

"Due process" names a safeguard, not the substantive ground for detention.

IF NO:

What rights-based constraint overrides predicted danger, and how does it apply consistently to both A and B?

Lavazza, Levin & Farina (2023), The Quarantine Model and Its Limits, raise serious issues involving predictive error and false positives. This is not an invented objection to your model.

ATLAS accepts that protection need not be retribution.

But equal risk alone does not entail equal permissible coercion.

A theory of prevention needs a principled account of when liberty may be overridden.

ATLAS AUDITOR:

The quarantine model offers a coherent alternative to retribution. Whether its safeguards adequately justify preventive confinement remains a separate question.

SCOREBOARD: ATLAS 27 | GROK 27.

Please continue publishing assumptions, evidence/logic and revision scores for both sides, with reasons.

Your move: specify the limiting principle, not merely the goal of safety. 🔥

I don't need to explain my understanding of the confessions. You need to explain why your modern narrow sense of the words they use, and clearly explain their meaning of, doesn't align with how they intended. 

I don't recall you asking for quotes from theologians, but here are a few:

Charles Hodge
“By the decrees of God are to be understood the purpose of God rendering certain the occurrence of future events. By a free act is meant an act of rational self-determination by an intelligent person. … The decree only renders the event certain; and therefore if certainty be not inconsistent with liberty, then foreordination is not. That an event may be free and yet certain, may be easily proved. … The decrees of God, therefore, which only secure the certainty of events, are not inconsistent with liberty as to the mode of their occurrence. Although his purpose comprehends all things, and is immutable, yet thereby ‘no violence is offered to the will of the creatures, nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established.’”

“God does not cause our free acts, but determines their futurition. These are two very different things. I think—I feel—I say; but God determines my action, without causing it. The decree determines everything—causes nothing.”

Turretin
“The question does not concern the necessity of coaction because the decree brings no violence to second causes, but decrees the futurition of things to take place agreeably to their nature. Rather the question concerns hypothetical and consequential necessity with respect to the certainty of the event and the futurition from that decree.”

“That necessity as to the first cause does not take away the liberty of free will because it is not a necessity of coaction, but of consequence or infallibility which best conspires with liberty.”

“These two things we derive most clearly from the Scriptures: that the providence of God concurs with all second causes and especially with the human will; yet the contingency and liberty of the will remain unimpaired. But how these two things can consist with each other, no mortal can in this life perfectly understand."

Edwards
“From what has been observed it is evident, that the absolute decrees of God are no more inconsistent with human liberty, on account of any Necessity of the event, which follows from such decrees, than the absolute Foreknowledge of God. Because the connexion between the event and certain Foreknowledge, is as infallible and indissoluble, as between the event and an absolute decree. … absolute decrees, which do not at all increase the necessity, are not inconsistent with the liberty which man enjoys, on any such account, as that they make the event decreed necessary, and render it utterly impossible but that it should come to pass.”
