text:
Let us begin with a case. In Chattogram, a BNP leader filed a case alleging disrespect to the national flag. The allegations were so absurd that even the BNP expelled the leader from the party. In other words, the very party that is now in power had, at one point, acknowledged through its own action that the case was unjustified. Yet Sannyasi Chinmoy Das has remained behind bars for nearly two years in connection with that very case. The person who initiated the case has been disowned by his own party, but the accused remains imprisoned. Do those in power have an answer to this glaring contradiction?
While Chinmoy was delivering a speech at Laldighi Maidan, a group of young men hoisted a saffron flag on a separate stand above the Bangladeshi national flag at New Market Square, nearly one kilometre away. One person delivered the speech; others raised the flag. Yet it was the former who ended up in prison. If this is the logic being applied, the speaker at any public gathering could be held responsible for any incident occurring anywhere in the surrounding area.
During a clash among lawyers near the court premises, lawyer Alif was killed. Chinmoy was also shown as arrested in connection with that murder case. Yet when Alif was killed, Chinmoy was sitting inside a police prison van, already detained in police custody. How could someone whom the state itself had confined be responsible for orchestrating another person's murder in full view of the state? No explanation has been forthcoming to this day. What better definition of a travesty of justice could there be?

Chinmoy's mother has died. While she was alive, she had only one wish: to see her son's face one last time. The state denied her that wish. Even accused murderers are sometimes permitted to attend the final rites of their loved ones. Here, however, a mother's final plea was rejected. Before the eyes of the entire country, a religious minority was humiliated in broad daylight, and no one appeared to feel the consequences.

Now let us turn to the statistics that the government used to demonstrate how well Hindus were doing in Bangladesh. Last year, the country had 33,000 Durga Puja mandaps—2,000 more than the previous year. On paper, that figure looks impressive in an official government statement. But during the same year, groups of Muslim clerics reportedly went from one mandap to another, tearing off the beards of the demon Mahishasura depicted in the idols, allegedly claiming that the beards insulted the image of Islam.
In a country where religious insult can supposedly be found in the facial hair of a demon sculpted from clay, measuring security by counting Puja mandaps is absurd. The greatest irony is that Jahangir, the then Home Affairs Adviser, described such arrangements as a “conspiracy” and threatened to arrest the organisers themselves. Those who had already been subjected to attacks were the very people who received the threats.
And this was not an isolated incident.

Deepu Chandra Das. Matua community families in Abhaynagar, Jashore. Hriday Ravidas of Kishoreganj. Families in Gangachara, Rangpur. The dismissal of 94 out of 99 Hindu trainees from SI training over an alleged failure to eat breakfast. The demolition of a Durga temple on railway land in Khilkhet in a manner described as deeply disrespectful.

These are not merely a list of unrelated mishaps. The circumstances of each incident differ, but the religious identity of those affected remains the same. To dismiss the fact that 94 out of 99 people belonged to the same religious community as mere coincidence would be an insult to statistics themselves.

The question now is: what are those in power doing?
The case filed by the BNP originated with a leader whom the party itself expelled, yet the accused in that case remains behind bars. Jamaat-e-Islami shares in parliamentary power, but finding its voice on the question of minority rights requires a microscope. One party makes promises, another shares in the exercise of power, and in between, a sannyasi spends year after year in prison.

When the government holds power, how long should it take to bring an end to a case that is being questioned on such fundamental grounds? Both parties owe the public an answer to this simple question.

Then why do Hindus in Bangladesh remain silent?
The reason is not an inability to speak; it is a calculation of risk. Most want the situation to change. But speaking out carries the fear of being singled out, and at the furthest end of that fear lies the possibility of losing one's life.
There is also a sense of inferiority born of being a numerical minority—a feeling that forces people to diminish themselves in their own country, day after day.

And then comes the most difficult question: who will stand behind them?
If someone dies or is arrested while protesting today, will anyone stand by their side tomorrow? Chinmoy's case itself offers a troubling answer. The man who took to the streets to speak up for his community has found that even the protests demanding justice for him remain weak.

No struggle by a minority has ever succeeded without the support of a larger force, and Bangladesh's Hindus do not have such a force standing behind them.
On one side, the beard of a demon depicted in a religious idol is torn off. On the other, a man sits in prison, unable to see his mother's face one last time.
Between these two scenes stands a country where the phrase “A Bangladesh for All” is no longer a slogan of unity. It has become a cruel joke.⁩

The AI data center selloff reflects fears about TIME and DEBT:

“Companies are borrowing enormous sums to build facilities that may not generate revenue for years. Will the eventual cash flow repay that debt?”

$FRMM’s recent management interview explains a strategy designed to address both concerns.

① A shorter path to revenue

Forum selected existing powered, permitted sites. Transformer installation, cooling upgrades and GPU deployment remain, but this reduces the wait compared with starting from land acquisition, new construction and grid connections.

② Balance contract pricing with reliable revenue

Shorter GPU contracts command higher hourly rates. Longer contracts offer lower rates but greater revenue visibility.

Forum aims to secure enough contracted revenue to recover its equipment investment without unnecessarily locking into low prices for too long. Management described current agreements as mostly 4–7 years, while expressing a preference for roughly 3–4 years on new projects, depending on terms.

③ Equipment-investment payback projected at approximately 2.5 years

The model assumes $4 per GPU-hour. Rudisill said pricing secured so far was higher and supported an approximately 2.5-year equipment-investment payback.

Management expects operating free cash flow to support further expansion and accelerated loan repayment. These are projections, not realized results.

④ Repay equipment loans within customer contract terms

Customer deposits help fund deployment. Customer compute payments are then intended to cover equipment-loan principal and interest.

Management says repayment is structured to finish by contract expiry—reducing the risk of customer revenue ending while equipment debt remains.

The important question is not simply “How much is borrowed?” but “What customer revenue supports repayment, and over what period?”

⑤ Keep generating revenue after the equipment loans are repaid

The GPUs remain owned assets after repayment. Management expects another 2–3 years of potential use beyond the initial contracts.

If that useful life materializes, Forum could rent out the equipment again after recovering its initial investment and repaying the original loans—a potential “bonus revenue” period.

⑥ Additional revenue outside the base model

Where customer contracts permit, unused GPU capacity could also be sold in hourly increments during existing contracts.

Management has excluded this potential upside from its base model pending actual operating experience.

⑦ Lower-cost power, tower partners and modular expansion

Forum compared regional electricity costs and prioritized attractive locations, including parts of the Southeast and Midwest.

Management highlighted SBA Communications’ Southeast footprint and Tillman Infrastructure’s towers in Texas and Florida as fitting its target regions and proximity to operating hubs.

The plan is to support surrounding 1–2 MW tower-based GPU clusters from central data center hubs. Nearby staff can maintain the installations, while capacity can be added in stages as demand develops.

This also serves enterprises that need smaller amounts of dedicated compute. For latency-sensitive applications such as real-time voice AI and gaming, placing GPUs closer to users can improve responsiveness.

Management also described discussions with another major tower operator about additional tower and real estate opportunities.

⑧ A future connection to https://t.co/Tc0sbi8IMX and tokenization

Beyond compute revenue, a longer-term opportunity is potentially connecting income-producing AI assets to tokenized investment products through https://t.co/Tc0sbi8IMX.

That could broaden investor access and potentially provide another funding channel for expansion. This is a strategic possibility, not a confirmed AI tokenization rollout announced in this interview.

The broader opportunity:

Bring existing sites into service sooner → use customer payments to recover investment and repay equipment loans → earn further revenue from the remaining GPUs → expand through tower partners → potentially connect those assets to tokenized investment markets.

Delivery, commissioning, customer credit and contract execution still matter. But Forum’s deployment timeline, repayment structure and expansion opportunities deserve to be assessed individually amid the sector-wide fear.
